SENSORY INTEGRATION ACTIVITIES
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > Understanding Stimming: Foundation Concepts > What is Stimming?
Self-stimulatory behaviour (stimming) refers to repetitive body movements, sounds, or manipulation of objects. Stimming serves critical neurological functions including: Self-regulation of the nervous system Sensory input management (seeking or avoiding) Emotional regulation during stress or excitement Communication when words are unavailable Cognitive processing and focus enhancement
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > Understanding Stimming: Foundation Concepts > Sensory Processing Framework
Sensory Seekers: Require MORE sensory input than typical to feel regulated Under-responsive nervous system Seeks intense, frequent sensory experiences May appear "always moving" or "sensation hungry" Sensory Avoiders: Require LESS sensory input than typical to feel regulated Over-responsive nervous system Overwhelmed by typical sensory levels May appear withdrawn or defensive Mixed Profile: Different responses across sensory systems May seek vestibular but avoid auditory Common in autism and sensory processing disorders
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 1. VISUAL STIMMING INTERVENTIONS > A. Light-Based Stimming > Level 1: Passive Light Watching
Causation: Over-stimulated (Avoider): Uses predictable light as focal point to block overwhelming visual environment Under-stimulated (Seeker): Craves visual input, light provides intense stimulation Sensitivity: Neurological fascination with how light behaves; calming effect of controlled visual input Sensory Profile: Seeker: Actively searches for light sources throughout day Avoider: Uses single light source to escape complex visual environment Description: Gazing at or tracking light sources without movement Manifestation 1: Staring at Sunlight Through Windows Physical Redirection Technique: "Gentle Interrupt and Redirect" Approach from side, avoiding blocking sunlight suddenly Gentle hand on shoulder, say name softly 2-3 times Once acknowledged, offer hand: "Let's walk together" Lead to alternative within 10 steps If resistance, wait 30 seconds and repeat No forcing - remain calm and patient
DIY Alternative Tool: Sun Catcher Window Clings Materials: White school glue, dish soap, food coloring, ziplock bags, tape Cost: Under $3 How to Make: Mix equal parts glue and dish soap in bowl Add 3-4 drops food coloring per color Pour into ziplock bag, seal tightly Tape to window at child's eye level Child squishes bag, watches colors mix in sunlight Provides controlled light interaction Duration: 10-15 minutes, 2-3x daily Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Flashlight Tag Cost: $2-5 (dollar store flashlight) Materials: Flashlight, colored paper on wall How to Use: Partially darken room Call out colors: "Catch the red circle!" Child shines flashlight on targets Add movement: crawl while finding targets Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Intense visual input + control + movement
Aluminum Foil Sun Sculptures Cost: $0 (household item) Materials: Aluminum foil, window sill How to Use: Crumple foil into various shapes (balls, animals, abstract) Place on window sill in direct sunlight Child rotates sculptures to see reflections change Create "sun gallery" with multiple pieces Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Creates dynamic light effects child controls Crystal/CD Prism Mobile Cost: $0-3 (old CDs or cheap crystals) Materials: CDs or crystals, string, coat hanger How to Use: Hang items from coat hanger at different lengths Suspend in sunny window Child can spin them, watch rainbow patterns Count how many rainbows they can make Duration: 10-20 minutes Why it works: Creates moving rainbow patterns, intense visual stimulation Water Spray Rainbow Making Cost: $2 (spray bottle)
Materials: Spray bottle with water, sunny outdoor area How to Use: Back to sun, spray water mist Create rainbows in spray Experiment with different spray patterns Jump through rainbow mist Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Movement + intense visual + outdoor proprioceptive input Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Dimmer Switch Light Box Cost: $8-12 Materials: Cardboard box, battery tea light, dimmer LED if possible How to Use: Create viewing box with small window Child controls when to look inside Predictable, contained light Can add colored tissue paper for gentle color Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Child has complete control, predictable, not overwhelming Shadow Theater Cost: $0 (household items) Materials: White sheet, lamp, toys How to Use: Hang sheet, place lamp behind child
Child makes shadows with toys Start with one toy, predictable movement Keep room otherwise dim Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Controlled light, calming activity Single Color Light Focus Cost: $3-5 (colored nightlight) Materials: One colored nightlight (blue or green calming) How to Use: Quiet corner setup Single light source Comfortable seating Child focuses when needed Duration: 3-5 minutes as needed Why it works: Simple, predictable, calming Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Heavy Work Before Light Play: Wall push-ups: 10 repetitions (hands flat on wall, push away) Carry stack of 5 heavy books across room Push laundry basket across floor Do BEFORE allowing light play Provides organizing proprioceptive input Duration: 5 minutes heavy work, then 5-10 minutes light play Visual Tracking Games:
Roll ball back and forth, child tracks with eyes (head stays still) Move flashlight slowly, child follows with eyes only Do 10 repetitions Builds visual control 5 minutes, 2x daily Scheduled Light Times: Morning: 5 minutes sun watching with parent Afternoon: 5 minutes flashlight play Evening: 3 minutes controlled light activity Use visual timer for each session Teaches self-regulation For AVOIDERS: Progressive Light Exposure: Week 1: Dim room, 2 minutes daily Week 2: Slightly brighter, 3 minutes daily Week 3: Normal room light, 5 minutes daily Week 4: Near window (not looking directly at sun), 3 minutes Gradual desensitization Always give warning: "In 1 minute we'll turn on light" Safe Space with Controlled Lighting: Create "light cave" under table with blanket
Child has flashlight with on/off control Safe base to retreat when overwhelmed 5-10 minutes as needed Grounding Activities: Before light exposure: 5 deep breaths together During: hold weighted toy or wear weighted vest After: tight hug (10-second squeeze) Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS (needs calming): Deep Pressure Massage: Child sitting or lying down Firm pressure on shoulders (like kneading bread dough) Count "1-2-3 squeeze" (gives warning and rhythm) Move down arms with squeezing pressure (shoulder to wrist) Squeeze each finger individually Pressure should be firm but never painful (check with child) Duration: 5-7 minutes Frequency: 2-3x daily, especially BEFORE anticipated light stimming times Why it works: Deep pressure calms nervous system, organizes sensory input Follow-Up Joint Compressions: After massage, gently press on each shoulder joint (count to 3)
Press on elbow joints Press on wrist joints Provides additional organizing input 2-3 minutes For AVOIDERS (needs organizing input): Slow, Predictable Strokes: Always announce: "I'm going to touch your right arm now" Gentle-to-moderate pressure (ask child's preference) Always move in same direction: shoulder to hand Slow count to 10 with each stroke Do one arm completely before other arm Duration: 3-5 minutes per arm Frequency: When child seems overwhelmed by visual environment Why it works: Predictable input helps nervous system organize Grounding Hand Hold: Sandwich child's hand between your hands Firm, steady pressure (not squeezing) Hold for count of 10 Release slowly 2-3 minutes when child is dysregulated Manifestation 2: Watching Reflections on Water or Mirrors Physical Redirection Technique: "Touch and Count" Method
Gently touch child's hand Count backwards from 5 aloud: "5...4...3...2...1" At "1" say calmly "Time to move" Guide (don't pull) toward next activity If resistance, use visual timer: "2 more minutes, then we go" Honor timer - builds trust DIY Alternative Tool: Reflection Sensory Bottle Materials: Clear plastic bottle (16-20 oz), water, cooking oil, glitter, mirror pieces, food coloring, hot glue Cost: Under $2 How to Make: Fill bottle 1/3 with water Add 1 tablespoon cooking oil Add glitter and small mirror pieces (break old compact mirror safely) Add 2-3 drops food coloring Fill remaining space with water Seal lid with hot glue (parent only) Child tilts bottle, watches oil and water separate, reflections shimmer Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Portable, controlled reflection experience
Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Mirror Dance Party Cost: $0 (household mirror) Materials: Full-length or large mirror, music player How to Use: Position child in front of mirror Play upbeat music Call out movements: "Touch your toes! Arms up high! Spin around!" Child watches self in mirror while moving Make silly faces together Copy each other's movements Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Combines intense visual feedback with movement Foil Water Table Cost: $3-5 Materials: Shallow pan, aluminum foil, water, food coloring, droppers How to Use: Line pan with foil (shiny side up) Add 1-2 inches water Child drops food coloring in water Swirls water with hands or tools Watches colored reflections on foil Can add small toys to create more reflections
Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Tactile + visual, child controls reflections Supervision: Required (water play) Reflective Sticker Art Cost: $4-6 Materials: Holographic stickers, black construction paper, light source How to Use: Give child sheet of holographic stickers Create patterns on black paper Hold up to light together Rotate paper to see reflections change Can layer stickers for different effects Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Creates art + intense reflective effects Mirror Maze Activity Cost: $5-10 (small handheld mirrors) Materials: 3-4 small mirrors, flashlight How to Use: Set up mirrors at angles Child uses flashlight to "bounce" light from mirror to mirror Try to hit target on wall Problem-solving + reflection play Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Active problem-solving with reflections
Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Calm Water Observation Cost: $0 (household items) Materials: Clear glass bowl, water, one drop food coloring How to Use: Fill bowl with water Child adds single drop of coloring Sit together and watch it slowly disperse Can add second drop after first disperses Quiet, meditative activity Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Predictable, gentle, calming visual input Mirror Box Peek Cost: $0 Materials: Small cardboard box, aluminum foil, small toy How to Use: Line inside of box with foil Cut viewing hole in one side Place small toy inside Child controls when to look Change toy daily for interest Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Contained, child controls exposure Still Water Reflection Cost: $0 Materials: Clear container with water, small objects
How to Use: Fill container, let water settle completely Place objects next to water (not in it) Look at reflections together No movement - just observation Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Predictable, no unexpected movement Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Proprioceptive Input Pre-Activity: Animal walks: Bear walk (hands and feet on ground, bottom up) across room 2x Crab walk (sitting, hands behind, feet in front, bottom up) across room 2x Bunny hops: 10 hops Duration: 3-5 minutes Do BEFORE reflection play Provides grounding input Structured Reflection Time: Use visual timer (Time Timer recommended) Set for 5 minutes "When timer is done, reflection time is over" When timer beeps, immediate transition to heavy work: Carry laundry basket Push against wall
Chair push-ups Teaches self-regulation and transitions Reflection Scavenger Hunt: List of items to find reflections of "Find reflection of: red toy, your hand, the lamp" Adds structure and purpose 10-15 minutes Prevents endless fixation For AVOIDERS: Gradual Reflection Exposure Protocol: Week 1: Reflections in dim light only, 30 seconds daily Small hand mirror in bathroom Look together with parent Week 2: Normal light, 1 minute daily Increase comfort gradually Week 3: Bright light, 2 minutes daily Near window but not direct sun Week 4: Multiple reflections, 3 minutes daily Can introduce water reflections Always give warning: "In 10 seconds we'll look at the mirror" Distance Control: Start observation from 10 feet away Week 2: Move to 7 feet Week 3: Move to 5 feet
Week 4: Move to 3 feet Child controls final distance Safe Base: Identify one spot as "safe base" with no reflections Child can return there when overwhelmed 2-3 minutes reset time Then try again Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Joint Compression Massage: Gently press on each finger joint (base, middle, tip) Firm pressure, count to 3 at each joint Press on wrist joint (front and back) Press on elbow joint Press on shoulder joint Work down: shoulder → elbow → wrist → fingers Duration: 3-5 minutes each arm Frequency: Before anticipated reflection-seeking behavior Why it works: Provides deep proprioceptive input that calms and organizes Squeezing Sequence: Squeeze hand (like handshake) count to 3 Squeeze forearm, count to 3 Squeeze upper arm, count to 3
Repeat 3x each arm Can be done quickly (2 minutes) Good for transitions For AVOIDERS: Brushing Protocol (Simplified): Note: Full Wilbarger Protocol requires OT training; this is simplified version Use soft-bristle brush (clean hairbrush works) Brush firmly on arms: shoulder to hand, 5 strokes each arm Always brush AWAY from body (never toward) Brush legs: hip to foot, 5 strokes each leg Firm pressure (not ticklish, not painful) Follow immediately with joint compressions: Press on shoulders, count to 3 Press on hips, count to 3 Duration: 5 minutes total Frequency: 2x daily minimum (before breakfast, before school/activities) Why it works: Helps desensitize tactile system, organizes sensory processing Preparation Massage: Before reflection activity Slow, deep strokes down arms (shoulder to hand) Count each stroke: 1...2...3...
5 strokes per arm Helps nervous system prepare 3 minutes Manifestation 3: Gazing at Fluorescent Lights Physical Redirection Technique: "Block and Replace" Method Position yourself between child and light (blocking view) Hold interesting object at child's eye level immediately Make noise with object (shake, tap, squeeze if it squeaks) When child looks at object, praise: "Good looking!" Guide away while maintaining interest in object Hand object to child for continued play Stay with them 2-3 minutes to ensure engagement DIY Alternative Tool: Light-Up Sensory Board Materials: Cardboard (12x12 inches), aluminum foil, battery string lights, pencil, tape Cost: $4-7 How to Make: Poke holes in cardboard in random or pattern design Wrap entire board in aluminum foil Tape battery string lights to back of board
Lights shine through holes creating light pattern Child can turn on/off Can create multiple boards with different patterns Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Mimics fluorescent light pattern but child has control Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Glow Stick Dance Party Cost: $5-8 for pack of glow sticks Materials: Glow sticks (multiple colors), music player, dark room How to Use: Activate 2-3 glow sticks Darken room completely Play energetic music Child holds glow sticks and dances wildly Watches light trails created by movement Can tape to feet/hands for more trails Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Intense visual + vestibular input, fully engaging Safety: Ensure glow sticks are intact (liquid inside can irritate) Strobe Flashlight Freeze Dance Cost: $6-10 (flashlight with strobe function)
Materials: Strobe flashlight, dark room, music How to Use: Darken room Adult controls strobe flashlight Call out actions: "Jump! Spin! Freeze! Touch toes!" Child sees themselves in strobe effect Adds unpredictability and excitement Duration: 10 minutes maximum (can be overstimulating) Why it works: Provides controlled intense light stimulation Caution: Not for children with seizure disorders DIY Lite-Brite Cost: $15 for commercial or $5 for DIY Materials: Pegboard, mini LED lights or glow sticks cut into pieces How to Use: Push lights through pegboard holes Create pictures and patterns Dark room enhances effect Child creates and controls light patterns Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Creative + intense visual input Light Painting Photography Cost: $5 (if you have phone/camera) Materials: Flashlight or glow stick, camera with long exposure, dark room
How to Use: Set camera to long exposure (or use app) Child "draws" in air with light Camera captures light trail Show child the "painting" created Try letters, shapes, spirals Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Creates permanent record of light play, very engaging Multiple Flashlight Patterns Cost: $8-12 (3-4 flashlights) Materials: Multiple flashlights, colored cellophane, rubber bands How to Use: Cover each flashlight with different color cellophane Child controls all flashlights Create overlapping colored lights on wall Watch colors mix and blend Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Intense visual control and experimentation Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single Nightlight Focus Cost: $3-5 Materials: One dim nightlight (blue or green preferred), comfortable seating How to Use: Set up in quiet corner
Single, predictable light source Child can sit and focus when overwhelmed No other lights in area Can add soft cushion or beanbag Duration: 3-5 minutes as needed Why it works: Simple, calming, child-controlled Soft Glow Jar Cost: $2-3 Materials: Mason jar, water, glow stick liquid OR battery tea light How to Use: Break glow stick, pour liquid into jar of water (seal tight) OR place battery tea light in jar Creates soft, contained glow Child can hold, look at, carry Not overwhelming or too bright Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Portable, controlled, gentle light Dimmer Lamp Control Cost: $12-15 (lamp with dimmer) Materials: Small lamp with dimmer switch How to Use: Child controls brightness level Can increase or decrease as needed
Practice adjusting: "Make it bright! Make it dim!" Provides sense of control Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Child controls intensity, not overwhelming Light Box Viewer Cost: $3-5 Materials: Shoebox, tissue paper, battery tea light, colored cellophane How to Use: Cut window in shoebox Cover with tissue paper Place light inside Can add colored cellophane for gentle color Child looks through window Contained, predictable Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Completely controlled viewing experience Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: "Light Menu" System: Create visual schedule with picture symbols Options: flashlight tag, glow sticks, light board, strobe play Child chooses from menu Set timer for chosen activity When timer ends, choose next activity or transition Teaches choice-making and prevents fixation Duration: 5-10 minutes per activity
Alerting Activities Before Controlled Light Play: Jumping jacks: 10-20 repetitions Spin in office chair: 5 rotations each direction (adult supervises/controls) Run in place: 30 seconds Dance to fast music: 3 minutes THEN: 10 minutes structured light play Satisfies sensory need in controlled, safer way Heavy Work Integration: Push wall (like pushing it down): 10 seconds x 3 reps Carry heavy object: 5 minutes Chair push-ups: 10 reps Do BETWEEN light activities Prevents escalation and over-arousal Light Play Circuit: Station 1: Flashlight play (3 minutes) Station 2: Heavy work - wall push-ups (2 minutes) Station 3: Glow stick activity (3 minutes) Station 4: Heavy work - carry books (2 minutes) Station 5: Light board play (3 minutes) Total: 15 minutes with built-in regulation
For AVOIDERS: Light Filtering Strategies: Sunglasses indoors during transition to bright rooms Start with very dark sunglasses Week 1: Wear during all transitions Week 2: Wear for half of transition Week 3: Wear entering room, then remove after 1 minute Week 4: Try without sunglasses for brief periods Gradually increase time without sunglasses (30 seconds daily increase) Creates bridge to tolerance Safe Base Protocol: Designate one dim area as "safe base" Could be corner with lamp, under table with blanket, small tent Child can return there when overwhelmed 2-3 minutes reset time Deep breaths, quiet time Then re-engage with environment No shame or punishment for using safe base Gradual Fluorescent Light Exposure: Week 1: Enter room with fluorescent lights for 30 seconds only
Can wear sunglasses Have preferred activity waiting Week 2: Increase to 1 minute Week 3: Increase to 2 minutes Week 4: Increase to 5 minutes Continue gradual increases Always give warning: "In 2 minutes we're going to the bright room" Predictable Light Schedule: Child knows exactly when they'll be in fluorescent-lit rooms Visual schedule with pictures Prepare 5 minutes before: "Soon we'll go to the bright room" Reduces anxiety through predictability Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Invigorating Massage: Fast, firm pressure taps on arms and legs (like drumming) March fingers up arms while counting: 1-2-3-4-5 up to shoulder March back down: 5-4-3-2-1 Tap rhythm on back (avoid spine): 1-2-3-4, 1-2-3-4 Rub arms vigorously (creates warmth) Duration: 2-3 minutes per limb Frequency: BEFORE allowing light interaction
Why it works: Provides alerting input that organizes nervous system, prevents fixation by pre-satisfying sensory need Wake-Up Technique: Brisk rubbing on arms and legs Gentle tapping on cheeks Rub palms together, then place on child's arms Quick, energizing 2 minutes Use when child is under-aroused and seeking intense input For AVOIDERS: Calming Touch Sequence: Child lies on stomach or sits calmly Slow, deep pressure on back (like spreading peanut butter) Move from shoulders to lower back 10 slow counts per stroke Avoid ticklish spots Pair with deep breathing: "Breathe in for 3...breathe out for 3" Duration: 5-7 minutes Frequency: When child appears overwhelmed by visual environment Why it works: Slow, rhythmic input organizes and calms nervous system Grounding Sequence: Firm pressure on shoulders (grounding)
Firm pressure on hips Gentle pressure on top of head Hold each for count of 5 Helps child feel "anchored" and safe 3-5 minutes Calming Sandwich: Child between two cushions or under weighted blanket Gentle pressure from above Hold for 1-2 minutes Can do while giving massage Very organizing and calming Manifestation 4: Tracking Car Headlights at Night Physical Redirection Technique: "Name and Redirect" Method Crouch to child's eye level (don't tower over them) Say name + gentle touch on shoulder Acknowledge what they're doing: "You're watching the car lights" Offer choice immediately: "Would you like to find lights inside or play with cars?" Guide to chosen activity within 5 seconds (important - don't delay) If choosing indoor lights: bring flashlight immediately
If choosing cars: bring toy cars immediately Stay with them through transition (2-3 minutes minimum) DIY Alternative Tool: Car Light Chase Board Materials: Poster board, markers, 2 small flashlights, 2 toy cars, rubber bands or tape, batteries Cost: $3-5 How to Make: Draw roads on poster board with black marker Add details: stop signs, buildings, trees Attach small flashlights to top of toy cars (rubber band or tape) Secure so flashlight beam points forward like headlights Darken room Child pushes cars along drawn roads Watches "headlights" illuminate path Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Replicates headlight experience, child has complete control Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Flashlight Road Race Cost: $2-5 (flashlight, masking tape) Materials: Masking tape, hallway or large room, toy cars, flashlight
How to Use: Create "road" on floor with masking tape (curves, intersections) Darken area Parent shines flashlight to illuminate road Child races cars along tape following light Switch roles: child holds flashlight, parent races cars Can add obstacles: pillows to drive around Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Movement + tracking + control Glow-in-Dark Car Track Cost: $8-12 OR DIY with $3-5 Materials: Glow-in-dark tape or glow sticks, masking tape, toy cars, flashlight DIY How to Use: Create track with masking tape Break glow sticks (carefully) and trace over tape Turn off lights Child races cars on glowing track Can make multiple tracks (race track, parking lot, city) Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Intense visual tracking in controlled environment LED Light Cars Collection
Cost: $10-15 (or DIY with $3-5) Materials: Multiple toy cars, LED button lights or mini flashlights, tape How to Use: Attach LED lights to cars Dark room Child creates "traffic patterns" Can organize parking lot, create races Incorporate crashing, chasing scenarios Build ramps for cars to drive down Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Child controls all variables, intense visual input Headlight Hide and Seek Cost: $3-5 (flashlights) Materials: 2-3 flashlights, toy cars, dark room How to Use: Hide toy cars around room Turn off lights Child uses flashlight to find cars When found, drive car with flashlight following it Parent can hide cars between rounds Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Movement + seeking + tracking Light Cone Traffic Game
Cost: $2-5 Materials: Flashlights, toy cars, small cones or blocks How to Use: Set up obstacle course with cones Darken room Child drives car through course Parent illuminates course with flashlight moving ahead of car Time trials: how fast can you complete? Switch roles Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Active participation, controlled tracking Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Slow Lantern Walk Cost: $3-6 (battery lantern) Materials: Battery lantern with dim setting, safe walking path How to Use: Set lantern to dimmest setting Child carries lantern slowly around room Can follow tape path on floor Move slowly and deliberately Quiet activity, no sudden movements - Can sing soft song while walking Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Child controls light movement, predictable, calming
Controlled Light Path Cost: $5-8 (battery tea lights) Materials: 10-15 battery tea lights, open floor space How to Use: Arrange tea lights in straight line on floor (10-15 feet) Child walks slowly along path Focus on each light as they pass Can count lights as they go Very predictable, no surprises Duration: 5 minutes, can repeat Why it works: Predictable, contained, calming visual input Single Car Light Play Cost: $2-3 Materials: One toy car with LED light attached, small contained area How to Use: Set up small "city" with blocks in contained space Child moves one car with light slowly through city Narrate journey: "The car is going to the store..." Calm, slow movements only Can repeat same route (predictable) Duration: 10 minutes
Why it works: One car, predictable, not overwhelming Stationary Light Cars Cost: $5-8 Materials: Several toy cars with LED lights, box or tray How to Use: Place cars in parking lot arrangement (not moving) Turn on lights Child looks at stationary display Can rearrange cars slowly No racing or sudden movements Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Visual input without movement component Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Movement + Light Tracking Combined: Therapy Ball Bouncing: Child sits on therapy ball or exercise ball Bounces while parent moves flashlight on wall Child tracks flashlight while bouncing 10 minutes Combines vestibular + visual input Satisfies dual sensory needs Flashlight Obstacle Course: Set up course: crawl under table, jump over pillow, walk on balance beam (tape line)
Child completes course while following flashlight beam you shine 10-15 minutes Heavy proprioceptive work + visual tracking Structured "Headlight Time" Protocol: Schedule specific evening time: 5-10 minutes watching from window Use visual timer child can see Warning at 2 minutes: "2 more minutes of watching" When timer ends, immediate transition to calming activity: Puzzle (known favorite) Reading books together Quiet building toys Teaches delayed gratification and self-regulation Child learns: "I get headlight time, but it has an end" Vestibular Alternatives: Swinging while tracking flashlight Spinning (controlled) then watching lights Rocking chair while watching controlled light display Provides vestibular input that may be underlying need For AVOIDERS: Distance Control Protocol: Week 1: Watch headlights from 20+ feet away from window Very brief (30 seconds to 1 minute)
Parent stays with child Week 2: Move 2 feet closer (18 feet away) Increase to 2 minutes Week 3: 16 feet away, 3 minutes Week 4: 14 feet away, 4 minutes Continue gradual approach Child can always move back if overwhelmed Builds visual tolerance slowly Light Predictability Training: Before watching: parent explains what will happen "Cars will drive by. Some will have bright lights." Count together: "In 5 seconds, a car will pass" Helps child anticipate, reduces overwhelm Practice 5 minutes, 3x weekly Makes unpredictable environment more predictable Safe Viewing Setup: Comfortable chair positioned at appropriate distance Weighted lap pad or stuffed animal to hold Parent sitting with child (physical grounding) Timer visible (knows when activity will end) Dim indoor lights (reduces contrast)
Alternative Focus Training: When car passes: parent points out something else "Look at that tree!" "See the moon?" Teaches attention flexibility Start with 1-2 redirections per session Gradually increase Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Rhythmic Pressure Massage: Press-release pattern on legs (like pumping brakes) Count rhythm aloud: "Press-2-3, release-2-3" Work from hips to ankles Firm, rhythmic pressure Duration: 5 minutes per leg Frequency: Before evening routine when headlight watching typically occurs Why it works: Provides organizing rhythm to nervous system, proprioceptive input calms seeking behavior Leg Compression Sequence: Squeeze thigh muscles (front and back) Squeeze calf muscles Press on knee joint Press on ankle joint Do each leg completely before moving to next 5 minutes total Calming and organizing For AVOIDERS: Grounding Touch Massage:
Child sits with feet flat on floor Firm pressure on tops of feet (like pressing into ground) Hold for count of 5 Firm pressure on shoulders (grounding) Hold for count of 5 Gentle pressure on top of head Hold for count of 5 Duration: 3-5 minutes Frequency: Before or after exposure to moving lights Why it works: Helps child feel "anchored" when visual environment feels chaotic and unpredictable Seated Grounding: Child sits in chair Your hands on their shoulders Firm, steady pressure Count together to 10 Deep breaths together 3 minutes Very calming before challenging visual activity Manifestation 5: Observing Light Patterns on Walls Physical Redirection Technique: "Acknowledge and Transition" Method Approach calmly, sit near child (not between them and wall)
Look at pattern with them briefly (10-15 seconds) - validates their interest Comment: "That's an interesting pattern" After brief observation together, offer: "Let's make our own patterns" Bring alternative activity to child (don't expect them to come to it) Demonstrate alternative: make shadow, shine flashlight, etc. Invite participation: "Want to try?" Stay engaged with alternative for 3-5 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Pattern Projection Wheel Materials: Flashlight, cardboard circle, scissors, tape, string Cost: Under $2 How to Make: Cut circle from cardboard (size of flashlight lens) Cut shapes in circle: stars, hearts, geometric patterns Tape circle over flashlight lens Optional: attach to string to create spinning projector Shine on wall to project pattern Can make multiple pattern wheels Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Child creates and controls patterns
Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Multiple Pattern Projector Cost: $10-15 OR DIY $3-5 Materials: Flashlight, multiple cardboard cutouts with different patterns, colored cellophane How to Use: Create 5-6 different pattern discs Add colored cellophane for color patterns Child switches patterns rapidly Create combination patterns (two flashlights) Experiment with distance (closer = smaller, farther = larger) Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Variety + control + intense visual input Prism Light Show Cost: $5-10 (prisms or crystals) Materials: Prisms or crystals, flashlight or sunlight, white wall How to Use: Shine light through prism Rotate prism to change rainbow patterns on wall Multiple prisms create complex patterns Child controls angle and movement Try different light sources (flashlight vs sunlight) Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Creates intense, dynamic patterns
Shadow Puppet Theater Cost: $0-3 Materials: Lamp, white sheet or wall, hands and cutout shapes How to Use: Create shadow animals with hands Cut animal shapes from cardboard on sticks Create stories with shadows Child controls all shadow movements Can involve whole body shadows Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Interactive pattern creation Kaleidoscope Effect Station Cost: $5-10 Materials: Kaleidoscope, flashlight, white surface How to Use: Look through kaleidoscope at light Rotate to change patterns Can project kaleidoscope pattern on wall (some types) Try different light intensities Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Ever-changing patterns, high visual interest Light and Texture Exploration Cost: $0-3 Materials: Flashlight, various textured items (lace, mesh, screens, colander) How to Use: Shine flashlight through textured items
Projects texture pattern on wall Try different distances and angles Layer multiple textures Child experiments with combinations Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Infinite variations, child-directed exploration Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single Static Pattern Cost: $0-3 Materials: Lamp with patterned lampshade, calm corner How to Use: Place lamp in quiet area Lampshade creates predictable pattern on wall Pattern never changes Child can observe when needed No movement or surprises Duration: 3-5 minutes as needed Why it works: Completely predictable, calming Controlled Dot Card Game Cost: $2 (index cards, marker) Materials: Index cards with dot patterns, flashlight How to Use: Draw simple dot patterns on cards (3-5 dots per card) Child shines flashlight to "connect the dots" Slow, deliberate movements Can trace patterns with finger first
Very structured activity Duration: 10 minutes Why it works: Predictable, structured, calming Single Shadow Object Cost: $0 Materials: One interesting object, lamp, wall How to Use: Place object to create shadow Shadow doesn't move Child can observe shadow Can slowly rotate object (child controls speed) One object per session (not overwhelming) Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Simple, controlled, predictable Night Light Pattern Box Cost: $5-8 Materials: Box, patterned nightlight, viewing window How to Use: Place nightlight in box Cut viewing window in box Creates contained pattern viewing Same pattern every time Child controls when to look Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Contained, predictable, not overwhelming Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Pattern Creation Activities: Active Pattern Making: Child creates patterns with their body
Jump and see shadow pattern change Dance and watch shadow dance 10 minutes Combines movement with visual interest Heavy Work + Pattern Time: 5 minutes heavy work (push-ups, carrying) 5 minutes pattern observation/creation 5 minutes heavy work 5 minutes pattern time Alternating regulates arousal level Structured Pattern Schedule: Morning: 5 minutes shadow play Midday: 5 minutes prism play Afternoon: 5 minutes flashlight patterns Evening: 3 minutes calm pattern observation Variety prevents fixation on environmental patterns Pattern Scavenger Hunt: List of patterns to find and recreate "Find: stripes, dots, circles, zigzag" Child finds pattern, then recreates with flashlight/shadows Active problem-solving with patterns 15-20 minutes For AVOIDERS: Gradual Pattern Complexity: Week 1: Single dot on wall (simplest pattern) Week 2: Three dots in line
Week 3: Simple shape (square) Week 4: Two simple shapes Very gradual increase in visual complexity Child signals when ready for next level Predictable Pattern Routine: Same pattern, same time, same duration daily "After breakfast, we look at the lampshade pattern for 5 minutes" Provides expected, safe visual input Reduces seeking environmental patterns at unexpected times Pattern Distance Control: Week 1: Observe pattern from 10 feet Week 2: Observe from 8 feet Week 3: Observe from 6 feet Child controls final distance Can always move back Safe Pattern Space: One designated area with calm, predictable pattern Child can retreat there when overwhelmed by environmental visual complexity 3-5 minutes reset time No time limit if truly needed Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Upper Body Alerting Massage:
Firm tapping on shoulders (like drumbeat) Quick rubbing on upper arms (creates warmth) Gentle karate chops on upper back (avoid spine) Squeeze neck muscles gently (sides only, never front) Duration: 3-5 minutes Frequency: Before pattern activities Why it works: Alerting input to upper body/visual system, organizes before intense visual activity Head and Neck Sequence: Gentle pressure on temples (circles) Gentle pressure at base of skull Massage neck muscles (sides, gentle) Provides input to visual and vestibular areas 5 minutes Helps organize visual processing For AVOIDERS: Calming Upper Body Massage: Slow, deep pressure on shoulders Slow strokes down arms (shoulder to hand) Each stroke counts to 10 Gentle pressure on upper back in circular motion Duration: 5-7 minutes Frequency: When child is overwhelmed by complex visual environment
Why it works: Slow, rhythmic, predictable input calms and organizes Head Calming Technique: Both hands gently cupping child's head Gentle, steady pressure Hold for count of 10 Very calming and grounding Child must be comfortable with head touch 2-3 minutes Can be very organizing for visual overwhelm Manifestation 6: Fixating on TV Static or Screensavers Physical Redirection Technique: "Planned Interruption" Method Don't turn off screen abruptly (causes distress) Set timer for 2 minutes where child can see it Sit near child: "When timer beeps, we'll turn off the screen" At 1 minute: "One more minute" When timer beeps, turn off screen immediately but calmly Have alternative ready in hand "Screen is sleeping. Let's play with this." If tantrum occurs: remain calm, maintain boundary, offer comfort
Stay consistent - child learns pattern DIY Alternative Tool: Moving Pattern Box Materials: Clear plastic container, water, oil, glitter, small beads, food coloring Cost: Under $3 How to Make: Fill container halfway with water Add 1/4 cup oil Add glitter, small beads, sequins Add food coloring Seal tightly with hot glue Child tilts and moves box, watches patterns shift and swirl Similar to TV static - constantly changing patterns Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Replicates random, changing visual patterns in controlled way Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Kinetic Sand Patterns Cost: $10-15 (kinetic sand) OR $3-5 (DIY sand + oil) Materials: Kinetic sand in contrasting colors, clear container, tools How to Use: Layer different colored sand in container Child mixes, swirls, creates patterns
Patterns constantly change (like static) Can add tools: rakes, stamps, cutters Tactile + visual stimulation Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Ever-changing patterns + tactile input Magnetic Sand Timer Race Cost: $8-12 (magnetic sand timers) Materials: Multiple magnetic sand timers, different colors How to Use: Set up 3-4 timers Flip simultaneously Watch magnetic patterns form as sand falls Race: which finishes first? Can use magnet to manipulate falling sand Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Mesmerizing movement patterns, interactive Bubble Machine Observation Cost: $10-15 (bubble machine) OR $3 (bubble solution, manual wand) Materials: Bubble machine or manual bubbles, outdoor/protected space How to Use: Set up bubble machine Child watches bubbles float, drift, pop Constantly changing patterns (like static) Can add movement: chase and pop bubbles
Try catching bubbles on wand Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Constantly changing, mesmerizing, adds movement option Rain Stick Observation Cost: $8-12 OR DIY $2-3 Materials: Rain stick (or make from paper towel tube, rice, nails) DIY How to Make: Push nails through paper towel tube in spiral pattern Add 1/2 cup rice or small beads Seal both ends Flip to create rain sound and movement inside How to Use: Child flips rain stick Watches and listens to contents cascade Visual + auditory stimulation Rhythmic, repetitive (like static) Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Self-contained, repetitive sensory input Ferrofluid Display Cost: $15-25 Materials: Ferrofluid display toy with magnet How to Use: Move magnet under ferrofluid Watch liquid form spike patterns Constantly changing formations (like static)
Very mesmerizing Older children can explore magnetic fields Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Unique, constantly changing patterns Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single Lava Lamp Cost: $10-20 Materials: One lava lamp (calming color like blue) How to Use: Place in quiet corner Slow, predictable movement Same pattern every time Child can watch when needed Very calming Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Predictable, slow, mesmerizing but not chaotic Simple Sand Timer Cost: $3-5 Materials: One large sand timer (3-5 minutes) How to Use: Child flips timer Watches sand fall Predictable, always the same Can use as transition timer Very calming Duration: 5-10 minutes (multiple flips) Why it works: Extremely predictable, soothing Single Fish Aquarium View Cost: Varies (or visit pet store/aquarium)
Materials: Small aquarium or visit to pet store How to Use: Watch one or few fish swim Gentle, predictable movement Calming visual input Can visit pet store weekly Duration: 10 minutes Why it works: Natural, calming, gentle movement Slow-Motion Bubble Viewer Cost: $3-5 Materials: Clear container, glycerin, water, bubble wand How to Use: Mix glycerin with water (makes bubbles move slower) Blow bubbles into container Watch them float slowly Very gentle, calm activity Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Slow, gentle, predictable Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Screen Time Replacement Protocol: When child seeks static/screensaver viewing: Offer choice from 3 alternatives (visual menu with pictures) Options prepared in advance Child chooses, engages for set time Timer shows when activity ends
Teaches: screensaver time can be replaced with other visual input Heavy Work Before Screen Use: If some screen time allowed: 10 minutes heavy work BEFORE screen time Wall push-ups, carrying objects, jumping Makes screen time less dysregulating Child more able to transition away Visual Variety Schedule: Throughout day, provide varied visual input: Morning: sand patterns Midday: bubble observation Afternoon: rain stick Evening: limited calm visual activity Prevents fixation on one source (TV static) For AVOIDERS: Predictable Visual Routine: Same visual activity, same time daily "After breakfast: 5 minutes lava lamp time" Provides expected, safe visual input Reduces anxiety about visual environment Child knows what to expect Gradual Complexity Introduction: Week 1: Simple sand timer (slowest, most predictable) Week 2: Add lava lamp (still slow but slightly more complex)
Week 3: Try sensory bottle (more movement) Week 4: Brief bubble observation (more variation) Very gradual increase in visual complexity Only move to next step when child comfortable Safe Visual Space: Designated corner with one predictable visual item Lava lamp or sand timer Child can retreat when overwhelmed No time limit Provides reset opportunity Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Face and Head Massage: Gentle pressure on temples (small circles) Gentle pressure on forehead (smooth from center outward) Massage around eyes (very gentle, never on eyes) Gentle pressure at base of skull Duration: 3-5 minutes Frequency: Before or instead of screen time Why it works: Provides input to visual processing areas, can satisfy some of the sensory seeking driving screen fixation Scalp Massage:
Gentle scratching/massaging of scalp Move fingers in small circles Cover whole head Many children find this very organizing 5 minutes Can help transition away from screen For AVOIDERS: Grounding Full Body Massage: Start at feet: firm pressure Move to legs: long, slow strokes Arms: shoulder to hand Back: slow, deep pressure Duration: 10 minutes full body Frequency: After overwhelming visual input or in place of screen time Why it works: Organizes entire nervous system, provides calming alternative to visual seeking Weighted Input: Weighted blanket or lap pad during massage Provides additional organizing input Very calming Can be used during alternatives to screen time Manifestation 7: Watching Sunrise/Sunset for Extended Periods Physical Redirection Technique: "Respectful Time Limit" Method Join child for part of observation (validates their interest)
Set visual timer at start: "We'll watch for 5 minutes" At 2 minutes remaining: "2 more minutes of watching" At 1 minute: "Almost time to go inside" When timer ends: "Sun watching is done. Time for [next activity]" Have next activity prepared and ready Physical guidance if needed (hand on shoulder, gentle steering) Praise cooperation: "Thank you for coming with me" If resistance: "We can watch again tomorrow at sunset time" DIY Alternative Tool: Sunrise/Sunset Sensory Bottle Materials: Clear plastic bottle, water, oil, liquid watercolors (orange, red, yellow), glitter, hot glue Cost: Under $3 How to Make: Fill bottle 1/3 with water Add drops of liquid watercolor: yellow, orange, red (sunset colors) Add glitter (gold/orange) Add 1/4 cup oil Fill rest with water
Seal with hot glue Child tilts bottle, watches colors swirl and blend like sunset Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Recreates sunset color patterns in controlled, portable way Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Sunset Painting Experience Cost: $5-8 (paints, paper) Materials: Watercolors or finger paints (sunset colors), large paper, brushes or fingers How to Use: After brief sunset observation (5 min), come inside to paint Recreate colors seen in sunset Use hands for tactile input Blend colors: "Watch red and yellow make orange!" Can do while sunset happening (paint while looking out window) Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Extends experience, adds tactile component, creates lasting product Flashlight Sunset Recreation Cost: $5-8 (flashlight, colored cellophane) Materials: Flashlight, red/orange/yellow cellophane, wall or ceiling
How to Use: Darken room Cover flashlight with sunset colors Project on ceiling Child controls "sunset" - can make it last as long as wanted Layer colors for different effects Move flashlight to show "sunset movement" Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Child has control over "sunset", intense visual input Sunset Photography Project Cost: $0 (if have phone/camera) Materials: Camera or phone, poster board for display How to Use: Take photo of sunset (child or parent) Print or view on device Can take series over several days Create sunset gallery Child can look at photos anytime Compare sunsets: "Which has more orange?" Duration: 5 min sunset observation + 15 min photo viewing/organizing Why it works: Captures moment permanently, provides continued access to visual interest
Color Gradient Light Box Cost: $8-12 Materials: Light box or tablet, gradient images (sunset colors) How to Use: Display color gradients that mimic sunset Child can choose different gradients Can create own gradients with drawing app Controlled, reproducible sunset experience Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Provides sunset-like visual without time limits Sunset Scavenger Hunt Cost: $0-3 Materials: Collection basket, outdoor space How to Use: During/after sunset, find objects matching sunset colors Orange leaves, yellow flowers, red berries, etc. Bring collection inside Sort by color Arrange in gradient (yellow to orange to red) Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Movement + color matching + collection Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Sunset Photo Book Cost: $5-10 (photo book or album) Materials: Printed sunset photos, album, comfortable viewing spot
How to Use: Create book of sunset photos (from internet or own photos) Child looks through book in quiet space Can look at same photos repeatedly (predictable) No time pressure (sun not actually setting) Very controlled viewing Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Predictable, contained, no time limit or pressure Single Sunset Color Focus Cost: $2-5 Materials: Paper or fabric in one sunset color (e.g., orange), lamp How to Use: Place orange paper near lamp Creates soft glow of one sunset color Child can look when desired Same every time (predictable) No overwhelming multiple colors Duration: 5 minutes as needed Why it works: Simplified, predictable, calming Sunset Story Time Cost: $0-10 (sunset-themed book) Materials: Book about sunsets, cozy reading spot How to Use:
Read story about sunset instead of watching actual sunset Same story can be read repeatedly Predictable and controlled Can look at sunset pictures in book Duration: 10 minutes Why it works: Addresses interest without overwhelming sensory input Gradual Sunset Viewing Cost: $0 Materials: Window with sunset view, timer How to Use: Week 1: Watch sunset for 30 seconds only Week 2: Watch for 1 minute Week 3: Watch for 2 minutes Very gradual increase Timer shows when viewing ends Duration: As tolerated (start very brief) Why it works: Builds tolerance gradually Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Sunset Routine with Movement: Watch sunset 5 minutes Immediate transition to movement: Run around yard 3 laps Jump on trampoline 20 times Bear crawl to house
Heavy proprioceptive input after intense visual Helps organize and transition Sunset Alternative Schedule: Can't watch actual sunset every day (weather, schedule) Create alternatives for each day: Monday: Sunset sensory bottle Tuesday: Sunset painting Wednesday: Watch actual sunset (5 min timed) Thursday: Flashlight sunset Friday: Sunset photo viewing Provides variety, reduces fixation Post-Sunset Heavy Work: After any sunset viewing/alternative: Carry heavy items inside Help with dinner prep (stirring, kneading) Push/pull activities Organizes nervous system after intense visual For AVOIDERS: Predictable Sunset Protocol: Same day each week (e.g., "Sunset Sunday") Same duration (start with 1-2 minutes) Same location Same person with child Predictability reduces anxiety Gradual Exposure with Control: Child holds timer They can end viewing early if desired Parent doesn't pressure to stay longer
Builds sense of control and safety Preparation Routine: 5 minutes before sunset viewing: Deep pressure hug Deep breaths together Put on comfortable clothes Bring comforting object Prepares nervous system Safe Base During Viewing: Can retreat inside at any time No pressure or disappointment "We can try again tomorrow" Builds positive association Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Intense Proprioceptive Massage: Firm squeezing massage on arms and legs Squeeze-hold-release pattern Count: "Squeeze 1-2-3, hold 1-2-3, release" Work from shoulders to hands, hips to feet Duration: 5-7 minutes Frequency: After sunset viewing or alternative Why it works: Helps transition from intense visual input, organizes nervous system, prepares for next activity Joint Loading: Press firmly on joints after massage Shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles Provides deep organizing input
3-5 minutes Very regulating after intense visual activity For AVOIDERS: Slow Calming Massage: Very slow, gentle pressure on back Count to 20 per stroke Predictable: same pattern every time Always top to bottom (shoulders to lower back) Duration: 7-10 minutes Frequency: Before or after sunset viewing Why it works: Extremely calming and organizing, helps nervous system manage visual experience Cocooning Technique: Wrap child snugly in blanket (burrito-style) Gentle rocking Deep pressure from blanket 5-10 minutes Very organizing Can do before or after sunset viewing
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 1. VISUAL STIMMING INTERVENTIONS > A. Light-Based Stimming > Level 2: Interactive Light Play
Causation: Over-stimulated: Attempts to control overwhelming environment by controlling one sensory element Under-stimulated: Creates intense, variable visual stimulation Sensitivity: Needs to understand light behavior through active experimentation Sensory Profile: Seeker: High intensity, fast switching, seeks maximum visual change Avoider: Slower, more controlled light manipulation; uses to self-soothe Description: Manipulating light sources or creating light effects Manifestation 1: Rapidly Flipping Light Switches On/Off (10-50+ times) Physical Redirection Technique: "Hand Over Hand Redirect" Method Approach calmly from child's side (not behind) Place your hand gently over child's hand on switch Don't force stop - just slow the flipping Say calmly: "Last three times. Let's count together" Count together: "One... two... three" (slowing pace) On "three," guide hand away from switch Immediately place alternative in their hand (fidget, toy)
Say: "Switch is resting now. Let's play with this instead" Guide to different area of room (away from switch) Stay engaged with alternative for 2-3 minutes minimum DIY Alternative Tool: Light Switch Fidget Board Materials: Wooden board or thick cardboard (12x8"), 3-4 light switches (hardware store), screws or hot glue, optional battery LED lights Cost: $5-8 How to Make: Purchase non-functional light switches from hardware store (or functional if adding lights) Screw or hot glue switches to board in pattern Optional: Wire switches to battery-operated LEDs so they actually control lights Decorate board (paint, stickers) Child can flip switches repeatedly without consequence Portable - can take to different rooms Duration: Unlimited (safe alternative) Why it works: Provides exact tactile and auditory feedback child seeks, no negative consequences
Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Multi-Switch Power Strip Station Cost: $8-12 Materials: Power strip with individual switches for each outlet (6 outlets), 6 different colored nightlights or small lamps How to Use: Plug nightlight into each outlet Each has own on/off switch Child controls which lights are on/off Create patterns: all on, alternating, only reds, etc. Count how many ways to arrange lights Play "Simon Says" with lights: "Turn on 3 lights!" Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Multiple switches, immediate visual feedback, creates patterns Clapper Light Game Cost: $8-15 Materials: Clap-on/clap-off lamp or multiple lamps How to Use: Child claps to control lights Adds movement and sound to light control Can play rhythm games: clap patterns Count claps needed Race: how fast can you turn it on?
Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Adds movement, child still controls light but through different action Pull-String Light Circuit Cost: $6-10 Materials: Multiple lamps with pull-chain switches (4-5), large room or multiple rooms How to Use: Set up lamps around space Child goes on "tour" turning each on/off Incorporates walking/movement Can create sequence: "First bedroom, then bathroom, then kitchen" Time trials: how fast can you turn them all on? Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Adds gross motor movement, reduces fixation on single switch Remote Control Light System Cost: $15-25 Materials: Smart bulbs with remote or app control, or remote control outlets How to Use: Child controls lights from distance with remote Can control multiple lights Some remotes have dimming function
Creates more complex interaction Can play games: "Make the bedroom light turn on from here!" Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Novel control method, more complex problem-solving Switch Counting Game Cost: $5-8 (DIY switch board) Materials: Switch board with counter How to Use: Parent holds tally counter or makes tally marks Count how many times child can flip switch in 1 minute Try to beat previous record Adds purpose and competition Structured endpoint (timer) Duration: 5-10 minutes (multiple rounds) Why it works: Adds structure, goal, and endpoint to switching behavior Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single Toggle Board Cost: $2-3 Materials: One switch mounted on small board, battery, single LED light How to Use: Child controls in quiet, contained space Predictable result every time
Low stimulation - single, dim light No overwhelming multiple options Child decides when to engage Duration: 3-5 minutes as needed Why it works: Simple, predictable, not overwhelming Dimmer Switch Play Cost: $8-12 Materials: Simple lamp with dimmer switch (or dimmer attachment) How to Use: Child controls brightness level gradually Not on/off (less jarring) Gentle, gradual visual changes Can find "just right" brightness Very controlled experience Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Gradual rather than sudden, child controls intensity Single Switch with Warning Light Cost: $5-8 Materials: Switch, timer, visual signal How to Use: Set timer for switch play duration Visual timer counts down When timer ends, switch play ends Child can see time remaining Predictable ending Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Time limit is visible and predictable
Flashlight On/Off Control Cost: $3-5 Materials: Flashlight with easy on/off button How to Use: Quiet space Child controls flashlight on/off Point at single target Can count on/off cycles Portable and contained Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Portable, controllable, simple Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Heavy Work Before Switch Play: Wall push-ups: Push against wall like trying to push it down, 10 seconds x 5 reps Carry stack of books: Heavy load across room and back, 3 trips Chair push-ups: Sit in chair, hands on seat beside hips, push body up, 10 reps Do BEFORE allowing switch play Duration: 5 minutes heavy work Then: structured 5-minute switch play with timer Provides organizing proprioceptive input first Switch Schedule System: Visual schedule with pictures
"Morning routine → breakfast → 5 minutes switch time → get dressed" Switch time has designated slot Use visual timer during switch time When timer ends, immediate transition to next scheduled activity Gradually reduce duration over weeks (5 min → 4 min → 3 min) Teaches that switch play has specific time and place Alternative Tactile Activities: Switch-flipping may be partly tactile seeking Provide alternatives: Pop-it fidget toys Button boards (sewing buttons on fabric) Snap bracelets (open/close repeatedly) Velcro strips (pull apart, press together) Clicking pens 10-15 minutes, 2-3x daily May reduce switch-seeking behavior For AVOIDERS: Gentle Introduction Protocol: Week 1: Child watches YOU flip switch 3x daily (1-2 flips only) Narrate: "I'm turning the light on now" No pressure for child to participate
Week 2: Hand-over-hand, you both flip together 3x daily (2-3 flips) Very gentle guidance Child can say "stop" anytime Week 3: Child flips independently 1-2x daily (3-5 flips maximum) Praise attempt No pressure for more Week 4: Child can flip up to 5x if desired Still limited duration Builds comfort and control Control Through Choice: Child chooses WHEN during day to have "switch time" Options: "After breakfast or before lunch?" Provides sense of control Reduces anxiety Duration: 2-3 minutes maximum Predictable Switch Routine: Same switch, same time, same duration daily Example: "Bathroom light switch, after brushing teeth, 2 minutes" Extreme predictability reduces stress Child knows exactly what to expect Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Finger Compressions: Gently squeeze each finger from base to tip
Firm pressure (not painful) Press on each knuckle joint: count to 3 Thumb, pointer, middle, ring, pinky - systematic Say: "Squeeze-1, squeeze-2, squeeze-3" at each joint Do both hands completely Duration: 3-5 minutes per hand Frequency: 2-3x daily, especially BEFORE access to light switches Why it works: Provides deep pressure to hands/fingers that are seeking stimulation through switch flipping, satisfies tactile seeking Hand Massage Sequence: After finger compressions Massage palm with thumbs in firm circles Squeeze along sides of hand Pull gently on each finger (traction) Clap child's hands together firmly (joint compression) 3-5 minutes Very organizing for hands For AVOIDERS: Hand Warm-Up Massage: Rub your hands together to warm them first Gently take child's hand (ask permission) Massage palms with your thumbs in slow, gentle circles
Very gentle, predictable pressure Count each circle: 1...2...3...up to 10 Same pattern every time Duration: 2-3 minutes per hand Frequency: Before switch-flipping activity or when anxious Why it works: Gentle, predictable input helps nervous system prepare for tactile experience, reduces anxiety Hand Sandwich: Place child's hand between your two hands Gentle, firm pressure (like sandwich) Hold for count of 10 Release slowly Repeat 3-5 times per hand Very calming 3 minutes total Manifestation 2: Waving Hands in Front of Lights to Create Shadows Physical Redirection Technique: "Catch and Transfer" Method Position yourself to side of child (don't block light source - disrupts and distresses them) Gently catch child's hands mid-wave (don't grab - gentle interception) Hold hands briefly and bring down slowly to their sides
Immediately transfer interesting object into their hands Object should be textured or interesting tactilely: squishy ball, textured toy, fidget Say enthusiastically: "Feel this!" while placing in hands Guide hands to explore object Within 10 seconds, guide to movement activity: jumping, crawling, running The quick transition prevents return to shadow play Praise when engaged: "Great playing!" DIY Alternative Tool: Shadow Theater Box Materials: Large cardboard box (shoebox or larger), white tissue paper or tracing paper, flashlight, tape, toys and hand puppets Cost: Under $2 How to Make: Cut out one full side of box (this becomes the "stage") Cover opening with white tissue paper or tracing paper Tape edges securely Place flashlight inside box shining toward paper screen Can cut small hole in back for flashlight beam
Child creates shadows on screen from outside with hands, toys, cutout figures Controlled shadow play environment Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Provides controlled shadow creation, child directs the experience, contained viewing area Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Shadow Dance Party Cost: $0-3 (household items) Materials: Large white sheet, bright lamp or flashlight, music player, open wall space How to Use: Hang white sheet on wall (tape or thumbtacks) Place bright lamp 3-5 feet behind child Child stands between lamp and sheet Play upbeat, energetic music Child dances, watches giant shadow copy movements Call out movements: "Jump! Spin! Touch your toes! Make yourself BIG!" Can dance with partner, make shadow touch Take photos/videos of shadow dances Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Intense visual feedback + vigorous movement, combines vestibular and visual input
Multiple Shadow Sources Cost: $5-8 (multiple flashlights) Materials: 3-4 flashlights (different brightness levels), darkened room, white wall How to Use: Give child multiple flashlights They shine from different angles Creates multiple shadows of same object/hand Shadows can be different sizes, colors (if using colored lights) Experiment: "What happens when shadows overlap?" Can trace shadow outlines on paper taped to wall Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Child controls all variables, complex problem-solving, intense visual play Shadow Puppet Show Performance Cost: $0-3 (cardboard, popsicle sticks) Materials: Cardboard cut into animal/character shapes, popsicle sticks, tape, lamp, white sheet/wall How to Use: Create puppet characters together (or use hands) Child performs shadow puppet show Can tell story: beginning, middle, end Can perform for family
Record shadow show Make different voices for characters Duration: 15-20 minutes preparation + performance Why it works: Narrative + creative + fine motor + visual Shadow Tracing Art Cost: $2-3 (large paper, crayons/markers) Materials: Large paper taped to wall, lamp, toys/objects, crayons How to Use: Create shadow of toy on paper Child traces shadow outline Move toy slightly, trace again Creates overlapping shadow art Can color in shapes Make shadow of own hand, trace, decorate Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Creates permanent product, adds fine motor component Shadow Size Experiment Cost: $0-2 Materials: One toy, flashlight or lamp, wall, measuring tape How to Use: Start with toy close to light source (small shadow) Move toy closer to wall (shadow gets bigger)
Measure shadow at different distances Create "giant shadow" and "tiny shadow" Experiment with different objects Scientific exploration Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Adds learning component, problem-solving, still provides visual input Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Gentle Shadow Tracing Cost: $0-2 (paper, pencil) Materials: One lamp, one small toy, paper, pencil How to Use: Place toy to create simple shadow Child traces shadow outline slowly Very calm, methodical activity One shadow at a time (not overwhelming) Predictable, controlled Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Slow, predictable, calming, cognitive task Shadow Matching Game Cost: $0-2 (paper, scissors) Materials: Cut simple shapes from paper (circle, square, triangle, star), lamp How to Use: Create shadow of shape Child matches paper shape to shadow Very structured, predictable
Clear right/wrong answer (cognitive safety) Can make more complex gradually Duration: 10 minutes Why it works: Structured, predictable outcomes, not overwhelming Single Hand Shadow Animals Cost: $0 Materials: Lamp, wall, parent's hands How to Use: Parent demonstrates one simple hand shadow (bird, dog) Show child slowly how to make it Practice together Make same shadow repeatedly (predictable) Can learn 2-3 animals over several weeks Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Simple, can be mastered, predictable, calming Static Shadow Observation Cost: $0 Materials: Interesting object, lamp, quiet space How to Use: Create shadow that doesn't move Child simply observes Can be familiar, comforting object No pressure to interact Can look as long as needed Duration: 5 minutes as needed Why it works: No demands, predictable, calming
Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Bilateral Coordination Activities Before Shadow Play: Clapping games with patterns: Pat head, clap hands, pat knees (repeat 10x) Drumming on table alternating hands: R-L-R-L for 1 minute Crossing midline: Touch right hand to left knee, left hand to right knee (20x) Duration: 5 minutes Do BEFORE shadow play Organizes motor system and both brain hemispheres Then: structured shadow play 10 minutes Whole Body Shadow Play: Instead of just hands creating shadows Child makes shapes with whole body Jumping jack shadow Ballerina pose shadow Tree pose shadow Star shape shadow Incorporates gross motor movement Less focus on hands only 10-15 minutes Provides more organizing proprioceptive input Shadow Play Circuit: Station 1: Shadow dancing (3 minutes) Station 2: Heavy work - wall push-ups (2 minutes)
Station 3: Shadow puppets (3 minutes) Station 4: Animal walks across room (2 minutes) Station 5: Shadow tracing (3 minutes) Total 15 minutes with built-in regulation breaks For AVOIDERS: Static Shadow Introduction: Week 1: Look at non-moving shadows only (toys, blocks) 1 minute daily Same shadow each day Week 2: Introduce slow-moving shadows (rolling ball creates moving shadow) 2 minutes daily Child controls ball speed Week 3: Parent creates simple hand shadows (child watches) 3 minutes daily Same shadows each time (predictable) Week 4: Child tries creating own simple hand shadow 5 minutes as tolerated Gradual introduction builds comfort and control Distance Control: Child decides how close to shadow activity Can observe from across room if needed Week 1: 10 feet away
Week 2: 8 feet Week 3: 6 feet Week 4: 4 feet or child's preference Child sets the pace Predictable Shadow Routine: Same time daily (e.g., "After dinner shadow time") Same duration (start with 5 minutes) Same location Same parent participating Predictability reduces anxiety Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Vigorous Hand Massage: Squeeze firmly up and down each finger (base to tip, tip to base) Make firm circles on palm with thumb pressure "Karate chop" (gentle chopping motion) on sides of hands Pull fingers gently (traction - gentle pulling provides joint input) Clap hands together (creates proprioceptive input) Rub hands together vigorously (creates warmth and tactile input) Duration: 3-5 minutes per hand Frequency: 2x daily, especially before times when shadow-play typically occurs
Why it works: Provides intense input to hands that are seeking stimulation, satisfies sensory need that drives hand-waving behavior Arm Massage Sequence: After hand massage Firm squeezing from shoulder to wrist Joint compressions: shoulder, elbow, wrist 5 minutes per arm Provides organizing input to entire upper extremity For AVOIDERS: Gentle Pressure Massage: Wrap child's hand in your hands (like gentle sandwich) Gentle, sustained pressure (not squeezing) Hold and count to 10 No rubbing or movement initially (can be overwhelming) Just steady, predictable pressure After child is comfortable (may take several sessions): add gentle circular massage on palm Duration: 2-3 minutes per hand Frequency: When child appears overwhelmed or before shadow activity Why it works: Calming, organizing, predictable input, builds trust and comfort with touch
Hand Holding Calm: Simply hold child's hands gently Steady, calm presence No massage movement (if child sensitive) Can progress to gentle massage over time 3-5 minutes Very calming Manifestation 3: Moving Objects Through Light Beams Physical Redirection Technique: "Intercept and Redirect" Method Don't remove light source abruptly Position yourself near child (not blocking light) Join the activity briefly: "I see you moving things through the light" After 30 seconds of joining, offer alternative: "Let's move things through water instead" Bring sensory bin or water table to child (don't expect them to come to it) Demonstrate: move object through water, make splash Hand object to child for them to try If resistant, set timer: "2 more minutes with the light, then we try the water"
Honor timer, then guide to alternative Stay engaged with new activity for 5 minutes minimum DIY Alternative Tool: Light Beam Tunnel Materials: Cardboard tube (paper towel roll or larger), flashlight, small objects (beads, small toys), clear tape or plastic wrap Cost: Under $2 How to Make: Cover one end of tube with clear plastic wrap (tape securely) Put small objects inside tube (beads, sequins, small toys) Cover other end with plastic wrap Shine flashlight through tube Child tilts and rotates tube, watches objects move through light beam Light illuminates objects as they tumble Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Controlled environment for moving objects through light, contained, portable Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Flashlight Object Chase Cost: $5-8 Materials: Flashlight, various small toys/objects, darkened room or hallway
How to Use: Darken space Parent shines flashlight creating beam on floor/wall Child places toy in beam Parent moves beam slowly, child "chases" toy to keep it in beam Switch roles: child controls flashlight, parent moves toy Race: how fast can you keep toy in the beam? Multiple objects: try to keep 2-3 in beam Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Movement + problem-solving + visual tracking + control Laser Pointer Toy Chase (with appropriate safety) Cost: $5-10 Materials: Low-power laser pointer (safe type), small toys with reflective elements, darkened room Safety: Never point at eyes, faces, or animals; adult supervision required How to Use: Adult controls laser pointer only Shine laser on floor/wall Child places toy to "catch" the light
Move laser, child chases with toy Can create patterns: circles, zigzags Add music for more engagement Duration: 10-15 minutes maximum Why it works: Intense visual tracking + movement + cause-effect Sunbeam Object Display Cost: $0-3 Materials: Sunny window, clear glass/plastic objects (beads, marbles, crystals, clear toys), string or shelf How to Use: Hang clear objects in sunny window on strings at different heights Objects catch sunlight, create rainbows Child moves objects through sunbeams Watches rainbows shift and change Can create "sun catcher mobile" Natural light provides intense visual input Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Natural light, child controls object movement, creates rainbows Overhead Projector Play Cost: $20-40 (or borrow/use at library) Materials: Overhead projector or light table, transparent objects (colored plastics, glass beads, clear toys), white wall/screen
How to Use: Place objects on projector surface Move objects, watch giant shadows/colored images on wall Overlap transparent colored objects to mix colors Create patterns and designs Very engaging visual display Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Large-scale visual display, child controls everything, color mixing Aquarium Light Exploration Cost: $5-10 Materials: Clear container with water, waterproof flashlight or glow sticks, floating/sinking objects How to Use: Fill clear container with water Add objects that float and sink Shine flashlight from different angles Watch light refract through water and objects Move objects through illuminated water Can add food coloring to water Duration: 20-30 minutes (water play requires supervision) Why it works: Combines water play, light play, and object manipulation Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS):
Single Object Light Path Cost: $0-2 Materials: One small toy, flashlight, quiet space How to Use: Shine flashlight on floor creating beam path Child moves one toy slowly along path Very controlled, predictable Can tape path on floor for consistency Same path every time Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Simple, predictable, not overwhelming, one object only Container Light Viewing Cost: $2-3 Materials: Clear container, 3-5 small transparent objects, flashlight How to Use: Place objects in container Shine light from below or side Child can tilt container slowly to move objects Contained, controlled environment Same objects each time (predictable) Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Contained, limited objects, predictable Stationary Light Observation Cost: $0-3 Materials: Objects placed in sunbeam or lamplight, no movement
How to Use: Arrange objects in light (don't move them) Child observes how light illuminates objects Can look at different times of day Very calm, no pressure to interact Duration: 5 minutes as needed Why it works: No movement requirement, just observation, calming Slow Motion Light Play Cost: $0-2 Materials: Flashlight, one object, table How to Use: Move object through light beam VERY slowly Count to 10 while moving Predictable, controlled speed Can practice "slow motion" together Calming pace Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Slow pace is calming, controlled, predictable Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Hand-Eye Coordination Circuit: Before/during light-object play, incorporate activities that provide similar input: Bean Bag Toss: Throw into targets (5 minutes) Catching Game: Toss and catch ball (5 minutes)
Marble Run: Watch marbles roll through channels (5 minutes) Then: Structured light-object play (10 minutes) Provides varied ways to practice object tracking Prevents fixation on one method Heavy Work Integration: Between light-object activities: Carry heavy objects across room Push/pull weighted cart Wall push-ups 3-5 minutes of heavy work between 5-minute light play sessions Organizes nervous system Makes transitions easier Whole Body Object Movement: Instead of just hands moving objects: Child crawls while pushing toy through light beam Kicks ball through sunbeam Jumps to intercept flying object in light Incorporates gross motor movement 15-20 minutes More organizing than fine motor only For AVOIDERS: Gradual Object-Light Introduction: Week 1: Look at objects in light (no touching/moving) - 2 minutes daily Week 2: Parent moves object slowly through light, child watches - 3 minutes daily
Week 3: Hand-over-hand: parent and child move object together - 5 minutes daily Week 4: Child moves object independently (if comfortable) - 5-10 minutes as tolerated Very gradual, child-paced progression Predictable Object Set: Use same 3 objects every time Same order of exploration Same duration Extreme predictability reduces anxiety Child knows exactly what will happen Distance and Control: Child decides: How close to light source How fast to move objects When to stop Parent doesn't direct or correct Builds sense of safety and control Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Bilateral Arm Massage: Massage both arms simultaneously (bilateral input is organizing) Firm pressure, squeeze from shoulders down to hands Then joint compressions: both shoulders, both elbows, both wrists Creates balance and organization between both sides
Duration: 5 minutes Frequency: Before fine motor/visual activities Why it works: Bilateral input helps integrate both brain hemispheres, organizes motor planning needed for precise object manipulation Hand Strengthening Massage: Press firmly on palm (like pressing dough) Squeeze each finger individually with firm pressure Child squeezes stress ball during/after massage 5 minutes per hand Builds strength and awareness May reduce need for repetitive object manipulation For AVOIDERS: Slow Predictable Touch: Always announce: "I'm going to touch your arm now" Very slow stroke from shoulder to fingertips Count each stroke: 1...2...3...4...5 Always same direction, same speed Child can say "stop" anytime Duration: 3-5 minutes per arm Frequency: Before object-light activities or when overwhelmed Why it works: Predictable, child has control, calming, prepares nervous system
Arm Wrapping: Gently wrap child's arm in soft blanket Provide deep pressure by holding wrapped arm Hold for count of 10 Very organizing and calming 3-5 minutes per arm Child may find this very soothing Manifestation 4: Using Flashlights to Create Patterns Physical Redirection Technique: "Pattern Transfer" Method Join child's flashlight pattern-making for 1 minute Acknowledge: "You're making interesting patterns!" Introduce alternative: "Let's make patterns with paint/chalk/blocks" Bring materials directly to child Create pattern with new material while child still has flashlight After 1-2 minutes: "Flashlight is tired now, let's keep making patterns this way" Guide child's hand to new material Help create first pattern together Gradually reduce your involvement as child engages Put flashlight out of sight (not aggressively - just "resting")
