DIY Alternative Tool: Pattern Beam Creator Materials: Flashlight, cardboard cutouts (shapes, patterns), colored cellophane sheets, rubber bands, tape Cost: Under $3 How to Make: Cut various pattern templates from cardboard (circles with holes, grids, star patterns) Attach to flashlight lens with rubber band Add colored cellophane over patterns for colored pattern projection Create 5-6 different pattern discs Child switches patterns by changing cardboard disc Projects different patterns on wall/ceiling Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Provides variety in pattern creation, child has control, can create complex patterns easily Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Multi-Flashlight Pattern Layering Cost: $8-12 (3-4 flashlights) Materials: Multiple flashlights, colored cellophane (different colors), rubber bands, pattern cutouts How to Use: Give child multiple flashlights Each has different color and/or pattern attachment
Child projects multiple patterns simultaneously Overlap patterns: "What happens when red circles overlap blue squares?" Create rhythm: flash patterns on/off in sequence Take photos of favorite pattern combinations Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Complex, child controls all variables, intense visual stimulation, problem-solving Glow Stick Pattern Writing Cost: $5-8 (glow sticks) Materials: Multiple glow sticks, dark room, camera with long exposure (or phone app) How to Use: Activate glow sticks Darken room completely Child "draws" patterns in air with glow stick Camera captures light trail (long exposure photo) Show child the pattern they created Try letters, shapes, spirals, random patterns Can spell name, create art Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Creates permanent record, very engaging, combines movement with pattern creation
Projector Pattern Show Cost: $15-30 (small LED projector) OR DIY with flashlight Materials: Projector or flashlight, transparent sheets with drawn patterns, overhead projector markers How to Use: Draw patterns on transparent sheets Project onto wall Child creates pattern "show" with sequence Can add music Perform for family Very large-scale patterns (exciting) Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Large-scale, dramatic, child creates and performs Reflective Pattern Board Cost: $5-8 Materials: Board covered in aluminum foil or mirror sheets, flashlight, various objects to create shadows How to Use: Shine flashlight on reflective board Place objects between light and board Creates reflected light patterns Experiment with different angles Move objects to change patterns Reflections multiply patterns Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Reflections create complex, interesting patterns, lots of variables to explore
Pattern Painting with Light Cost: $3-5 (if have camera) Materials: Flashlight, camera with long exposure capability, dark room or outdoor evening How to Use: Set camera to long exposure (or use app) Child creates patterns by moving flashlight while camera captures Try: circles, zigzags, spirals, writing Review "painting" created Print favorites Can create series/gallery Duration: 15-25 minutes Why it works: Permanent art creation, very engaging, novel Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Simple Pattern Template Cost: $0-2 (paper, flashlight) Materials: Paper with one simple pattern drawn, flashlight How to Use: Trace pattern on wall with flashlight beam Follow same pattern repeatedly (predictable) Can use stencil/template Very structured Same pattern can be repeated daily Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Predictable, structured, simple, success-oriented
Dot-to-Dot Light Cost: $0-2 Materials: Paper with dots numbered 1-5, tape to wall, flashlight How to Use: Tape paper to wall Child uses flashlight to "connect" dots in order Creates simple pattern Clear beginning and end Cognitive task (counting) + pattern making Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Structured, predictable outcome, not overwhelming Single Pattern Repetition Cost: $0-2 Materials: Flashlight, one simple pattern (circle) How to Use: Make same simple pattern (like circle) repeatedly Count: "Circle 1, circle 2, circle 3..." Very predictable Can increase count goal gradually Mastery-oriented Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Extremely predictable, builds confidence, clear structure Guided Pattern Following Cost: $0-2 Materials: Two flashlights How to Use: Parent makes simple pattern with flashlight Child copies pattern with their flashlight
Start with very simple (one circle) Gradually increase complexity Success-oriented Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Supported activity, clear model, builds skills gradually Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Pattern Creation Schedule: Vary pattern-making methods throughout day to prevent fixation: Morning: Flashlight patterns (5 min) Midday: Draw patterns on paper (10 min) Afternoon: Build patterns with blocks (10 min) Evening: Trace patterns in sand/rice (10 min) Satisfies need for pattern-making without fixation on flashlight method Each provides different sensory input Movement + Pattern Making: Create patterns while moving: Walk in pattern on floor (tape pattern to follow) Jump in pattern (hopscotch-style) Draw pattern with feet (in sand, with sidewalk chalk) Flashlight patterns while spinning or rocking 15-20 minutes Combines vestibular/proprioceptive with visual
Problem-Solving Pattern Challenges: Set specific challenges: "Can you make a pattern that uses 3 colors?" "Make a pattern that repeats 5 times" "Create the biggest pattern possible" Adds cognitive element Prevents mindless repetition 10-15 minutes For AVOIDERS: Gradual Pattern Complexity: Week 1: One simple line (flashlight traces line on wall) Week 2: Two lines (cross or parallel) Week 3: Simple shape (circle or square) Week 4: Pattern with two shapes Very gradual increase in complexity Only progress when child comfortable Predictable Pattern Time: Same time daily Same duration (5-10 minutes) Same patterns available Child chooses from 2-3 familiar options Extreme predictability Reduces anxiety Success-Oriented Pattern Making: All attempts praised No "wrong" patterns Focus on process, not perfect outcome Builds confidence 5-10 minutes
Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Wrist and Forearm Massage: Pattern-making involves repetitive wrist/hand movements Massage forearms with firm pressure Rotate wrists gently (with child's permission) Press on wrist joints (compression) Squeeze hands firmly Duration: 5 minutes per arm Frequency: Before and after pattern-making activities Why it works: Addresses muscles used in repetitive movements, provides organizing proprioceptive input, may reduce compulsive pattern-making by satisfying sensory need Upper Body Release: Pattern-making often involves tense shoulders/neck Massage shoulders and upper back Gentle neck stretches (child-directed) Arm circles (child does movement while you support) 5-7 minutes Releases tension from repetitive activity For AVOIDERS: Arm Cocooning: Wrap child's arm in soft blanket or towel Gentle pressure while wrapped Hold for count of 10 Unwrap slowly Duration: 3-5 minutes per arm
Frequency: Before pattern-making or when anxious Why it works: Contained, predictable, very calming, child can see what's happening Predictable Massage Routine: Exact same sequence every time Count each movement: "Stroke 1...2...3...4...5" Always shoulder to hand direction Never surprise movements 5 minutes Child knows exactly what to expect Manifestation 5: Playing with Laser Pointers on Walls Physical Redirection Technique: "Safe Redirect" Method (laser safety is critical) If child has laser, approach calmly from side (NOT from in front of beam path) Say calmly but firmly: "I need to hold the laser now" Trade immediately: "Here's a flashlight instead" (have ready) Remove laser from area completely (put out of reach) If child protests: acknowledge ("I know you like the laser") but maintain boundary ("Lasers can hurt eyes, flashlights are safe")
Engage with flashlight enthusiastically: "Can you shine it on the blue toy?" Demonstrate flashlight play actively Stay engaged for 3-5 minutes minimum Never allow child unsupervised access to laser pointers DIY Alternative Tool: Dot-Projection Flashlight Materials: Regular flashlight, black paper or cardboard, pin or nail, tape Cost: Under $1 How to Make: Cut circle from black paper (size of flashlight lens) Use pin to poke holes in paper in pattern (random dots, constellation pattern, smiley face, geometric design) Tape circle over flashlight lens Creates moving dot pattern on wall without laser danger Can make multiple pattern discs to change effects Child controls where dots appear Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Creates similar dot effect as laser pointer without safety risk, child has control
Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Multi-Flashlight Chase Game Cost: $4-8 (2-3 flashlights) Materials: Multiple flashlights (one for each hand), colored cellophane, dark room How to Use: Give child flashlight for each hand Cover each with different colored cellophane Darken room Call out challenges: "Make the lights meet in the middle!" "Race them across the wall!" "Make them dance together!" "Can you make them cross?" Add music for more engagement Chase the lights with your body too Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Intense visual tracking + bilateral coordination + movement + control Flashlight Target Game Cost: $2-3 (colored paper, flashlight) Materials: Colored paper targets taped to wall (various sizes/shapes), flashlight, timer How to Use: Create targets: red circles, blue squares, yellow stars (different sizes)
Call out target: "Hit the small red circle!" Child shines flashlight on correct target Time challenges: "How fast can you hit all 5 targets?" Accuracy challenges: "Hit only the green ones" Can add point system Increase distance for more challenge Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Adds structure and purpose, problem-solving, competitive element Glow Ball Fetch Game Cost: $5-8 (glow-in-dark ball) Materials: Glow-in-the-dark ball, flashlight, dark room or evening outdoor space How to Use: Shine flashlight on glow ball to "charge" it Ball glows brightly Throw ball, child fetches Ball glows in dark (exciting to find) Re-charge with flashlight, repeat Can play catch with glowing ball Add obstacles to navigate around Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Combines light play with gross motor movement, running, catching
Flashlight Maze Navigation Cost: $2-5 (masking tape, flashlight) Materials: Masking tape, flashlight, darkened room/hallway, small toy car or ball How to Use: Create maze on floor with masking tape Darken space Child uses flashlight to illuminate path ahead Navigate toy through maze following flashlight beam Time trials Create increasingly complex mazes Can crawl through maze themselves with flashlight Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Problem-solving + movement + light use + purpose-driven activity Shadow Tag with Flashlights Cost: $5-8 (2 flashlights) Materials: Two flashlights, dark space, players How to Use: Each person has flashlight "Tag" by shining flashlight on other person Can only tag person's shadow (harder!) Lots of running and movement Switch roles: one person creates shadows with toys, other "catches" shadows with flashlight
Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Vigorous movement + social play + light use Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Stationary Light Patterns Cost: $3-5 (patterned lampshade) Materials: Small lamp with decorative/patterned lampshade How to Use: Lamp creates stationary pattern on wall No movement (not overwhelming) Pattern never changes (predictable) Child can look when desired Can turn lamp on/off for control Duration: 3-5 minutes as needed Why it works: Stationary, predictable, calming, no demands Flashlight Tracing Activity Cost: $0-2 (paper, flashlight) Materials: Paper with simple shapes drawn, flashlight How to Use: Tape paper with shapes to wall Child traces shapes with flashlight beam Very slow, controlled movement Same shapes can be used repeatedly Clear task with beginning and end Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Structured, predictable, success-oriented
Single Target Focus Cost: $1-2 (one colored paper) Materials: One target (colored circle) on wall, flashlight How to Use: Child shines flashlight on single target only Can turn on/off Very simple, not overwhelming Same target daily (predictable) No complex instructions Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Extremely simple, predictable, achievable Controlled Flashlight Path Cost: $0-2 (tape, flashlight) Materials: Tape line on wall (simple path), flashlight How to Use: Child follows tape path slowly with flashlight beam Same path every time Can time self to see consistency (not speed) Very controlled, predictable movement Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Clear boundaries, predictable, calming Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Flashlight Obstacle Course: Combine flashlight use with movement: Set up course: crawl under table, jump over pillow, walk balance beam (tape line)
Parent shines flashlight showing path Child follows flashlight beam through course OR child uses flashlight to find way through dark course 10-15 minutes Heavy proprioceptive work + visual tracking Very organizing Structured Light Play Protocol: Visual timer: 10 minutes flashlight play When timer ends: 5 minutes heavy work Wall push-ups Carry books Jump on trampoline Then: 5 minutes calm activity (puzzle, books) Teaches modulation and transitions Purpose-Driven Flashlight Use: Give flashlight meaningful jobs: "Find all the red toys in this dark room" "Read this book with flashlight only" "Help me find my keys with the flashlight" Adds purpose, reduces mindless light-seeking 10-15 minutes per task For AVOIDERS: Predictable Light Path Protocol: Tape simple path on wall (circle or figure-8) Child traces same path daily with flashlight
Knows exactly what to expect Can master the path (confidence building) 5 minutes daily Gradual complexity increase (only when child ready) Co-Regulation with Flashlight: Adult holds flashlight with child (both hands on flashlight) Adult controls speed and direction initially Child feels control but with support Gradually release control to child (over days/weeks) 3-5 minutes daily Builds confidence and tolerance Distance from Activity: Week 1: Child watches parent use flashlight from distance Week 2: Child stands closer while parent uses flashlight Week 3: Hand-over-hand flashlight use Week 4: Independent use with support nearby Very gradual introduction Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Active Resistance Massage: Child makes fist, you gently try to open fingers (they resist) Then reverse: they try to make fist while you gently resist
Provides organizing input through active muscle engagement Do for each hand Then: squeeze hands firmly Duration: 5 minutes per hand Frequency: Before flashlight/light play activities Why it works: Satisfies sensory seeking through muscles, organizes proprioceptive system, may reduce need for intense visual seeking Bilateral Hand Work: Both hands worked simultaneously Squeeze both hands at same time Press on both wrists together Creates bilateral integration 5 minutes Very organizing For AVOIDERS: Predictable Stroke Massage: Always announce: "I'm going to touch your arm now" One hand flat on child's back Move in slow circle, clockwise only Count each circle: 1...2...3...up to 10 Child knows exactly what's coming Duration: 5 minutes Frequency: Before light play or when overwhelmed Why it works: Extreme predictability reduces anxiety, organizing rhythmic input, child maintains control (can say stop)
Contained Pressure: Place child's hand between two cushions Gentle pressure from above Hold for count of 10 Very calming and contained 3-5 minutes per hand Child can see and control entire experience Manifestation 6: Opening/Closing Blinds Repeatedly Physical Redirection Technique: "Countdown and Transfer" Method Don't forcibly stop blind manipulation (causes escalation) Approach and stand near child (not blocking blinds) Say: "You can open and close 5 more times, let's count" Count together: "One...two...three...four...five" On five: gently place hand over child's hand on blind cord/slats Guide hand away from blinds Immediately redirect to similar repetitive activity: "Let's open and close this instead" Hand them alternative (busy box, door/cabinet toy, pop-it fidget) Demonstrate enthusiastically Stay engaged for 3-5 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Mini Blind System Materials: Cardboard, popsicle sticks or straws, brads (split pins), string Cost: Under $3 How to Make:
Cut cardboard backing (8x10 inches) Attach 6-8 popsicle sticks horizontally using brads as pivots Sticks can rotate to "open" and "close" like blind slats Add string attached to bottom to pull (opens all slats at once) Child can manipulate individual slats or pull string Portable, can use anywhere Duration: Unlimited (safe alternative) Why it works: Replicates blind manipulation without actual blinds, satisfies repetitive open/close need Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Door/Cabinet Opening Station Cost: $0-5 (household items or cabinet locks) Materials: Multiple cabinets/doors with different types of closures (magnetic, latch, hook), or create board with various locks and latches How to Use: Set up station with 5-6 different opening mechanisms Child explores opening and closing each type Can time how fast they can open all
Add complexity: open in specific sequence Hide small toy in one - find it Each mechanism provides different tactile/proprioceptive feedback Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Variety of opening/closing experiences, problem-solving, fine motor challenge Flip Book Station Cost: $5-10 (or DIY with paper) Materials: Multiple flip books, or create own with index cards How to Use: Flip books create animation when pages flip rapidly Child flips pages open and closed repeatedly Visual reward for flipping action Can create own flip books (draw sequential images) Satisfies repetitive opening/closing motion Adds visual interest Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Combines repetitive motion with visual payoff Accordion Fold Paper Play Cost: $2-3 (colored paper) Materials: Paper strips, tape, decorating materials How to Use: Create accordion-folded paper (fold back and forth repeatedly)
Child opens and closes accordion Can make paper fan Decorate folds Create "expanding snake" or "stretching caterpillar" Satisfies open/close repetition Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Creative + repetitive motion + visual interest Curtain/Fabric Pull System Cost: $5-8 (fabric, dowel rod) Materials: Fabric hung on tension rod in doorway or between chairs, curtain rings How to Use: Hang fabric curtain at child's height Child can open and close repeatedly Safe alternative to window blinds Add weight to fabric for more resistance (organizing input) Can use as puppet theater backdrop Satisfies same motion as blinds Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Replicates blind motion, provides resistance, multi-purpose Jack-in-the-Box Collection Cost: $10-20 (or find used) Materials: Multiple jack-in-the-boxes with different mechanisms How to Use:
Turn crank to close/compress Opens/pops with surprise Satisfies repetitive opening motion Adds excitement and anticipation Can predict when pop will happen Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Repetitive motion + surprise element + cause-effect Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single Window Card Cost: $1-2 (cardboard, paper) Materials: Card with window flap that opens/closes How to Use: Create card with single window cut-out Attach flap with tape hinge Picture revealed when opened Very simple, one flap only Can change picture inside daily Controlled, predictable Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Simple, controlled, predictable outcome Book with Flaps Cost: $5-10 (flap book) Materials: Children's book with sturdy flaps (lift-the-flap book) How to Use: Read book together Child opens flaps to reveal pictures Same book can be read repeatedly (predictable)
Limited number of flaps (not overwhelming) Clear beginning and end Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Structured, predictable, combines reading with flapping motion Simple Box with Lid Cost: $0-2 (shoebox) Materials: Box with lid, small toy inside How to Use: Child opens lid to see toy Closes lid Very simple, repetitive Can change toy for continued interest Predictable action Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Very simple, achievable, predictable Controlled Blind Time Cost: $0 Materials: Actual window blinds (but controlled) How to Use: Designate specific blind for child's use Set clear rule: "Open 3 times, close 3 times, then done" Use visual counter (3 blocks, remove one each time) When all blocks gone, blind time is over Scheduled time daily (predictable)
Duration: 2-3 minutes (very controlled) Why it works: Allows behavior in controlled way, teaches limits, predictable Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Heavy Work Before Blind Play: Opening/closing blinds provides some resistance (organizing) Before allowing blind access, provide heavier resistance work: Push against wall: 10 seconds x 5 reps Carry stack of books: 3 trips across room Open/close heavy doors: 10 times Pull/push weighted cart Duration: 5-7 minutes Then: Brief, controlled blind opening time (5 minutes with timer) Satisfies need for resistance/proprioceptive input Blind Schedule System: Visual schedule showing when blind opening is allowed: Morning: 5 minutes when waking up (open blinds to let in light - functional) Evening: 5 minutes when sun sets (close blinds - functional) Makes blind interaction purposeful and scheduled
Reduces random blind manipulation throughout day Alternative Resistance Activities: Throughout day, provide activities with similar resistance: Therapy putty (pull apart, squeeze) Playdough (kneading, rolling) Clothespins (open and close on edge of can) Stress ball squeezing Opening and closing plastic containers with snap lids 10-15 minutes, 3-4x daily May reduce blind-seeking behavior For AVOIDERS: Gradual Blind Exposure: Many avoiders overwhelmed by sudden light changes from blind manipulation Week 1: Blinds stay in one position all week (open OR closed) Child observes but doesn't touch Week 2: Parent adjusts blinds once daily, child watches Prepares child: "I'm going to close the blinds now" Week 3: Hand-over-hand, child helps parent adjust once daily Very gentle guidance Week 4: Child adjusts independently (if comfortable) once daily
Controlled, scheduled time Builds tolerance for light changes gradually Predictable Blind Routine: Same time daily for blind adjustment "After breakfast, we open the bedroom blinds" Parent does it initially, child can watch Eventually child can participate Extreme predictability reduces anxiety Light Management: If child overwhelmed by bright light when blinds open: Use sheer curtains behind blinds (softens light) Open blinds gradually (1/4, then 1/2, then fully) Give warning: "Opening blinds in 10 seconds" Provide sunglasses if needed initially Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Forearm and Hand Massage: Blind manipulation uses forearm/hand muscles repeatedly Firm massage of forearms (squeeze from elbow to wrist) Massage palm with firm pressure Press on wrist joints (compression) Squeeze each finger Duration: 5 minutes per arm Frequency: 2-3x daily, especially before times when blind manipulation occurs
Why it works: Addresses muscles used in repetitive movement, provides organizing proprioceptive input directly to areas seeking stimulation Resistance Massage: Child pushes against your hands (you provide resistance) Press palms together, child pushes hard Provides organizing muscle input 3-5 minutes Satisfies need for resistance that drives blind manipulation For AVOIDERS: Gentle Arm Wrapping: Wrap child's arm in soft towel or blanket Gentle pressure while wrapped Hold for count of 10 Unwrap slowly Duration: 3-5 minutes per arm Frequency: When anxious about light/blind changes or before blind activities Why it works: Contained, predictable, very calming, organizes nervous system Slow Predictable Strokes: Always same pattern: shoulder to hand Very slow, count to 10 per stroke Gentle-moderate pressure (ask child's preference) 5 strokes per arm
5 minutes total Prepares nervous system for activity Manifestation 7: Shining Light Through Prisms or Crystals Physical Redirection Technique: "Join and Expand" Method Sit beside child and observe prism play with them (30-60 seconds) Comment positively: "The rainbows are beautiful" After brief observation, offer expansion: "Let's make rainbows in a new way" Bring alternative rainbow-making materials (CDs, water spray, oil on water) Demonstrate enthusiastically while child still has prism After 1-2 minutes: "The prism needs to rest now, let's keep making rainbows this way" Gently remove prism, immediately engage with alternative Stay engaged for 5+ minutes to ensure transition DIY Alternative Tool: Rainbow Reflection Box Materials: Shoebox, aluminum foil, old CDs or CD pieces, prisms or crystals (if available), flashlight Cost: Under $3 How to Make:
Line shoebox with aluminum foil (shiny side out) Hang CD pieces or small prisms from top of box with string Cut viewing window in one side Place flashlight in box shining on hanging pieces Light reflects, creates rainbow patterns inside box Child can look through window, rotate box, add/remove items Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Contained rainbow experience, child controls variables, portable Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Outdoor Water Spray Rainbows Cost: $2-5 (spray bottle or hose with mist setting) Materials: Spray bottle or garden hose, sunny outdoor space How to Use: Position with back to sun Spray water mist into air Creates rainbow in spray Experiment with different spray patterns Jump through rainbow mist Try to "catch" rainbow Can add bubbles to spray for more effect
Full body movement + intense visual Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Outdoor activity, movement, large-scale rainbows, tactile (water) + visual CD Mobile Rainbow Maker Cost: $0-3 (old CDs, string) Materials: 5-10 old CDs, string/fishing line, coat hanger or stick How to Use: Hang CDs from coat hanger at different lengths Suspend in sunny window CDs spin and create moving rainbows throughout room Child can spin CDs individually Watch rainbows dance on walls and ceiling Count how many rainbows visible Very mesmerizing Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Multiple rainbow sources, movement, child can control Oil and Water Rainbow Experiment Cost: $2-3 Materials: Clear container, water, cooking oil, food coloring, flashlight or sunlight How to Use: Fill container with water Add drops of oil (creates shimmering surface)
Shine light from side Creates rainbow effect on oil surface Add food coloring drops (spreads in patterns) Child controls additions, watches effects Swirl gently to change patterns Science + visual stimulation Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Hands-on experimentation, cause-effect, beautiful visual results Bubble Rainbow Station Cost: $3-5 (bubbles) Materials: Bubble solution, various bubble wands, sunny outdoor space or bright lamp How to Use: Blow bubbles in sunlight or bright lamp light Each bubble shows rainbow colors Try to catch bubbles and see rainbows up close Use different wand sizes (different rainbow sizes) Can add glycerin to bubble solution (longer-lasting bubbles = more rainbow viewing time) Very engaging Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Movement, outdoor activity, natural rainbow creation Rainbow Light Table Exploration
Cost: $20-40 (light table) or DIY with $5-10 Materials: Light table or DIY (clear container over lamp), transparent colored materials (cellophane, colored plastic, glass gems) How to Use: Place colored transparent items on light table Overlap items to create new colors Create patterns and designs Colors glow brilliantly Can trace on paper over designs Very engaging color/light exploration Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Intense visual input, child controls all variables, color learning Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single Rainbow Card Cost: $1-2 (rainbow sticker or drawing) Materials: Card with rainbow image, laminated if possible How to Use: Child can look at rainbow card when desired Same rainbow every time (predictable) Can carry in pocket No pressure to interact, just observation Calming, familiar
Duration: 3-5 minutes as needed Why it works: Predictable, portable, simple, controllable Gentle Prism Viewing (Controlled) Cost: $3-5 (small prism) Materials: Small prism, specific location (window sill) How to Use: Prism stays in one location Available at specific time daily (morning sunlight) Child can view for set time (5 minutes) Same conditions each day Very predictable Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Controlled conditions, predictable time, not overwhelming Rainbow Book Cost: $5-10 Materials: Book about rainbows (science or story) How to Use: Read together in calm space Look at rainbow pictures No actual light/prism stimulation (can be overwhelming) Same book can be read repeatedly Very predictable Duration: 10 minutes Why it works: Addresses interest without sensory overwhelm Single CD Sun Catcher
Cost: $0-1 (one CD) Materials: One CD hung in window How to Use: CD creates gentle moving rainbows Same location daily Child can observe when desired Not overwhelming (just one source) Calming, predictable Duration: 5 minutes as needed Why it works: Gentle, predictable, not overstimulating Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Rainbow Exploration Schedule: Provide variety of rainbow-making throughout day: Morning: CD rainbows in window (5 min) Midday: Outdoor spray rainbows (15 min) Afternoon: Bubble rainbows (15 min) Evening: Prism time (controlled, 5 min) Variety prevents fixation on prism only Each method provides different sensory input Rainbow Creation with Movement: Combine rainbow viewing with gross motor: Spray rainbows while running through mist Chase bubble rainbows and pop them Dance in rainbow light from spinning CD mobile
Jump to reach rainbows on ceiling 15-20 minutes Organizing proprioceptive/vestibular input with visual Science Exploration Approach: Make rainbow-seeking educational: Learn about light spectrum Predict where rainbow will appear Measure rainbow size Draw diagrams of light refraction Keep rainbow observation journal Adds cognitive element 20-30 minutes Prevents mindless fixation, adds purpose For AVOIDERS: Gradual Rainbow Introduction: Week 1: Look at rainbow pictures in books only - 5 minutes daily Week 2: View single CD rainbow from distance (10 feet) - 3 minutes daily Week 3: Move closer (5 feet) - 5 minutes daily Week 4: Brief prism viewing (if tolerated) - 2 minutes daily Very gradual sensory exposure Child sets the pace Predictable Rainbow Time: Same time daily ("Morning rainbow time after breakfast")
Same location (window sill in bedroom) Same duration (5 minutes) Same parent present Extreme predictability reduces anxiety Control and Choice: Child chooses: When to look at rainbow How long to look How close to get No pressure or expectations Builds sense of safety and control 5 minutes as child directs Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Visual System Massage: Gentle pressure on temples (small circles) Gentle pressure above eyebrows (smooth outward from center) Gentle pressure on forehead Massage around eye area (very gentle, avoid eyes themselves) Gentle pressure at base of skull (visual processing area) Duration: 3-5 minutes Frequency: Before or after intense visual activities (prism/rainbow viewing) Why it works: Provides organizing input to visual processing areas, may reduce intense visual seeking by satisfying some sensory need
Neck and Shoulder Release: Rainbow/prism viewing often involves tense neck position Gentle neck massage (sides only, never front) Shoulder massage with firm pressure Can help child rotate neck gently 5 minutes Releases tension from prolonged looking For AVOIDERS: Full Body Grounding: Start at feet (firm pressure) Move to legs (long, slow strokes) Arms (shoulder to hand) Back (deep, slow pressure) Duration: 10 minutes full body Frequency: After rainbow/light exposure or when overwhelmed Why it works: Organizes entire nervous system, provides calming alternative to visual input, very grounding Weighted Blanket Massage: Child under weighted blanket Gentle massage through blanket Provides deep pressure + massage benefits Very organizing and calming 10 minutes Can be very soothing after visual overstimulation Manifestation 8: Creating Rainbow Effects with CDs
Physical Redirection Technique: "Collection and Transition" Method Approach child playing with CD Join activity briefly: "That makes pretty rainbows!" After 30-60 seconds: "Let's collect the rainbows we made" Take photo of rainbow patterns (child can help) "Now the rainbows are saved! Let's make something else colorful" Offer alternative colorful activity (painting, colored blocks, kaleidoscope) Gently take CD: "CD is resting now" Immediately engage with alternative Show photo of rainbows later: "Remember the rainbows we saved?" DIY Alternative Tool: CD Rainbow Spinner Materials: Old CD, pencil or short dowel, hot glue, sunny space or lamp Cost: Under $1 How to Make: Hot glue pencil/dowel to center of CD (perpendicular, sticking up) Creates spinning top with CD as base Child spins on table or floor
CD creates rainbow blur while spinning Combines movement with rainbow effect Can make multiple with different designs on CD Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Active play with CD, creates dynamic rainbow effect, child controls speed and duration Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): CD Mobile Art Project Cost: $2-5 (old CDs, string, decorating materials) Materials: 10-15 old CDs, string, coat hanger or stick, paint/markers/stickers How to Use: Decorate CDs with paint, permanent markers, or stickers Hang at various lengths from mobile base Hang in sunny window or near lamp CDs spin creating rainbow light show throughout room Child can spin individual CDs Adjust positions to direct rainbows to different spots Large-scale project Duration: 30-45 minutes creation + ongoing viewing Why it works: Creative project + produces intense visual effect + permanent installation
CD Rainbow Hunt Game Cost: $0-2 (existing CDs) Materials: 5-10 CDs, sunny day or bright lamps, target markers (paper stars) How to Use: Place target markers around room Child uses CD to reflect light/rainbow onto targets "Hit the red star with your rainbow!" Time challenges Can play with partner (take turns) Adds purpose and problem-solving to CD play Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Purposeful activity, problem-solving, still provides visual input CD Kaleidoscope Viewer Cost: $3-5 (cardboard tube, CDs) Materials: Paper towel tube, 2-3 CD pieces (carefully cut or broken), tape, colored cellophane How to Use: Line inside of tube with CD pieces (reflective side in) Cover one end with colored cellophane Look through open end toward light Creates kaleidoscope effect
Turn to change patterns Can make multiple viewers Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Novel use of CD, creates contained viewing experience Outdoor CD Wind Chimes Cost: $2-5 (CDs, string, stick) Materials: Multiple CDs, string, stick or coat hanger, outdoor space How to Use: Hang CDs from stick at various lengths Hang outside where they catch wind CDs spin and create rainbows Make music/sound when touching Can check on them throughout day Combines visual + auditory + outdoor time Duration: 20 minutes setup + ongoing outdoor viewing Why it works: Outdoor activity, multisensory, child can check periodically CD Reflection Race Cost: $0-2 (CDs, toy cars) Materials: 2+ CDs, flashlight or sunlight, toy cars How to Use: Use CD to reflect light creating "path" on floor
Child races toy car following the light path Move CD to make path move (car chases) Can set up obstacle course Combines movement, problem-solving, light play Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Active, purposeful, still provides visual interest Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single CD Display Cost: $0-1 (one CD) Materials: One CD, stand or specific location How to Use: Place CD in designated spot (window sill) Creates gentle rainbow when sun hits it Same location daily Child can observe when desired No interaction required Duration: Brief observation as needed Why it works: Predictable, gentle, not demanding CD in Sensory Bottle Cost: $2-3 (bottle, CD pieces, glitter) Materials: Clear bottle, small CD pieces (edges smoothed), water, glitter How to Use: Place CD pieces in bottle with water and glitter
Seal tightly Child tilts bottle, watches CD pieces move and create gentle rainbow shimmer Contained, safe, controlled Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Contained, gentle visual input, safe CD Picture Frame Cost: $1-2 (CD, photo) Materials: CD, child's favorite photo, glue How to Use: Glue photo to center of CD Outer ring still creates rainbow Combines favorite image with gentle rainbow effect Can hang in window Comforting and predictable Duration: Brief viewing as needed Why it works: Combines comfort (familiar photo) with gentle visual interest Controlled CD Time Cost: $0 Materials: One CD, timer, specific time/place How to Use: "CD time" is 5 minutes daily Same time, same CD, same location Child can manipulate CD during this time Timer shows when time is ending
Extreme predictability Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Allows interest in controlled, predictable way Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: CD Rainbow Schedule: Designate specific times for CD rainbow play: Morning: 10 minutes CD mobile viewing Afternoon: 10 minutes CD rainbow hunt game Evening: 5 minutes calm CD viewing before bed Scheduled times prevent all-day seeking Teaches: "CD time has specific slots" Movement + CD Play: Combine CD use with movement: Dance while holding CD (watches rainbows move with dance) Run around room trying to "catch" CD mobile rainbows on body Jump to make hung CD swing (changes rainbow patterns) 15-20 minutes Adds organizing gross motor component Creative Projects: Turn CD interest into art projects: CD mosaic art (break CDs safely, create design)
Decorated CD ornaments CD sun catchers with tissue paper Creates lasting product Channels interest into creative outlet 30-45 minutes per project For AVOIDERS: Very Gradual CD Introduction: Week 1: CD in room but covered (gets used to presence) Week 2: CD uncovered but not in direct light (no rainbows yet) Week 3: CD in dim light (gentle rainbow effect) Week 4: CD in bright light briefly (2-3 minutes) Extremely gradual exposure Child controls progression Predictable CD Routine: One specific CD One specific location (window sill in child's room) One specific time (morning after breakfast) Same duration (5 minutes) Every element predictable and controlled Choice and Control: Child chooses all variables: Whether to look at CD How long to look How close to get
When to stop No pressure from adults Builds sense of safety Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Eye Area Massage (Very Gentle): Close eyes Very gentle pressure on closed eyelids (count to 3) Gentle circles on temples Gentle pressure above and below eyes (avoid eyes) Smooth from center of forehead outward Duration: 3-5 minutes Frequency: After intense visual activities Why it works: Provides calming input to overactive visual system, may reduce seeking by satisfying sensory need in that area Full Body Calming After Visual Intensity: After intense CD/rainbow play: Firm massage on arms and legs Deep pressure on back Joint compressions 10 minutes Helps transition from high visual stimulation to calm state For AVOIDERS: Grounding Before/After CD Exposure: Feet: firm pressure on soles
Legs: firm pressure, grounding strokes Place hands on shoulders: firm, steady pressure Count to 10 Duration: 5 minutes Frequency: Before and after CD viewing Why it works: Helps child feel "anchored" and safe, prepares nervous system for visual input or helps recover after Cocooning: Wrap snugly in blanket Gentle rocking Hold for 2-3 minutes Very calming after any overwhelming visual experience Can do before CD time as preparation
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 1. VISUAL STIMMING INTERVENTIONS > A. Light-Based Stimming > Level 3: Light-Induced Movement
Causation: Over-stimulated: Movement + light provides organizing input Under-stimulated: Combination of vestibular and visual creates intense experience Sensitivity: Integration of multiple sensory systems for regulation Sensory Profile: Seeker: Intense, prolonged sessions; seeks maximum stimulation Mixed: Movement seeking + specific visual preferences Description: Body movements designed to create or interact with light effects Manifestation 1: Spinning to See Light Blur and Streak Physical Redirection Technique: "Slow to Stop" Method DO NOT stop spinning abruptly (can cause vestibular dysregulation and distress) Match child's spin direction and spin alongside them While spinning together, gradually slow YOUR spin Narrate: "Slowing down...slower...slower..." Most children naturally slow to match your pace When both stopped, immediate hand-holding to provide grounding Guide to sitting activity immediately: puzzle, play-doh, books
Stay with child for 3-5 minutes (vestibular system needs time to stabilize) May need to sit or lie down briefly if dizzy DIY Alternative Tool: Spin Board with Light Strips Materials: Lazy Susan or office chair seat (rotating base), battery LED light strips, tape, cushion Cost: $8-15 How to Make: Attach cushion to rotating base (lazy Susan or office chair seat bottom) Attach battery LED light strips around edge of rotating base Secure with strong tape Lights face outward Turn on lights, child sits on cushion Adult controls spinning speed (pushes gently) Creates controlled light-streak effect Much safer than standing/spinning Duration: 5-10 minutes (with breaks) Why it works: Provides light-blur visual without dangerous standing spin, adult controls speed, sitting is safer
Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Spinning Glow Stick Trails Cost: $5-8 (pack of glow sticks) Materials: Glow sticks (multiple colors), string (optional), dark room or outdoor evening space, tape Safety: Ensure glow sticks intact (liquid can irritate skin) How to Use: Activate 2-3 glow sticks Darken space Option 1: Child holds glow sticks and spins with arms out (watches light trails) Option 2: Tape glow sticks to wrists/ankles, then spin/dance Option 3: Tie glow stick to string (secure knot), spin like lasso Intense light trails visible Take photos (captures trails) Duration: 5-10 minutes MAXIMUM (vestibular overload risk) Follow with: 5 minutes heavy work (push-ups, carrying) Why it works: Intense visual + vestibular, controlled environment, time-limited Sit-and-Spin with Light Circle Cost: $20-30 (Sit-n-Spin toy) or borrow
Materials: Sit-n-Spin toy, g glow sticks or battery tea lights How to Use: Arrange glow sticks in circle around Sit-n-Spin Darken room Child sits and spins Watches lights blur into circle Safer than standing (lower center of gravity) Adult supervises, enforces time limits Duration: 10 minutes with 2-minute breaks every few spins Why it works: Controlled spinning, sitting is safer, provides desired light-blur effect Merry-Go-Round Evening Play (if have access) Cost: $0 (playground equipment) OR $50-100 (backyard equipment) Materials: Playground merry-go-round, battery lights attached to rails, evening time Safety: Adult controls speed always, child sits/holds on How to Use: Attach battery lights to merry-go-round rails (securely) Evening/dusk timing Child sits on merry-go-round (never standing) Adult spins at controlled speed Lights create blur/trail effect
Enforce strict time limits Duration: 5-7 minutes MAXIMUM with breaks Follow with: Heavy work (climbing, swinging) Why it works: Combines vestibular + visual safely, adult-controlled speed Office Chair Spinning with Lights Cost: $0-5 (if have office chair) Materials: Office chair that spins, glow sticks or flashlight, darkened room Safety: Adult controls spinning, child seated with feet up How to Use: Child sits in office chair, feet tucked up (not dragging) Hold glow stick or flashlight Adult spins chair at controlled speed Child watches light blur Count rotations: "5 spins, then stop" Strictly enforce limits Duration: 5-10 minutes with frequent breaks Why it works: Seated (safer), adult controls speed, predictable stop point Dance Party with Ribbon Lights Cost: $5-10 (ribbon streamers, glow sticks)
Materials: Ribbon streamers with glow sticks attached to ends, music, darkened space How to Use: Attach activated glow stick to end of each ribbon Child holds ribbons and dances/spins Creates light trails with ribbon movement Can be less intense spinning (more dancing) Music provides rhythm and structure Duration: 10-15 minutes with movement breaks Why it works: Combines movement, music, visual trails, less intense than pure spinning Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Gentle Swing Rotation Cost: $0 (playground swing) Materials: Regular swing (not moving forward/back), one glow stick hung from swing Safety: Adult controls rotation speed completely How to Use: Child sits in swing Adult twists swing ropes 3-5 times (not more) Release for gentle rotation Hang single glow stick from swing chain
Very gentle spin with minimal visual input Child can say "stop" anytime Duration: 3-5 minutes MAX Why it works: Minimal vestibular input, gentle visual component, adult-controlled Rotating Light Display (Child Stays Still) Cost: $8-12 (rotating disco ball or light projector) Materials: Battery rotating disco ball or star projector How to Use: CHILD stays completely still (sitting or lying down) Turn on rotating light projector Lights move/spin around room Child gets visual input WITHOUT vestibular challenge Very gentle, non-threatening Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Visual input without vestibular demand, child feels safe and grounded Lazy Susan Observation Cost: $5-8 (lazy Susan) Materials: Lazy Susan, small toys or lights on it How to Use: Place toys/lights on lazy Susan Child OBSERVES while adult slowly rotates it
Child doesn't spin themselves Very slow, controlled rotation Child can say when to stop Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Observational only, no vestibular challenge to child Slow Rotation on Parent's Lap Cost: $0 Materials: Office chair or stool that rotates, parent, child How to Use: Child sits on parent's lap Parent rotates chair VERY slowly (1/4 turn at a time) Pause between rotations Child feels safe with parent Can hold comfort object Stop immediately if child uncomfortable Duration: 2-3 minutes MAX Why it works: Co-regulation with parent, minimal vestibular input, child feels safe Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Scheduled Spinning Protocol: Spinning MUST be controlled and scheduled to be safe: Morning: 5 minutes structured spinning (adult supervises/controls) After school: 5 minutes outdoor spinning play (merry-go-round or similar)
Before bed: 3 minutes gentle rocking (calming, not alerting) Provides vestibular input in safe, controlled doses Reduces dangerous random spinning throughout day Use visual timer for each session Spin + Crash Sequence: After spinning, child MUST do heavy work: Spin 5 rotations (adult-controlled speed) Immediate jump into crash pad or pile of pillows Repeat sequence 5-10 times Crash provides organizing proprioceptive input Helps vestibular system process spinning 10-15 minutes total Very important for safety and regulation Alternative Vestibular Activities: Provide other vestibular input to reduce spinning need: Swinging (forward/back) Rocking horse Therapy ball bouncing Log rolling Somersaults on mat 15-20 minutes, 2-3x daily May reduce spinning-seeking behavior Heavy Work Before Spinning: Always do heavy work BEFORE allowing spinning: Wall push-ups: 10 reps
Carry heavy items: 5 minutes Animal walks: 5 minutes Organizes nervous system Makes spinning less dysregulating Safer overall For AVOIDERS: Minimal Rotation Start: Begin with absolute minimum vestibular input: Week 1: Sit in office chair, adult rotates 1/4 turn (90 degrees) each direction once daily Week 2: Increase to 1/2 turn (180 degrees) Week 3: Full rotation VERY slowly Week 4: 2-3 rotations slowly (only if comfortable) Extremely gradual introduction Child can say "stop" anytime Build tolerance over months, not days Visual Reference During Spin: If any rotation attempted: Pick one object in room to focus on Try to find that object after each rotation Helps vestibular system stay organized Reduces dizziness and overwhelm Practice: 5 minutes, 2-3x weekly Grounding During/After Rotation:
Before: deep pressure hug During: parent's hands on shoulders (if on lap) After: immediate sitting, weighted lap pad Deep breaths together 5-10 minutes recovery time No Pressure Approach: Never force spinning/rotation Child must initiate or clearly consent Can work on tolerance without actual spinning: Watch others spin Spin toys Talk about spinning May never tolerate spinning - that's okay Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Pre-Spin Preparation Massage: Before any spinning activity: Firm pressure on shoulders and upper back (grounding) Joint compressions: press firmly on shoulder joints (count to 3) Press on hip joints (count to 3) Helps vestibular system prepare for input Duration: 3-5 minutes Why it works: Organizes proprioceptive system before vestibular challenge, safer spinning Post-Spin Organization Massage: Immediately after spinning stops:
Firm pressure on back in downward strokes (top to bottom) "Brushing" motion (firm, fast) down arms and legs Joint compressions on all major joints Helps reorganize nervous system Duration: 2-3 minutes Why it works: Helps nervous system reorganize after vestibular input, prevents prolonged dizziness/dysregulation Grounding Technique: Child sits or lies down Firm pressure on feet (pressing into ground/floor) Firm pressure on shoulders Hold each for count of 10 Very grounding after spinning For AVOIDERS: Grounding Touch Before Any Rotation: Before even minimal rotation: Child sits, feet flat on floor Place firm pressure on tops of shoulders Hold for count of 10 Gentle pressure on top of head (grounding) Say: "You are safe, I'm right here" Duration: 2-3 minutes Why it works: Helps child feel "anchored" and safe before vestibular challenge
Recovery Massage After Rotation: After any rotation (even minimal): Slow, deep pressure on back Very slow strokes (count to 10 per stroke) Predictable pattern Pair with deep breathing Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Calms nervous system, helps recover from vestibular experience Full Body Cocooning: Wrap child snugly in blanket after any spinning exposure Rock gently Provide deep pressure through blanket 5-10 minutes Very organizing and calming Manifestation 2: Jumping in and out of shadows Redirect Activities: Shadow hopscotch games Jumping on projected shapes or colors Shadow obstacle courses Floor projection interactive games Alternative Stimulation: Trampoline with shadow projections Floor piano mat with lights Interactive floor projections (beach, lava) Light-up floor tiles Regulation Through OT/SI: Structured jumping activities with counts Proprioceptive input through jumping (weighted vest)
Motor planning shadow games Bilateral coordination jumping patterns Massage Techniques: Leg compression massage post-activity Foot and ankle massage Quad and hamstring deep tissue work Hip flexor release massage Manifestation 3: Dancing in disco lights or strobe effects Redirect Activities: Structured dance party time Movement + light rhythm games Music and light sensory room time Choreographed light show participation Alternative Stimulation: Color-changing room lights with music sync LED dance props Glow stick dancing Black light dance room Regulation Through OT/SI: Rhythmic movement activities Gross motor coordination through dance Sensory diet inclusion with time limits Cool-down activities post-dancing Massage Techniques: Full body cool-down massage Sports massage techniques for active muscles Stretching with massage combination Rhythmic compression massage Manifestation 4: Moving head rapidly to create after images
Redirect Activities: Controlled head tracking exercises Vestibular board activities (balance board) Head movement games with purpose (find hidden objects) Neck strengthening activities Alternative Stimulation: Optical illusion cards and images Afterimage creation with high-contrast images Spinning top observation Strobe light viewers (controlled) Regulation Through OT/SI: Neck strengthening exercises Vestibular integration activities Postural awareness training Safe head movement boundaries Massage Techniques: Neck massage with caution (gentle only) Shoulder and upper trap massage Scalp massage for relaxation Suboccipital release (by trained therapist) Manifestation 5: Positioning body to catch/block sunbeams Redirect Activities: Sunbeam tracking and documentation Shadow measurement activities Sundial creation and use Light position science experiments Alternative Stimulation: Spotlight following games Beam blocker activities with materials Light and shadow theatre Body position photography in light
Regulation Through OT/SI: Body awareness activities Proprioceptive mapping exercises Gross motor positioning games Yoga poses in light/shadow Massage Techniques: Full body positional awareness massage Joint compression sequence Body segment massage (awareness) Postural alignment work Manifestation 6: Twirling near lamps to see rotating shadows Redirect Activities: Structured twirling with supervision Rotating shadow projection activities Spinning while holding light sources Controlled rotation on equipment Alternative Stimulation: Rotating disco ball observation Spinning light projectors Rotating color wheels Spinning fiber optic lights Regulation Through OT/SI: Vestibular activities with boundaries Heavy work before twirling Dizzy protocol (stop when dizzy, recovery time) Grounding activities post-spinning Massage Techniques: Vestibular calming massage (feet, legs) Deep pressure to counteract dizziness Grounding massage techniques Calming back and shoulder work
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 1. VISUAL STIMMING INTERVENTIONS > B. Object Visual Stimming > Level 1: Object Fixation
Causation: Over-stimulated: Predictable, repetitive visual input calms nervous system Under-stimulated: Mesmerizing motion provides needed visual stimulation Sensitivity: Pattern recognition and prediction provides cognitive comfort Sensory Profile: Seeker: Seeks out rotating objects actively; may create if unavailable Avoider: Uses as escape from complex visual environment Description: Extended visual attention to specific objects or patterns Manifestation 1: Staring at Spinning Washing Machine/Dryer (10-60+ minutes) Physical Redirection Technique: "Pre-Emptive Redirect" Method (Best to prevent fixation from starting) BEFORE laundry starts: Engage child in different room with preferred activity If already fixated: Approach from side, say name 2-3 times Hold interesting moving toy at child's eye level (between child and machine) Shake toy, make noise with it When eyes track toy, praise: "Good looking!" Say: "Let's go watch this instead"
Lead to different room while maintaining toy engagement Stay with toy activity for 5+ minutes If resistance: Set visual timer where child can see: "2 more minutes watching, then we play" Honor timer (builds trust), then guide away DIY Alternative Tool: Spin Drum Viewer Materials: Large clear plastic jar (pretzel or peanut container), lazy Susan or DIY rotating base, colorful objects (pom poms, beads, small toys) Cost: $3-5 How to Make: Use large clear container with lid Attach to lazy Susan base (or create rotating base from cardboard circle with pencil through center as axle) Fill container with colorful, moving objects: pom poms, beads, small lightweight toys, marbles Seal lid securely Child spins base, watches objects tumble inside Similar visual to washing machine but child controls it Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Replicates tumbling motion of washing machine, child has complete control, portable
Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Salad Spinner Visual Station Cost: $5-8 (salad spinner from kitchen store) Materials: Salad spinner, colorful items to spin (pom poms, beads, cut pieces of colored sponge, glitter in water) How to Use: Place colorful items in salad spinner Option 1: Dry items (pom poms, beads) - watch them whirl Option 2: Items in water with food coloring - intense color mixing Child pumps spinner handle (provides proprioceptive input) Watches items spin rapidly Can vary speed (slow pumps vs fast pumps) Take out items, rearrange, spin again Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Child controls speed and duration, tactile + visual input, cause-effect learning Box Fan with Ribbon Streamers Cost: $3-5 (ribbons) + box fan if don't have
Materials: Box fan, colorful ribbons or crepe paper streamers, tape Safety: Attach ribbons VERY securely to front grill of fan (not near blades), adult supervision required How to Use: Attach multiple colored ribbons to front of box fan Or hang ribbons near fan (not attached) where fan blows them Turn on fan (start low speed) Ribbons whip and move constantly Child watches movement Can try different speeds Can add more/fewer ribbons Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Constant movement similar to washing machine, auditory component, multiple colors DIY Bike Wheel Spinner Cost: $0-10 (old bike wheel or create cardboard version) Materials: Bike wheel or large cardboard wheel, axle (stick/dowel), colorful items attached to spokes (clothespins with colored paper, ribbons, cards) How to Make:
Mount bike wheel so it can spin freely (between two chairs, or create stand) Attach colorful items to spokes with clothespins Child spins wheel, watches colors blur How to Use: Outdoor activity works best Child spins wheel as fast or slow as desired Watches colors blur together Can add different items to change effect Very engaging Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Large-scale, outdoor activity, child controls completely Rock Tumbler Observation Cost: $20-40 (rock tumbler) Materials: Rock tumbler, rocks, water How to Use: Set up rock tumbler with rocks and water Motor runs, tumbles rocks (can watch through viewing window on some models) Similar sound and motion to washing machine Educational component (learning about rocks) Can check progress over days/weeks Duration: Brief observation sessions (5-10 min), ongoing project
Why it works: Similar sensory input, educational, creates anticipation Cement Mixer Toy Cost: $15-30 (toy cement mixer) Materials: Toy cement mixer truck with rotating drum, small objects to "mix" How to Use: Child cranks handle to make drum rotate Put small objects inside (beads, small toys) Watch/hear them tumble Similar to washing machine but child-controlled Can incorporate into play scenarios Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Replicates washing machine motion, child controls it, adds pretend play element Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Slow Rotation Spinner Cost: $5-8 (lazy Susan) Materials: Lazy Susan, single toy placed on it How to Use: Place one toy on lazy Susan Child spins SLOWLY by hand Controls speed completely Predictable, contained Can stop anytime Same toy can be used repeatedly
Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Child controls all variables, slow pace is calming, predictable Water Wheel in Bath Cost: $6-10 (bath water wheel toy) Materials: Water wheel toy, bathtub How to Use: Gentle water flow makes wheel spin slowly Calming, predictable rotation Bath time is already calming routine Can control water flow (speed) Quiet, gentle activity Duration: 10 minutes during bath time Why it works: Gentle, predictable, integrated into calming routine Snow Globe Observation Cost: $5-10 Materials: Snow globe (gentle, calming design) How to Use: Child shakes snow globe Watches particles settle slowly Calming, predictable motion Can be repeated Contained, portable Duration: 5 minutes as needed Why it works: Gentle movement, predictable, calming, contained Single Spinning Top Cost: $3-5 Materials: One simple spinning top
How to Use: Child spins top Watches it spin and slow down Predictable beginning and end Can master the skill Simple, not overwhelming Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Child controls completely, predictable pattern, simple Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Alternative Spinning Schedule: Provide variety of spinning/rotating activities throughout day: Morning: 5 minutes salad spinner play Midday: 5 minutes fan ribbon watching Afternoon: 5 minutes bike wheel spinner Evening: 5 minutes DIY spin drum Prevents fixation on washing machine specifically Each provides slightly different sensory input Controlled duration with timers Laundry Helper Jobs: Make washing machine time functional: Child helps load clothes (proprioceptive input from carrying) Can watch machine start (2 minutes) Then: transition to sorting clean laundry by color (continues engagement)
Folding washcloths (fine motor + proprioceptive) Turns fixation into functional participation 10-15 minutes total Physical Spinning Activities: Before/instead of washing machine watching: 10 log rolls across floor (provides vestibular input similar to watching spin) Spinning on office chair (5 rotations, adult controls) Then: watch spinning alternative (salad spinner) for 5 minutes Satisfies vestibular component of washing machine interest 15 minutes total Heavy Work Between Fixation: If child does watch washing machine briefly: 2 minutes watching 2 minutes heavy work (carrying, pushing) 2 minutes watching 2 minutes heavy work Prevents prolonged fixation Organizes nervous system For AVOIDERS: Predictable Laundry Routine: Establish what happens during laundry: Week 1: Child helps load washer BEFORE starting (functional task) Week 2: Can watch through window for 1 minute after loading
Week 3: Increase to 2 minutes if comfortable Week 4: Child can choose: watch 2 minutes OR go play elsewhere Builds sense of control and predictability Distance Graduated Exposure: If washing machine is overwhelming: Week 1: Watch from across room (15+ feet), 30 seconds Week 2: Move 3 feet closer, 1 minute Week 3: Move 3 feet closer, 1-2 minutes Continue gradual approach Child can always move back if uncomfortable Builds tolerance slowly Sound Management: Washing machine sound can be overwhelming: Offer headphones or earplugs Play calming music in room Close laundry room door Do laundry when child is engaged elsewhere Reduces auditory overwhelm Warning System: Always warn before starting washing machine: "In 5 minutes, I'll start the washing machine" "In 2 minutes..."
"Starting now" Reduces anxiety from unexpected sounds/movement Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Vestibular Grounding Massage: Watching spinning creates vestibular stimulation: Firm pressure on temples (gentle circles) - vestibular input Firm pressure at base of skull (where vestibular system processes) Massage neck (sides only) Provides organizing input to vestibular areas Duration: 3-5 minutes Frequency: When fixation on spinning begins or after watching spinning Why it works: Provides input to vestibular system without visual component, may satisfy some of the need driving washing machine fixation Full Body Proprioceptive Massage: After washing machine watching: Firm squeezing massage on all limbs Joint compressions (shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles) Helps reorganize after vestibular input from watching spin Duration: 7-10 minutes Very regulating For AVOIDERS: Predictable Rhythm Massage:
If child overwhelmed by washing machine: Pat shoulders in steady rhythm (like gentle drumbeat) Count: "1-2-3-4, 1-2-3-4" Very predictable pattern Can do while washing machine runs (competing sensory input) Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Predictable rhythm helps when visual/auditory environment feels chaotic Calming Back Massage: After washing machine exposure: Child lies on stomach Slow, deep pressure strokes on back Top to bottom only (organizing direction) Count to 10 per stroke Pair with deep breathing Duration: 7-10 minutes Very calming after overwhelming sensory experience Manifestation 2: Watching Fans or Ceiling Fans Rotate Physical Redirection Technique: "Engage and Reposition" Method Bring engaging toy/activity TO child (don't expect them to leave fan viewing) Play with toy yourself next to child, making sounds/commentary Position toy between child's face and fan view (blocking sightline)
When child looks at toy (even briefly), praise: "You're looking!" Hand toy to child immediately Physically guide them to different room or position facing away from fan If they try to reposition to see fan: "Fan time is over. Let's play with this." Offer choice between 2 activities (gives control): "Blocks or cars?" Stay engaged with chosen activity 5+ minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Hand-Held Pinwheel Station Materials: 3-5 pinwheels (buy or make from paper), foam block or pot of sand, small battery fan (optional), window Cost: $2-5 How to Make/Use: Purchase pinwheels or make from paper and straight pins on pencils Stick pinwheels in foam block so they stand upright Position near open window (wind spins them) OR use small battery fan
Child watches pinwheels spin Can blow on them (adds breath work - calming and organizing) Portable - can move to different locations Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Child-level, controllable spinning, can blow for control, portable Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Multi-Speed Fan with Attachments Cost: $8-15 (box fan if don't have) + $2-3 (ribbons) Materials: Box fan with 3 speeds, colorful ribbons/streamers, tape Safety: Secure ribbons to FRONT grill only, never near blades How to Use: Attach multiple colored ribbons to front of fan Child controls speed dial (low, medium, high) Watches different effects at different speeds Incorporate movement: child does jumping jacks in front of fan (feels wind + sees movement) Can remove/add ribbons to change visual Experiment with different materials: fabric strips, tissue paper
Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Child controls variables, multiple speeds = variety, adds movement option Toy Helicopter Launch Cost: $5-10 (pull-string helicopters) Materials: Multiple pull-string or launcher helicopters How to Use: Child launches helicopter Watches spinning blades as it flies Chase and retrieve (adds movement) Launch again Can have races with multiple helicopters Time how long they stay airborne Outdoor activity best Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Active participation, outdoor play, gross motor involvement, controlled spinning observation Spinning Toy Collection Station Cost: $10-20 total Materials: Variety of spinning toys: tops, dreidels, fidget spinners, gyroscopes, yo-yos How to Use: Set up spinning station with multiple options Child spins multiple toys simultaneously Compare: which spins longest? fastest? smoothest? Create patterns with spinning toys
Time trials Controlled, interactive spinning Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Variety prevents fixation on one source, child actively engages rather than passive watching, adds cognitive element Wind Spinner Garden Cost: $10-20 Materials: Multiple wind spinners/whirligigs, outdoor space How to Use: Place wind spinners in yard/garden at different heights Different designs spin at different rates Child can check on them throughout day Can predict: "Will it spin today? Is it windy enough?" Combines nature observation with spinning interest Outdoor time Duration: Brief observation periods throughout day (5 min each) Why it works: Outdoor activity, breaks up indoor fan fixation, adds weather/science learning Paper Plate Spinner Craft Cost: $3-5 Materials: Paper plates, markers/crayons, string, pencil How to Make Together: Decorate paper plate with spiral design or colors
Punch holes near edge Thread string through holes Pull string to make plate spin Creates optical illusion when spinning How to Use: Child pulls string to make own spinner Watches pattern blur Active participation in creating and using Duration: 30 minutes craft + 15 minutes play Why it works: Creative + functional, child creates tool for spinning observation Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single Slow Pinwheel Cost: $1-2 Materials: One pinwheel, quiet space How to Use: Child controls pinwheel completely Can blow on it gently (slow, controlled spin) Or hold in breeze Very gentle, predictable spinning No overwhelming speed or complexity Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Completely controllable, gentle, predictable, simple Slow-Motion Fan Observation Cost: $0 (existing fan) Materials: Fan on LOWEST speed setting only
How to Use: Fan on slowest setting Designated "fan watching time": 5 minutes before bed (routine) Same time daily (predictable) Can be part of calming bedtime routine Time limit enforced Duration: 5 minutes maximum Why it works: Predictable, slow pace is calming, integrated into routine Picture of Fan Cost: $0-2 Materials: Photo/drawing of fan, laminated How to Use: If actual fan too overwhelming Child can look at picture of fan Addresses interest without sensory overload Can carry picture Look when needed Duration: Brief viewing as needed Why it works: Static image, no movement, completely controllable Controlled Fan Schedule Cost: $0 Materials: Existing fan, visual timer, schedule How to Use: Specific fan watching time scheduled daily "After breakfast: 3 minutes fan time"
Visual timer shows remaining time When timer ends, fan time ends Extreme predictability Duration: 3-5 minutes Why it works: Allows interest but in controlled, predictable way Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Rotation Variety Protocol: Provide 5 different spinning activities throughout day: Morning: Spin tops competition (5 min) Midday: Pinwheel blowing (5 min) Afternoon: Salad spinner play (10 min) Late afternoon: Brief fan watching (5 min, controlled) Evening: Wind spinner check (outdoor, 5 min) Variety reduces fixation on ceiling fan specifically Each provides different type of spinning input Spin and Move Integration: Can't just watch fan passively - must incorporate movement: Watch fan for 2 minutes Do 10 jumping jacks Watch fan 2 minutes Do 10 jumping jacks Repeat 3-5 times
Movement breaks prevent prolonged fixation Adds organizing proprioceptive input 15-20 minutes total Heavy Work Alternatives: Before allowing fan watching: Wall push-ups: 10 reps Carry laundry basket: 3 trips Push against heavy door: 10 seconds x 5 Then: 5 minutes controlled fan watching Organizes nervous system first For AVOIDERS: Gradual Fan Exposure Protocol: Very slow introduction: Week 1: Fan off, child just looks at it stationary (3 min daily) Week 2: Fan on lowest speed, 30 seconds only Week 3: Increase to 1 minute Week 4: Increase to 2 minutes Week 5: Try medium speed 30 seconds (if tolerating low speed) Extremely gradual Child can always say "stop" Distance Control: Child controls proximity to fan: Start across room (15+ feet) Can move closer when ready
Can always move back No pressure to get close Builds sense of control and safety Fan Control Options: If possible, give child control: Remote control for fan Access to switch They decide on/off Builds confidence and reduces anxiety 5 minutes daily practice Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Head and Neck Organizing Massage: Watching overhead fans creates neck tension: Gentle pressure on temples (small circles) Gentle pressure at base of skull (vestibular input) Massage neck muscles (sides, gentle but firm) Gentle head rotations (child directs) Duration: 5 minutes Frequency: When child fixates on fan or after fan watching Why it works: Addresses tension from looking up, organizes visual/vestibular systems, may reduce seeking Shoulder Release: Looking up creates shoulder tension too: Massage shoulders with firm pressure
Gentle shoulder rolls (child does with guidance) Squeeze shoulder muscles 3-5 minutes Releases physical tension from fan watching For AVOIDERS: Shoulder Grounding: If fan is overwhelming: Both hands on child's shoulders Firm, steady pressure Gentle squeeze-and-release rhythm Count: "Squeeze 1-2-3, release 1-2-3" Duration: 5 minutes Frequency: Before fan exposure or when overwhelmed Why it works: Grounding input helps nervous system feel safe and organized Back Support: After fan exposure: Slow, deep pressure on back Top to bottom strokes Very calming Pair with deep breathing 7-10 minutes Helps recover from visual/auditory stimulation Manifestation 3: Gazing at Wheels Spinning on Toys Physical Redirection Technique: "Wheel Redirect" Method Don't remove toy abruptly (causes distress) Sit next to child at eye level Acknowledge: "You're watching the wheels spin"
After 10-15 seconds, offer related activity: "Let's race this car" Demonstrate racing car across floor If child continues spinning wheels: join them briefly Then: "Let's make the wheels go somewhere" - create ramp or road Encourage functional play: "Can the car go to the garage?" If persistent fixation: set timer "3 more minutes of spinning, then we race" Honor timer, redirect to functional wheel use DIY Alternative Tool: Wheel Observation Station Materials: Old toy cars (2-3), clear plastic box or container, lazy Susan or rotating base Cost: Under $3 How to Make: Mount toy cars upside down on rotating base (hot glue) Or place cars in clear box where wheels can spin freely Child can spin base to make all wheels spin at once
Or spin individual car wheels Controlled wheel-watching environment Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Designated place for wheel watching, contained, can be time-limited Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Wheel Spin Race Cost: $0-5 (using existing toy cars) Materials: Multiple toy cars with smooth-spinning wheels, timer How to Use: Line up cars on table edge Spin each car's wheels as hard as possible Time which wheels spin longest Record results Try different surfaces (table, floor, carpet) Scientific approach to wheel-spinning Adds cognitive element Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Structured activity, adds purpose, still satisfies wheel-watching need Gear and Wheel Building Set Cost: $15-25 Materials: Gear building toy set (interlocking gears and wheels) How to Use: Build elaborate gear systems Turn one gear, watch all connected gears/wheels spin
Create different configurations Problem-solve: how to make certain gear spin faster/slower Combines construction with wheel-watching Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Active construction, problem-solving, cause-effect learning, satisfies wheel interest Bicycle Wheel Observation (Real) Cost: $0 (child's bike) or $5-10 (used bike wheel) Materials: Bicycle, bike repair stand (or flip bike upside down), decorations (ribbon, cards) Safety: Adult supervision, ensure bike stable How to Use: Flip bike upside down or use repair stand Child spins pedals, watches wheel rotate Can attach cards/ribbons to spokes (makes noise, visual interest) Learn about how bikes work Outdoor activity Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Real-world connection, large-scale, educational, outdoor time Marble Run with Wheels Cost: $20-30 Materials: Marble run set with wheel/spinner elements How to Use:
Build marble run tracks Include wheel/spinner elements that activate when marble passes Watch wheels spin as marbles go by Combine construction, problem-solving, and wheel-watching Can time marble runs Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Active play, construction element, wheels spin with purpose (marble activates them) Water Wheel Play Cost: $8-15 (water wheel toy) Materials: Water wheel toy, bathtub or water table How to Use: Pour water over water wheel Watch wheel spin from water flow Experiment: fast pour vs slow pour Multiple water wheels in series Bath time or outdoor water play Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Combines water play with wheel watching, cause-effect, sensory input Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single Wheel Toy Cost: $0-3 Materials: One toy car with smooth wheels
How to Use: Child has access to one car only (not overwhelming) Can spin wheels in controlled, predictable way Same car daily (familiarity) Designated spot for wheel play Time-limited (5-10 minutes) Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Simple, predictable, not overwhelming, controlled Wheel Picture Book Cost: $5-10 Materials: Picture book about wheels, trucks, cars How to Use: Read together Look at wheel pictures No actual spinning (less stimulating) Same book repeatedly (predictable) Calm, quiet activity Duration: 10 minutes Why it works: Addresses interest without sensory stimulation, calming One Fidget Spinner Cost: $3-5 Materials: Single fidget spinner (smooth, quiet) How to Use: Contained wheel-like spinning Child controls completely Portable, can use when needed Not overwhelming Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Simple, controllable, portable, quiet
Controlled Wheel Time Cost: $0 Materials: Toy car from existing toys, timer How to Use: Scheduled "wheel time" daily 5 minutes after breakfast Visual timer shows remaining time Same car, same time, same place daily Predictable routine Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Allows behavior in controlled way, very predictable Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Functional Wheel Play: Redirect wheel-spinning to functional play: Race cars down ramps (wheels spin with purpose) Create parking garage (drive cars, park them) Build roads with tape, drive cars on roads Wash cars (wheels spin during "washing") Makes wheel interest part of functional play 20-30 minutes Wheel Observation Schedule: Designate specific times for wheel watching: Morning: 5 minutes wheel spin experiments Afternoon: 10 minutes marble run with wheel elements
Evening: 5 minutes controlled wheel watching Prevents all-day seeking Provides outlet at predictable times Heavy Work Between Wheel Watching: After wheel watching sessions: Push car up ramp (heavy work for hands) Carry toy bin across room Wall push-ups 5 minutes heavy work Organizes nervous system For AVOIDERS: Gradual Wheel Introduction: Week 1: Look at pictures of wheels (books, photos) Week 2: Touch stationary wheel (not spinning) Week 3: Parent spins wheel slowly while child watches from distance Week 4: Child touches wheel while parent spins slowly Week 5: Child spins wheel themselves (if comfortable) Very gradual, child-paced Predictable Wheel Routine: Same toy, same time, same place "After lunch: 5 minutes wheel play" Extreme predictability Child knows exactly what to expect Choice and Control:
