Child chooses: Which car to use How long to play (within limits) Where to play Builds sense of control and safety Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Hand and Finger Massage: Wheel-spinning uses hands/fingers intensively: Firm massage of palms Squeeze each finger individually Press on finger joints Rotate wrists gently Duration: 5 minutes per hand Frequency: Before and after wheel play Why it works: Addresses hands that seek tactile input through wheel-spinning, may reduce compulsive wheel-spinning Bilateral Hand Work: Work both hands simultaneously Squeeze both hands at once Bilateral movements Creates integration 5 minutes Very organizing For AVOIDERS: Gentle Hand Preparation: Before wheel play: Gently hold child's hands Warm hands by rubbing together Gentle palm massage Very gentle, predictable Duration: 3-5 minutes Why it works: Prepares hands for tactile experience, reduces anxiety
Hand Wrapping: Wrap child's hand in soft cloth Gentle pressure Hold for count of 10 Very calming and organizing 3 minutes per hand Manifestation 4: Observing Water Swirling Down Drain Physical Redirection Technique: "Water Redirect" Method Don't force child away from drain immediately Acknowledge: "You're watching the water go down" Set brief time limit: "You can watch one more time, then we do something else" Let water drain once more Before refilling sink/tub: "That was the last one. Now we're going to..." Offer water-related alternative immediately: "Let's make bubbles/play with water toys" If refilling water: block drain view with washcloth or bath mat Engage with alternative water play Stay engaged 5+ minutes to ensure transition DIY Alternative Tool: Vortex Bottle Materials: Two plastic bottles, tornado tube connector (or duct tape), water, glitter, food coloring Cost: $2-5 How to Make:
Fill one bottle 2/3 with water Add glitter and food coloring Connect two bottles at openings (tornado tube connector or tape securely) Flip so full bottle is on top Swirl in circles - creates vortex as water drains to bottom bottle Child controls vortex creation Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Portable drain/vortex simulation, child controls it completely, can use repeatedly Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Tornado Tube Science Experiment Cost: $5-8 (tornado tube connectors) Materials: 2-liter bottles, tornado tube connectors, water, various additions (glitter, beads, food coloring, oil) How to Use: Create multiple tornado bottles with different contents Bottle 1: Water + glitter Bottle 2: Water + oil + food coloring Bottle 3: Water + small beads Child swirls each, watches different vortex effects
Compare: which makes best vortex? Time how long each takes to drain Science + satisfies drain-watching interest Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Educational, multiple versions provide variety, child-controlled Water Table Drain Play Cost: $30-50 (water table) or DIY with $5 (large container) Materials: Water table or large container, drain plug, funnels, tubes How to Use: Fill water table Add funnels, tubes that drain Child pours water through funnels, watches it drain/swirl Pull drain plug, watch all water drain Can add food coloring, bubbles Outdoor activity Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Large-scale, outdoor, supervised water play, multiple drain-watching opportunities Bathroom Sink Science Station Cost: $0-5 (household items) Materials: Bathroom sink, various objects to test (corks, toy boats, sponges, small toys)
Safety: Adult supervision, establish rules (limited time, specific objects only) How to Use: Fill sink partially Add objects Pull plug, watch objects move as water drains Experiment: which objects get pulled toward drain? Which float away? Designated "science time" with structured endpoint Becomes educational activity Duration: 15-20 minutes (time-limited) Why it works: Makes drain interest educational, structured activity with beginning and end Funnel and Tube Waterfall Cost: $5-10 Materials: Funnels, clear plastic tubing, food coloring, water How to Use: Set up funnel system where water flows through tubes Child pours water into top funnel Watches it drain through tubes, creating visible flow Add food coloring for better visibility Can create elaborate systems Bathtub or outdoor activity Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Child controls water flow, can see entire path, cause-effect learning
Whirlpool Creation in Bucket Cost: $2-5 (bucket, spoon/stick) Materials: Large bucket, water, long spoon or stick, glitter How to Use: Fill bucket with water Add glitter or food coloring Child stirs rapidly in circular motion Creates whirlpool/vortex in bucket Watch it slow and stop Create again Child controls vortex creation Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Active creation of swirling water, immediate cause-effect, child-controlled Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Still Water Observation Cost: $0 Materials: Clear container, still water How to Use: Fill container with water Water stays still (no draining) Child can look when desired Very calm, predictable No movement (less stimulating) Duration: 5 minutes as needed Why it works: Water interest without swirling/draining stimulation One Vortex Bottle (Slow) Cost: $2-3
Materials: One tornado bottle, made with thicker liquid (add corn syrup to slow drain) How to Use: Single bottle with SLOW vortex Child controls when to flip Very slow, calm movement Predictable every time Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Slow pace, predictable, child-controlled Water Picture Book Cost: $5-10 Materials: Book about water cycle, drains, plumbing How to Use: Read together Look at pictures of water No actual water/draining Calm, quiet Educational Duration: 10 minutes Why it works: Addresses interest without sensory stimulation Controlled Drain Time Cost: $0 Materials: Sink or tub, timer How to Use: Scheduled "drain watching time" Once daily, 3 minutes maximum Fill sink, child watches it drain once Timer marks end of activity Very predictable routine Duration: 3 minutes
Why it works: Allows behavior in extremely controlled way Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Water Play Schedule: Designate times for supervised water play: Morning: 15 minutes water table play Afternoon: 10 minutes tornado bottle experiments Bath time: 5 minutes controlled drain watching Provides water/drain input at specific times Reduces seeking at inconvenient times Water Play Transitions: After drain watching, immediate transition to: Heavy work: wring out wet towels (heavy proprioceptive) Dry hands vigorously with towel (tactile input) Carry water bucket outside (if appropriate) 5 minutes heavy work after water play Helps organize nervous system Functional Water Activities: Channel drain interest into helpful tasks: Help wash dishes (water draining is functional) Water plants (pouring, watching water absorb) Help with laundry (watch washing machine drain - controlled setting)
Makes water interest purposeful For AVOIDERS: Gradual Water Introduction: Week 1: Look at picture of water draining Week 2: Watch parent fill/drain sink from distance (10 feet) Week 3: Move closer (5 feet), watch brief drain Week 4: Touch still water (no draining yet) Week 5: Watch drain from close distance (if comfortable) Extremely gradual Predictable Bath/Sink Routine: Establish what happens with water: Bath: water drains AFTER child out of tub (less overwhelming) Sink: child washes hands, leaves before drain opens Warning system: "In 2 minutes, water will drain" Predictability reduces anxiety Sound Management: Drain sound can be overwhelming: Leave room before draining Play music during drain time Use sink strainer (quieter draining) Reduces auditory component Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Vestibular Calming Massage:
Watching swirling water stimulates vestibular system: Gentle pressure on temples Pressure at base of skull Massage neck (sides only) Duration: 3-5 minutes Frequency: After drain watching Why it works: Calms vestibular stimulation from watching swirling motion Hand Massage After Water Play: Hands get wet during water play: Firm hand massage while drying Squeeze each finger Massage palms Organizing tactile input 3-5 minutes Helps transition from water play For AVOIDERS: Grounding After Water Exposure: If water/drains overwhelming: Firm pressure on feet (grounding) Firm pressure on shoulders Wrap in towel (deep pressure + warmth) Duration: 5-7 minutes Why it works: Helps child feel "anchored" after potentially overwhelming water experience Warmth and Pressure: Wrap child in warm towel after any water exposure Firm pressure through towel
Hold for 3-5 minutes Very comforting and organizing Manifestation 5: Fixating on Clocks or Timers Physical Redirection Technique: "Time Transfer" Method Don't cover or remove clock abruptly (causes anxiety) Approach and sit beside child at eye level Acknowledge: "You're watching the time" After 30 seconds, introduce alternative: "Let's use this timer for a game" Hand child visual timer or sand timer Demonstrate activity: "Let's see how many blocks we can stack before timer ends" Engage in timer-based activity together Gradually shift focus from clock to activity If persistent: "Clock watching time is over. Let's play with this timer instead" Remove from clock viewing area, engage with timer activity elsewhere DIY Alternative Tool: Personal Timer Collection Materials: Various timers (sand timer, visual timer, digital timer), container to store them Cost: $10-15 total How to Make/Assemble:
Collect 3-4 different types of timers Sand timer (3-5 minutes) - watch sand fall Visual timer (Time Timer style) - see red diminish Digital timer - see numbers count down Liquid motion timer - watch bubbles/liquid move Store in special box Child has designated "timer collection" to explore Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Provides controlled time-watching, child owns the timers, portable, variety prevents fixation on wall clock Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Timer Challenge Games Cost: $8-12 (visual timer) Materials: Visual timer, various activities How to Use: Set challenges: "How many jumping jacks in 1 minute?" "Build tallest tower before timer ends" "Find all red toys before beep" "Clean up race - beat the timer!" Makes time-watching functional and purposeful Child actively engaged, not passive watching
Competitive element adds excitement Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Combines time interest with active tasks, purposeful timer use, engaging Multiple Timer Station Cost: $15-25 (collection of timers) Materials: 5-6 different timers (sand, liquid motion, visual, digital, mechanical wind-up) How to Use: Set all timers simultaneously Watch different mechanisms: sand falling, liquid moving, numbers changing Compare: which finishes first? last? Line them up by speed Experiment with different time settings Science observation approach Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Variety prevents fixation, educational, child controls all timers Stopwatch Activities Cost: $5-10 (stopwatch) or use phone app Materials: Stopwatch, various activities to time How to Use: Child becomes "official timer" Time parent doing tasks: "How long to tie shoes?" Time self: "Can I beat my record for getting dressed?"
Time everyday events: "How long is dinner?" Keep log/chart of times Makes time-watching functional role Duration: Brief sessions throughout day (2-3 min each) Why it works: Gives child job/role, functional use of time interest, engaging Clock Building Activity Cost: $10-20 (clock kit) Materials: Build-your-own clock kit or craft supplies How to Use: Build functioning clock together Learn how clock mechanisms work Decorate clock face Child keeps finished clock in room Educational about time concepts Duration: 45-60 minutes project Why it works: Hands-on learning, creates understanding, functional end product Time-Lapse Observation Projects Cost: $0-5 (if have camera/phone) Materials: Camera or phone, tripod or stable surface, subjects that change over time How to Use: Set up camera to photograph same subject repeatedly Ice cube melting (take photo every 5 minutes)
Plant growing (photo daily) Shadow moving (photo every hour) Create time-lapse video Visual representation of time passing Duration: Setup 10 minutes, ongoing observation over hours/days Why it works: Makes time visible, scientific observation, engaging project Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Personal Sand Timer Cost: $3-5 Materials: One small sand timer (3 minutes) How to Use: Child's personal timer Can flip and watch when needed Predictable (always same duration) Portable (carry in pocket) Calming to watch sand fall Duration: 3-5 minutes as needed Why it works: Completely predictable, portable, calming, child-controlled Digital Clock in Room Cost: $10-15 Materials: Simple digital clock for child's room How to Use: Child has own clock to check Teaches time awareness Available when needed No fixation on kitchen/wall clocks
Part of room setup Duration: Brief checks as needed Why it works: Provides access to time info without fixation, child's own clock Time Picture Schedule Cost: $2-5 (printed pictures, clock images) Materials: Visual schedule with clock times shown How to Use: Picture schedule shows daily routine with clock times Child can look at schedule to see "what time" activities happen Satisfies time interest functionally Reduces anxiety about time Duration: Brief checks throughout day Why it works: Functional time use, reduces anxiety, predictable Controlled Clock Time Cost: $0 Materials: Existing clock, specific routine How to Use: Scheduled "clock checking time" "After breakfast, we check the clock together" Parent and child look at clock, discuss time Brief (1-2 minutes) Predictable routine Duration: 1-2 minutes daily
Why it works: Allows behavior in controlled, predictable way Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Functional Time Use: Make clock interest functional: "It's 3:00 - snack time! Let's check the clock" "In 5 minutes it will be 4:00 - time to clean up" Use clock/timer for transitions Teach time concepts functionally Integrates interest into daily life meaningfully Timer-Based Schedule: Use timers throughout day for structure: Morning: 10 minutes timer for getting dressed Homework: 15 minutes timer for focused work Play: 20 minutes timer for outdoor time Bed routine: 5 minutes timer for brushing teeth Child can watch timers - it's functional Satisfies time-watching need purposefully Time Experiments: Turn clock interest into learning: "How long does it take to...?" Estimate vs actual time experiments
Graph results Compare different activities 20-30 minutes structured learning Makes clock-watching educational For AVOIDERS: Predictable Time Routine: Establish when time is discussed: Check clock together at 3 specific times daily Morning: "Let's see what time we're leaving" Afternoon: "Let's check when dinner will be ready" Evening: "Let's see what time bedtime is" Predictable, anxiety-reducing Visual Schedule with Times: Show child what happens when: Pictures with clock times Child knows schedule Reduces anxiety about time Don't need to watch clock constantly Time Warnings: Help child understand time passing: "In 10 minutes, we'll leave" "5 minutes until bath time" "2 minutes left" Makes time predictable and less anxiety-inducing Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Focus and Attention Massage: Clock-watching often indicates need for regulation: Gentle pressure on temples (calming)
Massage forehead (smoothing outward from center) Gentle pressure on back of neck Helps regulate attention and focus Duration: 5 minutes Frequency: When clock fixation begins Why it works: May reduce compulsive checking behavior by providing organizing input Grounding Sequence: When fixation is strong: Firm pressure on shoulders Squeeze hands firmly Press on feet Full body grounding 5-7 minutes Helps child "come back" from fixation For AVOIDERS: Anxiety-Reducing Massage: Clock fixation often indicates time anxiety: Slow, rhythmic back massage Count each stroke: 1...2...3... Very predictable and calming Deep breathing together Duration: 7-10 minutes Frequency: When child seems anxious about time Why it works: Calms anxiety that may be driving clock-watching Calming Hold: Wrap child in hug or blanket Rock gently Rhythmic, predictable
5 minutes Very calming for time-related anxiety Manifestation 6: Watching Escalators or Elevators Move Physical Redirection Technique: "Movement Redirect" Method If in public place with escalator/elevator, acknowledge: "You like watching it move" Allow brief observation (1-2 minutes) - validate interest Set clear boundary: "We can watch two more people go up, then we continue shopping" Count together: "One...two...okay, time to go" Offer related movement activity: "Let's go find the stairs and walk up/down" Physical guidance away from escalator/elevator Engage immediately in alternative: "Can you help push the cart?" (movement input) If tantrum: remain calm, maintain boundary, physical redirection Later: process with child "I know you like watching it move. Next time we come, you can watch for 2 minutes again" DIY Alternative Tool: Marble Elevator Tower Materials: Cardboard, marbles, toilet paper tubes, tape, small cup or platform Cost: Under $5 How to Make:
Create vertical tower from cardboard Cut openings at different levels Insert toilet paper tube pieces as "elevator shafts" Create platform/cup that moves up and down (attached to string) Child pulls string to raise "elevator", releases to lower Drop marble down shaft - similar to elevator movement Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Replicates up/down movement, child controls it, portable Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Elevator Video Compilation Cost: $0 (YouTube/online videos) Materials: Device with internet, headphones How to Use: Find elevator/escalator compilation videos (many available) Designated viewing time: 10-15 minutes Can watch different types: glass elevators, escalators, unique designs Satisfies interest at home in controlled way Can discuss: "Which is your favorite?" Duration: 10-15 minutes controlled viewing Why it works: Provides access to interest without public fixation, time-limited, variety
Marble Run Elevator System Cost: $25-40 (elaborate marble run set) Materials: Marble run with elevator/lift components How to Use: Build marble run tracks Include elevator lift piece that brings marble back to top Turn crank or push lever to operate elevator Marble goes up (elevator) then down (run) Child controls entire system Can build different configurations Duration: 45-60 minutes Why it works: Combines construction, problem-solving, and elevator movement interest Pulley System Building Cost: $10-15 (pulleys, string, buckets) Materials: Simple pulley system, small buckets, objects to lift How to Use: Set up pulley between two points (tree branches, ceiling hook to floor) Attach bucket to rope Child pulls rope to raise bucket (like elevator) Release to lower Can lift toys, stuffed animals

Child pulls string to move platform up/down Load toys at different floors Can deliver messages between rooms Duration: 60 minutes building + ongoing play Why it works: Functional play, child creates and controls, can use repeatedly Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Elevator Button Board Cost: $5-8 (or DIY) Materials: Board with buttons (elevator style), lights/sounds optional How to Use: Child can press elevator-style buttons at home No actual movement (less overwhelming) Addresses button-pressing interest Controlled, predictable Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Addresses interest without overwhelming movement/sound Picture of Elevator/Escalator Cost: $0-2 (printed photo) Materials: Photo of elevator or escalator, laminated How to Use: Child can look at picture when interested No actual movement or sound Completely controllable Portable Duration: Brief viewing as needed

We can look for 1 minute, then we'll walk by" Rehearse at home Preparation reduces anxiety Duration: 5 minutes prep before outings Why it works: Predictability reduces overwhelm Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Stair/Ramp Use: When encountering escalator/elevator: Allow brief viewing (1-2 minutes)
Then: redirect to stairs "Let's use our bodies to go up/down" Provides vestibular + proprioceptive input Satisfies similar need through active participation Heavy Work Alternatives: Instead of passive escalator watching: Climb stairs with heavy backpack Carry grocery bags upstairs Push/pull activities Provides movement input that may underlie escalator interest Movement Schedule: Provide movement input throughout day: Morning: jump on trampoline Midday: climb playground equipment Afternoon: stairs up/down 5x Reduces seeking movement watching (escalator) For AVOIDERS: Gradual Exposure: Week 1: Look at picture of escalator/elevator Week 2: Watch video of escalator (can pause/control) Week 3: Visit location, observe from distance (20+ feet) Week 4: Move closer, brief viewing (1 minute) Week 5: Stand near escalator/elevator (if comfortable) Very gradual, child-paced Avoidance Strategies:
If too overwhelming: Plan routes that avoid escalators/elevators Use stairs instead Visit stores during off-peak (less movement) Headphones for sound management Reduces overwhelm Preparation and Warning: Before outing: "Today we might see an escalator" "If we see one, we'll walk by quickly" Visual schedule showing route Predictability reduces anxiety Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Vestibular Calming: After escalator watching (or instead of): Firm pressure on temples Pressure at base of skull Neck massage Calms vestibular stimulation from watching movement Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Organizes vestibular input from movement watching Proprioceptive Input: Provide alternative to movement watching: Firm squeezing on arms/legs Joint compressions Deep pressure massage 7-10 minutes May reduce need to watch movement For AVOIDERS: Grounding After Exposure: After encountering escalator/elevator:
Firm pressure on feet (grounding) Firm pressure on shoulders Slow, deep breathing together Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Helps recover from overwhelming movement/sound Full Body Calming: If very overwhelmed: Wrap in coat or blanket Firm pressure through wrap Sit quietly 5-10 minutes Very organizing after overwhelming experience Manifestation 7: Staring at Aquarium Fish Swimming Physical Redirection Technique: "Timed Viewing" Method Allow brief fish watching (validates interest) Set timer where child can see: "3 minutes of fish watching" Sit with child, observe together briefly At 2 minutes: "One more minute watching fish" When timer sounds: "Fish watching time is over" Offer related activity: "Let's draw/build/play with fish toys" Guide away from aquarium physically Engage with alternative activity Stay engaged 5+ minutes
Can return for another timed viewing later if appropriate DIY Alternative Tool: Fish in a Bottle Materials: Clear plastic bottle, water, blue food coloring, small plastic fish toys, glitter, oil, glycerin Cost: Under $5 How to Make: Fill bottle with water Add blue food coloring (ocean water) Add small plastic fish (2-3) Add glitter (sparkly like water) Add tablespoon of oil and glycerin (slows movement) Seal lid with hot glue Child tilts bottle, watches fish "swim" slowly through water Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Portable aquarium, child controls movement, can use repeatedly Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Aquarium Video with Activities Cost: $0 (YouTube aquarium videos) Materials: Device, aquarium video How to Use: Watch aquarium video (10-15 minutes controlled) While watching, do activities:
Count fish of each color Identify fish types Track one fish's movement Guess which direction fish will swim Adds cognitive element to watching Makes passive watching active Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Satisfies fish-watching interest, adds engagement, time-limited Pet Fish (Real Aquarium) Cost: $30-100 setup Materials: Small aquarium, fish, supplies How to Use: Child's own aquarium in bedroom Responsible for feeding, care Can watch during designated times Learn about fish care Makes interest purposeful and educational Duration: Brief viewing multiple times daily, care tasks daily Why it works: Functional, teaches responsibility, satisfies interest appropriately Fish Behavior Chart Cost: $2-5 (chart paper, markers) Materials: Clipboard, observation chart, pencil How to Use: Create scientific observation chart When viewing fish: note behaviors "Fish swam to left"
"Fish ate food" "Fish hid behind rock" Graph findings Makes fish-watching educational/scientific Duration: 15-20 minutes observation sessions Why it works: Purposeful watching, educational, structured Interactive Fish Toys Cost: $10-20 Materials: Swimming fish bath toys, electronic swimming fish How to Use: Bath time: add swimming fish toys Child watches them "swim" Can catch them (adds interaction) Electronic fish in water bowl - turn on/off, control Interactive rather than passive Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Child-controlled, interactive, adds tactile component Fish Craft Projects Cost: $5-10 (craft supplies) Materials: Paper, paints, colored paper, googly eyes, yarn How to Use: Create fish art after fish watching Make fish mobile to hang in room Paper bag fish puppets Channels fish interest into creativity Duration: 30-45 minutes
Why it works: Extends interest creatively, produces lasting product Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single Fish Picture Cost: $0-2 (printed image) Materials: Picture of fish, laminated How to Use: Child has picture to look at when desired No movement (less stimulating) Same picture every time (predictable) Portable Duration: Brief viewing as needed Why it works: No movement, predictable, controllable Fish Book Cost: $5-10 Materials: Picture book about fish How to Use: Read together in quiet space Look at fish pictures No actual movement Can read same book repeatedly Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Calm, predictable, no overwhelming movement One Toy Fish Cost: $3-5 Materials: Small stuffed or plastic fish How to Use: Child's personal fish toy Can hold, look at, carry
Comfort object Addresses interest without stimulation Duration: Available as needed Why it works: Portable comfort, no movement, child controls Controlled Aquarium Visit Cost: $0-15 (admission if zoo/aquarium) Materials: Social story, visual timer How to Use: If visiting aquarium: prepare extensively Social story about what will happen Plan specific fish to see (2-3 only) Timer for each viewing (2 minutes) Take breaks between tanks Plan escape route if overwhelmed Duration: Very brief, structured visit Why it works: Extreme structure and predictability Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Active Fish Engagement: Instead of passive watching: If own fish: feeding time (child feeds) Drawing fish while watching Mimicking fish movements with body Acting like fish (swimming movements) Adds active component Fish-Watching Schedule: Designate specific times:
Morning: 5 minutes fish watching After school: 5 minutes fish watching Before bed: 3 minutes fish watching Time-limited, scheduled Prevents all-day seeking Tracking Activities: Make watching purposeful: Pick one fish, track its path Draw map of where fish goes Count how many times fish surfaces Scientific observation 15-20 minutes structured For AVOIDERS: Distance Viewing: If aquarium overwhelming: Start 15-20 feet away Gradually move closer over weeks Child controls distance Builds tolerance slowly Limited Viewing: Brief exposures only: 1 minute viewing initially Gradually increase Always give warning before fish viewing Reduces overwhelm Preparation: Before aquarium visit: Look at pictures Watch short video Discuss what to expect Plan specific fish to see Preparation reduces anxiety Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Visual System Calming: After prolonged fish watching:
Gentle pressure on closed eyelids (very brief) Gentle circles on temples Pressure around eye area (avoid eyes) Forehead massage Duration: 3-5 minutes Why it works: Calms overactive visual system Full Body Organizing: After fish watching: Full body massage with firm pressure Joint compressions Helps transition from visual fixation 7-10 minutes For AVOIDERS: Calming Before/After: Before aquarium: Slow back massage Deep breathing Grounding pressure After aquarium: Same calming sequence Duration: 5-7 minutes each Why it works: Prepares nervous system for visual stimulation, helps recover after Safe Hold: If overwhelmed: Firm hug or wrap Rock gently Quiet reassurance 5 minutes as needed Manifestation 8: Observing Windshield Wipers During Rain Physical Redirection Technique: "Car Ride Management" Method In car during rain, acknowledge: "The wipers are moving"
Allow brief watching (1-2 minutes) Offer alternative focus: "Can you help me count red cars?" or "Let's listen to this song" If fixation continues: "Let's play I Spy" Engage actively - child must respond If severe fixation: pull over briefly, redirect attention fully before continuing Consider sitting child away from direct wiper view (middle seat if possible) Bring engaging toys/activities for car rides If regular issue: plan rainy day car activities in advance DIY Alternative Tool: Wiper Toy Board Materials: Cardboard, popsicle sticks or cardboard strips, brads (split pins), small toy car window outline Cost: Under $3 How to Make: Cut cardboard to look like car windshield Attach popsicle sticks as "wipers" using brads (they pivot) Child moves wipers back and forth
Can add blue cellophane for "rain" effect Portable for car rides Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Child controls wipers, portable, safe alternative Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Wiper Speed Game Cost: $0 (in actual car) Materials: Car windshield wipers Safety: Parent controls wipers while parked or safely pulled over How to Use: Make wiper observation educational Parked car: parent changes wiper speed Child identifies: "Slow! Medium! Fast!" Match rhythm: clap hands at wiper speed Count wiper swipes Makes passive watching interactive Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Educational, interactive, still satisfies interest Metronome Matching Cost: $10-15 (metronome) or free app Materials: Metronome or app How to Use: Wipers have rhythm - metronomes do too At home, use metronome Child watches pendulum swing back and forth (like wipers)
Change tempo (like wiper speeds) Can clap/move to beat Satisfies rhythmic movement interest Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Similar rhythmic back-forth motion Pendulum Play Cost: $2-5 (string, weight) Materials: String, weight (like a ball or rock), tape How to Use: Hang pendulum (doorway, tree branch) Child pushes, watches swing back and forth Similar motion to wipers Can try different weights/lengths Science experiment: which swings longest? Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Similar back-forth motion, child controls Fan Back-and-Forth Cost: $15-25 (oscillating fan) Materials: Oscillating fan (moves head side to side) How to Use: Turn on oscillating function Watch fan head move back and forth Similar motion to wipers Attach ribbons for more visual interest Can adjust speed Duration: 10-15 minutes
Why it works: Similar movement pattern, controllable Rhythmic Movement Activities Cost: $0-5 Materials: Music, various toys How to Use: Swinging on swing (back and forth like wipers) Rocking horse Metronome or music with steady beat Move body to rhythm Provides similar rhythmic, repetitive movement Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Satisfies underlying rhythmic movement need Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Wiper Picture Card Cost: $0-1 (print picture) Materials: Picture of windshield wipers How to Use: Static picture (no movement) Child can look when interested No actual movement to be overwhelmed by Portable Duration: Brief viewing as needed Why it works: Addresses interest without movement Car Ride Preparation Cost: $0 Materials: Social story, visual schedule How to Use: Before rainy car ride: prepare child
"We'll be in the car. The wipers will move. We'll look out the side window instead." Practice at home Reduces anxiety Duration: 5 minutes prep before drive Why it works: Predictability reduces overwhelm Alternative Seating Cost: $0 Materials: Car seat placement How to Use: Seat child where wipers less visible Middle seat, rear seat Provide engaging activities Reduces direct wiper exposure Duration: During car rides Why it works: Environmental modification Headphones and Audio Cost: $10-20 (child headphones) Materials: Headphones, favorite audiobook/music How to Use: During rainy car rides: headphones with engaging audio Diverts attention from wipers Reduces auditory component too Duration: During car rides Why it works: Competing sensory input diverts attention Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Car Ride Activities:
Plan engaging activities for rainy rides: I Spy games Counting games (red cars, trucks, etc.) Singing songs Audiobooks Fidget toys Engages attention elsewhere Wiper Time Limit: Allow brief wiper watching: "You can watch wipers for this song (3 minutes)" When song ends, redirect Timer or song marks end point Controlled viewing Movement Input: Before/after car ride: Heavy work activities Jumping, pushing, pulling May reduce wiper-seeking during ride 10 minutes before car ride For AVOIDERS: Minimize Exposure: Avoid driving in rain when possible If must drive: shortest route Park and wait for heavy rain to pass if child very distressed Child's comfort prioritized Preparation and Support: Before drive: Warn about wipers Offer comfort items Plan seating carefully During drive: Reassurance Distraction activities
Can pull over if too distressing Recovery Time: After rainy car ride: Quiet time Calming activities No rushing to next task 10-15 minutes minimum Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Rhythmic Massage: Wipers have rhythm - massage can too: Pat shoulders in steady rhythm Match massage rhythm to calm heartbeat (slower than wiper speed) Rhythmic pressure calms nervous system Duration: 5 minutes Frequency: Before/after car rides in rain Why it works: Provides rhythmic input in calming way Vestibular Calming: Wiper watching involves eye tracking: Gentle pressure on temples Pressure at base of skull Neck massage 5 minutes Calms visual tracking system For AVOIDERS: Pre-Ride Calming: Before rainy car ride: Slow, deep back massage Grounding pressure on shoulders/feet Deep breathing together Duration: 7-10 minutes
Why it works: Prepares nervous system for potentially overwhelming experience Post-Ride Recovery: After rainy car ride: Full body calming massage Wrap in blanket with pressure Quiet, calm environment 10-15 minutes Helps recover from stressful experience
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 1. VISUAL STIMMING INTERVENTIONS > B. Object Visual Stimming > Level 2: Object Manipulation
Causation: Over-stimulated: Creating order reduces environmental chaos Under-stimulated: Creating patterns provides visual and cognitive stimulation Sensitivity: Need for predictability and control Sensory Profile: Seeker: Large quantities, complex patterns, frequent changes Avoider: Simple, minimal arrangements; distress if disrupted Description: Handling objects to create visual effects Manifestation 1: Lining Up Toys in Precise Rows (50-200+ items) Physical Redirection Technique: "Respectful Interrupt" Method DO NOT disrupt the line (causes extreme distress and potential meltdown) Approach slowly and acknowledge child's work: "Wow, you made a really long line" Take photo of completed line: "Let's save your amazing line in a picture" Show child photo: "See? Your line is safe here" Say calmly: "Your line is saved in the picture. Now let's do [specific activity]" Offer choice for next activity: "Blocks or play-doh?"
If child wants line to stay: cover with sheet - "Your line will be here later, the sheet keeps it safe" If must clean up: involve child "Let's put each toy away together" (slower but respectful) Honor child's work even if seems unusual DIY Alternative Tool: Magnetic Lining Track Materials: Cookie sheet or metal board, magnetic tape, small toys or colored craft magnets, dry erase markers Cost: $5-8 How to Make: Use cookie sheet as base Stick magnetic tape to bottom of small toys Draw lines/grids on paper, place under cookie sheet (can see through) Child lines up magnetic toys on drawn lines Can rearrange without destroying line Can draw new lines for different configurations Portable, vertical option (put on wall) Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Allows extensive lining, can save arrangements, easy to rearrange
Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Large-Scale Lining Projects Cost: $0-5 (masking tape) Materials: Masking tape, ALL of child's toys (100-200+ items), large space (hallway, living room) How to Use: Create multiple lines with tape on floor (parallel lines, grid pattern) Child lines up EVERY toy they own Massive organizational project Photograph completed work extensively Can leave up for day(s) if possible Clean up becomes sorting activity Duration: 60-90 minutes or more Why it works: Satisfies need for extensive lining, provides deep engagement, creates sense of accomplishment Domino Rally Building Cost: $10-15 (domino set) or DIY with blocks Materials: 100+ dominoes or blocks How to Use: Child sets up elaborate domino arrangements Intricate lines, patterns, chain reactions Combines lining with exciting "destruction" Knock down and watch chain reaction
Can rebuild immediately Combines lining need with sensory payoff (visual, auditory) Duration: 45-60 minutes Why it works: Satisfies lining need, adds excitement, safe "destruction" at end Bead Stringing Patterns Cost: $5-10 (beads and string/pipe cleaners) Materials: Large beads, string or pipe cleaners, patterns How to Use: Create pattern sequences: AABBAABB or ABCABC String beads in specific patterns Creates "line" on string that's permanent Can wear as necklace (functional end product) More complex patterns for older children Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Creates permanent line, wearable product, pattern recognition Cityscape Building Project Cost: $10-20 (small building/vehicle toys) Materials: Small buildings, vehicles, people figures, masking tape How to Use: Create city layout with tape "roads" Line up buildings along streets Line up vehicles in traffic/parking lots
Arrange people in lines (waiting for bus, etc.) Functional play scenario that incorporates lining Duration: 60+ minutes Why it works: Makes lining functional, adds pretend play element, large-scale project Rainbow Color Gradient Cost: $5-10 (colored items) Materials: Items in rainbow colors (toys, blocks, cards, objects) How to Use: Sort all items by color Line up in rainbow order: ROY G BIV Within each color, organize by shade (light to dark) Create giant rainbow gradient Photograph result Very visually satisfying Duration: 45-60 minutes Why it works: Combines sorting and lining, visually beautiful, color learning Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Small Set Lining Cost: $0 Materials: 10 specific items only (cars, blocks, etc.) How to Use: Child lines up just 10 items Same 10 items daily (predictable)
Designated small area for lining When done, items return to container Not overwhelming Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Limited number not overwhelming, predictable, achievable Track Toys Cost: $8-15 (trains or cars with track) Materials: Train set or car track How to Use: Track provides "pre-lined" structure Child arranges cars/trains on track Combines lining with functional play Track makes it purposeful Can line up cars by color, size, etc. Duration: 20 minutes Why it works: Structure provided, combines lining with play Pegboard Pattern Cost: $5-10 Materials: Pegboard, colored pegs How to Use: Create simple lines with pegs Holes provide structure (not overwhelming) Limited space = limited number Can make patterns Clear endpoint (board fills up) Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Structured, limited scope, clear completion point
Picture Lining Card Cost: $2-3 (print pictures) Materials: Cards with lined-up toys pictured How to Use: Child looks at picture of lined toys Satisfies interest without actual lining Can carry picture No actual lining task (less demanding) Duration: 5 minutes as needed Why it works: Addresses interest without demands Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Gross Motor Lining: Make lining active: Line up pillows across room, jump on each in order Create obstacle course arranged in line Line up cones, weave through them Combines lining with movement 15-20 minutes Provides proprioceptive input + satisfies lining need Timed Lining Challenges: Add time element: "You have 10 minutes to make longest line possible" Timer creates endpoint Competition adds excitement When timer ends: 5 minutes heavy work before cleanup
Teaches time-limited engagement Functional Lining Jobs: Make lining helpful: Line up shoes by door (functional) Organize books by size (helpful) Set table with plates in row (purposeful) Line up laundry by color for folding Makes lining purposeful For AVOIDERS: Predictable Lining Routine: Same toys, same spot, same time daily "After breakfast: 10 minutes lining time with special cars" Provides expected sensory input Reduces need to line unexpectedly Very predictable Gradual Flexibility Training: Build tolerance for variations: Week 1: Line up toys exactly as child wants Week 2: Add one new toy to line Week 3: Suggest slight variation ("Can blue one go here instead?") Week 4: Try different location for line Very gradual cognitive flexibility building Choice Within Structure: Offer limited choices:
"Line up 10 cars OR 10 blocks" "Line can go here OR here" Child feels control but within structure Reduces anxiety Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Fingertip Massage: Lining involves intensive fine motor: Press firmly on each fingertip (like pressing button) Create pattern: thumb, pointer, middle, ring, pinky Repeat pattern 5 times each hand Firm pressure on each knuckle joint Squeeze fingers base to tip Duration: 5 minutes per hand Frequency: Before/during/after lining activity Why it works: Provides organizing pattern input to fingers, satisfies sensory seeking in hands that drives precise placement behaviors Hand and Forearm Massage: After extensive lining: Massage palms firmly Massage forearms (used in reaching/placing) Wrist rotations (gentle) Releases tension from repetitive movement 7-10 minutes Important after long lining sessions
For AVOIDERS: Proprioceptive Hand Massage: Before lining activity: Make "sandwich" with child's hand between your hands Firm pressure, hold for count of 10 Release slowly, count down 3-2-1 Repeat 3x per hand Duration: 3 minutes per hand Why it works: Organizing and grounding, prepares nervous system for precise motor task Calm Preparation: Before lining activity: Slow hand massage Gentle pressure Predictable strokes (count to 5 per stroke) 5 minutes total Reduces anxiety about upcoming activity Manifestation 2: Stacking Blocks to Specific Heights, Then Destroying Physical Redirection Technique: "Stack-Crash-Redirect" Method Allow child to complete stack and destruction cycle (important for completion) Don't interrupt mid-stack (causes frustration) After 2-3 stack-crash cycles, say: "Last tower! Then we build something new" Allow final stack and crash
Before child starts rebuilding: "Building time is changing. Let's build [specific structure]" Demonstrate new building project (house, garage, wall) If resistance: "You can crash this too when we're done!" Engage in structured building together Stay involved for 5+ minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Crash Tower Station Materials: Large cardboard blocks (made from boxes), soft foam blocks, plastic cups, designated crash area Cost: $5-10 How to Make: Create/collect stackable items specifically for crashing Designate "crash zone" (use mat or marked area) Can include: cardboard boxes, plastic cups, foam blocks, empty containers Store in specific bin labeled "crash towers" Child knows these are FOR stacking and crashing Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Designated materials for crashing, reduces need to destroy other structures, contained area
Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Giant Block Tower Competition Cost: $15-30 (large foam blocks) or DIY cardboard Materials: Large foam or cardboard blocks (20-50 pieces) How to Use: Build TALLEST possible tower Measure height before crash Count blocks used Photograph tower THEN: epic crash Try to beat previous record Combines building, measurement, excitement of crash Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Makes stack-crash purposeful, adds competition/measurement, satisfies destruction need Jenga-Style Challenge Cost: $10-15 (Jenga game) Materials: Jenga or similar stacking game How to Use: Stack all pieces into tower Take turns removing pieces (if playing with others) Tower eventually crashes Built-in crash element Can play competitively Combines fine motor skill, strategy, and eventual crash Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Structured game, crash is expected outcome, social option
Demolition Construction Site Cost: $10-20 (toy trucks, blocks) Materials: Blocks, toy bulldozers/dump trucks, hard hat (optional) How to Use: Build "buildings" with blocks Use bulldozer to "demolish" them Dump trucks haul away debris Rebuilding is part of construction site play Makes destruction part of purposeful play Can create whole city to demolish and rebuild Duration: 45-60 minutes Why it works: Makes crashing purposeful (demolition), adds pretend play, functional Bowling with Stacks Cost: $5-10 (or use existing items) Materials: Stackable items (cups, blocks), ball How to Use: Stack items like bowling pins Roll ball to knock down stacks Score points for knocks Combines stacking with purposeful crashing (bowling) Adds gross motor component (rolling ball) Can play with family Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Makes crashing part of game, social activity, purposeful
Crash Recording Project Cost: $0 (if have camera/phone) Materials: Camera/phone, blocks, slow-motion video capability How to Use: Build tower Record crash in slow-motion Watch video of crash repeatedly Analyze: how blocks fell, which fell first Create "crash compilation video" Makes crash event something to study and rewatch Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Extends crash interest, adds technology, can rewatch crashes without constant rebuilding Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Stable Building Only Cost: $0-10 Materials: Interlocking blocks (LEGO, Duplo) that stay together How to Use: Build structures that DON'T crash easily Blocks connect, creating stability No pressure to crash Can keep built structure No unexpected falling/noise Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Predictable, stable, no startling crashes Picture Building Cards Cost: $5-10 (building cards)
Materials: Cards showing simple block structures, blocks How to Use: Child builds what's shown on card Clear goal, clear completion No crashing required Can photograph completed build Very structured Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Clear structure, no destruction, achievable goals Controlled Crash Time Cost: $0 Materials: Blocks, visual schedule How to Use: If child wants to crash: scheduled "crash time" 5 minutes daily at specific time Child knows when crash will happen (not unexpected) Can build multiple small towers to crash in that time Contained, predictable Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Predictable, time-limited, child prepared Soft Blocks Only Cost: $10-20 (soft foam blocks) Materials: Soft, quiet blocks How to Use: If crash must happen: use soft blocks Makes crash quiet (less startling)
Soft landing (less overwhelming) Can still stack and knock down Reduces sensory impact Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Quieter, less overwhelming, gentler sensory experience Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Crash-Heavy Work Sequence: Make crashing part of organizing routine: Build tower Crash it Immediately: 10 wall push-ups Build again Crash again Immediately: carry blocks to container Repeat sequence 5x Incorporates heavy work between crashes Organizes nervous system Purposeful Destruction: Channel destruction need: Tear paper for art project (ripping = destruction) Crush aluminum cans for recycling Pop bubble wrap Smash clay and reform Provides destruction satisfaction without crashing towers constantly 15-20 minutes Building Challenges: Make stacking more complex: "Build a tower using ONLY red blocks" "Make a tower that's exactly 10 blocks"
"Build two towers same height" Adds cognitive challenge Reduces repetitive stack-crash cycle 20-30 minutes For AVOIDERS: Predictable Building: Structure to reduce anxiety: Build same structure daily (same height, same blocks) No crashing unless child chooses Photograph completed structures Can leave structures standing Predictability reduces stress Gradual Crash Introduction: If avoiding crashes due to sensory overwhelm: Week 1: Build only, no crashes Week 2: Parent gently lowers one block (not crashing) Week 3: Very gentle, controlled knock-down Week 4: Slightly less controlled crash Very gradual if crash is goal Choice and Control: Child decides: Whether to crash or keep How high to build When to stop Control reduces anxiety Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Proprioceptive Crash Simulation: Provide "crash" sensation through massage: Quick, firm taps on arms/legs (like blocks falling)
Firm pressure followed by release "Earthquake" massage - jiggle arms/legs gently Satisfies some destruction/crash sensory need Duration: 5 minutes Frequency: Before building time or instead of constant crashing Why it works: Provides some of intense proprioceptive sensation of crashing without actual destruction Post-Crash Calming: After crash session: Firm, organizing pressure on whole body Joint compressions Helps regulate after excitement 7-10 minutes Important transition For AVOIDERS: Gentle Building Preparation: Before building activity: Slow, gentle hand massage Calm, organizing touch Prepares for motor task Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Prepares nervous system for building task, reduces anxiety Safety Hold: If crash is distressing: Firm hug after crash Reassurance "You're safe, just blocks falling" Grounding pressure 3-5 minutes as needed Helps recover from startling crash
Manifestation 3: Watching Items Fall (Dominoes, Blocks, Marbles) Physical Redirection Technique: "Fall Completion Method" Allow child to complete falling sequence (important for closure) After 2-3 fall cycles, set boundary: "Two more times, then we try something new" Count together: "One fall...two falls...okay, now let's..." Before child resets: offer related activity "Let's make a ramp for cars to roll down" Demonstrate alternative that still has falling/rolling component If resistance: set timer "5 more minutes of falling, then we switch" Honor timer (builds trust for future) Transition to alternative with similar motion DIY Alternative Tool: Marble Maze Fall Tower Materials: Cardboard tubes (paper towel, wrapping paper), shoe box, tape, marbles, scissors Cost: Under $5 How to Make: Cut cardboard tubes into pieces Arrange at angles inside shoe box (creates zig-zag path)
Tape securely at different levels Drop marble at top, watches it fall/roll through maze Ends at bottom Child can modify maze arrangement Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Controlled falling, child can reset quickly, portable, adjustable Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Elaborate Marble Run System Cost: $25-50 (commercial marble run) Materials: Large marble run set with multiple tracks, spinners, bells How to Use: Build complex track system Drop marble at top Watch it fall, spin through elements, ring bells Combines construction, problem-solving, and falling motion Can time how long marble takes Try different configurations Duration: 60+ minutes Why it works: Extensive engagement, combines building with falling observation, adds sound element Water Fall Station Cost: $15-25 (water table or large container) Materials: Water table, funnels, tubes, containers, water
How to Use: Set up multi-level water fall system Pour water at top Watches it fall through levels Catches at bottom Can add food coloring for visibility Outdoor or bathroom activity Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Water falling, can repeat continuously, tactile + visual Domino Chain Reaction Videos/Building Cost: $10-20 (large domino set) Materials: 200+ dominoes How to Use: Set up elaborate domino patterns Create chain reactions Can incorporate other falling elements (books, blocks) Record the fall Watch videos of massive domino installations Duration: 45-90 minutes Why it works: Extensive setup time, dramatic fall, can film and rewatch Ball Drop Tower Cost: $15-30 (commercial toy) or DIY Materials: Ball drop tower toy or PVC pipes arranged vertically How to Use:
Drop balls at top Watch them cascade down levels Multiple balls create ongoing action Some towers have sound/light elements Can race multiple balls Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Continuous action, can add multiple balls, engaging Plinko Board Cost: $20-40 or DIY with $10 Materials: Board with pegs, balls or chips to drop How to Make DIY: Pegboard mounted vertically Insert pegs or nails at angles Drop ball at top Ball bounces off pegs falling to bottom Can add cups at bottom to catch How to Use: Drop ball, watch unpredictable path Try to land in specific cup Can play for points Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Unpredictable falling path (exciting), game element Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Slow Sand Timer
Cost: $5-10 (large sand timer) Materials: Large sand timer (5-10 minutes) How to Use: Watch sand fall slowly Very predictable Same every time Calming, meditative Can use as transition timer Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Slow, predictable, calming, contained Single Marble Down Tube Cost: $2-3 Materials: One clear tube, one marble How to Use: Hold tube vertical Drop marble Watch it fall (very simple) Predictable path No complex setup Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Simple, predictable, not overwhelming Coin Drop Jar Cost: $0-2 (jar, coins or buttons) Materials: Clear jar, coins or large buttons How to Use: Drop one coin at a time into jar Watch it fall Hear it clink Simple, repetitive Can count coins dropped Duration: 5-10 minutes
Why it works: Simple, auditory feedback gentle, achievable Controlled Domino Line Cost: $5-10 (small domino set) Materials: 20 dominoes How to Use: Set up SHORT line (not overwhelming) Knock down Predictable fall Quick to reset Not complex or long Duration: 10 minutes Why it works: Short, manageable, predictable Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Fall-Heavy Work Cycle: Alternate falling observation with physical work: Watch item fall 10 jumping jacks Reset, watch fall again Carry heavy item across room Repeat cycle Prevents prolonged passive watching Adds organizing movement Construction Focus: Emphasis on building/setup rather than just watching fall: "Let's make the most complex marble run possible" Focus on engineering, problem-solving Fall is reward for building Reduces fixation on fall itself 45-60 minutes building focus
Varied Falling Types: Provide different falling experiences: Morning: Water falls (outdoor) Afternoon: Marble run Evening: Sand timer (calming) Variety reduces fixation on one type For AVOIDERS: Predictable Falling: Same item, same path every time: One marble, one tube, daily Exactly the same setup Predictable outcome Brief (5 minutes) Reduces overwhelm Gradual Complexity: Start very simple: Week 1: Drop one item into container Week 2: Add one turn (tube at angle) Week 3: Two-part path Week 4: Three parts Very gradual increase Distance Control: Child controls proximity: Can watch from across room Move closer when comfortable Never forced Builds tolerance Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Vestibular Organizing: Watching items fall stimulates vestibular system: Gentle pressure on temples Pressure at base of skull Massage neck
Organizes visual tracking Duration: 5 minutes Frequency: After falling observation Why it works: Calms vestibular system stimulated by tracking falling objects Eye Rest: After intense watching: Gentle pressure on closed eyelids (very brief) Massage around eyes (not on eyes) Forehead smoothing Rests visual system 3-5 minutes For AVOIDERS: Grounding Before Activity: If falling is overwhelming: Grounding pressure before activity Feet, shoulders, hands "You are safe, I'm here" Prepares nervous system Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Creates safety before potentially overwhelming experience Calming After: After any falling observation: Slow back massage Deep pressure Quiet environment Helps recover 7-10 minutes Manifestation 4: Rolling Toys Back and Forth Watching Movement Physical Redirection Technique: "Roll Redirect" Method Don't stop rolling abruptly (causes distress) Join rolling activity: sit across from child, roll toy back and forth together
After 1-2 minutes of joint play: "Let's make the car go somewhere" Create destination: "Can you roll it into this garage?" Add functional element to rolling If continued fixation: "Last 5 rolls, then we build a city for the car" Count together: 1...2...3...4...5 Transition to functional car play (roads, buildings) Stay engaged in new activity 5+ minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Rolling Ramp Station Materials: Cardboard ramps at different angles, toy cars, target containers, measuring tape Cost: Under $5 How to Make: Create 3-4 ramps from cardboard at different angles (steep, medium, gentle) Set up with targets at bottom (cups, boxes to roll into) Add measuring tape to measure distance Child rolls cars down ramps Can experiment with different angles Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Adds purpose to rolling (scientific experiment), child controls, adds measurement/learning
Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Car Race Track Cost: $15-30 (commercial track) or DIY with tape Materials: Race track or tape roads, multiple cars, timer How to Use: Set up elaborate track system Race cars against each other Time each car's performance Create different track configurations Can add obstacles, jumps Purposeful rolling (racing) Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Makes rolling purposeful, competitive, adds construction element Bowling with Rolling Cost: $10-15 (toy bowling set or DIY) Materials: Toy bowling pins (or plastic bottles), ball How to Use: Set up pins Roll ball to knock them down Keep score Purposeful rolling with clear goal Can play with family Combines rolling with gross motor Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Purpose-driven rolling, social option, game with rules
Marble/Ball Run Maze Cost: $20-40 (commercial) or DIY $5-10 Materials: Marble run or pool noodles cut in half for ball paths How to Use: Build elaborate path systems Roll marble/ball through Watch it navigate curves, drops Can time runs Build increasingly complex paths Duration: 45-60 minutes Why it works: Combines construction with rolling observation, problem-solving Outdoor Rolling Course Cost: $0-10 (balls, outdoor items) Materials: Various balls, outdoor terrain, chalk How to Use: Create rolling obstacle course outside Roll ball around trees, through goals, down hills Mark course with chalk Time trials Different balls roll differently (observation) Incorporates movement, outdoors Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Outdoor activity, child moves with rolling object, varied terrain Rolling Distance Experiment Cost: $0-5 (measuring tape, toys)
Materials: Various rolling toys (cars, balls, cylinders), measuring tape, different surfaces How to Use: Scientific approach to rolling "How far does each toy roll?" Test on different surfaces: carpet, tile, wood Measure distances Graph results Makes rolling educational Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Educational, purpose-driven, combines science with rolling interest Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Single Car, Short Path Cost: $0 Materials: One toy car, short defined path (tape line) How to Use: Roll car on short path only (3-4 feet) Same path every time Predictable Can stop anytime Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Simple, contained, predictable Guided Rolling Cost: $0 Materials: Toy car, masking tape path How to Use: Create tape "road" on floor Car stays on road (guided)
Very controlled rolling Clear boundaries Duration: 10 minutes Why it works: Structured, clear path, not overwhelming Rolling in Container Cost: $0-3 (box, toy) Materials: Shallow box, toy car or ball How to Use: Roll toy within box boundaries Contained space Toy can't get away Predictable Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Completely contained, can't lose control Hand-Over-Hand Rolling Cost: $0 Materials: One toy How to Use: Adult and child roll toy together Adult's hand on child's hand Controlled, supported Child feels guidance Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Co-regulation, supported, safe Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Roll-Chase Sequence: Make rolling active: Roll car across room Child crawls/runs to get it Rolls it back Parent retrieves Adds gross motor movement 15-20 minutes
Prevents passive rolling fixation Functional Rolling: Make rolling purposeful: Roll ball to family member (back-forth game) "Delivery service" - roll cars with items to different rooms Roll ingredients in playdough Purposeful rolling tasks Integrates into daily activities Heavy Work with Rolling: Roll heavy items: Weighted ball Medicine ball Heavy toy truck Provides proprioceptive input 10-15 minutes More organizing than light rolling For AVOIDERS: Predictable Rolling Routine: Same toy, same path, same time: "After breakfast: 5 minutes car rolling" Same car, same location Extreme predictability Reduces anxiety Gradual Distance: Start with short rolls: Week 1: Roll 1 foot Week 2: Roll 2 feet Week 3: Roll 3 feet Gradually increase Builds confidence Slow Motion Rolling: Roll very slowly: Adult demonstrates slow roll
Child copies Calm, controlled pace Not overwhelming 5-10 minutes Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Hand and Arm Massage: Rolling uses hands/arms extensively: Massage hands firmly Massage forearms Wrist rotations Releases tension Duration: 5 minutes per arm Frequency: Before/after rolling play Why it works: Addresses muscles used, provides proprioceptive input to areas seeking stimulation Bilateral Integration: Both hands/arms worked together: Bilateral squeezing Both hands at once Creates integration 5 minutes Very organizing For AVOIDERS: Gentle Hand Preparation: Before rolling activity: Gentle hand massage Warm hands together first Very gentle, predictable Prepares for motor task Duration: 3-5 minutes Why it works: Prepares nervous system, reduces anxiety Calm Hand Hold: After rolling: Hold child's hands gently Steady pressure Calming presence Helps transition 3 minutes Manifestation 5: Dropping Items Repeatedly to Watch Them Fall
Physical Redirection Technique: "Drop Count Redirect" Method Don't stop dropping abruptly (causes tantrum) Count drops with child: "Let's drop it 10 more times" Count together: "1...2...3..." up to 10 At 10: "Dropping time is done. Now let's..." Offer alternative activity involving dropping but more structured "Let's drop things into this bucket" (adds target) Or "Let's stack these instead of drop" Physical redirection if needed (hand on shoulder, guide to new area) If infant/toddler in highchair: remove objects that are being dropped, offer alternative DIY Alternative Tool: Target Drop Station Materials: Large containers/buckets at different heights, various safe dropping items (pom poms, bean bags, balls), tape marks on floor Cost: Under $5 How to Make: Set up 3-4 containers at different heights (floor, low chair, higher shelf)
Mark floor with tape showing where to stand Provide various items to drop (pom poms, bean bags, soft balls) Child drops items aiming for containers Makes dropping purposeful (targeting) Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Adds purpose to dropping, targets provide goal, safe items, can practice aim Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Drop and Sort Game Cost: $5-10 (containers, items to drop) Materials: Multiple containers (different colors), colored objects to drop (pom poms, balls) How to Use: Match object color to container color Drop red pom pom in red bucket Combines dropping with sorting/matching Can time: "How fast can you drop all reds?" Adds cognitive element Can count items dropped Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Purpose-driven dropping, learning element, structured Kerplunk or Similar Game
Cost: $15-25 Materials: Kerplunk game or DIY version How to Make DIY: Clear container, straws, marbles Straws create web across container Drop marbles on top Pull straws, marbles drop through How to Use: Game with rules about dropping Take turns Count how many marbles drop Social play option Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Structured dropping game, social option, rules create boundaries Coin/Button Drop Bank Cost: $5-10 (piggy bank or create slot in container) Materials: Container with slot, coins or large buttons How to Use: Child drops coins into bank Functional dropping (saving money) Can count coins Hear satisfying clink When full, empty and count total Purposeful dropping with math learning Duration: 10-15 minutes per session Why it works: Functional, teaches saving, auditory feedback
Basketball/Netball Dropping Cost: $10-20 (small basketball hoop) or DIY Materials: Basketball hoop at child's height, soft ball How to Use: Drop/shoot ball into hoop Start very close (almost dropping in) Gradually move back Count baskets made Combines dropping motion with sport skill Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Sports skill development, purposeful, can progress difficulty Science Drop Experiments Cost: $0-5 (household items) Materials: Various objects (feather, ball, block, paper), stopwatch How to Use: Drop different items from same height "Which falls faster?" Observe and predict Time each fall Graph results Educational approach to dropping Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Makes dropping scientific, educational, purposeful observation Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Gentle Drop into Soft Container Cost: $0-3 Materials: Soft items (cotton balls, pom poms), soft container (fabric basket)
How to Use: Drop very soft items Quiet landing (not startling) Predictable, gentle Can retrieve and drop again Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Quiet, gentle, not overwhelming Controlled Drop with Timer Cost: $0 Materials: One item, container, timer How to Use: Drop one item at a time Count to 3 before each drop (predictable) Timer shows when dropping time ends (5 minutes) Very structured Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Highly structured, predictable, time-limited Hand-Over-Hand Dropping Cost: $0 Materials: Safe objects, container How to Use: Adult places hand over child's hand Drop together Shared control Very supported Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Co-regulation, child feels supported Drop Picture Cards Cost: $2 (print pictures) Materials: Pictures of items being dropped
How to Use: Look at pictures instead of actual dropping Less demanding than doing activity Can discuss what happens when things drop Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Addresses interest without demands Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Drop-Heavy Work Cycle: Alternate dropping with physical work: Drop 5 items 10 wall push-ups Drop 5 items Carry heavy bin Repeat cycle Prevents prolonged dropping fixation Adds organizing input Functional Dropping: Make dropping helpful: Drop laundry into basket Drop toys into cleanup bin Drop ingredients into bowl (cooking) Drop recycling into bin Integrates into daily tasks Retrieval Component: Add gross motor: Drop item Run to get it Drop again Adds movement, prevents passive dropping 15-20 minutes For AVOIDERS: Predictable Drop Schedule: Scheduled dropping time:
"After lunch: 5 minutes drop play" Same items, same container Predictable routine Reduces anxiety Gradual Introduction: Start with gentle drops: Week 1: Place items gently (no dropping) Week 2: Lower items slowly Week 3: Very gentle drop from low height Week 4: Normal drop from low height Extremely gradual Silent Drops: Use quiet items if noise overwhelming: Soft pom poms Fabric items Into soft basket Reduces auditory overwhelm Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Hand Release Massage: Dropping requires hand opening/releasing: Massage palms (helps with releasing) Gentle finger stretches Practice opening and closing hands with resistance Strengthens hand muscles Duration: 5 minutes per hand Frequency: Before/after dropping activity Why it works: Addresses hand muscles used in releasing, provides proprioceptive input Arm Weight: After repetitive dropping (arm fatigue):
Massage shoulders and arms Gentle arm lifts (parent supports) Releases tension 7-10 minutes For AVOIDERS: Gentle Hand Opening: If hand opening is difficult: Very gentle hand massage Help hand open gradually No forcing Gradual, supported Duration: 3-5 minutes Why it works: Prepares hand for releasing motion, gentle Calming After Dropping: After activity: Gentle hand holding Slow strokes on arms Calming presence Helps transition 5 minutes Manifestation 6: Spinning Objects (Tops, Fidget Spinners, Plates) Physical Redirection Technique: "Spin Transition" Method Allow completion of current spin (object slows and stops naturally) After 2-3 spins: "Last two spins, then we play something new" Count together: "One more spin...last spin...okay, spinning time is done" Before child can spin again: offer alternative "Let's roll this instead" or "Let's build with these"
Hand child non-spinning toy immediately Guide to different area if needed Stay engaged with alternative 5+ minutes Acknowledge interest: "I know you like spinning. We can spin again later." DIY Alternative Tool: Spinning Collection Station Materials: Various spinning toys (tops, fidget spinners, dreidels), lazy Susan, container Cost: $10-20 How to Make/Assemble: Collect 5-6 different types of spinning toys Store in special container Include: traditional tops, fidget spinners, gyroscopes, spin toys Add lazy Susan (can spin items on it) Designated "spinning station" Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Variety prevents fixation on one spinner, designated time/place, can explore different spin types Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Spinning Toy Competition Cost: $15-25 (variety of spinning toys) Materials: Multiple types: tops, fidget spinners, gyroscopes, dreidels
How to Use: Spin all toys simultaneously Which spins longest? Which spins fastest? Time each spinner Graph results Scientific approach to spinning Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Makes spinning purposeful, educational, comparison/measurement Pottery Wheel/Spin Art Cost: $20-40 (spin art machine) or DIY Materials: Spin art machine or lazy Susan, paper, paint How to Use: Place paper on spinning surface Drip paint while spinning Creates art from spinning motion Functional, creative spinning Produces artwork to keep Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Creative output, purposeful spinning, produces art Gyroscope Exploration Cost: $10-20 (gyroscope toy) Materials: Gyroscope How to Use: Learn how gyroscope works Spin and balance on different surfaces Try tricks (spin on finger, string) Educational about physics More complex than simple spinner
Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Educational, skill-building, physics concepts Beyblade/Battle Spinning Tops Cost: $15-30 Materials: Beyblade or similar battle tops, arena How to Use: Launch spinning tops in arena Tops battle/collide Last one spinning wins Can play with others Strategic element (which top to use) Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Game element, social option, strategy, purpose Create Spinners Project Cost: $5-10 (materials) Materials: Cardboard, markers, toothpicks or pencils, scissors How to Make: Cut circles from cardboard Decorate with markers/paint Push toothpick through center (axle) Creates custom spinner How to Use: Make multiple spinners Test which design spins best Combines art with spinning interest Duration: 45-60 minutes Why it works: Creative, builds understanding of how spinners work, custom designs Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS):
Single Slow Spinner Cost: $5-8 Materials: One simple top that spins slowly How to Use: Child controls completely Slow spin (not overwhelming) Same spinner every time Predictable Duration: 5-10 minutes Why it works: Slow, predictable, simple, one item only Guided Spinning Cost: $0 Materials: Spinner, adult support How to Use: Adult helps child spin Hand-over-hand support Controlled speed Child feels supported Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Co-regulation, supported, not overwhelming Spinning Picture Card Cost: $0-2 Materials: Picture of spinner How to Use: Look at picture instead of actual spinning Static image (no movement) Addresses interest without stimulation Duration: 3-5 minutes Why it works: No actual movement, controllable Timer Spinning Cost: $0 Materials: Spinner, timer How to Use: Spin for exactly 3 minutes
Timer shows when time ends Very predictable Same duration daily Duration: 3 minutes Why it works: Time-limited, predictable, structured Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Spin-Move Cycle: Alternate spinning with movement: Spin top 10 jumping jacks Spin again Run around house Repeat Prevents prolonged fixation Adds vestibular/proprioceptive input Functional Spinning: Make spinning purposeful: Spin dreidel for game Spin wheel for choice making Spin timer for activity duration Purposeful spinning integrated into activities Create Spinning Challenge: "Can you spin while standing on one foot?" "Spin it on different surfaces" "Make it spin in a circle while spinning" Adds motor challenge For AVOIDERS: Predictable Spin Routine: Same spinner, same time, same place: "After snack: 5 minutes spinner time" Extreme predictability Reduces anxiety Gradual Spin Speed:
Start very slow: Week 1: Roll spinner (not spinning) Week 2: Very slow spin Week 3: Gentle spin Week 4: Normal spin Builds tolerance Choice and Control: Child decides all variables: Which spinner How many spins When to stop Complete control Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Finger Dexterity Massage: Spinning requires fine motor control: Massage each finger individually Gentle finger rotations Press on fingertips Practice pinch grasp Duration: 5 minutes per hand Frequency: Before/after spinning Why it works: Addresses fine motor muscles, provides proprioceptive input to fingers Vestibular Calming: After watching spinning: Gentle pressure on temples Base of skull pressure Neck massage Calms visual tracking of spinning 5 minutes For AVOIDERS: Gentle Finger Preparation: Before spinning activity: Gentle finger massage No forcing or stretching
Warm hands together Very gentle, supportive Duration: 3-5 minutes Why it works: Prepares hands for fine motor task, reduces anxiety Hand Holding: After spinning: Gentle hand holding Steady, calm presence Helps transition 3 minutes
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 1. VISUAL STIMMING INTERVENTIONS > B. Object Visual Stimming > Level 3: Movement Tracking
Causation: Over-stimulated: Smooth tracking motion is organizing Under-stimulated: Dynamic movement provides visual interest Sensitivity: Visual system needs practice with motion tracking Sensory Profile: Seeker: Actively searches for movement to track Mixed: May seek tracking but avoid sudden movements Description: Following moving objects with eyes Manifestation 1: Tracking Birds, Airplanes, or Insects Flying Physical Redirection Technique: "Track and Transition" Method Allow brief tracking (1-2 minutes - validates interest) Acknowledge: "You see the bird flying!" After brief observation: "Let's count how many birds we see, then we'll..." Count 3-5 birds/planes together Then: "Now let's go [specific activity]" Physical guidance if needed (hand on shoulder) Offer related activity: "Let's pretend to be birds!" (arm flapping, jumping) Or: "Let's draw what we saw" Stay engaged with alternative 5+ minutes
DIY Alternative Tool: Flying Object Puppet Show Materials: Bird/butterfly/airplane pictures on popsicle sticks, flashlight, white sheet Cost: Under $3 How to Make: Cut out pictures of birds, butterflies, planes, insects Attach to popsicle sticks Child moves puppets across white sheet while parent shines light behind Creates flying shadows Child controls all movement Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Child creates flying motion, controlled environment, replicates outdoor experience indoors Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Flying Toy Collection Cost: $15-30 Materials: Various flying toys (helicopters, gliders, rockets, frisbees, kites) How to Use: Outdoor activity Child launches/throws flying toys Tracks their flight Retrieves and launches again Active participation instead of passive watching Can have distance competitions Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Active, outdoor, child creates flying motion, gross motor involvement
Bird Watching with Binoculars Cost: $10-20 (child binoculars) Materials: Binoculars, bird identification book, notebook How to Use: Structured bird watching activity Identify bird types Count birds seen Keep log Makes tracking purposeful/educational Can become ongoing hobby Duration: 20-30 minutes per session Why it works: Educational, structured, purposeful observation Bubble Chasing Cost: $3-5 (bubble solution) Materials: Bubble solution, bubble wands How to Use: Blow bubbles (or bubble machine) Child tracks bubbles floating Chases and pops them Combines tracking with active movement Can count bubbles caught Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Active participation, child controls pace, gross motor Drone Flying Cost: $30-100 (child-safe drone) Materials: Small, safe drone for children How to Use: Child controls drone Tracks it while flying Creates the flying motion
Learn about remote control Can do tricks, races Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Child in control, educational, combines tracking with operating skill Bird Feeder Project Cost: $10-20 (bird feeder, seed) Materials: Bird feeder, bird seed, window location How to Use: Set up bird feeder near window Scheduled bird watching times (morning, evening) Count birds that visit Identify types Keeps log Purposeful, educational Duration: Brief sessions (10 min) multiple times daily Why it works: Structured observation times, educational, ongoing project Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Bird Pictures/Videos Cost: $0-10 (book or videos) Materials: Picture book of birds or calm nature videos How to Use: Look at still pictures (no movement) Or very calm, slow bird videos Controlled, predictable Can pause video anytime
Duration: 10 minutes Why it works: No unexpected movement, controllable, calm Bird Mobile (Stationary) Cost: $5-10 Materials: Bird mobile to hang in room How to Use: Mobile moves gently with air Very slow, predictable Indoor, controlled Always available Duration: Brief viewing as desired Why it works: Gentle movement, predictable, calming Guided Bird Watching Cost: $0 Materials: Window view, parent support How to Use: Parent and child watch together Parent narrates: "Look, a bird..." Very brief (2-3 minutes) Parent provides structure and support Duration: 2-3 minutes Why it works: Co-regulation, brief, supported Indoor "Flying" Objects Cost: $3-5 Materials: Feather, tissue paper How to Use: Drop feather, watch it float down slowly Very gentle, predictable movement Indoor, controlled Child controls when it happens
