Controlled reflection viewing Time-limited Duration: 10-15 minutes Why it works: Child controls reflection, portable, time-limited Alternative Stimulation (For SEEKERS): Mirror Play Activities Cost: $5-15 (various mirrors) Materials: Handheld mirrors, tabletop mirrors, wall mirrors How to Use: Structured mirror activities Mirror games: make faces, copy expressions Use mirror for grooming (functional) Position mirror to reflect interesting things Purposeful reflection use Duration: 15-20 minutes Why it works: Purposeful, functional, controlled Reflective Art Projects Cost: $5-10 (aluminum foil, mirrors, shiny paper) Materials: Reflective art materials How to Use: Create art with reflective materials Aluminum foil sculptures Mirror mosaics Explore how reflections work Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Creative, educational, purposeful Photography of Reflections Cost: $0 (if have camera) Materials: Camera or tablet How to Use:
Take photos of interesting reflections Puddles, windows, mirrors, water Create reflection photo gallery Artistic exploration Duration: 20-30 minutes Why it works: Creative, purposeful, creates product Science of Reflections Cost: $5-10 (mirrors, materials) Materials: Mirrors, light source, objects How to Use: Explore how reflections work Angle experiments What reflects best? Educational approach Duration: 30-45 minutes Why it works: Educational, purposeful, exploratory Kaleidoscope Making Cost: $10-15 (materials) Materials: Mirrors, tube, colorful objects How to Make/Use: Create kaleidoscope Multiple reflections create patterns Functional reflection exploration Duration: 45 minutes creation + ongoing use Why it works: Creates tool for reflection viewing, purposeful Alternative Stimulation (For AVOIDERS): Limit Reflections Cost: $0-10 (covers) Materials: Covers for reflective surfaces How to Use: Cover mirrors when not needed Reduce reflective surfaces in environment
Limit exposure Duration: Ongoing Why it works: Environmental management Brief Mirror Time Cost: $0 Materials: Timer, mirror How to Use: Scheduled mirror time (3 minutes) For grooming purposes Time-limited Predictable Duration: 3 minutes Why it works: Controlled, predictable, brief Simple Reflections Only Cost: $0 Materials: One simple mirror How to Use: If must use mirror: one simple one No complex reflections Straightforward use Duration: 5 minutes Why it works: Simple, not overwhelming Alternative Visual Focus Cost: Varies Materials: Non-reflective activities How to Use: Activities without reflections Solid colored materials Matte surfaces Duration: Throughout day Why it works: Eliminates trigger Regulation Through Occupational Therapy: For SEEKERS: Scheduled Reflection Time: Designate specific times for reflection viewing: Morning: 5 minutes mirror time (grooming) Afternoon: 10 minutes reflection exploration activity
Prevents constant seeking Provides outlet at specific times Functional Reflection Use: Make all reflection viewing functional: Grooming (brushing hair, teeth) Getting dressed (checking outfit) Art projects Photography Never aimless reflection seeking Environmental Management: Limit available reflections: Cover unnecessary mirrors Position child away from windows Reduce reflective surfaces Makes seeking harder Purposeful Exploration: Channel interest educationally: Science of reflections Art projects Photography Purposeful and educational For AVOIDERS: Minimize Reflections: Cover mirrors when not needed Reduce reflective surfaces Simple environment Reduces overwhelm Functional Only: Use mirrors for function only: Brief grooming Time-limited Purpose-driven No Pressure: Never require mirror use May be uncomfortable Provide alternatives Respect discomfort Massage Techniques: For SEEKERS: Neck and Shoulder Release: Positioning for reflections creates neck/shoulder tension Massage neck (sides)
Shoulder massage Releases positioning tension Duration: 5-7 minutes Why it works: Releases physical tension from unusual positioning Full Body Awareness: Massage helps body awareness May reduce positioning seeking 10 minutes For AVOIDERS: General Calming: If reflections are overwhelming: Calming full body massage Reduces anxiety Grounding 10 minutes Grounding Touch: Shoulders and feet Helps feel grounded Not focused on reflections 5-7 minutes COMPREHENSIVE SENSORY DIET TABLE: RAPID EYE BLINKING Manifestation: Rapid Eye Blinking (2-3 blinks per second) PHYSICAL TECHNIQUES TO INTERRUPT RAPID BLINKING Technique 1: "Gentle Eye Coverage" (Primary Method) How to Perform: Approach child calmly, get at their eye level Say: "Let's give your eyes a rest" Ask permission: "Can I help your eyes feel better?" Warm your hands by rubbing them together for 5 seconds
Gently cup your hands over child's closed eyes (palming technique) Do NOT press on eyeballs - hands should create gentle darkness Hold for 10-20 seconds Remove hands slowly Immediately redirect to non-visual activity Why It Works: Provides darkness and warmth to tired eyes Interrupts the blinking pattern Gives visual system a break Feels soothing and calming When to Use: Anytime blinking is observed, especially if sustained for 30+ seconds Technique 2: "Cool Compress Redirect" How to Perform: Keep soft washcloth and cool (not cold) water accessible When blinking starts, say: "Your eyes look tired, let's cool them" Wet washcloth with cool water, wring out excess Have child close eyes Gently place cool washcloth over closed eyes Hold for 30-60 seconds Remove and immediately redirect to heavy work activity
Why It Works: Cool temperature provides sensory input Interrupts pattern Feels refreshing Physically blocks blinking ability temporarily When to Use: During transitions, after screen time, mid-afternoon fatigue Technique 3: "Face Massage Redirect" How to Perform: Have child close eyes Use firm (not hard) pressure Massage in this sequence: Forehead (horizontal strokes, 5 times) Temples (circular motions, 10 circles each side) Cheeks (downward strokes, 5 times) Around eye sockets (gentle circles, NOT on eyes) Total time: 2-3 minutes Finish with "eye palming" (hands cupped over closed eyes) Redirect to physical activity Why It Works: Provides proprioceptive input to face Relaxes facial muscles Redirects sensory seeking to different input Calming effect When to Use: Before bed, during peak blinking times, when child seems tense
DIY TOOLS & ALTERNATIVES (Inexpensive/Household Items) Tool 1: Eye Rest Station Materials Needed: Soft cloth or small hand towel Rice or dried beans (1 cup) Fabric or old sock Thread and needle (or rubber band) How to Make: Fill sock or fabric pouch with rice/beans Sew or tie closed securely Store in refrigerator (stays cool) Use as eye pillow - place over closed eyes for 2-5 minutes Cost: $0-2 (use household items) How to Use: Child lies down or sits comfortably Place cool eye pillow over closed eyes Set timer for 3-5 minutes Play calming music or audiobook Use during scheduled "eye rest breaks" throughout day Tool 2: Blink Awareness Chart Materials Needed: Paper or poster board Markers Stickers How to Make:
Draw simple chart with columns: "Morning / Afternoon / Evening" Create visual scale: 1 star = few blinks, 5 stars = lots of blinks Each day, child rates their blinking Track patterns over 2 weeks Cost: $0-3 How to Use: Increases awareness of blinking Helps identify triggers and patterns Rewards lower blinking days with special stickers Review weekly to adjust sensory diet Tool 3: "No-Screen" Activity Box Materials Needed: Cardboard box or bin Various non-visual activities What to Include: Audiobooks on device or CDs Playdough (homemade recipe: 1 cup flour, 1/2 cup salt, 1/2 cup water, food coloring) Therapy putty or clay Fidgets (stress balls, textured items) Building blocks Puzzles (tactile, not requiring intense visual focus) Musical instruments Sensory bottles Cost: $0-20 (use household items)
How to Use: Keep box readily accessible When screen time ends or blinking increases, immediately offer box Child chooses alternative activity Rotate items weekly to maintain interest Tool 4: Visual Break Timer Materials Needed: Kitchen timer, phone timer, or Time Timer visual timer Red and green construction paper How to Make: Red paper = "Eyes Working" time Green paper = "Eyes Resting" time Set timer for work/rest intervals Cost: $0-5 How to Use: During visual tasks (homework, reading): 15 minutes "eyes working" (red) Then 5 minutes "eyes resting" (green) - child must close eyes or do non-visual activity Repeat cycle Prevents visual fatigue before blinking starts Tool 5: Palming Practice Card Materials Needed: Index card Markers Laminate or clear tape How to Make:
Draw simple pictures showing palming steps: Step 1: Rub hands together Step 2: Cup hands over eyes Step 3: Keep covered for count of 10 Step 4: Remove slowly Laminate for durability Cost: $0-2 How to Use: Teach child to use independently Keep card in multiple locations (desk, bedroom, car) When eyes feel tired or adult says "palm," child follows card Empowers child to self-regulate ALTERNATIVE STIMULATION OPTIONS (Household Items) Alternative 1: Auditory Focus Activities Instead of visual stimulation, provide auditory input: Household Items: Music (various genres - let child choose) Audiobooks or podcasts Nature sounds (apps or YouTube audio only) Musical instruments (pots/pans, rice shakers, etc.) Singing, humming Following audio instructions (Simon Says audio version) How to Use: During times child would normally engage in visual activities
As reward or preferred activity During rest times Especially important during peak blinking times (mid-afternoon, evening) Alternative 2: Tactile Exploration Activities Household Items to Create Sensory Bins: Rice, beans, pasta (uncooked) Cotton balls Fabric scraps of different textures Sand (from sandbox or buy cheap) Water with dish soap (bubbles) Ice cubes Shaving cream Cooked spaghetti How to Use: Place in large container or baking dish Hide small toys to find Child explores with eyes CLOSED (intensifies tactile experience) Squeezing, pouring, burying hands 10-15 minute sessions Use during scheduled breaks from visual tasks Alternative 3: Proprioceptive "Heavy Work" Home Activities Zero-Cost Activities: Push against wall (10-second pushes, 10 reps) Carry laundry basket (make it heavy) Push furniture (move chairs to table) Carry groceries from car
Animal walks (bear walk, crab walk, frog jumps) Wall sits (back against wall, slide down like sitting) Push-ups (modified on knees okay) Carry heavy books Squeeze couch cushions Roll up in blanket burrito and "escape" How to Use: Every 60-90 minutes throughout day IMMEDIATELY before and after screen time When blinking is observed During transitions Before meals and bedtime Alternative 4: Vestibular Movement Activities Household Items: Office chair (for spinning - supervised) Blanket (for pulling child across floor) Couch cushions (for jumping) Stairs (for climbing up and down) Pillows (for crash pad) Activities: Controlled spinning (5-10 rotations maximum) Rocking in rocking chair Swinging (if playground nearby) Jumping on cushions/pillows Rolling across floor Somersaults Dancing with spins How to Use: For sensory seekers: Higher intensity, more repetitions
For sensory avoiders: Slow, gentle, gradual Always follow with heavy work (proprioceptive input) Use to "wake up" system when lethargic ACTIVITIES FOR SENSORY SEEKERS VS. AVOIDERS FOR SENSORY SEEKERS (Under-Responsive) with Rapid Blinking Key Characteristics: Blinks rapidly when BORED or under-stimulated Seeks out visual stimulation when not provided elsewhere Needs HIGH intensity sensory input May increase blinking when inactive Specific Activities: Morning: Trampoline jumping (50-100 jumps) Running around outside (10 minutes) Obstacle course with climbing, jumping, crawling Heavy breakfast prep (mixing, kneading, stirring) Crunchy, chewy breakfast foods Throughout Day: Schedule intense movement EVERY 60-90 minutes Proprioceptive activities: Pushing, pulling, carrying heavy items Oral motor: Chewy tubes, crunchy snacks, drinking thick smoothies through straw Vestibular: Spinning, swinging, jumping (controlled) Allow brief visual stimming (5 minutes) but then redirect to MOVEMENT
Key Strategy: Satisfy sensory hunger through MOVEMENT and PROPRIOCEPTION, not visual input Tire out the body so visual seeking decreases Red Flag: If blinking increases with more activity, child may actually be sensory avoider or mixed profile FOR SENSORY AVOIDERS (Over-Responsive) with Rapid Blinking Key Characteristics: Blinks rapidly when OVERWHELMED or overstimulated Tries to "block out" excessive visual input Needs LOWER intensity, CALMING sensory input May increase blinking in busy, bright, visually complex environments Specific Activities: Morning: Dim, quiet wake-up (gradual lighting) Gentle stretching (5 minutes) Quiet breakfast in calm environment Soft, preferred breakfast textures Predictable morning routine (no surprises) Throughout Day: Schedule calming breaks EVERY 90-120 minutes Deep pressure: Weighted blankets, tight hugs, compression Gentle rocking or slow swinging Quiet spaces for retreat when overwhelmed
Reduced visual complexity (clear, organized spaces) Sunglasses for bright environments Key Strategy: PREVENT overstimulation through environmental modifications Provide CALMING input before dysregulation occurs Allow frequent breaks in quiet, dim spaces Red Flag: If blinking continues even in calm environment, may need eye exam or medical evaluation SIMPLE INDICATORS TO IDENTIFY SENSORY PROFILE SENSORY SEEKER Indicators (Check all that apply): ☐ Child is constantly moving, rarely sits still
☐ Seeks out intense experiences (spinning, crashing, jumping)
☐ Touches everything, often roughly
☐ Appears to have endless energy
☐ Doesn't notice when called unless very loud
☐ Blinking INCREASES when bored or inactive
☐ Blinking DECREASES when engaged in intense activity
☐ Seeks out bright lights, stares at screens for long periods
☐ Seems to "need" visual stimulation
☐ Becomes more active when under-stimulated
If 5+ boxes checked = Likely SENSORY SEEKER SENSORY AVOIDER Indicators (Check all that apply): ☐ Easily overwhelmed by noise, light, crowds, or touch
☐ Covers ears, squints eyes, or withdraws from sensory input
☐ Prefers quiet, calm, predictable environments
☐ Complains about bright lights, prefers dim spaces
☐ Becomes distressed with unexpected changes
☐ Blinking INCREASES in busy, bright, or chaotic environments
☐ Blinking DECREASES in calm, quiet, dim spaces
☐ Prefers solitary, calm activities
☐ May close eyes or look away in bright/busy places
☐ Seems overwhelmed by "normal" sensory levels If 5+ boxes checked = Likely SENSORY AVOIDER MIXED PROFILE Indicators: ☐ Seeks input in some areas but avoids in others
☐ Responses vary by situation and time of day
☐ May love movement but hate loud sounds
☐ Blinking triggers seem inconsistent
☐ Sometimes seems to seek, sometimes avoid
If mixed indicators = Likely MIXED PROFILE (most common) For mixed profile: Observe carefully which sensory systems are seeking vs. avoiding, and adjust accordingly for each system. IMPORTANT MEDICAL NOTE When to Seek Medical Evaluation: Rapid eye blinking should be evaluated by healthcare providers if: ☐ Blinking is NEW or sudden onset
☐ Accompanied by other tics or repetitive movements
☐ Child complains of eye pain, headaches, or vision problems
☐ Blinking persists even with consistent sensory diet (4+ weeks)
☐ Blinking interferes significantly with daily functioning
☐ Eyes appear red, irritated, or watery
☐ Child frequently rubs eyes
☐ Only one eye affected
☐ Started after head injury Recommended Evaluations: Pediatric Ophthalmologist - Rule out vision problems, dry eyes, eye strain

Hand and finger massage Arm positioning support massage Postural alignment work Shoulder and neck relaxation Manifestation: Positioning self to see specific reflections Redirect Activities: Reflection exploration station Mirror positioning experiments Reflection photography projects Body awareness through reflection Alternative Stimulation: Multiple mirror types Reflective surfaces exploration Controllable reflection devices Mirror ball or disco ball Regulation Through OT/SI: Body awareness activities Spatial orientation exercises Proprioceptive mapping Self-image development activities Massage Techniques: Full body awareness massage Positional proprioceptive input Postural alignment massage Body segment differentiation work GENERAL MASSAGE PROTOCOLS FOR VISUAL STIMMING Pre-Stimming Massage (Regulation/Prevention) Duration: 5-10 minutes Purpose: Provide regulating input to reduce stimming intensity or need Deep pressure massage on arms and legs Joint compression sequence (shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles)
Proprioceptive input through compression Grounding foot massage During Stimming Transition Massage Duration: 2-5 minutes Purpose: Facilitate transition away from stimming Hand massage with deep pressure Shoulder and neck tension release Grounding techniques with massage Calming rhythmic strokes Post-Stimming Massage (Recovery) Duration: 5-15 minutes Purpose: Help nervous system recover and regulate Full body compression massage Postural fatigue relief (especially neck, shoulders, back) Eye area gentle massage (if appropriate) Grounding and centering techniques Specific Massage Techniques by Sensory Profile For Sensory Seekers (Under-Responsive): Firm, deep pressure massage Quick, vigorous strokes Joint compression with resistance Alerting techniques (brisk movements) For Sensory Avoiders (Over-Responsive): Slow, gentle, predictable strokes Deep pressure without surprises Calming, rhythmic patterns Gradual pressure changes For Mixed Profiles: Assess current state before beginning
Adjust pressure and pace accordingly Watch for sensory cues and adjust Combination techniques as needed KEY OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY PRINCIPLES Sensory Diet Integration: Incorporate activities throughout the day, not just when stimming occurs Environmental Modifications: Create spaces that support regulation Scheduled Sensory Breaks: Prevent overstimulation through proactive breaks Heavy Work Activities: Provide proprioceptive input regularly (pushing, pulling, carrying) Replacement Behaviors: Teach functionally equivalent alternatives Graduated Exposure: Slowly increase tolerance or decrease dependence Self-Advocacy Skills: Teach recognition of sensory needs and communication Collaboration: Work with OT for individualized sensory integration programs This comprehensive guide provides alternatives and regulation strategies while respecting that stimming serves important neurological functions. The goal is not elimination but regulation and providing safer, more socially acceptable alternatives when needed.
COMPREHENSIVE SENSORY DIET PROTOCOL FOR VISUAL STIMMING With Individualized Planning Tables PART 1: UNDERSTANDING SENSORY DIETS What is a Sensory Diet? A sensory diet is a carefully designed, personalized activity schedule that provides the sensory input a child's nervous system needs to stay focused, organized, and calm throughout the day. Just as we need food throughout the day to maintain energy, children need sensory input throughout the day to maintain optimal arousal and regulation. Key Principles: Proactive, not reactive: Activities are scheduled BEFORE dysregulation occurs Individualized: Based on each child's unique sensory profile Consistent: Regular schedule helps nervous system anticipate and regulate Flexible: Adjusts based on daily needs and responses Integrated: Woven naturally into daily routines PART 2: IDENTIFYING YOUR CHILD'S SENSORY PROFILE
Quick Identification Guide SENSORY SEEKER (Under-Responsive) Simple Indicators to Identify: Always moving, rarely sits still Seeks out intense experiences (spinning, crashing, loud noises) Doesn't notice when called unless very loud Touches everything, often roughly Seeks out bright lights, stares at spinning objects for long periods Appears to have endless energy May seem "sensory hungry" - always wanting MORE Increases stimming when bored or under-stimulated Seeks out strong smells, tastes, visual input May engage in rough play without seeming to notice pain Visual Stimming Characteristics: Long duration (30-60+ minutes if uninterrupted) High intensity movements (fast spinning, rapid hand movements) Actively seeks out light sources, spinning objects Creates intense visual effects Becomes more active when under-stimulated May have multiple visual stims happening simultaneously
SENSORY AVOIDER (Over-Responsive) Simple Indicators to Identify: Easily overwhelmed by noise, light, crowds, or touch Covers ears, eyes, or withdraws from sensory input Prefers quiet, calm, predictable environments Complains about clothing tags, seams, textures Avoids messy play, certain food textures May be labeled as "picky" or "difficult" Becomes distressed with unexpected changes Prefers solitary, calm activities May have strong reactions to sensory input others don't notice Stimming increases when overwhelmed or over-stimulated Visual Stimming Characteristics: Shorter duration (1-10 minutes at a time) Lower intensity, more controlled movements Uses stimming to BLOCK OUT overwhelming environment Focuses on predictable, calming visual input Increases stimming in busy, visually complex environments May close eyes, squint, or look away from visual complexity MIXED PROFILE Simple Indicators to Identify:
May seek input in some sensory systems (movement, visual) but avoid in others (sound, touch) Responses vary by situation and time of day May seek proprioceptive input but avoid vestibular Might love visual stimulation but hate loud sounds Responses can seem contradictory Often the most common profile in autism/SPD Visual Stimming Characteristics: Varies by context and arousal level May seek certain types of visual input while avoiding others Duration and intensity fluctuate based on overall regulation May combine seeking behaviors with avoidance strategies PART 3: SENSORY DIET STRUCTURE Daily Schedule Framework A sensory diet should provide input: Every 90-120 minutes throughout the day for most children Every 60-90 minutes for sensory seekers Every 2-3 hours for sensory avoiders (with gentler input)
Before and after challenging activities or transitions As needed when dysregulation signs appear Types of Sensory Activities Alerting Activities (increase arousal) For: Under-stimulated, lethargic, unfocused states Examples: Jumping, fast music, bright lights, crunchy foods Organizing Activities (maintain optimal arousal) For: Maintaining focus and regulation Examples: Heavy work, rhythmic activities, structured tasks Calming Activities (decrease arousal) For: Over-stimulated, anxious, hyperactive states Examples: Deep pressure, slow rocking, dim lights, quiet spaces PART 4: MANIFESTATION-SPECIFIC SENSORY DIET TABLES How to Use These Tables: Identify your child's visual stimming manifestations from the document Find the corresponding manifestation in the tables below Note your child's sensory profile (Seeker, Avoider, or Mixed) Follow the recommended sensory diet for that specific manifestation Customize timing based on when stimming typically occurs
Track effectiveness and adjust as needed TABLE 1: LIGHT-BASED STIMMING SENSORY DIET Manifestation: Staring at Sunlight Through Windows DIY Tools for This Manifestation: Light table: Clear plastic bin + string lights underneath Prism set: Order inexpensive glass prisms online ($5-10) Fiber optic lamp alternative: Flashlight + clear plastic strips Sunset lamp: Red/orange LED bulb ($3) in existing lamp Manifestation: Rapidly Flipping Light Switches (10-50+ times) DIY Replacement Tool - Arcade Button Board: Materials needed: Wooden board or thick cardboard (12" x 12") 6-10 arcade push buttons ($1-2 each online) OR doorbell buttons Battery-operated LED lights (optional) Hot glue or screws Instructions: Drill/cut holes for buttons in board Mount buttons securely If desired, wire buttons to LED lights (simple circuit) Let child push buttons for satisfying click sensation
Place in accessible location as alternative to light switches Physical Technique to Interrupt: "Hand Sandwich" - When approaching switches, gently place your hands on either side of child's hand (like sandwich), apply firm pressure, and guide away while saying "Let's push THIS button instead" (redirect to appropriate toy). Manifestation: Watching Ceiling Fan Rotate DIY Alternative - Personal Desktop Spinning Drum: Materials: Clear plastic container with lid (food storage) Drill one hole in center of lid Insert pencil through hole as axle Fill container with glitter, small objects, or colored water Spin pencil to rotate drum Child can control speed and duration Physical Technique to Interrupt: "Neck Nudge" - Gently place hand on back of child's head/neck, apply light pressure downward while saying "Let's look down here" and guide gaze to eye-level activity. Follow immediately with proprioceptive input (hand squeezes, shoulder compression).
TABLE 2: OBJECT VISUAL STIMMING SENSORY DIET Manifestation: Lining Up Toys (50-200+ items) DIY Alternative - Functional Lining Activity: Create "Lining with Purpose" stations: Domino Rally: Lines lead to knock-down (satisfies lining + destruction) Pathway Creation: Line items to create "road" for cars/balls Color Sorting: Line by color into different baskets (functional end) Counting Line: Line up while counting (educational purpose) Physical Technique to Interrupt: "Hand Redirect" - Approach from side, gently place your hand over child's hand mid-lining, apply firm pressure, then guide hand to pick up all items and place in bin. Say "Time to build/play a different way." Immediately provide heavy work alternative (carrying the bin, pushing it across floor). Manifestation: Watching Spinning Washing Machine/Dryer (10-60+ minutes) DIY Alternative - Personal Washing Machine Simulator: Materials:
Clear plastic jar with lid (large pickle jar) Fill 1/3 with water Add glitter, small waterproof toys, food coloring Shake/rotate to create "washing" effect Child can control when it "runs" Time limit: 5 minutes, then put away Physical Technique to Interrupt: "Full Body Redirect" - Stand between child and machine, block view with your body, open arms wide and say "Crash into me!" or "Let's go jump!" Use your body as physical barrier while immediately redirecting to movement activity. The proprioceptive input of crashing/hugging helps with transition. Manifestation: Spinning Objects (Tops, Fidget Spinners, Plates) DIY Spinning Collection (Inexpensive): Paper plate spinner: Poke pencil through center, spin like dreidel CD/DVD spinners: On pencil or finger Bottle cap spinners: Glue two caps together, spin
Cardboard spinners: Cut circles, decorate, spin on toothpick Lazy Susan: Rotate items on it Physical Technique to Interrupt: "Hand Covering" - Gently place your hand completely over the spinning toy AND child's hand, stop the motion, maintain firm pressure for 3-5 seconds. This provides proprioceptive input. Then say "Let's spin OUR bodies instead!" and redirect to physical spinning activity. TABLE 3: SELF-GENERATED VISUAL STIMMING SENSORY DIET Manifestation: Hand Flapping While Watching Hands DIY Alternative - Ribbon Wands: Materials: Wooden dowel or stick (12" long) Ribbons, scarves, or fabric strips (3-4 feet long) Tape or staple ribbons to stick Child waves wand to create visual effect Satisfies visual need + provides arm movement Physical Technique to Interrupt: "Arm Sandwich" - Approach child, gently but firmly grasp both upper arms (creating pressure), hold for 3-5 seconds while making eye contact and saying "Let's use these strong arms to _____" (push, carry, throw). The bilateral compression provides regulating input. Immediately redirect to heavy arm work.
Manifestation: Rapid Eye Blinking (2-3 blinks per second) minutes: Dim, calm wake-up<br>- No bright lights initially<br>- Gentle eye rest<br>- Gradual light exposure | Morning routine | | Mid-Morning | - 15 minutes: Outdoor play (natural light, not screens)<br>- Visual breaks every 20 minutes<br>- Eye exercises: Near/far focusing<br>- Proprioceptive input to head/face (gentle) | - 10 minutes: Reduced visual complexity<br>- Sunglasses if needed<br>- Frequent eye rest breaks<br>- Calm environment | Every 60-90 minutes | | Screen Time | - Limit to 20-minute periods<br>- MANDATORY 10-minute break after<br>- Blink awareness games<br>- Alternative activities prepared | - Limit to 10-minute periods<br>- Dim screen brightness<br>- Breaks every 10 minutes<br>- Reduce screen time overall | During any screen use | | After Lunch | - 15 minutes: Non-visual activity (audio books)<br>- Eye rest with cool compress<br>- Outdoor time without visual focus<br>- Gross motor play | - 20 minutes: Complete visual rest<br>- Dark room rest period<br>- Gentle music<br>- No visual demands | Quiet time | | Mid-Afternoon | - 20 minutes: Active play without visual focus<br>- Vestibular input (swinging, spinning)<br>- Eye palming exercises<br>- Oral motor activities | - 15 minutes: Sensory break in dim area<br>- Eye rest<br>- Gentle activities<br>- Reduced visual complexity | Peak blinking time | | Pre-Dinner | - 10 minutes: Heavy work activities<br>- Face/head massage (gentle around eyes)<br>- Deep pressure activities<br>- NO screens | - 10 minutes: Continued dim environment<br>- Eye rest period<br>- Gentle activities<br>- Transition preparation | Evening transition | | Evening | - 20 minutes: Active play (not screen)<br>- Family activities without visual focus<br>- Oral input: Chewy foods<br>- Deep pressure activities | - 30 minutes: Progressive dimming<br>- Minimal visual demands<br>- Calming activities<br>- Eye rest protocol | Evening wind-down | | Bedtime | - NO screens 1 hour before bed<br>- Eye massage/acupressure<br>- Dark room<br>- Calming routine | - Complete darkness<br>- Eye rest protocol<br>- Gentle face massage<br>- White noise only | Sleep preparation |
Important Note: Rapid blinking may indicate visual strain, dry eyes, or tic disorder. Consult pediatrician and pediatric ophthalmologist. DIY Eye Rest Station: Soft cloth or eye pillow (can make from sock filled with rice) Dim corner with cushions Calming music Timer for 5-10 minute eye rest periods Physical Technique to Interrupt: "Gentle Eye Coverage" - With child's permission, gently place your cupped hands over their closed eyes (like palming technique), hold for 10-20 seconds. This provides darkness and warmth, often stops blinking pattern. Say "Let's give your eyes a rest." Follow with different sensory input (tactile, proprioceptive). Manifestation: Finger Fluttering in Front of Eyes DIY Alternative - Sensory Hand Gloves: Materials: Old gloves Fill fingertips with different textures (rice, beans, sand, cotton)
Seal each fingertip Child wears gloves and manipulates fingers Provides tactile + proprioceptive input to hands Alternative: Finger lights (LED rings on fingers) Physical Technique to Interrupt: "Hand Press" - Approach child, take both hands gently but firmly, press palms together in prayer position between YOUR hands (creating hand sandwich), hold firm pressure for 5-10 seconds. Say "Let's feel these strong hands." Then immediately redirect to heavy hand activity (pushing wall, carrying object, squeezing putty). Vestibular input (1.5 minutes): Spinning (controlled), jumping, swinging Calming heavy work (30 seconds): Slow pushes, carrying heavy item For Sensory Avoiders in Dysregulation: 5-Minute Emergency Protocol: Immediate environment reduction (30 seconds): Dim lights, reduce noise, clear visual clutter Deep pressure (2 minutes): Weighted blanket, tight hug, compression Slow rhythmic movement (1 minute): Gentle rocking, slow swinging Calming tactile (1 minute): Soft textures, gentle massage Quiet space (30 seconds): Allow retreat to calm area PART 9: PARENT/TEACHER TRACKING SHEET Daily Stimming & Regulation Tracking Use this to identify patterns and adjust sensory diet: DATE: ___________ CHILD'S NAME: ___________________ ┌─────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────┐ │ TIME │ STIMMING OBSERVED│ DURATION │ WHAT HAPPENED │ INTERVENTION │ │ │ (Type/Intensity) │ │ BEFORE? │ USED │ ├─────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────┤ │ │ │ │ │ │

When to Adjust: Increase intensity/frequency if child still seeking Decrease intensity if child seems overwhelmed Change timing if current schedule doesn't match needs Add variety if child losing interest Consult OT if no improvement after 4 weeks PART 11: SCHOOL/THERAPY COLLABORATION SHEET Share with Teachers/Therapists STUDENT NAME: ___________________ DATE: ___________________ PRIMARY VISUAL STIMMING MANIFESTATIONS: 1. _________________________________________________________________ 2. _________________________________________________________________ 3. _________________________________________________________________ SENSORY PROFILE: ☐ Seeker ☐ Avoider ☐ Mixed EFFECTIVE INTERVENTIONS AT HOME: - _________________________________________________________________ - _________________________________________________________________ - _________________________________________________________________ SENSORY DIET RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCHOOL: MORNING (Before 10 AM): Activity: _____________________________________________________________ Frequency: Every _____ minutes Duration: _____ minutes MID-MORNING (10 AM - Lunch): Activity: _____________________________________________________________ Frequency: Every _____ minutes Duration: _____ minutes AFTERNOON (After Lunch): Activity: _____________________________________________________________ Frequency: Every _____ minutes Duration: _____ minutes

Alternative provided: ______________________________________________ ENVIRONMENTAL ACCOMMODATIONS NEEDED: ☐ Preferential seating (away from windows/visual distractions) ☐ Access to fidgets (specify): _______________________________________ ☐ Movement breaks every _____ minutes ☐ Reduced visual complexity in workspace ☐ Dimmer lighting or natural light ☐ Access to sensory space/break area ☐ Other: _____________________________________________________________ COMMUNICATION: Parent contact for dysregulation: ____________________________________ Daily communication method: ☐ Note home ☐ Email ☐ App ☐ Phone PART 12: KEY REMINDERS FOR SUCCESS The Golden Rules of Sensory Diets: CONSISTENCY IS CRUCIAL - Implementation must be daily and regular PREVENTION OVER REACTION - Provide input BEFORE dysregulation INDIVIDUALIZE - Every child is unique; adjust to your child's needs BE PATIENT - Changes take 2-4 weeks of consistent implementation
TRACK & ADJUST - Use tracking sheets to identify what works COLLABORATE - Work with OT, teachers, therapists RESPECT THE STIMMING - It serves a purpose; we're adding alternatives, not punishing PROPRIOCEPTIVE INPUT IS KING - Heavy work helps almost everyone TIMING MATTERS - Provide input at optimal times for regulation FLEXIBILITY - Some days need more, some need less; adjust accordingly Remember: Stimming is communication and regulation The goal is not elimination but regulation and alternatives Sensory diets empower children to regulate themselves Consistent implementation yields the best results You are the expert on your child; trust your observations
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 2. AUDITORY STIMMING
Understanding Sensory Profiles Quick Identification Guide Sensory Seekers: Child constantly makes loud noises Turns up volume on devices Bangs, crashes, or drops things frequently Seeks out noisy environments Never seems to "get enough" sound Sensory Avoiders: Covers ears frequently Complains sounds are "too loud" Becomes distressed in noisy places Prefers quiet, calm environments May have meltdowns from unexpected sounds
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 2. AUDITORY STIMMING > A. Vocal/Verbal Stimming > Level 1: Non-Speech Vocal Sounds
Causation: Over-stimulated: Self-generated sound blocks overwhelming auditory input Under-stimulated: Creates needed auditory stimulation Sensitivity: Oral-motor need + auditory seeking; soothing vibratory sensation Sensory Profile: Seeker: Loud, varied sounds; extended periods (hours) Avoider: Soft, consistent sounds; self-soothing humming Mixed: Creates sound to mask unpredictable environmental noise Description: Producing sounds without linguistic content MANIFESTATION 1: Humming (constant, melodic or monotone) Physical Redirection Technique: "The Bubble Breath Reset" Stand facing the child at eye level Take their hands gently in yours Say: "Let's blow giant bubbles together!" Demonstrate: Deep breath in through nose (4 counts), exhale slowly through rounded lips (6 counts) Make exaggerated bubble-blowing motions together Repeat 3-5 times until humming decreases This redirects the oral-motor need while regulating breathing DIY Alternative Tool: Homemade Kazoo
Materials: Empty toilet paper roll, wax paper, rubber band Assembly: Cover one end with wax paper, secure with rubber band, poke 3-4 small holes along the side Use: Child hums into open end (creates vibration sensation like humming but with purpose) Cost: Free from household items Alternative Stimulation (Inexpensive/Household): For Sensory Seekers: Vibrating toothbrush ($3-5) Let child press against cheeks, lips, chin while buzzing Provides oral-motor input + vibration Use for 2-3 minutes every hour DIY Humming Tube Use: Empty paper towel roll Child hums into it against wall/door Creates echo effect that amplifies feedback Teaches volume control: "loud hum" vs "quiet hum" Crunchy Foods Carrot sticks, apples, pretzels, crackers Chewing provides oral-motor input that satisfies same need Offer every 45-60 minutes
For Sensory Avoiders: Soft Humming Cloth Take a soft washcloth, roll it Child holds it against lips while humming softly Muffles sound, provides proprioceptive input Use during calm-down time Whisper Practice Create "whisper humming" game Child hums so quietly only they can hear it Reduces volume while maintaining stimulation Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "The Buzzing Bee Circuit" (15-20 minutes) Jump on pillows/couch cushions (2 min) - heavy work Hum loudly while doing jumping jacks (2 min) Push against wall while humming (2 min) - proprioceptive Roll like a log across floor humming (2 min) Crash into pillows humming (2 min) End with quiet humming in cozy corner (5 min) Why it works: Provides intense input to satisfy seeking, then gradually reduces
For Sensory Avoiders: "Quiet Voice Training" (10 minutes) Sit in calm, quiet space Practice different hum volumes with visual chart: Picture of mouse = tiny hum Picture of cat = medium hum Picture of lion = big hum Practice mouse humming (child's goal) Reward with preferred quiet activity Sensory Integration Therapy: Oral-Motor Protocol: Morning (before school): 5 minutes of oral activities Blow bubbles (2 min) Drink thick smoothie through straw (2 min) Chew gum or chewy tube (1 min) Midday: Quick oral input Crunchy snack Water bottle with straw (must suck hard) Evening: Calming oral input Warm soup through straw Gentle face massage (see massage section) Vestibular Integration: Swing before humming typically occurs (10 min) Rocking chair during homework These provide calming input that reduces need to hum
Massage Techniques: Oral-Facial Massage (5 minutes, 2-3x daily): Wash hands thoroughly Use unscented lotion or coconut oil Outside mouth: Gentle circles around lips (30 seconds each direction) Light pressure down from nose to chin (10 times) Tap gently around mouth with fingertips (30 seconds) Cheeks: Press palms against cheeks, gentle circles (1 minute) Tap along jaw line (30 seconds) Purpose: Provides proprioceptive input to oral area, reducing need for self-stimulation Neck and Shoulder Release (3 minutes): Child sits, adult stands behind Gentle pressure on shoulders, squeeze and release (1 min) Fingertips massage up neck to base of skull (1 min) Gentle head rolls (30 sec each direction) Purpose: Releases tension that may cause increased humming MANIFESTATION 2: Throat Clearing Repetitively (every 30-60 seconds)
Physical Redirection Technique: "The Lion Breath" Interrupt gently: "Let's do lion breath!" Have child kneel, hands on thighs Deep breath in through nose Exhale forcefully through wide-open mouth, stick tongue out, say "HAAA" Make fierce lion face Repeat 5 times This gives throat the strong sensation it's seeking DIY Alternative Tool: Straw and Water Bottle Materials: Sports water bottle with straw or narrow opening, water Use: Child must suck hard to get water (creates throat/swallowing sensation) Add: Few drops of lemon juice for extra throat sensation Cost: $2-5 for reusable bottle Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Bubble Blowing ($1 bubble solution) Every 30 minutes, blow 10-20 bubbles Requires throat control, provides oral-motor work Use thick bubble solution (more resistance) Thick Smoothies
Blend: frozen banana, yogurt, peanut butter Drink through narrow straw Swallowing thick liquid provides strong throat input Offer 2-3 times daily Chewy Foods Bagels, dried mango, fruit leather, gum Chewing and swallowing provides throat sensation Alternative to clearing For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Throat Comfort Warm (not hot) herbal tea with honey Sip slowly, focus on soothing sensation 2-3 times daily Soft Swallowing Practice Small sips of water every 10 minutes Teaches gentle swallowing vs. throat clearing Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Straw Olympics" (10-15 minutes) Cotton Ball Race: Blow cotton balls across table through straw Thick Shake Challenge: Drink thick smoothie through thin straw Bubble Mountain: Blow into cup of soapy water with straw Paper Pickup: Use straw to suck up small paper pieces and transfer
Whistle Practice: Make different sounds through straw Schedule: Before times when throat clearing typically increases For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Throat Training" (5-10 minutes) Practice gentle swallows with water Humming gently (vibrates throat softly) Whispering practice Blowing feathers gently Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Circuit (3x daily): Morning: Crunchy cereal, thick yogurt through straw, chewable vitamin Lunch: Chewy protein (chicken/beef), apple slices, water through straw Evening: Crunchy vegetables, smoothie, gum (if age-appropriate) Proprioceptive Input (before throat clearing episodes): Wall pushes (30 seconds) Chair push-ups (10 times) Heavy work (carry books, groceries) These calm nervous system, reducing stimming Massage Techniques: Throat and Neck Massage (3-4 minutes): IMPORTANT: Never press directly on throat/windpipe Technique: Stand behind seated child Very gentle fingertip massage along sides of neck (avoid front)
Small circles from behind ears down to shoulders (1 min each side) Gentle stretches: tilt head to each side, hold 10 seconds Shoulder squeezes (reduces tension that causes clearing) Jaw Release Massage (2 minutes): Locate jaw muscles (in front of ears) Gentle circular massage (30 seconds each side) Open mouth slightly, massage again Reduces overall oral-facial tension MANIFESTATION 3: Clicking Tongue Against Teeth Physical Redirection Technique: "The Tongue Workout" Stop the clicking by offering alternative: "Let's exercise our tongue!" Exercises: Touch tongue to nose (try 10 times) Touch tongue to chin (try 10 times) Move tongue side to side outside mouth (10 times) Roll tongue (if they can) in and out Lick lips in full circle (10 times) Provides similar oral-motor input without clicking sound
Do whenever clicking starts DIY Alternative Tool: Tongue Texture Board Materials: Small piece of cardboard (4"x4"), glue different textures Textures to glue: sandpaper square, felt piece, bubble wrap piece, aluminum foil piece, corrugated cardboard strip Use: Child licks different textures (provides tongue stimulation) Laminate or cover with clear packing tape for hygiene Wipe with antibacterial wipe between uses Cost: Free from household scraps Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Lollipops or Hard Candy ($2-3) Long-lasting (Dum-Dums, Jolly Ranchers) Tongue must work to lick/move candy Provides prolonged oral-motor input Use as "tongue tool" during high-clicking times Sour Candy ($1-2) Warheads, sour gummies, lemon drops Strong taste provides intense tongue stimulation Reduces need for clicking Limit to 2-3 per day (dental health) DIY Flavored Ice Chips
Freeze juice in ice cube trays Add popsicle stick halfway through freezing Child licks ice (strong tongue sensation) Cost: Pennies per serving Oral Motor Tools (household): Chewable straws Coffee stirrer sticks to hold between teeth Rubber pencil grips to chew For Sensory Avoiders: Soft Foods for Tongue: Yogurt, pudding, applesauce Spoon against tongue provides gentle input Less intense than clicking Gentle Licking Activities: Popsicles (slow licking) Soft ice cream Teaches controlled tongue movement Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Tongue Obstacle Course" (10 minutes, 2x daily): Station 1: Lick peanut butter off roof of mouth (1 min) Station 2: Use tongue to move small candy around mouth without chewing (2 min) Station 3: Lick different textures on texture board (2 min)
Station 4: Hold tongue depressor (popsicle stick) between teeth and lips (2 min) Station 5: Blow bubbles through wand (3 min) Purpose: Provides intense tongue work that satisfies seeking behavior For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Tongue Play" (5-8 minutes): Soft foods only: pudding, yogurt, smoothie Gentle tongue stretches (see redirection technique) Quiet mouth time with soft chewy tube Calming jaw massage Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Schedule: Every 90 minutes: Oral input activity Chew gum (if age 5+) Crunchy snack Drink through straw Chewy tube (ARK Therapeutics, $8-15, or DIY: clean rubber tubing) Before high-clicking times: Preventive input Heavy work: push/pull activities (5 min) Oral-motor: thick smoothie (2 min) Full Body Calming (reduces clicking): Weighted lap pad during seated activities (DIY: fill pillowcase with rice, sew shut)
Deep pressure: squeeze hands, arms, legs Rocking: rocking chair or therapy ball Massage Techniques: Comprehensive Oral-Facial Massage (5-7 minutes): Preparation: Child sits comfortably, relaxed External technique: Warm hands, use tiny amount of coconut oil Circles around mouth (1 min clockwise, 1 min counter-clockwise) Press gently on "smile lines" from nose to mouth corners (30 sec) Gentle taps all around mouth with fingertips (1 min) Massage jawline from chin to ears (1 min each side) Gentle pressure under chin (30 sec) Internal technique (if child allows): Wash hands thoroughly Use food-grade glove or finger cot Gentle pressure inside cheeks with index finger (30 sec each side) Gently massage gums (if teeth brushing is tolerated) Purpose: Provides deep proprioceptive input to mouth area
Neck-to-Mouth Calming Massage (3 minutes): Start at shoulders, work up neck to jaw Slow, firm strokes (calming to nervous system) End with gentle face strokes from forehead to chin Do before bed to reduce next-day clicking MANIFESTATION 4: Popping Lips Repeatedly Physical Redirection Technique: "Lip Work Station" When popping starts, offer: "Lip exercise time!" Quick Exercises: Press lips together hard, count to 10 (repeat 5x) Say "Mmm" with closed lips while pressing (10x) Blow raspberries (10x) Fish face: suck cheeks in (hold 5 sec, repeat 10x) Kiss hand loudly (10x) Blow kisses in all directions (20x) Provides lip proprioception without annoying sound Takes 2-3 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Lip Whistles/Kazoo Materials: Small piece of wax paper (1"x2"), fold in half Use: Hold folded edge between lips, blow gently (creates vibration like lip popping)
Alternative: Empty thread spool, blow across end Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Bubble Gum ($1-2) Blow bubbles repeatedly Provides lip work + proprioceptive input Make it a game: "How big can you blow?" Age-appropriate: 4+ years Lip Balm ($1-3) Strong flavors: mint, cherry, cinnamon Apply frequently (every 15 min during high-popping times) Provides lip sensation + taste Child focuses on licking lips instead of popping DIY Lip Activities: Blow painting: Diluted paint on paper, blow through straw to spread Feather blow: Blow feather, keep it in air as long as possible Whistle practice: Learning to whistle provides lip work Vibrating Lip Tools: Electric toothbrush (off) - child holds against lips ($3-5) Vibrating teether (if younger child, $5-8) For Sensory Avoiders:
Gentle Lip Care: Soft lip balm, unscented Gentle application (child does it themselves) Teaches awareness without over-stimulation Quiet Lip Activities: Sipping through straw (gentle lip press) Soft food on lips to lick off (yogurt, pudding) Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Lip Power Hour" (15-20 minutes, 2x daily): Bubble Blowing Station (5 min) Regular bubbles Blow through different sized wands Catch bubbles with wand (lip control) Resistance Blowing (5 min) Blow into balloon (creates resistance) Blow cotton balls through obstacle course Blow ping pong ball across water Lip Exercises (5 min) Hold button between lips and string (proprioceptive) Press lips around popsicle stick, pull gently Smile wide/pucker tight (alternate 20x) Cool Down (5 min) Drink thick smoothie through straw Chew gum
Gentle lip massage For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Lip Awareness" (8-10 minutes): Light touch around lips with soft brush (1 min) Apply lip balm (child does own application) Gentle blowing: feathers, tissue paper (3 min) Drinking through straw (3 min) Quiet time with preferred activity Sensory Integration: Prevention Protocol (every 60-90 min): Before popping typically occurs: Crunchy snack (apple, carrots, pretzels) Chewy snack (dried fruit, fruit leather) Heavy work task (push wall, carry items) Oral-motor toy (chewy tube, 2-3 min) Environmental Modifications: Provide vibration elsewhere: vibrating cushion, massager Proprioceptive input: weighted lap pad, compression clothing Reduce need for self-regulation: calmer environment overall Massage Techniques: Lip and Perioral Massage (4-5 minutes, 3x daily): Best times: Morning (before school), after school, before bed Technique:
Wash hands, small amount of coconut oil or unscented lotion Upper lip massage: Index fingers, start at center, massage outward to corners (10x) Gentle circles above upper lip (30 sec) Light tapping with fingertips (30 sec) Lower lip massage: Repeat same pattern on lower lip Gentle downward strokes under lower lip (10x) Full mouth circles: Both index fingers, circle around entire mouth (1 min each direction) Lip press: Gently press lips between thumb and index finger Work from center to corners (20 sec each side) Purpose: Deep proprioceptive input reduces need for lip popping Face-to-Shoulder Integration Massage (5 minutes): Connects oral-facial area to body for better regulation Start at lips, stroke down to jaw (10x) Jaw to neck (10x) Neck to shoulders (10x)
Shoulder squeeze and release (1 min) Return to gentle face strokes Purpose: Helps child feel whole-body connection, reducing isolated oral stimming 3. MANIFESTATION 5: Making "ahhh" or "eeee" Sounds Sustained Physical Redirection Technique: "The Volume Controller Game" When sustained sounds start, engage immediately Activity: "Let's play DJ! I'll show you volume levels!" Hand signals: Hand at floor = whisper "ahh" (level 1) Hand at waist = medium "ahh" (level 5) Hand at shoulders = loud "ahh" (level 10) Move your hand up and down, child matches with sound Gradually bring hand lower and lower End at whisper level Teaches volume control while allowing the sound Takes 2-3 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Singing/Humming Tube Materials: 2-3 feet of PVC pipe or pool noodle with hole through center (cut pool noodle if needed), duct tape (if sharp edges)
Assembly: If PVC, tape edges for safety. Pool noodle ready to use Use: Child makes sustained sounds into one end while other end is against wall, door, or floor Creates echo/vibration feedback Teaches directed sound vs. random vocalizations Cost: $3-5 at hardware store Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Kazoo or Harmonica ($1-5) Provides sustained sound + vibration Requires specific mouth position Can make "ahh" sounds through instrument Purposeful vs. random vocalization Voice Recording Device/App (Free phone app) Record child's sustained sounds Play back immediately Creates awareness + auditory feedback Turn into game: "Make longest 'ahh' sound" Singing Activities: Teach sustained notes in songs Children's songs with long vowels ("Old MacDonald" = "E-I-E-I-Ooooo") YouTube sing-alongs Makes stimming purposeful Vibrating Tools: Harmonica ($5-10)
Vibrating toy microphone ($10-15) DIY: Wax paper on comb, hum against it For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Sound Making: Whisper singing Soft "shh" sounds Gentle humming into pillow (dampens sound) Visual Sound Representation: Sound meter app (shows volume visually) Teaches child to see how loud they are Goal: keep in "green zone" Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Sustained Sound Circuit" (20 minutes): Breath Work (5 min) Blow up balloons (long exhalation) Blow pinwheels (sustained breath) Blow bubbles (controlled breath) Vocal Exploration (5 min) Make animal sounds (cow = long "moooo") Sing favorite songs with long notes Make sound effects (siren = "eeeee") Heavy Work (5 min) Push wall while making sound Carry heavy items while singing Jump while vocalizing Provides proprioceptive input with vocal stimming
Quiet Down (5 min) Gradually quieter vocalizations Whisper singing Silent lip movements Deep breathing For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Voice Play" (10 minutes): Soft humming (not sustained "ahh") Quiet songs Whisper practice Focus on control, not volume Sensory Integration: Vocal Regulation Schedule: Morning: Heavy proprioceptive work (reduces vocal stimming) Animal walks: bear crawl, crab walk (5 min) Push/pull: furniture moving, carrying books (5 min) This provides body input that may reduce need for vocal input Midday: Scheduled vocal outlets 5-minute "loud time" outside or designated room Child can be as loud as they want Then practice "quiet time" (whisper voices) Evening: Calming input Gentle rocking Soft music Massage (see below) Vestibular-Auditory Integration: Swing while singing (10 min) - vestibular input often reduces vocal stimming
Rock in rocking chair during homework Trampoline with songs (1 bounce = 1 word of song) Massage Techniques: Laryngeal Area and Chest Massage (5 minutes): IMPORTANT: Never press directly on throat Technique: Child lies down comfortably Chest massage: Flat palms on upper chest (below collarbones) Slow, firm strokes outward to shoulders (10x) Circular massage on chest muscles (1 min) Neck sides (avoid front): Very gentle fingertip massage on neck sides (30 sec each side) Work from behind ears down to shoulders Purpose: Relaxes muscles involved in vocalization Whole Body Calming Massage (10 minutes): Reduces overall need for vocal self-regulation Order: Shoulders and upper back (3 min) - firm pressure Arms: squeeze and release from shoulder to hand (1 min each) Hands: press firmly on palm, massage fingers (1 min each)
Legs: squeeze and release from thigh to foot (1 min each) Feet: firm pressure on soles (1 min each) Pressure: Firm and slow (activates parasympathetic nervous system) Best time: Before bed or after school (high-stimming times) MANIFESTATION 6: Screeching or Squealing Physical Redirection Technique: "The Pressure Release Valve" When screeching starts, immediately intervene with physical grounding Technique: Place firm hands on child's shoulders Make eye contact (if tolerated) Say: "Let's do strong arm pushes!" Guide child to wall Both push against wall together, hard as possible Count to 10 while pushing Release and shake arms out Repeat 3-5 times Provides intense proprioceptive input that often satisfies the need for intense vocalization The physical exertion redirects the energy DIY Alternative Tool: Screaming/Squeal Pillow
Materials: Old pillow or stuffed animal, fabric markers Decoration: Let child decorate with "loud voice" pictures Use: Designated pillow for screaming/squealing into Place in multiple locations (bedroom, playroom, car) Rule: "Big sounds go in the pillow, not in the air" Cost: Free (repurposed item) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Whistles ($1-3 for pack) Provide variety: slide whistle, train whistle, sports whistle Creates loud, high-pitched sound without vocal strain Can be scheduled: "Whistle time" 5 minutes every 2 hours Outdoor use preferred Musical Instruments - High Pitched Recorder/flute ($5-10) Toy saxophone ($8-15) Slide whistle ($3-5) Allows high-pitched sound creation purposefully DIY Sound Makers: Balloon squeaks: Let air out slowly (makes squealing sound) Styrofoam rub: Two pieces rubbed together (high-pitched squeak) Glass rim: Wet finger on glass rim (creates high tone)
Voice Amplifier/Microphone ($10-20 or phone app - free) Child can screech into microphone Hears own voice amplified Satisfies sensory need with control For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Alternatives: Silent scream practice (mouth open, no sound) Whisper screaming (teaches modulation) Humming instead of screeching Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Screech-to-Calm Protocol" (15-20 minutes, 2-3x daily): High Energy Release (5 min) Jump on trampoline or pillows while making loud sounds Run in place with vocal sounds Dance wildly to loud music Purpose: Releases pent-up energy that drives screeching Structured Loud Time (5 min) Designated "screaming zone" (outdoor or specific room) Set timer: "You have 5 minutes to be AS LOUD as you want" Screech, yell, squeal freely When timer ends: "Now we use quiet voices"
Purpose: Gives permission for the behavior in controlled way Heavy Work Transition (5 min) Immediately after loud time: Push-ups against wall (20x) Carry heavy books across room (10 trips) Squeeze therapy putty as hard as possible (2 min) Purpose: Proprioceptive input calms nervous system Quiet Activities (5 min) Weighted lap pad Gentle rocking Quiet book or calm toy Purpose: Practice being calm after being loud For Sensory Avoiders: "Volume Control Training" (10 minutes): Use visual volume chart (1-10, with pictures) Practice sounds at each level Reward staying at levels 1-3 Teach: "This sound is a 10. Can you make it a 5? A 3?" Sensory Integration: Preventive Sensory Diet (throughout day): Every 60-90 minutes: Heavy work break Carry laundry basket Push toy shopping cart filled with books
Animal walks (bear crawl, crab walk) Wall pushes Why: Proprioceptive input reduces need for vocal stimming Before high-risk times: Intensive proprioceptive "loading" 10 minutes of intense physical activity Examples: trampoline, crashing into pillows, tug-of-war Purpose: Pre-emptively satisfies sensory need Auditory-Vestibular Connection: Screeching often accompanies vestibular seeking Provide vestibular input proactively: Swinging (10 min, 3x daily) Spinning in office chair (10 spins each direction) Rolling down hills or across floor Often eliminates screeching behavior Deep Pressure Protocol: Compression vest or tight-fitting clothing (reduces arousal) Weighted lap pad during seated activities Body squeeze: Squeeze pillow between body and wall Purpose: Calming pressure reduces need for high-arousal behaviors Massage Techniques: Intensive Calming Massage (15 minutes, 2x daily - morning and evening): Purpose: Deep pressure massage significantly reduces screeching by calming the nervous system
Preparation: Quiet room, dim lights Use unscented massage oil or lotion Child lies on stomach Back Massage (5 min): Flat palms, firm pressure Long strokes from shoulders to lower back (20x) Circular motions on each side of spine (2 min) "Piano playing" with firm fingertips down back (1 min) More long strokes to finish (20x) Shoulder and Neck (3 min): Firm squeezes on shoulders (squeeze-hold-release, 20x) Thumb pressure on tight spots (hold 10 seconds each) Gentle neck massage on sides (never front) Arms and Hands (3 min): Squeeze down each arm from shoulder to hand (10x each arm) Press firmly on palms (30 sec each) Pull gently on each finger (5 sec each) Legs and Feet (4 min): Squeeze down each leg from hip to foot (10x each)
Firm pressure on soles of feet (1 min each) Press on each toe (5 sec each) Pressure Level: Should be firm - child should feel "squished" not tickled Response: Child often becomes very calm, sometimes sleepy "Emergency Calm-Down" Quick Massage (3 minutes): Use when screeching is imminent or happening: Firm shoulder squeezes (30 sec) Press palms together hard, child pushes against your hands (30 sec) Squeeze up and down arms quickly (30 sec) Firm pressure on top of head (gently press down 10 sec) Hand massage (squeeze each finger, 1 min) Deep breaths together while doing massage Purpose: Quick sensory reset to interrupt screeching pattern Oral-Facial Massage for Vocal Stimming (5 minutes): Often screeching involves tension in face/jaw Technique: Massage temples in circles (1 min)
Jaw massage: locate muscle in front of ears (1 min each side) Cheek massage: circles on cheeks (1 min) Chin and under-chin: firm pressure (1 min) Best timing: After screeching episode (prevents continuation) MANIFESTATION 7: Growling or Grunting Physical Redirection Technique: "Animal Power Moves" When growling/grunting starts, immediately engage Activity: "I hear you growling! Let's be strong animals!" Bear Crawl: Crawl on hands and feet, growling allowed (1 min) Gorilla Walk: Bent over, arms swinging, grunt allowed (1 min) Lion Pose: Yoga pose with deep breathing and roar (1 min) Elephant Trunk: Swinging arms, low groaning sounds (1 min) Rest Pose: Child's pose (yoga), quiet breathing (1 min) Channels the low vocal sounds into purposeful activity Proprioceptive input from animal movements often stops stimming
DIY Alternative Tool: Growl Box Materials: Cardboard box (shoebox size), decorate with "monster" or "animal" theme Use: Child growls/grunts into box opening Sound is muffled but child gets sensory feedback Can take to school in backpack Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Low-Frequency Sound Tools: Didgeridoo (toy version, $10-15) Tuba/trombone sounds on YouTube (play and imitate) Bass guitar or low notes on keyboard Provides low-frequency vibration similar to growling Vibrating Tools: Electric toothbrush - hold against cheeks, throat (external), chest ($5-10) Massager - handheld, use on jaw, neck, chest ($10-20) Creates similar vibratory sensation DIY Low Sound Makers: Tissue paper on comb: Hum low notes against it (vibration) PVC pipe: Hum into long pipe (amplifies low sounds) Cardboard tube: Hit on leg while vocalizing (percussion + vocalization)
Growl-Friendly Activities: Play "monster" or "dinosaur" games (growling is appropriate) Read books with animal sounds, emphasize growls "Dinosaur stomp" - stomp and growl together For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Low Sounds: Soft humming (low pitch) Gentle "ohhh" sounds Focus on soft, controlled vocalizations Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Deep Sound and Heavy Work Circuit" (20 minutes): Heavy Work Station (5 min) Push/pull heavy objects Carry weighted items Can growl/grunt during these activities (natural pairing) Purpose: These activities naturally involve low vocalizations Deep Pressure Station (5 min) Roll heavy therapy ball over body Squeeze under couch cushions Bear hugs from adult Can make low sounds during compression Purpose: Deep pressure satisfies sensory need Vocal Play Station (5 min) Explore different growl types: dog, bear, lion, monster
Practice loud vs. quiet growls Growl into different materials (pillow, box, tube) Purpose: Makes stimming purposeful and controlled Calming Station (5 min) Heavy blanket or weighted lap pad Deep breathing with low hums (not growls) Quiet activity with oral motor tool (chewy) Purpose: Transition to calm state For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Vocalization" (10 minutes): Soft humming (low tones okay) Gentle animal sounds (not aggressive) Reading stories with expression (varied tones) Singing gentle songs Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor and Proprioceptive Protocol: Target: The connection between oral-motor and whole-body proprioception Morning Routine (15 min): Crunchy breakfast (toast, cereal, apple) Heavy work: make bed, carry backpack Oral motor: chew gum or chewy tube (2 min) Purpose: Starts day with appropriate input Throughout Day (every 90 min):
Chewy snack (bagel, dried fruit, jerky) Heavy work task (carry books, push chairs) 2-3 min chewy tool Purpose: Prevents growling by satisfying needs proactively Before High-Risk Times: 10 minutes intensive proprioceptive work 5 minutes oral-motor activities Purpose: "Loading" the sensory system prevents stimming Jaw and Throat Connection: Growling involves jaw and throat tension Jaw exercises (5 min, 3x daily): Open mouth wide, close (20x) Move jaw side to side (20x) Pretend to chew big bites (20x) Chew actual resistive foods Purpose: Releases tension that may cause growling Massage Techniques: Jaw and Throat Release Massage (7 minutes): Purpose: Growling creates tension in jaw and throat; this releases it Jaw Muscle Massage (3 min): Locate masseter muscle (in front of ears, clench teeth to find it)
Place index and middle fingers on muscle Circular massage (1 min each side) Ask child to open mouth slightly, massage again (1 min each side) Gentle up-and-down strokes on jaw (30 sec each side) Throat Area (2 min): NEVER press on front of throat Massage sides of neck only Gentle circles from behind ears down to collarbones (1 min each side) Very light touch down front of neck (avoid pressure) Under Chin (1 min): Firm pressure under jaw/chin area Circular massage Press gently up toward jaw Face Connection (1 min): Stroke from jaw down to shoulders (10x) Helps connect areas and release overall tension Chest and Throat Vibration Release (5 minutes): Purpose: Growling creates vibration in chest/throat; this provides alternative input
Child lies on back Chest percussion: Cupped hands, gently "tap" on chest (like burping baby) 30-60 seconds, creates gentle vibration Chest massage: Flat palms, firm circular massage on upper chest (2 min) Stroke outward from center to shoulders (20x) Neck sides: Gentle massage from jaw to shoulders (1 min each side) Finish: Light fingertip tapping all over chest/neck area (1 min) Creates pleasant vibration sensation Full Body "Grounding" Massage (10 minutes): Purpose: Growling often indicates high arousal; this calms entire system Use before bed or after school Firm, slow strokes all over body Focus on: Back: long strokes (5 min) Arms and legs: squeeze and release (3 min) Feet: firm pressure (2 min) Child often stops growling significantly after this massage
Best practice: Daily massage routine MANIFESTATION 8: Buzzing Lips Physical Redirection Technique: "Lip Buzz to Breathing" When buzzing starts, gently interrupt Technique: "I hear your lips buzzing! Let's buzz into our hands!" Cup hands together making small opening Buzz lips into hands (creates feedback sensation) Then: "Now let's breathe the buzzing away" Deep breath in (nose), long exhale with lip buzz (purposeful) Repeat 10 times Gradually transition to exhale without buzz Transforms stim into breathing exercise Takes 2-3 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Buzz Bottle Materials: Empty plastic bottle (16-20 oz), water, dish soap Assembly: Fill 1/4 with water, add squirt of dish soap, secure lid Use: Remove lid, buzz lips against bottle opening (creates bubbles in liquid) Visual feedback + buzzing sensation
Cost: Free (household items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Kazoo ($1-2) Perfect lip-buzzing tool Creates purposeful sound Can play songs, makes it functional Portable (pocket-sized) Harmonica ($5-10) Requires controlled lip buzzing Produces musical tones Teaches lip position and control More sophisticated than kazoo DIY Buzzing Tools: Wax paper + comb: Hold wax paper over comb, buzz lips against it (vibration + sound) Balloon lips: Lips against inflated balloon, buzz (vibration feedback) Straw buzz: Buzz lips while holding straw (then blow through it) Musical Exploration: Brass instrument videos: Show how trumpets/trombones work (lip buzzing!) Practice trumpet buzzing: Lips together, buzz like brass player Turns stim into music education Bubble Activities: Bubble wands (must buzz/blow correctly) Bubble mixture: 1 cup water, 2 tbsp dish soap, 1 tbsp glycerin (makes stronger bubbles)
Bubble tricks (bubbles inside bubbles) For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Lip Activities: Soft lip massage (self-administered) Lip balm application (awareness without buzzing) Gentle blowing (no buzz) Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Lip Buzz Orchestra" (15-20 minutes, 2x daily): Warm-Up (3 min) Lip stretches: smile wide, pucker tight (20x) Lip rolls: blow air through lips loosely Gentle lip taps with fingers Buzz Exploration (5 min) Buzz at different pitches (high, medium, low) Buzz at different volumes (loud, medium, quiet) Buzz into different objects: Hands (cupped) Bottle with water Cardboard tube Against balloon Purpose: Makes buzzing purposeful and controlled Musical Buzzing (5 min) Kazoo playing Try to buzz songs (Mary Had a Little Lamb, etc.) Buzz rhythm patterns (buzz-buzz-pause-buzz) Purpose: Functional skill development
Oral-Motor Work (4 min) Chew tough foods (bagel, apple, jerky) Drink thick liquid through straw Chewy tube (2 min) Purpose: Satisfies oral-motor need Quiet Transition (3 min) Gentle lip massage Lip balm application Quiet breathing exercises Purpose: Calm down from activity For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Lip Exploration" (10 minutes): Very gentle lip touches (feather, cotton ball) Lip balm (teaches awareness) Soft blowing (feather, tissue paper) Whisper-breathing (lips almost closed) Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Sensory Diet: Morning (upon waking): Vibrating toothbrush (2 min) Crunchy breakfast Oral-motor exercises (see above) Every 60-90 minutes: Chewy snack or chewy tool Drink through straw (creates lip seal) 1-2 min of lip activities (bubbles, kazoo, etc.) Before times when buzzing typically occurs: 5 min intensive oral-motor input Heavy work (5 min)
Weighted lap pad Evening: Calming oral input (warm soup through straw) Lip massage No intense activities before bed Vestibular-Oral Connection: Lip buzzing often accompanies vestibular seeking Strategy: Provide vestibular input proactively Swing daily (10-15 min) Spin on office chair (10 spins each way) Rock in rocking chair during seated activities Result: Often reduces or eliminates lip buzzing Massage Techniques: Comprehensive Lip and Perioral Massage (6-8 minutes, 3x daily): Best times: Morning, after school, before bed Preparation: Wash hands thoroughly Tiny amount coconut oil or unscented lotion Child sits comfortably, relaxed Technique: Upper Lip (2 min): Index fingers, start at center of upper lip Firm circular massage moving outward to corners (30 sec) Return to center, press firmly and hold (10 sec)
Repeat massage outward (30 sec) Gentle tapping all around upper lip with fingertips (30 sec) Light feathery strokes (desensitizes, 30 sec) Lower Lip (2 min): Same pattern as upper lip Pay attention to center of lower lip (often most buzzing happens here) Firmer pressure here (child should feel "squished" feeling) Around Mouth (2 min): Both index fingers, start at center below nose Massage in large circles around entire mouth (1 min clockwise, 1 min counter-clockwise) Get close to lips but also massage the area around them Lip Press (1 min): Gently press lips between thumb (outside) and index finger (inside mouth if allowed) Work from center to corners Firm pressure (proprioceptive input) Hold pressure 5 sec in each spot Finish (1 min):
Light tapping all around mouth Gentle strokes outward from lips Deep breath together Quick "Buzzing Emergency" Massage (2 minutes): Use when buzzing is actively happening: Firm pressure on both lips simultaneously Press lips together (externally) with fingers (30 sec) Quick circular massage around mouth (30 sec) Press firmly on cheeks (30 sec) Lip stretches (smile/pucker) with gentle resistance from your fingers (30 sec) Purpose: Immediate sensory input that often stops the buzzing Face-to-Body Integration Massage (5 minutes): Purpose: Connects oral area to whole body (reduces isolated stimming) Start with lip massage (1 min) Stroke from lips down to jaw (10x) Jaw down to neck (10x) Neck down to shoulders (10x) Shoulder squeeze and hold (30 sec) Arms: squeeze down to hands (1 min each)
Hand massage (1 min each) Result: Child feels more "whole body" awareness, less focus on lips alone MANIFESTATION 9: Whistling Same Tune Repeatedly Physical Redirection Technique: "Whistle to Wind-Down" When repetitive whistling starts, acknowledge it Activity: "I hear you whistling! Let's turn it into a game!" Whistle Simon Says: "Whistle high" (demonstrate) "Whistle low" "Whistle loud" "Whistle soft" "Whistle fast" "Whistle slow" "Now... whistle silence!" (lips in position, no sound) Do 10-15 commands Gradually increase "silence" commands End with quiet breathing, lips relaxed Teaches control while honoring the need to whistle Takes 3-5 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Whistle Collection Box Materials: Small box or bag, collect different whistles Contents: Slide whistle (pitch changes) Train whistle Sports whistle Pea-less whistle (different sound)
DIY: Cut straws at angles (different pitches) Use: When child feels need to whistle, offer whistle from box Rotates, prevents obsessive focus on one tune Cost: $5-10 for collection Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Structured Whistle Time: Set timer: "You can whistle for 5 minutes" When timer ends: "Now it's quiet time" Gradually reduce time (5 min → 3 min → 1 min) Teaches delayed gratification Whistle Alternatives: Recorder ($5-8) - similar lip position, purposeful music Penny whistle/tin whistle ($10-15) - requires similar oral-motor control Ocarina ($10-20) - different sound, same concept All provide similar oral-motor feedback with purpose Whistle Games: "Name That Tune" - whistle songs, others guess "Whistle While You Work" - whistle while doing chores (makes it functional)
"Whistle Language" - create whistle codes with family Purpose: Makes stimming a social skill Breath Control Activities: Blow out candles (teaches breath control like whistling) Blow pinwheels at different speeds Blow cotton balls across finish line Purpose: Similar oral-motor without repetitive tune For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Alternatives: Humming softly (no whistling) Lip position practice without sound Visual music (watch music videos, no sound making) Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Whistle Skills Workshop" (15-20 minutes, 1-2x daily): Breath Control Station (5 min) Blow up balloons (requires similar lip position and breath) Blow through straw into water (bubbles) Blow cotton balls through obstacle course Purpose: Provides similar oral-motor without annoying repetitive tune Musical Whistle Station (5 min) Learn new whistle tunes (not repetitive single tune)
Whistle scales (do-re-mi-fa-so-la-ti-do) Whistle rhythm patterns (not melodies) Whistle with backing tracks (makes it purposeful) Purpose: Makes whistling educational Lip Work Station (5 min) Lip strengthening exercises: Press lips around popsicle stick, pull gently Lip push-ups: press lips together, release (30x) Hold button between lips attached to string, pull gently Drink thick liquid through straw Chewy tube Purpose: Satisfies oral-motor need differently Quiet Transition (5 min) Lip massage Quiet breathing Calm activity with hands (playdough, fidget) Purpose: Shifts focus away from lips For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Sound Exploration" (10 minutes): Soft humming (instead of whistling) Quiet singing Listening to music (not making it) Silent lip movements (pretend whistling) Sensory Integration: Whistling Prevention Protocol: Target: Provide sufficient oral-motor and auditory input to prevent whistling
Morning Routine: Crunchy breakfast Oral-motor exercises (5 min) Heavy work (make bed, carry backpack) Brief whistle time allowed (2-3 min) Throughout Day (every 90 min): Chewy snack or chewy tool Drink through straw 1-2 min purposeful whistling (scale, specific song) OR alternative (kazoo, harmonica) Heavy work task Before High-Risk Times: If whistling typically happens during homework/quiet time: 10 min active play before sitting Chewy tool available during work Whistle breaks every 20 minutes (1 min allowed) Evening: Calming input (no whistling practice before bed) Massage (see below) Auditory Sensory Diet: Whistling is auditory seeking behavior Provide alternative auditory input: Background music during activities White noise or nature sounds Audiobooks Singing songs together Purpose: Fills auditory need without whistling Massage Techniques: Lip and Jaw Release Massage (5-7 minutes, 2-3x daily):
Purpose: Whistling creates lip and jaw tension; this releases it Lip Massage (2 min): Circular massage around lips (1 min) Press and hold center of lips (10 sec) Gentle pulling/stretching of lips (20 sec) Light tapping around lips (30 sec) Jaw Massage (2 min): Locate jaw muscle (in front of ears) Circular massage (1 min each side) Child opens mouth slightly, massage again Cheek Massage (2 min): Palms on cheeks, circular massage (1 min) Fingertips massage inside of cheeks (if child allows) Gentle cheek presses (30 sec) Finish (1 min): Light strokes from lips outward to ears Gentle face taps Deep breath together Oral-Facial Desensitization Massage (5 minutes): Purpose: Sometimes whistling is due to oral sensitivity; this reduces it Use varied texures:
Soft brush (makeup brush) Washcloth (textured) Fingers (firm pressure) Technique: Stroke around mouth with each texture (30 sec each) Gradually increase pressure Include lips directly (if tolerated) Progression: Start with least sensitive areas (cheeks) Move toward more sensitive (lips) If child resists, backoff Do: 2x daily for 2-3 weeks Result: Often reduces oral stimming behaviors Full Face and Neck Calming Massage (8-10 minutes): Best time: Before bed (prevents nighttime/morning whistling) Forehead (1 min): Fingertips, stroke from center outward (20x) Gentle circles on temples Eyes/Nose (1 min): Light pressure on bridge of nose Gentle circles around eye sockets (not eyes themselves) Cheeks and Jaw (3 min): Full palm circular massage on cheeks Jaw muscle massage (detailed above) Mouth/Lips (2 min): Detailed lip massage (as above)
Neck (2 min): Stroke from jaw down to shoulders (20x) Gentle neck massage (sides only) Finish (1 min): Light feathery touches all over face Very calming to nervous system
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 2. AUDITORY STIMMING > A. Vocal/Verbal Stimming > Level 2: Echolalia (Repetitive Speech)
Causation: Over-stimulated: Predictable verbal patterns reduce anxiety Under-stimulated: Creates auditory + motor planning stimulation Sensitivity: Processing language through repetition; communication attempt Sensory Profile: Seeker: High volume, frequent scripting throughout day Avoider: Soft, self-directed scripting for comfort Communication: Using scripts functionally despite appearing stimming Description: Repeating words, phrases, or scripts MANIFESTATION 1: Immediate Echolalia (Repeating Just-Heard Phrases Instantly) Physical Redirection Technique: "Echo to Answer Bridge" 1.
