When immediate echolalia occurs, don't ignore or punish Technique: You say: "Do you want juice?" Child echoes: "Do you want juice?" You respond: "I hear you saying 'Do you want juice?' Let's change it! Say 'I want juice'" (model with exaggerated emphasis on "I") Guide their hand to their chest when saying "I" If child still echoes: Offer choice: "Show me - point to juice or milk"
Accept non-verbal response Celebrate: "Great communication!" Gently shapes echolalia toward functional communication Physical element: Use hand-over-hand to help child point to themselves when using "I" DIY Alternative Tool: Communication Choice Board Materials: Piece of cardboard, print or draw pictures of common items/activities Sections: Foods, Activities, Feelings, People Laminate or cover with clear contact paper Add velcro dots Use: Instead of echoing questions, child points to answer Advanced: Create sentence strips "I want ___" (child adds picture) Cost: $5 for laminating sheets, otherwise free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Echo Games (purposeful echolalia): "Echo Canyon": Speak into cardboard tube, child echoes (makes it a game) "Telephone Game": Whisper phrase, child repeats (functional echoing) "Robot Repeat": Adult says phrase, child "robot repeats" in robot voice (adds element of play)
Purpose: Makes echolalia purposeful and fun Recording Devices: Voice recording app (free on phone) Child records self saying phrases Plays back immediately Provides auditory feedback Can practice saying NEW things (not just echoing) Verbal Routines: Teach songs/rhymes with repetition "Call and response" songs Example: Adult: "Who let the dogs out?" Child: "Woof, woof, woof, woof!" Makes echolalia social and purposeful For Sensory Avoiders (Communication-Focused): Visual Supports: Picture cards for communication Written choices Reduces pressure to speak immediately Processing Time: Count to 10 after asking question (gives time to formulate response) Use visual timer Reduces anxiety that causes echolalia Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Playful Language Circuit" (20-25 minutes, 2x daily): Heavy Work First (5 min) Jumping, crashing, pushing Calms body before language work
Many children echo less when proprioceptively regulated Echo Play Station (5 min) Purposeful echoing games (see above) Echo with actions (echo + clap, echo + jump) Makes echolalia fun and intentional Language Expansion (7 min) Script: Adult says "I want snack" Child echoes: "I want snack" Adult: "Great! Now add which snack!" (models: "I want crackers") Practice expanding echoed phrases Celebrate attempts, even if imperfect Choice Practice (5 min) Offer choices for everything "Crackers or pretzels?" (hold up both) If child echoes: Gently shape "Which one? Point!" Accept pointing, signing, any communication Sensory-Language Integration (3 min) Sensory bin (rice, beans, water beads) Practice labeling: "I feel..." (textures) "I found..." (objects in bin) Language + sensory = more engagement For Communication-Focused: "Communication Building Blocks" (15-20 minutes):
Use visuals extensively (less pressure to speak) Honor ALL communication (pointing, nodding, echolalia) Gently model without pressure Celebrate small changes in echo patterns Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Before Language Activities: Theory: Oral-motor regulation improves speech control Protocol (5 min before language activities): Crunchy snack Drink through straw Chewy tube (2 min) Lip/jaw exercises Result: Often reduces echolalia Proprioceptive Regulation for Language: Heavy work before communication demands: Carry heavy books Wall pushes Chair push-ups During communication: Weighted lap pad Fidget tool in hand Allows body to be calm while language is stressed Reduce Auditory Overload: Less language = less echolalia Strategies: Use simple, short phrases One instruction at a time Pause between sentences Reduce background noise during conversations Purpose: Makes language processing easier
Massage Techniques: Oral-Motor Preparatory Massage (5 minutes, before language activities): Purpose: Prepares oral-motor system for speech, reducing echolalia Facial Warm-Up (2 min): Gentle face massage (forehead to chin) Wake up facial muscles Lip and Mouth Focus (3 min): Circular massage around lips (1 min) Jaw massage (1 min) Cheek massage, inside if allowed (1 min) Do this: Before school, before therapy, before homework Calming Body Massage for Overall Regulation (10 minutes, 2x daily): Theory: Calm body = better language control Full body massage (see previous detailed instructions) Focus on: Back (calming long strokes) Arms and hands (grounding) Legs and feet (security) Timing: After school (when echolalia typically increases), before bed Quick "Communication Prep" Massage (2-3 minutes): Use before asking questions/making demands:
Shoulder squeeze (30 sec) Arm squeeze down to hands (30 sec) Hand massage (1 min) One deep breath together Then ask question/make request Purpose: Helps child be more regulated and available for communication MANIFESTATION 2: Delayed Echolalia (Repeating Movie/TV Lines Hours or Days Later) Physical Redirection Technique: "Script to Story Bridge" When child starts scripting movie lines, engage immediately Technique: Child says: "To infinity and beyond!" (Toy Story script) You respond: "Oh! You're thinking about Toy Story! Let's act it out with our bodies!" Actions: Jump high (like Buzz flying) - 10 jumps Pretend to be Woody (walk like cowboy) - 1 minute Freeze like toys when humans come - practice 5 times Crash into pillows (like movie action scene) Then redirect: "Now let's tell me about YOUR day using YOUR words"
If child continues scripting: "Show me with actions" (accept non-verbal) Transforms verbal script into physical play Provides proprioceptive input that often reduces need to script DIY Alternative Tool: Script Book/Journal Materials: Notebook, markers, stickers Purpose: Designated place for scripts Use: When child starts scripting, offer: "Let's write/draw that in your script book!" Child writes favorite lines Draws pictures of scenes Can revisit book during "script time" (scheduled) Contains the behavior to specific times/places Cost: $2-3 for notebook Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Scheduled Script Time (15-20 min, 2-3x daily): Set timer: "This is script time!" Child can repeat any scripts they want When timer ends: "Script time is over, now it's [activity] time" Gradually reduce duration Purpose: Honors the need while setting boundaries
Props and Acting: Provide costumes, props from favorite shows Act out scripts (makes it purposeful play) Invite others to participate Transform stim into imaginative play Recording Scripts: Voice memo app (free) Child records favorite scripts Can listen during designated times Creates library of scripts Purpose: External storage reduces need to repeat verbally Script Writing: Encourage child to write own scripts "What happens AFTER this scene?" Create new stories with favorite characters Purpose: Moves from repetition to creativity Video Making: Use tablet/phone camera Child acts out scripts on video Can watch later (designated times) Makes scripting a productive activity For Communication-Focused: Script Translation: When child scripts, ask: "What are you feeling?" Scripts often communicate emotions Example: Child scripts: "Elsa runs away" (Frozen)
Might mean: "I feel overwhelmed" Help child learn to recognize this connection Visual Emotion Charts: Match scripts to emotions "When you say that line, how do you feel?" Gradually build emotional vocabulary Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "From Script to Play" Protocol (30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Heavy Work Opening (5 min) Proprioceptive input calms nervous system Reduces compulsive scripting Activities: jumping, crashing, pushing Scheduled Script Time (10 min) "This is YOUR time to say anything you want!" Child scripts freely Adult listens without judgment Can video record if child wants Purpose: Fills the need Script to Action (10 min) Take scripts and make them physical Example with "Lion King": "Simba runs" = run in place "Circle of Life" = spin in circles
"Stampede scene" = jump on couch cushions Purpose: Channels verbal into physical Expansion Practice (5 min) Adult models expanding scripts: Child: "Hakuna Matata" Adult: "Yes! That means no worries! What do YOU have no worries about?" Gently encourage original thought Accept any attempt, even more scripting Celebrate small variations in scripts For Communication-Focused: "Script Detective" Activity (15-20 minutes): Identify the Script (5 min) When child scripts, write it down Ask: "What show/movie is that from?" Build awareness Find the Feeling (5 min) "How does [character] feel in that scene?" "How do YOU feel right now?" Connect script to emotion Alternative Expression (5 min) "Let's think of another way to say that feeling" Model: "You could say 'I feel worried' or 'I need space'"
Practice new phrases Choice Practice (5 min) Offer: "You can say the script OR the new phrase" Honor both choices Gradually child may choose new phrases Sensory Integration: Vestibular-Language Connection: Theory: Scripting often accompanies vestibular seeking or regulation needs Protocol: Before scripting typically occurs: Swing (10-15 min) Spin activities (office chair, playground) Rocking (rocking chair during activities) During high-script times: Therapy ball to sit on (gentle bouncing while scripting) Rocking while allowing scripts Result: Vestibular input often reduces scripting significantly Proprioceptive Loading: Heavy work before language demands: Morning: 15 min heavy work before school After school: 15 min heavy work before homework Evening: 10 min heavy work before dinner Types: Pushing/pulling heavy objects Carrying groceries, laundry, books Animal walks Wall pushes
Result: Calm, regulated body = less compulsive scripting Auditory Environment Management: Reduce script triggers: Limit screen time (less exposure to scripts) If child watches show, watch together and discuss (makes it interactive, not just input) Provide alternative auditory input (music, audiobooks, nature sounds) Purpose: Less script input = less script output Massage Techniques: Pre-Language Activity Massage (7-10 minutes): Best time: Before situations requiring functional communication (school, social events, therapy) Purpose: Calms nervous system, making functional language more accessible Shoulders and Upper Back (3 min): Firm squeezes on shoulders (20x) Circular massage on upper back Reduces tension that increases scripting Arms to Hands (2 min): Squeeze down arms (10x each) Firm palm massage Finger pulls (5 sec each finger) Grounding effect Legs to Feet (2 min):
Squeeze down legs (10x each) Firm foot massage Full body grounding Finish: Head to Toe Connection (2 min): Light touch from head down spine to feet Helps child feel "whole" and present Reduces dissociative scripting "Script Interrupt" Quick Massage (3-5 minutes): Use when scripting is excessive/problematic: Interrupt gently: "Let's take a massage break" Quick sequence: Shoulder squeeze (30 sec) Hand massage (1 min each hand) Foot massage (1 min each foot) Deep pressure down arms and legs (1 min) Often child stops or significantly reduces scripting Then redirect to activity Bedtime Calming Massage for Next-Day Prevention (15 minutes): Purpose: Deep calm before sleep = less scripting next day Full body massage (detailed in previous sections) Extra time on: Back (long, slow strokes)
Hands (detailed massage) Feet (deep pressure) Use slow, rhythmic movements Can pair with calming music or white noise Child often falls asleep during or shortly after Result: Better sleep = better regulation = less scripting MANIFESTATION 3: Repeating Own Words (Palilalia) Physical Redirection Technique: "Word to Movement" When child repeats own words, acknowledge and redirect Technique: Child says: "I want juice, I want juice, I want juice" You respond: "I heard you say 'I want juice' THREE times! Let's jump three times!" Jump together (or clap, stomp, etc.) Then: "Now let's use one-time words. Say 'juice please' ONE time" Model saying it once Immediately honor request (give juice) Positive reinforcement: "Great one-time words!" Creates awareness of repetition Pairs language with movement (proprioceptive input)
DIY Alternative Tool: One-Time Word Visual Materials: Index card, draw 1 mouth, write "ONE TIME WORDS" Laminate or cover with contact paper Use: When child starts repeating, show card Point to one mouth Say: "One-time words" Can carry in pocket/backpack Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Counting/Rhythm Integration: When child repeats, count repetitions together "Let's count! One, two, three... you said it three times!" Make it a math/counting game Then: "Now let's say it ONE time" Purpose: Adds awareness without shame Echo Microphone (controlled): Toy microphone with echo effect ($10-15) Or phone app with echo Child speaks into it Hears repetition from device (not self) Satisfies need for repetition externally May reduce self-repetition Percussion with Words: Each word = one drum beat
If child repeats, they drum multiple times Creates awareness through another modality Can practice "one beat" (one word) For Communication-Focused: Processing Time Support: Palilalia often indicates processing difficulty Strategies: Give more time to formulate thoughts Visual supports Reduce pressure to speak quickly May reduce repetition Completion Phrases: When child repeats: "I want... I want... I want..." Gently complete: "...juice? Crackers? What do you want?" Helps child finish thought Reduces stuck repetition Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "One-Time Word Practice" (15-20 minutes, 2-3x daily): Proprioceptive Opening (5 min) Heavy work (calms nervous system) Jumping, crashing, squeezing Often reduces verbal perseveration Repetition Games (5 min) Make repetition purposeful: "Repeat after me: jump, jump, jump" (do action 3x) "Now say AND do it ONE time: jump!" (1x)
Practice controlled repetition vs. one-time Builds awareness and control Communication Practice (5 min) Request items using "one-time words" Visual reminder (card) visible Immediate reinforcement when successful If child repeats: Gentle redirect, try again Transition Activity (5 min) Quiet activity with oral-motor input Chewy tube (hard to talk while chewing) Reduces verbal behavior Calming For Communication-Focused: "Thought Completion Support" (10-15 minutes): Visual sentence strips: "I want ____" with picture choices Child completes sentence once Reduces verbal searching/repetition Processing time practice: Ask question Count to 10 silently (give processing time) Accept answer even if repeated Alternative communication: Pointing Sign language for common words Written words (if able) Reduces pressure on verbal system Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Regulation: Theory: Mouth/speech area needs sensory input Protocol (every 60-90 minutes):
Chewy snack or chewy tool (2-3 min) Drink through straw Oral-motor exercises Result: Satisfied oral-motor system = less verbal perseveration Body-Language Integration: Pair all language with movement: Jumping while talking Bouncing on ball during communication Walking during conversation Theory: Movement often regulates and organizes speech Result: May reduce repetition Reduce Verbal Demands: Less pressure = less perseveration Strategies: Accept non-verbal communication Don't force responses Allow processing time Reduce question frequency Environment becomes less verbally stressful Massage Techniques: Oral-Facial Release Massage (7-10 minutes, 3x daily): Purpose: Palilalia may involve oral-facial tension Jaw Focus (3 min): Locate jaw muscles (in front of ears) Firm circular massage (1 min each side) Child opens/closes mouth slowly during massage Releases jaw tension Mouth and Lips (3 min):
Circular massage around mouth Gentle lip massage Under-chin firm pressure Face Connection (2 min): Massage from jaw to ears Ears to neck Neck to shoulders Releases overall tension Finish (2 min): Light tapping all over face Gentle face strokes Deep breath together Calming Full-Body Massage (15 minutes, 1-2x daily): Best times: After school (high perseveration time), before bed Purpose: Overall nervous system regulation Follow detailed full-body massage from previous sections Slow, rhythmic movements Firm pressure (calming) Effect: Significantly reduces all verbal stimming behaviors Hand Massage for Grounding (5 minutes, as needed): Use when palilalia is active: Take child's hands Firm massage on palms (1 min each) Squeeze each finger (10 sec each) Press firmly on pressure points Pull gently on fingers
Often interrupts verbal perseveration cycle Grounding effect helps child become more present MANIFESTATION 4: Scripting Entire Scenes from Media (5-30+ minutes) Physical Redirection Technique: "Scene to Movement Story" When extended scripting begins, interrupt gently with action Technique: "I hear you telling that story! Let's act it out with BIG movements!" Assign movements to each part: Character 1 dialogue = jumping Character 2 dialogue = spinning Action scenes = running in place Quiet scenes = slow motion Do movements together while child scripts After 5 minutes: "Great! Now let's do something else. What do you want to do?" Offer heavy work activity Allows scripting while adding proprioceptive input Makes it active rather than passive Easier to transition from (movement to new movement)
DIY Alternative Tool: Script Schedule Board Materials: Poster board, velcro, picture cards Sections: "Script Time" and "Other Activity Time" Pictures of activities in each section Use: Visual schedule showing when scripting is allowed Child can see: "Script time at 3pm for 15 minutes, then playtime" Teaches scripting has a time and place Cost: $5 for velcro dots Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Structured Script Sessions (20-30 min, 1-2x daily): Designated script time with rules: Specific location (script corner) Specific duration (timer) Props available (puppets, costumes) When timer ends, transition to active play Purpose: Contains behavior, prevents all-day scripting Video Self-Modeling: Record child acting out scripts Watch together Discuss: "What happened in YOUR video?" Gradually helps child see self as actor, not just scripter
Can create "movie library" of their performances Script Journals: Beautiful notebook for favorite scripts Child writes or draws scenes Can illustrate Becomes cherished item Externalizes scripts (reduces need to repeat verbally) Interactive Script Play: Find others to participate Assign roles Example: Child scripts Frozen Child is Elsa Sibling/parent is Anna Perform together Transforms solo stim into social play Script Variations: Encourage changing the script: "What if Elsa went to the beach instead?" "What if Anna had superpowers too?" Start small, celebrate creativity Moves from rigid repetition to flexible thinking For Communication-Focused: Script-to-Life Connection: When child scripts: "That reminds me of when YOU..." Connect script themes to child's real experiences Example: Child scripts: "Simba lost his dad" You: "Yes, and you felt sad when grandpa moved away"
Helps child use memories instead of scripts Emotion Identification: "How does [character] feel in this scene?" "Have you ever felt that way?" Builds emotional vocabulary May reduce need for scripts to express feelings Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Script Integration Circuit" (40-45 minutes, 1x daily): Heavy Work Opening (10 min) Intensive proprioceptive input Jumping, crashing, pulling, pushing Calms system before language focus Structured Script Time (15 min) Designated time and space Props and costumes available Can video record Full permission to script Timer visible Purpose: Fills the bucket Script-to-Movement (10 min) Act out script with big movements Jump scenes Crash scenes Spin scenes Transitions from verbal to physical Alternative Expression (10 min) Art about the script (draw favorite scene) Build with blocks (make setting)
Playdough (make characters) Channels obsession into creative outlets Calm Transition (5 min) Quiet sensory activity Weighted lap pad Gentle rocking Prepares for next activity For Communication-Focused: "From Script to Communication" Program (30 minutes, daily): Identify the function (10 min) When child scripts, ask yourself: "What is this communicating?" Common functions: Anxiety (scripts predictable dialogue) Excitement (shares favorite things) Processing (works through themes) Connection (shares interests) Teach alternative expression (10 min) Model alternative ways to express the function: Anxious → "I feel worried" Excited → "I really like [topic]" Processing → Talk about feelings directly Connection → "Let's watch together" Practice and reinforce (10 min) Role play using new phrases Celebrate any functional communication Allow scripts but also introduce alternatives Sensory Integration:
Intensive Proprioceptive Protocol: Theory: Extended scripting often indicates under-regulated nervous system Daily Schedule: Morning (before school): 20 min heavy work Animal walks Carrying heavy items Pushing/pulling Every 2 hours during day: 10 min proprioceptive break Wall pushes Chair push-ups Carry/organize items After school (high-script time): 30 min intensive Playground (climbing, swinging, sliding) Trampoline Crash pad play Evening: 15 min calming proprioceptive Gentle rocking Joint compressions Massage Result: Well-regulated body may reduce scripting by 50-70% Vestibular Integration: Scripting often accompanies vestibular seeking Provide vestibular input proactively: Swing daily (15-20 min minimum) Spinning activities (controlled) Rolling, tumbling Rocking chair available all day Many children stop scripting when vestibular needs are met Environmental Modifications: Reduce script triggers: Limit screen time (1 hour per day maximum)
When watching, watch together and discuss Introduce variety (not same shows repeatedly) Increase novelty: New experiences New places New activities Reduces perseveration on familiar scripts Massage Techniques: Comprehensive Regulation Massage (20-25 minutes, 1-2x daily): Best times: After school (before peak scripting), before bed Purpose: Deep nervous system regulation to reduce compulsive scripting Back (7 min): Long, firm strokes head to toe (50x) Circular massage on each side of spine (2 min) Firm pressure down spine with thumbs (1 min) More long strokes (20x) Shoulders, Arms, Hands (5 min): Firm shoulder squeezes (2 min) Squeeze down arms (1 min each) Detailed hand massage (1 min each) Legs and Feet (5 min): Squeeze down legs from hip (1 min each) Detailed foot massage (2 min each)
Firm pressure on soles Neck and Head (3 min): Gentle neck massage (sides only) Scalp massage Face massage Full Body Integration (3 min): Light strokes from head to toes (20x) Helps child feel whole and integrated Often dramatically reduces dissociative scripting Quick Grounding Massage for Active Scripting (5 minutes): Use when child is in extended scripting episode: Interrupt gently: "Pause for a minute, let's do squeeze massage" Technique: Firm squeezes shoulders (30 sec) Squeeze down arms to hands (1 min) Press firmly on palms (30 sec each) Squeeze down legs to feet (1 min) Press firmly on feet (30 sec each) Deep pressure hug (30 sec) Often breaks scripting cycle Can then redirect to different activity Preventive Daily Massage Routine (15 minutes, morning or evening):
Purpose: Consistent daily massage prevents excessive scripting Same time every day (creates routine) Full body massage (described above) Focus on calming, regulating Consistent deep pressure = regulated nervous system = less scripting Many parents report 60-80% reduction in scripting with daily massage routine MANIFESTATION 5: Repeating Questions Instead of Answering Physical Redirection Technique: "Question to Action Response" When child repeats question, provide physical grounding first Technique: You ask: "What do you want for snack?" Child repeats: "What do you want for snack?" You respond: "Let's show with our bodies! Point to what you want!" (take child's hand, guide to choices) If still no response: "Let's do jumping choice! Jump for crackers!" (demonstrate) Child jumps or doesn't Try next: "Jump for pretzels!"
Accept non-verbal communication Physical grounding: Hand on shoulder while asking again: "Show me, point" Reduces pressure of verbal response Provides proprioceptive input (calming) Teaches alternative communication DIY Alternative Tool: Answer Choice Board Materials: Piece of cardboard, divided into sections For common questions, provide visual answer options Example for "What do you want for snack?": Pictures: crackers, cheese, apple, pretzels Child points instead of answering verbally Laminate for durability Can make multiple boards for different question types Cost: Free (use magazine pictures) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Question Games (purposeful repetition): Play games where repeating questions is the goal: "Echo Game": Adult asks question, child echoes, then adult answers "Interview Game": Child is reporter, asks same question to different people Makes repetition functional and fun
Physical Response System: Teach: "You don't have to say words, show me!" For yes/no: Jump for yes, stomp for no For choices: Point, walk to it, bring it to adult Reduces verbal pressure For Communication-Focused: Processing Time Support: Question repetition often = processing difficulty Strategies: Ask question Count to 20 silently (give time) Offer visual choices Simplify question Example: Original: "What do you want to do this afternoon?" Simplified: "Park or home?" (with pictures) Visual Question-Answer Scripts: Create visual scripts: Picture of question being asked Arrow Picture of answer options Practice following script Teaches: question → answer format Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Question-Answer Circuit" (20 minutes, 2x daily): Heavy Work Opening (5 min) Calms nervous system Jumping, pushing, pulling
Regulated body = better communication Question Practice with Actions (7 min) Ask simple question If child repeats: "Show me with your body!" Practice physical responses: Yes = jump No = sit down "I want this" = point Reward all communication attempts Visual Support Practice (5 min) Use choice boards Practice pointing to answers Gradually reduce visual supports (if able) Calm Transition (3 min) Oral-motor input (chewy, drink through straw) Weighted lap pad Quiet activity For Communication-Focused: "Alternative Communication Training" (15 minutes, daily): Identify communication barriers (5 min) Why does child repeat questions? Processing difficulty? Doesn't understand? Anxious? Verbal apraxia? Determine root cause Teach alternatives (7 min) Sign language for common words Picture exchange Pointing Gestures Any communication is valid Practice in low-pressure settings (3 min)
Preferred activities Familiar people Gradually generalize Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Before Language Demands: Prepare mouth/speech system: 5 min oral-motor activities before: Mealtimes (asking questions common) Homework time Social situations Activities: Chew crunchy/chewy foods Drink through straw Lip/jaw exercises Chewy tube Result: Better speech motor control Reduce Verbal Demands Globally: Less questions = less repetition Strategies: Offer choices before child must ask Use statements instead of questions Example: Instead of "What do you want?", say "Here are crackers and cheese" Accept non-verbal communication Lower pressure environment Proprioceptive Integration Throughout Day: Every 60-90 min: Heavy work (5-10 min) Calms nervous system Better availability for communication Less verbal perseveration Massage Techniques: Pre-Communication Massage (5-7 minutes): Use before situations requiring answering questions: Oral-Facial Preparation (3 min):
Face massage (forehead to chin) Lip and mouth massage Jaw massage Wakes up speech system Body Grounding (3 min): Shoulder squeezes Arm squeezes to hands Hand massage (firm pressure) Grounding for better presence Finish (1 min): Deep pressure hug One deep breath together Calming Massage for Communication Anxiety (10 minutes): If question repetition stems from anxiety: Back (4 min): Long, slow strokes Very calming Arms and Hands (3 min): Squeeze and release Grounding hand massage Legs and Feet (3 min): Squeeze and release Firm foot pressure Overall effect: Reduces anxiety, may improve communication Hand Massage for Immediate Support (3 minutes): Use during or after question-repeating episode: Hold child's hands Firm palm massage (1 min each) Squeeze each finger (10 sec each)
Press pressure points Grounding and calming Often helps child MANIFESTATION 6: Reciting Commercials, Jingles, or Songs Verbatim Physical Redirection Technique: "Jingle to Jive" When child begins reciting jingle/commercial, join in with movement Technique: Child starts: "Like a good neighbor, State Farm is there!" You respond: "I hear that commercial! Let's dance it!" Create dance moves for each line: "Like a good neighbor" = wave to neighbor "State Farm" = jump twice "is there" = point Do together 2-3 times Then transition: "Great dancing! Now let's do [heavy work activity]" Wall pushes (20x) Carry something heavy across room Allows the jingle while adding proprioceptive input Makes it interactive instead of perseverative Easier to transition from movement to new movement DIY Alternative Tool: Jingle Jar
Materials: Jar or container, popsicle sticks, markers Write favorite jingles/songs on sticks Rule: Can pick ONE jingle from jar at designated times After reciting once, jingle goes back in jar Choose different one next time Limits repetition, adds element of choice/control Cost: Free (household items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Scheduled Jingle Time (10-15 min, 2-3x daily): Set timer Child can recite any jingles/commercials Can perform them (act out) Can record them (video/audio) When timer ends: "Jingle time is over" Transition to physical activity Purpose: Contains the behavior Create Original Jingles: Use obsession productively "Let's make a jingle about YOUR day!" "Let's make a commercial for your favorite toy!" Start with copying structure, fill in new words Example: Original: "I'm lovin' it" (McDonald's)
New: "I'm playing it!" (about their toy) Moves from repetition to creativity Jingle Performance Stage: Designate area as "stage" Child performs jingles there (not everywhere) Can use toy microphone Family can be "audience" at designated times Makes it purposeful entertainment, not perseveration Music Substitution: Replace commercial jingles with actual songs Teach children's songs with similar catchy rhythms Provide access to kid-friendly music Channels need for repetitive music into more appropriate content Rhythm Instruments: Percussion instruments ($10-20 set) Play rhythm of jingle without words Drums, shakers, tambourine Transforms verbal into musical/physical For Communication-Focused: Jingle-to-Communication Bridge: When child recites jingle, explore why: "That's a food commercial! Are you hungry?" "That's about toys! Do you want to play?" Teach: "Instead of the jingle, you can say 'I'm hungry'"
Helps child connect jingle to underlying need Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Musical Movement Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Heavy Work Opening (5 min) Intensive proprioceptive input Jumping, crashing, pushing Calms system before language focus Jingle Performance (10 min) Designated stage/area Child performs favorite jingles With props, costumes, instruments Can video record Family participates as audience Purpose: Makes it social and purposeful Jingle Transformation (7 min) Take jingle, change it: Different words (keep melody) Different melody (keep words) Different speed (fast/slow) Different volume (loud/whisper) Teaches flexibility Musical Instruments (5 min) Play jingle rhythms on instruments No words, just music Channels verbal into physical Quiet Transition (3 min) Calm sensory activity Weighted lap pad Gentle rocking Oral-motor input (chewy) For Communication-Focused:
"From Jingle to Language" Program (20 minutes, daily): Identify the trigger (5 min) When does child recite jingles most? When anxious? When excited? When bored? Random/constant? Understanding trigger helps intervention Teach functional alternatives (10 min) For each common jingle, teach alternative: Food jingle → "I'm hungry" or point to picture Toy jingle → "I want to play" or bring toy Random jingle → "I need a break" or sensory activity Practice alternatives with role-play Reinforce functional communication (5 min) When child uses alternative (even once!): Celebrate! Immediate reinforcement Continue allowing jingles but reward alternatives Sensory Integration: Auditory Diet Modification: Theory: Jingle recitation = auditory seeking/regulation Provide alternative auditory input: Throughout day: Background music (instrumental, calming) Nature sounds White noise Audiobooks Reduce commercial exposure:
Limit TV watching Skip commercials (DVR, streaming) Pre-screen content Result: Less jingle input = less jingle output Proprioceptive Protocol: Heavy work every 90 minutes (10 min): Reduces need for auditory self-regulation Provides body-based regulation instead Before high-jingle times: 15-20 min intensive proprioceptive work Often prevents jingle recitation Oral-Motor Satisfaction: Jingles involve oral-motor system Provide alternative oral-motor input: Chewy foods/tools every hour Drinks through straws Crunchy snacks Singing activities (purposeful vs. perseverative) May reduce jingle recitation by 40-50% Massage Techniques: Oral-Facial and Throat Massage (8-10 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Jingle recitation involves significant oral-facial-throat muscle use Face and Jaw (3 min): Massage temples (1 min) Jaw muscles (1 min each side) Releases tension from excessive verbalization Lip and Mouth (2 min): Circular massage around mouth
Lip massage (center to corners) Under-chin pressure Throat Area (2 min): NEVER front of throat Sides of neck only Gentle circles from jaw to shoulders Releases vocal tension Shoulder and Neck (2 min): Firm shoulder squeezes Neck massage These areas tense during extensive vocalization Finish (1 min): Light face touches Deep breath together Full Body Calming Massage (15-20 minutes, daily): Best time: Evening (before bed) Purpose: Overall regulation reduces all verbal stimming Complete full-body routine (described in previous sections) Extra focus on: Back (long, calming strokes) Arms and hands (grounding) Feet (security) Consistent daily massage often reduces jingle recitation by 50-70% Quick "Jingle Interrupt" Massage (3-4 minutes): Use when excessive jingle recitation is occurring: Hand focus: Take child's hands Firm palm massage (1 min each)
Squeeze each finger Press pressure points Shoulder squeeze: Firm pressure on shoulders (30 sec) Deep pressure hug: Full body squeeze (30 sec) Often interrupts verbal perseveration Redirect to quiet activity after MANIFESTATION 7: Repeating Specific Words (10-100+ times) Physical Redirection Technique: "Word Count to Movement Count" When child repeats specific word, acknowledge and redirect Technique: Child repeats: "Blue, blue, blue, blue, blue..." You respond: "I hear you saying 'blue'! Let's count how many times!" Count together while child continues After reaching 10: "You said blue TEN times! Now let's do ten jumps!" Jump together (counting) Then: "Great! Now let's try ONE time. Say 'blue' once." If successful: Immediate positive reinforcement If continues repeating: "Let's give our mouth a rest" (offer chewy toy)
Creates awareness without shame Provides proprioceptive alternative Takes 3-5 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Word Tally Board Materials: Small whiteboard or laminated paper, dry-erase marker Use: When child repeats word, make tally mark for each repetition Show child: "You said it 5 times! Now let's erase and try saying it once" Visual representation of repetition Some children self-regulate when they see tally marks growing Cost: $3-5 for small whiteboard Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Word Percussion: Each repetition = one drum beat/clap/stomp Makes repetition musical Can practice: "Say and clap once" vs. "Say and clap five times" Brings control and awareness Word Writing: Instead of saying word repeatedly, write it repeatedly Whiteboard, paper, sidewalk chalk Transforms verbal into visual-motor Some children satisfied by writing instead of speaking
Word Games: Make repetition purposeful: "How many times can you say 'jump' while jumping?" "Say 'stomp' every time you stomp" "Say 'clap' with each clap" Connects word to action Recording and Playback: Record child saying word once (clearly, purposefully) Play back when child feels need to repeat External repetition may reduce internal need For Communication-Focused: Identify the Function: Why is child repeating this word? Processing it? Likes how it sounds/feels? Trying to communicate something? Anxiety/stimming? Understanding helps intervention Expand Single Word: When child repeats "blue, blue, blue" Model expansion: "Yes, blue! Blue sky! Blue car! Blue shirt!" Gradually teaches word goes in sentences May reduce isolated repetition Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Word Work Circuit" (15-20 minutes, 2-3x daily): Proprioceptive Opening (5 min)
Heavy work (calms nervous system) Often reduces verbal perseveration immediately Purposeful Repetition (5 min) Make word repetition a game: "Say 'jump' five times while jumping" "Say 'push' while pushing wall" "Say 'squeeze' while squeezing putty" Controlled, purposeful repetition One-Word Practice (3 min) Practice saying word ONCE Immediate reinforcement "You said it one time! Great job!" Gradually increase intervals between repetitions Oral-Motor Alternative (4 min) Chewy tool (hard to talk while chewing) Drink through straw Crunchy snack Satisfies oral-motor need differently Quiet Transition (3 min) Calm activity Weighted lap pad Reduces arousal For Communication-Focused: "Word Expansion Training" (10-15 minutes, daily): Accept the word (2 min) Child says: "Car, car, car, car" You respond: "Yes! Car! You're thinking about cars!" Don't shame or stop (yet)
Model expansion (5 min) "Car! Red car! Fast car! Big car! Toy car!" Show how word can grow Encourage child to add descriptor Celebrate any attempt Alternative expression (5 min) "Instead of saying 'car' many times, can you show me a car?" Point, bring, draw, etc. Reduces verbal perseveration Practice new patterns (3 min) "Let's practice: Say 'car' once, then tell me more" May need visual support Gradual progress is fine Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Sensory Diet: Target: Satisfy oral-motor needs to reduce verbal perseveration Every 60-90 minutes: Chewy snack or chewy tool (3-5 min) Drink through straw (creates oral work) Crunchy food (carrots, apples, pretzels) Oral-motor exercises (lip, jaw, tongue) Result: Satisfied oral-motor system = less word repetition Reduce Verbal Pressure:
Less language demand = less perseveration Strategies: Accept non-verbal communication Don't force verbal responses Reduce questions Give processing time Creates calmer verbal environment Full Body Regulation: Word repetition often = under-regulated nervous system Proprioceptive protocol: Morning: 15-20 min heavy work Every 2 hours: 10 min heavy work break After school: 30 min intensive play Evening: 15 min calming input Well-regulated body = less verbal stimming Massage Techniques: Jaw and Oral-Facial Release (6-8 minutes, 3x daily): Purpose: Word repetition creates jaw/facial tension Best times: After episodes of word repetition, before bed, morning Jaw Focus (3 min): Locate masseter muscle (clench teeth to find it) Firm circular massage (1 min each side) Child opens mouth slightly, massage again (1 min) Releases primary tension area
Face and Mouth (2 min): Circular massage around mouth Cheek massage (palms, circular motions) Temple massage Throat and Neck (2 min): Sides of neck only (never front) Gentle massage from jaw to shoulders Releases vocal tension Finish (1 min): Light tapping on face Gentle strokes Deep breath together Hand-to-Mouth Connection Massage (5 minutes): Purpose: Grounding hands often reduces oral stimming Hand massage (3 min): Detailed palm massage (1 min each) Squeeze each finger (5 sec each) Press pressure points firmly Pull gently on fingers Hand to face connection (2 min): Guide child's hands to their own face Teach self-massage Hand on cheeks, gentle pressure Self-awareness and grounding Full Body Regulation Massage (15 minutes, 1-2x daily): Best times: After school (high-stimming time), before bed
Complete full-body massage (previous sections) Slow, firm, rhythmic Deep regulation reduces all verbal stimming significantly Parents report 50-80% reduction with consistent daily massage MANIFESTATION 8: Repeating Specific Words (10-100+ times) Physical Redirection Technique: "Word Count to Movement Count" When child repeats specific word, acknowledge and redirect Technique: Child repeats: "Blue, blue, blue, blue, blue..." You respond: "I hear you saying 'blue'! Let's count how many times!" Count together while child continues After reaching 10: "You said blue TEN times! Now let's do ten jumps!" Jump together (counting) Then: "Great! Now let's try ONE time. Say 'blue' once." If successful: Immediate positive reinforcement If continues repeating: "Let's give our mouth a rest" (offer chewy toy) Creates awareness without shame Provides proprioceptive alternative
Takes 3-5 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Word Tally Board Materials: Small whiteboard or laminated paper, dry-erase marker Use: When child repeats word, make tally mark for each repetition Show child: "You said it 5 times! Now let's erase and try saying it once" Visual representation of repetition Some children self-regulate when they see tally marks growing Cost: $3-5 for small whiteboard Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Word Percussion: Each repetition = one drum beat/clap/stomp Makes repetition musical Can practice: "Say and clap once" vs. "Say and clap five times" Brings control and awareness Word Writing: Instead of saying word repeatedly, write it repeatedly Whiteboard, paper, sidewalk chalk Transforms verbal into visual-motor Some children satisfied by writing instead of speaking Word Games:
Make repetition purposeful: "How many times can you say 'jump' while jumping?" "Say 'stomp' every time you stomp" "Say 'clap' with each clap" Connects word to action Recording and Playback: Record child saying word once (clearly, purposefully) Play back when child feels need to repeat External repetition may reduce internal need For Communication-Focused: Identify the Function: Why is child repeating this word? Processing it? Likes how it sounds/feels? Trying to communicate something? Anxiety/stimming? Understanding helps intervention Expand Single Word: When child repeats "blue, blue, blue" Model expansion: "Yes, blue! Blue sky! Blue car! Blue shirt!" Gradually teaches word goes in sentences May reduce isolated repetition Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Word Work Circuit" (15-20 minutes, 2-3x daily): Proprioceptive Opening (5 min)
Heavy work (calms nervous system) Often reduces verbal perseveration immediately Purposeful Repetition (5 min) Make word repetition a game: "Say 'jump' five times while jumping" "Say 'push' while pushing wall" "Say 'squeeze' while squeezing putty" Controlled, purposeful repetition One-Word Practice (3 min) Practice saying word ONCE Immediate reinforcement "You said it one time! Great job!" Gradually increase intervals between repetitions Oral-Motor Alternative (4 min) Chewy tool (hard to talk while chewing) Drink through straw Crunchy snack Satisfies oral-motor need differently Quiet Transition (3 min) Calm activity Weighted lap pad Reduces arousal For Communication-Focused: "Word Expansion Training" (10-15 minutes, daily): Accept the word (2 min) Child says: "Car, car, car, car" You respond: "Yes! Car! You're thinking about cars!" Don't shame or stop (yet)
Model expansion (5 min) "Car! Red car! Fast car! Big car! Toy car!" Show how word can grow Encourage child to add descriptor Celebrate any attempt Alternative expression (5 min) "Instead of saying 'car' many times, can you show me a car?" Point, bring, draw, etc. Reduces verbal perseveration Practice new patterns (3 min) "Let's practice: Say 'car' once, then tell me more" May need visual support Gradual progress is fine Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Sensory Diet: Target: Satisfy oral-motor needs to reduce verbal perseveration Every 60-90 minutes: Chewy snack or chewy tool (3-5 min) Drink through straw (creates oral work) Crunchy food (carrots, apples, pretzels) Oral-motor exercises (lip, jaw, tongue) Result: Satisfied oral-motor system = less word repetition Reduce Verbal Pressure:
Less language demand = less perseveration Strategies: Accept non-verbal communication Don't force verbal responses Reduce questions Give processing time Creates calmer verbal environment Full Body Regulation: Word repetition often = under-regulated nervous system Proprioceptive protocol: Morning: 15-20 min heavy work Every 2 hours: 10 min heavy work break After school: 30 min intensive play Evening: 15 min calming input Well-regulated body = less verbal stimming Massage Techniques: Jaw and Oral-Facial Release (6-8 minutes, 3x daily): Purpose: Word repetition creates jaw/facial tension Best times: After episodes of word repetition, before bed, morning Jaw Focus (3 min): Locate masseter muscle (clench teeth to find it) Firm circular massage (1 min each side) Child opens mouth slightly, massage again (1 min) Releases primary tension area
Face and Mouth (2 min): Circular massage around mouth Cheek massage (palms, circular motions) Temple massage Throat and Neck (2 min): Sides of neck only (never front) Gentle massage from jaw to shoulders Releases vocal tension Finish (1 min): Light tapping on face Gentle strokes Deep breath together Hand-to-Mouth Connection Massage (5 minutes): Purpose: Grounding hands often reduces oral stimming Hand massage (3 min): Detailed palm massage (1 min each) Squeeze each finger (5 sec each) Press pressure points firmly Pull gently on fingers Hand to face connection (2 min): Guide child's hands to their own face Teach self-massage Hand on cheeks, gentle pressure Self-awareness and grounding Full Body Regulation Massage (15 minutes, 1-2x daily): Best times: After school (high-stimming time), before bed
Complete full-body massage (previous sections) Slow, firm, rhythmic Deep regulation reduces all verbal stimming significantly Parents report 50-80% reduction with consistent daily massage
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 2. AUDITORY STIMMING > A. Vocal/Verbal Stimming > Level 3: Vocal Play and Experimentation
Causation: Over-stimulated: Creative vocal expression regulates emotions Under-stimulated: Intense auditory + proprioceptive input from vocal production Sensitivity: Exploring auditory-motor connection; speech motor planning practice Sensory Profile: Seeker: Loud, varied, prolonged vocal experimentation Creative: Using vocal stimming as play and exploration Description: Exploring vocal capabilities and sound production MANIFESTATION 1: Changing Pitch Rapidly (High to Low Repeatedly) Physical Redirection Technique: "Pitch to Posture" When child makes rapid pitch changes, connect to body position Technique: "I hear your voice going up and down! Let's match with our bodies!" High pitch = reach arms up high, on tiptoes Low pitch = squat down low Do together: Make sound AND movement Practice 10 times Then: "Now let's just move without sound" Continue movements silently (10x)
Transition to different activity (heavy work) Connects vocal play to body awareness Provides proprioceptive and vestibular input Easier to transition to quiet when paired with movement DIY Alternative Tool: Pitch Slider Visual Materials: Cardboard strip (12" tall), draw arrow slider, velcro or paper clip Labels: Top = "High Voice", Middle = "Medium Voice", Bottom = "Low Voice" Use: Child moves arrow while making sounds at that pitch Creates visual representation of pitch Can practice "keeping arrow in middle" (moderate voice) Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Musical Instruments with Pitch: Slide whistle ($3-5) - perfect for pitch exploration Xylophone ($10-15) - different pitches, structured Keyboard/piano app (free) - endless pitch variety Purpose: Channels pitch exploration into music Singing Activities: Teach songs with pitch variation
"Do-Re-Mi" from Sound of Music (scales) Practice opera singing (exaggerated highs/lows) Animal sounds (mouse = high, bear = low) Makes pitch play purposeful Pitch Games: "Copycat Pitch" - adult makes pitch, child copies "High-Low Game" - adult says "high!" child makes high sound "Pitch Freeze Dance" - music stops, hold current pitch Structured pitch exploration Recording Play: Record pitch experiments Play back and discuss "That was high! That was low!" Creates awareness For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Pitch Exploration: Whisper humming (gentle pitches) Soft singing Less intense than loud pitch changes Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Voice and Body Integration Circuit" (20-25 minutes, 1-2x daily): Vestibular Opening (5 min) Swinging (often regulates vocal pitch seeking) Spinning (controlled) Rocking Vestibular input often reduces vocal stimming
Structured Pitch Play (7 min) Pitch exploration with rules: High pitch = jump Low pitch = crouch Medium = stand normal Practice all three (control) Use instruments (xylophone, slide whistle) Purposeful vs. random pitch changes Singing and Music (5 min) Learn songs with pitch variety Practice scales Musical games Educational pitch use Oral-Motor Work (5 min) Chewy foods/tools Drink through straw Hard to make pitch changes while chewing! Alternative oral-motor input Quiet Transition (3 min) Calming activity Weighted lap pad Gentle rocking Reduces arousal For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Voice Control" (10-15 minutes): Practice moderate pitch (not extreme highs/lows) Use visual pitch meter (show where voice should be) Reward staying in "comfortable" range Gradual desensitization to pitch variety Sensory Integration: Vestibular-Vocal Connection:
Theory: Pitch changes often accompany vestibular seeking Provide vestibular input proactively: Morning: 15 min swinging Throughout day: Access to rocking chair After school: 20 min playground (swings, slides, climbing) Evening: Gentle rocking Result: Satisfied vestibular system = reduced pitch play (often 60-70% reduction) Oral-Motor Satisfaction: Every 60-90 min: Chewy snack or tool Crunchy food Drink through straw Oral exercises Satisfied oral-motor system = less vocal play Auditory Environment: Provide rich auditory input: Music (variety of genres) Nature sounds Audiobooks Fills auditory needs without child needing to create own sounds Massage Techniques: Throat and Vocal Area Massage (6-8 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Pitch changes use throat/vocal cords extensively; this releases tension External Throat Area (3 min): NEVER press on front of throat/windpipe
Massage sides of neck only Gentle circles from jaw to collarbones (1 min each side) Very light touch down front (no pressure) Jaw and Face (3 min): Jaw muscle massage Face massage (releases overall tension) Temple massage Shoulder and Neck (2 min): Firm shoulder squeezes Neck sides massage Releases tension that accumulates from vocal play Full Body Calming Massage (15 minutes, 1x daily minimum): Best time: Evening Complete full-body massage Extra focus on upper body (where vocal tension lives) Slow, rhythmic, calming Overall regulation reduces vocal stimming significantly Quick "Voice Rest" Massage (3 minutes): Use when pitch play is excessive: Firm shoulder squeeze (30 sec) Neck sides massage (1 min) Jaw massage (1 min) Offer chewy immediately after (gives mouth something else to do)
MANIFESTATION 2: Volume Modulation (Whispering to Shouting) Physical Redirection Technique: "Volume Meter Body Match" When child modulates volume rapidly, create body-based volume system Technique: "Your voice is going loud and quiet! Let's make our bodies match!" Volume 1 (whisper) = lie flat on floor Volume 5 (normal) = sit Volume 10 (shout) = stand with arms stretched up Practice together: Call out volumes, child matches body position Make sounds at each level (10 times) Gradually stay at lower volumes/positions longer End at "volume 1" lying down, quiet breathing Creates physical awareness of volume Provides proprioceptive input (calming) Visual/kinesthetic learning of volume control DIY Alternative Tool: Volume Control Board Materials: Poster board, draw thermometer/meter with 1-10 scale Add pictures at each level:
1-3: Mouse (quiet) 4-6: Person talking (normal) 7-10: Lion roaring (loud) Arrow or clothespin that moves Use: Show child current volume, teach desired volume "You're at 10! Let's move to 5!" Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Designated Loud Time and Space: Create "loud zone" (outside, basement, specific room with door) Set timer: 10 minutes of "loud time" Child can be as loud as they want Timer ends: "Now we use inside voices" Purpose: Satisfies need for loud while teaching boundaries Volume Games: "Volume Dial" - adult calls numbers, child matches volume "Simon Says Volumes" - "Simon says whisper!" "Simon says shout!" "Volume Freeze Dance" - freeze at whatever volume playing when music stops Makes volume control a fun skill
Musical Instruments: Drums (loud option) Cymbals (loud option) Kazoo, whistle (moderately loud) Allows loud sound-making without voice strain Alternative to vocal loudness Outdoor Activities: Yelling/shouting allowed outside "Shouting contests" in open spaces Cheering practice Appropriate loud outlets Sound Meter Apps: Free decibel meter apps Visual feedback of volume Game: "Can you keep it in the green zone?" Teaches self-monitoring For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Voice Practice: Visual charts showing "inside voice" range Reward staying quiet Noise-canceling headphones if overwhelmed by own loudness Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Volume Control Training Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): High-Energy Opening (5 min) LOUD activities allowed: Jumping while shouting Running while yelling Crashing into pillows with loud sounds Purpose: Releases need for loud, high-energy vocal output
Structured Volume Practice (10 min) Level 10 Practice (2 min): Shout as loud as possible (outdoor or designated room) Scream into pillows Practice maximum volume safely Level 5 Practice (3 min): Normal talking voice Practice conversations Sing at moderate volume Level 1 Practice (3 min): Whisper practice Silent lip movements Very quiet humming Transitions (2 min): Practice moving between volumes smoothly "10 to 5 to 1" sequence Builds control Instrument Play (7 min) Loud instruments (drums, cymbals) Quiet instruments (bells, shakers) Practice loud and soft playing Alternative to vocal volume Oral-Motor Work (5 min) Chewy foods/tools (hard to be loud while chewing) Thick drinks through straws Quiet mouth activities Calming Transition (3 min) Weighted lap pad Gentle rocking Quiet breathing Reduces overall arousal
For Sensory Avoiders: "Comfortable Volume Maintenance" (15 minutes): Find child's comfortable volume (usually quiet) Practice maintaining that volume Use visual supports (volume meter) Reward consistency Gradually expand range slightly (if appropriate) Sensory Integration: Proprioceptive Regulation for Volume Control: Theory: Loud vocalizations often indicate under-regulated nervous system Heavy work protocol (intensive): Before times when shouting typically occurs: 15-20 min heavy proprioceptive work Examples: Wall pushes (3 sets of 20) Carrying heavy items back/forth (5 min) Tug-of-war (5 min) Pushing/pulling furniture Animal walks (bear crawl, crab walk) Throughout day (every 90 min): 10 min proprioceptive break Heavy work tasks Result: Well-regulated body = better volume control (often 50-60% reduction in shouting) Vestibular Input: Shouting often accompanies high vestibular arousal Provide vestibular input proactively:
Swinging (15 min, 2-3x daily) Spinning activities Active play (running, jumping, climbing) May significantly reduce need for loud vocalizations Environmental Modifications: Reduce environmental loudness: Turn down TV, music Reduce background noise Quieter home environment Child may match environmental volume (quieter environment = quieter child) Massage Techniques: Vocal Cord and Throat Soothing Massage (8-10 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Shouting strains vocal cords; this soothes and releases tension CRITICAL: Never massage directly on front of throat/windpipe Preparation: Warm hands Small amount of coconut oil or lotion Child lies down comfortably External Throat (sides only) (3 min): Very gentle circular massage on sides of neck Start below ears, work down to collarbones (1 min each side) Light touch (this area is sensitive) Avoid any pressure on front of throat
Jaw and Face (3 min): Jaw muscle massage (firm) Cheek massage Temple massage Releases facial tension from loud talking Chest and Upper Back (3 min): Upper chest massage (below collarbones) Firm circular motions If child can turn over: massage between shoulder blades This area tenses during shouting Finish (1 min): Very light strokes down neck (sides) Light tapping on chest Deep, slow breathing together Full Body "Volume Down" Massage (20 minutes, 1x daily): Best time: Evening (helps set calm tone for night) Purpose: Deep overall calming reduces high-arousal behaviors like shouting Complete full-body massage: Back: Long, slow, firm strokes (7 min) Arms/hands: Squeeze and release (4 min) Legs/feet: Firm pressure (6 min) Head/face: Gentle massage (3 min) Key elements: SLOW movements (activates parasympathetic nervous system)
FIRM pressure (calming, not tickling) RHYTHMIC (predictable, soothing) Result: Consistent daily massage often reduces shouting by 60-80% Emergency "Volume Down" Quick Massage (3-5 minutes): Use when child is actively shouting/being very loud: Approach calmly "Let's take a quiet massage break" Quick sequence: Firm hands on shoulders, squeeze (30 sec) Squeeze down arms to hands (1 min) Detailed hand massage, firm pressure (1 min each hand) If child sitting: firm pressure on top of head (gentle push down, 10 sec) Deep pressure hug (30 sec) Often child calms immediately Voice volume typically drops Can then redirect to quiet activity MANIFESTATION 3: Testing Vocal Effects (Echoes in Bathrooms, Tunnels) Physical Redirection Technique: "Echo Hunt to Body Sound" When child seeks echoes, provide alternative sound exploration
Technique: "You like hearing echoes! Let's make body sounds instead!" Teach body percussion: Clapping (different speeds, patterns) Stomping (loud, soft, rhythms) Slapping thighs Snapping fingers (if able) Chest thumping Create rhythms together (5 min) Then: "Now let's use our echo tunnel!" (provide cardboard tube) Speak into tube for echo effect (2 min) Transition to quiet activity with proprioceptive input Provides auditory feedback through non-vocal and controlled vocal means Easier to redirect (portable tube vs. running to bathroom) DIY Alternative Tool: Echo Tube Kit Materials: Long cardboard tubes (paper towel, wrapping paper tubes) PVC pipe sections (various lengths, 1-3 feet) Decorate with stickers, duct tape Use: Child speaks, hums, sings into tubes Different lengths = different echo effects Keep in multiple locations (bedroom, playroom, car)
Cost: $5-10 for PVC at hardware store, tubes free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Designated Echo Exploration Time (10-15 min, 1-2x daily): Allow child to explore echoes in bathroom, hallways Set timer When timer ends: "Echo time is done" Satisfies need in controlled way Echo Recording: Use recording app with echo/reverb effects Child records voice with effects Can listen repeatedly External echo reduces need to seek spaces Echo Games: "Echo Hide and Seek" - shout in different rooms, family finds by echo "Echo Contest" - who can make longest echo "Echo Patterns" - repeat rhythm patterns with echo Makes it purposeful play Musical Echo Tools: Singing bowls ($15-30) Tuning forks ($10-20) Chimes and bells These create sustained, echo-like sounds Alternative to vocal echo-seeking
Outdoor Echo Exploration: Find outdoor spaces with echoes (tunnels, parking garages, under bridges) Scheduled "echo adventures" Appropriate places to shout and hear echoes Healthy outlet for interest For Sensory Avoiders: Soft Sound Exploration: Gentle sounds instead of loud echoes Quiet music with reverb Soft singing Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Sound Science Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Proprioceptive Opening (5 min) Heavy work (regulates before auditory seeking) Often reduces intensity of echo-seeking Structured Echo Exploration (10 min) Science approach: "Let's be sound scientists!" Experiment with different spaces: Bathroom (strong echo) Bedroom (soft echo) Outside (no echo) Inside tube (medium echo) Discuss differences Make chart of findings Purpose: Makes it educational, purposeful Echo Tube Play (7 min) Multiple tubes (different lengths)
Test different sounds: Whispers Normal voice Singing Humming Compare and contrast Controlled echo exploration Musical Echo (5 min) Instruments with sustained sound (bells, singing bowls) Listen to sound fade Similar satisfaction to echo Transition to Quiet (3 min) Oral-motor input (chewy) Calm activity Reduces auditory arousal For Communication-Focused: "Why Echo?" Discussion (if child can engage): Explore what child likes about echoes "It makes my voice big!" "It sounds cool!" "It feels good in my throat!" Understanding helps provide alternatives Sensory Integration: Auditory Regulation: Theory: Echo-seeking = auditory processing/seeking behavior Provide rich auditory environment: Throughout day: Background music (varied genres) Nature sounds White noise options Audiobooks Specific echo alternatives: Headphones with reverb/echo effects Sound apps with voice modification Karaoke with echo effects
Purpose: Satisfied auditory needs reduce echo-seeking Proprioceptive Connection: Echo-seeking often accompanies high arousal Heavy work protocol: Before bathroom trips (if echo-seeking common there) Throughout day (every 90 min) Result: Calmer body = less compulsive echo-seeking Vestibular Input: Swinging while vocalizing (combines needs): Swing and sing Swing and hum Satisfies multiple sensory systems simultaneously Often reduces need for echo-seeking Massage Techniques: Ear and Auditory System Massage (6-8 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Calms auditory system, may reduce auditory seeking Ear Massage (3 min): Gentle massage of outer ears Rub earlobes (1 min) Trace around outer ear with fingertips (1 min each ear) Very light pressure (ears are sensitive) Around Ears (2 min): Massage in circles around ears (not inside) Temple area (1 min)
Behind ears down to jaw (1 min) Face and Jaw (2 min): Face massage (general calming) Jaw massage Releases tension Finish (1 min): Very light touches all over face and ears Calming to auditory system Throat and Chest Massage (5-7 minutes): Purpose: Echo-seeking involves significant vocalization Throat area massage (sides only, never front) Chest massage (firm, circular) Shoulder and neck (releases tension) See detailed technique in previous sections Full Body Calming Massage (15 minutes, 1x daily): Best time: Evening Complete full-body routine Reduces overall sensory seeking behaviors Consistent daily massage = less echo-seeking MANIFESTATION 4: Creating Sound Effects (Explosions, Vehicles, Animals) Physical Redirection Technique: "Sound Effect Theater" When child makes sound effects repetitively, transform into structured play Technique: "You're making great sound effects! Let's make a movie!"
Assign roles: Child does sound effects, adult acts out story Example: Adult: "The car drives..." Child: "Vroom vroom!" (while pushing toy car) Adult: "It crashes!" Child: "CRASH!" (while crashing toy) Adult: "The engine breaks..." Child: "Sputter sputter" (while examining toy) Do 5-minute "scene" Then switch: "Now let's do quiet scene" (whisper sounds) Transition to physical activity (heavy work) Makes sound effects purposeful and social Gives opportunity to practice control (loud vs. quiet effects) Easier to end when part of structured play DIY Alternative Tool: Sound Effects Board Materials: Poster board, pictures of items that make sounds Sections: Vehicles, Animals, Weather, Actions (crash, boom, etc.) Buttons (drawn) next to each picture Use: Child "pushes button" (points) and makes that sound effect once
Visual control and organization Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Sound Effects Recording Studio: Voice recorder or phone app Create "library" of sound effects Record each effect clearly Can play back for own entertainment Externalizes the sounds Sound Effect Videos: YouTube: "Sound effects for kids" Child listens instead of constantly creating Can request specific effects Alternative to self-generated sounds Sound Effect Books: Books with sound buttons Press for effects External sound source Voice Modification Apps: Apps that change voice (robot, monster, etc.) Child makes sounds, app modifies Engaging and controlled Cost: Free apps available Foley Art (Real Sound Effects): Teach how movie sound effects are made Make real sounds: Coconut halves = horse hooves Crinkled cellophane = fire Shaking sheet metal = thunder
Channels interest into creative activity For Communication-Focused: Sound Effect Communication: Some children use sound effects functionally "Vroom vroom" = want to play with cars "Boom" = building blocks fell Honor and expand: "Yes, big crash! The blocks fell down!" Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Sound Studio Circuit" (30-35 minutes, 1-2x daily): Active Opening (5 min) Heavy work (calming) Big movements (jumping, crashing) Can make sound effects DURING activity "Jump explosion!" (jump and say "BOOM") Combines proprioceptive with vocal Structured Sound Effects (10 min) Recording session: Create sound effects library Record each effect once, clearly Organize by category Can listen to recordings Purpose: Makes it organized and purposeful Sound Effect Stories (10 min) Create stories together Child provides sound effects at appropriate times
Adult narrates, child provides sounds Example: Adult: "Once upon a time, a car drove down the road..." Child: "Vroom vroom!" Adult: "Suddenly, a dog barked!" Child: "Woof woof!" Social, interactive, purposeful Foley Art Creation (7 min) Make real sound effects Experiment with objects Record real sounds Creative and educational Quiet Transition (3 min) Oral-motor input Calm activity Reduces vocal arousal For Communication-Focused: "Sound Effect Expansion" (15-20 minutes): When child makes sound effect, expand: Child: "Vroom!" Adult: "Yes! Car! Red car! Fast car!" Model using words instead of sounds: "You can say 'car' or 'I want car'" Accept both sound effects and words Gradually child may add words to sound effects Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Satisfaction: Sound effects use mouth/tongue/lips extensively Provide alternative oral-motor input:
Every 60-90 min: chewy snack or tool Crunchy foods Drinks through straw Whistles, kazoos, harmonicas May reduce sound effect creation by 40-50% Proprioceptive Pairing: Allow sound effects DURING proprioceptive activities: Jumping with "boom!" Pushing with "vroom!" Crashing with "crash!" Satisfies both needs simultaneously Often reduces random sound effects (reserves them for active play) Auditory Environment: Provide sound effect alternatives: Sound effect apps Sound effect videos Movies/shows with interesting sounds Reduces need to create own constantly Massage Techniques: Oral-Facial-Throat Massage (8-10 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Sound effects use oral-facial muscles intensively Lip and Mouth (3 min): Detailed circular massage around mouth Lips (center to corners) Inside cheeks if child allows Jaw (2 min): Masseter muscle focus Firm circular massage Open/close mouth during massage
Tongue and Palate (2 min): If child allows, gentle pressure on tongue with cloth-covered finger Palate massage (very gentle) Most kids won't allow this - skip if uncomfortable Throat (2 min): Sides only (never front) Gentle massage Finish (1 min): Light face tapping Deep breath Full Body Regulation Massage (15 minutes, 1x daily): Complete routine Reduces overall need for vocal stimming Consistent massage = less sound effect creation Hand Massage for Grounding (5 minutes, as needed): Use when sound effects are excessive: Take child's hands Firm, detailed hand massage Squeeze each finger Press pressure points Grounding often reduces vocal behaviors Redirect to quiet activity using hands (playdough, fidget, drawing) MANIFESTATION 5: Beatboxing or Rhythmic Sounds Physical Redirection Technique: "Beat to Body Rhythm"
When child begins beatboxing/making rhythmic sounds, join and redirect Technique: "I hear your rhythm! Let's make it with our whole body!" Match child's rhythm with body percussion: Clapping on beats Stomping on beats Slapping thighs on beats Chest thumping on beats Do together for 2-3 minutes Then: "Now let's do our rhythm while doing work!" Carry heavy items to the rhythm Push wall to the rhythm March to the rhythm Gradually slow rhythm down End with slow, calm rhythm (rocking, swaying) Transforms vocal rhythm into physical rhythm Provides proprioceptive and vestibular input Natural transition from fast/loud to slow/calm DIY Alternative Tool: Rhythm Board Materials: Piece of wood or thick cardboard, drumsticks or wooden spoons Decorate with music notes Use: Child drums rhythm instead of beatboxing
Portable (can take in car, to school) Visual/physical outlet for rhythm need Cost: Free (household items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Real Percussion Instruments: Drum set (toy version $30-50, or real if budget allows) Bongos ($20-30) Djembe ($40-80) Hand drums ($15-25) Allows rhythm creation without vocal strain Purposeful musical expression Beatboxing Lessons: YouTube tutorials for kids Turn interest into actual skill Structured practice (designated times) Makes stimming into music education Rhythm Apps and Games: Drum pad apps (free) Rhythm games (many free options) Child creates rhythms digitally Can save and replay External creation reduces constant vocal beatboxing Body Percussion Classes/Videos: Stomp-style body percussion Cup song rhythms Hand clapping games Channels rhythm into structured activity DIY Percussion Instruments: Shakers: Empty bottles with rice/beans
Drums: Overturned buckets, pots with wooden spoons Tambourine: Paper plates with bells Rain stick: Paper towel tube, nails, rice Cost: Free from household items For Communication-Focused: Rhythm as Communication: Some children use rhythm to regulate or communicate Slow rhythm = calm Fast rhythm = excited/anxious Teach recognizing and using rhythm intentionally Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Rhythm Integration Circuit" (30-35 minutes, 1-2x daily): Heavy Work with Rhythm (8 min) All proprioceptive activities done to rhythm: Jump to rhythm (2 min) Push wall to rhythm (2 min) Carry items to rhythm (2 min) Stomp to rhythm (2 min) Purpose: Satisfies proprioceptive and rhythm needs together Percussion Exploration (10 min) Multiple instruments available Create rhythms on each Record favorite rhythms Practice playing softly and loudly
Fast and slow Structured, purposeful rhythm creation Body Percussion (7 min) Clapping patterns Stomping patterns Full body rhythm routine Can follow video tutorials Transforms vocal into physical Rhythm Games (7 min) "Copycat Rhythm" - adult claps pattern, child copies "Rhythm Freeze" - create rhythm, freeze on command "Fast-Slow Game" - start fast, gradually slow down Teaches control and flexibility Quiet Transition (3 min) Very slow, gentle rhythm (rocking, swaying) Gradually silence Deep breathing Oral-motor input (chewy) For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Rhythm Exploration" (10-15 minutes): Soft, slow rhythms only Quiet instruments (bells, soft shakers) Focus on calming rhythms No loud or fast rhythms Sensory Integration: Vestibular-Rhythm Connection: Theory: Rhythm often connects to vestibular system Provide vestibular input with rhythm: Swing to rhythm: Push swing in rhythm
Rock to rhythm: Rocking chair with beat Bounce to rhythm: Therapy ball bouncing Throughout day: Rocking chair access during seated activities Movement breaks every 90 minutes Swinging daily (15-20 min) Result: Satisfied vestibular system often reduces rhythmic vocal stimming by 60-70% Oral-Motor Satisfaction: Beatboxing uses mouth/lips/tongue intensively Alternative oral-motor input every 60-90 min: Chewy snacks/tools Crunchy foods Drinks through straws Whistles, kazoos, harmonicas Reduces need for vocal rhythm creation Auditory Environment: Provide rhythmic auditory input: Music with strong beats (drum-heavy genres) Metronome sounds Rhythm-focused songs Fills auditory/rhythm need without child needing to create constantly Massage Techniques: Rhythmic Massage (10-15 minutes, 1-2x daily): Purpose: Use massage WITH rhythm to satisfy need Unique approach for rhythmic stimming: All massage strokes done in rhythm:
Count: "1, 2, 3, 4" while massaging Tap in rhythm on back Pat in rhythm on legs Clap hands on child's body in rhythm (gentle) Back (5 min): Rhythmic tapping all over back (2 min) Rhythmic strokes down back (2 min) Rhythmic circles (1 min) Arms and Legs (5 min): Rhythmic squeezing down arms Rhythmic squeezing down legs Rhythmic tapping on limbs Finish (3 min): Slow the rhythm down gradually Very slow, gentle taps Eventually stop Silence and stillness Purpose: Satisfies rhythm need through touch instead of sound Oral-Facial Massage (7-8 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Releases tension from beatboxing Lips and mouth (detailed massage, 3 min) Jaw muscles (firm massage, 2 min) Cheeks and face (2 min) Throat sides (1 min)
See detailed techniques in previous sections "Beat Box Break" Quick Massage (3-4 minutes): Use when beatboxing is excessive: Rhythmic shoulder taps (1 min) Rhythmic arm squeezes (1 min) Rhythmic hand massage (1 min) Gradually slow rhythm End with stillness Offer drum or instrument after massage MANIFESTATION 6: Singing Same Song 20-100+ Times Physical Redirection Technique: "Song to Movement Routine" When child sings repetitively, create movement choreography Technique: "You love that song! Let's make dance moves for it!" Create specific movements for each part: Example with "Twinkle Twinkle": "Twinkle twinkle" = hand twinkles above head "Little star" = crouch down small "How I wonder" = hands on hips, look around "What you are" = point up Continue for whole song Do choreography together (5 times)
Then: "Now let's do the moves WITHOUT singing!" Silent dancing to song in their head (5 times) Transition to different active play Allows the song while adding movement Easier to transition from vocal to silent Provides proprioceptive and vestibular input DIY Alternative Tool: Song Ticket System Materials: Index cards, draw musical notes, jar Each card = one song performance Start with 10 tickets per day Each time child sings complete song, use one ticket When tickets gone: "Song time is over today, tomorrow you get more!" Visual, concrete limit on repetition Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Designated Song Time (15-20 min, 2-3x daily): Set timer Child can sing as much as they want Can record performances When timer ends: transition to quiet activity
Contains behavior to specific times Song Variations: Encourage changing the song: Different tempo (fast, slow, medium) Different volume (loud, whisper, medium) Different style (opera, rap, country) Different language (make up words) Builds flexibility while honoring the interest Karaoke Apps/Videos: Sing-along videos on YouTube Karaoke apps (many free) Provides structured singing activity Can record performances Makes it purposeful entertainment Music Lessons: Voice lessons (if interested) Choir or singing group Turns stimming into skill development Appropriate outlet for singing interest Song Writing: Encourage creating NEW songs Start by changing words to familiar melody Eventually create original melodies Moves from repetition to creativity Musical Instruments: Play song on instrument instead of singing Piano, keyboard, xylophone, recorder Alternative musical expression For Communication-Focused: Song as Communication:
Sometimes repetitive singing communicates: Emotion (happy = upbeat song) Memory (song reminds them of experience) Desire (wants to watch movie the song is from) Explore: "That song makes you think of ___?" Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Musical Expression Circuit" (30-40 minutes, 1-2x daily): Active Musical Opening (8 min) Sing favorite songs WHILE doing heavy work: Jump while singing (3 min) Dance energetically while singing (3 min) March and sing (2 min) Purpose: Combines proprioceptive with vocal** Structured Performance Time (10 min) Set up "stage" area Child performs favorite songs (with limits) Can use microphone (toy or real) Family can be audience Time limit enforced Makes it special performance, not constant background Song Variations (8 min) Practice singing favorite song in different ways:
Opera style (2 min) Whisper singing (2 min) Fast version (2 min) Slow version (2 min) Builds flexibility Alternative Music Activities (10 min) Instruments (play song on xylophone, keyboard) Song writing (create new verses) Drawing while listening to song Non-vocal music engagement Quiet Transition (4 min) Very quiet humming (no words) Gentle lip massage Oral-motor input (chewy) Silent activity For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Music Engagement" (15 minutes): Quiet singing (not repetitive) Listening to music (not singing) Soft instruments Focus on variety, not repetition Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Protocol: Theory: Singing uses oral-motor system extensively Provide alternative oral-motor input: Every 60-90 minutes: Chewy snack or tool (3-5 min) Crunchy food Drink through straw Whistling, kazoo playing Before high-singing times: 5 min intensive oral-motor work
Reduces subsequent singing Result: Satisfied oral-motor needs = 40-50% reduction in repetitive singing Vestibular Integration: Swinging while singing: Allows both behaviors simultaneously Often satisfies both needs 15-20 min daily Rocking while allowing singing: Rocking chair during "song time" Calming vestibular input Result: May significantly reduce random singing Auditory Environment Management: Provide rich musical environment: Background music throughout day Variety of genres Audiobooks, podcasts for kids Purpose: Fills auditory need without child creating constant sound Can reduce repetitive singing by 30-40% Massage Techniques: Comprehensive Vocal System Massage (10-12 minutes, 2x daily): Best times: After singing episodes, before bed Purpose: Extensive singing causes significant vocal/throat tension Throat Area (3 min): NEVER front of throat Sides of neck only Gentle circular massage from jaw to collarbones
