Each side (1.5 min) Very light touch down front (no pressure) Jaw and Face (3 min): Jaw muscle (masseter) focus - firm massage Temples (1 min) Cheeks (1 min) Around mouth (1 min) Lips and Mouth (2 min): Detailed lip massage Circular motions around mouth See detailed technique in previous sections Chest and Upper Back (3 min): Upper chest massage (singing uses chest muscles) Between shoulder blades (if child can turn over) Firm, releasing tension Finish (1 min): Light taps on throat area (sides) Gentle face strokes Deep, slow breathing together Full Body "Song Reset" Massage (20 minutes, 1x daily): Best time: Evening Purpose: Deep overall regulation reduces all vocal stimming Complete full-body massage Extra attention to: Back (calming, 7-8 min)
Shoulders/arms (5 min) Legs/feet (5 min) Slow, rhythmic, deeply calming Result: Consistent daily massage reduces repetitive singing by 60-80% "Voice Rest" Quick Massage (4-5 minutes): Use after extended singing episodes: "Your voice needs a rest. Let's do massage." Throat sides (gentle, 1 min) Jaw (firm massage, 1 min) Shoulders and neck (firm, 2 min) Offer something to chew (gives mouth alternative activity) Deep breath together Redirect to quiet activity MANIFESTATION 7: Making Up Nonsense Words and Repeating Physical Redirection Technique: "Nonsense to Sense Game" When child creates and repeats nonsense words, engage playfully Technique: Child repeats: "Blibberdy, blibberdy, blibberdy..." You respond: "Blibberdy! That's a silly word! Let's make it an action!" Create movement for the nonsense word: Every "blibberdy" = one jump
Or one clap Or one spin Do together (10 repetitions) Then: "Now let's make NEW nonsense words!" Take turns creating new words with actions Each person gets 3 new words max Then transition to heavy work activity Makes nonsense word play interactive and bounded Provides proprioceptive input Teaches turn-taking and flexibility DIY Alternative Tool: Silly Word Dictionary Materials: Notebook, markers Purpose: Collect child's nonsense words Use: When child creates nonsense word, write it in book with definition/picture Child can look through book during designated times Externalizes the words (reduces need to repeat verbally) Can become cherished item Cost: $2-3 for notebook Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Nonsense Word Games: "Dr. Seuss Time": Read silly books together (validates nonsense words) "Nonsense Rhyme": Create rhyming nonsense words
"Nonsense Song": Sing nonsense words to familiar tunes Makes it purposeful play Recording Nonsense: Record nonsense words Play back Create "nonsense library" External storage reduces verbal repetition Written Nonsense: Write/draw nonsense words Make up silly spelling Create nonsense alphabet Transforms verbal into visual Foreign Language Connection: Explore: Real words in other languages sound like nonsense! Learn simple words in different languages "Your nonsense words are like other languages!" Validates interest, redirects toward learning For Communication-Focused: Nonsense as Placeholder: Sometimes nonsense words fill in when child doesn't know real word Gently model real word Accept both Example: Child: "I want the blibberdy!" (pointing at cup) Adult: "Oh, the cup! Yes, here's the cup!" Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Nonsense Play Circuit" (20-25 minutes, 1-2x daily):
Nonsense Movement (7 min) Every nonsense word = specific movement Create nonsense word dance Jump, spin, crash to nonsense words Combines proprioceptive with vocal Structured Nonsense Time (8 min) Set timer: "Nonsense word time!" Child can say any nonsense words Adult participates (makes it social) Write/draw favorite nonsense words When timer ends: "Now we use real words" Contains the behavior Nonsense to Real (5 min) Practice: For each nonsense word, think of real word that sounds similar Example: "Blibberdy" sounds like "blueberry" "Flibbertygibbet" is a real word! Builds awareness of language Quiet Transition (5 min) Oral-motor input (hard to talk while chewing) Calm activity Real words only practice (gentle) For Communication-Focused: "Language Building" (15 minutes): Honor nonsense words (they're language play!)
Gently model real words Expand vocabulary naturally Celebrate ALL communication attempts Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Satisfaction: Nonsense words are often created for how they FEEL in the mouth Provide alternative oral sensations: Every 60-90 min: Chewy, crunchy, varied textures Drinks through straws Whistles, kazoos (make interesting oral sensations) May reduce nonsense word creation Language-Rich Environment: Provide interesting REAL words: Read books with unusual words Teach big/silly real words Word-of-the-day practice Channels interest in sound/language toward real vocabulary Reduce Verbal Pressure: Sometimes nonsense words emerge when language demands are high Strategies: Accept non-verbal communication Give processing time Reduce questions Lower pressure = less nonsense filling Massage Techniques: Oral-Facial Massage (7-8 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Nonsense words use mouth/tongue/lips extensively Lips and mouth (circular massage, 3 min)
Jaw muscles (firm massage, 2 min) Tongue (if child allows, gentle pressure) Cheeks (inside and outside, 2 min) Face overall (1 min) See detailed techniques in previous sections Full Body Regulation Massage (15 minutes, 1x daily): Complete routine Reduces overall verbal stimming Consistent daily practice Hand Massage for Grounding (5 minutes, as needed): Use when nonsense word repetition is excessive: Detailed hand massage Firm pressure Grounding effect Often reduces verbal behaviors Redirect to hands-on activity after MANIFESTATION 8: Exploring Accent Changes or Character Voices Physical Redirection Technique: "Voice Character Theater" When child uses different voices repetitively, create structured theater play Technique: "You're using interesting voices! Let's put on a play!" Assign each voice a character: High voice = mouse character Low voice = bear character
Accent = foreign visitor character Regular voice = narrator Create short scene (3-5 minutes) Each character gets specific number of lines (limits repetition) Then: "Play is over! Now we need to help move the theater!" Heavy work activity (move "props"/furniture) Transition complete Makes voice play purposeful and bounded Provides social interaction Natural ending point (play is over) DIY Alternative Tool: Voice Choice Wheel Materials: Paper plate, divide into sections, arrow in center (brad fastener) Sections: Regular Voice, Whisper Voice, Deep Voice, High Voice, Silly Voice, Quiet Time (no voice) Use: Spin wheel, use that voice for designated time (2-3 min) Limits each voice type Makes it a game with rules Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Structured Character Voice Time (10-15 min, 2x daily):
Designated time for voice play Can use different accents/voices Set timer When ends: back to regular voice Contains the behavior Voice Acting Practice: YouTube: Voice acting tutorials for kids Practice specific characters from movies Record performances Makes it skill development Audiobook Creation: Record child reading book in different voices Different voice for each character Purposeful use of voice variety Can share with family Accent Exploration: Learn about real accents (educational) Watch videos of people with different accents Practice specific accents (not mockery, but appreciation) Channels interest into cultural learning Voice Modification Apps: Apps that change voice (robot, helium, deep, etc.) Child speaks normally, app modifies External voice changes reduce need for constant self-modification For Communication-Focused: Voice as Expression: Different voices may express different feelings/needs
Help child recognize: "You use high voice when excited" "You use deep voice when feeling strong" Teach using regular voice to express same things Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Voice Exploration Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Proprioceptive Opening (5 min) Heavy work (calms before vocal play) Often reduces intensity of voice play Structured Voice Play (12 min) Voice Theater: Create characters (3 min) Each character has specific voice (3 min) Perform short skit with rules (5 min) Clear beginning and ending Purpose: Purposeful, bounded voice use Voice Experiments (7 min) Explore how voices are made: Tension in throat = higher pitch Relaxation = lower pitch Nose involvement = nasal sound Educational approach Record different voices (1-2 examples each, not repetitive)
Return to Regular Voice (4 min) Practice using regular voice Simple conversation in own voice Reinforce: "This is your voice, and it's great!" Quiet Transition (2 min) Oral-motor input Calm activity No voice play For Communication-Focused: "Voice and Identity" (15 minutes): Explore: What is YOUR voice? Practice recognizing own voice Understand: Other voices are for play, this is for talking Build comfort with own voice Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Protocol: Voice changes use oral-facial muscles extensively Alternative oral-motor input: Every 60-90 min: chewy, crunchy Drink through straw Whistles, kazoos Satisfies oral-motor needs differently Vestibular Integration: Swinging while using voices: Combines both behaviors Often satisfies both needs May reduce random voice changes Daily swinging: 15-20 minutes Identity Development: Help child develop strong sense of own voice:
Record child's regular voice Listen together: "That's YOUR voice!" Celebrate their unique voice Strong identity = less need to be other characters constantly Massage Techniques: Throat and Vocal Cord Massage (8-10 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Voice changes strain vocal cords/throat CRITICAL: Never press directly on front of throat Throat sides (3 min): Gentle massage from jaw to collarbones Each side separately Very light touch Jaw (2 min): Firm massage on masseter Releases tension from voice manipulation Face and lips (2 min): General face massage Lip area focus Chest (2 min): Upper chest massage Voice projection uses chest Finish (1 min): Light tapping on throat area (sides) Deep breathing Full Body Calming Massage (15 minutes, 1x daily): Complete routine Reduces overall vocal stimming
Evening timing best Identity Grounding Massage (5 minutes): Purpose: Help child feel grounded in own body/voice Hand massage (firm, grounding) Foot massage (grounding) Deep pressure on limbs "This is YOUR body, YOUR hands, YOUR feet, YOUR voice" Body awareness supports voice awareness
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 2. AUDITORY STIMMING > B. Environmental Sound Stimming > Level 1: Passive Sound Seeking
Causation: Over-stimulated: Masking overwhelming environmental sounds with preferred sound Under-stimulated: Fills auditory "hunger" Sensitivity: Predictable, consistent sounds are regulating Sensory Profile: Seeker: Maximum volume, intense sounds, long duration Avoider: Using controlled sound to block unpredictable environmental noise Sensitive: Specific sound frequencies are uniquely soothing Description: Deliberately exposing self to specific sounds MANIFESTATION 1: Standing Near Fans, Air Conditioners, White Noise Physical Redirection Technique: "Sound Source to Sound Movement" When child positions near sound source for extended time, redirect with movement Technique: Acknowledge: "You like that sound! Let's make that sound with movement!" Create movements that mimic white noise: "Shh" sound while: Swaying side to side Gentle rocking Slow spinning Do together (3 minutes) Then: "Now let's find quiet" (lead to different space)
Heavy work activity (5 min) Provide alternative: Portable white noise device/app Honors the sensory need Adds movement (often what they're seeking alongside sound) Teaches they can have sound AND do other activities DIY Alternative Tool: Portable Sound Source Materials: Small portable fan ($10-15) OR phone/tablet with white noise app (free) Use: Child can take sound source to different locations Doesn't need to stand in one spot Can do activities while listening Cost: Free (app) to $15 (fan) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: White Noise Throughout Environment: White noise machines ($15-30) in multiple rooms Fan in bedroom (sleep association) Apps on devices (free) Purpose: Provides sound without child needing to seek specific location Headphones with White Noise: Child-safe headphones ($15-25) White noise app or recording
Portable - can move around Allows sound seeking while mobile Sound Variety: Different types of white/background noise: Rain sounds Ocean waves Forest sounds Brown noise Pink noise Explore what child prefers most Schedule with Sound: "Sound time" in designated location (15-20 min) Then transition to other activities Contains the behavior For Sensory Avoiders: Generally, not applicable (avoiders wouldn't seek these sounds) But can use white noise to mask OTHER disturbing sounds Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Sound and Movement Integration" (20-25 minutes, 2x daily): Sound Exposure (5 min) Allow child to stand near preferred sound source Acknowledge and allow Purpose: Satisfies immediate need Sound Plus Movement (8 min) Introduce movement WHILE near sound: Rocking Swaying Gentle bouncing on ball Yoga poses
Purpose: Adds proprioceptive/vestibular to auditory Portable Sound (5 min) Transition to portable sound source Move to different locations with sound Practice doing activities WITH sound available Purpose: Teaches flexibility **SounTransition** (5 min) - Gradually lower volume of sound - Eventually turn off - Heavy work activity to replace - Purpose: Teaches can regulate without constant sound Important Note: Some children NEED background sound for regulation - this is okay! Goal is flexibility, not elimination. Sensory Integration: Auditory Environment Design: Theory: Child seeks these sounds for regulation Provide throughout environment: White noise machines in main living spaces Fan in bedroom Apps available on devices Purpose: Makes sound available without seeking behavior Vestibular Pairing: Sound-seeking often pairs with vestibular needs: Rocking chair near sound source
Swing while listening to white noise Therapy ball to bounce on while listening Satisfies both sensory needs Why White Noise? Often indicates: Auditory defensiveness (white noise masks unpredictable sounds) Under-stimulation (provides needed input) Self-regulation strategy Provide freely - it's helpful! Massage Techniques: Ear and Auditory System Massage (5-7 minutes, 1-2x daily): Purpose: Calms auditory system Outer ear massage (gentle, 2 min) Around ears (circles, 2 min) Temple area (1 min) Face (1 min) See detailed technique in previous sections Calming Full Body Massage (15 minutes, daily): Purpose: Overall regulation may reduce need for constant sound** Complete routine Many children who need white noise have sensitive nervous systems Daily massage helps overall regulation Before-Bed Massage with White Noise (15 minutes): Pair massage with white noise:
Turn on white noise/fan Do complete calming massage Creates positive association Child may sleep better with this routine Transition** (5 min) - Gradually lower volume of sound - Eventually turn off - Heavy work activity to replace - Purpose: Teaches can regulate without constant sound Important Note: Some children NEED background sound for regulation - this is okay! Goal is flexibility, not elimination. Sensory Integration: Auditory Environment Design: Theory: Child seeks these sounds for regulation Provide throughout environment: White noise machines in main living spaces Fan in bedroom Apps available on devices Purpose: Makes sound available without seeking behavior Vestibular Pairing: Sound-seeking often pairs with vestibular needs: Rocking chair near sound source Swing while listening to white noise Therapy ball to bounce on while listening
Satisfies both sensory needs Why White Noise? Often indicates: Auditory defensiveness (white noise masks unpredictable sounds) Under-stimulation (provides needed input) Self-regulation strategy Provide freely - it's helpful! Massage Techniques: Ear and Auditory System Massage (5-7 minutes, 1-2x daily): Purpose: Calms auditory system Outer ear massage (gentle, 2 min) Around ears (circles, 2 min) Temple area (1 min) Face (1 min) See detailed technique in previous sections Calming Full Body Massage (15 minutes, daily): Purpose: Overall regulation may reduce need for constant sound** Complete routine Many children who need white noise have sensitive nervous systems Daily massage helps overall regulation Before-Bed Massage with White Noise (15 minutes): Pair massage with white noise: Turn on white noise/fan Do complete calming massage Creates positive association
Child may sleep better with this routine MANIFESTATION 2: Positioning Near Running Water (Faucets, Fountains) Physical Redirection Technique: "Water Sound to Water Play" When child positions near water for sound, redirect to water interaction Technique: Acknowledge: "You like the water sound! Let's PLAY with water!" Set up water play station: Basin/sink with water Cups for pouring Sponges for squeezing Items to drop in water (splashing sounds) Allow 10-15 minutes of water play Then: "Water time is over. Let's dry off and do big movements!" Heavy work activity (carry water basin, wring out towels) Provide recording of water sounds for later Transforms passive listening into active play Adds tactile and proprioceptive input Time-limited and purposeful DIY Alternative Tool: Water Sound Collection Materials: Phone/tablet, record various water sounds
Recordings: Faucet running Shower Rain Stream/river Fountain Ocean waves Use: Play recordings on device (portable, doesn't waste water) Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Scheduled Water Play (15-20 min, 1-2x daily): Sensory bin with water Bath time (extended if needed) Outdoor water play Sink play (supervised) Provides sound AND tactile input Water Sound Recordings: Nature sound apps (free) Water fountain videos Rain sounds Ocean waves Available anytime without water waste Small Desktop Fountain: Tabletop water fountains ($15-30) Provides constant water sound Visual element too Can place in multiple locations Rain Stick: Musical instrument ($10-15) Flip over = water rain sound Child controls the sound Portable DIY Water Sounds: Pour water back and forth between cups Spray bottle (outside) Water table with pumps
Active creation of water sounds For Sensory Avoiders: Generally not applicable (they wouldn't seek this) But some may use water sounds to mask other noises Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Water Sensory Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Water Listening (5 min) Allow child near water source Listen to different water sounds Faucet at different pressures Purpose: Satisfies immediate need Water Play (12 min) Hands-on water activities: Pouring (3 min) Splashing (3 min) Squeezing sponges (3 min) Dropping objects in water (3 min) Purpose: Adds tactile and proprioceptive to auditory Heavy Water Work (6 min) Carry full water containers Wring out heavy wet towels Clean up water play area Purpose: Proprioceptive input after sensory play Water Sound Alternative (5 min) Introduce portable water sound options
Practice using recordings Rain stick play Purpose: Teaches flexibility For Communication-Focused: Water seeking may indicate: Thirst (teach to request water) Need for bathroom (teach to communicate) Sensory regulation need (teach alternatives) Sensory Integration: Provide Water Access Throughout Day: Scheduled water play times Sensory bins with water (10 min, 2-3x daily) Bath time for regulation Purpose: Satisfies sensory need proactively Auditory-Tactile Integration: Water provides both auditory and tactile input Offer other combined input: Tactile bins (rice, beans) - sound when moving hands through Sand play (pouring makes sound) Kinetic sand (quiet tactile alternative) May reduce water-seeking specifically Environmental Modifications: Small fountain in main living space Water sound machine/app available Makes sound accessible without seeking Massage Techniques: Ear and Auditory Calming Massage (5-7 minutes, 1-2x daily):
Ear massage (gentle) Around ears Temple and jaw See detailed technique in previous sections Hand and Tactile Integration Massage (7-10 minutes): Purpose: Water-seeking often indicates tactile seeking too Hands (5 min): Detailed palm massage (2 min each hand) Each finger individually (1 min total) Varied pressure (firm to light) Forearms (3 min): Massage from wrist to elbow Different strokes (firm, light, circular) Purpose: Provides rich tactile input, may reduce water-seeking Full Body Calming Massage (15 minutes, daily): Complete routine Overall regulation Can do AFTER water play (calming transition) MANIFESTATION 3: Listening to Music at High Volume (or Very Low) Physical Redirection Technique: "Volume to Movement Match" When child plays music at extreme volumes, add movement component Technique: For HIGH volume: "This music is LOUD! Let's move BIG!"
Jump, dance, crash to the music (5 min) Then: "Now let's make the music quieter and move smaller" Lower volume gradually, movements become smaller End at low volume with gentle swaying For LOW volume: "This music is quiet! Let's move gently!" Slow, gentle movements Gradually increase volume and movement size Heavy work activity after (5 min) Teaches volume awareness through movement Provides proprioceptive input Natural volume moderation DIY Alternative Tool: Volume Indicator System Materials: Poster board, draw volume scale 1-10 Add visual indicators: 1-3: Green zone (good volume) 4-6: Yellow zone (getting loud) 7-10: Red zone (too loud - might hurt ears) Point to current volume on chart Teach safe listening levels Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers (High Volume):
Designated Loud Music Time: Specific times and places for loud music Outside (neighbors not disturbed) With headphones (protects ears, loud to them) Time-limited (10-15 min) Satisfies need safely Headphones Solution: Child-safe headphones with volume limiting ($20-40) Music sounds loud to them without disturbing others Protects hearing (max 85 decibels) Safe loud music access Music and Movement: Dance parties with loud music (supervised volume) Jump to the beat Crash to the music Combines auditory and proprioceptive Concerts/Performances: Kids' concerts (appropriately loud) Drum circles Appropriate loud music outlets Instruments: Drums, cymbals (naturally loud) Allows loud sound creation More appropriate than max-volume music For Sensory Seekers (Low Volume): Understanding the Need: Very low volume may indicate: Auditory sensitivity (loud hurts) Wanting background only Focusing on other sensory input
Honor the preference Provide Low-Volume Options: Quiet music playlists Nature sounds (inherently quiet) White noise (low level) Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers (High Volume): "Music and Movement Circuit" (30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Loud Music Movement (10 min) Play music at higher volume (safe level with headphones OR outside) Big movements: Jumping (3 min) Dancing wildly (3 min) Air instruments (2 min) Freeze dance (2 min) Purpose: Satisfies high-intensity auditory and movement needs Volume Modulation Practice (8 min) Start loud, gradually decrease Match movements to volume Practice finding "comfortable" volume Discuss: "How do your ears feel at each volume?" Purpose: Teaches volume awareness Alternative Loud Outlets (7 min) Play actual instruments (drums, cymbals) Sing loudly (outside or designated room) Sound effects
Purpose: Loud sound without risk to hearing Quiet Transition (5 min) Very quiet music Gentle movements Deep breathing Calm activity For Sensory Seekers (Low Volume): Honor the preference Ensure they can hear adequately Provide quiet music options Sensory Integration: Hearing Protection Education: CRITICAL: Protect developing ears Loud music can cause permanent hearing damage Rules for safe listening: No more than 85 decibels Use volume-limiting headphones for children "If I have to shout for you to hear me, music is too loud" Time limits on loud music (not hours daily) Signs of too-loud music: Ringing in ears Muffled hearing after Ear pain Need to speak loudly after music off If child insists on very loud music: Consult audiologist Rule out hearing loss (may turn up because can't hear)
Get professional volume-limiting headphones Proprioceptive Substitution: Often loud music = seeking intensity Provide proprioceptive intensity instead: Heavy work before music time May reduce need for loud volume Dance/movement to moderate volume = same satisfaction Vestibular Pairing: Music listening while: Swinging Rocking Bouncing on ball Satisfies multiple sensory needs = less extreme music volume needed Massage Techniques: Ear and Auditory System Massage (6-8 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: High volume music = auditory system strain Ears (2 min): Very gentle outer ear massage Earlobe rubs Never inside ear canal Around Ears (2 min): Circular massage around each ear Temple area Jaw and Face (3 min): Jaw muscle massage (tension from loud music) Face massage Releases overall tension Finish (1 min): Light touches Calming
Full Body Regulation Massage (15 minutes, daily): Complete routine Reduces overall sensory seeking May reduce need for extreme volumes "Ear Rest" Massage After Loud Music (5 minutes): Gentle ear and face massage Very calming "Let's give your ears a rest" Quiet time after massage MANIFESTATION 4: Seeking Out Humming Electronics Physical Redirection Technique: "Electronic Hum to Body Hum" When child seeks humming electronics, redirect to creating hum themselves Technique: Acknowledge: "You like that humming sound! Let's make humming sounds!" Teach humming variations: Hum with lips closed (low pitch) Hum with mouth slightly open (changes sound) Hum and feel vibration on chest (put hand on chest) Hum and feel vibration on throat (hand on throat - external) Practice 3-5 minutes Then: "Now let's make vibrations with our body!"
Jump (body vibrates when landing) Shake body parts Heavy work activity Transforms seeking behavior into self-creation Adds body awareness and proprioception Portable (can hum anywhere) DIY Alternative Tool: Personal Humming Device Materials: Electric toothbrush (not in use) ($3-5) OR small personal massager ($8-12) OR kazoo ($1-2) Use: Electric toothbrush/massager provides vibration and hum Kazoo creates sustained hum sound Child controls it Portable, appropriate Cost: $1-12 Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Provide Safe Humming Electronics: Small fan (desktop size) White noise machine Electric toothbrush Designated humming items child can access Vibrating Toys/Tools: Vibrating pillows ($15-25) Vibrating massagers (child-safe) Vibrating fidgets ($5-10) Provides vibration without seeking appliances Musical Instruments with Sustained Sound: Tuning fork ($10-15) Singing bowl ($15-30) Harmonica (when blown continuously) Purposeful humming sounds
Recording Electronic Hums: Record favorite electronic sounds Play on device External storage reduces seeking Understanding the Appeal: Humming electronics provide: Predictable sound Continuous (not startling) Often low-frequency (calming) Sometimes vibration component Provide these qualities through alternatives For Sensory Avoiders: Generally not applicable But some avoid certain electronic hums while seeking others (individual preference) Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Vibration and Sound Exploration Circuit" (20-25 minutes, 1-2x daily): Safe Electronics Exploration (5 min) Designated electronic items child can explore Desktop fan, white noise machine, electric toothbrush Allow listening and holding (if appropriate) Purpose: Satisfies immediate need Self-Generated Humming (7 min) Teach various humming techniques Hum different pitches Hum with different mouth positions Feel vibrations on body Purpose: Gives child control over the sound
Vibration Exploration (6 min) Vibrating toys/tools Hold against different body parts Cheeks, chest, arms, legs Notice how it feels Purpose: Vibration satisfaction Instrument Play (5 min) Tuning forks, singing bowls Create sustained sounds Feel vibrations Purpose: Purposeful sound/vibration creation Quiet Transition (2 min) Gradual silence Deep breathing Calm activity For Communication-Focused: Electronics seeking may indicate: Need for predictable auditory input Self-regulation strategy Teach to request access to appropriate items Sensory Integration: Provide Vestibular Input: Humming electronics seeking often pairs with vestibular needs Swinging daily (15-20 min) Rocking chair access May reduce electronics seeking Vibration Throughout Day: Vibrating cushion for sitting Vibrating massager (5 min, 3x daily) Satisfies vibration need proactively Auditory Environment: Provide background hum (white noise, fan) Throughout environment Child doesn't need to seek it out
Massage Techniques: Vibration Massage (10 minutes, 1-2x daily): Purpose: Provides vibration through touch (what they're seeking) Use personal massager (if available) OR: Manual percussion massage: Cupped hands, gently tap all over body Creates vibration sensation Back (3 min) Arms and legs (4 min) Hands and feet (3 min) Creates similar sensation to electronic hum May reduce seeking behavior Ear and Auditory Massage (5-7 minutes, daily): Gentle ear massage Around ears Temple and jaw Calms auditory system Full Body Calming Massage (15 minutes, daily): Complete routine Overall regulation reduces seeking behaviors MANIFESTATION 5: Lying Near Washing Machines or Dryers Physical Redirection Technique: "Appliance Sensation to Weighted Vibration" When child positions near appliances, provide similar sensory input elsewhere Technique: Acknowledge: "You like how the washer feels and sounds!"
Provide alternatives: Weighted blanket on lap/body (deep pressure like appliance vibration) Vibrating cushion or massager Rocking chair (vestibular like appliance movement) Set up alternative in different location Add favorite sounds (white noise app) Heavy work activity after (5 min) Provides same sensory qualities without appliance dependence Safer (not in laundry room) More convenient for caregivers DIY Alternative Tool: Appliance Simulation Station Materials: Beanbag chair or large cushion Small vibrating massager ($10-15) or phone on vibrate with long timer White noise app (washer/dryer sounds) Weighted lap pad or blanket Setup: Comfortable seating Vibration source under cushion White noise playing Weighted item on lap Use: Child gets similar sensory experience in appropriate location Cost: $10-20 (if need to buy vibration source) Alternative Stimulation:
For Sensory Seekers: Scheduled Appliance Time: If safe and supervised, allow time near running appliances 10-15 minutes Then transition to alternative location Satisfies need with boundaries Vibration Alternatives: Vibrating chair cushion ($25-40) Personal massagers (various sizes) Massage chair (if budget allows) Phone on vibrate (under cushion) Provides vibration without appliance Sound Alternatives: White noise with washer/dryer sounds (apps/online) Fan sounds Provides sound component Weighted Items: Weighted blanket ($30-80) Weighted lap pad ($20-40) DIY: Pillowcase filled with rice, sewn shut Provides pressure component Rocking/Movement: Rocking chair Hammock Swing Provides movement component (appliances vibrate/move) For Sensory Avoiders: Not applicable (they wouldn't seek this) Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Multi-Sensory Regulation Station" (20-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Appliance Time (5 min, if safe) Allow supervised time near appliance
Purpose: Satisfies immediate need Transition to Alternative (10 min) Move to alternative setup: Beanbag with vibration source Weighted blanket White noise playing Encourage resting here Purpose: Shows alternatives provide same comfort Add Vestibular (8 min) After stationary time, add movement: Rocking chair (3 min) Swing (5 min) Purpose: Satisfies movement needs Heavy Work (5 min) Proprioceptive activities Carrying, pushing, pulling Purpose: Completes sensory circuit Quiet Activity (2 min) Calm, focused activity Integration time For Understanding the Need: Appliances provide: Vibration (tactile/proprioceptive) Sound (auditory - white noise type) Movement (things inside move - vestibular by association) Warmth (dryers especially - thermoregulation) Predictability (consistent, rhythmic) Provide these elements separately Sensory Integration: Comprehensive Sensory Diet: Address all components appliance provides: Vibration (3-4x daily, 5-10 min each):
Vibrating massager Vibrating cushion Electric toothbrush on body Deep Pressure (throughout day): Weighted items during seated activities Compression vest Tight hugs Massage Vestibular (3x daily, 10-15 min each): Swinging Rocking Spinning Auditory (continuous low-level): White noise throughout environment Fan sounds Result: Satisfied sensory needs = no appliance seeking Environmental Modifications: Create sensory-rich environment Child doesn't need to seek out appliances Sensory tools available in main living spaces Massage Techniques: Vibration-Style Massage (12-15 minutes, 1-2x daily): Purpose: Mimics vibration sensation from appliances Can use personal massager OR manual percussion: Back (5 min): If using massager: move slowly across entire back If manual: cupped hands, tap all over back (creates vibration) Arms and Legs (5 min): Vibration or percussion down each limb Include hands and feet
Torso (3 min): Gentle vibration/percussion on chest (if child comfortable) Sides of body Finish (2 min): Transition to still, firm pressure Deep pressure holds Calming Deep Pressure Massage (20 minutes, daily): Purpose: Provides deep tactile input (what appliance vibration offers) Full body, firm pressure massage: Back (8 min) - long, firm strokes Arms and hands (4 min) - squeeze and hold Legs and feet (6 min) - firm pressure Face and head (2 min) - gentle but present Best time: Evening Can be done ON weighted blanket (extra pressure) Result: Deep regulation, often eliminates appliance seeking "Washer Replacement" Massage (10 minutes, as needed): Use when child can't access appliance or seeking is problematic: Heavy weighted blanket on child Firm massage through blanket
Creates cocoon-like pressure Play white noise during massage Very satisfying for these children MANIFESTATION 6: Listening to Same Song 30-500+ Times Consecutively Physical Redirection Technique: "Song Repetition to Movement Routine" When child plays same song excessively, create physical engagement Technique: "You really love this song! Let's make it a workout!" Assign specific movement to each repetition: Play 1-5: Dance and jump Play 6-10: March around room Play 11-15: Do stretches Play 16-20: Wall pushes during song Play 21: "Last time! Big finale dance!" Count plays together Visual chart showing countdown to "last play" After final play: Heavy work activity, then completely different music Makes repetition purposeful (exercise routine) Adds proprioceptive input Clear ending point DIY Alternative Tool: Song Counter Card Materials: Index card, draw boxes (10-20 boxes)
Each box = one song play Child checks off box each time song plays When all boxes checked: Song time ends Visual, concrete limit Next day: New card Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Song Ticket System: Child gets 10-15 "plays" of favorite song per day Use tickets, tokens, or checkmarks When gone: "That song is done for today. Choose different song." Teaches delayed gratification and variety Song Variations: Same song, different versions: Original Cover versions Instrumental Slowed down Sped up Different language Honors the obsession while adding variety Create With the Song: Draw while listening (each play = one drawing) Dance choreography (perfect moves over many plays) Learn every word Makes repetition productive Song Journal: Write about why they love this song
Draw pictures inspired by it Track how many times played Externalizes obsession Scheduled Song Blocks: "Song time" = 20 minutes Can play favorite on repeat during that time Timer ends = different activity Contains the behavior For Communication-Focused: Extreme song repetition may indicate: Regulation need (predictability is calming) Processing (learning language/concepts from song) Emotional connection (song represents feeling/memory) Explore: "What do you love about this song?" Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Song Integration Circuit" (30-40 minutes, 1-2x daily): Controlled Song Repetition (15 min) Play favorite song with structure: Plays 1-5: Active dancing (heavy movements) Plays 6-10: Instrument play (drums, shakers) Plays 11-15: Drawing/creating to song Plays 16-20: Quieter listening with weighted lap pad Purpose: Satisfies need with variety of engagement
Song Variations (10 min) Introduce different versions of same song Discuss differences Which version do you like best? Purpose: Expands flexibility New Music Exploration (8 min) "Let's find songs LIKE your favorite!" Similar genre, tempo, artist Play 2-3 new songs Purpose: Gradually expands repertoire Heavy Work Transition (5 min) No music Proprioceptive activities Purpose: Reset from auditory focus Quiet Activity (2 min) Silent or very quiet background music Calm task For Understanding the Pattern: Why same song repeatedly? Predictability: Every note known = calming Auditory seeking: Fills auditory need intensely Processing: Child may be analyzing/learning Regulation: Known music regulates emotions Obsessive interest: Common in autism/ADHD Not harmful in moderation, but needs boundaries Sensory Integration: Auditory Regulation Protocol: Provide rich, varied auditory environment:
Throughout day: Variety of music (curated playlists) Audiobooks Podcasts for kids Nature sounds Prevents fixation on single song Scheduled "favorite song time": 15-20 min, 2x daily Can play favorite song Limited repetitions (10-15) Rest of day: variety Proprioceptive Pairing: Listen to song WHILE: Swinging Jumping on trampoline Bouncing on therapy ball Satisfies multiple needs simultaneously May reduce need for hundreds of plays Transition Strategies: Moving away from single song obsession: Week 1: Unlimited plays (baseline) Week 2: 100 plays per day (still high but limited) Week 3: 50 plays per day Week 4: 30 plays per day Week 5: 20 plays per day Week 6: 15 plays per day (maintenance) Gradual reduction reduces anxiety Massage Techniques: Ear Rest Massage (6-8 minutes, 2x daily):
Purpose: Hundreds of song plays = auditory fatigue Ears (2 min): Gentle outer ear massage Earlobes Very soothing Around Ears (2 min): Circular massage around each ear Temple area Jaw (2 min): Jaw tension from auditory processing Firm massage on masseter Face and Head (2 min): Overall calming Scalp massage Do this: After intense listening sessions, before bed Full Body Regulation Massage (15-20 minutes, daily): Purpose: Overall regulation reduces obsessive behaviors Complete routine Consistent daily massage reduces song repetition by 40-60% (parent reports) Deep pressure particularly effective "Music Break" Massage (5 minutes, as needed): Use to interrupt excessive song playing: "Let's take a music break and do massage" Hand massage (grounding) Shoulder massage (calming) Offer different activity after Often child accepts break more easily with massage transition
MANIFESTATION 7: Playing Videos for Specific Sound Effects Only Physical Redirection Technique: "Sound Effect Hunt to Creation" When child plays videos repeatedly for sound effects, redirect to creating sounds Technique: "You love that sound effect! Let's make it ourselves!" Identify the sound (explosion, animal, vehicle, etc.) Create the sound: Vocally (voice sound effects) With instruments (drums for explosions, shakers for rain) With objects (crumpling paper for fire, coconut halves for horses) With body (stomping, clapping) Practice creating effect (5 min) Record their sound effects Play back instead of video Heavy work activity after Transforms passive watching into active creating Reduces screen time Develops creative skills DIY Alternative Tool: Sound Effects Audio Library Materials: Phone/tablet, audio recording app (free) Create library of sound effects:
Record from videos (audio only) Record child making sound effects Download sound effect files (free online) Organize by category Use: Play audio only (no video needed) Portable Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Sound Effect Videos → Audio Files: Extract audio from videos Create playlist of just the sounds Eliminates repetitive video watching Provides sound without screen time Sound Effect Apps: Free soundboard apps Hundreds of effects Child taps button = sound plays More variety, less repetition Interactive control Create Own Sound Effects: Foley art supplies: Various objects for sound creation Coconut halves (horse hooves) Cellophane (fire crackle) Gravel in box (walking sounds) Leather gloves (bird wings) Purposeful, creative activity Sound Effect Books: Books with sound buttons Press for effects
No screen needed Cost: $10-20 Musical Instruments: Many create sound-effect-like sounds: Rainstick (rain/water) Ocean drum (waves) Thunder drum (thunder) Whistles (birds, wind) Musical rather than video For Communication-Focused: Using sound effects from videos may indicate: Interest in how sounds are made Preference for specific auditory input Difficulty expressing interest verbally Teach: "You can ask for sounds!" Create sound request system Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Sound Production Circuit" (30-35 minutes, 1-2x daily): Limited Video Time (5 min) Allow watching video for sound effects With rules: Only 5 minutes Only 3 replays Timer visible Purpose: Satisfies immediate need with boundaries Sound Identification (5 min) After watching: "What sounds did you hear?" List them together Discuss how each is made Purpose: Analytical rather than just consuming
Sound Recreation (12 min) Recreate each sound effect from video: Vocally (5 min) With objects/instruments (5 min) Record own versions (2 min) Purpose: Active creation instead of passive consumption Sound Effect Performance (8 min) Create scene/story Child provides live sound effects Family participates Purpose: Social, purposeful use of sound interest Alternative Activity (5 min) No screens, no sounds Tactile or proprioceptive activity Purpose: Sensory variety For Screen Time Reduction: Goal: Reduce video dependency for sounds Strategy: Provide richer sound environment without screens Success: Child satisfied without constant video playing Sensory Integration: Auditory Environment Without Screens: Provide rich sound environment: Sound effect playlists (audio only) Nature sound machines Musical instruments accessible Sound toys (buttons, switches) Result: Auditory needs met without screens Visual-Auditory Separation:
Teach: Can have sounds without watching videos Provide audio-only options Reduces screen time significantly Proprioceptive Integration: Heavy work before typical video times: 15 min intensive proprioceptive input Often eliminates desire for videos During audio listening: Swing, rock, bounce on ball Satisfies multiple needs Massage Techniques: Eye and Face Relief Massage (7-10 minutes, after screen time): Purpose: Screen time = eye strain; this relieves it Eye Area (3 min): NEVER touch eyes directly Gentle pressure on closed eyelids (very light) Massage around eye sockets (avoid eyeball) Bridge of nose Face (3 min): Full face massage Forehead, cheeks, jaw Releases tension Ears (2 min): Ear massage (auditory relief) Around ears Scalp (2 min): Gentle scalp massage Very relaxing Full Body "Screen Detox" Massage (20 minutes):
Use after day of excessive screen time: Complete full-body routine Extra calming and grounding Helps reset from screen stimulation Often child more balanced next day Hand and Finger Massage (5 minutes, daily): Purpose: Screens involve fine motor (tapping, swiping); this relieves tension Detailed hand massage Each finger individually Wrists and forearms Grounding and calming MANIFESTATION 8: Seeking Out Nature Sounds (Rain, Wind, Ocean) Physical Redirection Technique: "Nature Sound to Nature Experience" When child seeks nature sounds, provide real nature experience when possible Technique: Acknowledge: "You love rain sounds! Let's experience rain!" If raining: Go outside briefly (supervised, appropriate clothing) If not raining: Create rain experience: Shower with door open (steam + sound) Spray bottle (creates rain sound) Pour water (rain sound)
Rain stick instrument 10 minutes of "rain experience" Then: Indoor heavy work activity Provide recording for later Transforms auditory seeking into multi-sensory experience More regulating than sound alone Builds appreciation for nature DIY Alternative Tool: Nature Sound Collection Materials: Phone/tablet, nature sound apps (free) or recordings Collect variety: Rain (light, heavy, thunderstorm) Ocean (waves, calm, storm) Wind (gentle, strong) Forest (birds, rustling leaves) Stream/river Waterfall Use: Available anytime, any location Headphones for portable use Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Nature Sound Machines: White noise machines with nature options ($20-40) In bedroom, main living area Constant availability Real Nature Exposure: Regular outdoor time: Parks, forests, beaches Listen to actual nature sounds More regulating than recordings Weather experiences: Play in rain (supervised, safe)
Feel wind Listen to storms (from safety) Nature Sound Instruments: Rain stick ($10-20) Ocean drum ($20-40) Wind chimes (outside window, $10-30) Thunder drum ($30-50) Child creates nature sounds Water Features: Desktop fountain ($15-30) Aquarium (moving water sound) Real water sounds at home Nature Videos: Long-form nature videos (waves, rain, forest) Visual + auditory Can loop For Sensory Avoiders: Some nature sounds (thunder) may be aversive Provide gentle nature sounds only (rain, stream) Low volume Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Nature Sensory Circuit" (30-35 minutes, 1-2x daily): Nature Sound Listening (7 min) Comfortable position Play nature sounds Close eyes and listen Identify different sounds in recording Purpose: Mindful listening Multi-Sensory Nature Experience (15 min) If outdoors possible: Nature walk (10 min)
Sit and listen (5 min) If indoors: Water play (rain simulation) Fan (wind simulation) Natural materials (leaves, sticks, stones) Nature sounds playing Purpose: Full sensory immersion Nature Creation (10 min) Create nature sounds with instruments Draw/paint while listening to nature Build nature scene with toys/materials Purpose: Creative engagement with interest Quiet Integration (3 min) Gradually fade nature sounds Deep breathing Calm transition For Understanding the Need: Why nature sounds? Predictable yet varied (rain continues but each drop different) Low frequency (calming to nervous system) Non-threatening (no social demands, no unexpected loud noises) Regulating (scientifically proven calming effects) Healthy interest! Encourage nature connection Sensory Integration: Nature-Based Regulation: Use nature for daily regulation: Morning: Nature walk or outdoor play (15-20 min) Throughout day: Nature sounds playing (low volume)
Transitions: Brief nature sound breaks Evening: Nature sounds for calming before bed Result: Nature becomes primary regulation tool Outdoor Sensory Diet: Daily outdoor time non-negotiable: 30-60 minutes minimum All weather (with appropriate gear) Parks, yards, nature areas Combines: Auditory (nature sounds) Vestibular (movement in space) Proprioceptive (climbing, running, digging) Visual (natural light, scenery) Tactile (natural textures) Often reduces ALL stimming behaviors by 40-60% Nature Connection Building: Teach about nature Observe birds, weather, seasons Build relationship with natural world Deepens the interest positively Massage Techniques: "Nature Massage" (15-20 minutes, daily): Purpose: Pair massage with nature sounds for deep regulation Setup: Play nature sounds (rain, ocean, forest) Dim lighting Comfortable position Massage: Complete full-body routine Slow strokes (match rhythm of waves/rain) Very calming
Best time: Evening before bed Result: Incredibly regulating; combines auditory and tactile calming Foot Massage "Grounding in Nature" (10 minutes): Purpose: Feet connect us to earth; this grounds while honoring nature interest Both feet, detailed massage: Soles (firm pressure, 3 min each foot) Toes (each one, 2 min total) Tops of feet (1 min each) Ankles (1 min total) While doing: Play nature sounds Talk about walking in nature "Imagine walking on grass, sand, forest floor" Very grounding and calming Ear Massage for Nature Sounds (5 minutes): Purpose: Ears receive nature sounds; this honors that connection Gentle ear massage While playing favorite nature sounds Creates positive association Very soothing
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 2. AUDITORY STIMMING > B. Environmental Sound Stimming > Level 2: Sound Creation
Causation: Over-stimulated: Creating predictable sound provides control Under-stimulated: Generates needed auditory + tactile input Sensitivity: Cause-effect understanding; sound-touch connection Sensory Profile: Seeker: Loud, frequent, varied sound creation all day Avoider: Soft, rhythmic tapping as self-soothing Mixed: Loud sounds + simultaneous tactile input Description: Actively producing environmental sounds MANIFESTATION 1: Tapping Objects Rhythmically (Fingers, Pencils, Toys) Physical Redirection Technique: "Tap to Total Body Rhythm" When child taps repetitively, expand to full-body rhythm Technique: Join the tapping: "I hear your rhythm! Let's make it bigger!" Match their rhythm with full body: Stomp feet to their rhythm Clap hands to their rhythm Pat thighs to their rhythm March around room to their rhythm Do together 2-3 minutes Gradually slow the rhythm End with slow, heavy movements (push wall to slow rhythm)
Transition to quiet activity with fidget in hands Expands small motor into gross motor Provides proprioceptive input Natural rhythm to stillness progression DIY Alternative Tool: Rhythm Fidget Box Materials: Small box, various tappable items Contents: Pencils with erasers (good tapping) Wooden stick Small drum or pot Textured surfaces (corrugated cardboard, bubble wrap) Quiet tapping options (soft surfaces) Use: Designated items for tapping Rules: Can tap these items, not random objects Cost: Free (household items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Legitimate Percussion: Drums (various sizes, $15-50) Practice pad (quiet drum alternative, $15-25) Bongos ($20-30) Cajón (box drum, $40-80) Turns stim into musical skill Tapping Fidgets: Fidget cube with buttons ($5-10) Pop-it toys (satisfying taps, $3-8) Mechanical keyboard (for typing/tapping satisfaction, $30+) Clickers (quiet, $2-5)
Appropriate tapping outlets Rhythm Apps and Games: Drum pad apps (free) Rhythm games Digital tapping Body Percussion: Teach structured body percussion Clapping games Stomp routines Purposeful rhythm Scheduled Tapping Time: 10-15 min, 2-3x daily Can tap freely Timer ends = quiet hands time Contains behavior For Sensory Avoiders: If child IS the avoider and others tap: Noise-canceling headphones Quiet spaces Communication about noise sensitivity Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Rhythm Development Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Free Tapping (5 min) Allow tapping on various surfaces Explore different sounds Purpose: Satisfies immediate need Structured Rhythm (10 min) Learn actual rhythm patterns Simple beats (quarter notes, eighth notes) Copy adult's patterns Create own patterns Purpose: Educational, purposeful Body Rhythm (7 min) Full body percussion
Stomp-tap-clap combinations Purpose: Expands from fingers to whole body Heavy Work Rhythm (5 min) Do proprioceptive activities to rhythm Jump to beats Push wall to beats Purpose: Combines sensory needs Quiet Hands (3 min) Practice still hands Hold therapy putty (can squeeze but not tap) Gentle hand massage Purpose: Regulation after intense motor For Fine Motor Development: Tapping = fine motor practice Can be channeled into: Typing Piano/keyboard Drumming Functional skills Sensory Integration: Proprioceptive Hand/Arm Protocol: Theory: Tapping = seeking proprioceptive input to hands/arms Provide alternative input (every 60-90 min): Hand activities: Therapy putty (squeeze, pull) Playdough (knead, pound) Stress ball Hand weights (lift, hold) Arm activities: Wall pushes Carry heavy items Pulling activities Result: Satisfied proprioceptive needs = 40-50% reduction in tapping
Vestibular Pairing: Allow tapping WHILE: Swinging Rocking Bouncing on ball Satisfies multiple needs simultaneously Environmental Modifications: Provide appropriate tapping surfaces Quiet options during quiet times Louder options during active times Reduces inappropriate tapping Massage Techniques: Hand and Arm Intensive Massage (10-12 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Tapping uses hands/arms extensively; provides deep input Hands (5 min): Detailed palm massage (firm pressure, 2 min each hand) Each finger individually (pull, squeeze, rotate) Between knuckles Wrists (circular massage) Forearms (4 min): Firm squeezes from elbow to wrist (2 min each arm) Circular massage on forearm muscles Upper Arms and Shoulders (3 min): Squeeze upper arms Shoulder squeezes Connects hands to body Do this: Before times when tapping typically increases, after tapping sessions Finger Massage for Fine Motor Regulation (5 minutes, as needed):
Use when tapping is excessive: Take child's hand Massage each finger slowly (30 sec each = 5 min total both hands) Firm pressure Pull gently on each finger Rotate each finger Press firmly on fingertips Often stops tapping immediately Very grounding Full Body "Fidget Release" Massage (15 minutes, daily): Complete routine Extra attention to: Hands and arms (primary tapping tools) Back (overall calming) Reduces ALL fidgeting behaviors including tapping MANIFESTATION 2: Banging on Surfaces Repeatedly Physical Redirection Technique: "Bang to Controlled Impact" When child bangs surfaces, redirect to appropriate impact activities Technique: Acknowledge: "You want to make loud banging! Let's bang the RIGHT way!" Provide appropriate alternatives immediately: Drum with hands (on actual drum or overturned pot) Pound playdough on table
Hammer toy workbench Stomp feet on ground (body banging) Do together 5 minutes Then: Heavy work without noise (push wall, carry items) Teach: "We bang on drums and pots, not on walls and furniture" Redirects destructive banging to appropriate outlets Provides proprioceptive input (what they're seeking) Protects furniture and walls DIY Alternative Tool: Bang Station Materials: Overturned sturdy pot or bucket Wooden spoons or drumsticks Old phone book or thick magazine (for pounding) Cushion to bang on floor Setup: Designated "banging corner" Rule: Can bang HERE only Cost: Free (household items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Legitimate Banging Outlets: Drums (full set if possible, $50-200) Punching bag (child-size, $30-60) Hammer toys (workbench, $20-40) Stomp toys (stomp rockets, $15-25) Purpose: Appropriate impact activities
Outdoor Banging: Sticks on trees (supervised) Rocks on rocks Digging and pounding in dirt Natural, appropriate outlets Heavy Work Alternatives: Provides same proprioceptive without noise: Wall pushes (silent but forceful) Pushing furniture Carrying heavy items If proprioception is primary need, noise unnecessary Scheduled Banging Time: 10-15 min, 2-3x daily Designated location (outside, basement, specific room) Can bang as much as wanted Timer ends = quiet time Contains behavior Music Lessons: Drum lessons Percussion classes Turns stim into skill For Sensory Avoiders (if others bang): Noise-canceling headphones Warning before banging activities Quiet spaces available Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Impact and Proprioception Circuit" (30-35 minutes, 1-2x daily): Controlled Banging (8 min) Drums, pots, appropriate surfaces With rhythm patterns (not random) Loud and soft banging
Fast and slow Purpose: Purposeful, controlled impact Heavy Work (10 min) Wall pushes (3 min) - forceful without noise Carrying heavy items (3 min) Tug-of-war (2 min) Pushing/pulling furniture (2 min) Purpose: Provides proprioceptive without auditory Aggressive Play (8 min) Punching bag Pillow fighting Wrestling with adult (safe) Crash pad jumping Purpose: Releases physical energy appropriately Pounding Activities (6 min) Pound playdough (2 min) Hammer toy workbench (2 min) Meat tenderizer on playdough (2 min) Purpose: Controlled pounding Quiet Transition (3 min) Gentle activities Deep breathing Weighted lap pad Reduces arousal For Understanding the Need: Why banging? Proprioceptive seeking (impact through hands/arms) Auditory seeking (loud sound) Cause-effect exploration (I bang = sound happens) Emotional expression (anger, frustration, excitement) Sensory feedback (body needs strong input)
Not misbehavior - sensory need or communication attempt Sensory Integration: Intensive Proprioceptive Protocol: Theory: Banging = intense proprioceptive seeking Provide throughout day (every 90 min): 10-15 min heavy work breaks: Pushing Pulling Carrying Jumping Crashing Before high-risk times: 20 min intensive proprioceptive "loading" Often prevents banging completely Result: Satisfied proprioceptive system = 60-80% reduction in banging Appropriate Outlets Always Available: Drums in playroom Punching bag accessible Heavy items to carry Never without appropriate outlet Environmental Modifications: Protect surfaces if banging continues Foam padding on walls (temporary) Move fragile items While working on behavior Massage Techniques: Hand, Arm, and Shoulder Intensive Massage (12-15 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Banging uses hands/arms/shoulders intensively; deep massage satisfies Hands (4 min): Very firm palm massage (2 min each hand)
Squeeze each finger hard Press firmly on knuckles Child should feel significant pressure Forearms (3 min): Very firm squeezes from elbow to wrist As much pressure as child tolerates comfortably Upper Arms (3 min): Firm squeezes Can't be too gentle - needs to feel it Shoulders (4 min): Very firm shoulder squeezes (20-30x) Press down on shoulders firmly Shoulder compressions Pressure level: FIRM - child needs strong proprioceptive input Do this: Before times when banging typically occurs, after banging episodes Joint Compression Protocol (5-7 minutes, 3-4x daily): Purpose: Provides deep joint input (what banging provides) Hands and wrists: Press palms together hard (10 sec) Compress wrist joints (push hand toward forearm gently, 5 sec) Elbows: Bend arm, press on elbow to compress joint (5 sec, repeat 5x)
Shoulders: Press down on shoulders firmly (10 sec, repeat 5x) Can teach child to do self-compressions Very regulating for banging behavior Full Body Deep Pressure Massage (20 minutes, 1-2x daily): Best times: After school (high-banging time), before bed Complete routine with FIRM pressure These children need deep, strong input Not gentle, relaxing massage - FIRM, organizing massage Focus on: Arms (5 min) Legs (5 min) Back (8 min) Hands/feet (2 min) Result: Deep daily massage can reduce banging by 70-90%** MANIFESTATION 3: Scratching or Rubbing Textured Surfaces for Sound Physical Redirection Technique: "Scratch Sound to Tactile Exploration" When child scratches surfaces for sound, redirect to rich tactile play Technique: Acknowledge: "You like that scratching sound! Let's find MORE textures!" Texture hunt:
Gather various textured items (fabric, sandpaper, bubble wrap, corrugated cardboard, velvet, burlap) Explore each with hands (rubbing, scratching) Notice sounds AND feelings Which is loudest? Softest? Roughest? Smoothest? 10 minutes exploration Then: Hands-on activity (playdough, finger painting) Heavy work after Expands auditory seeking into tactile seeking More developmentally appropriate Richer sensory experience DIY Alternative Tool: Texture Scratch Board Materials: Piece of plywood or thick cardboard (12"x12"), glue various textures Textures: Sandpaper squares (various grits) Velcro strips Corrugated cardboard Bubble wrap Fabric scraps (corduroy, velvet, burlap) Aluminum foil Window screen mesh Use: Child scratches each section Different sounds and feelings Appropriate outlet Cost: $5-10 for materials Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Sensory Bins with Textured Materials: Rice, beans, sand, pasta Run hands through = scratching sound
Appropriate tactile and auditory input 10-15 min, 2-3x daily Scratch-Specific Items: Scratch art (black paper that reveals colors when scratched, $5-10) Scratch-off lottery cards (used, free from adults) Velcro board (pulling apart makes satisfying sound) Purpose: Appropriate scratching Musical Scratching: Guiro (Latin percussion instrument, scrape stick across, $10-20) Washboard (musical instrument, $15-25) Purpose: Turns scratching into music Textured Fidgets: Fidgets with various textures Can rub/scratch in hand Portable Appropriate, discreet Tactile Play: Playdough (knead, scratch with tools) Kinetic sand (mold, scratch patterns) Finger painting (tactile satisfaction) Rich tactile alternatives For Sensory Avoiders: If child IS avoider, scratching may be defensive behavior (uncomfortable with touch, seeking control) Provide gradual tactile desensitization Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Tactile-Auditory Integration Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily):
Texture Exploration (10 min) Multiple textured surfaces Scratch, rub, explore each Notice sounds AND feelings Chart favorite textures Purpose: Mindful exploration Tactile Play (10 min) Sensory bins (rice, beans, sand) Playdough or kinetic sand Finger painting or shaving cream Purpose: Rich tactile input Scratching Instruments (5 min) Guiro or washboard Purposeful scratching sounds Learn rhythm patterns Purpose: Musical outlet Hand Heavy Work (3 min) Therapy putty (pull, squeeze) Hand weights Finger exercises Purpose: Proprioceptive to hands Hand Massage (2 min) Detailed hand massage Various textures (lotion, dry, textured cloth) Purpose: Calming integration For Tactile Sensitivity (if scratching is defensive): Tactile Desensitization Program: Gradual exposure to textures Start with tolerated textures Slowly introduce challenging ones Build tolerance over weeks/months Sensory Integration: Tactile Sensory Diet:
Provide rich tactile input throughout day: Every 60-90 min: Tactile bin play (5 min) Textured fidget (available constantly) Tactile activities (playdough, etc.) Before scratching typically occurs: 10 min intensive tactile input May prevent scratching behavior Result: Satisfied tactile needs = less surface scratching Hand Proprioceptive Input: Scratching = seeking hand/finger input Provide alternatives: Therapy putty (throughout day) Stress balls Hand exercises Playing with small manipulatives Satisfies hand needs differently Environmental Modifications: Provide appropriate surfaces to scratch Protect inappropriate surfaces While teaching discrimination Massage Techniques: Hand and Finger Intensive Massage (10-12 minutes, 3x daily): Purpose: Provides deep tactile input to hands (what scratching seeks) Palms (3 min): Firm circular massage (1.5 min each hand) Press firmly all over palm Knead palm muscles
Fingers (5 min): Each finger individually (30 sec each = 5 min both hands) Pull firmly Squeeze Rotate at each joint Press on fingertips and fingernails Between Fingers (2 min): Massage between each finger Press into webbing Backs of Hands (2 min): Firm massage Press on knuckles Do this: Before times when scratching occurs, multiple times daily Very satisfying for these children Textured Hand Massage (7-10 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Provides tactile variety (what they seek when scratching different surfaces) Use DIFFERENT textures during massage: Smooth: Regular lotion massage (2 min) Rough: Textured cloth massage (2 min) Bumpy: Use massage ball with nubs (2 min) Vibration: Use massager on hands (2 min) Dry brush: Soft brush on hands (2 min) Provides rich tactile variety
Satisfies seeking for different tactile-auditory combinations Full Body Tactile Massage (15 minutes, daily): Use varied pressures and textures during massage Not just hands - whole body needs tactile input Some children scratch because overall tactile system under-responsive Rich full-body tactile = less hand scratching MANIFESTATION 4: Crinkling Paper or Plastic (5-30+ minutes) Physical Redirection Technique: "Crinkle to Crush" When child crinkles paper/plastic extensively, redirect to purposeful crushing Technique: Acknowledge: "You like that crinkling sound! Let's CRUSH things!" Provide alternatives: Stack of old newspaper (can crumple forcefully) Bubble wrap (satisfying pops AND crinkles) Empty water bottles (crush and crinkle) Paper bags (loud crinkle) Make it purposeful: "Let's make the smallest ball possible!" or "Let's fill this bag with crushed paper!" 5-10 minutes of intensive crushing
Then: Heavy work without noise Dispose of crushed items (cleanup = proprioceptive) Allows the behavior with boundaries Provides hand/arm proprioceptive input Time-limited and purposeful DIY Alternative Tool: Crinkle Box Materials: Box or bag, fill with crinkly materials Contents: Newspaper sheets Tissue paper Cellophane Bubble wrap Plastic shopping bags Aluminum foil Parchment paper Use: Designated crinkle materials Can crinkle/crush these only Cost: Free (collected items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Scheduled Crinkle Time: 10-15 min, 2-3x daily Access to crinkly materials Timer ends = put materials away Contains behavior Bubble Wrap Activities: Bubble wrap sheets ($5 for large sheet) Pop and crinkle Walk on it (pops under feet) Highly satisfying Crinkle Toys: Baby crinkle toys (crinkly fabric, $5-10) Crinkle paper in fidget pouch
Appropriate, portable Crushing Activities: Crush cans for recycling (supervised, older children) Crush cereal boxes before recycling Functional crushing Sensory Bins with Crinkly Materials: Shredded paper Crinkle cut paper Run hands through = sound Tactile and auditory Art with Crinkly Materials: Tissue paper collage (crinkle while gluing) Aluminum foil sculptures (crinkle and shape) Purposeful crinkling For Sensory Avoiders: If others crinkle and it bothers child: Headphones Designated quiet spaces Communication about noise sensitivity Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Crinkle and Crush Circuit" (20-25 minutes, 2x daily): Controlled Crinkling (7 min) Various crinkly materials Explore different sounds Fast vs slow crinkling Loud vs quiet Purpose: Mindful exploration Crushing Activities (8 min) Crush paper into balls (3 min) Pop bubble wrap (2 min)
Crush empty bottles (3 min) Purpose: Forceful, proprioceptive Hand Heavy Work (5 min) Therapy putty (pull, squeeze, twist) Stress ball Hand grip strengthener Purpose: Hand proprioception without noise Crinkle Art (3 min) Create something with crinkled materials Purposeful Hand Massage (2 min) Calming hand massage Transition to quiet For Understanding the Need: Why crinkling? Auditory: Satisfying sound Tactile: Interesting hand sensation Proprioceptive: Crushing uses hand/arm muscles Control: Child controls sound creation Repetitive: Predictable, calming Multi-sensory behavior (auditory + tactile + proprioceptive) Sensory Integration: Hand-Focused Sensory Diet: Provide rich hand input throughout day: Every 60 min: Hand activity (putty, fidget, manipulative toy) 3-5 minutes Before high-crinkle times: 10 min intensive hand activities May prevent crinkling Result: Satisfied hand needs = less crinkling
Auditory Alternatives: Provide other satisfying sounds ASMR videos (crinkling sounds, $0 - free online) Sound machines Fills auditory need without materials waste Proprioceptive Substitution: Heavy work for hands/arms May satisfy same need without crinkling Try: Does heavy work reduce crinkling? Massage Techniques: Intensive Hand and Forearm Massage (12-15 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Crinkling = intense hand use; deep massage satisfies Hands (6 min): Very firm palm massage (3 min each hand) Each finger (pull, squeeze, rotate) Between fingers Knuckles (firm pressure) Forearms (4 min): Firm squeezes from elbow to wrist (2 min each) Circular massage on muscles Wrists (3 min): Circular massage around wrists Flex and extend while massaging Upper Arms and Shoulders (2 min): Connect hands to body Firm squeezes
Do this: Multiple times daily, especially before typical crinkling times Textured Hand Massage (8-10 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Crinkling provides varied tactile input; replicate through massage Use different textures: Smooth lotion (2 min) Textured cloth (2 min) Rough (textured glove or brush, 2 min) Cool (use cold lotion or ice pack briefly, 1 min) Warm (use warm towel, 1 min) Vibration (massager, 2 min) Provides rich sensory variety May reduce need for crinkling Full Body Regulation Massage (15 minutes, daily): Complete routine Extra focus on hands and arms Overall regulation reduces all stimming behaviors MANIFESTATION 5: Shaking Containers with Items Inside Physical Redirection Technique: "Shake to Musical Rhythm" When child shakes containers repeatedly, transform into musical activity Technique: Acknowledge: "You're making a shaker! Let's make MUSIC!"
Provide proper shakers or make them together: DIY shaker: Empty bottle + rice/beans + tape Create rhythm patterns: Shake-shake-pause-shake Fast shaking, slow shaking Loud and quiet Play music, shake along to beat March while shaking (vestibular + auditory) Heavy work after (5 min) Transforms random shaking into musical activity Adds structure and purpose Can participate with others (social) DIY Alternative Tool: Shaker Collection Materials: Various empty containers, rice/beans/buttons/beads Create different shakers: Small bottle (high-pitched shake) Large bottle (low-pitched shake) Metal container (louder) Plastic container (quieter) Decorate each Different contents = different sounds Cost: Free (household items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Actual Musical Shakers: Maracas ($5-10 pair) Egg shakers ($3-5) Shaker tubes ($5-8) Rain stick ($10-20) Purpose: Legitimate instruments Shaker Games:
"Guess what's inside!" (shake to identify contents) "Loudest shaker contest" "Follow the rhythm" (adult shakes pattern, child copies) Purposeful shaking Music Classes: Percussion classes Music Together classes (toddler/preschool) Social, educational Sound-Making Sensory Bins: Containers buried in rice/beans Find and shake each one Combines tactile seeking with auditory Scheduled Shaking Time: 10 min, 2-3x daily Can shake freely Timer ends = quiet time Contains behavior For Sensory Avoiders (if shaking bothers them): Headphones during others' shaking time Quiet spaces Warning before shaking activities Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Shake and Move Circuit" (25 minutes, 2x daily): Free Shaking Exploration (5 min) Multiple shakers/containers Explore different sounds Purpose: Satisfies immediate need Musical Shaking (10 min) Play music, shake to beat Learn rhythm patterns
Shake-and-dance Play with others (turn-taking) Purpose: Structured, social** Shaking with Movement (7 min) March while shaking Jump while shaking Spin while shaking Purpose: Vestibular + auditory + proprioceptive Hand Heavy Work (3 min) Therapy putty Stress ball Purpose: Hand proprioception without noise For Understanding the Need: Why shaking? Auditory: Satisfying repetitive sound Proprioceptive: Arm movement, hand grip Vestibular: Rhythmic movement Visual: Watching items move inside (if transparent) Control: Child creates and controls sound Multi-sensory behavior Sensory Integration: Vestibular-Auditory Integration: Theory: Shaking often accompanies vestibular seeking Provide vestibular input: Swinging (15-20 min daily) Spinning Rocking Allow shaking WHILE swinging: Combine both needs May reduce random shaking Result: Satisfied vestibular system = less shaking Arm and Hand Proprioceptive Protocol: Shaking = arm movement + hand grip
Provide alternatives every 60-90 min: Carrying heavy items (5 min) Pulling/pushing activities Hand exercises (putty, stress ball) May reduce shaking by 40-50% Auditory Environment: Rich auditory input Music playing Reduces need to create own sounds Massage Techniques: Arm, Hand, and Shoulder Massage (12-15 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Shaking uses arms/hands/shoulders extensively Shoulders (3 min): Firm squeezes (20x) Circular massage Upper Arms (2 min): Squeeze from shoulder to elbow (10x each arm) Forearms (4 min): Firm squeezes from elbow to wrist (2 min each) Circular massage on muscles Hands (5 min): Detailed hand massage (see previous descriptions) Very firm pressure Do this: Before typical shaking times, after shaking episodes Joint Compression for Arms (5 minutes, 3x daily): Purpose: Provides deep proprioceptive input shaking seeks
Wrist compressions: Gently compress wrist joint (5 sec, 5x) Elbow compressions: Bend arm, compress elbow joint (5 sec, 5x) Shoulder compressions: Press down on shoulders firmly (10 sec, 5x) Can teach child self-compressions Very regulating Full Body "Shake Release" Massage (15 minutes, daily): Complete routine Focus on upper body (arms, shoulders, back) Deep, firm pressure Reduces shaking behavior significantly MANIFESTATION 6: Clicking Pens or Switches (100+ times) Physical Redirection Technique: "Click to Count and Stop" When child clicks repetitively, add counting structure Technique: Acknowledge: "You like clicking! Let's count your clicks!" Count together: "1, 2, 3... up to 20!" After 20: "Great! Now let's do 20 jumps instead of clicks!" Jump together (proprioceptive) Offer alternative: "Here's a quiet fidget for your hands now"
Provide silent fidget (therapy putty, stress ball) Teach: "Clicking time is done. Now it's quiet fidget time." Puts limits on clicking Redirects to proprioceptive activity Provides alternative hand occupation DIY Alternative Tool: Click Alternatives Box Materials: Small box with various quiet fidgets Contents: Therapy putty Stress ball Tangle toy (twisted coils) Smooth stones Fidget cube (quiet side) Stretchy string Use: When clicking urge arises, choose from box All silent alternatives Cost: $10-15 for variety Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Clicker Toys (Designated): Fidget clicker (designed for this purpose, $5-8) Tally counter (satisfying clicks, $3-5) Designated pens (can click THESE pens only) Purpose: Appropriate clicking outlet Button/Switch Toys: Big button toys (large satisfying clicks) Light switches (play switches, not functional ones) Keyboard (old keyboard for clicking/typing)
Purpose: Appropriate button pressing Quiet Alternatives: Silent pen (no click mechanism) Pop-it fidget (quiet pops) Squeeze fidgets Purpose: Hand occupation without noise Scheduled Clicking Time: 5 min, 2-3x daily Can click designated item Timer ends = quiet fidget Contains behavior Click Counting Game: See how many clicks in 1 minute Try to beat record Makes it purposeful competition Time-limited For Sensory Avoiders (if clicking bothers them): Use silent fidgets only Headphones if others click Communicate about noise sensitivity Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Click Control Circuit" (15-20 minutes, 2-3x daily): Controlled Clicking (5 min) Designated clicker or pen Structured clicking: 10 fast clicks 10 slow clicks 10 loud clicks 10 quiet clicks STOP Purpose: Control and awareness Finger Exercises (5 min)
Finger isolation exercises Therapy putty work Finger push-ups on table Purpose: Finger proprioception without clicking Hand Heavy Work (5 min) Squeeze stress ball (50x) Pull therapy putty Hand grip strengthener Purpose: Hand muscle work without noise Quiet Fidget Practice (3 min) Practice using silent fidgets Find favorites Purpose: Alternatives to clicking Hand Massage (2 min) Calming hand massage Transition away from stimulation For Understanding the Need: Why clicking? Auditory: Satisfying click sound Tactile: Button press sensation Proprioceptive: Finger/hand muscle use Visual: Pen mechanism moving Control: Predictable cause-effect Rhythm: Can click in patterns Common in ADHD/autism (fidgeting, stimming) Sensory Integration: Hand and Finger Sensory Diet: Provide rich hand input throughout day: Every 45-60 min: 3-5 min hand activity Therapy putty, stress ball, fidget
Before high-risk times: 10 min intensive hand work Reduces clicking urge Result: Satisfied hand needs = 50-70% reduction in clicking Auditory Alternatives: Provide other satisfying sounds Music, white noise Reduces need for self-generated clicking Fidget Training: Teach appropriate fidget use Always have quiet fidget available Substitute clicking with silent fidgeting Massage Techniques: Intensive Hand and Finger Massage (10-12 minutes, 3-4x daily): Purpose: Clicking = intense finger use; deep massage satisfies Each finger individually (6 min): Pull firmly on each finger (10 sec each) Squeeze each finger along its length Rotate each finger at each joint Press firmly on fingertip and nail 30 seconds per finger = 5 min both hands Extra time on clicking finger (index typically) Palms (3 min): Very firm circular massage
Press thumbs deeply into palm Knead palm muscles Between Fingers (2 min): Massage webbing between each finger Firm pressure Wrists (1 min): Circular massage Flex and extend Do this: Multiple times daily, especially before situations requiring quiet hands Finger Joint Compression (5 minutes, 4x daily): Purpose: Provides deep joint input (what clicking provides) Each finger: Gently compress each joint (3 joints per finger) Hold compression 5 seconds All 10 fingers = 150 seconds = 2.5 min Knuckles: Press down on each knuckle firmly (10 sec each) Wrists: Compress wrist joints Very regulating for clicking behavior Can teach child to do this themselves Full Hand Proprioceptive Routine (8 minutes, 3x daily): Hand massage (4 min) Joint compressions (2 min) Hand exercises (squeeze ball, 2 min)
Complete hand sensory circuit Often eliminates clicking for several hours MANIFESTATION 7: Slamming Doors or Cabinets Physical Redirection Technique: "Slam to Safe Impact" When child slams doors/cabinets, redirect to appropriate impact immediately Technique: Intervene: "Stop! Doors stay open or close gently. Let's slam the RIGHT way!" Provide immediate alternatives: Crash pad or pile of pillows (slam into it) Punching bag (hit it) Stomp on ground (forceful stomping) Clap hands loudly (creates noise without damage) Do 2 minutes of appropriate impact Heavy work activity after (push wall, carry items) Return to door: "Now show me gentle door closing" (practice 5 times) Redirects destructive behavior immediately Provides impact/noise outlet Teaches appropriate vs. inappropriate DIY Alternative Tool: Safe Slam Board Materials: Piece of thick plywood, foam padding, hinges
