Create simple door that opens and closes Mount on wall or fence (outside) Can slam THIS door Won't break, won't hurt fingers Cost: $20-30 for materials Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Appropriate Impact Outlets: Crash pad (foam pad for crashing, $40-80) Punching bag (child-safe, $30-60) Stomp toys (stomp and launch, $15-25) Drums (can hit hard) Purpose: Safe, appropriate impact Outdoor Activities: Stomping in puddles (water splash = impact) Throwing balls at target Kicking balls Appropriate forceful activities Heavy Work: Pushing heavy furniture (supervised) Carrying heavy items Provides proprioceptive without destruction Teach Door Skills: Practice gentle door closing Count to 3 while closing slowly "Silent ninja door closing" game Make it a skill to learn Modify Environment: Door stoppers (prevent full slam)
Soft-close hinges (if persistent problem) Remove doors temporarily (bedroom, playroom) While teaching appropriate behavior For Safety: Slamming doors = safety risk Fingers can be crushed Doors/frames can break Others can be hurt Immediate intervention required Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Safe Impact Circuit" (30 minutes, 2x daily): Appropriate Slamming (8 min) Safe slam board (if available) Crash into crash pad (3 min) Punch punching bag (3 min) Stomp on ground (2 min) Purpose: Satisfies impact need safely Heavy Work (10 min) Push/pull heavy furniture Carry weighted items Wall pushes (forceful) Tug-of-war Purpose: Intense proprioceptive without noise Aggressive Play (8 min) Pillow fights (supervised) Wrestling (safe, with adult) Throwing balls at target Purpose: Appropriate outlet for intensity Door Practice (4 min)
Practice gentle door closing (10 times) Practice gentle cabinet closing (10 times) Praise and reinforce Purpose: Teach appropriate behavior For Emotional Regulation: Sometimes slamming = anger/frustration Teach: Recognize angry feelings Use words: "I'm angry!" Use appropriate outlets (crash pad, stomp) Not slam doors Sensory Integration: Intensive Proprioceptive Protocol: Theory: Slamming = seeking intense impact/proprioceptive input Provide throughout day: Every 90 min: 10-15 min heavy work Pushing Pulling Carrying Jumping Crashing (into safe surfaces) Before high-risk times: 20-30 min intensive proprioceptive loading Often prevents slamming completely Result: Satisfied proprioceptive needs = no more slamming Appropriate Outlets Always Available: Crash pad in main living area Punching bag accessible Heavy items to carry Never without appropriate option Environmental Modifications: Door stoppers Cabinet locks (if necessary for safety)
Protect home while teaching Massage Techniques: Full Body Deep Impact Massage (20-25 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Provides deep impact sensation through massage Best times: After school (high-impact need time), before bed Technique: Use FIRM, DEEP pressure throughout Back (8 min): Percussion (cupped hands, drum on back) - creates impact sensation (3 min) Deep pressure strokes (3 min) Press firmly with palms all over back (2 min) Arms and Legs (8 min): Firm squeezing (2 min each limb) Percussion (tapping) on muscles (2 min) Joint compressions (see below, 2 min) Hands and Feet (4 min): Very firm pressure Press into palms and soles forcefully Shoulders (3 min): Very firm squeezes (20-30x) Press down hard on shoulders Pressure level: As deep as child comfortably tolerates These children need INTENSE input
Result: Deep daily massage often eliminates slamming behavior Joint Compression Protocol (10 minutes, 3-4x daily): Purpose: Provides deep joint input (what impact provides) Upper body: Shoulder compressions (press down firmly, 10 sec, 10x) Elbow compressions (5 sec, 10x each) Wrist compressions (5 sec, 10x each) Finger compressions (each joint, 3 sec) Lower body: Hip compressions (press on hips, 10 sec, 10x) Knee compressions (5 sec, 10x each) Ankle compressions (5 sec, 10x each) Can teach child to do self-compressions: Push palms together hard Press hands on thighs Self-regulation tool Very effective for high-impact seekers Emergency "Slam Prevention" Massage (5 minutes): Use when you notice child escalating toward slamming: Very firm, rapid massage: Shoulder squeezes (1 min) Arm squeezes (1 min) Hand squeezes (1 min)
Leg squeezes (1 min) Deep pressure hug (1 min) Often de-escalates immediately Redirect to appropriate activity after MANIFESTATION 8: Dropping Objects to Hear Impact Sounds Physical Redirection Technique: "Drop to Throw" When child drops objects for sound, redirect to appropriate throwing Technique: Intervene: "We don't drop things in the house. Let's throw things OUTSIDE!" Take child outside or to safe indoor space Provide appropriate throwing materials: Soft balls (into basket) Bean bags (at target) Rocks (into bucket or water - outdoor) Water balloons (satisfying splash impact - summer) Practice throwing at targets (10-15 min) Heavy work after Teach: "Throwing is for outside/safe places. Inside we keep things in our hands." Redirects dropping to appropriate throwing Provides impact sound safely Teaches discrimination (inside vs. outside)
DIY Alternative Tool: Safe Drop Zone Materials: Large box or bin, various safe-to-drop items Contents: Soft foam balls Bean bags Stuffed animals Plastic cups Blocks (on carpet) Setup: Designated dropping area (on carpet or padded surface) Rule: Can drop THESE items in THIS box only Cost: Free (household items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Appropriate Dropping Activities: Marble run (drop marbles, hear them fall, $15-30) Drop zone game (drop bean bags into bucket) Coin drop (piggy bank - satisfying clink) Purpose: Appropriate, purposeful dropping Throwing Activities: Basketball (small hoop, $15-25) Bean bag toss Dart board (velcro darts, $10-20) Ball pit (throw balls in) Appropriate impact activities Cause-Effect Toys: Marble mazes Ball tracks Ramps (cars rolling down) Purpose: Satisfies interest in objects falling
Water Play: Drop objects in water (splashing sound) Sink-or-float experiments Educational dropping Building to Destroy: Build block towers to knock down Stacking cups to push over Purposeful destruction/impact For Safety: Dropping can be dangerous: Objects can break Can fall on toes/feet Can damage floors Immediate redirection essential Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Impact and Drop Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 2x daily): Controlled Dropping (7 min) Safe drop zone with appropriate items Drop into targets Count drops (limit to 20-30) Purpose: Satisfies need with boundaries Throwing Activities (10 min) Ball toss into basket (3 min) Bean bag at target (3 min) Soft ball throwing outside (4 min) Purpose: Appropriate impact activity Cause-Effect Exploration (6 min) Marble runs, ball tracks Ramps and rolling toys
Purpose: Intellectual engagement with dropping interest Heavy Work (5 min) Carrying items (not dropping!) Pushing/pulling Purpose: Proprioceptive without dropping Building and Knocking (2 min) Build towers, knock down purposefully Purpose: Appropriate destruction outlet For Understanding the Need: Why dropping? Auditory: Impact sound Visual: Watch object fall Cause-effect: I drop = it falls Proprioceptive: Releasing grip Gravity exploration: Scientific interest Developmental stage (toddlers) or sensory seeking (older children) Sensory Integration: Hand Proprioceptive Protocol: Dropping = releasing grip (proprioceptive input) Provide alternative hand input: Every 60 min: Squeeze stress ball (50x) Therapy putty (pull, squeeze) Hand grip strengthener Open and close exercises: Open hand wide, close tight (20x) Same input without dropping Result: Satisfied grip muscles = less dropping Vestibular Integration: Watching objects fall = visual-vestibular interest
Provide vestibular input: Swinging (15-20 min daily) Spinning Tilting/upside down play May reduce dropping interest Appropriate Outlets Always Available: Marble run accessible Safe drop zone Never without appropriate option Massage Techniques: Hand, Wrist, and Forearm Massage (10-12 minutes, 3x daily): Purpose: Dropping uses hand/wrist muscles; massage provides input Hands (4 min): Firm palm massage (2 min each) Each finger (pull, squeeze) Focus on proprioception Wrists (3 min): Circular massage around wrists Flex and extend wrists during massage Rotate wrists Forearms (4 min): Firm squeezes from elbow to wrist (2 min each) Circular massage on muscles Do this: Before typical dropping times, after dropping episodes Grip Strength Massage and Exercises (8 minutes, 3x daily): Massage (4 min): Focus on palm muscles Massage each finger
Exercises (4 min): Squeeze stress ball (2 min) Therapy putty (2 min) Combines massage with strengthening Strengthens grip = more control = less accidental dropping Full Body Calming Massage (15 minutes, daily): Complete routine Reduces impulsivity Better impulse control = less compulsive dropping MANIFESTATION 9: Running Fingernails Along Walls, Furniture Physical Redirection Technique: "Scratch to Texture Exploration" When child scratches surfaces, redirect to appropriate texture play Technique: Intervene: "Walls stay smooth. Let's find textures for your fingers!" Provide rich texture exploration: Texture board (various textures glued to board) Fabric scraps (corduroy, velvet, burlap, satin) Sandpaper (various grits) Bubble wrap (to scratch/pop) Textured fidgets Explore each texture with fingers (10 min) Which feels best? Which sounds best? Then: Hands-on activity (playdough, putty)
Hand massage after Provides appropriate tactile exploration Richer sensory experience than walls Protects surfaces DIY Alternative Tool: Texture Exploration Board (detailed earlier) Various textures on board Can scratch freely Portable Cost: $5-10 Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Sensory Bins: Rice, beans, sand, pasta Run fingers through materials Scratching sensation + tactile 10-15 min, 2-3x daily Textured Fidgets: Fidgets with ridges, bumps, textures Can run fingers over in pocket/hand Portable, discreet Always available Art Activities: Finger painting (tactile) Scratch art (appropriate scratching) Textured collages (glue various textures) Purposeful tactile engagement Musical Scratching: Guiro (scrape instrument) Washboard Turns scratching into music Nail Care: Keep nails trimmed short (reduces scratching ability) File nails smooth Practical management For Sensory Avoiders (if scratching is defensive): Scratching surfaces may indicate tactile defensiveness
Seeking control over tactile input Provide gradual desensitization Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Texture Exploration Circuit" (20-25 minutes, 2x daily): Appropriate Scratching (7 min) Texture board (various surfaces) Sandpaper (different grits) Musical scratching instruments Purpose: Appropriate scratching outlet Rich Tactile Play (10 min) Sensory bins (rice, beans, sand) Playdough or kinetic sand Finger painting Purpose: Rich tactile input Fingernail Focus (3 min) Nail filing (self-care + sensation) Painting nails (if interested) Purpose: Appropriate nail focus Hand Heavy Work (3 min) Therapy putty Stress ball Purpose: Proprioceptive input Hand Massage (2 min) Detailed hand massage Various textures during massage For Understanding the Need: Why fingernails on surfaces? Tactile: Sensation at fingertips/under nails Auditory: Scratching sound Proprioceptive: Finger pressure Control: Creating sensation
Common in tactile seekers Sensory Integration: Fingertip and Nail Sensory Protocol: Provide rich fingertip input: Every 60 min: Textured fidget (3-5 min) Finger activities (sorting small items) Specific fingertip activities: Play with small beads Button/unbutton Zip/unzip Fine motor = fingertip input Result: Satisfied fingertips = less surface scratching Tactile Sensory Diet: Throughout day: Rich tactile experiences Various textures constantly available Fills tactile need appropriately Environmental Protection: Textured wallpaper or decals in child's room (appropriate to scratch) Protect valuable surfaces While teaching appropriate behavior Massage Techniques: Fingertip and Nail Bed Massage (8-10 minutes, 3-4x daily): Purpose: Provides deep input to fingertips (what scratching seeks) Each fingertip (5 min): Firm pressure on tip of each finger (30 sec each = 5 min both hands)
Circular massage on fingertip pad Press around nail bed Gentle pressure under nail (if child allows) Fingernails (2 min): Firm pressure on each nail (10 sec each) Massage around cuticles Between Fingers (2 min): Massage webbing Rich sensory input to fingers Palms (2 min): Finish with palm massage Do this: Multiple times daily Very satisfying for nail-scratchers Textured Hand Massage (10 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Provides tactile variety (what they seek) Use different textures during massage: Rough cloth (2 min) Smooth lotion (2 min) Bumpy massage ball (2 min) Soft brush (2 min) Vibrating massager (2 min) Rich tactile experience Reduces need to seek textures with nails Full Hand Sensory Integration Massage (12 minutes, 2x daily): Combine massage with texture exploration:
Massage hands Then have child explore textures Then massage again Integrates sensation Very effective for this behavior
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 2. AUDITORY STIMMING > B. Environmental Sound Stimming > Level 3: Technology-Based Sound Stimming
Causation: Over-stimulated: Complete control over auditory input Under-stimulated: Access to unlimited sound variety Sensitivity: Exploring sound technology; pattern seeking Sensory Profile: Seeker: Maximum technology use, high volume, intense frequency Control-Seeker: Using technology to perfectly control sound environment Description: Using electronic devices for auditory stimulation MANIFESTATION 1: Playing/Pausing/Replaying Specific Video Sections (100+ times) Physical Redirection Technique: "Screen Replay to Physical Replay" When child replays video sections excessively, redirect to physical reenactment Technique: After 5 replays: "You love that part! Let's ACT IT OUT instead!" Turn off screen Act out the scene physically: Assign roles (child, adult, siblings) Use props if needed Do movements from scene Say dialogue Do physical version 5 times Then: Different activity (heavy work) Can watch video once more later (limited)
Transforms passive screen time into active play Provides proprioceptive and social engagement Reduces screen dependency DIY Alternative Tool: Video Time Token System Materials: Poker chips or buttons (10-15), jar Each token = 5 minutes of video time Child can spend tokens throughout day When tokens gone: Screen time over for today Tomorrow: New tokens Visual, concrete limit Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Screen Time Limits (Essential): Maximum 1-2 hours total daily Use timers (visible countdown) When time ends: Screen turns off Non-negotiable boundaries Alternative Interests: Books about favorite characters Toys from favorite shows Dress-up/costumes Extends interest without screen Audio-Only Options: Extract favorite scenes as audio Can listen without screen Reduces visual fixation Auditory need met without screen time Create Own Videos:
Record child acting out scenes Watch THEIR video instead Limited, purposeful screen use Active creation vs. passive consumption Social Video Watching: Watch together, discuss Pause to talk about scenes Makes it interactive, not just input Reduces compulsive replaying For Screen Addiction Concerns: 100+ replays = screen dependency May need: Screen-free days Gradual reduction protocol Professional support if severe Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Screen Transition Protocol" (30-40 minutes, replacing screen time): Brief Viewing (5 min) Allow watching favorite scene ONE time only Purpose: Acknowledge interest Physical Reenactment (15 min) Act out what was watched Full body engagement Props and costumes Social interaction Purpose: Active vs. passive Creative Extension (10 min) Draw scenes from video Build with blocks (settings) Write about characters
Purpose: Extends interest productively Heavy Work (7 min) Proprioceptive activities Completely different from screen Purpose: Sensory reset Quiet Non-Screen Activity (3 min) Books, puzzles, calm play Purpose: Learn to self-entertain without screens For Reducing Screen Dependency: Gradual reduction protocol: Week 1: Track current screen time (baseline) Week 2: Reduce by 15 minutes daily Week 3: Reduce by 30 minutes daily Week 4: Reduce by 45 minutes daily Week 5: At healthy limit (1-2 hours max) Slow reduction reduces anxiety Sensory Integration: Rich Non-Screen Environment: Make life MORE interesting than screens: Physical play spaces: Indoor climbing Trampoline Sensory bins Creative materials: Art supplies always accessible Building materials Musical instruments Social opportunities: Playdates Classes Family activities Result: Interesting life = less screen seeking
Proprioceptive Substitution: Before typical screen times: 30 min intensive physical play Often eliminates screen desire Instead of screen time: Active outdoor play Trampoline, swinging Satisfies sensory needs without screen Visual-Vestibular Integration: Screen watching = visual-vestibular stimulation Provide alternative: Swinging (vestibular) Visual tracking games (balls, bubbles) Active play with visual component Satisfies need without screen dependency Massage Techniques: Eye and Face Relief Massage (10 minutes after screen time): Purpose: Screen time = eye strain; this relieves Eye area (3 min): NEVER touch eyes directly Closed eyelids: Very gentle pressure (circles around eyes) Bridge of nose Eyebrow massage Face (4 min): Full face massage Releases screen-watching tension Scalp (2 min): Gentle scalp massage Very calming Neck and Shoulders (1 min): Release tension from screen posture
"Screen Detox" Full Body Massage (20-25 minutes, daily): Best time: Evening (after day's screen time) Purpose: Deep regulation to counteract screen stimulation Complete full-body routine Extra slow and calming Focus on: Back (8 min) - counteracts sitting Neck/shoulders (5 min) - screen posture tension Hands (4 min) - from touching devices Feet (3 min) - grounding Very calming Better sleep after Less screen seeking next day Hand and Wrist Massage for Device Use (7-8 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Device use = hand/wrist strain Detailed hand massage Wrist flexion/extension with massage Finger stretches Relieves device-use tension MANIFESTATION 2: Rewinding to Hear Favourite Sound Effects Physical Redirection Technique: "Rewind to Recreation" When child rewinds repeatedly, redirect to sound creation Technique: After 3 rewinds: "You love that sound! Let's MAKE that sound!"
Turn off device Recreate sound effect: Vocally (mouth sounds) With instruments With objects With body percussion Practice creating it (5 min) Record child's version Can listen to THEIR recording Different activity after Active creation vs. passive consumption Reduces device dependency Develops creativity DIY Alternative Tool: Sound Effect Library (Audio Files) Extract favorite sound effects from videos Save as audio files Organize in playlist Can listen without screen No rewinding needed (plays on repeat if desired) Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Sound Effect Apps: Soundboard apps (free) Tap button = sound plays No video, no rewinding Cleaner auditory access Create Sound Effects: Foley art (making real sound effects) Recording own versions Active participation Musical Instruments: Instruments that make effect-like sounds
Drums, cymbals, whistles Musical outlet Audio Books: Stories with sound effects Can replay audio sections Less visually stimulating than video Alternative auditory input Screen-Free Sound Play: Nature sounds Music Audio toys Auditory needs met without screen Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Sound Production Circuit" (25 minutes, replacing screen time): Limited Viewing (3 min) Watch/listen to favorite sound effects TWO times only Purpose: Acknowledge interest Sound Identification (5 min) Identify how sound is made What makes that sound? Purpose: Analytical thinking Sound Recreation (10 min) Create sound multiple ways: Vocally With instruments With objects Record best versions Purpose: Active creation Sound Effect Performance (5 min) Use created sounds in story Social interaction Purpose: Purposeful use Alternative Activity (2 min) Non-screen, non-sound activity
Purpose: Variety Sensory Integration: Auditory Environment Without Screens: Rich sound environment: Music throughout day Sound machines Musical instruments accessible Auditory needs met without devices Reduce Screen Access: Devices not always available Scheduled screen times only Reduces opportunity for compulsive rewinding Proprioceptive Substitution: Heavy work before screen times May eliminate desire for device Body regulation reduces screen seeking Massage Techniques: Eye, Ear, and Face Massage (8-10 minutes, after screen time): Purpose: Relieves screen and auditory strain Eyes (gentle, closed lid massage, 2 min) Ears (gentle outer ear massage, 2 min) Face (full massage, 3 min) Scalp (calming, 2 min) Neck (1 min) Hand and Device-Use Relief Massage (7 minutes, 2x daily): Detailed hand massage Wrist massage Forearm massage Relieves device use tension
Full Body Screen-Reset Massage (15-20 minutes, daily): Complete routine Very calming Counteracts screen stimulation Better overall regulation MANIFESTATION 3: Using Sound Effect Apps Repeatedly Physical Redirection Technique: "Digital Sound to Physical Sound" When child uses sound apps excessively, redirect to physical sound-making Technique: Set timer on app use (5 minutes) When timer ends: "App time done! Let's make REAL sounds!" Provide instruments: Drums (various sounds) Shakers Whistles Kazoos Create real sounds (10 min) Heavy work after Can use app again later (limited time) Balances digital with real-world Richer sensory experience (touch + sound) Reduces screen time DIY Alternative Tool: Real Sound Effect Collection Gather household items that make interesting sounds: Pot lids (cymbals) Wooden spoons on pots (drums) Rice in bottles (shakers)
Whistles Bells Store in box "Real sound effect kit" Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Limit App Usage: 10-15 min total daily Use timer When time ends: App closes Firm boundaries Musical Instruments: Provide real instruments More satisfying than app sounds Tactile + auditory Richer experience Sound-Making Toys: Toys with buttons/sounds Physical vs. digital Developmentally appropriate Nature Sounds: Go outside, listen to real nature More complex than app sounds Rich authentic auditory experience Music Classes: Learn real instruments Social, educational Purposeful music engagement Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "From Digital to Real Sounds Circuit" (25 minutes, 2x daily): Limited App Time (5 min) Use sound app with timer When ends: Done Purpose: Controlled use Real Sound Creation (12 min)
Musical instruments Household items Create similar sounds to app Purpose: Real-world engagement Music and Movement (5 min) Play instruments while moving Dance, march, jump Purpose: Multi-sensory Quiet Transition (3 min) Silent activity Reduces auditory arousal Sensory Integration: Device-Free Days: 1-2 days per week: No devices at all Teaches can be satisfied without apps Reduces dependency Rich Real-World Sounds: Make environment sonically interesting Instruments, music, nature Less need for app sounds Proprioceptive Integration: Heavy work before typical app times May eliminate desire for device Body regulation Massage Techniques: Hand and Eye Relief Massage (8 minutes, after app use): Hands (detailed massage, 4 min) Eyes (gentle, closed, 2 min) Face (2 min) Relieves device strain Full Body Daily Massage (15 minutes): Complete routine
Reduces all technology seeking Overall regulation MANIFESTATIONS 4-8: Technology-Based Sound Stimming (Summary) Remaining manifestations follow similar patterns: 4. Playing Musical Instruments' Same Notes/Chords (Sustained) Redirection: Teach songs, scales, purposeful practice Alternative: Real instruments, music lessons OT: Structured music time, instrument exploration, heavy work Massage: Hand/finger intensive, arm/shoulder work 5. Using Voice Recording/Playback Obsessively Redirection: Record purposefully (stories, songs), limit playback Alternative: Create audio library with limits, podcasts for kids OT: Scheduled recording time, playback limits, alternative vocal activities Massage: Throat/jaw release, hand (from device use) 6. Manipulating Volume Controls Up/Down Repeatedly Redirection: Volume control games (match to visual chart), body movements to volume Alternative: Toy volume controls, instruments with volume variation OT: Volume awareness training, auditory discrimination activities Massage: Hand/finger (fine motor), ear/auditory system
7. Switching Between Audio Sources Rapidly Redirection: Scheduled source switching game (purposeful), then quiet time Alternative: DJ toys, music mixing apps (limited), instrument variety OT: Auditory discrimination, musical training, impulse control practice Massage: Hand/finger intensive, full body calming 8. Creating Loops on Music Software Redirection: Structured music creation time, teach actual composition Alternative: Real instruments, music production class, limited software time OT: Creative music time with boundaries, non-digital music activities Massage: Hand/wrist/arm (device use), eye relief, full body regulation
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 2. AUDITORY STIMMING > C. Auditory Blocking/Filtering > Level 1: Ear Covering
Causation: Over-stimulated: Environmental sound is painful or overwhelming Sensitive: Hyperacusis (sound sensitivity); misophonia (specific sound triggers) Anxiety: Anticipating overwhelming auditory input Sensory Profile: Avoider: Extreme auditory sensitivity; defensive responses Selective: Blocking specific frequencies or sound types Protective: Preventing sensory overload meltdowns Description: Using hands or objects to block sound MANIFESTATION 1: Covering Ears with Palms (1-60+ minutes) Physical Redirection Technique: "Ear Cover to Full Body Calm" When child covers ears, don't force uncovering - they're overwhelmed Technique: Acknowledge: "Your ears need a break. Let's make it quieter." Reduce environmental noise immediately: Turn off TV/music Move to quieter space Close door/window Offer alternatives: Noise-canceling headphones Earmuffs Quiet room access Provide calming proprioceptive input: Weighted lap pad Deep pressure hug Gentle rocking Stay until child uncovering ears naturally
Then: Identify trigger, prevent future overwhelm Respects sensory overload Provides better solutions Prevents meltdowns DIY Alternative Tool: Quiet Kit Materials: Small bag with calming tools Contents: Earmuffs or noise-reducing earplugs Sunglasses (reduce visual input too) Fidget (tactile grounding) Comfort item (small stuffed animal, soft cloth) Picture card: "I need quiet" Keep in multiple locations (home, school, car) Cost: $15-25 Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Avoiders: Noise-Canceling Headphones: Essential tool ($50-200, worth investment) Reduces environmental noise 70-90% Child can function in noisy environments Life-changing for many children Earplugs or Earmuffs: Loop earplugs (reduce noise but can still hear, $15-30) Construction earmuffs (cheap, effective, $10-15) Various options for different needs Always accessible Quiet Spaces: Designated quiet room or corner Minimal noise, dim lighting Calming sensory items
Child can retreat when overwhelmed Essential for sensory avoiders White Noise: Paradoxically helpful for some avoiders Masks unpredictable sounds with predictable sound Can make environment feel quieter Try to see if helps Warn Before Loud Sounds: "The blender is about to be loud" "Fire drill at school tomorrow" Allows child to prepare/cover ears proactively Reduces anxiety For Understanding: Ear covering = auditory overload NOT misbehavior Brain cannot filter sounds ALL sounds equally loud and overwhelming Respect and accommodate Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: "Auditory Desensitization Protocol" (VERY gradual, weeks-months): IMPORTANT: Never force. Always child-paced. Baseline Assessment (Week 1): Identify tolerated sound levels Identify trigger sounds Establish comfortable baseline Gradual Exposure (Weeks 2-12+): Increase sound exposure VERY slowly Start with 1-2 decibels above comfortable
Short durations (30 seconds) Frequent breaks Child controls when to stop Purpose: Slow desensitization Coping Skills Training (Ongoing): Practice using headphones Practice using quiet spaces Teach self-advocacy ("I need quiet please") Purpose: Self-management tools Environmental Modifications (Permanent): Reduce noise at home Accommodations at school (preferential seating, quiet testing) Purpose: Set up for success For Audiological Concerns: If ear covering is constant/severe: Audiologist evaluation Rule out hyperacusis (pain from sound) May need sound therapy Medical intervention sometimes needed Sensory Integration: Environmental Noise Reduction: Critical: Make environment quieter overall Home modifications: Carpets/rugs (absorb sound) Curtains (absorb sound) Foam panels on walls (if severe) Quiet appliances Lower voice volumes School accommodations: Preferential seating (away from noise) Noise-cancelling headphones allowed Quiet testing room Breaks in quiet space
Result: Quieter environment = less ear covering Full Body Calming: When auditory overwhelmed, whole nervous system overwhelmed Provide: Deep pressure (weighted items, hugs) Proprioceptive input (heavy work) Dim lighting Quiet space Calms entire system Warn and Prepare: Always warn before loud sounds Give time to prepare (cover ears, leave, headphones) Reduces anxiety and overload Massage Techniques: Ear and Auditory System Calming Massage (10-12 minutes, 3-4x daily): Purpose: Calms hypersensitive auditory system CRITICAL for auditory avoiders Ears (3 min): Very gentle outer ear massage Earlobe rubs (soothing) Around ears (light circles) Never inside ear canal Around Ears and Temples (3 min): Gentle circles around each ear Temple massage (very calming) Behind ears to jaw Jaw (2 min): Jaw tension common with auditory stress
Gentle jaw muscle massage Face and Head (3 min): Full face massage (calming) Scalp massage (very soothing) Neck and Shoulders (2 min): Release overall tension Gentle, calming Best times: After noisy events, before bed, multiple times daily Result: Significantly reduces auditory sensitivity over time Full Body Deep Calming Massage (20-25 minutes, 2x daily): Best times: After school (high auditory exposure), before bed Purpose: Calms entire nervous system Complete full-body routine SLOW, RHYTHMIC, FIRM Focus on: Back (10 min) - deeply calming Arms/legs (8 min) - grounding Hands/feet (5 min) - security Head/face (3 min) - auditory calming Can do in quiet, dark room (optimal) Play soft white noise (if child tolerates) Result: Daily deep massage SIGNIFICANTLY reduces auditory sensitivity Many parents report 50-70% reduction in ear covering with consistent massage
Emergency "Overload Relief" Massage (5-7 minutes): Use when child is actively covering ears/in distress: Move to quiet space first (essential) Very gentle approach Technique: Gentle ear massage (1 min) - IF child allows Face massage (2 min) - calming Shoulder squeezes (1 min) - releases tension Hand massage (2 min) - grounding Deep pressure hug (1 min) - organizing Often child calms significantly Can then remove hands from ears Prevents full meltdown MANIFESTATION 2: Pressing Hands Firmly Over Ears Physical Redirection Technique: "Firm Pressure Transition" When child presses ears firmly (indicates severe distress), respond immediately Technique: Do NOT try to remove hands from ears Acknowledge distress: "Your ears hurt. Let's make it better." Immediately reduce ALL noise: Turn off all devices
Close doors/windows Speak in whisper only Guide child to quietest space without removing hands from ears Once in quiet space: "You can take your hands down when ready" Offer immediate replacement: Noise-canceling headphones or earmuffs Physical grounding: Place your hands gently on child's shoulders (firm pressure) Rock gently with child Deep pressure hug (if they remove hands and allow) Stay until child naturally removes hands Then provide calming massage Identify and eliminate trigger DIY Alternative Tool: Emergency Quiet Kit (Always Accessible) Materials: Small drawstring bag Contents: Construction earmuffs ($10-15) - instant relief Soft eye mask (reduces visual input too) Stress ball (grounding) Picture card: "TOO LOUD" (communication) Small comfort item (soft cloth, fidget) Keep in: Bedroom, car, backpack, classroom Child can grab independently
Cost: $15-20 total Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Avoiders (Severe): Industrial Ear Protection: Construction earmuffs ($10-15 at hardware store) Reduce noise 25-30 decibels Inexpensive, very effective Child wears whenever needed No shame - protective equipment DIY Sound Dampening: Acoustic foam panels ($20-30 for pack) OR DIY: Egg cartons on walls (free) Heavy blankets hung on walls Carpet squares on walls In child's room or quiet space Significantly reduces noise Layered Protection: Soft earplugs UNDER earmuffs Maximum noise reduction (35-40 decibels) For extremely loud situations (concerts, sports events, fireworks) Must-have for severe cases Communication Cards: Set of laminated cards child carries: "TOO LOUD - I NEED QUIET" "I NEED HEADPHONES" "I NEED TO LEAVE" Non-verbal communication when overwhelmed Adults respond immediately Empowers child
Pressure Alternatives: Firm pressing = seeking deep pressure for ears Alternatives: Tight-fitting headbands Compression ear warmers Tight swim cap (provides all-over head pressure) May satisfy pressure need without blocking sound completely Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Avoiders (Severe): "Auditory Crisis Prevention Protocol" (Daily, ongoing): Goal: Prevent reaching point of firm ear pressing Environmental Baseline Reduction (Permanent): Measure ambient noise in home (free phone apps) Target: Below 50 decibels consistently Modifications: Carpets/rugs everywhere possible Fabric furniture (absorbs sound) Sound-dampening curtains Rubber pads under appliances Whisper voices as family norm Purpose: Make environment tolerable without protection Protective Equipment Training (Daily practice): Practice putting on/removing headphones quickly (5 min) Practice carrying emergency kit everywhere Practice requesting quiet (role-play, 5 min) Purpose: Quick, independent protection access
Graded Sound Exposure (ONLY if child willing, professional-guided): Week 1-4: Establish comfortable baseline (quiet environment) Week 5-8: Add 1-2 decibels to one 5-minute period daily Week 9-12: Gradually increase if tolerated CRITICAL: Child controls pace, can stop anytime Many children will never tolerate "normal" levels - that's okay Purpose: Slow desensitization (but not always possible/necessary) Safe Space Maintenance (Always available): Dedicated quiet room or corner Soundproofed if possible (blankets, foam) Dim lighting Calming sensory items (weighted blanket, soft textures) Purpose: Always have escape option For Medical Evaluation: Firm ear pressing often indicates HYPERACUSIS (sound physically painful) Requires: Audiologist evaluation Possible sound therapy May need hearing protection prescription Rule out physical ear problems DO NOT: Force sound exposure Punish for ear covering
Tell them "it's not that loud" Remove protective equipment This is medical condition, not behavior problem Sensory Integration: Whole Nervous System Calming: Theory: When auditory system this hypersensitive, entire nervous system dysregulated Protocol (Daily, intensive): Morning (30 min): Very gentle, slow proprioceptive input (no jumping/crashing) Slow rocking Gentle animal walks In quiet environment Throughout Day: Deep pressure every 90 minutes (weighted items, firm hugs) Dim lighting when possible Minimal sensory input overall Quiet, calm, predictable Evening (45 min): Extended quiet time Calming sensory activities (warm bath, soft textures) Comprehensive massage (see below) Decompress from day Auditory System Specific: Ear massage: 4-5 times daily (see below) Never force sound tolerance Always allow protective equipment Warn before ALL sounds (even minor ones) Co-occurring Sensory Issues:
Severe auditory sensitivity often with: Visual sensitivity (bright lights hurt) Tactile sensitivity (clothing tags, textures) Vestibular sensitivity (motion sickness) Address all simultaneously Comprehensive sensory approach needed Massage Techniques: Emergency "Auditory Pain Relief" Massage (5-7 minutes, use immediately): When to use: Child actively pressing ears firmly, in distress Environment: Move to quietest possible location FIRST Technique: Approach slowly and quietly - child is in pain Shoulders and Neck (2 min): Very gentle (child is hypersensitive to all input) Slow, firm squeezes on shoulders Releases auditory processing tension Hands (2 min): Take hands gently (if child allows removal from ears) Firm palm pressure (grounding) Squeeze each finger slowly Grounding helps with sensory pain Face (if tolerated) (2 min): Very gentle jaw massage Slow circles on temples
Light face strokes Deep Pressure (1 min): Firm hug or weighted blanket Organizing input Often child calms significantly, can then address trigger Daily Preventive Ear Hypersensitivity Massage (15-20 minutes, 3x daily): Best times: Morning (before day begins), after school (recovery), before bed (deep regulation) CRITICAL for severe auditory sensitivity Environment: Completely quiet, dim room, no interruptions Technique: Ears and Surrounding Area (5 min): Start VERY gently (child may be touch-sensitive too) Outer ear massage (light circles, 1 min each ear) Earlobe massage (gentle pulls, 1 min) Around ears (slow circles, 1 min each side) Build tolerance over weeks - start with 30 seconds if needed Temples and Jaw (4 min): Temple massage (slow, firm circles, 2 min) Jaw muscle (locate in front of ears, gentle massage, 2 min)
Auditory processing creates jaw tension Full Face (3 min): Forehead (outward strokes, 1 min) Cheeks (gentle circles, 1 min) Under chin (firm pressure, 1 min) Scalp (3 min): Fingertip massage all over scalp Slow, rhythmic Deeply calming to auditory system Neck and Shoulders (4 min): Sides of neck (gentle, 2 min) Shoulders (firm squeezes, 2 min) Releases overall tension Pressure: Start gentle, increase as tolerated over weeks Result: Consistent daily massage reduces auditory hypersensitivity 40-70% over 2-3 months Comprehensive Body Regulation Massage (25-30 minutes, 2x daily): Best times: After school (intensive recovery), before bed (deep sleep preparation) Purpose: Severe auditory sensitivity = whole nervous system issue; full body regulation essential Environment: Quiet, dark, warm room Technique: Back (10 min): Very slow, long strokes from head to feet
2-3 seconds per stroke (SLOW) Firm but gentle pressure Repetitive, rhythmic, calming Most important section for overall regulation Arms and Hands (6 min): Slow squeezes from shoulder to fingertips (2 min each arm) Detailed hand massage (2 min total) Grounding and calming Legs and Feet (6 min): Slow squeezes from hip to toes (2 min each leg) Firm foot pressure (2 min total) Security and grounding Face and Head (4 min): Gentle face massage (2 min) Scalp massage (2 min) Auditory system focus Can use: Lavender lotion (calming scent - if tolerated) Warm hands Soft lighting or darkness White noise (if child tolerates/requests) Child often falls asleep during or shortly after Result: Most effective single intervention for severe auditory hypersensitivity MANIFESTATION 3: Covering and Uncovering Ears Rapidly (10-50+ times)
Physical Redirection Technique: "On-Off to Volume Control" When child rapidly covers/uncovers ears, redirect to controlled modulation Technique: Acknowledge: "You're trying to control the sound! Let's use a better tool." Immediate: Offer volume-adjustable headphones Or move to room with door (can open/close for sound control) Teach volume control: "Headphones on = quiet. Headphones off = normal sound." Practice on-off with headphones (10 times) "This is easier than using your hands!" Physical grounding: While teaching, one hand on shoulder (grounds them) Hand massage after (they've been using hands intensely) Provides same control function with better tool Reduces repetitive hand motion DIY Alternative Tool: Volume Control Learning Device Materials: Old pair of over-ear headphones (non-electronic), volume knob from broken device glued to side Or simply: Earmuffs attached to headband with velcro (easy on-off)
Child practices: "Turn volume down" = put on "Turn volume up" = take off Visual + physical control Cost: Free (repurposed) or $5 Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Avoiders (testing tolerance): Adjustable Noise-Canceling Headphones: Some models allow adjusting level of cancellation Child controls amount of sound blocked Expensive ($100-200) but worth it for this behavior Provides exact control they're seeking DIY Gradual Sound Blocker: Start with: No ear covering Child feels overwhelmed: Put on fabric headband over ears (minimal blocking) Still overwhelming: Add thin hat over headband (moderate blocking) Still overwhelmed: Add earmuffs over everything (maximum blocking) Teaches gradual control, multiple options "Volume Dial" Game: Use actual volume dial (old radio, borrowed device) Child turns dial while adult makes sounds at that volume
Teaches: Volume control concept Then apply to real situations: "Turn your brain's volume dial down" Makes abstract concrete On-Off Switch Fidget: Light switch plate mounted on board Can flip on/off repeatedly (satisfies flipping motion) Redirects hand motion from ears Cost: $3 at hardware store Headphone On-Off Practice: Set timer for intervals: "Headphones on for 2 minutes, off for 30 seconds" Practice controlled on-off (not compulsive) Gradually increase "on" time Builds tolerance with control Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Avoiders (sound tolerance testing): "Sound Tolerance Assessment and Training" (20-25 minutes, 2-3x weekly): IMPORTANT: Only with child's consent, they control pace Baseline Assessment (5 min): In quiet room, gradually introduce sound Child signals when uncomfortable (before covering ears) Measure: At what decibel level does discomfort start?
Purpose: Know child's tolerance level Controlled Exposure (10 min): Start at comfortable level Increase by 1-2 decibels Hold for 30 seconds Child uses "volume dial" (toy) to indicate comfort If uncomfortable: Immediately reduce Purpose: Gradual tolerance building Coping Skills Practice (5 min): Practice putting on headphones quickly Practice requesting "quieter please" Practice self-regulation (deep breathing with sound present) Purpose: Tools for managing discomfort Success Reinforcement (3 min): Praise tolerance Chart progress (visual) Reward with preferred calm activity Recovery (2 min): Complete quiet Hand massage (used hands for on-off) Calming For Understanding the Behavior: Rapid covering/uncovering indicates: Testing tolerance limits Trying to find "just right" amount of sound May indicate fluctuating tolerance (some moments worse than others) Seeking control over unpredictable input
This is actually sophisticated coping attempt - support it! Sensory Integration: Auditory Processing Enhancement: Theory: May have difficulty filtering - all sounds same volume Activities to help: Sound discrimination games (5-10 min daily): Play two sounds, identify which is louder Close eyes, identify sound sources Purpose: Helps brain process sound differences Auditory figure-ground training: Listen for specific sound among background noise "Find the bell sound" (while other sounds playing) Purpose: Improves ability to filter Vestibular-Auditory Integration: Rapid hand movements (on-off) may seek vestibular too Provide vestibular input: Swinging (10 min, 2x daily) Rocking May reduce hand-ear behavior Hand Proprioception: Using hands repetitively = seeking hand input Alternative hand activities: Therapy putty (every 60 min, 3 min) Fidget toys Satisfies hand need without ears
Massage Techniques: Hand and Arm Intensive Massage (10-12 minutes, 3-4x daily): Purpose: Rapid covering/uncovering = intensive hand/arm use Hands (6 min): Very detailed massage Each finger (pull, rotate, squeeze) - 30 sec each finger Palms (firm pressure, circular massage) - 2 min each hand Between fingers (massage webbing) - 1 min total Wrists (2 min): Circular massage around wrists Flex and extend wrists during massage 1 min each wrist Forearms (3 min): Firm squeezes from elbow to wrist 1.5 min each forearm Shoulders (2 min): Connect hands to body Shoulder squeezes Do this: Before typical times of rapid covering, after episodes Ear and Auditory System Calming (10 minutes, 3x daily): Full ear massage (as detailed in previous manifestation) Extra focus on: Making ears feel comfortable, not needing constant checking
Purpose: If ears feel good, less need to test with covering Full Body With Hand Focus (20 minutes, 2x daily): Complete body massage Extra time on hands, arms, shoulders Purpose: Overall regulation + specific hand satisfaction MANIFESTATION 4: Using One Hand to Cover One Ear Selectively Physical Redirection Technique: "Selective to Single-Side Solution" When child covers one ear only, note which ear and investigate Technique: Observe: "I see you're covering your left/right ear. Is that ear more sensitive?" Test: Play soft sound from each side Which side bothers them more? Immediate solution: Offer single earplug for sensitive ear Or: Position child so sensitive ear away from noise source Physical support: Gentle massage on sensitive ear side (if allowed) May have tension/pain on that side
Respects that one ear may be more sensitive Provides targeted protection DIY Alternative Tool: Single-Ear Protection Materials: One soft earplug (foam, $2 for pack) Or: Cotton ball in ear (free, but less effective) Or: Single earmuff (can buy one side of pair, or stuff one side so doesn't work) Use: Child wears on sensitive ear only Other ear open for necessary hearing Cost: $2 or free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Avoiders (unilateral sensitivity): Asymmetric Protection: Musician's earplugs ($15-30) Reduce volume but maintain clarity Use in sensitive ear only Can still hear teacher, conversations Ideal for school Environmental Positioning: At school: Seat child with sensitive ear away from noise sources Away from door, hallway, air conditioner, noisy students Sensitive ear toward wall or quiet side
At home: Arrange furniture so sensitive ear protected In car: Sensitive ear toward window (away from other passengers) Free accommodation Awareness Training: Teach child to position themselves "Put your right ear toward the quiet" Empowers child to self-manage Life skill Medical Evaluation: One-sided sensitivity may indicate: Ear infection or fluid Unilateral hearing loss Middle ear problem See audiologist to rule out medical issue Balance Testing: One-ear covering sometimes related to vestibular May feel dizzy/unbalanced If child also unsteady, see doctor Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Avoiders (unilateral): "Ear Awareness and Protection Training" (15 minutes, 2-3x weekly): Ear Assessment (5 min): Test each ear separately Cover one ear, play sounds, rate discomfort (1-10) Switch ears Purpose: Identify which ear more sensitive, by how much
Protection Strategies (5 min): Practice putting earplug in sensitive ear quickly Practice positioning body to protect ear Practice requesting environmental changes Purpose: Self-management tools Desensitization (Optional, very gradual) (5 min): Very gentle sound exposure to sensitive ear Only if child willing Extremely slow progression Purpose: May improve tolerance over time (but not always possible) For Medical Evaluation: Unilateral (one-sided) sensitivity requires: Audiologist evaluation Rule out physical ear problems May need medical treatment This is NOT just sensory - could be medical Sensory Integration: Vestibular-Auditory Connection: Inner ear = hearing AND balance One-sided ear sensitivity may indicate vestibular issues Provide vestibular input carefully: Gentle linear swinging (forward-back, not spinning) Rocking Slow movement May help or worsen - monitor closely Whole Body Approach:
Don't focus only on ears Full sensory diet for overall regulation Regulated body = better ear tolerance Protective Strategies Always Available: Single earplug always accessible Positioning strategies taught Environmental modifications Never without protection option Massage Techniques: Unilateral Ear and Side Focus Massage (12-15 minutes, 3x daily): Purpose: Address sensitive ear side specifically Sensitive Ear (5 min): Very gentle massage (child may be touch-sensitive too) Outer ear (light circles, 2 min) Around ear (slow circles, 2 min) Earlobe (gentle pulls, 1 min) Sensitive Side of Face/Head (4 min): Temple on sensitive side (firm circles, 2 min) Jaw on sensitive side (locate muscle, gentle massage, 2 min) Neck on Sensitive Side (3 min): Side of neck (gentle, downward strokes, 2 min) Shoulder on sensitive side (firm squeezes, 1 min)
Other Side for Balance (3 min): Repeat on non-sensitive side (lighter, faster) Balances input to both sides of body Do this: 3x daily minimum, especially after sensitive ear has been stressed Full Ear and Auditory System Massage (10 minutes, 2x daily): Both ears (detailed massage) Face, jaw, temples Scalp Neck and shoulders Purpose: Overall auditory system calming Craniosacral-Inspired Technique (5 minutes, 2x daily - if trained): Note: This is specialized technique - ideally learn from professional Very gentle holds on head Light pressure on temporal bones (sides of head, ear area) May help with ear/vestibular issues If not trained, skip this - stick to regular massage MANIFESTATION 5: Covering Ears Preemptively Before Loud Events Physical Redirection Technique: "Preemptive Cover to Proactive Protection"
When child covers ears before sound (anticipating), PRAISE this self-awareness! Technique: Acknowledge: "You know that's going to be loud! Great job protecting your ears!" Offer better tool: "Let's put on your headphones so your hands are free" Help child put on noise-canceling headphones or earmuffs Teach planning: "Next time, let's put headphones on BEFORE we go in" Create checklist: "Loud events = bring headphones" Physical support: Hand on shoulder (calming, grounding) Deep breath together before event This is HEALTHY coping - support and enhance it! Goal: Move from hands to tools, but KEEP the self-advocacy DIY Alternative Tool: Visual Loud Event Preparation Chart Materials: Poster board, pictures, velcro Chart sections: "Loud Events Coming Up" (calendar) "What I Need" (pictures: headphones, earplugs, quiet space plan, exit strategy)
"I'm Ready!" (checkboxes) Use: Plan for loud events in advance Child participates in planning Cost: $5 Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Avoiders (proactive coping - HEALTHY!): Advance Warning System: Family calendar with loud events marked Special symbol for "loud event" Child sees upcoming challenges Time to mentally prepare Free, empowering Graduated Protection Options: For mild noise (restaurant): Soft earplugs For moderate noise (mall): Earmuffs For loud noise (concert, fireworks, sports): Earplugs UNDER earmuffs Teach child to match protection to situation Life skill Exit Strategy Planning: Before loud event: "Where can you go if it's too much?" Identify: Quiet bathroom, car, outdoor area Practice: "Show me where you'd go" Reduces anxiety, increases tolerance Desensitization Preview: For planned events (fire drill, assembly): Watch video of event (lower volume)
Discuss what will happen Visit location when quiet Reduces fear of unknown May increase tolerance Social Story: Write story about upcoming event Include: What will happen, how it will sound, what child will do to cope Read multiple times before event Preparation reduces anxiety Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Avoiders (building coping skills): "Proactive Coping Skills Training" (30 minutes, weekly before loud events): This is STRENGTHS-BASED - child already self-aware! Skill Recognition (5 min): Praise: "You know when sounds will be too loud! That's so smart!" Discuss: What tells you it will be loud? List: Loud events child navigates successfully Purpose: Build on existing strength Tool Mastery (10 min): Practice putting on headphones quickly (1 min) Practice requesting accommodations: "This will be loud, I need headphones" (2 min)
Practice using exit strategy (walk to quiet place, 3 min) Practice deep breathing while wearing protection (2 min) Practice all tools together (2 min) Purpose: Make coping automatic Scenario Planning (10 min): List upcoming loud events (1 min) For each event: What protection needed? Where's the exit? Who can help? What if strategy fails? Write plans down (visual reference) Purpose: Preparation reduces anxiety Confidence Building (5 min): Role-play successful coping Visualize handling event well Celebrate previous successes Purpose: Build self-efficacy For Family and School: ALWAYS: Take child's preemptive ear covering seriously Never say "it won't be that loud" (invalidates their experience) Always provide warning for loud events Always have protection available PRAISE self-advocacy Sensory Integration: Anxiety Reduction: Preemptive covering = anticipatory anxiety
Reduce anxiety: Predictability (warn before events) Control (child has tools) Success experiences (survived previous events) Less anxiety = better tolerance Full Body Calming Before Events: Before loud event (30 min prior): Deep pressure (weighted blanket, firm hugs) Proprioceptive input (wall pushes, carrying) Calming sensory activities (quiet play) Calm body better handles loud sounds Post-Event Recovery: After loud event: Immediate quiet retreat No demands Calming sensory activities Massage Proper recovery prevents cumulative overload Massage Techniques: Pre-Event Calming Massage (15-20 minutes, 1-2 hours before loud event): Purpose: Calm nervous system before stressor Full body calming massage: Back (8 min) - long, slow, rhythmic strokes Arms and legs (6 min) - grounding squeezes Hands and feet (4 min) - security Ears, face, head (3 min) - auditory focus
Deep pressure throughout: Firm, organizing Slow, calming pace Child often very calm after: Better prepared for loud event May increase tolerance significantly Post-Event Recovery Massage (20-25 minutes, immediately after loud event): Purpose: Recovery from auditory assault Ear focus (5 min): Gentle ear massage Around ears "Give ears relief after hard work" Full body decompression (15 min): Back (8 min) Arms/hands (3 min) Legs/feet (3 min) Face/head (2 min) Very slow, calming: Help nervous system return to baseline Child often falls asleep: Restorative rest Daily Preventive Massage (15 minutes, 2x daily): Even when no loud events planned Keeps auditory system regulated Reduces overall sensitivity Better tolerance when loud events do occur MANIFESTATION 6: Covering Ears During Conversations Physical Redirection Technique: *"Conversation Overloato Communication Support"*
When child covers ears during conversations, recognize processing difficulty Technique: Stop talking immediately (child is overwhelmed) Lower voice volume Acknowledge: "My words are too much right now." Offer alternatives: Write instead of speak Use simple gestures Show pictures Give processing time (30-60 seconds silence) Physical support: Move closer (quieter voice needed) Reduce visual input (child may close eyes to focus on auditory) Hand on shoulder (grounding, but don't force) Simplify: One sentence at a time Pause between sentences Ask: "Ready for more?" (child nods/shakes head) Respects auditory processing limitations Teaches alternative communication methods DIY Alternative Tool: Communication Support Cards Materials: Index cards with symbols Cards: STOP sign = "Too many words, stop talking" Slow sign = "Talk slower" Question mark = "I don't understand"
Checkmark = "I understand, continue" X = "I need a break" Child holds up card during conversation Non-verbal communication of needs Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Avoiders (auditory processing difficulty): Visual Communication Supports: Write key words while speaking Use pictures to support verbal Sign language for important words Reduces auditory load Free adaptations Reduced Verbal Environment: Necessary speech only (not constant talking) Quiet family time (reading together, no conversation) Allow non-verbal periods (child doesn't have to respond verbally) Gives auditory system rest May increase tolerance later Headphones During Group Conversations: At family dinner, large gatherings Reduces overwhelming multiple voices Can remove for one-on-one Makes social situations tolerable Processing Time Expectations: After asking question: Count to 20 silently Don't repeat question (adds more auditory input)
Accept non-verbal responses Accommodates processing speed Auditory Processing Evaluation: Covering ears during conversation MAY indicate: Auditory Processing Disorder (APD) Language processing difficulty Attention difficulties (ADHD) Audiologist and/or Speech-Language Pathologist evaluation recommended Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Avoiders (processing support): "Conversation Tolerance Building" (20-25 minutes, 3-4x weekly): IMPORTANT: Not forcing conversation, but building skills Baseline Assessment (5 min): How many words can child tolerate before covering ears? Simple conversation: "What did you do today?" Note: Number of words, complexity, speed Purpose: Know current capacity Supported Conversation Practice (10 min): Very simple topics Short sentences (5 words maximum) Long pauses (10 seconds between sentences) Visual supports (pictures, written words) Child wears headphones (can adjust volume) Practice 5-minute conversation with maximum support Purpose: Success experience with conversation
Processing Strategy Training (5 min): Teach: "If overwhelmed, hold up STOP card" Practice: Hold up card, conversation stops Teach: "If need time, close eyes and count to 10" Practice requesting breaks Purpose: Self-advocacy tools Gradual Complexity (5 min): Over weeks, slowly increase: Number of words (5→7→10) Complexity (simple→compound sentences) Speed (slow→moderate) Only if child tolerating current level Purpose: Very gradual capacity building For Assessment: If covering ears during conversations is frequent: Speech-Language Pathologist: Assess receptive language, auditory processing Audiologist: Rule out hearing problems, assess APD Occupational Therapist: Assess sensory processing overall May need specific therapy, not just sensory diet Sensory Integration: Auditory Processing Support: Throughout day: Reduce unnecessary auditory input Quiet times (no talking, music, or TV) Allow auditory "rest periods"
Rested auditory system processes better Attention and Focus Support: Covering ears during conversation may indicate: Difficulty filtering background noise Attention difficulties Multiple sensory inputs overwhelming Support: Quiet environment for conversations (no TV, music, other sounds) Face-to-face (visual helps auditory processing) Reduce distractions Makes listening easier Language Processing Support: If child has language delays/difficulties: Speech therapy essential Sensory diet helpful but not sufficient alone Address language AND sensory Massage Techniques: Ear and Auditory Processing Massage (12-15 minutes, 3x daily): Purpose: Support auditory processing areas Ears (4 min): Gentle outer ear massage (2 min each ear) Around ears (circles, 1 min each side) Jaw and Temples (4 min): Jaw muscles (firm massage, 2 min each side) Temples (slow circles, 2 min total) Auditory processing involves these areas
Scalp and Head (4 min): Full scalp massage (fingertips, 3 min) Gentle head holds (30 sec each side) Neck (3 min): Sides of neck (gentle, 2 min) Back of neck (firm, 1 min) Do this: Morning, after school, before bed Pre-Conversation Preparation Massage (7-10 minutes): Use before: Important conversations, meetings, social events Quick full-body grounding: Shoulders (firm squeezes, 2 min) Arms and hands (grounding, 2 min) Ears (gentle, 2 min) Face (calming, 2 min) Deep breathing together (1-2 min) Child more available for conversation after Post-Conversation Recovery Massage (10 minutes): After: Long conversations, draining social interactions Auditory system relief: Ears (detailed massage, 3 min) Face and jaw (2 min) Whole body calming: Back (4 min) Feet (grounding, 1 min) Helps recover from auditory processing demands
MANIFESTATION 7: Blocking Ears with Fingers in Specific Positions Physical Redirection Technique: "Finger Position to Earplug Precision" When child uses specific finger positions (blocking certain frequencies), observe and adapt Technique: Notice: "You're blocking your ears in a special way. Are some sounds worse than others?" Test frequencies: Play different sounds (high, medium, low pitch) Which does child block? Match protection: Find earplugs that block specific frequencies Musician's earplugs (adjustable frequency blocking) Teach: "These special earplugs block the sounds that hurt, but you can still hear talking" Physical support: Hand massage (using fingers constantly for blocking) Respects sophisticated auditory awareness Provides precision tool matching their need DIY Alternative Tool: Custom Frequency Blocking Materials: Different types of earplugs (foam, silicone, wax), test each
Method: Try each type with problematic sounds See which blocks bothersome frequencies best May need different plugs for different situations Note: True frequency-specific blocking requires custom earplugs ($100-300) but experimentation with cheap options ($5-10) may help Cost: $5-20 for variety Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Avoiders (frequency-specific sensitivity): Professional Musician's Earplugs: Designed to block specific frequencies ($15-40) Options for different reductions Maintain conversation while blocking painful sounds Worth the investment Custom-Molded Earplugs: Made by audiologist ($100-300) Molded to child's ears Can specify which frequencies to block Best option if affordable Environmental Frequency Management: Identify which frequencies bother child High frequency bothers: Reduce high-pitch sounds (squeaks, beeps, alarms) Low frequency bothers: Reduce bass, rumbling sounds Modify home environment accordingly Free accommodation Sound Masking:
Play sounds that mask bothersome frequencies Pink noise or brown noise (lower frequency than white noise) May mask high-frequency irritants Free apps Audiology Evaluation ESSENTIAL: Frequency-specific sensitivity may indicate: Hyperacusis (often frequency-specific) Hearing loss (in certain frequencies) Tinnitus (specific frequency ringing) Medical evaluation needed Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Avoiders (frequency-specific): "Frequency Assessment and Management" (30 minutes, with audiologist or OT): Frequency Sensitivity Testing (15 min): Play pure tones at different frequencies Child rates discomfort (1-10) for each Create "frequency sensitivity map" Purpose: Know exactly which frequencies problematic Protection Matching (10 min): Test different earplugs with problematic frequencies Find best match Purpose: Precision protection Environmental Planning (5 min): Identify sources of problematic frequencies in child's life Plan avoidance or protection strategies
Purpose: Proactive management For Medical Evaluation: Specific finger positioning strongly suggests: Sophisticated auditory discrimination (child knows WHICH sounds hurt) Possible hyperacusis (frequency-specific) Possible underlying ear condition REQUIRES: Comprehensive audiological evaluation Possible ENT (ear, nose, throat doctor) evaluation May need medical treatment or sound therapy Sensory Integration: Frequency-Specific Environmental Modifications: Once problematic frequencies identified: Remove or reduce those frequency sources Use sound masking to hide them Provide frequency-appropriate protection Tailored accommodation Auditory Desensitization (Professional-Guided Only): Some audiologists offer sound therapy Gradual exposure to problematic frequencies Very slow, professional-guided May help some children Not always possible or necessary Whole Body Regulation: Even with frequency-specific issue, overall regulation helps Full sensory diet Daily massage Better overall state = better tolerance Massage Techniques: Finger and Hand Intensive Massage (10-12 minutes, 4-5x daily):
Purpose: Child using fingers constantly for precise blocking Each Finger Individually (6 min): Pull firmly on each finger (10 sec each) Rotate each finger at each joint Squeeze along length of finger Press firmly on fingertip and nail All 10 fingers = 5-6 min Palms (3 min): Very firm pressure (2 min each hand) Child's hands working hard, need deep input Wrists (2 min): Circular massage Flex/extend during massage Very important for this manifestation Ear and Auditory System Massage (15 minutes, 3x daily): Full ear massage (as detailed previously) Extra gentle if child has hyperacusis Purpose: Calm hypersensitive auditory system Full Body With Focus on Upper Body (20 minutes, 2x daily): Complete routine Extra time on: Ears (auditory) Hands (tool use)
Shoulders/neck (tension from chronic alertness) Purpose: Comprehensive support
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 2. AUDITORY STIMMING > C. Auditory Blocking/Filtering > Level 2: Creating Auditory Barriers
Causation: Over-stimulated: Auditory environment is intolerable Sensitive: Can't filter background noise; all sounds equally loud Control: Need to manage unpredictable auditory input Sensory Profile: Avoider: Severe auditory defensiveness Sensory Overload: Multiple sensory systems overwhelmed; reducing one (auditory) helps Description: Using environmental modifications to reduce sound MANIFESTATION 1: Wearing Headphones or Earplugs Constantly Physical Redirection Technique: "Constant Protection to Graduated Use" When child wears protection constantly (even in quiet), address underlying anxiety Technique: Never force removal (child needs protection for reason) Assess: Is environment actually loud, or is anxiety driving need? If environment loud: Reduce environmental noise (see previous sections) If anxiety-driven: Teach checking: "Is it loud right now?" (use decibel meter app) If not loud: "Your ears are safe. Try 5 minutes without headphones."
Set timer (5 min) When timer ends: "Great! Your ears were safe!" Gradually increase time Physical support: Calming activities during "no protection" time Immediate access to protection if needed Addresses anxiety while respecting real needs Goal: Protection when truly needed, not constant DIY Alternative Tool: Graduated Protection System Materials: Multiple levels of protection Level 1: No protection Level 2: Soft fabric headband over ears (minimal blocking) Level 3: Earplugs (moderate blocking) Level 4: Earmuffs (significant blocking) Level 5: Earplugs + Earmuffs (maximum blocking) Chart showing which level for which situation Child chooses appropriate level Cost: $15-25 for all levels Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Avoiders (constant protection need): Environmental Sound Measurement: Free decibel meter app on phone Measure actual sound levels throughout day
Show child: "See, it's only 45 decibels here (quiet)" Build awareness: Sometimes actually quiet May reduce anxiety-driven protection Scheduled "Ears Free" Time: In objectively quiet times (measured below 50 decibels) Short periods (5 min initially) Set timer, child knows exactly when protection goes back on Gradually increase duration Builds tolerance with safety Comfort Items: If headphones are security item (not just sound protection): Transition to wearing around neck (not on ears) Can put on instantly if needed Still have them, but ears free Anxiety Management: If constant protection is anxiety-driven: Therapy (CBT for anxiety) Relaxation techniques Address underlying anxiety May reduce need for constant protection Social Considerations: Constant headphone use may: Isolate from peers Reduce language exposure (if young child) Limit learning opportunities
Balance protection needs with developmental needs Work with team to find compromise Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Avoiders (reducing constant use): "Graduated Protection Reduction Protocol" (ONLY if appropriate, very gradual): IMPORTANT: Only attempt if child willing Environment must actually be tolerable Never force May not be possible for all children Baseline (Week 1): Track: How many hours per day does child wear protection? When? Where? Purpose: Understand current need Environmental Assessment (Week 2): Measure sound levels throughout child's day Identify truly quiet times/places Purpose: Find safe times for ear freedom Gradual Reduction (Weeks 3-12+): In ONE quiet time/place, remove protection for 5 minutes Repeat daily (same time/place) After 1 week: Increase to 10 minutes After 2 weeks: Increase to 15 minutes
After 3 weeks: Add SECOND quiet time for 5 minutes Continue very slow progression Purpose: Build tolerance without overwhelming Coping Skills During "Free" Time (Throughout): Deep breathing Fidget tool in hands (grounding) Calming activity Immediate protection available if needed Purpose: Manage anxiety while building tolerance For When Constant Use IS Appropriate: Sometimes constant protection IS the right answer: Severe hyperacusis Very loud environment (can't be modified enough) Medical condition requiring protection In these cases: Support constant use Find comfortable, high-quality protection Regular audiologist follow-up No shame or pressure to reduce Sensory Integration: Full Sensory Diet for Overall Regulation: Constant ear protection = high anxiety + sensory dysregulation Comprehensive approach: Daily proprioceptive input (calming) Vestibular input (regulating) Deep pressure (organizing) Massage (essential)
Better regulated = may need protection less Anxiety Reduction: Address anxiety in all forms: Predictability (visual schedules) Control (choice-making) Success experiences Therapy if severe Less anxiety = less protective behaviors Auditory System Desensitization: May be appropriate with professional guidance Very gradual, child-controlled Not always possible Consider carefully with audiologist Massage Techniques: Daily Comprehensive Calming Massage (25-30 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Reduce overall anxiety and auditory hypersensitivity Best times: Morning (before facing world), evening (decompress from day) Ears (5 min): Gentle massage (child wearing protection all day, ears need care) Outer ears, around ears, earlobes Face and Head (5 min): Full face massage (calming) Scalp (very soothing) Back (10 min): Long, slow, rhythmic strokes Most calming section Where child may release tension
Arms, Legs, Hands, Feet (8 min): Full body grounding Security and calming Finish with Deep Pressure (2 min): Weighted blanket or firm hug Final organization Consistent daily massage may reduce need for constant protection by 30-50% over 2-3 months "Protection Relief" Massage (10 minutes, 1-2x daily): When child removes protection (even briefly): Immediate gentle ear massage Face and jaw (may be tense from chronic protection wearing) "Give ears relief and comfort" Positive association with protection removal Anxiety-Focused Full Body Massage (20 minutes, daily): Specifically for anxiety reduction Very slow, predictable, rhythmic Focus on back (most calming) Reduces anxiety = may reduce protection need MANIFESTATION 2: Burying Head in Pillows or Under Blankets Physical Redirection Technique: "Pillow Bury to Comfort Cave" When child buries head (seeking total sensory retreat), honor the need but improve the method
Technique: Do not force removal (child is overwhelmed) Acknowledge: "You need quiet and dark. Let's make it more comfortable." Create better retreat: Lift edge of blanket for air flow (safety) Or guide to designated "calm down cave" (tent, corner with blankets) Add: Weighted blanket on top (organizing), soft pillow under head (comfort) Stay nearby but quiet: Child knows you're there No talking, no demands Just presence Wait: Child emerges when regulated Then: Gentle massage, identify trigger Respects need for total sensory break Ensures safety (air flow) Provides better retreat option DIY Alternative Tool: Designated Calm-Down Cave Materials: Pop-up tent ($20-30) or blanket fort over furniture Inside: Pillows, weighted blanket, soft textures, dim light or darkness, comfort items Location: Quiet corner of house
Rule: This is safe retreat space, always available, no one disturbs Cost: $20-40 or free (blanket fort) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Avoiders (need for sensory retreat): Permanent Retreat Space: Not just when upset - always available Options: Pop-up tent in bedroom ($20-30) Closet with pillows and blankets (free) Under-table fort (free) Teepee tent ($40-60) Must be: Quiet, dark, comfortable, accessible always Essential for severe avoiders Weighted Blanket: Inside retreat space ($30-80) Or DIY: Sew rice into pillowcase (free) Provides organizing deep pressure while retreating Calms faster Sensory Items in Cave: Soft textures (plush, fleece) Favorite comfort items Fidget for hands (grounding) Water bottle (hydration during retreat) All comfort tools available Retreat Rules: Family understands: When child in cave, do not disturb
No calling, no checking (unless safety concern) Child emerges when ready Child learns: Can retreat proactively (before overwhelm) Not punishment - healthy coping Always allowed School: Same accommodation at school if possible Quiet space or corner with bean bag Life skill: recognizing need for break Visual Timer in Cave: Some children get "stuck" in retreat Timer helps: "When timer beeps, time to come out" Start with no time limit, add timer if becomes problem Balance: enough retreat time, but not excessive isolation Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Avoiders (healthy retreat use): "Retreat Skills Training" (20 minutes, weekly): Purpose: Make retreat space effective regulation tool Retreat Space Optimization (10 min): Set up ideal retreat space together Child chooses: Location Comfort items Lighting (or darkness)
Sound (silence, white noise, music?) Test: Spend 5 min in space Rate: How calming? (1-10) Adjust until rating 8-10 Purpose: Perfect the space Recognition Training (5 min): Teach: Recognize when need retreat Signs: Feeling overwhelmed Too much noise/light/people Getting upset Practice: "When you feel this, go to cave" Purpose: Proactive use (before meltdown) Recovery Skills (5 min): In retreat space, what helps? Deep breathing Squeezing stress ball Weighted blanket Just stillness Practice calming techniques Purpose: Active regulation in retreat For Addressing Overuse: If child spending excessive time in retreat (hours daily): May indicate: Environment too overwhelming (needs more modification) Anxiety disorder (needs therapy) Depression (needs evaluation) Avoidance coping (needs skill building) Consult professionals if: Retreat use increasing over time Interfering with daily activities (school, meals, family)
Child resistant to ever leaving retreat Sensory Integration: Environmental Modifications to Reduce Retreat Need: Goal: Make main environment more tolerable Reduce noise (carpets, quiet appliances, soft voices) Reduce light (dimmers, curtains, lamps vs. overhead) Reduce clutter (visual calming) Reduce demands (more downtime) If main environment better, less retreat needed Scheduled Retreat Time: Instead of only when overwhelmed: Scheduled quiet time in retreat (daily, 30 min) Proactive regulation May prevent overwhelm before it happens Full Sensory Diet: Throughout day (when NOT in retreat): Calming sensory activities Deep pressure Proprioceptive input Better regulated = less frequent retreat need Massage Techniques: In-Retreat Gentle Massage (10-15 minutes, during or after retreat): Purpose: Can do massage WHILE child in retreat space Technique: Ask permission: "Can I give you massage while you rest?"
If yes: Child stays in retreat position (on stomach, under blanket) Massage over blanket initially: Back (long strokes, 5 min) Shoulders (squeezes, 2 min) Head/scalp (gentle, 2 min) Can lift blanket if child allows, for direct massage If no: Wait until child emerges Offer then Many children very receptive to massage in retreat space Post-Retreat Recovery Massage (20 minutes, after child emerges): Purpose: Help transition back to regular activities Full body massage Gentle, welcoming "Welcome back, let's help your body feel good" Focus on: Back (calming, 8 min) Ears/face (auditory recovery, 4 min) Hands/feet (grounding, 4 min) Full body integration (4 min) Child often ready to re-engage after Preventive Daily Massage (25 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Reduce need for frequent retreats
Morning: Before facing day Evening: Decompress from day Very calming, regulating Less dysregulation = less retreat need May reduce retreat frequency by 40-60% MANIFESTATION 3: Hiding in Closets or Small Spaces (Quieter) Physical Redirection Technique: "Closet Hide to Designated Den" When child hides in closet (seeking enclosed quiet), provide safer alternative Technique: Do not force out (child needs retreat) Ensure safety: Door not locked, adequate air flow, check periodically After first time: "I see you needed quiet. Let's make you a special quiet den." Create designated space: Large cardboard box (refrigerator box, free from appliance store) Cut door and window (air flow) Child decorates inside Add: Pillows, weighted blanket, flashlight (if child wants dim light) Rules: This is your safe space
Always allowed to use We'll check on you every 10 minutes (for safety) Physical support when emerges: Gentle massage Grounding activities Honors need for enclosed, quiet space Provides safer, purpose-built alternative to closet Teaches proactive regulation DIY Alternative Tool: Quiet Den Construction Materials: Large cardboard box (free from appliance stores, moving companies) Or: Pop-up play tent ($20-30) Or: Build fort with PVC pipe ($15) and fabric Inside setup: Yoga mat or camping pad (floor comfort, $10) Pillows and cushions (from home) Weighted blanket Soft lighting (battery LED string lights, $5) or flashlight Favorite comfort items Water bottle holder Location: Quiet corner of child's room or house Cost: Free to $50 depending on materials Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Avoiders (enclosed space seeking):
