Massage Techniques: Oral-Facial Massage (5 minutes, 2-3x daily): Wash hands thoroughly Use unscented lotion or coconut oil Outside mouth: Gentle circles around lips (30 seconds each direction) Light pressure down from nose to chin (10 times) Tap gently around mouth with fingertips (30 seconds) Cheeks: Press palms against cheeks, gentle circles (1 minute) Tap along jaw line (30 seconds) Purpose: Provides proprioceptive input to oral area, reducing need for self-stimulation Neck and Shoulder Release (3 minutes): Child sits, adult stands behind Gentle pressure on shoulders, squeeze and release (1 min) Fingertips massage up neck to base of skull (1 min) Gentle head rolls (30 sec each direction) Purpose: Releases tension that may cause increased humming MANIFESTATION 2: Throat Clearing Repetitively Physical Redirection Technique: "The Lion Breath"
Interrupt gently: "Let's do lion breath!" Have child kneel, hands on thighs Deep breath in through nose Exhale forcefully through wide-open mouth, stick tongue out, say "HAAA" Make fierce lion face Repeat 5 times This gives throat the strong sensation it's seeking DIY Alternative Tool: Straw and Water Bottle Materials: Sports water bottle with straw or narrow opening, water Use: Child must suck hard to get water (creates throat/swallowing sensation) Add: Few drops of lemon juice for extra throat sensation Cost: $2-5 for reusable bottle Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Bubble Blowing ($1 bubble solution) Every 30 minutes, blow 10-20 bubbles Requires throat control, provides oral-motor work Use thick bubble solution (more resistance) Thick Smoothies Blend: frozen banana, yogurt, peanut butter
Drink through narrow straw Swallowing thick liquid provides strong throat input Offer 2-3 times daily Chewy Foods Bagels, dried mango, fruit leather, gum Chewing and swallowing provides throat sensation Alternative to clearing For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Throat Comfort Warm (not hot) herbal tea with honey Sip slowly, focus on soothing sensation 2-3 times daily Soft Swallowing Practice Small sips of water every 10 minutes Teaches gentle swallowing vs. throat clearing Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Straw Olympics" (10-15 minutes) Cotton Ball Race: Blow cotton balls across table through straw Thick Shake Challenge: Drink thick smoothie through thin straw Bubble Mountain: Blow into cup of soapy water with straw Paper Pickup: Use straw to suck up small paper pieces and transfer
Whistle Practice: Make different sounds through straw Schedule: Before times when throat clearing typically increases For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Throat Training" (5-10 minutes) Practice gentle swallows with water Humming gently (vibrates throat softly) Whispering practice Blowing feathers gently Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Circuit (3x daily): Morning: Crunchy cereal, thick yogurt through straw, chewable vitamin Lunch: Chewy protein (chicken/beef), apple slices, water through straw Evening: Crunchy vegetables, smoothie, gum (if age-appropriate) Proprioceptive Input (before throat clearing episodes): Wall pushes (30 seconds) Chair push-ups (10 times) Heavy work (carry books, groceries) These calm nervous system, reducing stimming Massage Techniques: Throat and Neck Massage (3-4 minutes): IMPORTANT: Never press directly on throat/windpipe Technique: Stand behind seated child Very gentle fingertip massage along sides of neck (avoid front)
Small circles from behind ears down to shoulders (1 min each side) Gentle stretches: tilt head to each side, hold 10 seconds Shoulder squeezes (reduces tension that causes clearing) Jaw Release Massage (2 minutes): Locate jaw muscles (in front of ears) Gentle circular massage (30 seconds each side) Open mouth slightly, massage again Reduces overall oral-facial tension MANIFESTATION 3: Clicking Tongue Against Teeth Physical Redirection Technique: "The Tongue Workout" Stop the clicking by offering alternative: "Let's exercise our tongue!" Exercises: Touch tongue to nose (try 10 times) Touch tongue to chin (try 10 times) Move tongue side to side outside mouth (10 times) Roll tongue (if they can) in and out Lick lips in full circle (10 times) Provides similar oral-motor input without clicking sound
Do whenever clicking starts DIY Alternative Tool: Tongue Texture Board Materials: Small piece of cardboard (4"x4"), glue different textures Textures to glue: sandpaper square, felt piece, bubble wrap piece, aluminum foil piece, corrugated cardboard strip Use: Child licks different textures (provides tongue stimulation) Laminate or cover with clear packing tape for hygiene Wipe with antibacterial wipe between uses Cost: Free from household scraps Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Lollipops or Hard Candy ($2-3) Long-lasting (Dum-Dums, Jolly Ranchers) Tongue must work to lick/move candy Provides prolonged oral-motor input Use as "tongue tool" during high-clicking times Sour Candy ($1-2) Warheads, sour gummies, lemon drops Strong taste provides intense tongue stimulation Reduces need for clicking Limit to 2-3 per day (dental health) DIY Flavored Ice Chips
Freeze juice in ice cube trays Add popsicle stick halfway through freezing Child licks ice (strong tongue sensation) Cost: Pennies per serving Oral Motor Tools (household): Chewable straws Coffee stirrer sticks to hold between teeth Rubber pencil grips to chew For Sensory Avoiders: Soft Foods for Tongue: Yogurt, pudding, applesauce Spoon against tongue provides gentle input Less intense than clicking Gentle Licking Activities: Popsicles (slow licking) Soft ice cream Teaches controlled tongue movement Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Tongue Obstacle Course" (10 minutes, 2x daily): Station 1: Lick peanut butter off roof of mouth (1 min) Station 2: Use tongue to move small candy around mouth without chewing (2 min) Station 3: Lick different textures on texture board (2 min)
Station 4: Hold tongue depressor (popsicle stick) between teeth and lips (2 min) Station 5: Blow bubbles through wand (3 min) Purpose: Provides intense tongue work that satisfies seeking behavior For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Tongue Play" (5-8 minutes): Soft foods only: pudding, yogurt, smoothie Gentle tongue stretches (see redirection technique) Quiet mouth time with soft chewy tube Calming jaw massage Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Schedule: Every 90 minutes: Oral input activity Chew gum (if age 5+) Crunchy snack Drink through straw Chewy tube (ARK Therapeutics, $8-15, or DIY: clean rubber tubing) Before high-clicking times: Preventive input Heavy work: push/pull activities (5 min) Oral-motor: thick smoothie (2 min) Full Body Calming (reduces clicking): Weighted lap pad during seated activities (DIY: fill pillowcase with rice, sew shut)
Deep pressure: squeeze hands, arms, legs Rocking: rocking chair or therapy ball Massage Techniques: Comprehensive Oral-Facial Massage (5-7 minutes): Preparation: Child sits comfortably, relaxed External technique: Warm hands, use tiny amount of coconut oil Circles around mouth (1 min clockwise, 1 min counter-clockwise) Press gently on "smile lines" from nose to mouth corners (30 sec) Gentle taps all around mouth with fingertips (1 min) Massage jawline from chin to ears (1 min each side) Gentle pressure under chin (30 sec) Internal technique (if child allows): Wash hands thoroughly Use food-grade glove or finger cot Gentle pressure inside cheeks with index finger (30 sec each side) Gently massage gums (if teeth brushing is tolerated) Purpose: Provides deep proprioceptive input to mouth area
Neck-to-Mouth Calming Massage (3 minutes): Start at shoulders, work up neck to jaw Slow, firm strokes (calming to nervous system) End with gentle face strokes from forehead to chin Do before bed to reduce next-day clicking MANIFESTATION 4: Popping Lips Repeatedly Physical Redirection Technique: "Lip Work Station" When popping starts, offer: "Lip exercise time!" Quick Exercises: Press lips together hard, count to 10 (repeat 5x) Say "Mmm" with closed lips while pressing (10x) Blow raspberries (10x) Fish face: suck cheeks in (hold 5 sec, repeat 10x) Kiss hand loudly (10x) Blow kisses in all directions (20x) Provides lip proprioception without annoying sound Takes 2-3 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Lip Whistles/Kazoo Materials: Small piece of wax paper (1"x2"), fold in half Use: Hold folded edge between lips, blow gently (creates vibration like lip popping)
Alternative: Empty thread spool, blow across end Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Bubble Gum ($1-2) Blow bubbles repeatedly Provides lip work + proprioceptive input Make it a game: "How big can you blow?" Age-appropriate: 4+ years Lip Balm ($1-3) Strong flavors: mint, cherry, cinnamon Apply frequently (every 15 min during high-popping times) Provides lip sensation + taste Child focuses on licking lips instead of popping DIY Lip Activities: Blow painting: Diluted paint on paper, blow through straw to spread Feather blow: Blow feather, keep it in air as long as possible Whistle practice: Learning to whistle provides lip work Vibrating Lip Tools: Electric toothbrush (off) - child holds against lips ($3-5) Vibrating teether (if younger child, $5-8) For Sensory Avoiders:
Gentle Lip Care: Soft lip balm, unscented Gentle application (child does it themselves) Teaches awareness without over-stimulation Quiet Lip Activities: Sipping through straw (gentle lip press) Soft food on lips to lick off (yogurt, pudding) Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Lip Power Hour" (15-20 minutes, 2x daily): Bubble Blowing Station (5 min) Regular bubbles Blow through different sized wands Catch bubbles with wand (lip control) Resistance Blowing (5 min) Blow into balloon (creates resistance) Blow cotton balls through obstacle course Blow ping pong ball across water Lip Exercises (5 min) Hold button between lips and string (proprioceptive) Press lips around popsicle stick, pull gently Smile wide/pucker tight (alternate 20x) Cool Down (5 min) Drink thick smoothie through straw Chew gum
Gentle lip massage For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Lip Awareness" (8-10 minutes): Light touch around lips with soft brush (1 min) Apply lip balm (child does own application) Gentle blowing: feathers, tissue paper (3 min) Drinking through straw (3 min) Quiet time with preferred activity Sensory Integration: Prevention Protocol (every 60-90 min): Before popping typically occurs: Crunchy snack (apple, carrots, pretzels) Chewy snack (dried fruit, fruit leather) Heavy work task (push wall, carry items) Oral-motor toy (chewy tube, 2-3 min) Environmental Modifications: Provide vibration elsewhere: vibrating cushion, massager Proprioceptive input: weighted lap pad, compression clothing Reduce need for self-regulation: calmer environment overall Massage Techniques: Lip and Perioral Massage (4-5 minutes, 3x daily): Best times: Morning (before school), after school, before bed Technique:
Wash hands, small amount of coconut oil or unscented lotion Upper lip massage: Index fingers, start at center, massage outward to corners (10x) Gentle circles above upper lip (30 sec) Light tapping with fingertips (30 sec) Lower lip massage: Repeat same pattern on lower lip Gentle downward strokes under lower lip (10x) Full mouth circles: Both index fingers, circle around entire mouth (1 min each direction) Lip press: Gently press lips between thumb and index finger Work from center to corners (20 sec each side) Purpose: Deep proprioceptive input reduces need for lip popping Face-to-Shoulder Integration Massage (5 minutes): Connects oral-facial area to body for better regulation Start at lips, stroke down to jaw (10x) Jaw to neck (10x) Neck to shoulders (10x)
Shoulder squeeze and release (1 min) Return to gentle face strokes Purpose: Helps child feel whole-body connection, reducing isolated oral stimming MANIFESTATION 5: Making "ahhh" or "eeee" Sounds Sustained Physical Redirection Technique: "The Volume Controller Game" When sustained sounds start, engage immediately Activity: "Let's play DJ! I'll show you volume levels!" Hand signals: Hand at floor = whisper "ahh" (level 1) Hand at waist = medium "ahh" (level 5) Hand at shoulders = loud "ahh" (level 10) Move your hand up and down, child matches with sound Gradually bring hand lower and lower End at whisper level Teaches volume control while allowing the sound Takes 2-3 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Singing/Humming Tube Materials: 2-3 feet of PVC pipe or pool noodle with hole through center (cut pool noodle if needed), duct tape (if sharp edges)
Assembly: If PVC, tape edges for safety. Pool noodle ready to use Use: Child makes sustained sounds into one end while other end is against wall, door, or floor Creates echo/vibration feedback Teaches directed sound vs. random vocalizations Cost: $3-5 at hardware store Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Kazoo or Harmonica ($1-5) Provides sustained sound + vibration Requires specific mouth position Can make "ahh" sounds through instrument Purposeful vs. random vocalization Voice Recording Device/App (Free phone app) Record child's sustained sounds Play back immediately Creates awareness + auditory feedback Turn into game: "Make longest 'ahh' sound" Singing Activities: Teach sustained notes in songs Children's songs with long vowels ("Old MacDonald" = "E-I-E-I-Ooooo") YouTube sing-alongs Makes stimming purposeful Vibrating Tools: Harmonica ($5-10)
Vibrating toy microphone ($10-15) DIY: Wax paper on comb, hum against it For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Sound Making: Whisper singing Soft "shh" sounds Gentle humming into pillow (dampens sound) Visual Sound Representation: Sound meter app (shows volume visually) Teaches child to see how loud they are Goal: keep in "green zone" Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Sustained Sound Circuit" (20 minutes): Breath Work (5 min) Blow up balloons (long exhalation) Blow pinwheels (sustained breath) Blow bubbles (controlled breath) Vocal Exploration (5 min) Make animal sounds (cow = long "moooo") Sing favorite songs with long notes Make sound effects (siren = "eeeee") Heavy Work (5 min) Push wall while making sound Carry heavy items while singing Jump while vocalizing Provides proprioceptive input with vocal stimming
Quiet Down (5 min) Gradually quieter vocalizations Whisper singing Silent lip movements Deep breathing For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Voice Play" (10 minutes): Soft humming (not sustained "ahh") Quiet songs Whisper practice Focus on control, not volume Sensory Integration: Vocal Regulation Schedule: Morning: Heavy proprioceptive work (reduces vocal stimming) Animal walks: bear crawl, crab walk (5 min) Push/pull: furniture moving, carrying books (5 min) This provides body input that may reduce need for vocal input Midday: Scheduled vocal outlets 5-minute "loud time" outside or designated room Child can be as loud as they want Then practice "quiet time" (whisper voices) Evening: Calming input Gentle rocking Soft music Massage (see below) Vestibular-Auditory Integration: Swing while singing (10 min) - vestibular input often reduces vocal stimming
Rock in rocking chair during homework Trampoline with songs (1 bounce = 1 word of song) Massage Techniques: Laryngeal Area and Chest Massage (5 minutes): IMPORTANT: Never press directly on throat Technique: Child lies down comfortably Chest massage: Flat palms on upper chest (below collarbones) Slow, firm strokes outward to shoulders (10x) Circular massage on chest muscles (1 min) Neck sides (avoid front): Very gentle fingertip massage on neck sides (30 sec each side) Work from behind ears down to shoulders Purpose: Relaxes muscles involved in vocalization Whole Body Calming Massage (10 minutes): Reduces overall need for vocal self-regulation Order: Shoulders and upper back (3 min) - firm pressure Arms: squeeze and release from shoulder to hand (1 min each) Hands: press firmly on palm, massage fingers (1 min each)
Legs: squeeze and release from thigh to foot (1 min each) Feet: firm pressure on soles (1 min each) Pressure: Firm and slow (activates parasympathetic nervous system) Best time: Before bed or after school (high-stimming times) MANIFESTATION 6: Screeching or Squealing Physical Redirection Technique: "The Pressure Release Valve" When screeching starts, immediately intervene with physical grounding Technique: Place firm hands on child's shoulders Make eye contact (if tolerated) Say: "Let's do strong arm pushes!" Guide child to wall Both push against wall together, hard as possible Count to 10 while pushing Release and shake arms out Repeat 3-5 times Provides intense proprioceptive input that often satisfies the need for intense vocalization The physical exertion redirects the energy DIY Alternative Tool: Screaming/Squeal Pillow
Materials: Old pillow or stuffed animal, fabric markers Decoration: Let child decorate with "loud voice" pictures Use: Designated pillow for screaming/squealing into Place in multiple locations (bedroom, playroom, car) Rule: "Big sounds go in the pillow, not in the air" Cost: Free (repurposed item) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Whistles ($1-3 for pack) Provide variety: slide whistle, train whistle, sports whistle Creates loud, high-pitched sound without vocal strain Can be scheduled: "Whistle time" 5 minutes every 2 hours Outdoor use preferred Musical Instruments - High Pitched Recorder/flute ($5-10) Toy saxophone ($8-15) Slide whistle ($3-5) Allows high-pitched sound creation purposefully DIY Sound Makers: Balloon squeaks: Let air out slowly (makes squealing sound) Styrofoam rub: Two pieces rubbed together (high-pitched squeak) Glass rim: Wet finger on glass rim (creates high tone)
Voice Amplifier/Microphone ($10-20 or phone app - free) Child can screech into microphone Hears own voice amplified Satisfies sensory need with control For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Alternatives: Silent scream practice (mouth open, no sound) Whisper screaming (teaches modulation) Humming instead of screeching Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Screech-to-Calm Protocol" (15-20 minutes, 2-3x daily): High Energy Release (5 min) Jump on trampoline or pillows while making loud sounds Run in place with vocal sounds Dance wildly to loud music Purpose: Releases pent-up energy that drives screeching Structured Loud Time (5 min) Designated "screaming zone" (outdoor or specific room) Set timer: "You have 5 minutes to be AS LOUD as you want" Screech, yell, squeal freely When timer ends: "Now we use quiet voices"
Purpose: Gives permission for the behavior in controlled way Heavy Work Transition (5 min) Immediately after loud time: Push-ups against wall (20x) Carry heavy books across room (10 trips) Squeeze therapy putty as hard as possible (2 min) Purpose: Proprioceptive input calms nervous system Quiet Activities (5 min) Weighted lap pad Gentle rocking Quiet book or calm toy Purpose: Practice being calm after being loud For Sensory Avoiders: "Volume Control Training" (10 minutes): Use visual volume chart (1-10, with pictures) Practice sounds at each level Reward staying at levels 1-3 Teach: "This sound is a 10. Can you make it a 5? A 3?" Sensory Integration: Preventive Sensory Diet (throughout day): Every 60-90 minutes: Heavy work break Carry laundry basket Push toy shopping cart filled with books
Animal walks (bear crawl, crab walk) Wall pushes Why: Proprioceptive input reduces need for vocal stimming Before high-risk times: Intensive proprioceptive "loading" 10 minutes of intense physical activity Examples: trampoline, crashing into pillows, tug-of-war Purpose: Pre-emptively satisfies sensory need Auditory-Vestibular Connection: Screeching often accompanies vestibular seeking Provide vestibular input proactively: Swinging (10 min, 3x daily) Spinning in office chair (10 spins each direction) Rolling down hills or across floor Often eliminates screeching behavior Deep Pressure Protocol: Compression vest or tight-fitting clothing (reduces arousal) Weighted lap pad during seated activities Body squeeze: Squeeze pillow between body and wall Purpose: Calming pressure reduces need for high-arousal behaviors Massage Techniques: Intensive Calming Massage (15 minutes, 2x daily - morning and evening): Purpose: Deep pressure massage significantly reduces screeching by calming the nervous system
Preparation: Quiet room, dim lights Use unscented massage oil or lotion Child lies on stomach Back Massage (5 min): Flat palms, firm pressure Long strokes from shoulders to lower back (20x) Circular motions on each side of spine (2 min) "Piano playing" with firm fingertips down back (1 min) More long strokes to finish (20x) Shoulder and Neck (3 min): Firm squeezes on shoulders (squeeze-hold-release, 20x) Thumb pressure on tight spots (hold 10 seconds each) Gentle neck massage on sides (never front) Arms and Hands (3 min): Squeeze down each arm from shoulder to hand (10x each arm) Press firmly on palms (30 sec each) Pull gently on each finger (5 sec each) Legs and Feet (4 min): Squeeze down each leg from hip to foot (10x each)
Firm pressure on soles of feet (1 min each) Press on each toe (5 sec each) Pressure Level: Should be firm - child should feel "squished" not tickled Response: Child often becomes very calm, sometimes sleepy "Emergency Calm-Down" Quick Massage (3 minutes): Use when screeching is imminent or happening: Firm shoulder squeezes (30 sec) Press palms together hard, child pushes against your hands (30 sec) Squeeze up and down arms quickly (30 sec) Firm pressure on top of head (gently press down 10 sec) Hand massage (squeeze each finger, 1 min) Deep breaths together while doing massage Purpose: Quick sensory reset to interrupt screeching pattern Oral-Facial Massage for Vocal Stimming (5 minutes): Often screeching involves tension in face/jaw Technique: Massage temples in circles (1 min)
Jaw massage: locate muscle in front of ears (1 min each side) Cheek massage: circles on cheeks (1 min) Chin and under-chin: firm pressure (1 min) Best timing: After screeching episode (prevents continuation) MANIFESTATION 7: Growling or Grunting Physical Redirection Technique: "Animal Power Moves" When growling/grunting starts, immediately engage Activity: "I hear you growling! Let's be strong animals!" Bear Crawl: Crawl on hands and feet, growling allowed (1 min) Gorilla Walk: Bent over, arms swinging, grunt allowed (1 min) Lion Pose: Yoga pose with deep breathing and roar (1 min) Elephant Trunk: Swinging arms, low groaning sounds (1 min) Rest Pose: Child's pose (yoga), quiet breathing (1 min) Channels the low vocal sounds into purposeful activity Proprioceptive input from animal movements often stops stimming
DIY Alternative Tool: Growl Box Materials: Cardboard box (shoebox size), decorate with "monster" or "animal" theme Use: Child growls/grunts into box opening Sound is muffled but child gets sensory feedback Can take to school in backpack Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Low-Frequency Sound Tools: Didgeridoo (toy version, $10-15) Tuba/trombone sounds on YouTube (play and imitate) Bass guitar or low notes on keyboard Provides low-frequency vibration similar to growling Vibrating Tools: Electric toothbrush - hold against cheeks, throat (external), chest ($5-10) Massager - handheld, use on jaw, neck, chest ($10-20) Creates similar vibratory sensation DIY Low Sound Makers: Tissue paper on comb: Hum low notes against it (vibration) PVC pipe: Hum into long pipe (amplifies low sounds) Cardboard tube: Hit on leg while vocalizing (percussion + vocalization)
Growl-Friendly Activities: Play "monster" or "dinosaur" games (growling is appropriate) Read books with animal sounds, emphasize growls "Dinosaur stomp" - stomp and growl together For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Low Sounds: Soft humming (low pitch) Gentle "ohhh" sounds Focus on soft, controlled vocalizations Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Deep Sound and Heavy Work Circuit" (20 minutes): Heavy Work Station (5 min) Push/pull heavy objects Carry weighted items Can growl/grunt during these activities (natural pairing) Purpose: These activities naturally involve low vocalizations Deep Pressure Station (5 min) Roll heavy therapy ball over body Squeeze under couch cushions Bear hugs from adult Can make low sounds during compression Purpose: Deep pressure satisfies sensory need Vocal Play Station (5 min) Explore different growl types: dog, bear, lion, monster
Practice loud vs. quiet growls Growl into different materials (pillow, box, tube) Purpose: Makes stimming purposeful and controlled Calming Station (5 min) Heavy blanket or weighted lap pad Deep breathing with low hums (not growls) Quiet activity with oral motor tool (chewy) Purpose: Transition to calm state For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Vocalization" (10 minutes): Soft humming (low tones okay) Gentle animal sounds (not aggressive) Reading stories with expression (varied tones) Singing gentle songs Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor and Proprioceptive Protocol: Target: The connection between oral-motor and whole-body proprioception Morning Routine (15 min): Crunchy breakfast (toast, cereal, apple) Heavy work: make bed, carry backpack Oral motor: chew gum or chewy tube (2 min) Purpose: Starts day with appropriate input Throughout Day (every 90 min):
Chewy snack (bagel, dried fruit, jerky) Heavy work task (carry books, push chairs) 2-3 min chewy tool Purpose: Prevents growling by satisfying needs proactively Before High-Risk Times: 10 minutes intensive proprioceptive work 5 minutes oral-motor activities Purpose: "Loading" the sensory system prevents stimming Jaw and Throat Connection: Growling involves jaw and throat tension Jaw exercises (5 min, 3x daily): Open mouth wide, close (20x) Move jaw side to side (20x) Pretend to chew big bites (20x) Chew actual resistive foods Purpose: Releases tension that may cause growling Massage Techniques: Jaw and Throat Release Massage (7 minutes): Purpose: Growling creates tension in jaw and throat; this releases it Jaw Muscle Massage (3 min): Locate masseter muscle (in front of ears, clench teeth to find it)
Place index and middle fingers on muscle Circular massage (1 min each side) Ask child to open mouth slightly, massage again (1 min each side) Gentle up-and-down strokes on jaw (30 sec each side) Throat Area (2 min): NEVER press on front of throat Massage sides of neck only Gentle circles from behind ears down to collarbones (1 min each side) Very light touch down front of neck (avoid pressure) Under Chin (1 min): Firm pressure under jaw/chin area Circular massage Press gently up toward jaw Face Connection (1 min): Stroke from jaw down to shoulders (10x) Helps connect areas and release overall tension Chest and Throat Vibration Release (5 minutes): Purpose: Growling creates vibration in chest/throat; this provides alternative input
Child lies on back Chest percussion: Cupped hands, gently "tap" on chest (like burping baby) 30-60 seconds, creates gentle vibration Chest massage: Flat palms, firm circular massage on upper chest (2 min) Stroke outward from center to shoulders (20x) Neck sides: Gentle massage from jaw to shoulders (1 min each side) Finish: Light fingertip tapping all over chest/neck area (1 min) Creates pleasant vibration sensation Full Body "Grounding" Massage (10 minutes): Purpose: Growling often indicates high arousal; this calms entire system Use before bed or after school Firm, slow strokes all over body Focus on: Back: long strokes (5 min) Arms and legs: squeeze and release (3 min) Feet: firm pressure (2 min) Child often stops growling significantly after this massage
Best practice: Daily massage routine MANIFESTATION 8: Buzzing Lips Physical Redirection Technique: "Lip Buzz to Breathing" When buzzing starts, gently interrupt Technique: "I hear your lips buzzing! Let's buzz into our hands!" Cup hands together making small opening Buzz lips into hands (creates feedback sensation) Then: "Now let's breathe the buzzing away" Deep breath in (nose), long exhale with lip buzz (purposeful) Repeat 10 times Gradually transition to exhale without buzz Transforms stim into breathing exercise Takes 2-3 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Buzz Bottle Materials: Empty plastic bottle (16-20 oz), water, dish soap Assembly: Fill 1/4 with water, add squirt of dish soap, secure lid Use: Remove lid, buzz lips against bottle opening (creates bubbles in liquid) Visual feedback + buzzing sensation
Cost: Free (household items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Kazoo ($1-2) Perfect lip-buzzing tool Creates purposeful sound Can play songs, makes it functional Portable (pocket-sized) Harmonica ($5-10) Requires controlled lip buzzing Produces musical tones Teaches lip position and control More sophisticated than kazoo DIY Buzzing Tools: Wax paper + comb: Hold wax paper over comb, buzz lips against it (vibration + sound) Balloon lips: Lips against inflated balloon, buzz (vibration feedback) Straw buzz: Buzz lips while holding straw (then blow through it) Musical Exploration: Brass instrument videos: Show how trumpets/trombones work (lip buzzing!) Practice trumpet buzzing: Lips together, buzz like brass player Turns stim into music education Bubble Activities: Bubble wands (must buzz/blow correctly) Bubble mixture: 1 cup water, 2 tbsp dish soap, 1 tbsp glycerin (makes stronger bubbles)
Bubble tricks (bubbles inside bubbles) For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Lip Activities: Soft lip massage (self-administered) Lip balm application (awareness without buzzing) Gentle blowing (no buzz) Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Lip Buzz Orchestra" (15-20 minutes, 2x daily): Warm-Up (3 min) Lip stretches: smile wide, pucker tight (20x) Lip rolls: blow air through lips loosely Gentle lip taps with fingers Buzz Exploration (5 min) Buzz at different pitches (high, medium, low) Buzz at different volumes (loud, medium, quiet) Buzz into different objects: Hands (cupped) Bottle with water Cardboard tube Against balloon Purpose: Makes buzzing purposeful and controlled Musical Buzzing (5 min) Kazoo playing Try to buzz songs (Mary Had a Little Lamb, etc.) Buzz rhythm patterns (buzz-buzz-pause-buzz) Purpose: Functional skill development
Oral-Motor Work (4 min) Chew tough foods (bagel, apple, jerky) Drink thick liquid through straw Chewy tube (2 min) Purpose: Satisfies oral-motor need Quiet Transition (3 min) Gentle lip massage Lip balm application Quiet breathing exercises Purpose: Calm down from activity For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Lip Exploration" (10 minutes): Very gentle lip touches (feather, cotton ball) Lip balm (teaches awareness) Soft blowing (feather, tissue paper) Whisper-breathing (lips almost closed) Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Sensory Diet: Morning (upon waking): Vibrating toothbrush (2 min) Crunchy breakfast Oral-motor exercises (see above) Every 60-90 minutes: Chewy snack or chewy tool Drink through straw (creates lip seal) 1-2 min of lip activities (bubbles, kazoo, etc.) Before times when buzzing typically occurs: 5 min intensive oral-motor input Heavy work (5 min)
Weighted lap pad Evening: Calming oral input (warm soup through straw) Lip massage No intense activities before bed Vestibular-Oral Connection: Lip buzzing often accompanies vestibular seeking Strategy: Provide vestibular input proactively Swing daily (10-15 min) Spin on office chair (10 spins each way) Rock in rocking chair during seated activities Result: Often reduces or eliminates lip buzzing Massage Techniques: Comprehensive Lip and Perioral Massage (6-8 minutes, 3x daily): Best times: Morning, after school, before bed Preparation: Wash hands thoroughly Tiny amount coconut oil or unscented lotion Child sits comfortably, relaxed Technique: Upper Lip (2 min): Index fingers, start at center of upper lip Firm circular massage moving outward to corners (30 sec) Return to center, press firmly and hold (10 sec)
Repeat massage outward (30 sec) Gentle tapping all around upper lip with fingertips (30 sec) Light feathery strokes (desensitizes, 30 sec) Lower Lip (2 min): Same pattern as upper lip Pay attention to center of lower lip (often most buzzing happens here) Firmer pressure here (child should feel "squished" feeling) Around Mouth (2 min): Both index fingers, start at center below nose Massage in large circles around entire mouth (1 min clockwise, 1 min counter-clockwise) Get close to lips but also massage the area around them Lip Press (1 min): Gently press lips between thumb (outside) and index finger (inside mouth if allowed) Work from center to corners Firm pressure (proprioceptive input) Hold pressure 5 sec in each spot Finish (1 min):
Light tapping all around mouth Gentle strokes outward from lips Deep breath together Quick "Buzzing Emergency" Massage (2 minutes): Use when buzzing is actively happening: Firm pressure on both lips simultaneously Press lips together (externally) with fingers (30 sec) Quick circular massage around mouth (30 sec) Press firmly on cheeks (30 sec) Lip stretches (smile/pucker) with gentle resistance from your fingers (30 sec) Purpose: Immediate sensory input that often stops the buzzing Face-to-Body Integration Massage (5 minutes): Purpose: Connects oral area to whole body (reduces isolated stimming) Start with lip massage (1 min) Stroke from lips down to jaw (10x) Jaw down to neck (10x) Neck down to shoulders (10x) Shoulder squeeze and hold (30 sec) Arms: squeeze down to hands (1 min each)
Hand massage (1 min each) Result: Child feels more "whole body" awareness, less focus on lips alone MANIFESTATION 9: Whistling Same Tune Repeatedly Physical Redirection Technique: "Whistle to Wind-Down" When repetitive whistling starts, acknowledge it Activity: "I hear you whistling! Let's turn it into a game!" Whistle Simon Says: "Whistle high" (demonstrate) "Whistle low" "Whistle loud" "Whistle soft" "Whistle fast" "Whistle slow" "Now... whistle silence!" (lips in position, no sound) Do 10-15 commands Gradually increase "silence" commands End with quiet breathing, lips relaxed Teaches control while honoring the need to whistle Takes 3-5 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Whistle Collection Box Materials: Small box or bag, collect different whistles Contents: Slide whistle (pitch changes) Train whistle Sports whistle Pea-less whistle (different sound)
DIY: Cut straws at angles (different pitches) Use: When child feels need to whistle, offer whistle from box Rotates, prevents obsessive focus on one tune Cost: $5-10 for collection Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Structured Whistle Time: Set timer: "You can whistle for 5 minutes" When timer ends: "Now it's quiet time" Gradually reduce time (5 min → 3 min → 1 min) Teaches delayed gratification Whistle Alternatives: Recorder ($5-8) - similar lip position, purposeful music Penny whistle/tin whistle ($10-15) - requires similar oral-motor control Ocarina ($10-20) - different sound, same concept All provide similar oral-motor feedback with purpose Whistle Games: "Name That Tune" - whistle songs, others guess "Whistle While You Work" - whistle while doing chores (makes it functional)
"Whistle Language" - create whistle codes with family Purpose: Makes stimming a social skill Breath Control Activities: Blow out candles (teaches breath control like whistling) Blow pinwheels at different speeds Blow cotton balls across finish line Purpose: Similar oral-motor without repetitive tune For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Alternatives: Humming softly (no whistling) Lip position practice without sound Visual music (watch music videos, no sound making) Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Whistle Skills Workshop" (15-20 minutes, 1-2x daily): Breath Control Station (5 min) Blow up balloons (requires similar lip position and breath) Blow through straw into water (bubbles) Blow cotton balls through obstacle course Purpose: Provides similar oral-motor without annoying repetitive tune Musical Whistle Station (5 min) Learn new whistle tunes (not repetitive single tune)
Whistle scales (do-re-mi-fa-so-la-ti-do) Whistle rhythm patterns (not melodies) Whistle with backing tracks (makes it purposeful) Purpose: Makes whistling educational Lip Work Station (5 min) Lip strengthening exercises: Press lips around popsicle stick, pull gently Lip push-ups: press lips together, release (30x) Hold button between lips attached to string, pull gently Drink thick liquid through straw Chewy tube Purpose: Satisfies oral-motor need differently Quiet Transition (5 min) Lip massage Quiet breathing Calm activity with hands (playdough, fidget) Purpose: Shifts focus away from lips For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Sound Exploration" (10 minutes): Soft humming (instead of whistling) Quiet singing Listening to music (not making it) Silent lip movements (pretend whistling) Sensory Integration: Whistling Prevention Protocol: Target: Provide sufficient oral-motor and auditory input to prevent whistling
Morning Routine: Crunchy breakfast Oral-motor exercises (5 min) Heavy work (make bed, carry backpack) Brief whistle time allowed (2-3 min) Throughout Day (every 90 min): Chewy snack or chewy tool Drink through straw 1-2 min purposeful whistling (scale, specific song) OR alternative (kazoo, harmonica) Heavy work task Before High-Risk Times: If whistling typically happens during homework/quiet time: 10 min active play before sitting Chewy tool available during work Whistle breaks every 20 minutes (1 min allowed) Evening: Calming input (no whistling practice before bed) Massage (see below) Auditory Sensory Diet: Whistling is auditory seeking behavior Provide alternative auditory input: Background music during activities White noise or nature sounds Audiobooks Singing songs together Purpose: Fills auditory need without whistling Massage Techniques: Lip and Jaw Release Massage (5-7 minutes, 2-3x daily):
Purpose: Whistling creates lip and jaw tension; this releases it Lip Massage (2 min): Circular massage around lips (1 min) Press and hold center of lips (10 sec) Gentle pulling/stretching of lips (20 sec) Light tapping around lips (30 sec) Jaw Massage (2 min): Locate jaw muscle (in front of ears) Circular massage (1 min each side) Child opens mouth slightly, massage again Cheek Massage (2 min): Palms on cheeks, circular massage (1 min) Fingertips massage inside of cheeks (if child allows) Gentle cheek presses (30 sec) Finish (1 min): Light strokes from lips outward to ears Gentle face taps Deep breath together Oral-Facial Desensitization Massage (5 minutes): Purpose: Sometimes whistling is due to oral sensitivity; this reduces it Use varied texures:
Soft brush (makeup brush) Washcloth (textured) Fingers (firm pressure) Technique: Stroke around mouth with each texture (30 sec each) Gradually increase pressure Include lips directly (if tolerated) Progression: Start with least sensitive areas (cheeks) Move toward more sensitive (lips) If child resists, back off Do: 2x daily for 2-3 weeks Result: Often reduces oral stimming behaviors Full Face and Neck Calming Massage (8-10 minutes): Best time: Before bed (prevents nighttime/morning whistling) Forehead (1 min): Fingertips, stroke from center outward (20x) Gentle circles on temples Eyes/Nose (1 min): Light pressure on bridge of nose Gentle circles around eye sockets (not eyes themselves) Cheeks and Jaw (3 min): Full palm circular massage on cheeks Jaw muscle massage (detailed above) Mouth/Lips (2 min): Detailed lip massage (as above)
Neck (2 min): Stroke from jaw down to shoulders (20x) Gentle neck massage (sides only) Finish (1 min): Light feathery touches all over face Very calming to nervous system LEVEL 2: Echolalia (Repetitive Speech) CAUSATION Over-Stimulated Causation: Mechanism: Predictable verbal patterns reduce anxiety during overwhelming situations How it works: Language processing is complex cognitive task During overwhelm, brain simplifies by using pre-memorized scripts Echolalia requires less processing than original language Repetition creates predictability in chaotic sensory environment Familiar words/phrases are comforting during stress Examples: Child scripts movie dialogue during loud, busy classroom (predictable language during overwhelming environment) Repeats commercials while in crowded store (familiar script reduces anxiety) Echoes phrases when multiple people talking (simplifies language processing) Clinical note: Echolalia often increases during transitions, new situations, or sensory-overwhelming environments
Under-Stimulated Causation: Mechanism: Creates auditory stimulation + motor planning stimulation simultaneously How it works: Auditory component: Provides auditory input when environment quiet/boring Motor planning component: Speech requires complex motor planning (lips, tongue, jaw, breath coordination) Repetition allows practice of motor plans without cognitive load of creating new language Provides both auditory and motor satisfaction Examples: Scripting entire scenes during independent quiet time (fills auditory void with familiar language) Repeating own words during boring tasks (creates auditory and motor stimulation) Reciting jingles while waiting (fills time with familiar verbal patterns) Clinical note: Often decreases when engaged in stimulating activity Sensitivity Causation: Dual purpose: Processing language through repetition + communication attempt Processing mechanism: Auditory processing difficulty: Child hears language but doesn't immediately process meaning
Repetition buys time: Echoing allows child to "replay" language internally while processing Each repetition deepens processing (like reading sentence multiple times to understand) Eventually, meaning extracted through repeated exposure to same phrase Communication attempt: Functional echolalia: Using memorized scripts to communicate needs Example: "Do you want juice?" (heard from parent) used by child to mean "I want juice" Scripts are form of expressive language when original language generation difficult May be only available communication method at that moment Examples: Immediate echolalia: Repeating question instead of answering (processing what was asked) Delayed echolalia: Movie scripts used functionally ("Elsa runs away" when child wants to leave) Palilalia: Repeating own words while searching for next word Clinical note: Often child KNOWS what they want to say but can't generate language; scripts fill gap
SENSORY PROFILE Seeker Profile: Characteristics: High volume scripting/echoing Frequent throughout day (constant verbal output) Loud, exuberant recitation Extensive scripts (entire scenes, long passages) Seems to enjoy the sound of own voice Uninhibited about when/where scripting occurs Presentation: Constant background of scripts, echoes, repetitions Volume often too loud for setting Scripts during all activities May script while simultaneously doing other activities Doesn't seem to notice others' reactions Neurological basis: Under-responsive auditory system (needs intense verbal output) May also have motor planning seeking (enjoys complex speech motor patterns) High arousal state (scripts maintain arousal level) Support needs: Designated script times (contains behavior) Alternative vocal outlets (singing, instruments) Heavy proprioceptive work (may reduce verbal seeking) Oral-motor alternatives (chewing, drinking through straws) Avoider Profile: Characteristics:
Soft, self-directed scripting Quiet volume (comforting to self, not broadcasting) Scripts for comfort during stress Often combined with self-soothing behaviors (rocking, hugging self) May script while alone or quietly to self even when others present Presentation: Gentle, almost whispered scripting Increases during anxiety or overwhelm Decreases when calm and comfortable Scripts seem to calm child Protective of script content (private) Neurological basis: Using scripts as regulation during overwhelm Familiar language is anxiety-reducing Soft volume indicates not seeking auditory input, but using for emotional regulation Support needs: Allow scripts as regulation tool Teach other anxiety management strategies Reduce overall anxiety and overwhelm Don't interrupt scripts (they're serving important function) Communication Profile: Characteristics: Using scripts functionally despite appearing to be stimming Scripts have communicative intent (though not always obvious)
May be only available expressive language method Scripts are purposeful (if you interpret correctly) Presentation: Scripts appear random but are actually communicating needs/thoughts Example: "It's raining, it's pouring" when child wants to go outside (rain scene from movie = outside) Example: "Time for bed" (repeated from parent) when child is tired Pattern matching reveals communicative function Neurological basis: Expressive language difficulty (can't generate original language easily) Receptive language better than expressive (understands more than can say) Scripts are learned expressive language chunks Support needs: Learn child's script meanings (takes time and observation) Honor scripts as valid communication Gently expand (model alternatives without requiring child to use them) Speech-language therapy (teach more flexible communication) MANIFESTATION 1: Immediate Echolalia (Repeating Just-Heard Phrases Instantly)
Physical Redirection Technique: "Echo to Answer Bridge" When immediate echolalia occurs, don't ignore or punish Technique: You say: "Do you want juice?" Child echoes: "Do you want juice?" You respond: "I hear you saying 'Do you want juice?' Let's change it! Say 'I want juice'" (model with exaggerated emphasis on "I") Guide their hand to their chest when saying "I" If child still echoes: Offer choice: "Show me - point to juice or milk" Accept non-verbal response Celebrate: "Great communication!" Gently shapes echolalia toward functional communication Physical element: Use hand-over-hand to help child point to themselves when using "I" DIY Alternative Tool: Communication Choice Board Materials: Piece of cardboard, print or draw pictures of common items/activities Sections: Foods, Activities, Feelings, People
Laminate or cover with clear contact paper Add velcro dots Use: Instead of echoing questions, child points to answer Advanced: Create sentence strips "I want ___" (child adds picture) Cost: $5 for laminating sheets, otherwise free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Echo Games (purposeful echolalia): "Echo Canyon": Speak into cardboard tube, child echoes (makes it a game) "Telephone Game": Whisper phrase, child repeats (functional echoing) "Robot Repeat": Adult says phrase, child "robot repeats" in robot voice (adds element of play) Purpose: Makes echolalia purposeful and fun Recording Devices: Voice recording app (free on phone) Child records self saying phrases Plays back immediately Provides auditory feedback Can practice saying NEW things (not just echoing) Verbal Routines: Teach songs/rhymes with repetition "Call and response" songs
Example: Adult: "Who let the dogs out?" Child: "Woof, woof, woof, woof!" Makes echolalia social and purposeful For Sensory Avoiders (Communication-Focused): Visual Supports: Picture cards for communication Written choices Reduces pressure to speak immediately Processing Time: Count to 10 after asking question (gives time to formulate response) Use visual timer Reduces anxiety that causes echolalia Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Playful Language Circuit" (20-25 minutes, 2x daily): Heavy Work First (5 min) Jumping, crashing, pushing Calms body before language work Many children echo less when proprioceptively regulated Echo Play Station (5 min) Purposeful echoing games (see above) Echo with actions (echo + clap, echo + jump) Makes echolalia fun and intentional Language Expansion (7 min) Script: Adult says "I want snack"
Child echoes: "I want snack" Adult: "Great! Now add which snack!" (models: "I want crackers") Practice expanding echoed phrases Celebrate attempts, even if imperfect Choice Practice (5 min) Offer choices for everything "Crackers or pretzels?" (hold up both) If child echoes: Gently shape "Which one? Point!" Accept pointing, signing, any communication Sensory-Language Integration (3 min) Sensory bin (rice, beans, water beads) Practice labeling: "I feel..." (textures) "I found..." (objects in bin) Language + sensory = more engagement For Communication-Focused: "Communication Building Blocks" (15-20 minutes): Use visuals extensively (less pressure to speak) Honor ALL communication (pointing, nodding, echolalia) Gently model without pressure Celebrate small changes in echo patterns Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Before Language Activities: Theory: Oral-motor regulation improves speech control Protocol (5 min before language activities):
Crunchy snack Drink through straw Chewy tube (2 min) Lip/jaw exercises Result: Often reduces echolalia Proprioceptive Regulation for Language: Heavy work before communication demands: Carry heavy books Wall pushes Chair push-ups During communication: Weighted lap pad Fidget tool in hand Allows body to be calm while language is stressed Reduce Auditory Overload: Less language = less echolalia Strategies: Use simple, short phrases One instruction at a time Pause between sentences Reduce background noise during conversations Purpose: Makes language processing easier Massage Techniques: Oral-Motor Preparatory Massage (5 minutes, before language activities): Purpose: Prepares oral-motor system for speech, reducing echolalia Facial Warm-Up (2 min): Gentle face massage (forehead to chin) Wake up facial muscles Lip and Mouth Focus (3 min): Circular massage around lips (1 min)
Jaw massage (1 min) Cheek massage, inside if allowed (1 min) Do this: Before school, before therapy, before homework Calming Body Massage for Overall Regulation (10 minutes, 2x daily): Theory: Calm body = better language control Full body massage (see previous detailed instructions) Focus on: Back (calming long strokes) Arms and hands (grounding) Legs and feet (security) Timing: After school (when echolalia typically increases), before bed Quick "Communication Prep" Massage (2-3 minutes): Use before asking questions/making demands: Shoulder squeeze (30 sec) Arm squeeze down to hands (30 sec) Hand massage (1 min) One deep breath together Then ask question/make request Purpose: Helps child be more regulated and available for communication Comprehensive Guide to Managing Auditory Stimming in Children PART 3: Continued Detailed Manifestations
MANIFESTATION 2: Delayed Echolalia (Repeating Movie/TV Lines Hours or Days Later) Physical Redirection Technique: "Script to Story Bridge" When child starts scripting movie lines, engage immediately Technique: Child says: "To infinity and beyond!" (Toy Story script) You respond: "Oh! You're thinking about Toy Story! Let's act it out with our bodies!" Actions: Jump high (like Buzz flying) - 10 jumps Pretend to be Woody (walk like cowboy) - 1 minute Freeze like toys when humans come - practice 5 times Crash into pillows (like movie action scene) Then redirect: "Now let's tell me about YOUR day using YOUR words" If child continues scripting: "Show me with actions" (accept non-verbal) Transforms verbal script into physical play Provides proprioceptive input that often reduces need to script
DIY Alternative Tool: Script Book/Journal Materials: Notebook, markers, stickers Purpose: Designated place for scripts Use: When child starts scripting, offer: "Let's write/draw that in your script book!" Child writes favorite lines Draws pictures of scenes Can revisit book during "script time" (scheduled) Contains the behavior to specific times/places Cost: $2-3 for notebook Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Scheduled Script Time (15-20 min, 2-3x daily): Set timer: "This is script time!" Child can repeat any scripts they want When timer ends: "Script time is over, now it's [activity] time" Gradually reduce duration Purpose: Honors the need while setting boundaries Props and Acting: Provide costumes, props from favorite shows Act out scripts (makes it purposeful play) Invite others to participate Transform stim into imaginative play
Recording Scripts: Voice memo app (free) Child records favorite scripts Can listen during designated times Creates library of scripts Purpose: External storage reduces need to repeat verbally Script Writing: Encourage child to write own scripts "What happens AFTER this scene?" Create new stories with favorite characters Purpose: Moves from repetition to creativity Video Making: Use tablet/phone camera Child acts out scripts on video Can watch later (designated times) Makes scripting a productive activity For Communication-Focused: Script Translation: When child scripts, ask: "What are you feeling?" Scripts often communicate emotions Example: Child scripts: "Elsa runs away" (Frozen) Might mean: "I feel overwhelmed" Help child learn to recognize this connection Visual Emotion Charts: Match scripts to emotions "When you say that line, how do you feel?"
Gradually build emotional vocabulary Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "From Script to Play" Protocol (30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Heavy Work Opening (5 min) Proprioceptive input calms nervous system Reduces compulsive scripting Activities: jumping, crashing, pushing Scheduled Script Time (10 min) "This is YOUR time to say anything you want!" Child scripts freely Adult listens without judgment Can video record if child wants Purpose: Fills the need Script to Action (10 min) Take scripts and make them physical Example with "Lion King": "Simba runs" = run in place "Circle of Life" = spin in circles "Stampede scene" = jump on couch cushions Purpose: Channels verbal into physical Expansion Practice (5 min) Adult models expanding scripts: Child: "Hakuna Matata" Adult: "Yes! That means no worries! What do YOU have no worries about?"
Gently encourage original thought Accept any attempt, even more scripting Celebrate small variations in scripts For Communication-Focused: "Script Detective" Activity (15-20 minutes): Identify the Script (5 min) When child scripts, write it down Ask: "What show/movie is that from?" Build awareness Find the Feeling (5 min) "How does [character] feel in that scene?" "How do YOU feel right now?" Connect script to emotion Alternative Expression (5 min) "Let's think of another way to say that feeling" Model: "You could say 'I feel worried' or 'I need space'" Practice new phrases Choice Practice (5 min) Offer: "You can say the script OR the new phrase" Honor both choices Gradually child may choose new phrases Sensory Integration: Vestibular-Language Connection: Theory: Scripting often accompanies vestibular seeking or regulation needs
Protocol: Before scripting typically occurs: Swing (10-15 min) Spin activities (office chair, playground) Rocking (rocking chair during activities) During high-script times: Therapy ball to sit on (gentle bouncing while scripting) Rocking while allowing scripts Result: Vestibular input often reduces scripting significantly Proprioceptive Loading: Heavy work before language demands: Morning: 15 min heavy work before school After school: 15 min heavy work before homework Evening: 10 min heavy work before dinner Types: Pushing/pulling heavy objects Carrying groceries, laundry, books Animal walks Wall pushes Result: Calm, regulated body = less compulsive scripting Auditory Environment Management: Reduce script triggers: Limit screen time (less exposure to scripts) If child watches show, watch together and discuss (makes it interactive, not just input) Provide alternative auditory input (music, audiobooks, nature sounds)
Purpose: Less script input = less script output Massage Techniques: Pre-Language Activity Massage (7-10 minutes): Best time: Before situations requiring functional communication (school, social events, therapy) Purpose: Calms nervous system, making functional language more accessible Shoulders and Upper Back (3 min): Firm squeezes on shoulders (20x) Circular massage on upper back Reduces tension that increases scripting Arms to Hands (2 min): Squeeze down arms (10x each) Firm palm massage Finger pulls (5 sec each finger) Grounding effect Legs to Feet (2 min): Squeeze down legs (10x each) Firm foot massage Full body grounding Finish: Head to Toe Connection (2 min): Light touch from head down spine to feet Helps child feel "whole" and present Reduces dissociative scripting "Script Interrupt" Quick Massage (3-5 minutes):
Use when scripting is excessive/problematic: Interrupt gently: "Let's take a massage break" Quick sequence: Shoulder squeeze (30 sec) Hand massage (1 min each hand) Foot massage (1 min each foot) Deep pressure down arms and legs (1 min) Often child stops or significantly reduces scripting Then redirect to activity Bedtime Calming Massage for Next-Day Prevention (15 minutes): Purpose: Deep calm before sleep = less scripting next day Full body massage (detailed in previous sections) Extra time on: Back (long, slow strokes) Hands (detailed massage) Feet (deep pressure) Use slow, rhythmic movements Can pair with calming music or white noise Child often falls asleep during or shortly after Result: Better sleep = better regulation = less scripting MANIFESTATION 3: Repeating Own Words (Palilalia)
Physical Redirection Technique: "Word to Movement" When child repeats own words, acknowledge and redirect Technique: Child says: "I want juice, I want juice, I want juice" You respond: "I heard you say 'I want juice' THREE times! Let's jump three times!" Jump together (or clap, stomp, etc.) Then: "Now let's use one-time words. Say 'juice please' ONE time" Model saying it once Immediately honor request (give juice) Positive reinforcement: "Great one-time words!" Creates awareness of repetition Pairs language with movement (proprioceptive input) DIY Alternative Tool: One-Time Word Visual Materials: Index card, draw 1 mouth, write "ONE TIME WORDS" Laminate or cover with contact paper Use: When child starts repeating, show card Point to one mouth Say: "One-time words" Can carry in pocket/backpack
Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Counting/Rhythm Integration: When child repeats, count repetitions together "Let's count! One, two, three... you said it three times!" Make it a math/counting game Then: "Now let's say it ONE time" Purpose: Adds awareness without shame Echo Microphone (controlled): Toy microphone with echo effect ($10-15) Or phone app with echo Child speaks into it Hears repetition from device (not self) Satisfies need for repetition externally May reduce self-repetition Percussion with Words: Each word = one drum beat If child repeats, they drum multiple times Creates awareness through another modality Can practice "one beat" (one word) For Communication-Focused: Processing Time Support: Palilalia often indicates processing difficulty Strategies: Give more time to formulate thoughts Visual supports Reduce pressure to speak quickly
May reduce repetition Completion Phrases: When child repeats: "I want... I want... I want..." Gently complete: "...juice? Crackers? What do you want?" Helps child finish thought Reduces stuck repetition Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "One-Time Word Practice" (15-20 minutes, 2-3x daily): Proprioceptive Opening (5 min) Heavy work (calms nervous system) Jumping, crashing, squeezing Often reduces verbal perseveration Repetition Games (5 min) Make repetition purposeful: "Repeat after me: jump, jump, jump" (do action 3x) "Now say AND do it ONE time: jump!" (1x) Practice controlled repetition vs. one-time Builds awareness and control Communication Practice (5 min) Request items using "one-time words" Visual reminder (card) visible Immediate reinforcement when successful If child repeats: Gentle redirect, try again Transition Activity (5 min) Quiet activity with oral-motor input
Chewy tube (hard to talk while chewing) Reduces verbal behavior Calming For Communication-Focused: "Thought Completion Support" (10-15 minutes): Visual sentence strips: "I want ____" with picture choices Child completes sentence once Reduces verbal searching/repetition Processing time practice: Ask question Count to 10 silently (give processing time) Accept answer even if repeated Alternative communication: Pointing Sign language for common words Written words (if able) Reduces pressure on verbal system Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Regulation: Theory: Mouth/speech area needs sensory input Protocol (every 60-90 minutes): Chewy snack or chewy tool (2-3 min) Drink through straw Oral-motor exercises Result: Satisfied oral-motor system = less verbal perseveration Body-Language Integration: Pair all language with movement: Jumping while talking Bouncing on ball during communication Walking during conversation Theory: Movement often regulates and organizes speech
Result: May reduce repetition Reduce Verbal Demands: Less pressure = less perseveration Strategies: Accept non-verbal communication Don't force responses Allow processing time Reduce question frequency Environment becomes less verbally stressful Massage Techniques: Oral-Facial Release Massage (7-10 minutes, 3x daily): Purpose: Palilalia may involve oral-facial tension Jaw Focus (3 min): Locate jaw muscles (in front of ears) Firm circular massage (1 min each side) Child opens/closes mouth slowly during massage Releases jaw tension Mouth and Lips (3 min): Circular massage around mouth Gentle lip massage Under-chin firm pressure Face Connection (2 min): Massage from jaw to ears Ears to neck Neck to shoulders Releases overall tension Finish (2 min): Light tapping all over face Gentle face strokes Deep breath together Calming Full-Body Massage (15 minutes, 1-2x daily):
Best times: After school (high perseveration time), before bed Purpose: Overall nervous system regulation Follow detailed full-body massage from previous sections Slow, rhythmic movements Firm pressure (calming) Effect: Significantly reduces all verbal stimming behaviors Hand Massage for Grounding (5 minutes, as needed): Use when palilalia is active: Take child's hands Firm massage on palms (1 min each) Squeeze each finger (10 sec each) Press firmly on pressure points Pull gently on fingers Often interrupts verbal perseveration cycle Grounding effect helps child become more present MANIFESTATION 4: Scripting Entire Scenes from Media (5-30+ minutes) Physical Redirection Technique: "Scene to Movement Story" When extended scripting begins, interrupt gently with action Technique: "I hear you telling that story! Let's act it out with BIG movements!"
Assign movements to each part: Character 1 dialogue = jumping Character 2 dialogue = spinning Action scenes = running in place Quiet scenes = slow motion Do movements together while child scripts After 5 minutes: "Great! Now let's do something else. What do you want to do?" Offer heavy work activity Allows scripting while adding proprioceptive input Makes it active rather than passive Easier to transition from (movement to new movement) DIY Alternative Tool: Script Schedule Board Materials: Poster board, velcro, picture cards Sections: "Script Time" and "Other Activity Time" Pictures of activities in each section Use: Visual schedule showing when scripting is allowed Child can see: "Script time at 3pm for 15 minutes, then playtime" Teaches scripting has a time and place
Cost: $5 for velcro dots Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Structured Script Sessions (20-30 min, 1-2x daily): Designated script time with rules: Specific location (script corner) Specific duration (timer) Props available (puppets, costumes) When timer ends, transition to active play Purpose: Contains behavior, prevents all-day scripting Video Self-Modeling: Record child acting out scripts Watch together Discuss: "What happened in YOUR video?" Gradually helps child see self as actor, not just scripter Can create "movie library" of their performances Script Journals: Beautiful notebook for favorite scripts Child writes or draws scenes Can illustrate Becomes cherished item Externalizes scripts (reduces need to repeat verbally) Interactive Script Play: Find others to participate Assign roles Example: Child scripts Frozen Child is Elsa Sibling/parent is Anna
Perform together Transforms solo stim into social play Script Variations: Encourage changing the script: "What if Elsa went to the beach instead?" "What if Anna had superpowers too?" Start small, celebrate creativity Moves from rigid repetition to flexible thinking For Communication-Focused: Script-to-Life Connection: When child scripts: "That reminds me of when YOU..." Connect script themes to child's real experiences Example: Child scripts: "Simba lost his dad" You: "Yes, and you felt sad when grandpa moved away" Helps child use memories instead of scripts Emotion Identification: "How does [character] feel in this scene?" "Have you ever felt that way?" Builds emotional vocabulary May reduce need for scripts to express feelings Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Script Integration Circuit" (40-45 minutes, 1x daily):
Heavy Work Opening (10 min) Intensive proprioceptive input Jumping, crashing, pulling, pushing Calms system before language focus Structured Script Time (15 min) Designated time and space Props and costumes available Can video record Full permission to script Timer visible Purpose: Fills the bucket Script-to-Movement (10 min) Act out script with big movements Jump scenes Crash scenes Spin scenes Transitions from verbal to physical Alternative Expression (10 min) Art about the script (draw favorite scene) Build with blocks (make setting) Playdough (make characters) Channels obsession into creative outlets Calm Transition (5 min) Quiet sensory activity Weighted lap pad Gentle rocking Prepares for next activity For Communication-Focused: "From Script to Communication" Program (30 minutes, daily): Identify the function (10 min) When child scripts, ask yourself: "What is this communicating?"
Common functions: Anxiety (scripts predictable dialogue) Excitement (shares favorite things) Processing (works through themes) Connection (shares interests) Teach alternative expression (10 min) Model alternative ways to express the function: Anxious → "I feel worried" Excited → "I really like [topic]" Processing → Talk about feelings directly Connection → "Let's watch together" Practice and reinforce (10 min) Role play using new phrases Celebrate any functional communication Allow scripts but also introduce alternatives Sensory Integration: Intensive Proprioceptive Protocol: Theory: Extended scripting often indicates under-regulated nervous system Daily Schedule: Morning (before school): 20 min heavy work Animal walks Carrying heavy items Pushing/pulling Every 2 hours during day: 10 min proprioceptive break Wall pushes Chair push-ups Carry/organize items After school (high-script time): 30 min intensive
Playground (climbing, swinging, sliding) Trampoline Crash pad play Evening: 15 min calming proprioceptive Gentle rocking Joint compressions Massage Result: Well-regulated body may reduce scripting by 50-70% Vestibular Integration: Scripting often accompanies vestibular seeking Provide vestibular input proactively: Swing daily (15-20 min minimum) Spinning activities (controlled) Rolling, tumbling Rocking chair available all day Many children stop scripting when vestibular needs are met Environmental Modifications: Reduce script triggers: Limit screen time (1 hour per day maximum) When watching, watch together and discuss Introduce variety (not same shows repeatedly) Increase novelty: New experiences New places New activities Reduces perseveration on familiar scripts Massage Techniques: Comprehensive Regulation Massage (20-25 minutes, 1-2x daily): Best times: After school (before peak scripting), before bed Purpose: Deep nervous system regulation to reduce compulsive scripting
Back (7 min): Long, firm strokes head to toe (50x) Circular massage on each side of spine (2 min) Firm pressure down spine with thumbs (1 min) More long strokes (20x) Shoulders, Arms, Hands (5 min): Firm shoulder squeezes (2 min) Squeeze down arms (1 min each) Detailed hand massage (1 min each) Legs and Feet (5 min): Squeeze down legs from hip (1 min each) Detailed foot massage (2 min each) Firm pressure on soles Neck and Head (3 min): Gentle neck massage (sides only) Scalp massage Face massage Full Body Integration (3 min): Light strokes from head to toes (20x) Helps child feel whole and integrated Often dramatically reduces dissociative scripting Quick Grounding Massage for Active Scripting (5 minutes):
Use when child is in extended scripting episode: Interrupt gently: "Pause for a minute, let's do squeeze massage" Technique: Firm squeezes shoulders (30 sec) Squeeze down arms to hands (1 min) Press firmly on palms (30 sec each) Squeeze down legs to feet (1 min) Press firmly on feet (30 sec each) Deep pressure hug (30 sec) Often breaks scripting cycle Can then redirect to different activity Preventive Daily Massage Routine (15 minutes, morning or evening): Purpose: Consistent daily massage prevents excessive scripting Same time every day (creates routine) Full body massage (described above) Focus on calming, regulating Consistent deep pressure = regulated nervous system = less scripting Many parents report 60-80% reduction in scripting with daily massage routine MANIFESTATION 5: Repeating Questions Instead of Answering
Physical Redirection Technique: "Question to Action Response" When child repeats question, provide physical grounding first Technique: You ask: "What do you want for snack?" Child repeats: "What do you want for snack?" You respond: "Let's show with our bodies! Point to what you want!" (take child's hand, guide to choices) If still no response: "Let's do jumping choice! Jump for crackers!" (demonstrate) Child jumps or doesn't Try next: "Jump for pretzels!" Accept non-verbal communication Physical grounding: Hand on shoulder while asking again: "Show me, point" Reduces pressure of verbal response Provides proprioceptive input (calming) Teaches alternative communication DIY Alternative Tool: Answer Choice Board Materials: Piece of cardboard, divided into sections For common questions, provide visual answer options Example for "What do you want for snack?":
Pictures: crackers, cheese, apple, pretzels Child points instead of answering verbally Laminate for durability Can make multiple boards for different question types Cost: Free (use magazine pictures) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Question Games (purposeful repetition): Play games where repeating questions is the goal: "Echo Game": Adult asks question, child echoes, then adult answers "Interview Game": Child is reporter, asks same question to different people Makes repetition functional and fun Physical Response System: Teach: "You don't have to say words, show me!" For yes/no: Jump for yes, stomp for no For choices: Point, walk to it, bring it to adult Reduces verbal pressure For Communication-Focused: Processing Time Support: Question repetition often = processing difficulty Strategies: Ask question Count to 20 silently (give time)
Offer visual choices Simplify question Example: Original: "What do you want to do this afternoon?" Simplified: "Park or home?" (with pictures) Visual Question-Answer Scripts: Create visual scripts: Picture of question being asked Arrow Picture of answer options Practice following script Teaches: question → answer format Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Question-Answer Circuit" (20 minutes, 2x daily): Heavy Work Opening (5 min) Calms nervous system Jumping, pushing, pulling Regulated body = better communication Question Practice with Actions (7 min) Ask simple question If child repeats: "Show me with your body!" Practice physical responses: Yes = jump No = sit down "I want this" = point Reward all communication attempts Visual Support Practice (5 min) Use choice boards Practice pointing to answers
Gradually reduce visual supports (if able) Calm Transition (3 min) Oral-motor input (chewy, drink through straw) Weighted lap pad Quiet activity For Communication-Focused: "Alternative Communication Training" (15 minutes, daily): Identify communication barriers (5 min) Why does child repeat questions? Processing difficulty? Doesn't understand? Anxious? Verbal apraxia? Determine root cause Teach alternatives (7 min) Sign language for common words Picture exchange Pointing Gestures Any communication is valid Practice in low-pressure settings (3 min) Preferred activities Familiar people Gradually generalize Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Before Language Demands: Prepare mouth/speech system: 5 min oral-motor activities before: Mealtimes (asking questions common) Homework time Social situations Activities: Chew crunchy/chewy foods Drink through straw Lip/jaw exercises Chewy tube Result: Better speech motor control Reduce Verbal Demands Globally: Less questions = less repetition
Strategies: Offer choices before child must ask Use statements instead of questions Example: Instead of "What do you want?", say "Here are crackers and cheese" Accept non-verbal communication Lower pressure environment Proprioceptive Integration Throughout Day: Every 60-90 min: Heavy work (5-10 min) Calms nervous system Better availability for communication Less verbal perseveration Massage Techniques: Pre-Communication Massage (5-7 minutes): Use before situations requiring answering questions: Oral-Facial Preparation (3 min): Face massage (forehead to chin) Lip and mouth massage Jaw massage Wakes up speech system Body Grounding (3 min): Shoulder squeezes Arm squeezes to hands Hand massage (firm pressure) Grounding for better presence Finish (1 min): Deep pressure hug One deep breath together Calming Massage for Communication Anxiety (10 minutes): If question repetition stems from anxiety:
Back (4 min): Long, slow strokes Very calming Arms and Hands (3 min): Squeeze and release Grounding hand massage Legs and Feet (3 min): Squeeze and release Firm foot pressure Overall effect: Reduces anxiety, may improve communication Hand Massage for Immediate Support (3 minutes): Use during or after question-repeating episode: Hold child's hands Firm palm massage (1 min each) Squeeze each finger (10 sec each) Press pressure points Grounding and calming **Often helps chil reset and try again** MANIFESTATION 6 Reciting Commercials, Jingles, or Songs Verbatim Physical Redirection Technique: "Jingle to Jive" When child begins reciting jingle/commercial, join in with movement Technique: Child starts: "Like a good neighbor, State Farm is there!" You respond: "I hear that commercial! Let's dance it!"
Create dance moves for each line: "Like a good neighbor" = wave to neighbor "State Farm" = jump twice "is there" = point Do together 2-3 times Then transition: "Great dancing! Now let's do [heavy work activity]" Wall pushes (20x) Carry something heavy across room Allows the jingle while adding proprioceptive input Makes it interactive instead of perseverative Easier to transition from movement to new movement DIY Alternative Tool: Jingle Jar Materials: Jar or container, popsicle sticks, markers Write favorite jingles/songs on sticks Rule: Can pick ONE jingle from jar at designated times After reciting once, jingle goes back in jar Choose different one next time Limits repetition, adds element of choice/control Cost: Free (household items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers:
Scheduled Jingle Time (10-15 min, 2-3x daily): Set timer Child can recite any jingles/commercials Can perform them (act out) Can record them (video/audio) When timer ends: "Jingle time is over" Transition to physical activity Purpose: Contains the behavior Create Original Jingles: Use obsession productively "Let's make a jingle about YOUR day!" "Let's make a commercial for your favorite toy!" Start with copying structure, fill in new words Example: Original: "I'm lovin' it" (McDonald's) New: "I'm playing it!" (about their toy) Moves from repetition to creativity Jingle Performance Stage: Designate area as "stage" Child performs jingles there (not everywhere) Can use toy microphone Family can be "audience" at designated times Makes it purposeful entertainment, not perseveration Music Substitution: Replace commercial jingles with actual songs
Teach children's songs with similar catchy rhythms Provide access to kid-friendly music Channels need for repetitive music into more appropriate content Rhythm Instruments: Percussion instruments ($10-20 set) Play rhythm of jingle without words Drums, shakers, tambourine Transforms verbal into musical/physical For Communication-Focused: Jingle-to-Communication Bridge: When child recites jingle, explore why: "That's a food commercial! Are you hungry?" "That's about toys! Do you want to play?" Teach: "Instead of the jingle, you can say 'I'm hungry'" Helps child connect jingle to underlying need Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Musical Movement Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Heavy Work Opening (5 min) Intensive proprioceptive input Jumping, crashing, pushing Calms system before language focus Jingle Performance (10 min) Designated stage/area Child performs favorite jingles
With props, costumes, instruments Can video record Family participates as audience Purpose: Makes it social and purposeful Jingle Transformation (7 min) Take jingle, change it: Different words (keep melody) Different melody (keep words) Different speed (fast/slow) Different volume (loud/whisper) Teaches flexibility Musical Instruments (5 min) Play jingle rhythms on instruments No words, just music Channels verbal into physical Quiet Transition (3 min) Calm sensory activity Weighted lap pad Gentle rocking Oral-motor input (chewy) For Communication-Focused: "From Jingle to Language" Program (20 minutes, daily): Identify the trigger (5 min) When does child recite jingles most? When anxious? When excited? When bored? Random/constant? Understanding trigger helps intervention Teach functional alternatives (10 min) For each common jingle, teach alternative: Food jingle → "I'm hungry" or point to picture
Toy jingle → "I want to play" or bring toy Random jingle → "I need a break" or sensory activity Practice alternatives with role-play Reinforce functional communication (5 min) When child uses alternative (even once!): Celebrate! Immediate reinforcement Continue allowing jingles but reward alternatives Sensory Integration: Auditory Diet Modification: Theory: Jingle recitation = auditory seeking/regulation Provide alternative auditory input: Throughout day: Background music (instrumental, calming) Nature sounds White noise Audiobooks Reduce commercial exposure: Limit TV watching Skip commercials (DVR, streaming) Pre-screen content Result: Less jingle input = less jingle output Proprioceptive Protocol: Heavy work every 90 minutes (10 min): Reduces need for auditory self-regulation Provides body-based regulation instead Before high-jingle times: 15-20 min intensive proprioceptive work Often prevents jingle recitation Oral-Motor Satisfaction:
Jingles involve oral-motor system Provide alternative oral-motor input: Chewy foods/tools every hour Drinks through straws Crunchy snacks Singing activities (purposeful vs. perseverative) May reduce jingle recitation by 40-50% Massage Techniques: Oral-Facial and Throat Massage (8-10 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Jingle recitation involves significant oral-facial-throat muscle use Face and Jaw (3 min): Massage temples (1 min) Jaw muscles (1 min each side) Releases tension from excessive verbalization Lip and Mouth (2 min): Circular massage around mouth Lip massage (center to corners) Under-chin pressure Throat Area (2 min): NEVER front of throat Sides of neck only Gentle circles from jaw to shoulders Releases vocal tension Shoulder and Neck (2 min): Firm shoulder squeezes Neck massage These areas tense during extensive vocalization Finish (1 min):
