Light face touches Deep breath together Full Body Calming Massage (15-20 minutes, daily): Best time: Evening (before bed) Purpose: Overall regulation reduces all verbal stimming Complete full-body routine (described in previous sections) Extra focus on: Back (long, calming strokes) Arms and hands (grounding) Feet (security) Consistent daily massage often reduces jingle recitation by 50-70% Quick "Jingle Interrupt" Massage (3-4 minutes): Use when excessive jingle recitation is occurring: Hand focus: Take child's hands Firm palm massage (1 min each) Squeeze each finger Press pressure points Shoulder squeeze: Firm pressure on shoulders (30 sec) Deep pressure hug: Full body squeeze (30 sec) Often interrupts verbal perseveration Redirect to quiet activity after MANIFESTATION 7: Repeating Specific Words (10-100+ times) Physical Redirection Technique: "Word Count to Movement Count"
When child repeats specific word, acknowledge and redirect Technique: Child repeats: "Blue, blue, blue, blue, blue..." You respond: "I hear you saying 'blue'! Let's count how many times!" Count together while child continues After reaching 10: "You said blue TEN times! Now let's do ten jumps!" Jump together (counting) Then: "Great! Now let's try ONE time. Say 'blue' once." If successful: Immediate positive reinforcement If continues repeating: "Let's give our mouth a rest" (offer chewy toy) Creates awareness without shame Provides proprioceptive alternative Takes 3-5 minutes DIY Alternative Tool: Word Tally Board Materials: Small whiteboard or laminated paper, dry-erase marker Use: When child repeats word, make tally mark for each repetition Show child: "You said it 5 times! Now let's erase and try saying it once"
Visual representation of repetition Some children self-regulate when they see tally marks growing Cost: $3-5 for small whiteboard Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Word Percussion: Each repetition = one drum beat/clap/stomp Makes repetition musical Can practice: "Say and clap once" vs. "Say and clap five times" Brings control and awareness Word Writing: Instead of saying word repeatedly, write it repeatedly Whiteboard, paper, sidewalk chalk Transforms verbal into visual-motor Some children satisfied by writing instead of speaking Word Games: Make repetition purposeful: "How many times can you say 'jump' while jumping?" "Say 'stomp' every time you stomp" "Say 'clap' with each clap" Connects word to action Recording and Playback: Record child saying word once (clearly, purposefully) Play back when child feels need to repeat
External repetition may reduce internal need For Communication-Focused: Identify the Function: Why is child repeating this word? Processing it? Likes how it sounds/feels? Trying to communicate something? Anxiety/stimming? Understanding helps intervention Expand Single Word: When child repeats "blue, blue, blue" Model expansion: "Yes, blue! Blue sky! Blue car! Blue shirt!" Gradually teaches word goes in sentences May reduce isolated repetition Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Word Work Circuit" (15-20 minutes, 2-3x daily): Proprioceptive Opening (5 min) Heavy work (calms nervous system) Often reduces verbal perseveration immediately Purposeful Repetition (5 min) Make word repetition a game: "Say 'jump' five times while jumping" "Say 'push' while pushing wall" "Say 'squeeze' while squeezing putty" Controlled, purposeful repetition One-Word Practice (3 min) Practice saying word ONCE
Immediate reinforcement "You said it one time! Great job!" Gradually increase intervals between repetitions Oral-Motor Alternative (4 min) Chewy tool (hard to talk while chewing) Drink through straw Crunchy snack Satisfies oral-motor need differently Quiet Transition (3 min) Calm activity Weighted lap pad Reduces arousal For Communication-Focused: "Word Expansion Training" (10-15 minutes, daily): Accept the word (2 min) Child says: "Car, car, car, car" You respond: "Yes! Car! You're thinking about cars!" Don't shame or stop (yet) Model expansion (5 min) "Car! Red car! Fast car! Big car! Toy car!" Show how word can grow Encourage child to add descriptor Celebrate any attempt Alternative expression (5 min) "Instead of saying 'car' many times, can you show me a car?" Point, bring, draw, etc.
Reduces verbal perseveration Practice new patterns (3 min) "Let's practice: Say 'car' once, then tell me more" May need visual support Gradual progress is fine Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Sensory Diet: Target: Satisfy oral-motor needs to reduce verbal perseveration Every 60-90 minutes: Chewy snack or chewy tool (3-5 min) Drink through straw (creates oral work) Crunchy food (carrots, apples, pretzels) Oral-motor exercises (lip, jaw, tongue) Result: Satisfied oral-motor system = less word repetition Reduce Verbal Pressure: Less language demand = less perseveration Strategies: Accept non-verbal communication Don't force verbal responses Reduce questions Give processing time Creates calmer verbal environment Full Body Regulation: Word repetition often = under-regulated nervous system Proprioceptive protocol: Morning: 15-20 min heavy work Every 2 hours: 10 min heavy work break
After school: 30 min intensive play Evening: 15 min calming input Well-regulated body = less verbal stimming Massage Techniques: Jaw and Oral-Facial Release (6-8 minutes, 3x daily): Purpose: Word repetition creates jaw/facial tension Best times: After episodes of word repetition, before bed, morning Jaw Focus (3 min): Locate masseter muscle (clench teeth to find it) Firm circular massage (1 min each side) Child opens mouth slightly, massage again (1 min) Releases primary tension area Face and Mouth (2 min): Circular massage around mouth Cheek massage (palms, circular motions) Temple massage Throat and Neck (2 min): Sides of neck only (never front) Gentle massage from jaw to shoulders Releases vocal tension Finish (1 min): Light tapping on face Gentle strokes Deep breath together
Hand-to-Mouth Connection Massage (5 minutes): Purpose: Grounding hands often reduces oral stimming Hand massage (3 min): Detailed palm massage (1 min each) Squeeze each finger (5 sec each) Press pressure points firmly Pull gently on fingers Hand to face connection (2 min): Guide child's hands to their own face Teach self-massage Hand on cheeks, gentle pressure Self-awareness and grounding Full Body Regulation Massage (15 minutes, 1-2x daily): Best times: After school (high-stimming time), before bed Complete full-body massage (previous sections) Slow, firm, rhythmic Deep regulation reduces all verbal stimming significantly Parents report 50-80% reduction with consistent daily massage MANIFESTATION 8: Functional Echolalia (Using Scripts to Communicate Needs) Physical Redirection Technique: "Script Recognition and Expansion" When child uses script functionally, honor it AND expand
Technique: Child says: "Do you want to go outside?" (script from parent, means "I want to go outside") You respond: First, honor the communication: "Yes! You want to go outside!" (acknowledge understanding) Physical grounding: Take child's hand, walk toward door Model expansion: "You can say 'I want outside' or 'Outside please'" (simplified) Guide child's hand to point to door (non-verbal option) Go outside (fulfill request immediately to reinforce communication) Over time, gently shape script toward more direct language Key: NEVER punish functional echolalia - it's communication! Accept script, honor intent, gently model alternatives DIY Alternative Tool: Communication Script Cards Materials: Index cards, pictures, words Create cards for common needs: "I want..." + pictures of common items "I need..." + pictures (break, help, bathroom)
"I feel..." + emotion pictures Child can use script OR card Gradually may transition from script to card to words Cost: Free (print pictures or draw) Alternative Stimulation: For All Children Using Functional Echolalia: IMPORTANT NOTE: Functional echolalia is communication, not pure stimming. Goal is to honour and expand, not eliminate. Visual Communication Supports: Picture cards Communication boards Written words (if reading) Sign language Provides alternatives to scripts Script Library: Accept that child has library of scripts Help them build functional script library: Scripts for requesting Scripts for protesting Scripts for social greetings Honor their communication style while expanding Video Modelling: Record videos of child using functional scripts successfully Watch together Discuss what they communicated Model slight variations Builds awareness and flexibility
Social Stories: Create stories about communicating needs Include child's scripts as valid options Also show alternative ways to communicate same thing Normalizes multiple communication methods Occupational Therapy Activities: For All Children: "Communication Expansion Program" (20-25 minutes, daily): Relationship Building (5 min) Play preferred activity together No communication demands Build trust and connection Foundation for communication work Script Honoring (5 min) Child uses scripts to communicate Adult responds to intent immediately Example: Child: "Do you want juice?" (means "I want juice") Adult: "Yes! You want juice!" (gives juice) Reinforces: scripts work for communication Gentle Modeling (7 min) After honoring script, model alternative: "You can also say 'juice please' or point to juice" No pressure to use alternative Just expose to options Repeat over many sessions
Alternative Communication Practice (5 min) Practice using visuals, signs, gestures Make it playful, not demanding Celebrate ALL communication attempts Sensory Integration (3 min) End with sensory activity (calming) Oral-motor input (chewy, crunchy snack) Proprioceptive input (squeezes, pressure) Important Principles: Never punish functional echolalia - it's working communication Always honor the intent - respond to what they mean Gently expand - offer alternatives without pressure Celebrate all communication - scripts, words, gestures, visuals Progress is slow - months to years, not days to weeks Sensory Integration: Reduce Communication Pressure: Stress increases echolalia Create low-pressure environment: Accept all communication forms Give processing time (count to 20) Don't demand verbal responses Provide visual supports Result: Less stress = more flexible communication Oral-Motor Regulation: Before communication opportunities:
5 min oral-motor input Crunchy/chewy snack Drink through straw Chewy tool Prepares speech system May increase variety in communication Overall Body Regulation: Regulated body = better communication Daily proprioceptive protocol: Morning heavy work (15 min) Breaks every 90 min (10 min) After school (30 min intensive) Evening calming (15 min) Well-regulated child communicates more effectively Massage Techniques: Pre-Communication Massage (7-10 minutes): Use before situations requiring communication Purpose: Prepares nervous system and speech mechanism Oral-Facial Prep (3-4 min): Face massage (forehead to chin) Lip and mouth massage Jaw massage Wakes up and prepares speech system Body Grounding (3-4 min): Shoulder squeezes (firm) Arms to hands squeeze Firm hand massage Grounds and calms Integration (2 min): Light touch from head to hands Helps child feel present and connected
Deep breath together Do before: School, therapy, social events, any communication-heavy activities Daily Regulation Massage (15-20 minutes): Best time: Evening before bed Purpose: Overall nervous system regulation supports all communication Full body massage (see detailed descriptions in previous sections) Focus on: Calming (slow, rhythmic) Deep pressure (regulating) Consistency (same routine daily) Result: Better overall regulation supports more flexible communication patterns "Communication Success" Reward Massage (5 minutes): Use after child communicates successfully (with scripts or otherwise) Positive association with communication: Gentle, pleasant massage Shoulder and back (feels good) Hands (grounding and rewarding) "You communicated so well! Let's celebrate with massage!" Positive reinforcement through sensory input LEVEL 3: Vocal Play and Experimentation CAUSATION Over-Stimulated Causation: Mechanism: Creative vocal expression regulates emotions during overwhelm
How it works: Emotional arousal (anxiety, frustration, excitement) needs outlet Vocal experimentation provides emotional release Creating/controlling sounds gives sense of agency during loss of control Exploration is organizing (focused activity) during chaotic internal state Transforms overwhelming emotions into manageable vocal play Examples: Rapid pitch changes when anxious (expressing internal emotional fluctuation) Volume modulation when frustrated (yelling = emotional release; whispering = calming) Making sound effects when overstimulated (channeling energy into vocal creativity) Clinical note: Vocal play often increases during emotional dysregulation; decreases when calm Under-Stimulated Causation: Mechanism: Intense auditory + proprioceptive input from vocal production How it works: Vocal production provides dual stimulation: Auditory: Hearing own voice variations Proprioceptive: Intense feedback from throat, mouth, chest vibration Experimentation creates novelty and interest
Different sounds create different sensory experiences Fills sensory need when environment isn't providing enough input Exploration is inherently stimulating and engaging Examples: Exploring pitch changes during boring task (creates auditory variety) Making sound effects during independent play (adds excitement to activity) Singing same song repeatedly (provides consistent sensory input during under-stimulation) Clinical note: Decreases when environment provides adequate stimulation Sensitivity Causation: Triple mechanism: Exploring auditory-motor connection + speech motor planning practice + proprioceptive satisfaction Auditory-motor exploration: Child discovering connection between motor actions (tongue, lips, breath) and resulting sounds Experimenting with cause-effect relationships Learning to control vocal production Developing auditory-motor feedback loop Speech motor planning: Vocal play is practice for speech production Trying different mouth positions, tongue placements, vocal tensions Building motor programs for speech sounds
May be particularly important for children with speech delays (extra practice needed) Proprioceptive satisfaction: Vocal production creates strong proprioceptive feedback (throat, mouth, chest, face) Different vocalizations create different proprioceptive patterns Child seeking specific proprioceptive experiences through vocal play Examples: Making up nonsense words (exploring speech sounds) Accent changes (experimenting with different motor patterns) Beatboxing (complex motor planning + auditory + proprioceptive) Clinical note: Often more complex and varied in children with speech/language involvement SENSORY PROFILE Seeker Profile: Characteristics: Loud, varied vocal experimentation Prolonged sessions (can play for 30+ minutes) Maximum volume and intensity Tries every possible variation Uninhibited about social context Seems energized by vocal play Presentation: Constant vocal exploration throughout day Very loud (screaming, yelling, shouting experiments) Wide variety of sounds (pitches, volumes, effects)
Socially inappropriate timing (doesn't stop in quiet settings) Increases vocal complexity over time Neurological basis: Under-responsive auditory and proprioceptive systems (needs intense input) High sensory threshold Seeks maximum stimulation from vocal production Support needs: Designated loud/quiet times and places Structured vocal play (music class, voice lessons) Heavy proprioceptive work (alternative to vocal seeking) Social skills training (appropriate times for loud vocalizations) Creative Profile: Characteristics: Using vocal stimming as play and exploration Purposeful experimentation (trying to achieve specific effects) Often imaginative component (character voices, sound effects in play) More regulated and controlled than pure seekers Able to stop/modulate when needed Presentation: Vocal play integrated into activities (not constant background) Creates characters with different voices Experiments to find interesting sounds Often can explain what trying to do ("I'm being a robot")
Social context awareness (may perform for others or play privately) Neurological basis: Normal range of sensory responsiveness Using vocal exploration as creative play (developmentally appropriate) May have speech/language interest or talent Support needs: Encourage and channel creativity (drama, voice acting) Teach appropriate times/places Provide creative outlets Generally less intervention needed (this is more typical play) MANIFESTATION 1: Changing Pitch Rapidly (High to Low Repeatedly) Physical Redirection Technique: "Pitch to Posture" When child makes rapid pitch changes, connect to body position Technique: "I hear your voice going up and down! Let's match with our bodies!" High pitch = reach arms up high, on tiptoes Low pitch = squat down low Do together: Make sound AND movement Practice 10 times Then: "Now let's just move without sound"
Continue movements silently (10x) Transition to different activity (heavy work) Connects vocal play to body awareness Provides proprioceptive and vestibular input Easier to transition to quiet when paired with movement DIY Alternative Tool: Pitch Slider Visual Materials: Cardboard strip (12" tall), draw arrow slider, velcro or paper clip Labels: Top = "High Voice", Middle = "Medium Voice", Bottom = "Low Voice" Use: Child moves arrow while making sounds at that pitch Creates visual representation of pitch Can practice "keeping arrow in middle" (moderate voice) Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Musical Instruments with Pitch: Slide whistle ($3-5) - perfect for pitch exploration Xylophone ($10-15) - different pitches, structured Keyboard/piano app (free) - endless pitch variety Purpose: Channels pitch exploration into music
Singing Activities: Teach songs with pitch variation "Do-Re-Mi" from Sound of Music (scales) Practice opera singing (exaggerated highs/lows) Animal sounds (mouse = high, bear = low) Makes pitch play purposeful Pitch Games: "Copycat Pitch" - adult makes pitch, child copies "High-Low Game" - adult says "high!" child makes high sound "Pitch Freeze Dance" - music stops, hold current pitch Structured pitch exploration Recording Play: Record pitch experiments Play back and discuss "That was high! That was low!" Creates awareness For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Pitch Exploration: Whisper humming (gentle pitches) Soft singing Less intense than loud pitch changes Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Voice and Body Integration Circuit" (20-25 minutes, 1-2x daily): Vestibular Opening (5 min) Swinging (often regulates vocal pitch seeking)
Spinning (controlled) Rocking Vestibular input often reduces vocal stimming Structured Pitch Play (7 min) Pitch exploration with rules: High pitch = jump Low pitch = crouch Medium = stand normal Practice all three (control) Use instruments (xylophone, slide whistle) Purposeful vs. random pitch changes Singing and Music (5 min) Learn songs with pitch variety Practice scales Musical games Educational pitch use Oral-Motor Work (5 min) Chewy foods/tools Drink through straw Hard to make pitch changes while chewing! Alternative oral-motor input Quiet Transition (3 min) Calming activity Weighted lap pad Gentle rocking Reduces arousal For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Voice Control" (10-15 minutes): Practice moderate pitch (not extreme highs/lows) Use visual pitch meter (show where voice should be) Reward staying in "comfortable" range
Gradual desensitization to pitch variety Sensory Integration: Vestibular-Vocal Connection: Theory: Pitch changes often accompany vestibular seeking Provide vestibular input proactively: Morning: 15 min swinging Throughout day: Access to rocking chair After school: 20 min playground (swings, slides, climbing) Evening: Gentle rocking Result: Satisfied vestibular system = reduced pitch play (often 60-70% reduction) Oral-Motor Satisfaction: Every 60-90 min: Chewy snack or tool Crunchy food Drink through straw Oral exercises Satisfied oral-motor system = less vocal play Auditory Environment: Provide rich auditory input: Music (variety of genres) Nature sounds Audiobooks Fills auditory needs without child needing to create own sounds Massage Techniques: Throat and Vocal Area Massage (6-8 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Pitch changes use throat/vocal cords extensively; this releases tension External Throat Area (3 min):
NEVER press on front of throat/windpipe Massage sides of neck only Gentle circles from jaw to collarbones (1 min each side) Very light touch down front (no pressure) Jaw and Face (3 min): Jaw muscle massage Face massage (releases overall tension) Temple massage Shoulder and Neck (2 min): Firm shoulder squeezes Neck sides massage Releases tension that accumulates from vocal play Full Body Calming Massage (15 minutes, 1x daily minimum): Best time: Evening Complete full-body massage Extra focus on upper body (where vocal tension lives) Slow, rhythmic, calming Overall regulation reduces vocal stimming significantly Quick "Voice Rest" Massage (3 minutes): Use when pitch play is excessive: Firm shoulder squeeze (30 sec) Neck sides massage (1 min) Jaw massage (1 min) Offer chewy immediately after (gives mouth something else to do)
MANIFESTATION 2: Volume Modulation (Whispering to Shouting) Physical Redirection Technique: "Volume Meter Body Match" When child modulates volume rapidly, create body-based volume system Technique: "Your voice is going loud and quiet! Let's make our bodies match!" Volume 1 (whisper) = lie flat on floor Volume 5 (normal) = sit Volume 10 (shout) = stand with arms stretched up Practice together: Call out volumes, child matches body position Make sounds at each level (10 times) Gradually stay at lower volumes/positions longer End at "volume 1" lying down, quiet breathing Creates physical awareness of volume Provides proprioceptive input (calming) Visual/kinesthetic learning of volume control DIY Alternative Tool: Volume Control Board Materials: Poster board, draw thermometer/meter with 1-10 scale Add pictures at each level:
1-3: Mouse (quiet) 4-6: Person talking (normal) 7-10: Lion roaring (loud) Arrow or clothespin that moves Use: Show child current volume, teach desired volume "You're at 10! Let's move to 5!" Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Designated Loud Time and Space: Create "loud zone" (outside, basement, specific room with door) Set timer: 10 minutes of "loud time" Child can be as loud as they want Timer ends: "Now we use inside voices" Purpose: Satisfies need for loud while teaching boundaries Volume Games: "Volume Dial" - adult calls numbers, child matches volume "Simon Says Volumes" - "Simon says whisper!" "Simon says shout!" "Volume Freeze Dance" - freeze at whatever volume playing when music stops Makes volume control a fun skill
Musical Instruments: Drums (loud option) Cymbals (loud option) Kazoo, whistle (moderately loud) Allows loud sound-making without voice strain Alternative to vocal loudness Outdoor Activities: Yelling/shouting allowed outside "Shouting contests" in open spaces Cheering practice Appropriate loud outlets Sound Meter Apps: Free decibel meter apps Visual feedback of volume Game: "Can you keep it in the green zone?" Teaches self-monitoring For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Voice Practice: Visual charts showing "inside voice" range Reward staying quiet Noise-canceling headphones if overwhelmed by own loudness Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Volume Control Training Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): High-Energy Opening (5 min) LOUD activities allowed: Jumping while shouting Running while yelling Crashing into pillows with loud sounds Purpose: Releases need for loud, high-energy vocal output
Structured Volume Practice (10 min) Level 10 Practice (2 min): Shout as loud as possible (outdoor or designated room) Scream into pillows Practice maximum volume safely Level 5 Practice (3 min): Normal talking voice Practice conversations Sing at moderate volume Level 1 Practice (3 min): Whisper practice Silent lip movements Very quiet humming Transitions (2 min): Practice moving between volumes smoothly "10 to 5 to 1" sequence Builds control Instrument Play (7 min) Loud instruments (drums, cymbals) Quiet instruments (bells, shakers) Practice loud and soft playing Alternative to vocal volume Oral-Motor Work (5 min) Chewy foods/tools (hard to be loud while chewing) Thick drinks through straws Quiet mouth activities Calming Transition (3 min) Weighted lap pad Gentle rocking Quiet breathing Reduces overall arousal
For Sensory Avoiders: "Comfortable Volume Maintenance" (15 minutes): Find child's comfortable volume (usually quiet) Practice maintaining that volume Use visual supports (volume meter) Reward consistency Gradually expand range slightly (if appropriate) Sensory Integration: Proprioceptive Regulation for Volume Control: Theory: Loud vocalizations often indicate under-regulated nervous system Heavy work protocol (intensive): Before times when shouting typically occurs: 15-20 min heavy proprioceptive work Examples: Wall pushes (3 sets of 20) Carrying heavy items back/forth (5 min) Tug-of-war (5 min) Pushing/pulling furniture Animal walks (bear crawl, crab walk) Throughout day (every 90 min): 10 min proprioceptive break Heavy work tasks Result: Well-regulated body = better volume control (often 50-60% reduction in shouting) Vestibular Input: Shouting often accompanies high vestibular arousal Provide vestibular input proactively:
Swinging (15 min, 2-3x daily) Spinning activities Active play (running, jumping, climbing) May significantly reduce need for loud vocalizations Environmental Modifications: Reduce environmental loudness: Turn down TV, music Reduce background noise Quieter home environment Child may match environmental volume (quieter environment = quieter child) Massage Techniques: Vocal Cord and Throat Soothing Massage (8-10 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Shouting strains vocal cords; this soothes and releases tension CRITICAL: Never massage directly on front of throat/windpipe Preparation: Warm hands Small amount of coconut oil or lotion Child lies down comfortably External Throat (sides only) (3 min): Very gentle circular massage on sides of neck Start below ears, work down to collarbones (1 min each side) Light touch (this area is sensitive) Avoid any pressure on front of throat
Jaw and Face (3 min): Jaw muscle massage (firm) Cheek massage Temple massage Releases facial tension from loud talking Chest and Upper Back (3 min): Upper chest massage (below collarbones) Firm circular motions If child can turn over: massage between shoulder blades This area tenses during shouting Finish (1 min): Very light strokes down neck (sides) Light tapping on chest Deep, slow breathing together Full Body "Volume Down" Massage (20 minutes, 1x daily): Best time: Evening (helps set calm tone for night) Purpose: Deep overall calming reduces high-arousal behaviors like shouting Complete full-body massage: Back: Long, slow, firm strokes (7 min) Arms/hands: Squeeze and release (4 min) Legs/feet: Firm pressure (6 min) Head/face: Gentle massage (3 min) Key elements: SLOW movements (activates parasympathetic nervous system)
FIRM pressure (calming, not tickling) RHYTHMIC (predictable, soothing) Result: Consistent daily massage often reduces shouting by 60-80% Emergency "Volume Down" Quick Massage (3-5 minutes): Use when child is actively shouting/being very loud: Approach calmly "Let's take a quiet massage break" Quick sequence: Firm hands on shoulders, squeeze (30 sec) Squeeze down arms to hands (1 min) Detailed hand massage, firm pressure (1 min each hand) If child sitting: firm pressure on top of head (gentle push down, 10 sec) Deep pressure hug (30 sec) Often child calms immediately Voice volume typically drops Can then redirect to quiet activity MANIFESTATION 3: Testing Vocal Effects (Echoes in Bathrooms, Tunnels) Physical Redirection Technique: "Echo Hunt to Body Sound" When child seeks echoes, provide alternative sound exploration
Technique: "You like hearing echoes! Let's make body sounds instead!" Teach body percussion: Clapping (different speeds, patterns) Stomping (loud, soft, rhythms) Slapping thighs Snapping fingers (if able) Chest thumping Create rhythms together (5 min) Then: "Now let's use our echo tunnel!" (provide cardboard tube) Speak into tube for echo effect (2 min) Transition to quiet activity with proprioceptive input Provides auditory feedback through non-vocal and controlled vocal means Easier to redirect (portable tube vs. running to bathroom) DIY Alternative Tool: Echo Tube Kit Materials: Long cardboard tubes (paper towel, wrapping paper tubes) PVC pipe sections (various lengths, 1-3 feet) Decorate with stickers, duct tape Use: Child speaks, hums, sings into tubes Different lengths = different echo effects Keep in multiple locations (bedroom, playroom, car)
Cost: $5-10 for PVC at hardware store, tubes free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Designated Echo Exploration Time (10-15 min, 1-2x daily): Allow child to explore echoes in bathroom, hallways Set timer When timer ends: "Echo time is done" Satisfies need in controlled way Echo Recording: Use recording app with echo/reverb effects Child records voice with effects Can listen repeatedly External echo reduces need to seek spaces Echo Games: "Echo Hide and Seek" - shout in different rooms, family finds by echo "Echo Contest" - who can make longest echo "Echo Patterns" - repeat rhythm patterns with echo Makes it purposeful play Musical Echo Tools: Singing bowls ($15-30) Tuning forks ($10-20) Chimes and bells These create sustained, echo-like sounds Alternative to vocal echo-seeking
Outdoor Echo Exploration: Find outdoor spaces with echoes (tunnels, parking garages, under bridges) Scheduled "echo adventures" Appropriate places to shout and hear echoes Healthy outlet for interest For Sensory Avoiders: Soft Sound Exploration: Gentle sounds instead of loud echoes Quiet music with reverb Soft singing Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Sound Science Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Proprioceptive Opening (5 min) Heavy work (regulates before auditory seeking) Often reduces intensity of echo-seeking Structured Echo Exploration (10 min) Science approach: "Let's be sound scientists!" Experiment with different spaces: Bathroom (strong echo) Bedroom (soft echo) Outside (no echo) Inside tube (medium echo) Discuss differences Make chart of findings Purpose: Makes it educational, purposeful Echo Tube Play (7 min) Multiple tubes (different lengths)
Test different sounds: Whispers Normal voice Singing Humming Compare and contrast Controlled echo exploration Musical Echo (5 min) Instruments with sustained sound (bells, singing bowls) Listen to sound fade Similar satisfaction to echo Transition to Quiet (3 min) Oral-motor input (chewy) Calm activity Reduces auditory arousal For Communication-Focused: "Why Echo?" Discussion (if child can engage): Explore what child likes about echoes "It makes my voice big!" "It sounds cool!" "It feels good in my throat!" Understanding helps provide alternatives Sensory Integration: Auditory Regulation: Theory: Echo-seeking = auditory processing/seeking behavior Provide rich auditory environment: Throughout day: Background music (varied genres) Nature sounds White noise options Audiobooks Specific echo alternatives: Headphones with reverb/echo effects Sound apps with voice modification Karaoke with echo effects
Purpose: Satisfied auditory needs reduce echo-seeking Proprioceptive Connection: Echo-seeking often accompanies high arousal Heavy work protocol: Before bathroom trips (if echo-seeking common there) Throughout day (every 90 min) Result: Calmer body = less compulsive echo-seeking Vestibular Input: Swinging while vocalizing (combines needs): Swing and sing Swing and hum Satisfies multiple sensory systems simultaneously Often reduces need for echo-seeking Massage Techniques: Ear and Auditory System Massage (6-8 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Calms auditory system, may reduce auditory seeking Ear Massage (3 min): Gentle massage of outer ears Rub earlobes (1 min) Trace around outer ear with fingertips (1 min each ear) Very light pressure (ears are sensitive) Around Ears (2 min): Massage in circles around ears (not inside) Temple area (1 min)
Behind ears down to jaw (1 min) Face and Jaw (2 min): Face massage (general calming) Jaw massage Releases tension Finish (1 min): Very light touches all over face and ears Calming to auditory system Throat and Chest Massage (5-7 minutes): Purpose: Echo-seeking involves significant vocalization Throat area massage (sides only, never front) Chest massage (firm, circular) Shoulder and neck (releases tension) See detailed technique in previous sections Full Body Calming Massage (15 minutes, 1x daily): Best time: Evening Complete full-body routine Reduces overall sensory seeking behaviors Consistent daily massage = less echo-seeking MANIFESTATION 4: Creating Sound Effects (Explosions, Vehicles, Animals) Physical Redirection Technique: "Sound Effect Theater" When child makes sound effects repetitively, transform into structured play Technique: "You're making great sound effects! Let's make a movie!"
Assign roles: Child does sound effects, adult acts out story Example: Adult: "The car drives..." Child: "Vroom vroom!" (while pushing toy car) Adult: "It crashes!" Child: "CRASH!" (while crashing toy) Adult: "The engine breaks..." Child: "Sputter sputter" (while examining toy) Do 5-minute "scene" Then switch: "Now let's do quiet scene" (whisper sounds) Transition to physical activity (heavy work) Makes sound effects purposeful and social Gives opportunity to practice control (loud vs. quiet effects) Easier to end when part of structured play DIY Alternative Tool: Sound Effects Board Materials: Poster board, pictures of items that make sounds Sections: Vehicles, Animals, Weather, Actions (crash, boom, etc.) Buttons (drawn) next to each picture Use: Child "pushes button" (points) and makes that sound effect once
Visual control and organization Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Sound Effects Recording Studio: Voice recorder or phone app Create "library" of sound effects Record each effect clearly Can play back for own entertainment Externalizes the sounds Sound Effect Videos: YouTube: "Sound effects for kids" Child listens instead of constantly creating Can request specific effects Alternative to self-generated sounds Sound Effect Books: Books with sound buttons Press for effects External sound source Voice Modification Apps: Apps that change voice (robot, monster, etc.) Child makes sounds, app modifies Engaging and controlled Cost: Free apps available Foley Art (Real Sound Effects): Teach how movie sound effects are made Make real sounds: Coconut halves = horse hooves Crinkled cellophane = fire Shaking sheet metal = thunder
Channels interest into creative activity For Communication-Focused: Sound Effect Communication: Some children use sound effects functionally "Vroom vroom" = want to play with cars "Boom" = building blocks fell Honor and expand: "Yes, big crash! The blocks fell down!" Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Sound Studio Circuit" (30-35 minutes, 1-2x daily): Active Opening (5 min) Heavy work (calming) Big movements (jumping, crashing) Can make sound effects DURING activity "Jump explosion!" (jump and say "BOOM") Combines proprioceptive with vocal Structured Sound Effects (10 min) Recording session: Create sound effects library Record each effect once, clearly Organize by category Can listen to recordings Purpose: Makes it organized and purposeful Sound Effect Stories (10 min) Create stories together Child provides sound effects at appropriate times
Adult narrates, child provides sounds Example: Adult: "Once upon a time, a car drove down the road..." Child: "Vroom vroom!" Adult: "Suddenly, a dog barked!" Child: "Woof woof!" Social, interactive, purposeful Foley Art Creation (7 min) Make real sound effects Experiment with objects Record real sounds Creative and educational Quiet Transition (3 min) Oral-motor input Calm activity Reduces vocal arousal For Communication-Focused: "Sound Effect Expansion" (15-20 minutes): When child makes sound effect, expand: Child: "Vroom!" Adult: "Yes! Car! Red car! Fast car!" Model using words instead of sounds: "You can say 'car' or 'I want car'" Accept both sound effects and words Gradually child may add words to sound effects Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Satisfaction: Sound effects use mouth/tongue/lips extensively Provide alternative oral-motor input:
Every 60-90 min: chewy snack or tool Crunchy foods Drinks through straw Whistles, kazoos, harmonicas May reduce sound effect creation by 40-50% Proprioceptive Pairing: Allow sound effects DURING proprioceptive activities: Jumping with "boom!" Pushing with "vroom!" Crashing with "crash!" Satisfies both needs simultaneously Often reduces random sound effects (reserves them for active play) Auditory Environment: Provide sound effect alternatives: Sound effect apps Sound effect videos Movies/shows with interesting sounds Reduces need to create own constantly Massage Techniques: Oral-Facial-Throat Massage (8-10 minutes, 2-3x daily): Purpose: Sound effects use oral-facial muscles intensively Lip and Mouth (3 min): Detailed circular massage around mouth Lips (center to corners) Inside cheeks if child allows Jaw (2 min): Masseter muscle focus Firm circular massage Open/close mouth during massage
Tongue and Palate (2 min): If child allows, gentle pressure on tongue with cloth-covered finger Palate massage (very gentle) Most kids won't allow this - skip if uncomfortable Throat (2 min): Sides only (never front) Gentle massage Finish (1 min): Light face tapping Deep breath Full Body Regulation Massage (15 minutes, 1x daily): Complete routine Reduces overall need for vocal stimming Consistent massage = less sound effect creation Hand Massage for Grounding (5 minutes, as needed): Use when sound effects are excessive: Take child's hands Firm, detailed hand massage Squeeze each finger Press pressure points Grounding often reduces vocal behaviors Redirect to quiet activity using hands (playdough, fidget, drawing) Comprehensive Guide to Managing Auditory Stimming in Children MANIFESTATION 5: Beatboxing or Rhythmic Sounds
Physical Redirection Technique: "Beat to Body Rhythm" When child begins beatboxing/making rhythmic sounds, join and redirect Technique: "I hear your rhythm! Let's make it with our whole body!" Match child's rhythm with body percussion: Clapping on beats Stomping on beats Slapping thighs on beats Chest thumping on beats Do together for 2-3 minutes Then: "Now let's do our rhythm while doing work!" Carry heavy items to the rhythm Push wall to the rhythm March to the rhythm Gradually slow rhythm down End with slow, calm rhythm (rocking, swaying) Transforms vocal rhythm into physical rhythm Provides proprioceptive and vestibular input Natural transition from fast/loud to slow/calm DIY Alternative Tool: Rhythm Board Materials: Piece of wood or thick cardboard, drumsticks or wooden spoons
Decorate with music notes Use: Child drums rhythm instead of beatboxing Portable (can take in car, to school) Visual/physical outlet for rhythm need Cost: Free (household items) Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Real Percussion Instruments: Drum set (toy version $30-50, or real if budget allows) Bongos ($20-30) Djembe ($40-80) Hand drums ($15-25) Allows rhythm creation without vocal strain Purposeful musical expression Beatboxing Lessons: YouTube tutorials for kids Turn interest into actual skill Structured practice (designated times) Makes stimming into music education Rhythm Apps and Games: Drum pad apps (free) Rhythm games (many free options) Child creates rhythms digitally Can save and replay External creation reduces constant vocal beatboxing Body Percussion Classes/Videos: Stomp-style body percussion Cup song rhythms Hand clapping games Channels rhythm into structured activity
DIY Percussion Instruments: Shakers: Empty bottles with rice/beans Drums: Overturned buckets, pots with wooden spoons Tambourine: Paper plates with bells Rain stick: Paper towel tube, nails, rice Cost: Free from household items For Communication-Focused: Rhythm as Communication: Some children use rhythm to regulate or communicate Slow rhythm = calm Fast rhythm = excited/anxious Teach recognizing and using rhythm intentionally Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Rhythm Integration Circuit" (30-35 minutes, 1-2x daily): Heavy Work with Rhythm (8 min) All proprioceptive activities done to rhythm: Jump to rhythm (2 min) Push wall to rhythm (2 min) Carry items to rhythm (2 min) Stomp to rhythm (2 min) Purpose: Satisfies proprioceptive and rhythm needs together Percussion Exploration (10 min) Multiple instruments available Create rhythms on each
Record favorite rhythms Practice playing softly and loudly Fast and slow Structured, purposeful rhythm creation Body Percussion (7 min) Clapping patterns Stomping patterns Full body rhythm routine Can follow video tutorials Transforms vocal into physical Rhythm Games (7 min) "Copycat Rhythm" - adult claps pattern, child copies "Rhythm Freeze" - create rhythm, freeze on command "Fast-Slow Game" - start fast, gradually slow down Teaches control and flexibility Quiet Transition (3 min) Very slow, gentle rhythm (rocking, swaying) Gradually silence Deep breathing Oral-motor input (chewy) For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Rhythm Exploration" (10-15 minutes): Soft, slow rhythms only Quiet instruments (bells, soft shakers) Focus on calming rhythms No loud or fast rhythms Sensory Integration: Vestibular-Rhythm Connection: Theory: Rhythm often connects to vestibular system
Provide vestibular input with rhythm: Swing to rhythm: Push swing in rhythm Rock to rhythm: Rocking chair with beat Bounce to rhythm: Therapy ball bouncing Throughout day: Rocking chair access during seated activities Movement breaks every 90 minutes Swinging daily (15-20 min) Result: Satisfied vestibular system often reduces rhythmic vocal stimming by 60-70% Oral-Motor Satisfaction: Beatboxing uses mouth/lips/tongue intensively Alternative oral-motor input every 60-90 min: Chewy snacks/tools Crunchy foods Drinks through straws Whistles, kazoos, harmonicas Reduces need for vocal rhythm creation Auditory Environment: Provide rhythmic auditory input: Music with strong beats (drum-heavy genres) Metronome sounds Rhythm-focused songs Fills auditory/rhythm need without child needing to create constantly Massage Techniques: Rhythmic Massage (10-15 minutes, 1-2x daily): Purpose: Use massage WITH rhythm to satisfy need
Unique approach for rhythmic stimming: All massage strokes done in rhythm: Count: "1, 2, 3, 4" while massaging Tap in rhythm on back Pat in rhythm on legs Clap hands on child's body in rhythm (gentle) Back (5 min): Rhythmic tapping all over back (2 min) Rhythmic strokes down back (2 min) Rhythmic circles (1 min) Arms and Legs (5 min): Rhythmic squeezing down arms Rhythmic squeezing down legs Rhythmic tapping on limbs Finish (3 min): Slow the rhythm down gradually Very slow, gentle taps Eventually stop Silence and stillness Purpose: Satisfies rhythm need through touch instead of sound Oral-Facial Massage (7-8 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Releases tension from beatboxing Lips and mouth (detailed massage, 3 min) Jaw muscles (firm massage, 2 min)
Cheeks and face (2 min) Throat sides (1 min) See detailed techniques in previous sections "Beat Box Break" Quick Massage (3-4 minutes): Use when beatboxing is excessive: Rhythmic shoulder taps (1 min) Rhythmic arm squeezes (1 min) Rhythmic hand massage (1 min) Gradually slow rhythm End with stillness Offer drum or instrument after massage MANIFESTATION 6: Singing Same Song 20-100+ Times Physical Redirection Technique: "Song to Movement Routine" When child sings repetitively, create movement choreography Technique: "You love that song! Let's make dance moves for it!" Create specific movements for each part: Example with "Twinkle Twinkle": "Twinkle twinkle" = hand twinkles above head "Little star" = crouch down small "How I wonder" = hands on hips, look around "What you are" = point up
Continue for whole song Do choreography together (5 times) Then: "Now let's do the moves WITHOUT singing!" Silent dancing to song in their head (5 times) Transition to different active play Allows the song while adding movement Easier to transition from vocal to silent Provides proprioceptive and vestibular input DIY Alternative Tool: Song Ticket System Materials: Index cards, draw musical notes, jar Each card = one song performance Start with 10 tickets per day Each time child sings complete song, use one ticket When tickets gone: "Song time is over today, tomorrow you get more!" Visual, concrete limit on repetition Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Designated Song Time (15-20 min, 2-3x daily): Set timer Child can sing as much as they want
Can record performances When timer ends: transition to quiet activity Contains behavior to specific times Song Variations: Encourage changing the song: Different tempo (fast, slow, medium) Different volume (loud, whisper, medium) Different style (opera, rap, country) Different language (make up words) Builds flexibility while honoring the interest Karaoke Apps/Videos: Sing-along videos on YouTube Karaoke apps (many free) Provides structured singing activity Can record performances Makes it purposeful entertainment Music Lessons: Voice lessons (if interested) Choir or singing group Turns stimming into skill development Appropriate outlet for singing interest Song Writing: Encourage creating NEW songs Start by changing words to familiar melody Eventually create original melodies Moves from repetition to creativity Musical Instruments: Play song on instrument instead of singing Piano, keyboard, xylophone, recorder
Alternative musical expression For Communication-Focused: Song as Communication: Sometimes repetitive singing communicates: Emotion (happy = upbeat song) Memory (song reminds them of experience) Desire (wants to watch movie the song is from) Explore: "That song makes you think of ___?" Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Musical Expression Circuit" (30-40 minutes, 1-2x daily): Active Musical Opening (8 min) Sing favorite songs WHILE doing heavy work: Jump while singing (3 min) Dance energetically while singing (3 min) March and sing (2 min) Purpose: Combines proprioceptive with vocal** Structured Performance Time (10 min) Set up "stage" area Child performs favorite songs (with limits) Can use microphone (toy or real) Family can be audience Time limit enforced Makes it special performance, not constant background
Song Variations (8 min) Practice singing favorite song in different ways: Opera style (2 min) Whisper singing (2 min) Fast version (2 min) Slow version (2 min) Builds flexibility Alternative Music Activities (10 min) Instruments (play song on xylophone, keyboard) Song writing (create new verses) Drawing while listening to song Non-vocal music engagement Quiet Transition (4 min) Very quiet humming (no words) Gentle lip massage Oral-motor input (chewy) Silent activity For Sensory Avoiders: "Gentle Music Engagement" (15 minutes): Quiet singing (not repetitive) Listening to music (not singing) Soft instruments Focus on variety, not repetition Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Protocol: Theory: Singing uses oral-motor system extensively Provide alternative oral-motor input: Every 60-90 minutes: Chewy snack or tool (3-5 min) Crunchy food Drink through straw
Whistling, kazoo playing Before high-singing times: 5 min intensive oral-motor work Reduces subsequent singing Result: Satisfied oral-motor needs = 40-50% reduction in repetitive singing Vestibular Integration: Swinging while singing: Allows both behaviors simultaneously Often satisfies both needs 15-20 min daily Rocking while allowing singing: Rocking chair during "song time" Calming vestibular input Result: May significantly reduce random singing Auditory Environment Management: Provide rich musical environment: Background music throughout day Variety of genres Audiobooks, podcasts for kids Purpose: Fills auditory need without child creating constant sound Can reduce repetitive singing by 30-40% Massage Techniques: Comprehensive Vocal System Massage (10-12 minutes, 2x daily): Best times: After singing episodes, before bed Purpose: Extensive singing causes significant vocal/throat tension Throat Area (3 min): NEVER front of throat
Sides of neck only Gentle circular massage from jaw to collarbones Each side (1.5 min) Very light touch down front (no pressure) Jaw and Face (3 min): Jaw muscle (masseter) focus - firm massage Temples (1 min) Cheeks (1 min) Around mouth (1 min) Lips and Mouth (2 min): Detailed lip massage Circular motions around mouth See detailed technique in previous sections Chest and Upper Back (3 min): Upper chest massage (singing uses chest muscles) Between shoulder blades (if child can turn over) Firm, releasing tension Finish (1 min): Light taps on throat area (sides) Gentle face strokes Deep, slow breathing together Full Body "Song Reset" Massage (20 minutes, 1x daily): Best time: Evening Purpose: Deep overall regulation reduces all vocal stimming
Complete full-body massage Extra attention to: Back (calming, 7-8 min) Shoulders/arms (5 min) Legs/feet (5 min) Slow, rhythmic, deeply calming Result: Consistent daily massage reduces repetitive singing by 60-80% "Voice Rest" Quick Massage (4-5 minutes): Use after extended singing episodes: "Your voice needs a rest. Let's do massage." Throat sides (gentle, 1 min) Jaw (firm massage, 1 min) Shoulders and neck (firm, 2 min) Offer something to chew (gives mouth alternative activity) Deep breath together Redirect to quiet activity MANIFESTATION 7: Making Up Nonsense Words and Repeating Physical Redirection Technique: "Nonsense to Sense Game" When child creates and repeats nonsense words, engage playfully Technique: Child repeats: "Blibberdy, blibberdy, blibberdy..." You respond: "Blibberdy! That's a silly word! Let's make it an action!"
Create movement for the nonsense word: Every "blibberdy" = one jump Or one clap Or one spin Do together (10 repetitions) Then: "Now let's make NEW nonsense words!" Take turns creating new words with actions Each person gets 3 new words max Then transition to heavy work activity Makes nonsense word play interactive and bounded Provides proprioceptive input Teaches turn-taking and flexibility DIY Alternative Tool: Silly Word Dictionary Materials: Notebook, markers Purpose: Collect child's nonsense words Use: When child creates nonsense word, write it in book with definition/picture Child can look through book during designated times Externalizes the words (reduces need to repeat verbally) Can become cherished item Cost: $2-3 for notebook Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Nonsense Word Games: "Dr. Seuss Time": Read silly books together (validates nonsense words)
"Nonsense Rhyme": Create rhyming nonsense words "Nonsense Song": Sing nonsense words to familiar tunes Makes it purposeful play Recording Nonsense: Record nonsense words Play back Create "nonsense library" External storage reduces verbal repetition Written Nonsense: Write/draw nonsense words Make up silly spelling Create nonsense alphabet Transforms verbal into visual Foreign Language Connection: Explore: Real words in other languages sound like nonsense! Learn simple words in different languages "Your nonsense words are like other languages!" Validates interest, redirects toward learning For Communication-Focused: Nonsense as Placeholder: Sometimes nonsense words fill in when child doesn't know real word Gently model real word Accept both Example: Child: "I want the blibberdy!" (pointing at cup) Adult: "Oh, the cup! Yes, here's the cup!" Occupational Therapy Activities:
For Sensory Seekers: "Nonsense Play Circuit" (20-25 minutes, 1-2x daily): Nonsense Movement (7 min) Every nonsense word = specific movement Create nonsense word dance Jump, spin, crash to nonsense words Combines proprioceptive with vocal Structured Nonsense Time (8 min) Set timer: "Nonsense word time!" Child can say any nonsense words Adult participates (makes it social) Write/draw favorite nonsense words When timer ends: "Now we use real words" Contains the behavior Nonsense to Real (5 min) Practice: For each nonsense word, think of real word that sounds similar Example: "Blibberdy" sounds like "blueberry" "Flibbertygibbet" is a real word! Builds awareness of language Quiet Transition (5 min) Oral-motor input (hard to talk while chewing) Calm activity Real words only practice (gentle) For Communication-Focused:
"Language Building" (15 minutes): Honor nonsense words (they're language play!) Gently model real words Expand vocabulary naturally Celebrate ALL communication attempts Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Satisfaction: Nonsense words are often created for how they FEEL in the mouth Provide alternative oral sensations: Every 60-90 min: Chewy, crunchy, varied textures Drinks through straws Whistles, kazoos (make interesting oral sensations) May reduce nonsense word creation Language-Rich Environment: Provide interesting REAL words: Read books with unusual words Teach big/silly real words Word-of-the-day practice Channels interest in sound/language toward real vocabulary Reduce Verbal Pressure: Sometimes nonsense words emerge when language demands are high Strategies: Accept non-verbal communication Give processing time Reduce questions Lower pressure = less nonsense filling Massage Techniques: Oral-Facial Massage (7-8 minutes, 2-3x daily):
Purpose: Nonsense words use mouth/tongue/lips extensively Lips and mouth (circular massage, 3 min) Jaw muscles (firm massage, 2 min) Tongue (if child allows, gentle pressure) Cheeks (inside and outside, 2 min) Face overall (1 min) See detailed techniques in previous sections Full Body Regulation Massage (15 minutes, 1x daily): Complete routine Reduces overall verbal stimming Consistent daily practice Hand Massage for Grounding (5 minutes, as needed): Use when nonsense word repetition is excessive: Detailed hand massage Firm pressure Grounding effect Often reduces verbal behaviors Redirect to hands-on activity after MANIFESTATION 8: Exploring Accent Changes or Character Voices Physical Redirection Technique: "Voice Character Theater" When child uses different voices repetitively, create structured theater play Technique: "You're using interesting voices! Let's put on a play!"
Assign each voice a character: High voice = mouse character Low voice = bear character Accent = foreign visitor character Regular voice = narrator Create short scene (3-5 minutes) Each character gets specific number of lines (limits repetition) Then: "Play is over! Now we need to help move the theater!" Heavy work activity (move "props"/furniture) Transition complete Makes voice play purposeful and bounded Provides social interaction Natural ending point (play is over) DIY Alternative Tool: Voice Choice Wheel Materials: Paper plate, divide into sections, arrow in center (brad fastener) Sections: Regular Voice, Whisper Voice, Deep Voice, High Voice, Silly Voice, Quiet Time (no voice) Use: Spin wheel, use that voice for designated time (2-3 min) Limits each voice type Makes it a game with rules
Cost: Free Alternative Stimulation: For Sensory Seekers: Structured Character Voice Time (10-15 min, 2x daily): Designated time for voice play Can use different accents/voices Set timer When ends: back to regular voice Contains the behavior Voice Acting Practice: YouTube: Voice acting tutorials for kids Practice specific characters from movies Record performances Makes it skill development Audiobook Creation: Record child reading book in different voices Different voice for each character Purposeful use of voice variety Can share with family Accent Exploration: Learn about real accents (educational) Watch videos of people with different accents Practice specific accents (not mockery, but appreciation) Channels interest into cultural learning Voice Modification Apps: Apps that change voice (robot, helium, deep, etc.) Child speaks normally, app modifies External voice changes reduce need for constant self-modification
For Communication-Focused: Voice as Expression: Different voices may express different feelings/needs Help child recognize: "You use high voice when excited" "You use deep voice when feeling strong" Teach using regular voice to express same things Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: "Voice Exploration Circuit" (25-30 minutes, 1-2x daily): Proprioceptive Opening (5 min) Heavy work (calms before vocal play) Often reduces intensity of voice play Structured Voice Play (12 min) Voice Theater: Create characters (3 min) Each character has specific voice (3 min) Perform short skit with rules (5 min) Clear beginning and ending Purpose: Purposeful, bounded voice use Voice Experiments (7 min) Explore how voices are made: Tension in throat = higher pitch Relaxation = lower pitch Nose involvement = nasal sound
Educational approach Record different voices (1-2 examples each, not repetitive) Return to Regular Voice (4 min) Practice using regular voice Simple conversation in own voice Reinforce: "This is your voice, and it's great!" Quiet Transition (2 min) Oral-motor input Calm activity No voice play For Communication-Focused: "Voice and Identity" (15 minutes): Explore: What is YOUR voice? Practice recognizing own voice Understand: Other voices are for play, this is for talking Build comfort with own voice Sensory Integration: Oral-Motor Protocol: Voice changes use oral-facial muscles extensively Alternative oral-motor input: Every 60-90 min: chewy, crunchy Drink through straw Whistles, kazoos Satisfies oral-motor needs differently Vestibular Integration: Swinging while using voices: Combines both behaviors Often satisfies both needs May reduce random voice changes Daily swinging: 15-20 minutes
Identity Development: Help child develop strong sense of own voice: Record child's regular voice Listen together: "That's YOUR voice!" Celebrate their unique voice Strong identity = less need to be other characters constantly Massage Techniques: Throat and Vocal Cord Massage (8-10 minutes, 2x daily): Purpose: Voice changes strain vocal cords/throat CRITICAL: Never press directly on front of throat Throat sides (3 min): Gentle massage from jaw to collarbones Each side separately Very light touch Jaw (2 min): Firm massage on masseter Releases tension from voice manipulation Face and lips (2 min): General face massage Lip area focus Chest (2 min): Upper chest massage Voice projection uses chest Finish (1 min): Light tapping on throat area (sides) Deep breathing Full Body Calming Massage (15 minutes, 1x daily):
Complete routine Reduces overall vocal stimming Evening timing best Identity Grounding Massage (5 minutes): Purpose: Help child feel grounded in own body/voice Hand massage (firm, grounding) Foot massage (grounding) Deep pressure on limbs "This is YOUR body, YOUR hands, YOUR feet, YOUR voice" Body awareness supports voice awareness SECTION 1: QUICK REFERENCE GUIDES A. EMERGENCY INTERVENTION QUICK GUIDE For Rapid Response When Stimming Escalates or Meltdown Imminent: B. 5-MINUTE SENSORY RESET PROTOCOL Use anytime, anywhere - portable regulation: Step 1 (60 seconds): Proprioceptive Input Wall pushes (10 hard pushes) OR Chair push-ups (10 times) OR Carry something heavy Step 2 (60 seconds): Deep Pressure Shoulder squeezes (firm, 10 times) Arm squeezes down to hands Deep pressure hug Step 3 (60 seconds): Hand Grounding
Detailed hand massage Press each finger firmly Palm pressure Step 4 (90 seconds): Breathing + Vestibular Gentle rocking OR swaying Deep breaths together (5 slow breaths) Step 5 (30 seconds): Transition Offer appropriate fidget or activity State what happens next Result: Most children significantly calmer, ready to proceed C. SENSORY PROFILE IDENTIFICATION FLOWCHART Use this to quickly identify your child's sensory profile: START: Does your child... ├─ Make lots of sounds/seek loud noises? │ └─ YES → AUDITORY SEEKER │ ├─ Do they also cover ears sometimes? │ │ └─ YES → MIXED SEEKER/AVOIDER │ │ └─ NO → PURE SEEKER │ └─ Follow SEEKER protocols │ └─ NO → Do they cover ears/avoid noise? └─ YES → AUDITORY AVOIDER └─ Follow AVOIDER protocols
└─ NO → Do they seem unbothered by sound? └─ TYPICAL AUDITORY PROCESSING └─ Standard sensory diet for overall regulation Detailed Characteristics: PURE SEEKER: Makes sounds constantly (humming, singing, sound effects) Turns volume up high Bangs, taps, clicks things Loves loud environments Never covers ears Seems to "need" sound Under-responsive to sound PURE AVOIDER: Covers ears frequently Complains sounds are too loud Distressed by normal environmental sounds Avoids noisy places Melts down from sound Seeks quiet constantly Over-responsive to sound MIXED SEEKER/AVOIDER: Makes own sounds (seeking) BUT covers ears to environmental sounds (avoiding) Wants control over auditory input Loves own sounds, hates unexpected sounds Complex profile - needs both protocols SECTION 2: AGE-SPECIFIC MODIFICATIONS TODDLERS (18 months - 3 years) Modifications to standard protocols:
Attention Span: Shorten all activities to 1-3 minutes More frequent breaks Follow child's lead more Massage: Shorter sessions (5-10 min instead of 15-20) More playful approach ("tickle massage," "squeeze game") May need to massage during play Build tolerance gradually Heavy Work: Make it play-based: "Help mommy carry!" (light items they can manage) Animal walks as games Push toy shopping carts Pull wagons with toys Oral-Motor: More food-based (natural) Less tolerance for tools (may resist chewy tubes) Use: crunchy/chewy foods throughout day Communication: More visual supports needed Less verbal instruction Model behaviors, don't explain Sensory Diet: Every 45-60 min (vs. 90 min for older) Shorter duration each activity More play-based integration PRESCHOOL (3-5 years) Modifications: Attention Span: 3-7 minutes per activity Can follow simple 2-step directions
Beginning to understand cause-effect Massage: 10-15 minutes tolerable Can understand "massage time" May request massage themselves Can learn some self-massage Heavy Work: Structured games work well: "Strong man/woman" challenges Animal walk races Obstacle courses Can help with real chores: Carrying groceries (light bags) Helping move furniture Yard work (raking, pulling weeds) Oral-Motor: Can use chewy tubes if introduced properly Understands taking turns Can participate in "oral motor games" Sensory Diet: Every 60-90 minutes 5-10 minutes per activity Can follow visual schedule SCHOOL-AGE (6-12 years) Standard protocols work well, plus: Added Responsibilities: Can track own sensory needs (with visual supports) Can request breaks/tools Can do self-massage techniques Can advocate: "I need quiet" or "I need to move" School Integration: Written sensory diet for school
Teacher collaboration essential Can have classroom "sensory job" (carry papers, organize shelves) May need formal 504 or IEP accommodations Peer Awareness: Age where teasing begins Teach discrete self-regulation May need social skills support Educate peers (if child agrees) Independence Building: Teach to recognize own dysregulation Practice using tools independently Build self-advocacy skills Create "sensory toolbox" they manage ADOLESCENTS (13-18 years) Significant modifications needed: Privacy and Autonomy: May resist massage (body awareness, privacy) Offer alternatives: Self-massage techniques Massage therapist (professional) Weighted blankets instead Other proprioceptive tools Self-Direction: Should largely manage own sensory diet by this age May need reminders, but driving own schedule Independence is goal Social Considerations: Discrete tools critical (won't use obvious items) May resist headphones (social stigma) Need "cool" looking tools
Stress increases (hormones, academics, social) Accommodations: May still need school accommodations Self-advocacy critical for college/work Build life skills for independent sensory management Heavy Work Options: Exercise/sports Weight training Job responsibilities (manual labor) Yard work, household projects SECTION 3: COMORBIDITY CONSIDERATIONS AUDITORY STIMMING + AUTISM Unique Considerations: Stimming as Communication: May be expressing emotion May be seeking regulation May be processing information Never suppress - provide appropriate outlets Sensory Sensitivity: Often MORE severe than ADHD May have multiple sensory sensitivities (auditory + visual + tactile) Need comprehensive sensory support Predictability Critical: Strict routines essential Visual schedules mandatory Transitions very difficult Prepare for changes extensively Social Impact: Stimming may isolate from peers Need social skills support Teach appropriate times/places (not eliminate) Build peer understanding
Recommended Approach: Occupational therapy (sensory integration) Speech therapy (if echolalia significant) ABA (if desired) - focused on REPLACEMENT behaviors, not suppression Sensory diet absolutely essential Daily massage critical AUDITORY STIMMING + ADHD Unique Considerations: Fidgeting Connection: Auditory stimming IS fidgeting Provides focus for some children May worsen with medication (increased focus on one behavior) Need movement breaks more frequently Impulsivity: Less control over stimming Harder to redirect Need very structured environment External controls initially (timers, schedules) Attention: May not notice own stimming Less awareness of impact on others Need explicit teaching about volume, timing Visual reminders helpful Medication Interaction: Stimulant medication may INCREASE or DECREASE stimming Monitor closely when starting/adjusting meds Some children stim less (more regulated) Some stim more (more focused/intense)
Recommended Approach: Medication management (psychiatrist) Occupational therapy (sensory + motor planning) Behavioral support (structure, routines) Very frequent movement breaks (every 30-45 min) Fidgets ALWAYS available Sensory diet essential AUDITORY STIMMING + ANXIETY Unique Considerations: Stimming as Coping: Increases with anxiety Self-soothing mechanism May indicate emotional distress Reducing anxiety reduces stimming Triggers: Stressful situations increase stimming Anticipatory anxiety triggers preemptive stimming Social anxiety may worsen in groups Need anxiety management strategies Sensory Sensitivity Connection: Anxiety makes sensory sensitivities WORSE Sensory overload triggers anxiety Vicious cycle Must address both simultaneously Recommended Approach: Therapy (CBT for anxiety) Anxiety management skills Deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation Sensory diet (calming focus) MORE massage (anxiety responds excellently) Eliminate/reduce anxiety triggers when possible Medication if severe (psychiatrist) AUDITORY STIMMING + SENSORY PROCESSING DISORDER (SPD)
Unique Considerations: Multiple Sensory Systems Affected: Not just auditory May have tactile, vestibular, proprioceptive issues too Need comprehensive sensory diet Auditory is one piece of larger puzzle Complex Sensory Profile: May be seeker in some areas, avoider in others Example: Auditory seeker, tactile avoider Need individualized assessment OT evaluation essential Behavioral Manifestations: "Sensory meltdowns" common Difficulty with transitions Emotional dysregulation Sleep problems Feeding issues (if oral-tactile sensitive) Recommended Approach: Occupational therapy (specialized in SPD) - ESSENTIAL Comprehensive sensory integration therapy Home sensory diet (all systems, not just auditory) Environmental modifications (all sensory inputs) Daily massage absolutely critical May need 3-6 months intensive OT SECTION 4: CULTURAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL ADAPTATIONS LIMITED RESOURCES / LOW-INCOME FAMILIES Free/Minimal Cost Alternatives: Instead of Expensive Equipment:
Trampoline ($100-300) → Jumping on mattress, couch cushions on floor Crash pad ($80-150) → Pile of pillows, bean bag Therapy swing ($60-200) → Playground swings (free), sheet tied to tree Weighted blanket ($50-150) → DIY: sew rice into pillowcase Noise-canceling headphones ($100-300) → Construction earmuffs ($10-15) Sensory bins ($20-40) → Rice/beans from pantry, large bowl Instead of Professional Therapy: OT ($100-200/session) → YouTube videos, free library books Massage therapist → Parent-provided massage (free) Expensive fidgets → Household items (bubble wrap, rubber bands, paper clips) Free Resources: Public library (books on sensory processing) YouTube (OT exercises, massage techniques) School-based services (free OT/PT if qualify) Community centers (free play spaces, playgrounds) Nature (outdoor play is free) Food-Based Sensory: Store-brand equivalents of all foods
Freeze vegetables for crunch (cheaper than fresh) Dried beans for sensory bins (very cheap) Water play (free) SMALL LIVING SPACES (Apartments, Small Homes) Adaptations When Space Limited: Heavy Work Without Space: Wall pushes (any wall) Chair push-ups (any chair) Carrying: groceries, laundry, full water bottles Stairs (if available) - up and down repeatedly Isometric exercises (push hands together, push against doorframe) Vestibular Without Equipment: Rocking in any chair Spinning (clear small space, 5-10 spins) Head movements (up/down, side to side) Rolling across floor (can do in hallway) Sound Creation Management: Outdoor time essential (make noise outside) Bathroom = best echo room (allow appropriate use) Headphones for child (contains sound) Designated "loud times" (when neighbors not home) Communicate with neighbors (explain, prevent complaints)
Quiet Spaces: Closet with pillows (instant quiet retreat) Under table with blanket fort Bathroom (quietest room in most apartments) Bathtub with pillows (surprisingly effective) SCHOOL IMPLEMENTATION GUIDE For Teachers and School Staff: Classroom Accommodations: For Seekers: Fidget basket (child can choose as needed) Movement breaks every 45-60 minutes Flexible seating (wobble stool, ball chair, standing desk) Sensory job (carry messages, organize materials) Chew tool available at desk (necklace, pencil topper) Allow humming during independent work (if not disruptive) For Avoiders: Preferential seating (away from noise sources) Noise-canceling headphones (as needed) Access to quiet space (library, counselor's office, empty classroom) Warning before bells, announcements, fire drills Quiet testing room (standard accommodation) Volume control on classroom activities Movement Breaks (All Students Benefit): Every 45-60 minutes
3-5 minutes Options: Stretching Brain Gym exercises Walk around room Animal walks Chair push-ups Communication with Family: Daily/weekly reports on stimming behaviors Triggers identified at school What worked, what didn't Consistency between home and school essential Legal Accommodations: 504 Plan (for sensory processing disorder) IEP (if qualifies for special education) Accommodations to include: Movement breaks Sensory tools Quiet space access Modified environment Extra time (if sensory processing slows work) SECTION 5: SPECIALIZED PROTOCOLS PROTOCOL 1: Intensive 2-Week "Reset" Protocol Use when behaviors are severe or out of control: Purpose: Intensive sensory input for 2 weeks to "reset" nervous system Schedule: Week 1-2 (Every Day): Morning (60 minutes): 30 min outdoor heavy play (running, climbing, jumping) 15 min oral-motor circuit (eating, chewing, drinking)
15 min massage Midday (30 minutes): 15 min heavy work 10 min vestibular (swinging, spinning) 5 min oral-motor Afternoon (60 minutes): 30 min intensive outdoor play 20 min massage 10 min quiet sensory bin Evening (30 minutes): 25 min comprehensive massage 5 min quiet activity Total Daily: 3+ hours intensive sensory input After 2 Weeks: Re-assess behaviors Most children show 60-80% reduction Transition to maintenance schedule (standard sensory diet) Continue daily massage indefinitely Important: Very intensive - requires full commitment May need to take time off work/school But VERY effective Like "sensory boot camp" PROTOCOL 2: Gradual Elimination Protocol (For Problem Behaviors) When one behavior must be reduced/eliminated: Example: Excessive Same-Song Listening Baseline Week: Track current frequency (e.g., 500 plays per day)
No changes yet Week 1: 25% Reduction Reduce to 375 plays per day Use ticket system (375 tickets) Intensive sensory diet to compensate Daily massage increased Week 2: 50% Reduction Reduce to 250 plays per day Continue support Introduce more alternatives Week 3: 75% Reduction Reduce to 125 plays per day Heavy support needed May see increased other stimming (allow) Week 4: Final Goal 50 plays per day (or whatever goal is) Maintain with ongoing support Keys to Success: Slow reduction (not cold turkey) Increase other sensory support Allow replacement behaviors Consistent daily massage Patience (behaviors may worsen temporarily) PROTOCOL 3: Non-Verbal Child Protocol Modifications for children who cannot communicate verbally: Assessment Challenges: Cannot tell you what helps Cannot request tools
Must observe carefully Observation Focus: What reduces stimming? What increases it? What calms child? What agitates? Modified Sensory Diet: Offer multiple options, see what child chooses Child's choices indicate needs Follow child's lead more Communication Systems: Picture cards ("I need quiet," "I need to move") Visual schedule of sensory activities Child can point/indicate needs Massage: Especially critical (non-verbal input) May be primary regulation tool Some non-verbal children very touch-averse (start slow) Others crave massage Tools Always Available: Fidgets visible and accessible Headphones accessible Quiet space clearly marked Child can self-direct to tools PROTOCOL 4: Crisis Prevention and Management Preventing Sensory Meltdowns: Early Warning Signs (Learn Your Child's): Increased stimming Covering ears more Seeking input more intensely Becoming non-verbal Increased muscle tension
Red face/ears Rapid breathing Level 1 Intervention (Early Signs): Immediate sensory input Quick hand massage (2 min) Deep pressure hug Offer fidget/tool Remove from triggering environment Quiet space Level 2 Intervention (Escalating): 5-minute sensory reset protocol (see earlier) Remove ALL unnecessary input Quiet, dim, calm Deep pressure if tolerated Level 3 (Meltdown in Progress): Safety first (ensure child and others safe) Remove ALL sensory input possible Quiet, dark space Allow meltdown to run course Stay close but don't force interaction Deep pressure if tolerated (weighted blanket, firm hug) Wait After Meltdown: Child needs recovery (30 min - 2 hours) Quiet space Gentle massage when allowed No demands No discussing what happened (yet) Later (Hours or Next Day): Identify trigger Prevent in future
Teach coping skills (if child able) Increase preventive sensory diet SECTION 6: VISUAL SUPPORTS AND TOOLS PRINTABLE VISUAL SCHEDULES Create these for your child: Daily Sensory Diet Visual Schedule: [Picture of breakfast] Morning Routine ↓ [Picture of jumping] Movement Break ↓ [Picture of hands] Massage Time ↓ [Picture of school] School ↓ [Picture of playground] Big Play Time ↓ [Picture of drum] Noise Time ↓ [Picture of hands massaging] Massage ↓ [Picture of bed] Bedtime Feelings and Tools Chart: How I Feel → What Helps 😫 Too much noise → [Headphones picture] 😤 Need to move → [Jumping picture] 😰 Overwhelmed → [Quiet space picture] 😊 Feel good → [Happy activities] Volume Control Visual: Level 10: 🦁 ROARING (Too loud) Level 7: 📢 Outdoor voice
Level 5: 👥 Talking voice ← Use this! Level 3: 🤫 Library voice Level 1: 🐭 Mouse whisper SOCIAL STORIES Example: "When My Ears Need a Break" Sometimes sounds feel too loud to me. When sounds feel too loud, my ears hurt. It's okay to need quiet. When I need quiet, I can: - Put on my headphones - Go to my quiet space - Ask for help Other people understand. Taking care of my ears helps me feel better. Example: "Making Sounds at the Right Time" I like to make sounds. Sounds are fun! There are good times and places for loud sounds. Loud sounds are okay: - Outside - In my room - During noise time Quiet sounds are better:
- At school - At the library - When others are sleeping I can choose the right sound for the right place. SECTION 7: FAMILY SUPPORT FOR PARENTS Self-Care is Essential: You Cannot Pour from Empty Cup: Parenting sensory child is EXHAUSTING You need breaks You need support This is marathon, not sprint Respite Care: Arrange regular breaks (weekly if possible) Trade childcare with trusted friend/family Hire sitter (even for 2 hours) Use school extended day programs Support Groups: Online communities (Facebook groups for sensory kids) Local support groups (autism, ADHD, SPD) Talk to other parents who understand Share resources and strategies Your Own Regulation: Your stress affects child Practice self-regulation Deep breathing, exercise, meditation Model calm behavior Partnership with Co-Parent:
United approach essential Both must follow sensory diet Communicate about what works Support each other Divide responsibilities (one does massage, one does heavy work) Siblings: They need attention too Explain sibling's needs age-appropriately Individual time with each child Teach siblings to help (if appropriate) Watch for resentment FOR EDUCATORS Understanding is Key: These are NOT Behavior Problems: Stimming = neurological need Not defiance Not attention-seeking Not controllable without support Your Role: Provide accommodations Follow sensory diet at school Communicate with family Educate peers (with permission) Be flexible Classroom Management: Stimming child may need different rules Example: Can hum during independent work Example: Can leave to quiet space without asking Explain to class (with family permission): "Jamie's brain needs movement breaks" "Emma's ears are sensitive, we use quiet voices"
Builds empathy When Behaviors Disrupt: Redirect to appropriate alternative immediately Remove from situation if needed Contact family to problem-solve Adjust sensory diet at school Success Stories: Many stimming children thrive with support Often highly intelligent, creative Accommodations help them access their potential Your support makes enormous difference SECTION 8: FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS Q: Will my child outgrow auditory stimming? A: Some children reduce stimming as they mature and develop better regulation skills. Others continue to stim into adulthood. With appropriate support, stimming typically becomes: Less frequent Less intense More socially appropriate (right times/places) Better controlled Goal is not elimination, but management and appropriate expression. Q: Should I stop my child from stimming? A: No. Stimming serves important regulatory functions. Suppressing stimming without addressing underlying needs leads to:
Increased anxiety Worse behaviors elsewhere Meltdowns Psychological harm Instead: Redirect to appropriate alternatives, address sensory needs proactively. Q: How long before I see improvement? A: With consistent implementation of sensory diet and daily massage: Some improvement: 1-2 weeks Significant improvement: 3-4 weeks Maximum benefit: 2-3 months Must be CONSISTENT. Sporadic implementation won't work. Q: What if my child refuses massage? A: Some children (especially adolescents, trauma survivors, or tactile defensive) refuse massage.
