Alternatives: Start with just hands or feet Very brief sessions (2-3 minutes) Massage over clothes initially Let them control (they stop when want) Weighted blankets (passive deep pressure) Compression clothing Professional massage therapist (some prefer stranger) Don't force. Build trust slowly. Q: Can medication help? A: Medication doesn't specifically treat stimming, but may help underlying conditions:
ADHD medication: May reduce fidgeting/stimming in some children Anxiety medication: May reduce anxiety-driven stimming Sleep medication: Better sleep = better regulation = less stimming Consult psychiatrist. Medication should SUPPLEMENT sensory diet, not replace it. Q: What about ABA therapy? A: Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) can be helpful IF focused on: Teaching replacement behaviors Building skills Improving quality of life NOT if focused on: Suppressing stimming through punishment "Quiet hands" approach Eliminating behaviors without teaching alternatives Many autistic adults report trauma from ABA. Choose therapists carefully. Sensory-based approaches often more effective and less harmful. Q: My child's stimming doesn't seem sensory-related. Could it be something else? A: Differential diagnosis - other causes of repetitive behaviors: OCD (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder): Compulsions driven by anxiety, intrusive thoughts
Tic Disorders: Involuntary movements/sounds, preceded by urge Stereotypies: Motor stereotypies (hand flapping, head rocking) - may be separate from sensory Habit: Some behaviors become habits after starting as stims If unsure, seek evaluation from developmental pediatrician or neurologist. Q: School won't provide accommodations. What do I do? A: Legal rights under Section 504 and IDEA: Steps: Request evaluation in writing (school must respond within 30 days) If qualify (most sensory kids do), develop 504 Plan or IEP Include all needed accommodations in written plan School legally required to follow plan If school refuses: Request mediation (free) File complaint with state education department Consult education advocate or lawyer Document everything in writing You have legal rights. Use them. Q: Is there a cure?
A: Sensory Processing Disorder is neurological - no "cure." BUT: With support, children learn better regulation Develop coping skills Some children improve dramatically Many adults manage well with accommodations Think of it like needing glasses - not cured, but managed well with right supports. FINAL WORDS This comprehensive guide represents evidence-based practices, clinical experience, and input from occupational therapists, parents, and autistic adults. Key Takeaways: Stimming is communication and regulation - respect it Daily massage is the most powerful intervention - prioritize it Sensory diets must be consistent - commit fully Environmental modifications are essential - change the environment, not the child Professional support is available - seek it when needed You are not alone - millions of families navigate this
Improvement is possible - with patience, consistency, and comprehensive support Your child is not broken. Their nervous system processes sensory information differently. With understanding, accommodation, and support, they can thrive. Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 3. TACTILE (TOUCH) STIMMING > A. Self-Touch Stimming > Level 1: Skin-Based Stimming
Causation: Over-stimulated: Self-touch is grounding and organizing Under-stimulated: Skin provides accessible tactile input Sensitivity: Exploring tactile boundaries; body awareness development Anxiety: Self-soothing through familiar touch patterns Sensory Profile: Seeker: Firm pressure, extensive touching, long duration Avoider: Light touch on self to "wake up" defensive system Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviour (BFRB): Picking/pulling may indicate separate condition Description: Touching or manipulating own skin Manifestation 1: Rubbing Arms, Legs, or Face (Continuous/Rhythmic) PHYSICAL TECHNIQUE TO INTERRUPT: "Compression Redirect" Approach child calmly and quietly Place both your hands firmly (not harshly) over their hands/arms where they're rubbing Apply deep pressure for 5-10 seconds - compress the area they were rubbing Say: "Let me help you feel your arms/face" Slowly remove your hands while guiding their hands to their lap
Immediately provide alternative (see below) Why it works: Deep pressure provides the tactile input they're seeking but in a more intense, organizing way. It interrupts the pattern and satisfies the sensory need. DIY ALTERNATIVE TOOL: "Sensory Arm Bands" Materials Needed (all under $5): Wide elastic bands (can use wide hair ties, elastic from old clothing, or ace bandage) Optional: Velcro strips Textured fabric scraps (corduroy, fleece, velvet, burlap) How to Make: Cut elastic to fit around child's upper arm or forearm (snug but not tight) Sew or glue textured fabric pieces onto the elastic Create 2-4 bands with different textures Alternative: Use ace bandage wrapped firmly but comfortably around arm How to Use: Child wears bands on arms (where they typically rub)
When urge to rub arises, child rubs the textured bands instead Provides tactile input without skin damage Can be worn under clothing discreetly For face rubbing: Create textured wristband - child rubs wristband then brings to face to smell/touch Cost: $0-5 ALTERNATIVE STIMULATION (Household/Inexpensive): For Sensory SEEKERS: Textured Lotion Application (Organizing Activity) Use thick lotions (coconut oil, vitamin E cream, unscented lotion) Child applies with FIRM pressure to arms/legs Use long, deep strokes Do 2-3 times daily (morning, after school, bedtime) Cost: $3-10 for lotion Why it works: Provides intense tactile input + proprioception through pressure Dry Brushing Program Use soft vegetable brush, makeup brush, or clean paintbrush Child brushes own arms/legs with firm strokes Follow brushing with joint compressions Do every 90-120 minutes when rubbing is frequent
Cost: $1-3 for brush Why it works: Provides organized tactile input that calms nervous system Textured Fabric Squares Collection Gather fabric scraps: corduroy, velvet, burlap, satin, fleece Keep in small pouch or ziplock bag Child rubs fabric pieces instead of skin Rotate textures to maintain interest Cost: $0 (use old clothing/fabric scraps) Resistance Band Arm Work Use exercise band, rubber band, or stretchy fabric Pull, stretch, twist the band Wrap around arms firmly and remove Provides heavy work + tactile input Cost: $1-5 or free (old tights/stockings work) For Sensory AVOIDERS: Predictable Touch Schedule Set timer for scheduled touch times Child CONTROLS when/where they're touched Start with 30 seconds, gradually increase Use child's preferred pressure level Cost: Free Soft Fabric Sleeves
Cut soft cotton or silk sleeves from old clothing Child wears to prevent light touch triggers Gradually introduce during calm times only Cost: Free (repurpose old clothes) Self-Application Tools Cotton balls, soft makeup sponges, silk scarves Child applies touch to self (more tolerable) Start with hands/arms, work toward face slowly Cost: $1-5 OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY ACTIVITIES: For Sensory SEEKERS - Regulation Activities: Heavy Work Before Rubbing Typically Occurs: Wall pushes: 10 reps, holding 10 seconds each Chair push-ups: Sit in chair, push up with arms, 10 reps Carry heavy items (books, laundry basket, water jugs) Animal walks: Bear walk, crab walk across room Frequency: Every 60-90 minutes Tactile Discrimination Activities: Texture matching games (eyes closed, find matching fabrics) "Feely bag" - identify objects by touch only
Sand/rice writing - draw letters/shapes Builds body awareness and tactile processing Proprioceptive Input: Joint compressions: Press down on shoulders, compress joints Squeeze play: Therapy putty, stress balls, playdough Body sock or stretchy fabric - child pushes against resistance For Sensory AVOIDERS - Desensitization Activities: Gradual Exposure Protocol (Wilbarger Method - Modified): Start with child's preferred texture Apply to least sensitive area (usually hands/arms) Use deep pressure (more tolerable than light touch) 3-5 minutes, 2-3x daily NEVER force - child must consent Tolerance Building: Play-based texture exploration (their choice to participate) Messy play with boundaries (wear gloves initially) Tactile bins with preferred items only at first Gradually introduce new textures over weeks/months MASSAGE TECHNIQUES: For Sensory SEEKERS: Deep Pressure Massage (Morning/Evening Routine)
Duration: 10-15 minutes Pressure: FIRM (child should say "just right") Technique: Long, deep strokes down arms (shoulder to hand) Knead muscle tissue like bread dough Compress joints (shoulder, elbow, wrist) Roll arms between your palms Frequency: 2-3 times daily minimum Sports Massage Technique Quick, vigorous strokes Deep tissue work on arms, legs Joint mobilization Use before activities to "wake up" system For Sensory AVOIDERS: Gentle, Predictable Massage (Only with Permission) Duration: 5-10 minutes Pressure: Deep but slow (avoid light touch) Technique: Warn before touching ("I'm going to touch your arm now") Use whole hand contact (not fingertips) Slow, predictable strokes Child controls start/stop Frequency: Only when child requests or consents Self-Massage Teaching Teach child to massage own arms/legs Provides control and predictability
Use visual schedule showing technique Can use massage tools (roller, ball) Manifestation 2: Scratching Skin (Not Itchy) Repeatedly PHYSICAL TECHNIQUE TO INTERRUPT: "Hand Covering and Pressure" When scratching begins, approach calmly Gently but firmly place your hand OVER their hand (stopping scratching motion) Apply firm pressure - press their hand against the area they were scratching Hold for 10-15 seconds Say: "Let's press instead of scratch" Guide hand to alternative scratching tool Why it works: Provides the sensory input they seek (pressure on skin) without causing damage. Teaches alternative that satisfies need. DIY ALTERNATIVE TOOL: "Scratch Pad Boards" Materials Needed: Cardboard squares (4x4 inches) Textured materials: sandpaper, bubble wrap, corrugated cardboard, velcro strips, fabric scraps Glue or tape String or keyring to attach boards together
How to Make: Cut 5-10 cardboard squares Glue different textures onto each square Punch hole in corner of each Thread onto keyring or string Keep in pocket or attached to backpack How to Use: When urge to scratch arises, child scratches the texture board instead Different textures provide variety Can be scratched firmly without damage Portable for school/outings Make multiple sets (one for each location) Cost: $0-3 ALTERNATIVE STIMULATION: For Sensory SEEKERS: Velcro or Scratch Paper Velcro strips sewn onto clothing wristband Scratch paper pads (like scratch-off lottery tickets) Textured wallpaper samples Emery boards or nail files How to use: Child scratches alternative instead of skin Cost: $1-5 Body Brushing Program Surgical brush, vegetable brush, or makeup brush Brush arms/legs with firm strokes
Follow with lotion application Every 2 hours during high-scratching times Cost: $1-3 Resistance Scratching Activities Scratch in kinetic sand Scratch designs in foam sheets Scratch with stick in dirt/sand outside Satisfies scratching urge with resistance Cost: $5-10 for kinetic sand, free for outdoor options For Sensory AVOIDERS: (Less common for scratching, but if present:) Skin Protection Cotton gloves or long sleeves Bandaids over scratched areas Reduces accidental scratching Cost: $3-10 OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY ACTIVITIES: Regulation Through Proprioception: Scratching often indicates need for intense tactile + proprioceptive input Heavy work activities BEFORE typical scratching times: Push/pull heavy objects Carry weighted items Wall pushes, floor pushes Digging in garden Kneading dough Tactile Substitution Activities: Texture bins: Rice, beans, sand - run hands through Resistive activities: Therapy putty, stress balls
Messy play: Shaving cream, finger paint, mud Provides intense tactile without skin damage MASSAGE TECHNIQUES: Pre-Scratching Prevention Massage: Firm stroking massage on typical scratch areas Deep pressure kneading Scratching motion WITH lotion (satisfies urge safely) Joint compressions Duration: 5-10 minutes Frequency: Before typical scratching times (morning, after school, evening) Post-Scratching Healing Massage: Gentle lotion application to scratched areas Promotes healing Provides soothing alternative Use therapeutic lotion (vitamin E, aloe) Manifestation 3: Pinching Self (Arms, Hands, Legs) PHYSICAL TECHNIQUE TO INTERRUPT: "Pinch Redirect with Resistance" When pinching observed, approach immediately Gently separate fingers from pinch Place therapy putty, stress ball, or rolled washcloth in their hand Say: "Pinch THIS instead - squeeze as hard as you can" Demonstrate firm squeezing Stay with child for 2-3 minutes ensuring they engage with alternative
Why it works: Satisfies the proprioceptive need (firm pressure) without self-harm. Redirects impulse to appropriate object. DIY ALTERNATIVE TOOL: "Pinch and Resistance Toys" Materials Needed: Clothespins (wooden or plastic) Small binder clips Thick rubber bands Balloons filled with flour, rice, or playdough Old tennis ball How to Make: Option 1 - Pinch Clothespin Board: Cardboard or wooden board Draw simple picture outline Child pinches clothespins around edge of picture Requires repeated pinching motion Option 2 - Resistance Ball: Fill balloon with flour or rice Tie securely (double knot) Child squeezes/pinches repeatedly Make 2-3 with different resistances Option 3 - Tennis Ball Pincher: Cut slit in old tennis ball (adult does this) Child pinches to open "mouth" Can feed it small objects
Strong resistance satisfies pinching urge How to Use: Keep in pocket, on desk, in car When pinching urge arises, use tool immediately Pinch/squeeze 20-50 times Provides intense proprioceptive input Can be used discretely Cost: $0-5 ALTERNATIVE STIMULATION: For Sensory SEEKERS: Therapy Putty or Homemade Playdough Commercial therapy putty OR Homemade: 1 cup flour, 1/2 cup salt, 1/2 cup water, food coloring Pinch, pull, squeeze, roll Add small objects to hide and find (beads, coins) 10-20 minute sessions, 3-4x daily Cost: $5-10 commercial, $1-2 homemade Clothespin Activities Pinch clothespins onto cardboard Transfer pompoms with clothespin "pinchers" Build structures with clothespins Strengthens hands + satisfies pinching Cost: $2-5 for clothespin set Binder Clip Chain Connect 10-20 small binder clips together Child opens and closes repeatedly
Portable, quiet, intense resistance Cost: $3-5 Pinching Sensory Bins Fill container with dried beans/rice Hide small items Child uses fingers to pinch and find items Provides tactile + proprioceptive input Cost: $2-5 For Sensory AVOIDERS: (Unlikely to pinch, but if mixed profile:) Gentle Resistance Tools Soft foam, cotton balls Softer alternatives for pinching Less intense sensation Cost: $1-3 OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY ACTIVITIES: Heavy Resistance Activities (Pinching Alternative): Pinching often indicates HIGH proprioceptive need Activities providing similar input: Hand Strengthening: Squeeze water from sponges Wring out wet towels Use hole punch on paper (heavy duty) Crack nuts with nutcracker Use tongs to transfer objects Resistive Crafts: Cutting thick cardboard with scissors Tearing thick paper or cardboard Stapling projects (heavy duty stapler) Leather punching crafts
Kitchen Activities: Kneading bread dough Mashing potatoes Peeling vegetables (with supervision) Opening jars with resistance Frequency: Before typical pinching times and every 90 minutes MASSAGE TECHNIQUES: Deep Tissue Hand/Arm Massage: Preparation: Warm hands by rubbing together Technique: Deep pressure kneading of arms (shoulder to hand) Focus on areas typically pinched Pinching massage: Use YOUR fingers to firmly pinch along arms/legs (providing sensation they seek) Hand massage: Squeeze each finger, compress palm Joint compressions: Press shoulder, elbow, wrist joints Duration: 10 minutes Frequency: 2-3 times daily (morning, mid-afternoon, bedtime) Pinching Massage Technique (Paradoxical): Use YOUR hands to pinch child's arms/legs firmly (not painfully) Provides the sensation they're seeking Satisfies neurological need Often reduces self-pinching significantly Get child's permission first Manifestation 4: Picking at Skin, Scabs, Cuticles
IMPORTANT NOTE: Skin picking can be Body-Focused Repetitive Behavior (BFRB) or excoriation disorder, which may require clinical intervention beyond sensory strategies. If picking causes significant damage, scarring, infection, or distress, consult dermatologist and therapist specializing in BFRBs. PHYSICAL TECHNIQUE TO INTERRUPT: "Hand Occupation Technique" When picking observed, approach calmly (no judgment) Gently take child's hands in yours Guide hands to hold fidget object or texture item Keep their hands occupied for 3-5 minutes Say: "Let's keep these busy hands working on something else" Provide hand activity immediately (see alternatives) Why it works: Picking often occurs unconsciously. Occupying hands prevents access to skin while providing alternative sensory input. DIY ALTERNATIVE TOOL: "Picking Alternative Kit" Materials Needed: Small container (mint tin, pencil case)
Variety of picking alternatives Items to Include (all under $10 total): Fake skin picking tools: Glue dried on wax paper (can peel off repeatedly) Dried Elmer's glue on plastic sheet Price tag stickers on laminated card (can pick off and reapply) Textured stickers to peel Cuticle alternatives: Bandaids with adhesive to pick Tape rolled into loops (pick at edges) Putty or slime to pick apart Foam pieces to tear Texture items: Rough stones Textured fabric Bubble wrap Velcro strips How to Make: Collect items above Place in portable container Keep multiple kits (home, school, car) Refresh items weekly How to Use: When picking urge arises, open kit Use each item for 2-3 minutes Satisfies picking urge without skin damage Kit can be used discretely
Cost: $5-10 ALTERNATIVE STIMULATION: For Sensory SEEKERS (Most Common Profile for Pickers): Peel-Off Activities Dried glue on wax paper - child peels repeatedly Orange peeling - satisfying resistance Sticker peeling from sheet Tape removal from surfaces Egg peeling after boiling Cost: $0-3 Why it works: Provides picking sensation without damage Texture Picking Boards Cork board with pushpins to remove/replace Foam board with toothpicks inserted (pick out) Clay or playdough with embedded objects to pick out Cost: $3-10 Fidget Tools for Picking Urges Tangle toys (can pick apart and reassemble) Thinking putty (pick and pull) Kinetic sand (pick and shape) Magnetic putty (pick at pieces) Cost: $5-15 Functional Picking Activities Snap peas/green beans (remove strings) Pomegranate seed removal Corn silk removal Herb leaf picking (basil, cilantro)
Cost: Cost of food items For Sensory AVOIDERS: (Rare for picking, as picking is usually seeking behavior) OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY ACTIVITIES: Picking Prevention Through Hand Occupation: Scheduled "Hands Busy" Times: Every 60-90 minutes: 10-minute hand activity Therapy putty exercises Stress ball squeezing Hand crafts (beading, lacing, weaving) Fine Motor Activities (Keeps Hands Engaged): Beading/jewelry making Lacing cards or shoes Small Lego building Threading activities Embroidery or sewing (supervised) Model building Awareness Building: Tally counter: Click each time picking urge noticed Awareness is first step to redirection No punishment, just data collection Reward for using alternatives Sensory Integration Activities: Often picking indicates tactile + proprioceptive + visual integration need Multi-sensory activities: Cooking (measuring, mixing, kneading) Gardening (digging, pulling weeds, planting) Crafts requiring multiple senses
Building/construction projects MASSAGE TECHNIQUES: Hand and Arm Deep Pressure Massage: Cuticle Area Focus (if picking cuticles): Massage each finger individually Deep pressure on nail beds Cuticle oil massage (olive oil works) Press firmly on each fingertip Duration: 5-10 minutes per hand Frequency: 3-4x daily Full Arm Massage (if picking arms/legs): Long, deep strokes Kneading muscle tissue Pay extra attention to picked areas Lotion with firm pressure Duration: 10 minutes Frequency: Morning and evening minimum Sensory Substitution Massage: Light scratching massage along arms (with permission) Provides picking-like sensation in controlled way Use fingernails to lightly scratch in patterns Then follow with deep pressure Child often finds this satisfying Manifestation 5: Touching Face Repeatedly (10-100+ times/day) PHYSICAL TECHNIQUE TO INTERRUPT: "Face Redirect with Proprioceptive Input"
When face touching observed, approach from side Gently guide hands away from face Immediately place hands on firm surface (table, wall) Have child push HARD against surface for 10 seconds Repeat 3 times Say: "Let's wake up these hands with pushing instead" Provide alternative fidget for hands Why it works: Face touching often indicates need for proprioceptive input to hands OR sensory input to face. Providing heavy work to hands often reduces face touching. DIY ALTERNATIVE TOOL: "Hand Fidget Necklace" Materials Needed: Cord or thick string (30 inches) Beads with large holes Textured items that can be strung: wooden beads, plastic rings, buttons, fabric pieces Optional: Essential oil (lavender) on wooden beads How to Make: Cut cord to necklace length (adjustable based on child's size)
String variety of textured beads/items Tie securely Add drop of essential oil to wooden beads (if child tolerates smell) How to Use: Child wears necklace When urge to touch face arises, manipulates necklace instead Fidgeting with necklace keeps hands occupied Can bring necklace to nose to smell (if essential oil used) Provides tactile input to hands instead of face Discrete for school use Cost: $2-8 ALTERNATIVE STIMULATION: For Sensory SEEKERS: Hand Fidgets (Keep Hands Busy) Therapy putty in pocket Stress ball Tangle toy Fidget cube Textured fabric square Why it works: Provides tactile input to hands, reducing need to touch face Cost: $3-15 Face Alternatives (If Face Input Needed) Soft washcloth: Child rubs on face (cleaner than hands) Facial massage with lotion (structured time)
Face painting/makeup play (provides face stimulation) Cooling face mist spray Cost: $2-10 Oral Motor Input (Often Linked to Face Touching) Chewy tubes or chewable jewelry Crunchy/chewy snacks Drinking through straw (resistive) Blowing activities (bubbles, whistles) Cost: $5-15 for chewies, $0-5 for food Proprioceptive Hand Work: Hand exercises with therapy putty Squeezing stress balls Clothespin activities Finger push-ups against table Cost: $5-10 For Sensory AVOIDERS: (Usually not face-touching, but if mixed profile with face sensitivity:) Desensitization Tools: Soft makeup brushes for gentle face touch Cotton balls Silk fabric Child controls all face touch Cost: $3-10 OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY ACTIVITIES: Prevention Through Hand Engagement: Scheduled Hand Activities (Every 90 min): Therapy putty exercises Stress ball squeezing routines Hand crafts Building activities Keeps hands too busy to touch face
Oral Motor Activities (If Face Touching Related to Oral Seeking): Drinking thick liquids through straw Chewing gum (if appropriate age) Blowing exercises Eating crunchy/chewy foods Provides oral input, reducing face seeking Heavy Work for Upper Body: Wall pushes Chair push-ups Carrying heavy items Animal walks (bear, crab) Organizes nervous system, reduces stimming Awareness Activities: Place small sticker on back of hand When child feels sticker, it cues them that hand is moving toward face Can pause and redirect Non-punitive awareness building MASSAGE TECHNIQUES: Facial Massage (With Permission - Provides Input Child Seeks): Preparation: Wash child's face and your hands Technique: Forehead: Horizontal strokes, firm pressure Temples: Circular massage Cheeks: Downward strokes Jaw: Massage along jawline Around mouth: Gentle circles Chin: Press and release
Duration: 5-10 minutes Frequency: 2-3 times daily (morning, after school, bedtime) Why it works: Provides organized, calming facial input that satisfies need Hand Massage (Reduces Hand-to-Face Impulse): Deep pressure massage on each hand Squeeze each finger Press palm firmly Roll hands between your palms Joint compressions on wrists Duration: 5 minutes per hand Frequency: Before times when face-touching is highest Combined Approach: Face massage (provides face input child seeks) Immediately followed by hand heavy work (redirects hands) Most effective when done proactively before face-touching escalates Manifestations: Stroking hair or beard-not available Running hands over body surfaces-not avalable Squeezing parts of body (arms, legs, hands)-not available
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 3. TACTILE (TOUCH) STIMMING > A. Self-Touch Stimming > Level 2: Hair Manipulation
Causation: Over-stimulated: Hair texture is calming and predictable Under-stimulated: Hair provides multi-sensory input (tactile, visual, smell) Sensitivity: Texture-seeking; soothing repetitive motion BFRB: Trichotillomania (hair-pulling disorder) requires clinical attention Sensory Profile: Seeker: Constant hair touching throughout day; intense pulling Avoider: Gentle stroking for self-soothing Mixed: Hair as multi-sensory tool (sight, smell, touch simultaneously) Description: Playing with, pulling, or arranging hair Manifestation 1: Twirling Hair Around Fingers (10-60+ minutes) IMPORTANT NOTE: Excessive hair pulling (trichotillomania) is a BFRB that requires clinical intervention. If child is pulling out hair, creating bald spots, or experiencing distress, consult mental health professional specializing in BFRBs. PHYSICAL TECHNIQUE TO INTERRUPT: "Hand Substitution Technique" When hair twirling observed, approach calmly Gently guide twirling hand away from hair Place twist/fidget toy immediately in that hand
Guide fingers through twisting motion with toy Say: "Let's twist THIS instead - same motion, different object" Model the twisting motion with toy Stay with child 2-3 minutes to ensure engagement Why it works: Maintains the satisfying twisting motion but redirects to appropriate object. Muscle memory is satisfied. DIY ALTERNATIVE TOOL: "Hair-Twist Substitute Collection" Materials Needed: Pipe cleaners (chenille stems) Yarn or embroidery thread Ribbons Twist ties from bread bags Spiral phone cord (old style) Tangle toy (if purchasing) How to Make: Option 1 - Personal Twisting Kit: Gather 5-10 twistable items Place in small pouch or tin Include items with hair-like texture (yarn, embroidery thread) Include items with satisfying twist (pipe cleaners, twist ties) **Option 2 - Wearable Twist Alternative:**
Braid several pieces of yarn together (12-18 inches) Attach to backpack, belt loop, or bracelet Child twists yarn braid instead of hair Replace when worn out Option 3 - DIY Tangle Toy: Cut plastic straw into 1-inch segments (20 pieces) Thread elastic cord through all segments Tie ends together Creates twistable, bendable toy How to Use: Keep twist alternatives in pocket, on desk, attached to body When urge to twirl hair arises, immediately grab alternative Twist for 2-5 minutes until urge passes Can be used discretely (under desk, in pocket) Cost: $0-5 ALTERNATIVE STIMULATION: For Sensory SEEKERS: Twisting/Manipulation Activities: Friendship bracelet making (twisting, braiding) Pipe cleaner crafts (constant twisting) Twist ties into sculptures Twisting wire for crafts Finger knitting or crochet (repetitive motions)
Cost: $3-10 Why it works: Satisfies twisting motor pattern with appropriate objects Hair-Like Textures to Manipulate: Yarn pompom making Fringe-making with paper or fabric String or rope braiding Tassel-making Cost: $2-8 Fidget Tools with Twisting: Commercial tangle toys Rubik's cube or similar twist puzzles Fidget spinner Twisty puzzle toys Cost: $5-15 Functional Twisting Activities: Twisting wet towels (laundry help) Opening jars (resistance + twisting) Using screwdriver (supervised) Wind-up toys Cost: Free (using household tasks) For Sensory AVOIDERS: (Rare for hair twirling, as this is usually seeking behavior) OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY ACTIVITIES: Hand and Finger Engagement: Fine Motor Activities (Keeps Hands Busy): Beading with small beads Sewing or embroidery Lacing activities Small Lego or building toys Model building Jewelry making Duration: 15-20 minute sessions
Frequency: 3-4 times daily Bilateral Coordination Activities: Clapping games with patterns Hand jive games Playing instruments (piano, guitar) Cutting and crafts requiring two hands Why: Keeps both hands engaged, reduces one-hand-to-hair pattern Heavy Work for Hands: Therapy putty exercises Squeezing stress balls Hand strengthening activities Provides proprioceptive input hands are seeking Frequency: Every 60-90 minutes Replacement Habit Training: When urge to twirl hair noticed, immediately: Grasp twist toy Twist 20 times Place hands in lap or on table Take 3 deep breaths Practice sequence 10 times daily even when not twirling Creates new neural pathway MASSAGE TECHNIQUES: Hand and Finger Massage (Reduces Hair-Twirling Impulse): Technique: Massage each finger individually, twisting motion Deep pressure on palm Roll each finger between thumb and fingers (twisting sensation)
Compress knuckles and finger joints Hand massage with lotion in twisting motions Duration: 5-10 minutes per hand Frequency: 3-4 times daily, especially before high-twirling times Why it works: Provides proprioceptive input to hands and satisfies twisting motor pattern Scalp Massage (Provides Hair/Scalp Input): Technique: Firm circular motions across entire scalp Gentle tugging of hair (with permission) Pressure point massage on head Use fingertips, firm pressure Duration: 5-10 minutes Frequency: Morning and bedtime Why it works: Provides organized sensory input to scalp area that child seeks Combined Approach: Scalp massage (satisfies scalp/hair sensory need) Immediately followed by hand massage with twisting motions Then provide twist fidget Most effective when done proactively Manifestation 2: Pulling Hair (May Indicate Trichotillomania) CRITICAL NOTE: Hair pulling that results in hair loss, bald spots, or significant distress is likely trichotillomania, a BFRB requiring professional treatment. Please consult:
Dermatologist (assess scalp damage) Mental health professional specializing in BFRBs Consider Habit Reversal Training (HRT) or Comprehensive Behavioral Model (ComB) The following strategies are supplementary, not replacement for professional treatment. PHYSICAL TECHNIQUE TO INTERRUPT: "Immediate Gentle Intervention" When pulling observed, approach very calmly (no alarm or judgment) Gently place your hand over their hand Slowly guide hand away from hair Place high-resistance fidget in hand immediately Apply deep pressure to their hand/arm Say calmly: "I see your hand needed something to do. Let's use this." Stay with child, providing support Why it works: Non-judgmental intervention prevents shame while providing immediate alternative. Deep pressure regulates. DIY ALTERNATIVE TOOL: "Pulling Resistance Kit" Materials Needed: Items that provide resistance when pulled Textured items similar to hair
Items to Include: Yarn or String Ball: Wrap yarn into tight ball Child can pull strands out Provides hair-like texture + pulling resistance Cost: $2-5 Rubber Band Board: Pegboard or board with nails Stretch rubber bands between pegs Child pulls and releases rubber bands Provides resistance similar to hair pulling Cost: $5-10 Velcro Strips: Two pieces of velcro attached together Child pulls apart (resistance) and resticks Can be worn on wrist Cost: $2-5 Therapy Putty with Embedded Items: Hide small beads or items in therapy putty Child pulls items out (resistance) Satisfies pulling urge Cost: $5-10 How to Make Portable Kit: Small container (mint tin) Include 3-4 pulling alternatives Keep multiple kits (home, school, car, bathroom) Refresh weekly Cost: $10-15 total
ALTERNATIVE STIMULATION: For Sensory SEEKERS (Most Common for Pulling): High-Resistance Pulling Activities: Resistance bands (pull and stretch) Pulling taffy or stretchy candy Stretching therapy putty Pulling apart toy pop-beads Tug-of-war games Cost: $5-15 Why it works: Provides intense proprioceptive pulling sensation Hair-Like Textures to Pull: Troll doll hair Yarn or string to pull apart Fringe on fabrics to manipulate Long-fiber fur fabric pieces Cost: $3-10 Fidget Tools: Therapy putty (extra firm) Stretchy strings or cords Pull-apart toys Magnetic putty Cost: $5-15 For Complex BFRB (Trichotillomania): Professional intervention required May need Cognitive Behavioral Therapy May need medication evaluation Habit Reversal Training Support groups These tools are supplementary only OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY ACTIVITIES: Intensive Proprioceptive Input (Reduces Pulling Urges): Heavy Resistance Activities: Pull heavy wagon or cart
Tug-of-war games (with adult or resistance band) Pulling weeds in garden Opening tight jars Resistance band exercises Duration: 10-15 minutes Frequency: Every 60-90 minutes, before high-pulling times Hand Strengthening: Therapy putty exercises (especially pulling and stretching) Squeezing activities Climbing activities (playground, rock wall) Hanging from bars Why: Provides intense proprioceptive input to arms/hands Awareness and Replacement Training: Teach child to recognize pulling urge BEFORE it happens Body scan: "Where do I feel the urge?" (hands, scalp, tension) Replacement behavior: When urge noticed, immediately: Squeeze stress ball 20 times OR Do 10 wall pushes OR Pull resistance band 10 times Practice replacement even when not pulling (builds habit) Environmental Modifications: Keep hands busy during high-risk times (TV watching, reading, homework) Fidgets always accessible
Barriers (hats, headbands) during high-risk situations Mirrors covered if pulling happens while looking in mirror MASSAGE TECHNIQUES: Intensive Hand/Arm Massage (Reduces Pulling Impulse): Preparation: Firm pressure throughout Technique: Deep tissue massage of arms (shoulder to fingertips) Focus on pulling muscles (biceps, forearms) Compress each finger joint Pulling massage: Gently pull each finger (with permission) Hand massage with kneading Duration: 15 minutes Frequency: Minimum 3 times daily (morning, mid-afternoon, bedtime) Scalp Massage (Desensitization and Organized Input): Technique: Firm pressure circular motions across scalp Cover all areas where pulling occurs Gentle hair tugging (with permission) Use coconut oil or hair oil for added sensory input Duration: 10 minutes Frequency: Daily, preferably before bedtime Why it works: Provides organized sensory input to scalp, may reduce urge to pull
IMPORTANT: Trichotillomania requires professional treatment. These are supportive strategies only. Manifestations: Stroking hair rhythmically- not available Combing fingers through hair repeatedly-not available Braiding/unbraiding small sections constantly-not avalable Touching/feeling hair texture-not avaiuilable Rubbing hair against face or lips-not avaiilable Smelling hair while touching-not available
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 3. TACTILE (TOUCH) STIMMING > A. Self-Touch Stimming > Level 3: Nail and Cuticle Stimming
Causation: Over-stimulated: Focused activity calms anxiety Under-stimulated: Fingertips have high nerve density; intense input Sensitivity: Oral-motor seeking (nail biting) + tactile BFRB: Excoriation (skin-picking) or onychophagia may require treatment Sensory Profile: Seeker: Intense, frequent, may cause damage Anxiety-Related: Increases during stress; may not be purely sensory BFRB: Compulsive nature indicates clinical condition beyond stimming Description: Manipulating nails, cuticles, or fingertips Manifestation 1: Biting Nails (Onychophagia) PHYSICAL TECHNIQUE TO INTERRUPT: "Mouth Redirect with Oral Alternative" When nail biting observed, approach calmly Gently guide hand away from mouth IMMEDIATELY place chewable item in mouth (chewy tube, gum, crunchy snack) Say: "Let's give your mouth something else to chew" Keep oral alternative accessible at all times Why it works: Nail biting provides oral-motor input. Replacing with appropriate chewable satisfies the same need.
DIY ALTERNATIVE TOOL: "Chew and Fidget Toolkit" Materials Needed: Chewable alternatives (various textures and resistances) Hand fidgets Items to Include: DIY Chewable Necklace: Food-grade silicone beads (can purchase online, $10-15) OR coffee stirrer straws cut into 1-inch pieces and strung on cord Child wears and chews when urge arises Cost: $5-15 Household Chewables: Clean pencil eraser (new, unused) Coffee stirrer straws Clean plastic tubing (aquarium tubing from hardware store) Licorice or dried fruit leather Cost: $2-8 Hand Fidgets (Keeps Hands from Mouth): Stress ball Therapy putty Textured fabric square Keeps hands occupied so they don't go to mouth Cost: $5-10 How to Make Complete Kit: Small pencil case or pouch Include 2-3 chewable items Include 2-3 hand fidgets Keep multiple kits (home, school, car)
Refresh monthly Cost: $15-25 total ALTERNATIVE STIMULATION: For Sensory SEEKERS (Most Common for Nail Biting): Oral Motor Alternatives: Chewy tubes or chewable jewelry Gum (if age-appropriate) Crunchy foods (carrots, celery, apples, pretzels) Chewy foods (dried mango, fruit leather, bagels, jerky) Drinking through straw (resistive) Blowing activities (whistles, bubbles, kazoo) Cost: $10-20 for chewables, $5-10 for food Why it works: Provides oral-motor sensory input child seeks Hand Alternatives (Keeps Hands Busy): Therapy putty Stress balls Fidget cube Tangle toys Pop-it toys Cost: $5-15 Nail Care Alternatives: Nail file kept accessible - file nails instead of biting Nail brush - scrub nails when urge arises Clear nail polish with bitter taste (some children respond) Bandaids on fingertips (physical barrier) Cost: $5-15 Functional Oral Activities:
Chewing gum during homework/screen time Drinking water through straw frequently Eating crunchy snacks during high-risk times Cost: Cost of food items For Sensory AVOIDERS: (Unlikely to bite nails, as this is seeking behavior) OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY ACTIVITIES: Oral Motor Regulation: Oral Motor Exercises (Satisfies Oral Need): Blowing through straw into water (make bubbles) Blowing cotton balls across table Whistles, kazoos, harmonicas Drinking thick smoothies through straw Duration: 5-10 minutes Frequency: Before typical nail-biting times (3-4x daily) Heavy Work (Whole Body Regulation): Nail biting often increases when under-stimulated Vigorous physical activity every 90 minutes: Jumping jacks (20 reps) Wall pushes (10 reps, 10 seconds each) Animal walks (bear, crab, frog) Carrying heavy items Regulates nervous system, reduces nail biting Hand Engagement Activities: Keeps hands too busy to go to mouth
Fine motor crafts: beading, lacing, building Therapy putty exercises Squeezing activities Duration: 15-20 minutes Frequency: 3-4 times daily Awareness Training: Self-Monitoring: Tally counter: Child clicks each time they notice urge to bite Awareness without judgment Identify high-risk times (homework, TV, car rides, stress) Target interventions to those times Replacement Habit: When urge noticed: Step 1: Place hands flat on surface or in pockets Step 2: Take 3 deep breaths Step 3: Grab oral alternative (chewable) Step 4: Use for 2-3 minutes Practice this sequence 5 times daily even when not biting Creates new neural pathway MASSAGE TECHNIQUES: Oral-Facial Massage (Provides Oral-Motor Input): Preparation: Wash hands Technique: Jaw massage: Circular motions on jaw muscles Cheek massage: Inside cheeks (with gloved finger or outside cheeks)
Around mouth: Firm circles around lips Chin and jaw: Firm pressure along jawline Duration: 5-10 minutes Frequency: 2-3 times daily (especially before high-risk times) Why it works: Provides organized oral-motor sensory input Hand and Finger Massage (Reduces Hand-to-Mouth Impulse): Technique: Deep pressure massage on each hand Individual finger massage (pull gently, compress joints) Palm pressure with kneading Fingertip compression Nail bed pressure (ironically satisfying) Duration: 5-10 minutes per hand Frequency: 3-4 times daily Combined Approach: Oral-facial massage (satisfies oral need) Hand massage (reduces hand-to-mouth movement) Immediately provide chewable alternative Most effective before high-risk times (homework, bedtime, car rides) Manifestations: Picking cuticles until bleeding- not available Peeling skin around nails-not available Scratching nails against each other-not available Filing or scraping nails obsessively-not available
Pressing on nail beds- not available Pulling hangnails repeatedly-not available
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 3. TACTILE (TOUCH) STIMMING > B. Object Tactile Stimming > Level 1: Texture Exploration
Causation: Over-stimulated: Predictable textures are organizing Under-stimulated: Variety of textures provides rich sensory input Sensitivity: Tactile discrimination development; sensory exploration Comfort: Specific textures are emotionally regulating Sensory Profile: Seeker: Touches everything; seeks novel textures constantly Avoider: Selective about textures; distressed by certain feels Selective: Craves specific texture (soft) but avoids others (sticky, rough) Description: Seeking and touching various textures Manifestations: Rubbing soft fabrics (blankets, clothing) constantly Touching smooth surfaces (tables, walls, glass) Seeking rough textures (sandpaper, concrete, carpet) Running hands over textured walls or surfaces Touching everything in environment (compulsive) Collecting textured objects to touch repeatedly Carrying "comfort items" for texture (specific blankets, toys) Rubbing tags on clothing or objects
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 3. TACTILE (TOUCH) STIMMING > B. Object Tactile Stimming > Level 2: Manipulative Play
Causation: Over-stimulated: Focused tactile activity blocks overwhelming input Under-stimulated: Resistance and texture provide rich input Sensitivity: Proprioceptive + tactile integration; cause-effect learning Motor Planning: Developing fine motor skills through repetition Sensory Profile: Seeker: High intensity, long duration, seeks resistive materials Texture-Selective: Specific materials preferred (wet vs dry, smooth vs rough) Proprioceptive: Needs resistance + tactile simultaneously Description: Handling and manipulating objects for tactile feedback Manifestations: Squeezing stress balls or fidgets (100-500+ squeezes) Playing with putty, slime, or playdough (30+ minutes) Kneading or molding clay repeatedly Crumpling paper or fabric Tearing paper into small pieces (10-100+ sheets) Rolling objects between hands or fingers Squishing foam or squishy toys Manipulating kinetic sand for hours
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 3. TACTILE (TOUCH) STIMMING > B. Object Tactile Stimming > Level 3: Temperature and Unusual Tactile Seeking
Causation: Over-stimulated: Extreme temperatures "reset" tactile system Under-stimulated: Need intense tactile input to register sensation Sensitivity: Under-responsive to typical tactile input; needs extreme Danger: May indicate severe under-responsiveness requiring safety measures Sensory Profile: Extreme Seeker: High pain threshold; seeks intense sensations Temperature Seeking: Specific need for hot or cold input Safety Concern: May not feel pain appropriately; risk of injury Description: Seeking extreme or unusual tactile experiences Manifestations: Seeking cold (ice, frozen items) to touch repeatedly Seeking warmth (heating pads, warm water) excessively Touching hot surfaces (carefully or dangerously) Playing in water for hours (bath, sink, hose) Walking barefoot to feel surfaces Seeking sticky substances (glue, tape adhesive) Touching wet or slimy things (mud, gel, food) Seeking pain sensations (pressing hard, scratching firmly)
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 3. TACTILE (TOUCH) STIMMING > C. Tactile Defensive/Avoidant Stimming > Level 1: Touch Rejection
Causation: Over-stimulated: Preventing tactile input that causes distress Sensitive: Severe tactile defensiveness; protecting vulnerable areas Control: Need to manage tactile environment completely Anxiety: Fear-based avoidance of unpredictable touch Sensory Profile: Extreme Avoider: Cannot tolerate typical touch experiences Protective: Behavioral strategies to prevent sensory assault Anxious: Touch avoidance tied to anxiety disorder may require therapy Description: Actively avoiding or rejecting touch sensations Manifestations: Refusing to touch certain textures (tags, wool, sticky) Extreme reaction to unexpected touch Only wearing specific soft clothing Refusing messy play (paint, mud, food textures) Walking on tiptoes to avoid floor sensations Constantly brushing off perceived sensations ("bugs") Refusing to hold certain objects Washing hands excessively after touching things
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 3. TACTILE (TOUCH) STIMMING > C. Tactile Defensive/Avoidant Stimming > Level 2: Self-Protective Touch Behaviors
Causation: Over-stimulated: Preventing tactile input that causes distress Sensitive: Severe tactile defensiveness; protecting vulnerable areas Control: Need to manage tactile environment completely Anxiety: Fear-based avoidance of unpredictable touch Sensory Profile: Extreme Avoider: Cannot tolerate typical touch experiences Protective: Behavioral strategies to prevent sensory assault Anxious: Touch avoidance tied to anxiety disorder may require therapy Description: Using touch to prevent unwanted tactile input Manifestations: Keeping arms crossed to prevent touch Wearing long sleeves/pants even when hot Wearing gloves to avoid direct touch Using tools instead of hands (fork for everything, sticks) Walking with hands in pockets constantly Positioning body to prevent incidental touch Maintaining large personal space (3-6 feet)
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 3. TACTILE (TOUCH) STIMMING > C. Tactile Defensive/Avoidant Stimming > Level 3: Aggressive Touch Responses
Causation: Over-stimulated: Touch triggers neurological pain or extreme distress Sensitive: Severe tactile defensiveness; touch perceived as threat Trauma: Previous negative tactile experiences create fear Neurological: Possible underlying pain disorders or extreme sensitivity Sensory Profile: Crisis-Level Avoider: Touch triggers fight-or-flight response Medical Concern: Requires occupational therapy evaluation Safety: Behaviors protect from neurologically painful input Description: Fight-or-flight reactions to touch Manifestations: Hitting or pushing when touched unexpectedly Screaming or crying when touched Fleeing from touch situations Meltdowns after haircuts, teeth brushing, etc. Refusing medical exams or procedures involving touch Extreme tantrums about clothing or bathing Vomiting or gagging from texture experiences
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 4. PROPRIOCEPTIVE STIMMING
(Body Position and Movement Awareness)
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 4. PROPRIOCEPTIVE STIMMING > A. Joint and Muscle Stimming > Level 1: Pressing and Pushing
Causation: Over-stimulated: Deep pressure is calming and organizing Under-stimulated: Muscles and joints "hungry" for input Sensitivity: Proprioceptive system under-responsive; needs intense input Calming: Deep pressure releases calming neurotransmitters Sensory Profile: Seeker: Seeks heavy, intense pressure throughout day Self-Regulating: Using pressure to calm anxious nervous system Under-Responsive: Needs extreme input to feel body position Description: Applying pressure to joints and muscles Manifestation 1: Pushing Hands Together (Prayer Position, 10-60 seconds) Manifestation 1: Pushing Hands Together (Prayer Position) Physical Redirect Technique: Place your hand gently on the child's shoulder and say their name softly. Guide them to take 3 deep breaths with you, counting slowly "1...2...3" on each inhale and exhale. This interrupts the pattern without startling. DIY Alternative Tool: Homemade Therapy Putty: Mix 2 cups white glue + 1½ cups liquid starch + food coloring. Knead for 5-10 minutes until it forms a ball. Store in airtight container. Child squeezes and presses putty between palms with same motion as prayer pressing.
Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Rice-filled sock: Fill a thick sock with 2 cups uncooked rice, tie tightly. Child squeezes between palms for 30-60 seconds, releases, repeats. Towel squeezes: Roll a hand towel tightly, child presses it between palms as hard as they can, hold 10 seconds, release. Playdough press: Regular playdough from store. Flatten balls between palms, press hard, feel resistance. Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Wall push-ups: Stand arm's length from wall, push against it counting to 10, release. Repeat 10 times. Heavy books carry: Stack 3-5 heavy books, child carries across room and back, pressing books together tightly. Compression sandwich: Child lies on stomach, place large couch cushion on back, apply gentle pressure for 2-3 minutes. For Avoiders: Gentle hand massage: Using lotion, massage palms in small circles, warning before each touch.
Self-applied pressure: Teach child to squeeze their own forearms gently, they control pressure. Predictable press routine: Press hands together for count of 5 only, same time each day. Massage Techniques: Palm pressure massage: Place thumbs in child's palm center, press firmly in small circles for 30 seconds each hand Finger compression: Gently squeeze each finger from base to tip, providing deep pressure Hand sandwich: Place child's hand between your two palms, press firmly for 10 seconds, release Manifestation 2: Pressing Palms Against Walls/Doors/Furniture Physical Redirect Technique: Walk calmly to the child, kneel to their eye level, place your hand over theirs on the wall and say "I see you need strong pushing. Let's do wall pushes together instead." Guide them through 5 controlled wall push-ups.
DIY Alternative Tool: Wall Push Board: Take a sturdy cardboard box (12"x12"), cover with textured fabric (corduroy, velvet), tape securely to wall at child's chest height. Mark target spots with colored tape. Child pushes specific spots with palms. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Pushing doors open: Assign child to push open all doors in the house (when safe), using full palm pressure Furniture push: Have child push heavy ottoman or chair across room (on carpet for safety), emphasizing palm pressure Wall ball: Inflate a beach ball halfway, child presses it against wall with palms, holds for 10 seconds Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Wheelbarrow walks: Hold child's legs while they walk on hands across room, 3-5 trips Resistance band pushes: Tie resistance band to doorknob, child pushes away with palms 20 times
Pushing race: Child pushes large cardboard box filled with books across room as fast as possible For Avoiders: Gentle wall lean: Just lean shoulder against wall for 20 seconds, building up tolerance Self-controlled push: Child decides how hard and how long to push against wall Visual timer push: Push against wall only while 30-second sand timer runs, predictable end Massage Techniques: Forearm rolling massage: Using a rolling pin, roll firmly up and down child's forearms for 1-2 minutes Palm pressure points: Press firmly on the meaty part of palm below thumb for 15 seconds Wrist compressions: Gently squeeze around wrist joint, hold for 5 seconds, release, repeat 5 times Manifestation 3: Leaning Body Weight onto Surfaces Physical Redirect Technique: Approach from the side, gently touch their back and say "Your body needs pressure. Let's try a better way." Guide them to lie face-down on the floor with a pillow under their chest.
DIY Alternative Tool: Lap Weight: Sew together two 12"x16" pieces of denim fabric on 3 sides. Fill with 3-4 lbs of dried beans or rice, sew closed. Child places on lap when sitting. Alternatively, use a backpack filled with books (2-5 lbs depending on child's size). Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Couch cushion press: Stack 2-3 couch cushions on child (lying on stomach), leave for 5-10 minutes Bean bag chair sitting: Child burrows into bean bag chair, letting it conform around them Mattress sandwich: Child lies between mattress and box spring or under mattress edge Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Burrito roll: Roll child tightly in blanket, apply gentle pressure along body, unroll slowly Pillow crash: Stack soft pillows, child jumps/crashes into them 15-20 times
Under-table work: Have child do homework/activities lying under heavy table with weighted lap pad For Avoiders: Light blanket draping: Gently drape light blanket over shoulders, they decide when to remove Pillow hug: Child hugs pillow to chest while sitting, controls pressure themselves Partial coverage: Only cover legs or torso, not whole body at once Massage Techniques: Back pressure massage: Child lies face down, use flat palms to press firmly along both sides of spine (never directly on spine) from shoulders to hips Shoulder compressions: Place hands on tops of shoulders, press down firmly for 10 seconds Full body pressure: Child lies down, use a large exercise ball to roll over back, legs, arms with firm pressure Manifestation 4: Hugging Self Tightly/Squeezing Arms
Physical Redirect Technique: Sit beside child, mirror their hug position, then say "I'll count to 5 while you hug tight, then we'll try bear hugs." Count slowly, then offer a firm 10-second hug. DIY Alternative Tool: Compression Vest: Cut the bottom and sleeves off a stretchy athletic compression shirt one size too small. Child wears this under regular clothes. Or use a snug-fitting swim shirt (rash guard) worn regularly. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Tight clothing layers: Have child wear snug undershirt plus another fitted shirt Scarf wrap: Wrap a long scarf around torso snugly (not constricting breathing), tuck in ends Elastic bands: Use elastic exercise band, wrap around chest/arms under adult supervision, feels like a hug Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers:
Bear hug squeezes: Adult gives 5-10 firm bear hugs throughout day, holding 10-15 seconds each Sleeping bag time: Child gets into sleeping bag, zip it up, roll gently back and forth Lycra body sock: Purchase inexpensive lycra fabric (1-2 yards), sew into tube shape, child gets inside and stretches against it For Avoiders: Side-by-side sitting: Sit close with light shoulder contact, no hugging Hand squeeze: Just squeeze hands instead of full body hugs Warned hugs: Always ask "5-second hug?" so they can prepare and consent Massage Techniques: Arm squeeze massage: Starting at shoulder, squeeze down arm to wrist using both hands, firm pressure, 3-5 times per arm Bicep/tricep compressions: Squeeze upper arm muscles for 5 seconds, release, repeat 5 times each arm
Forearm pressure strokes: Use flat palm to press firmly down forearm from elbow to wrist, slow strokes Manifestation 5: Pressing Knees Together or Apart Forcefully Physical Redirect Technique: Kneel in front of child, place your hands gently on their knees and say "Let's give your legs strong work to do." Have them stand and do 10 squats with you, or march in place with high knees for 30 seconds. DIY Alternative Tool: Resistance Knee Band: Cut a 2-inch wide strip from an old bicycle inner tube to create a circular band (20-24 inches around). Child places band around knees and pushes out against resistance, or around ankles for pushing in. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Pillow squeeze: Place a firm couch pillow between knees, child squeezes hard for 10 seconds, releases, repeats 10 times
Ball squeeze: Use a partially inflated soccer ball or basketball between knees, squeeze rhythmically Resistance sitting: Tie a belt around chair legs at knee height, child pushes knees out against belt while sitting Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Crab walk races: Walk sideways in crab position (bottom up, hands and feet down) across room Scissor kicks: Lying on back, kick legs out and in repeatedly, 20-30 times Frog jumps: Squat down, jump forward like a frog, emphasizing the leg push-off, 15-20 jumps For Avoiders: Gentle leg swings: Standing, swing one leg forward and back slowly, 10 times each leg Seated knee lifts: While sitting, simply lift one knee up and down slowly, 10 times each Ankle rolls: Sit and rotate ankles in circles, 10 each direction, less intense than knee movements
Massage Techniques: Thigh compressions: Using both hands, squeeze thigh muscles firmly from hip to knee, 5 times each leg Calf squeezes: Squeeze calf muscle with both hands, hold 5 seconds, release, repeat 5 times per leg Knee joint pressure: Place hands on either side of knee, press inward gently for 10 seconds Manifestation 6: Pushing Fingertips Together Physical Redirect Technique: Gently tap the child's wrist and say "Let's make your fingers strong a different way." Guide them to spread fingers wide like a star, hold for 5 seconds, then make a fist, repeating 5 times. DIY Alternative Tool: Finger Resistance Board: Cut a piece of cardboard (8"x8"), poke 10 small holes, thread thick rubber bands through holes vertically. Child pushes fingers against rubber band resistance. Or glue clothespins around the edge of a small box, child squeezes them open.
Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Clothespin squeezing: Give child 20-30 clothespins to squeeze open and attach around edge of coffee can, 2-3 times daily Chip clip exercises: Collect 10 chip clips, child squeezes them open and clips onto cardboard repeatedly Finger push-ups: Fingertips only on table, do mini push-ups using just finger strength, 10 repetitions Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Playdough strength: Hide small objects (beads, coins) in playdough, child digs them out using finger strength Stress ball squeezes: Squeeze stress ball or tennis ball 50-100 times with each hand Hand gripper tool: Buy inexpensive hand strengthener from dollar store, squeeze 20-30 times per hand For Avoiders: Gentle finger touches: Touch fingertip to fingertip gently on each hand, no pressure Finger painting: Light sensory play without intense pressure
Puppet play: Use finger puppets which provide light pressure they control Massage Techniques: Finger pulls: Gently grasp each finger and pull from base to tip with firm pressure, 2-3 times per finger Fingertip pressure: Press firmly on pad of each fingertip for 5 seconds Hand web massage: Massage the webbing between thumb and index finger with deep circular motions Manifestation 7: Sitting/Lying Under Heavy Objects Physical Redirect Technique: Approach calmly, lift edge of object slightly and say "I see you need heavy feeling. Let's get your special heavy blanket instead." Help them transition to proper weighted item. DIY Alternative Tool: Homemade Weighted Blanket: Purchase 2-3 yards of fleece fabric and 5-10 lbs of poly pellets (craft store) or dried rice. Create pockets by sewing horizontal lines across fabric every 6 inches, fill pockets evenly with pellets, sew closed. Should weigh approximately 10% of child's body weight. Or simply fill multiple ziplock bags with rice (1 lb each), layer 5-6 bags between two sheets, safety pin together.
Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Book stack: While child lies on stomach reading/watching, place 3-5 heavy books across their back Weighted stuffed animal: Fill old stuffed animal with rice or beans through small opening, sew closed (2-3 lbs), place on child's lap or chest Couch cushion cocoon: Stack couch cushions on top of child (ensure they can breathe), leave for 10-15 minutes Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Weighted lap time: Child sits with weighted object (5-10 lbs) on lap during calm activities (reading, TV, homework) Compression tunnel: Create tunnel with couch cushions, child crawls through tight space repeatedly Body wrap: Wrap child firmly in blanket, roll them gently back and forth like a log For Avoiders: Light blanket only: Use regular light blanket, let them add layers if wanted
Feet only weights: Place small weight (1-2 lbs) on feet while lying down, not whole body Gradual introduction: Start with 1 minute under weight, slowly increase over weeks Massage Techniques: Deep pressure massage: Using flat palms, press firmly down child's back, legs, arms, holding each area for 5-10 seconds Rolling pin massage: Use a rolling pin to roll firmly over child's back, legs, arms (through clothing) for 2-3 minutes Weighted ball massage: Use a small medicine ball (2-3 lbs) to roll over body parts with firm pressure Manifestation 8: Squeezing Between Furniture and Walls Physical Redirect Technique: Crouch near the space and say softly "Your body wants tight squeezes. Let's find a better squeeze spot." Guide them to a safer tight space you've prepared, like between two large pillows.
DIY Alternative Tool: Squeeze Box: Take a large cardboard box, line three sides with thick foam or pillows, create an opening on one side. Child climbs in and gets compression from three sides safely. Or create a "reading nook" by draping heavy blankets over chairs placed close together. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Pillow press: Place child between couch back and 3-4 firm couch pillows pressed against them Sleeping bag squeeze: Child gets into sleeping bag, you zip it up and place pillows on both sides Chair sandwich: Two dining chairs facing each other with cushions, child sits between getting squeezed Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Lycra swing: Purchase 2-3 yards of lycra fabric, tie ends to create hammock/swing, child gets inside and it wraps around them
Foam roller tunnel: Line up 3-4 foam pool noodles on floor, child rolls through them Tight space crawling: Create obstacle course through tight spaces (under tables, between cushions) child crawls through repeatedly For Avoiders: Open-ended spaces: Provide three-sided boxes/spaces with open front so they never feel trapped Quick escape: Any tight space must allow immediate exit Beside not inside: Sit beside narrow spaces rather than in them Massage Techniques: Side compression massage: Child lies on side, press firmly along entire side of body from shoulder to hip for 10 seconds Limb sandwich: Sandwich each arm between your two hands, squeeze firmly from shoulder to wrist, repeat for legs Spinal pressure: Child lies face down, use palms to press on either side of spine (not directly on it) with firm, steady pressure
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 4. PROPRIOCEPTIVE STIMMING > A. Joint and Muscle Stimming > Level 2: Pulling and Stretching
Causation: Over-stimulated: Stretching tension releases regulation Under-stimulated: Pulling provides strong proprioceptive feedback Sensitivity: Body needs to know where it is in space constantly Motor Planning: Exploring body capabilities and limits Sensory Profile: Seeker: Constant pulling and stretching all day Joint-Focused: Specific attention to joint sensations Mixed: Combines proprioceptive + auditory (cracking sounds) Description: Creating tension in joints and muscles Manifestation 1: Pulling on own Fingers (Cracking Knuckles) 20-100+ times daily Physical Redirect Technique: Place your hand gently over theirs and say "Let's give your fingers a better stretch." Guide them to interlace fingers and push palms away from body, stretching arms forward fully, hold 10 seconds, release, repeat 3 times. DIY Alternative Tool: Finger Stretcher: Cut 5 small slits (1 inch apart) in a thick rubber band. Child places fingertips in slits and stretches band outward, providing resistance and stretch without pulling joints. Or thread elastic cord through buttons, child pulls cord to stretch.
Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Putty finger pull: Use therapy putty or playdough, pinch pieces and pull apart with fingers 30-50 times Rubber band stretches: Loop rubber bands around pairs of fingers, spread fingers apart to stretch band, 10 repetitions per finger combination Towel twisting: Give child a small hand towel, twist it tightly with both hands in opposite directions, 15-20 repetitions Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Monkey bar hanging: Hang from monkey bars or sturdy door frame pull-up bar for 10-30 seconds, repeat 5-10 times Tug of war: Play tug-of-war with rope or towel, 2-3 minutes of pulling Stretchy toys: Give child stretchy rubber toys (stretch armstrong type), pull and stretch repeatedly For Avoiders: Gentle yoga: Simple child-friendly yoga poses with gentle stretching (cat-cow, child's pose)
Slow finger movements: Slowly open and close hands without pulling, focusing on smooth movement No-force stretches: Stretches where they decide how far to go, no pulling Massage Techniques: Finger traction: Hold base of each finger firmly, gently pull finger straight out from hand for 5 seconds, repeat each finger Knuckle massage: Use thumb to massage around each knuckle joint in firm circles for 15 seconds Hand stretching massage: Gently bend each finger backward and forward at each joint, providing controlled stretch Manifestation 2: Stretching Arms Overhead Repeatedly Physical Redirect Technique: Stand beside child, raise your arms with theirs and say "Let's do big stretches together properly." Lead them through 5 overhead reaches with 5-second holds, breathing deeply with each stretch. DIY Alternative Tool: Resistance Stretch Band: Use an old bicycle inner tube or resistance band (dollar store). Child holds both ends, stretches band overhead and outward slowly, hold for 10 seconds, release. Repeat 10 times. Mark start and end points to show progress.
Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Door frame stretches: Child stands in doorway, places palms on frame above head, leans forward gently for 10 seconds Towel pulls: Hold towel with both hands, raise overhead, pull ends apart creating tension, hold 10 seconds Wall climbing: Child stands arm's length from wall, "climbs" wall with fingertips, reaching higher each time Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Star jumps: Jump with arms and legs spread wide like a star, 20-30 repetitions Swimming motions: Practice swimming arm strokes (freestyle, backstroke) standing up, 2-3 minutes Ribbon dancing: Attach ribbons/streamers to stick, child creates big overhead movements For Avoiders: Seated arm raises: Raise arms only to shoulder height while sitting, less intense Forward reaches: Reach forward instead of overhead, gentler stretch
Supported stretches: Lean on wall or furniture while stretching, feels more secure Massage Techniques: Arm traction: Hold wrist firmly, gently pull arm straight away from shoulder socket for 10 seconds, each arm Shoulder rolling massage: Massage shoulder muscles with firm circular motions while gently rotating arm Tricep stretch massage: Support elbow, gently bend arm behind head while massaging tricep muscle Manifestation 3: Pulling Legs Into Chest and Releasing Physical Redirect Technique: Sit on floor beside child, mirror their position and say "Let's do knee hugs together the right way." Guide them to pull both knees to chest, hold 10 seconds, release slowly, repeat 5 times with controlled breathing. DIY Alternative Tool: Leg Stretcher Loop: Cut an old belt or make a loop from sturdy fabric (24-30 inches around). Child lies on back, places loop around one foot, holds ends, gently pulls leg toward chest using strap, controls stretch intensity. Switch legs.
Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Chair leg stretches: Sit on chair, lift one foot onto another chair, lean forward to stretch hamstring, 30 seconds each leg Doorway leg stretch: Lie near doorway, place one leg up against door frame, scoot closer to increase stretch Towel leg pulls: Lie on back, loop towel around foot, hold ends, pull leg toward body Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Bridge pose: Lie on back, plant feet, lift hips high, hold 10 seconds, lower, repeat 10 times Bicycle kicks: Lie on back, pedal legs in air like riding bicycle, 1-2 minutes Happy baby pose: Lie on back, grab feet, pull knees toward armpits, rock gently side to side For Avoiders: Partial leg lifts: Just lift leg slightly without pulling to chest, gentler movement
Supported stretches: Place folded towel under knee when stretching, adds comfort Slow movements: Move legs very slowly through range of motion without forcing Massage Techniques: Hip flexor massage: Child lies on back, massage the front of hip/upper thigh area with firm pressure Hamstring strokes: Use flat palm to press firmly down back of thigh from hip to knee repeatedly Leg compressions: Squeeze leg muscles (thigh and calf) firmly, hold 5 seconds, release, work down entire leg Manifestation 4: Hanging from Bars or Furniture Physical Redirect Technique: Stand nearby for safety, place hand near child's waist and say "I see you need hanging time. Let's count how long you can hang safely." Count slowly to 10-30 seconds, encourage them to drop down gently, rest, repeat.
DIY Alternative Tool: Safe Hanging Bar: Install an over-door pull-up bar (inexpensive, hardware store) in a doorway at appropriate height. Place thick rug or exercise mat underneath. Supervise all hanging activities. Or use a sturdy tree branch with adult supervision. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Doorway hang: Child hangs from top of doorframe (if strong enough and door is stable) with adult support Table edge hang: Child lies on stomach on sturdy table, holds edge with hands, dangles upper body off edge safely (adult holds legs) Bed side hang: Child lies perpendicular on bed, dangles arms off side, lets them hang down heavily Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Arm wrestling: Wrestle with adult or peer for 2-3 minutes, using arm strength Carrying activities: Child carries heavy bags of groceries, laundry baskets, stacks of books
Climbing opportunities: Playground climbing structures, rock climbing wall, tree climbing (supervised) For Avoiders: Standing arm holds: Just hold arms out to sides for 10-20 seconds, no hanging Support hanging: Hang with feet still touching ground, partial weight only Short durations: Hang for only 3-5 seconds, very brief exposure Massage Techniques: Shoulder decompression: Child sits, you stand behind, place hands on shoulder tops, gently pull upward to decompress joints Arm hanging massage: Let child's arm hang loosely, massage from shoulder to fingertips with firm downward strokes Upper back release: Massage upper back and shoulder blade areas with firm circular motions Manifestation 5: Tugging on Clothing or Accessories Physical Redirect Technique: Gently touch the child's hand and say "Your hands need pulling work. Let's find something better to tug." Hand them a resistance band or stretchy toy and demonstrate gentle pulling motion.
DIY Alternative Tool: Tug Bracelet: Braid together 3 strands of thick elastic cord (12 inches each), tie ends together to form bracelet. Child wears on wrist, can pull and stretch it without damaging clothing. Or attach a stretchy hair tie to belt loop for pulling. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Velcro strip: Sew 3-4 inch strip of velcro to inside of sleeve or pocket, child can press and pull apart repeatedly (satisfying sound too) Zipper pulls: Attach key ring or beaded zipper pull to backpack/jacket, child fidgets with this instead Stretchy shoelaces: Use elastic shoelaces, child can pull and stretch while sitting Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Resistance band exercises: Pull resistance band in various directions, 20-30 repetitions per movement Heavy pulling tasks: Pull wagon filled with heavy items, drag laundry basket across room
Pulley system: Create simple pulley with rope over closet rod, child pulls objects up and down For Avoiders: Smooth textures: Provide silk/satin ribbons to hold, gentle sensory input Minimal tugging: Light fidget items that don't require hard pulling Soft sensory items: Soft stretchy materials that give easily without resistance Massage Techniques: Arm length strokes: Stroke firmly from shoulder to fingertips, following direction of pulling motion Wrist rotations with pressure: Hold child's hand, rotate wrist in circles while applying gentle pressure Forearm compressions: Squeeze forearm muscles rhythmically from elbow to wrist Manifestation 6: Pulling Hair (Proprioceptive, not just tactile) Physical Redirect Technique: Gently place your hand on child's arm (not the hair-pulling hand directly) and say softly "Let's give your hands something else to pull." Immediately offer a stress ball or putty and model squeezing it yourself.
DIY Alternative Tool: Pull Strings Toy: Take a small cardboard box, punch holes around it, thread thick yarn through holes with beads on ends inside. Child pulls strings in and out through holes. Or attach multiple hair ties to a carabiner clip on their belt loop for pulling. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Head massage instead: Teach child to massage their own scalp with fingertips firmly, providing proprioceptive input without pulling Thick rubber band pulls: Place thick rubber bands around a sturdy plastic container, child pulls and releases bands Brush hair firmly: Use a paddle brush to brush hair with firm strokes 50-100 times, providing scalp pressure Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Scalp massage with pressure: Adult provides firm scalp massage, pressing fingers into scalp and moving in circles, 2-3 minutes
Hair play alternatives: Play with toy troll dolls or dolls with long hair that can be pulled Hat wearing: Wear tight swim cap or headband that provides scalp pressure For Avoiders: Gentle head touches: Very light hair brushing or touching, child controls duration No scalp pressure: Avoid head-focused sensory activities Redirect to hands: Any sensory input focuses on hands instead of head Massage Techniques: Scalp pressure point massage: Use fingertips to press firmly all over scalp in small circles, 3-5 minutes Hairline compressions: Press firmly along hairline from center to sides with fingertips Temple and crown massage: Apply firm pressure to temples and crown of head in circular motions Manifestation 7: Stretching Neck and Back Frequently Physical Redirect Technique: Stand behind child, place hands gently on shoulders and say "Let's do proper neck stretches together." Guide them through controlled neck rolls (5 each direction) and shoulder rolls (10 each direction).
DIY Alternative Tool: Neck Support Roll: Roll a hand towel tightly, secure with rubber bands. Child lies on back with roll under neck for 2-3 minutes. Or fill a tube sock with rice, tie off, heat in microwave for 30 seconds (test temperature), place on shoulders/neck. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Wall corner stretches: Stand in corner, place forearms on each wall, lean forward to stretch chest and neck, 30 seconds Book balance: Balance light book on head while walking, promotes neck awareness without excessive stretching Chin tucks: Press chin back toward neck (making double chin) hold 5 seconds, release, repeat 10 times Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Backbends: Lying on floor, plant hands by ears, push up into bridge/backbend position, hold 10 seconds
Foam roller back: Lie on back on foam roller (lengthwise), roll slowly for 2-3 minutes Cat-cow stretches: On hands and knees, alternate between arching back up and dropping belly down, 15-20 repetitions For Avoiders: Minimal stretching: Just gentle head turns left and right, 3-5 repetitions Supported positions: Lie with neck on pillow roll, letting gravity do gentle stretch No forced movements: Only stretch as far as comfortable, no pushing limits Massage Techniques: Neck muscle massage: Massage along sides of neck (avoid front/throat) with firm pressure, upward strokes Trapezius squeeze: Squeeze the muscle between neck and shoulder, hold 5 seconds, release, repeat along entire trapezius Upper back pressure: Press firmly along upper back muscles parallel to spine, 30-second holds at different points
Manifestation 8: Tug-of-War with Objects or People Physical Redirect Technique: Join in briefly, then say "Let's make this tug-of-war a proper game with rules." Set up a formal tug-of-war with a towel or rope, mark a line, pull for 30 seconds, rest, repeat 3-5 times. DIY Alternative Tool: Resistance Tug Rope: Braid together 3 old t-shirts into a thick rope (3-4 feet long), tie loops on each end. Secure one end to table leg, child pulls on other end. Or make two loops for two-player tug-of-war. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Stretch bands: Use exercise resistance bands, loop around sturdy furniture leg, child pulls while walking backward Dog pull toy: Even without a dog, use a dog tug rope toy against a secured anchor point
Sheet twist: Two people hold opposite ends of a sheet, twist in opposite directions, feel resistance Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Rope climbing: If possible, provide access to climbing rope (gym class, playground) Wagon pulling: Fill wagon with heavy items, pull friend or sibling around yard Resistance walking: Tie exercise band around waist, secure to starting point, walk forward against resistance For Avoiders: Gentle pulling: Pull very light objects with minimal resistance Push instead: Redirect to pushing activities which may feel more comfortable Side-by-side: Work together pulling something rather than against each other Massage Techniques: Full arm traction: Hold wrist firmly, gently pull arm straight away from body for 10 seconds, each arm Shoulder socket mobilization: With bent elbow, gently rotate arm in socket while pulling slightly
Lat muscle massage: Massage the large muscle along side of back (latissimus) with firm pressure strokes
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 4. PROPRIOCEPTIVE STIMMING > A. Joint and Muscle Stimming > Level 3: Heavy Work Activities
Causation: Over-stimulated: Intense muscle work organizes nervous system Under-stimulated: High proprioceptive need; muscles crave resistance Sensitivity: Severe under-responsiveness requires intense input Regulation: Using physical exertion to modulate arousal level Sensory Profile: Extreme Seeker: Constant movement seeking all day Regulator: Uses heavy work before/after difficult situations Athletic: Thrives with constant physical challenges Description: Engaging in resistive physical activities Manifestation 1: Carrying Heavy Objects (Books/Bags/Furniture) Unnecessarily Physical Redirect Technique: Approach child, acknowledge their effort "I see you're working hard carrying heavy things. Let's give you a special job." Assign specific heavy carrying tasks on schedule - morning book stack to room, evening laundry basket, etc. DIY Alternative Tool: Weighted Backpack System: Take child's regular backpack, sew or safety-pin small ziplock bags inside (1 lb each). Start with 2-3 lbs, can add more. Create "carrying schedule" chart - specific times child wears weighted backpack for 15-20 minutes.
