Hold their hands up in front of face, move their hands slowly side to side, up and down, have them follow with eyes (no spinning). Say "Your eyes can do interesting things without spinning too." Then allow brief (5-10) controlled spins if desired. DIY Alternative Tool: Visual Alternatives to Spinning: Sensory bottle: Make bottle with water, glitter, small objects - child shakes and watches swirl (visual stimulation without spinning self)
Pinwheel: Child holds pinwheel, blows/runs to make it spin, watches blur (spinning object, not self) Ceiling fan watching: Designated time watching ceiling fan spin (2-3 minutes max), satisfies visual spinning need Spinning light toy: Light spinner or LED poi provides visual blur without self-spinning Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Dizzy glasses: If safe, briefly wear glasses with prism lenses or look through kaleidoscope - visual blur without spinning Spin art: Art activity spinning paper with paint - watches paint blur and create patterns Fidget spinner: Hold fidget spinner close to face, watch it blur - visual stimulation Fast movement watching: Watch trains, cars, or ball rolling quickly for visual blur (child remains still) Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Visual tracking exercises: Follow moving object with eyes (ball swinging on string, finger moving), develops eye control reducing spinning need for visual input
Optokinetic stimulation: Watch videos with moving patterns (trains passing, scrolling patterns) - provides visual vestibular input without self-movement Bilateral eye movements: EMDR-style bilateral eye movements (following finger side-to-side) - therapeutic visual-vestibular integration Visual-motor activities: Activities integrating vision and movement (catch, tennis, tracking games) For Avoiders: Stable visual field: Avoid all spinning objects, blurred vision, fast movements Slow, controlled visual environment: Calm, stable visual surroundings Central vision focus: Activities using central focused vision only, no peripheral blur Predictable visual input: Same visual environment, no surprises Massage Techniques: Eye area massage: Gentle massage around eyes (orbital bones, temples), 2-3 minutes - relaxes eye muscles Scalp and neck massage: Massage scalp, base of skull, neck - affects visual-vestibular integration, 5-7 minutes Hand massage before spinning: Massage hands thoroughly before allowing spinning, 3 minutes each hand - provides hand sensory input
Calming transition massage: After spinning/watching blur, slow, organizing massage, 10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Visual-vestibular integration: Spinning while watching hands integrates two sensory systems - not inherently bad, just needs structure Controlled visual blur: Practice creating visual blur through safer methods (spinning objects, not self) Eye exercises: Vision therapy exercises may reduce need for extreme visual-vestibular seeking Manifestation 7: Spinning at Different Speeds (Slow to Fast) Physical Redirect Technique: Observe child's spinning speeds. Approach and say "I notice you spin at different speeds. Let's practice that with control." Guide through structured progression: 5 spins slow speed (1 per second), 5 spins medium speed (2 per second), 5 spins fast speed (3 per second), immediate stop, sit down, rest 2 minutes. Praises their speed variation ability while adding structure.
DIY Alternative Tool: Speed-Controlled Spinning: Metronome speed control: Use metronome app at different BPMs (60, 120, 180), spin to each beat, child learns to control speed Music speed variation: Create playlist of songs at different BPMs, spin to tempo of music Speed zones: Mark three floor spots - SLOW (blue tape), MEDIUM (yellow tape), FAST (red tape), spin at appropriate speed in each zone Video recording: Record child's spinning at different speeds, watch together, discuss which speeds feel best Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Office chair speed control: Adult spins child in office chair at controlled different speeds Record player watching: Watch record spin at 33 RPM, then 45 RPM, then 78 RPM (if available) - visual speed differences Fan speed variation: Turn ceiling fan to different speeds, watch and discuss how each looks different
Ball rolling races: Roll balls at different speeds, observe differences Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Speed variation training: Structured practice of different speeds builds vestibular modulation - important skill Tempo-based activities: Dance to different tempo music, run at different speeds, activities with pace variation Speed awareness: Practice identifying and controlling own movement speed in various activities Variable intensity: Day's vestibular diet includes slow activities (gentle rocking), medium (walking), fast (running, jumping) For Avoiders: Slow only: If any movement, only very slow, controlled speed Predictable pace: Same speed every time, no variation Advance warning: Always warn before any speed changes Personal control: Child controls all speed changes themselves Massage Techniques: Variable speed massage: Massage at different speeds (slow strokes, medium, fast tapping) mirroring child's speed variation interests
Rhythm-responsive massage: Match massage rhythm to child's preferred movement rhythms Vestibular modulation massage: After varied-speed spinning, massage that modulates from fast to slow progressively, 10 minutes Sensory integration focus: Massage that helps organize varied sensory input received, 10-15 minutes Vestibular Integration: Modulation skill: Ability to spin at different speeds indicates good vestibular modulation - skill to support and structure Speed safety: Teach that some speeds safer than others (moderate safer than extreme fast) Real-world application: Speed control transfers to other activities (running, biking, skating) Manifestation 8: Spinning with Arms Extended or Tucked Physical Redirect Technique: Notice child's arm position during spinning. Say "Spin check - show me arms out spinning" (child does 5 spins arms extended), "Now show me arms in spinning" (child does 5 spins arms tucked), "Which do you feel more?" Discuss how different arm positions feel different. Then structure: 5 spins each way with rest between, practice body awareness during spinning.
DIY Alternative Tool: Arm Position Awareness: Position sequence chart: Create visual chart showing different arm positions during spinning (arms out, arms up, arms at sides, arms crossed), child follows sequence Mirror observation: Spin in front of mirror with different arm positions, observe how it looks and feels different Arm weight variation: Hold light objects (scarves) while spinning vs. heavy objects (water bottles) - explores how weight affects spinning Tape positions: Use colored tape on floor to indicate which arm position to use in each spinning zone Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Arm movement activities: Activities focusing on arm positions (arm circles, arm stretches, swimming motions) without spinning Weighted arm bands: Wear wrist weights during spinning (if safe and supervised), changes sensory experience
Ribbon wands: Hold ribbon wands during spinning, creates visual effect with arm movements Different hand holds: Spin while holding different objects (ball, scarf, beanbag) explores proprioceptive variation Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Proprioceptive arm exploration: Activities exploring arm sensations (push-ups, arm wrestling, carrying heavy items) separate from spinning Bilateral arm activities: Activities using both arms (catching large ball, jumping jacks, swimming strokes) Arm strengthening: Building arm strength may change spinning sensation (arm exercises, climbing, hanging) Varied arm spinning: Practice all arm position variations with structure - builds body awareness For Avoiders: Arms at sides only: If any spinning, arms stay close to body, safest feeling position Supported arms: Arms holding onto stable support during any movement No free-moving arms: Avoid activities with unsupported arm movement
Proprioceptive arm input: Heavy work for arms instead (pushes, carrying) without spinning Massage Techniques: Comprehensive arm massage: Thorough massage of entire arm from shoulder to fingertips, 5 minutes each arm Shoulder girdle massage: Massage shoulder complex deeply (different arm positions work different shoulder muscles), 7-10 minutes Bilateral arm massage: Massage both arms simultaneously, supports bilateral integration Proprioceptive arm input massage: Deep pressure, compressions along entire arm, 5 minutes each Vestibular Integration: Centrifugal force exploration: Different arm positions change experience of centrifugal force during spinning - legitimate exploration Body awareness building: Varying arm positions builds proprioceptive and vestibular integration Physics learning: Can teach about physics concepts (centrifugal force, momentum, balance) through spinning variations
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 5. VESTIBULAR STIMMING > B. Rotational Movement Stimming > Level 2: Spinning Objects or Self on Equipment
Causation: Over-stimulated: Equipment-based spinning provides controllable intense input Under-stimulated: Needs maximum vestibular stimulation available Sensitivity: Severe vestibular under-responsiveness; typical movement insufficient Thrill-Seeking: May seek dizziness or disorientation sensation Proprioceptive: Rolling provides vestibular + full-body pressure input Sensory Profile: Extreme Seeker: Uses equipment to achieve maximum spinning intensity Speed Seeker: Focuses on fastest possible rotation Duration Seeker: Prolonged spinning sessions (30-90+ minutes) Manifestation 1: Spinning on Office/Desk Chairs (50-200+ Spins Per Session) Physical Redirect Technique: Approach spinning child, place hand on chair back (not stopping abruptly - safety risk) and say "Spin countdown - 5 more spins!" Count down 5...4...3...2...1...stop! Have child stand immediately, do 10 jumping jacks, shake out legs, drink water. After 2-minute break, may return for another controlled session (max 20 spins this time). Set kitchen timer visible to child for next session.
DIY Alternative Tool: Office Chair Spin Management: Spin tracker: Use tally counter or app, child clicks after each spin, set maximum per session (50 spins) Timer system: Set timer for 3 minutes, spin only while timer runs, mandatory 5-minute break between sessions Resistance modification: Add friction to chair (place on carpet instead of hard floor, or add resistance to wheels) making spinning harder/slower Token system: 4 tokens per day, each = one 3-minute spin session, teaches self-regulation Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Sit-and-spin toy: Provide sit-and-spin (even for older kids), safer than office chair spinning Lazy Susan sitting: Child sits on large sturdy lazy Susan on floor, adult or child controls spin speed Rotating stool: Use piano bench or rotating drum throne instead of wheeled office chair (safer, more controlled)
Swivel chair with limits: Use office chair with swivel but lock wheels (allows spinning, prevents rolling away) Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured chair spin routine: 20 spins, 3-minute break, 20 spins, 3-minute break, 20 spins, done (3x daily maximum) Spin variations: Practice different speeds, directions, with arms in/out - adds variety Alternative rotational input: When chair unavailable, use spinning activities (pirouettes, somersaults, rolling down hills) Chair spin with purpose: Spin in chair while doing activity (counting backward, reciting alphabet, catching bean bags) - integrates spinning with cognition For Avoiders: Non-swivel seating: Only stationary chairs Locked position: If chair swivels, lock it facing forward Ground contact: Feet always flat on floor, no floating/spinning Stability first: All seating prioritizes stability over any movement
Massage Techniques: Post-spinning grounding massage: Immediate 10-minute firm pressure massage after spinning sessions Neck and upper back focus: Chair spinning can strain neck from centrifugal force, massage thoroughly 5-7 minutes Vestibular calming points: Massage base of skull, behind ears, temples - directly affects vestibular system, 5 minutes Leg grounding: Massage legs from hip to ankle, helping child "feel the ground" again, 5 minutes Vestibular Integration: Controlled stopping: Practice stopping smoothly from various speeds - builds vestibular control Bilateral direction: Equal spins both directions (25 right, 25 left) - bilateral vestibular development Recovery monitoring: Watch for signs of overstimulation (nausea, headache, disorientation) - indicates need to reduce Manifestation 2: Using Playground Merry-Go-Rounds for Extended Periods Physical Redirect Technique: Approach merry-go-round, make eye contact with child and say "Time check! You've been spinning X minutes. Let's do 5 more spins and then take a break." Count 5 rotations aloud, help child dismount safely when dizzy. Immediate activity: walk around playground perimeter once, do 10 squats, sit and drink water for 3 minutes. May return to merry-go-round after break for 10-minute session maximum.
DIY Alternative Tool: Merry-Go-Round Management: Rotation counter: Adult counts rotations aloud, set limit per session (20-30 rotations) Timed turns: Set timer for 5 minutes, that's one turn, then another child's turn (if group), encourages limited sessions Speed governor: Adult controls speed, keeps it moderate not extreme, teaches safe spinning Direction protocol: 10 rotations clockwise, stop, 2-minute break, 10 rotations counterclockwise - bilateral and controlled Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): DIY spinning platform: Create safe spinning platform - lazy Susan on ground with cushion on top, child sits and spins (adult supervises) Tire swing: Tire swing provides rotational input safer than merry-go-round (one person, slower) Disc swing: Rotating disc swing allows child to control own spinning Rotating office chair outside: Bring office chair outside on patio, supervised spinning in controlled environment
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Playground rotation schedule: Merry-go-round 10 min, other equipment 10 min, merry-go-round 10 min - prevents exclusive focus on spinning Cooperative play: Teach taking turns spinning vs. riding, social skills while getting vestibular input Speed variation: Practice slow spins, medium spins, fast spins with breaks between - teaches modulation Group activities: Group games on merry-go-round (sing songs, count together) makes spinning more purposeful For Avoiders: No merry-go-round: Avoid entirely, use other playground equipment Stationary seating: Sit on stationary equipment only Watching from distance: May watch others from safe, stable location Alternative playground fun: Slides (straight, not spiral), monkey bars, climbing structures Massage Techniques: Full body integration massage: After intense merry-go-round use, 15-20 minute comprehensive massage integrating vestibular input
Anti-nausea pressure points: If child feels nauseous, firm pressure on wrist pressure point (P6/Nei Guan), 2-3 minutes Bilateral symmetrical massage: Massage both sides equally simultaneously, supports bilateral vestibular processing Grounding techniques: Very heavy, firm pressure massage focusing on feet and legs, 10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Gradual intensity reduction: Start session at desired speed, gradually slow down before stopping (prevents abrupt vestibular change) Eyes open vs. closed: Brief periods with eyes closed intensifies vestibular input (only if safe and supervised) Post-spinning transitions: After merry-go-round, quiet activities (reading, drawing) help organize vestibular input Manifestation 3: Spinning on Sit-and-Spin Toys Beyond Typical Age Physical Redirect Technique: Approach child on sit-and-spin, kneel beside and say "Let's count your spins today." Count 20 spins together aloud. Say "Great spinning! Now your body needs a spin break." Help them off, do 10 star jumps together, walk around room. Set timer for 15 minutes - when it beeps, may return to sit-and-spin for another 20-spin session.
DIY Alternative Tool: Sit-and-Spin Alternatives: DIY rotating platform: Large lazy Susan with cushion duct-taped on top, child sits and spins (adult supervision) Office chair at child height: Adjust office chair to lowest setting for child-appropriate spinning Rotating drum throne: Musician's drum throne spins smoothly, supports more weight than sit-and-spin Upgrade: If child too heavy for sit-and-spin, purchase rotating disk swing or platform swing for similar input Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Spinning while sitting variations: Spin on stool, lazy Susan, office chair, rotation board - variety of spinning options Spinning objects instead: Spin tops, fidget spinners, lazy Susan with toys on it - visual spinning satisfaction Body spinning: When can't use sit-and-spin, do standing spins, somersaults, cartwheels - body-based rotation Rocking alternatives: When spinning urge hits, use rocking chair or therapy ball as alternative vestibular input
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Scheduled sit-and-spin time: 10 minutes morning, 10 minutes afternoon, 10 minutes evening - structured access Sit-and-spin games: Play games while spinning (count backward, alphabet, catch bean bags) - cognitive integration Speed challenges: "Can you spin super slow?" "Now medium" "Now fast" - teaches speed modulation Position variations: Sit different ways on sit-and-spin (legs out, crossed, kneeling) - proprioceptive variation For Avoiders: No spinning toys: Avoid all spinning equipment Stable toys only: Play with toys/equipment that don't move or spin Observation: May watch others use spinning toys from distance Alternative fun: Push toys, building toys, art supplies - non-vestibular activities Massage Techniques: Post-spin organizing massage: 10-minute massage after spinning focusing on organizing nervous system Hip and lower back: Sitting position on sit-and-spin strains hips/back, massage thoroughly, 5-7 minutes
Vestibular calming: Massage sub-occipital area, temples, behind ears, 5 minutes Proprioceptive emphasis: Deep pressure massage all body parts, adds organizing proprioceptive input after vestibular activity Vestibular Integration: Age-appropriate discussion: Validate need for spinning while helping child understand some toys typically for younger kids Upgrade options: Transition to age-appropriate spinning options (disc swing, office chair, rotating stool) Reducing dependence: Gradually introduce other vestibular activities reducing exclusive sit-and-spin use Manifestation 4: Rolling Down Hills Repeatedly (10-30+ Rolls) Physical Redirect Technique: Stand at bottom of hill where child will finish rolling. After they complete roll and stop, say "Great roll! Stand up and check in with your body." Have them stand, describe how they feel, walk around in circle. Count together: "That was roll number X. Let's do 3 more rolls, then try something different." After 3 more rolls, redirect to different activity (running up hill, somersaults on flat ground, climbing tree).
DIY Alternative Tool: Hill Rolling Management: Roll counter: Child carries counter clicker, clicks after each roll (builds awareness), set daily limit (20-30 rolls) Rotation protocol: 5 rolls down, run up, 5 rolls down, different activity 10 min, return if desired Direction variation: Roll down left shoulder leading, walk up, roll down right shoulder leading - bilateral input Course markers: Mark different rolling paths with cones (straight, diagonal, curved) - adds variety and purpose Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Indoor rolling: Roll across room on carpet or mat, provides rotation without hill (safer, more controlled) Log rolls: Lie on flat ground, roll like log sideways 10 times - rotational input without hills Somersault circuit: Set up indoor somersault path with mats, controlled rolling
Sleeping bag rolls: Get in sleeping bag, roll across floor - contained rolling with deep pressure Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured rolling routine: 10 rolls down hill, 5-minute break doing different activity, 10 more rolls if desired, done Rolling variations: Log rolls (arms at sides), pencil rolls (arms overhead), tuck rolls - provides variety Vestibular circuit: Rolling down hills as part of larger circuit including swinging, spinning, jumping Natural vestibular play: Rolling is natural, healthy vestibular activity - support with structure rather than eliminating For Avoiders: No rolling: Avoid all rolling activities Stable ground play: Activities on flat, stable ground only Walk hills: If on hills, walk up and down carefully, no rolling Gentle alternatives: Rocking chair, gentle swinging - minimal vestibular input only
Massage Techniques: Full body massage post-rolling: 15 minutes comprehensive massage, rolling affects entire body Shoulder and arm focus: Rolling stresses shoulders/arms, deep massage 5-7 minutes each side Neck alignment massage: Rolling can jar neck, gentle massage ensuring proper alignment, 5 minutes Grass/dirt removal: If needed, clean skin gently, then provide calming massage, 10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Visual-vestibular integration: Rolling down hills provides intense visual input (world spinning) plus vestibular - very integrative Bilateral practice: Equal rolls leading with each shoulder supports bilateral development Proprioceptive bonus: Rolling on ground provides full-body proprioceptive input plus vestibular - highly organizing Manifestation 5: Somersaults or Forward Rolls (20-50 Consecutive) Physical Redirect Technique: Count child's consecutive somersaults. When they reach 10, say "Pause! Somersault check-in." Have them stop, stand up, walk in straight line across room (tests balance/coordination). If walking straight easily, allow 10 more somersaults. If wobbly, say "Your vestibular system needs rest" - do different activity for 5 minutes before any more somersaults.
DIY Alternative Tool: Somersault Management System: Rep counter: Use counter app or tally marks, set maximum per session (30 somersaults) Circuit integration: 10 somersaults, 10 jumping jacks, 10 squats, rest, repeat circuit - embeds somersaults in larger routine Direction protocol: 15 forward rolls, rest 3 minutes, 15 backward rolls (if skilled), rest - bilateral vestibular input Mat requirement: Somersaults only allowed on designated mat/soft surface - contains activity, ensures safety Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Crash mat tumbling: Stack couch cushions, child does somersaults onto/over cushions - soft, safe tumbling Incline somersaults: Use couch cushions to create slight incline, somersault down incline (increases sensation) Barrel rolls: Roll sideways instead of forward - different rotational plane, varies input Egg rolls: Curl in ball, roll sideways - vestibular plus proprioceptive compression
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Gymnastics class enrollment: Structured tumbling class teaches proper technique, provides vestibular input appropriately Daily tumbling routine: 15-minute routine including somersaults, cartwheels, rolls - structured vestibular time Somersault games: Somersault races, somersault counting games, Simon Says with somersaults Progression training: Forward rolls → backward rolls → dive rolls → aerials (as age/skill appropriate) For Avoiders: No inverted positions: Avoid all activities putting head below heart Horizontal activities: Activities maintaining upright or horizontal position only Gentle rolling: If must roll, only gentle side-to-side rocking on back Stable ground: All activities with head upright and body stable Massage Techniques: Neck and upper back priority: Somersaults stress neck, very thorough massage of neck and upper back, 7-10 minutes Spinal alignment check: Gentle massage along entire spine ensuring alignment, 5 minutes
Shoulder girdle massage: Massage shoulders and upper arms which bear weight during rolls, 5 minutes Vestibular integration massage: Sub-occipital massage, behind ears, jaw - calms vestibular system, 5 minutes Vestibular Integration: Proper technique: Teach correct somersault form (tuck chin, round back, roll on shoulders not head) - protects neck Bilateral skills: Practice forward rolls and backward rolls - challenges vestibular system differently Integration activities: After somersaults, activities requiring balance and coordination (walking balance beam, one-foot standing) - integrates vestibular input Manifestation 6: Cartwheels in Repetitive Sequences Physical Redirect Technique: Count child's consecutive cartwheels. After 10, say "Cartwheel break! Show me your best tree pose." Have them do tree pose (yoga balance pose) for 30 seconds each leg. This tests their balance and gives vestibular break. Then allow 10 more cartwheels if balance was good. If wobbly, extend break to 5 minutes with different activities.
DIY Alternative Tool: Cartwheel Structure System: Cartwheel line: Use tape to create straight line on floor, practice cartwheels along line (improves form, creates structure) Rep limit chart: Visual chart showing cartwheel limits per session (20 cartwheels), child marks off each one Alternating sides: Must alternate: right-hand-lead cartwheel, left-hand-lead cartwheel, repeat - bilateral development Cartwheel circuit: 5 cartwheels, 5 push-ups, 5 cartwheels, 10 jumping jacks, 5 cartwheels, rest - integrated circuit Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Outdoor cartwheel space: Designate safe outdoor area (soft grass, away from obstacles) for cartwheel practice Crash mat cartwheels: Place mat or cushions, practice cartwheels landing on soft surface Cartwheel progressions: Bunny hops → handstands → cartwheels - builds up to cartwheels properly Video recording: Record cartwheels, watch together analyzing form - increases body awareness
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Gymnastics/dance class: Structured class teaching cartwheels and other tumbling skills Cartwheel challenges: Cartwheel over objects, one-handed cartwheels, roundoffs - progressive difficulty Daily practice routine: 10-15 minutes structured practice including warm-up, cartwheels, cool-down Bilateral emphasis: Equal practice both sides, tracks which side needs more work For Avoiders: No inversions: Avoid cartwheels and all inverted positions Horizontal tumbling: If any tumbling, only rolls with head staying relatively level Feet-on-ground: All activities keep feet on ground, no inverting Slow movements: Any movement slow, controlled, never fast/inverted Massage Techniques: Wrist and hand massage: Cartwheels stress wrists heavily, thorough massage 5 minutes each hand/wrist Shoulder decompression: After bearing body weight, massage shoulders and gently decompress joints, 5 minutes Core massage: Cartwheels require strong core, massage abdominal and back muscles, 7 minutes
Hip flexor release: Cartwheel position uses hip flexors intensely, massage front of hips, 3 minutes each Vestibular Integration: Spotting technique: Teach to "spot" (look at hands/ground) during cartwheel - improves orientation and reduces dizziness Bilateral development: Cartwheel practice both directions develops bilateral vestibular and motor planning Body awareness: Cartwheels require and build body awareness in space (proprioception + vestibular) Manifestation 7: Rolling Across Floor or Ground Physical Redirect Technique: As child is rolling repeatedly, count rolls aloud. At roll 15, say "Rolling pause!" Have them stop in lying position, then guide them to stand up slowly. Do "grounding check": stomp feet firmly 10 times, press palms together hard for 10 seconds. Ask "How does your body feel?" Then allow 10 more rolls if body feels organized. If dizzy/disoriented, 5-minute break with heavy work (wall push-ups, carrying something heavy).
DIY Alternative Tool: Rolling Management System: Rolling mat/path: Designate specific mat or taped path for rolling, contains activity to appropriate space Direction cue cards: Alternate cards showing left roll vs. right roll - ensures bilateral rolling Rolling counter: Tallies rolls per session, maximum 30 rolls per session Activity integration: Roll 10 times → build with blocks 5 minutes → roll 10 times → puzzle 5 minutes - alternates vestibular with organizing activities Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Sleeping bag rolling: Child gets in sleeping bag (unzipped or zipped), rolls across floor - contained rolling with compression Blanket rolling: Roll child up in blanket (burrito roll), they roll to unroll themselves - compression plus rotation Carpet rolling vs. smooth floor: Roll on both surfaces - different proprioceptive feedback with same vestibular input
Obstacle rolling: Create path with pillows/objects to roll around - adds cognitive planning to rolling Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Rolling games: Log rolling races, roll to target, roll while holding object - purposeful rolling Indoor/outdoor rolling: Vary environment - indoor on carpet, outdoor on grass - different sensory experiences Rolling relay: Family rolling relay races - social, fun, structured vestibular activity Variations: Pencil rolls (arms overhead), hug rolls (arms crossed), parachute rolls (under billowing parachute) - variety maintains interest For Avoiders: No rolling: Avoid all rolling activities Seated movement: If needs movement, seated rocking or swaying only Straight-path walking: Walk forward only, no diagonal or circular paths Stable activities: Building, art, reading - no vestibular demand Massage Techniques: Full body surface massage: Rolling involves entire body surface, massage all areas, 15 minutes
Shoulder and hip focus: These joints bear weight during rolling, massage surrounding muscles thoroughly, 5 minutes each Integration massage: Massage while child lies in various positions rolling puts them through - integrates sensory experience Calming conclusion: End with slow, rhythmic strokes from head to toe, 5 minutes Vestibular Integration: Multi-sensory integration: Rolling provides vestibular (rotation) + proprioceptive (pressure on body) + tactile (floor contact) - very integrative activity Speed variation: Practice slow controlled rolls vs. fast rolls - teaches vestibular modulation Environmental awareness: Roll with eyes open observing surroundings - integrates visual with vestibular Manifestation 8: Seeking Rides That Spin (Teacups, Gravitron) Physical Redirect Technique: At amusement park or fair, before child goes on spinning ride, establish agreement: "You can ride the teacups two times today. After first ride, we'll do three other rides, then second teacup ride." Use visual schedule showing ride order. After each spinning ride, mandatory 15-minute break doing non-spinning activities (eating, watching shows, slow rides) before next ride.
DIY Alternative Tool: Amusement Ride Management: Ride tokens: Give child 2-3 tokens for spinning rides per park visit, unlimited tokens for non-spinning rides, teaches moderation Rotation schedule: Visual schedule: spin ride → 3 other rides → spin ride → 3 other rides Timer between spins: After spinning ride, set 20-minute timer, no spinning rides until timer done Ride diary: Track which rides, how many times, how felt afterward - builds self-awareness Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Home spinning alternatives: When craving amusement park spins, use office chair spinning, merry-go-round at playground, rolling down hills Virtual reality: VR experiences can provide visual spinning sensation (if available and age-appropriate) Spin simulation videos: Watch POV videos of spinning rides - visual vestibular input without actual spinning
Anticipation activities: Before park visit, satisfy spinning needs with home activities reducing intensity of park seeking Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Variety emphasis: At park, ensure trying many different types of rides (drops, fast, spinning, water) - not all spinning Spin with company: Ride spinning rides with friend/family, makes it social experience not just sensory seeking Post-ride grounding: After intense spinning ride, grounding activities (eating, drinking, sitting quietly) before next ride Build tolerance gradually: Start park visit with gentle rides, build to more intense, end with calmer - eases into/out of vestibular overload For Avoiders: No spinning rides: Avoid teacups, gravitron, any spinning rides Alternative park fun: Gentle rides (train, ferris wheel stopped at top, carousel), shows, games, food Exit strategy: If accidentally on spinning ride, know it's OK to ask operator to stop
Preparation: If family members going on spin ride, find comfortable waiting spot away from ride Massage Techniques: Post-park recovery massage: After amusement park with spinning rides, thorough evening massage, 20-30 minutes Anti-nausea techniques: If nauseous after rides, pressure on wrist P6 point, cool compress on neck, 5-10 minutes Vestibular integration: Gentle massage of sub-occipital area, temples, jaw - helps integrate intense vestibular input, 5-7 minutes Grounding massage: Very firm, deep pressure massage focusing on legs and feet - helps ground after floating/spinning sensations, 10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Tolerance building: Regular exposure to varied vestibular input (with limits) can build healthy vestibular tolerance Self-regulation learning: Amusement parks teach limits - feeling nauseous/dizzy indicates "too much" - important self-awareness Recovery time: Body needs 20-30 minutes to fully recover from intense spinning ride - respecting this teaches body awareness
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 5. VESTIBULAR STIMMING > B. Rotational Movement Stimming > Level 3: Head/Eye Rotational Stimming
Causation: Over-stimulated: Isolated head movement provides controlled vestibular input Under-stimulated: Head movements stimulate semicircular canals directly Sensitivity: Exploring vestibular system capabilities Tic-like: May have obsessive-compulsive features; feels "incomplete" without movement Visual-Vestibular: Combining eye and head movement for multi-sensory effect Sensory Profile: Focused Seeker: Targets specific vestibular canals with precise movements Compulsive: May feel urge to complete specific number or pattern Mixed: Combines visual + vestibular seeking Description: Rotating head or eyes while body remains stable Manifestation 1: Rapid Side-to-Side Head Shaking (10-50+ Shakes) Physical Redirect Technique: When observing rapid head shaking, approach from front, establish eye contact, place hands gently on sides of child's head (not restricting, just providing sensory input) and say "Head pause." Hold steady gentle pressure for 10 seconds. Then guide through controlled head movements: 5 slow "no" shakes (count together), then hold head still, deep breath. Repeat: 5 slow shakes, stillness, breath, three times total.
DIY Alternative Tool: Head Movement Management: Neck wrap sensory input: Soft scarf or neck warmer worn around neck provides proprioceptive input reducing shaking urge Head shake counter: Child uses counter to track head shakes, set daily maximum (100 shakes), builds awareness Alternative head movements: Create chart showing appropriate head movements (yes nods, ear-to-shoulder tilts, looking up/down) as alternatives to vigorous shaking Shake timer: Allow 30 seconds of head shaking, then 5 minutes stillness (with timer) - structured access Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Cold/warm compress: Apply to back of neck 5 minutes - strong sensory input may reduce head movement seeking Weighted hood: Hoodie with small weights sewn in around hood (½-1 oz) provides gentle head/neck awareness Headphones with music: Music through headphones provides auditory input that may reduce head movement need
Head massage self-care: Teach child to massage own scalp/neck instead of shaking - appropriate self-regulation Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured head movement routine: Morning and evening - 10 yes nods, 10 no shakes, 10 ear-to-shoulder each side, 5 head circles each direction - satisfies need with structure Vestibular alternatives: When head shaking urge hits, redirect to whole-body vestibular (spinning 5 times, somersault, rocking chair) Neck strengthening: Exercises strengthening neck muscles (resist hand pressure on head from all directions, 10 reps) - may change sensation seeking "Headbanging" to music: Structured time with appropriate music allowing head movement (supervised, not dangerous) - appropriate outlet For Avoiders: Minimal head movement: Keep head as still as possible, turn whole body rather than just head
Supported head: Use pillows, headrests, furniture to support head when sitting/lying Slow, gentle movements: Any head movement very slow and controlled Avoid triggers: Stay away from situations triggering head movement (loud noises, bright lights, chaos) Massage Techniques: Sub-occipital release: Gentle but firm massage at base of skull where it meets neck, 5-7 minutes - directly affects vestibular system Neck muscle massage: Thorough massage of all neck muscles (front, sides, back), 10 minutes - releases tension from head shaking Scalp massage: Firm pressure scalp massage with fingertips, 5 minutes - very organizing for vestibular system Jaw and temple massage: Head shaking can create jaw/temple tension, gentle massage 3-5 minutes Vestibular Integration: Semicircular canal stimulation: Head shaking directly stimulates vestibular semicircular canals - very intense input
Bilateral stimulation: Side-to-side shaking stimulates lateral canals bilaterally - integrative Gradual reduction: Goal is reducing frequency/intensity as vestibular system matures and receives input through other activities Manifestation 2: Head Rolling in Circular Patterns Physical Redirect Technique: Observe child rolling head in circles. Approach from front, establish eye contact and say "Let's do slow, controlled head circles together." Guide them through 5 very slow head circles in one direction (counting), stop, hold head straight for 10 seconds, then 5 slow circles other direction. Emphasize "slow and controlled" throughout. After, have them stand and do 10 jumping jacks to redirect energy. DIY Alternative Tool: Head Rolling Management: Circle counter and direction tracker: Chart tracking head rolls - must do equal numbers each direction (5 right circles, 5 left circles)
Mirror practice: Practice head rolls in front of mirror - increases body awareness and control Neck pillow: U-shaped travel pillow worn during high-risk times (homework, TV) gently discourages excessive head movement Replacement behavior: When head rolling urge hits, do shoulder rolls instead - similar sensation, less vestibular intensity Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Rolling objects instead: Roll balls, marbles, toy cars in circles on floor - visual circular motion without head involvement Hula hoop spinning: Spin hula hoop on arm - circular visual input Stirring activities: Vigorous stirring activities (mixing dough, stirring paint) - circular arm movements replacing head circles Drawing circles: Draw large circles on paper or whiteboard repeatedly - visual-motor circular activity Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Whole body circles: Instead of head circles, do full body spins/rotations - more organizing vestibular input
Structured neck mobility routine: Stretching routine including safe, controlled head movements, 5 minutes 2x daily Vestibular diet: Comprehensive vestibular activities reducing isolated head movement seeking Proprioceptive neck input: Neck strengthening exercises, resistance to head movements from different angles For Avoiders: No head rolling: Avoid all circular head movements Linear head movements only: If any head movement, only up/down or side/side, no circles Neck support: Always use proper head/neck support when sitting or lying Slow, minimal movement: Keep head movement minimal and very controlled Massage Techniques: 360-degree neck massage: Massage entire circumference of neck thoroughly, 10 minutes - addresses all muscles used in head rolling Sub-occipital and upper cervical: Focus on top of neck/base of skull area, 5-7 minutes - calms vestibular system
Shoulder and upper back: Head rolling often accompanies shoulder tension, massage thoroughly, 7 minutes Craniosacral techniques: Gentle craniosacral therapy techniques (if trained) can be very effective for head movement stims Vestibular Integration: Multiple canal stimulation: Circular head movements stimulate all three semicircular canals - very intense vestibular input Bilateral integration: Circles both directions important for balanced bilateral vestibular development Vision-vestibular: Head rolling while watching creates strong visual-vestibular integration (world appears to move) Manifestation 3: Looking Up and Spinning Only Eyes Physical Redirect Technique: When notice child looking up with spinning eyes, approach calmly, place hand on shoulder and say "Let's rest your eyes." Have them close eyes for 10 seconds, then open and look straight ahead at specific object for 10 seconds. Then allow brief (5 seconds) looking up/eye movement, then back to forward gaze. Practice this pattern: forward gaze 30 seconds, up gaze with eye movement 5 seconds, repeat.
DIY Alternative Tool: Eye Movement Management: Visual tracking exercises: Create or purchase visual tracking tools (follow moving object with eyes, letter/number searches) - appropriate eye movements Eye rest timer: Set timer for 10 minutes, child must rest eyes (look at distance, close eyes briefly) when timer sounds Structured looking up: Designate times/places where looking up appropriate (cloud watching outside, looking at stars) - channels behavior appropriately Eye movement game cards: Cards showing different eye movement patterns (up, down, circles, side-to-side) child follows - structured eye exercise Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Ceiling decorations: Put interesting but not overstimulating things on ceiling (glow stars, mobile) giving purpose to looking up Flashlight tracking: In darkened room, shine flashlight on ceiling, child tracks with eyes - controlled visual input
Bubble watching: Blow bubbles, child tracks them upward with eyes - purposeful upward gaze Ball toss tracking: Toss ball up, child tracks with eyes only (head still) - eye-tracking exercise Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Vision therapy exercises: Specific eye exercises from vision therapist or online resources - appropriate visual input Where's Waldo/I Spy books: Intensive visual scanning activities - satisfies visual seeking appropriately Tracking games: Follow flying objects (birds, planes, butterflies, balls) with eyes Visual-vestibular integration: Activities combining vision and vestibular (swinging while looking at target, spinning and locating objects) For Avoiders: Stable visual field: Keep eyes focused on stable, non-moving objects Minimal eye movement: Reduce eye movement requirements Central vision: Activities using central focused vision, avoid peripheral scanning Predictable visual environment: Same visual surroundings, no surprises
Massage Techniques: Eye area gentle massage: Very gentle massage around eyes (on orbital bones, not eyeballs), 2-3 minutes - relieves eye strain Temple and brow massage: Massage temples and eyebrow area with gentle pressure, 3 minutes - relieves visual tension Sub-occipital focus: Base of skull massage affects visual and vestibular centers, 5 minutes Face massage: Gentle massage of entire face including jaw, 5 minutes - often very calming Vestibular Integration: Visual-vestibular connection: Looking up while moving eyes strongly integrates visual and vestibular systems Semicircular canal stimulation: Upward gaze with eye movement particularly stimulates superior canals Vision therapy: Professional vision therapy may address underlying visual-vestibular integration issues driving this behavior Manifestation 4: Tilting Head at Extreme Angles While Moving Physical Redirect Technique: When observe extreme head tilting, approach from front where child can see you, say "Head position check." Place hands gently on sides of head, guide back to neutral center position, have them hold for 10 seconds. Say "This is strong, centered head." Allow brief (5 seconds) head tilt if desired, then back to center. Practice: center 30 seconds, tilt 5 seconds, center 30 seconds.
DIY Alternative Tool: Head Position Management: Position mirror: Small mirror positioned so child can see own head position - visual feedback encourages neutral position Posture reminder: Soft neck support or collar (not restrictive) provides proprioceptive reminder of head position Head position photos: Take photos of neutral vs. tilted head positions, child refers to photos for self-correction Balance challenge: Balance bean bag on head during activities - encourages neutral head position Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Structured tilting time: Designated times (5 minutes 2x daily) for exploring head positions with supervision Mirror exploration: Explore different head positions in mirror - increases body awareness Yoga head positions: Poses involving head position (ear to shoulder stretches, neck circles) - appropriate head movement outlet Photography from angles: Take photos from different angles, look at how perspective changes - explores tilting concept safely
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Vestibular input through body: Satisfy vestibular needs through whole-body tilting (lying on wedge, inverting on furniture edges, cartwheels) Neck strengthening: Build neck strength to better control head position Proprioceptive neck input: Activities providing input to neck (wearing weighted vest, carrying items on head, resistance exercises) Body awareness training: Activities building overall body position awareness including head position For Avoiders: Neutral head always: Keep head in neutral center position always Supported positions: Use furniture, pillows to support head in neutral No tilting: Avoid all activities requiring head tilting Turn whole body: Turn entire body rather than tilting head to see things Massage Techniques: Neck realignment massage: Gentle massage encouraging proper neck alignment, 7-10 minutes Unilateral focus: May need extra massage on one side if child favors tilting one direction, 5 minutes
Upper trap release: Tilted head position often creates tight upper trapezius, massage thoroughly, 5 minutes each side Suboccipital release: Base of skull massage, 5 minutes - helps reset vestibular system Vestibular Integration: Otolithic stimulation: Head tilting stimulates otolithic organs (utricle and saccule) - gravity/linear acceleration receptors Spatial orientation: Extreme tilting challenges brain's sense of vertical - child may be exploring spatial concepts Visual-vestibular conflict: Tilted head creates mismatch between visual horizontal and vestibular sense of vertical - interesting but potentially disorganizing Manifestation 5: Head Nodding Repetitively (Up-Down 20-100+ Times) Physical Redirect Technique: Count child's head nods. At 20 nods, say "Nod pause!" Place hand gently on top of head and say "Let's do yes nods the slow way." Guide through 10 very slow, deliberate yes nods, counting together. Then hold head still, deep breath, 10 seconds. Say "Now your neck has had its exercise." If nodding resumes quickly, redirect to different activity entirely.
DIY Alternative Tool: Nodding Management System: Nod counter: Use counter app, set daily limit (100 nods), child tracks own nodding Replacement nods: When nodding urge hits, do 5 slow controlled nods, then stop - satisfies urge briefly Conversation nods: Channel nodding into appropriate context (nodding during conversations to show listening) - functional use Puppet nodding: Use puppet or toy, make it nod instead of nodding own head Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Bobblehead toy: Provide bobblehead toy to tap/make nod - visual nodding satisfaction Yes/No game: Game requiring head nods for yes, shakes for no - functional head movement Rocking motion: Redirect to rocking whole body instead of just head Chin tucks: Replace nodding with chin tuck exercises (press chin toward chest, hold 5 sec) - strengthening vs. repetitive movement
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Full body movement: Redirect to whole body activities providing vestibular input (bowing, bending forward-back, somersaults) Structured neck exercise: Include head nods in exercise routine (10 nods as part of warm-up stretching) Music with beat: Nod to music beat for one song only - channels nodding into musical activity Weighted hood or hat: Wear weighted item on head during high-risk times - provides awareness reducing automated nodding For Avoiders: Minimal head movement: Keep head still as much as possible Supported head: Use headrest, pillow, furniture support Avoid nodding triggers: Reduce exposure to situations triggering head nodding Alternative affirmation: Use words, thumbs up, or other gestures instead of head nodding Massage Techniques: Front and back neck massage: Nodding uses both anterior and posterior neck muscles, massage both thoroughly, 10 minutes
Suboccipital release: Massage base of skull intensively, 5-7 minutes - area of high vestibular processing Upper back and shoulders: Nodding often accompanies shoulder tension, massage 7 minutes Jaw release: Repetitive nodding can create jaw tension, massage jaw muscles, 3 minutes each side Vestibular Integration: Vertical canal stimulation: Up-down head movement primarily stimulates anterior and posterior semicircular canals Rhythmic stimulation: Repetitive nodding provides rhythmic vestibular input - may be organizing for some children Functional use: Encourage using head nods appropriately (indicating yes, showing understanding) - functional application of movement Manifestation 6: Combining Head Rotation with Body Spinning Physical Redirect Technique: When child is spinning body while also moving head, say loudly "Stop and sit!" (safety concern - this combination very disorienting). Once stopped and sitting, say "Spinning your body OR moving your head, not both together - that's too much for your brain." Model body spinning with head stable (5 spins), then standing still with head movements (5 nods). Enforce rule: body spinning = head still, OR head moving = body still.
DIY Alternative Tool: Separation Training System: Visual rule chart: Chart showing "Body spins, head still" (picture) and "Head moves, body still" (picture) - clear visual rule Progressive practice: Week 1 - only body spinning allowed, Week 2 - only head movements allowed, Week 3 - can choose one but never combine Supervision requirement: Combined head-body movement only allowed with direct adult supervision for safety Alternative integration: Supervised activities appropriately combining movement (dance, gymnastics, martial arts) - structured integration Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Spinning with visual focus: Spin body while keeping eyes focused on one stable point - integrates spinning with visual stability Seated spinning: Sit in office chair and spin - head naturally comes along but less disorienting than standing Slow combinations: Very slow body turns with head movements - much less disorienting
Mirror practice: Practice combinations in front of mirror - visual feedback reduces dangerous disorientation Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured integration activities: Dance, figure skating, gymnastics routines combining body and head movement with instruction/supervision Progressive challenge: Master body spinning alone, master head movements alone, then carefully introduce combinations with supervision Safety education: Teach about vestibular system, why combining can cause falls/injury, build understanding Spotting technique: Teach dancer's spotting (head stays focused on point as long as possible during spin) - safer integration For Avoiders: No combinations: Never combine body and head movement Body still, head still: Prefer both body and head remaining still Minimal movement: Any movement minimal and highly controlled Supported positions: Always supported by furniture or person Massage Techniques:
Full vestibular reset massage: After combined head-body movement, comprehensive massage focusing on vestibular calming, 15-20 minutes Neck intensive focus: Neck takes strain from both movements, very thorough neck massage, 10 minutes Grounding emphasis: Heavy, firm pressure massage emphasizing grounding after disorienting combination, 10 minutes Sub-occipital and cranial: Gentle craniosacral techniques if trained, or focused sub-occipital release, 7-10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Intense combined input: Combining head rotation with body spinning provides extremely intense vestibular input - potentially disorganizing Safety concern: This combination significantly increases fall/injury risk due to extreme disorientation Professional support: Child seeking this level of vestibular input may benefit from occupational therapy vestibular assessment Manifestation 7: Rolling Eyes in Sockets Deliberately Physical Redirect Technique: When notice eye rolling, approach and say "Let's rest your eyes." Have child close eyes for 10 seconds. Then open eyes, look straight ahead at specific object for 10 seconds (point to object). Allow brief (5 seconds) eye rolling if still desired, then back to forward focus. If eye rolling continues excessively, redirect to different activity using vision differently (reading, I Spy book, video).
DIY Alternative Tool: Eye Movement Management: Eye tracking alternatives: Provide appropriate eye movement activities (following moving object, visual tracking games, eye exercise routines) Eye rest schedule: Timer every 20 minutes reminds child to rest eyes (close 20 seconds, or look at distance) Visual stimulation alternatives: Fidget spinner, optical illusion books, kaleidoscope - visual interest without eye rolling Mirror self-monitoring: Practice eye movements in mirror - builds awareness Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Where's Waldo type books: Intensive visual scanning appropriately Flashlight tag: Shine flashlight patterns on wall, child follows with eyes Visual scavenger hunts: Lists of things to find visually around house Stereogram/Magic Eye books: Books requiring eye focus/divergence - appropriate visual challenge Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Vision therapy: Professional vision therapy if underlying visual tracking/processing issues
Visual-motor activities: Activities integrating vision with movement (catch, tennis, visual tracking games) Appropriate eye exercises: Structured eye exercises from vision therapist or optometrist Visual sensory diet: Throughout day, varied visual activities (near/far focus, tracking, scanning) satisfying visual needs For Avoiders: Stable visual targets: Look only at stable, non-moving objects Reduce visual demands: Minimize activities requiring eye movements Central focus only: Use central focused vision, avoid peripheral/moving targets Dim lighting: If visual environment overwhelming, reduce lighting intensity Massage Techniques: Eye area gentle massage: Very gentle massage around eyes on orbital bones, 2-3 minutes Temple massage: Firm pressure on temples with circular motions, 2 minutes Forehead massage: Massage forehead and eyebrow area, 3 minutes - relieves visual tension Face and scalp massage: Full face and scalp massage, 7-10 minutes - very organizing for visual system
Vestibular Integration: Visual-vestibular link: Eye movements directly connect to vestibular system through VOR (vestibulo-ocular reflex) Proprioceptive eye muscles: Eye rolling provides proprioceptive feedback from eye muscles - may be seeking this input Vision-vestibular therapy: Some children benefit from vision therapy addressing visual-vestibular integration Manifestation 8: Head Movements While Watching TV or During Activities Physical Redirect Technique: When observe head movements during TV/activities, pause the show/activity. Say "Head position check." Guide head to neutral centre position, have child hold still for 10 seconds feeling neutral position. Resume show for 5 minutes, then pause again for position check. Gradually increase time between checks as child maintains neutral position longer. If can't maintain, may need movement break (jumping jacks, run around room). DIY Alternative Tool: Activity Position Management:
Head position reminder: Place small mirror beside TV/activity space so child can monitor own head position Position checks: Set timer for every 10 minutes during activities, check head position when timer sounds Supported seating: Chair with high back and headrest encourages neutral head position during activities Activity modifications: Adjust activity setup (TV height, book angle, desk position) to encourage natural neutral head position Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Movement breaks: Every 15-20 minutes during sedentary activities, 2-minute movement break including appropriate head movements Fidget tools: Provide hand fidgets during TV/activities - redirects movement to hands instead of head Varied positioning: Watch TV/do activities from different positions (sitting, lying, standing) to vary input Active watching: Combine TV with activity (bouncing on therapy ball, gentle rocking chair) - provides movement outlet
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Pre-activity vestibular input: Before sedentary activities, 10 minutes vestibular activity (spinning, swinging, jumping) may reduce head movement during activity Movement integrated: Do homework on therapy ball, watch TV in rocking chair - legitimizes movement need Frequent breaks: Structure sedentary time with frequent active breaks (20 min activity, 3 min movement, repeat) Positioning variety: Change position frequently during activities - floor, chair, standing desk, beanbag For Avoiders: Supported positions: Very stable, supported seating for all activities Predictable setup: Same setup every time, no changes Short durations: Limit sedentary activity time to what can tolerate comfortably Calm activities only: Choose calming, non-stimulating activities Massage Techniques: Pre-activity calming massage: Before sedentary activities, 5-minute calming massage may reduce fidgeting/head movements
Post-activity release: After activities involving head movements, thorough neck and shoulder massage, 7-10 minutes Ongoing light touch: During activities (if tolerated), gentle hand on shoulder or light scalp massage provides organizing input Evening comprehensive: Thorough full-body massage at day's end, 15-20 minutes, integrating all day's vestibular input Vestibular Integration: Vestibular regulation: Head movements during activities may indicate under-stimulated vestibular system seeking input Sensory diet timing: Ensure robust vestibular sensory diet throughout day reduces seeking during quiet times Activity modifications: Some children need movement during learning/watching - this is OK and can be accommodated
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 5. VESTIBULAR STIMMING > C. Movement Pattern Stimming > Level 1: Pacing and Walking Patterns
Causation: Over-stimulated: Rhythmic pacing organizes thoughts and emotions Under-stimulated: Movement provides continuous vestibular + proprioceptive input Sensitivity: Needs movement to process information or manage anxiety Cognitive: Pacing aids thinking, problem-solving, or emotional processing Toe-Walking: May indicate tight Achilles tendons, sensory seeking, or neurological pattern Sensory Profile: Seeker: Constant movement throughout day; can't think while still Anxious Pacer: Increases during stress or emotional dysregulation Toe-Walker: Seeking proprioceptive input through calves; avoiding heel contact sensation Description: Repetitive walking or movement paths Manifestation 1: Pacing Back and Forth (10-60+ Minutes) Physical Redirect Technique: When child has been pacing for extended time, walk alongside them for a few paces, then gently touch their shoulder and say "Let's take a pacing pause." Guide them to stop, stand still, plant feet firmly, take 3 deep breaths. Say "Your body has been walking a lot. Let's try sitting for 10 minutes with something interesting." Offer engaging seated activity. Set timer - after 10 minutes, brief pacing allowed if needed.
DIY Alternative Tool: Pacing Management System: Pacing path: Use colored tape to create specific pacing path (10-15 feet), pacing allowed only on path (contains behavior) Pacing timer: Set timer for pacing sessions (10 minutes pacing, 10 minutes seated/different activity) Step counter: Child wears pedometer or uses phone app, tracks steps, set daily maximum Pacing chart: Visual schedule showing when pacing allowed (after school 15 min, before bed 10 min) and when other activities required Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Treadmill walking: If available, structured treadmill time provides walking outlet with purpose Walking chores: Channel pacing into functional walking (carry items back and forth, deliver messages) Walking meditation: Teach mindful walking practice - slow, intentional walking with breath focus Indoor walking track: Create designated walking route through house, child walks circuit specific number of times
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured walking times: 15-minute walking sessions 3x daily (morning, afternoon, evening) with specific routes/destinations Walking with purpose: Dog walking, mail getting, trash taking - functional walking Nature walks: Daily outdoor walks in neighborhood or park - provides vestibular input plus environmental richness Walking meetings: Have conversations while walking together - makes pacing social and purposeful For Avoiders: Minimal walking: Reduce walking to necessary only Seated activities priority: Plan day around seated activities Short distances: Keep all walking distances very short Assistive devices: Use wagon, cart, or assistance for carrying items to reduce walking Massage Techniques: Leg and foot focus: After extended pacing, thorough leg massage from hip to ankle, 10 minutes each leg Foot reflexology: Deep pressure massage on soles of feet, 5 minutes each - very grounding after pacing
Hip and lower back: Pacing can strain these areas, massage thoroughly, 7-10 minutes Calming transition massage: After pacing, slow rhythmic massage transitioning to stillness, 10-15 minutes Vestibular Integration: Linear vestibular input: Back-and-forth pacing provides linear vestibular stimulation - organizing for many Cognitive processing: Many people pace while thinking/problem-solving - movement aids cognition Anxiety regulation: Pacing often increases with anxiety - address underlying anxiety while providing movement alternatives Manifestation 2: Walking in Circles or Figure-8 Patterns Physical Redirect Technique: Observe child's circular/figure-8 walking pattern. Join them briefly walking the pattern, then say "Let's change our path to straight." Take their hand (if accepted) and walk straight line together across room and back, counting steps. Repeat 3 times. Then allow brief return to circular pattern if desired, but encourage varying patterns throughout day.
DIY Alternative Tool: Pattern Walking Management: Multiple path options: Create different taped paths on floor - straight, curved, zigzag - child chooses but must vary Pattern cards: Make cards showing different walking patterns (circle, figure-8, straight, square), child draws card and follows that pattern Transition protocol: 5 minutes circle walking, 5 minutes straight walking, 5 minutes figure-8, rest Outdoor chalk patterns: Draw various walking patterns with chalk outside, child follows patterns Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Labyrinths: Draw or print finger labyrinths child traces with finger - same pattern concept without full-body walking Dance patterns: Teach dance steps following patterns (box step, grapevine) - structured pattern walking Sports drills: Soccer dribbling in patterns, basketball dribbling circuits - purposeful pattern movement Indoor track variety: Create circuit through house with different movement types at each station
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Pattern exploration: Encourage trying many different walking patterns - builds motor planning Obstacle courses: Create courses requiring various movement patterns and directions Sports participation: Soccer, basketball, tennis - sports with patterned movements Dance/movement class: Structured classes teaching choreographed patterns For Avoiders: Straight paths only: Simple, straight walking paths Minimal turns: Reduce turning and directional changes Supported walking: Hold hand or rail while walking Predictable routes: Same walking route every time Massage Techniques: Bilateral leg massage: Circular walking may use one side more than other, ensure equal bilateral massage, 10 minutes each leg Hip rotator massage: Circular walking uses hip rotators intensely, massage deeply, 5 minutes each side Balance integration: Massage while child practices standing balance - integrates proprioception with vestibular
Core massage: Circular/pattern walking requires core stability, massage abdominal and back muscles, 7 minutes Vestibular Integration: Multi-directional input: Circular and figure-8 patterns provide complex vestibular input from multiple directions Motor planning: Complex patterns require and build motor planning skills Spatial awareness: Pattern walking develops spatial awareness and body navigation skills Manifestation 3: Specific Routes Through Rooms (Same Path 20-100+ Times) Physical Redirect Technique: After child has walked their specific route multiple times, intercept at a point in the route, gently touch their arm and say "Let's try a new route today." Guide them through alternative path through rooms. Walk new route together 3 times. Then say "Tomorrow let's try another different route." Create variety gradually while respecting need for some routine.
DIY Alternative Tool: Route Management System: Route rotation chart: Create 3-4 different approved routes, chart shows which route for which day (builds flexibility) Route counter: Track how many times child walks specific route, set maximum per day (50 times) Route timer: Set timer - walk specific route for 10 minutes, then must change to different activity for 20 minutes Treasure hunt routes: Hide small items along various routes, finding items requires walking different paths Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Functional routes: Make routes purposeful - walking route to collect laundry, walking route to set table - functional purpose Delivery person game: Give child items to deliver to different rooms following various routes Different movements on route: Walk route different ways (tiptoe, heel-toe, backward, sideways) - maintains route but varies input
Timed challenges: "Can you walk the route in under 2 minutes?" - adds challenge element Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured routine flexibility: Gradually introduce route variations - helps build cognitive flexibility while maintaining structure Active routes: Make routes include vestibular activities (spin at corner, jump over line, crawl under table) Social routes: Walk routes with family members, take turns choosing routes Map making: Draw maps of different routes, plan new routes together For Avoiders: Consistent routes: Allow same predictable route if provides comfort Supported walking: Walk routes with adult nearby Visual route markers: Use visual cues marking the safe, preferred route Minimal changes: Introduce any route changes very gradually with preparation Massage Techniques: Repetitive movement release: Massage addressing muscle imbalances from repetitive route walking, 10-15 minutes
Leg symmetry focus: Ensure both legs massaged equally even if route favors one side Calming routine massage: If route walking is anxiety-driven, calming massage before known triggers, 10 minutes Evening integration: End-of-day massage integrating all repetitive movements, 15-20 minutes Vestibular Integration: Predictability vs. flexibility: Balance child's need for predictable vestibular input with building flexibility Cognitive-motor link: Specific routes may help cognitive processing - respect this while expanding repertoire OCD features: If route-walking has compulsive features, may benefit from OCD-specific interventions alongside sensory strategies Manifestation 4: Walking on Toes Consistently (Toe-Walking) Physical Redirect Technique: When notice toe-walking, approach child and say "Let's check your feet." Have them stop, look down at feet together. Say "Let's put heels down" and guide them to lower heels to floor. Walk beside them for 10 steps with flat feet, praising "Great flat-foot walking!" If toe-walking resumes, immediately repeat. May need frequent reminders until pattern changes.
DIY Alternative Tool: Toe-Walking Intervention System: Heel strikes practice: Paint or tape heels of shoes with bright color, child tries to make heel marks on floor when walking Ankle weights: Very light ankle weights (½-1 lb) make toe-walking harder, encourage flat-foot walking Heel-first stepping stones: Create path with marked spots for heels to land on Mirror walking: Walk past mirror, child observes own walking style - builds awareness Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Calf stretching routine: Multiple daily calf stretches (may have tight Achilles tendons), 5 minutes 3x daily Heel walking practice: Practice walking on heels only (opposite of toe-walking) 2 minutes 3x daily Barefoot time: Maximum barefoot time at home - easier to feel heel contact without shoes Sensory paths: Create textured walking paths, child must feel textures with full foot (encourages flat-foot walking)
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Heavy heel stepping: Practice stomping, marching, heavy heel strikes - opposite of toe-walking Squatting activities: Deep squats stretch calves (often tight in toe-walkers), do throughout day Foot massage before walking: Massage feet before walking activities, 3 minutes each foot, increases foot awareness Professional assessment: Persistent toe-walking may need physical therapy assessment for Achilles tightness For Avoiders: Supported walking: Use railings, furniture, or hand-holding while learning flat-foot walking Slow practice: Very slow, controlled walking practice focusing on heel-toe pattern Comfortable footwear: Ensure shoes support flat-foot walking comfortably Short practice sessions: Brief practice sessions (2-3 minutes) multiple times daily Massage Techniques: Calf deep massage: Tight calves common in toe-walkers, deep massage 5-7 minutes each calf daily Achilles tendon attention: Gentle massage of Achilles tendon, 2-3 minutes each
Foot flexion massage: Massage while gently dorsiflexing foot (bringing toes toward shin), stretches calf Full leg massage: Comprehensive leg massage from hip to toes, 10 minutes each leg Vestibular Integration: Proprioceptive seeking: Toe-walking provides intense calf proprioceptive input - may be sensory-seeking behavior Vestibular compensation: Some children toe-walk to compensate for poor vestibular processing Medical evaluation: Persistent toe-walking should be evaluated by pediatrician/physical therapist to rule out neurological causes Manifestation 5: Marching or Stomping While Walking Physical Redirect Technique: When child is marching/stomping, join them briefly marching in place together. Then say "Let's change to quiet cat feet walking." Demonstrate exaggerated tiptoeing quietly, have them try for 10 steps. Alternate: 10 steps loud marching, 10 steps quiet walking. Builds awareness of different walking styles and control.
DIY Alternative Tool: Walking Style Management: Volume control game: Create "volume cards" - loud (red), medium (yellow), quiet (green) - child draws card and walks that volume Marching time vs. quiet time: Visual schedule showing when marching appropriate (outside, gym, designated times) vs. when quiet walking needed (library, bedtime, quiet hours) Step-o-meter with style: Track not just steps but style - marching steps vs. quiet steps, aim for balance Drum march: Designate times for marching to drumbeat (structured, appropriate outlet), rest of time quiet walking Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Marching band play: Create marching band activities with pots/pans instruments - appropriate stomping outlet Dance style practice: Practice different walking styles (tiptoe, march, shuffle, glide) - builds movement repertoire Heavy work alternative: When marching urge hits, redirect to heavy work (carrying, pushing) providing proprioceptive input
Outdoor stomping: Designate outside area for loud marching/stomping, inside requires quiet feet Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured marching time: 10-15 minutes 2-3x daily of approved marching/stomping time Proprioceptive alternatives: Other activities providing impact (jumping, running, stomping in designated areas) Marching games: Follow the leader marching, freeze march, marching to music Sports with impact: Activities with jumping, running, stomping (basketball, dance, martial arts) For Avoiders: Quiet walking always: Practice only soft, quiet walking Carpet/soft surfaces: Walk on soft surfaces that naturally quiet footsteps Gentle movement: All movement slow, controlled, gentle Noise sensitivity: May be avoiding loud sounds, provide quiet environment Massage Techniques: Heel and foot deep massage: Stomping impacts heels, deep massage of heels and entire foot, 5 minutes each Calf and shin massage: Marching uses these muscles intensely, massage both front and back of lower leg, 5 minutes each
Hip and knee joint massage: Impact travels up leg to hips, massage around these joints, 3 minutes each Spinal massage: Impact transmitted up through spine, gentle spinal massage, 5-7 minutes Vestibular Integration: Proprioceptive seeking: Stomping/marching provides strong proprioceptive input through joints - often seeking this Auditory feedback: May also seek auditory feedback from loud footsteps Energy level: High-energy children may naturally march - need appropriate outlets for their energy Manifestation 6: Walking Along Lines, Cracks, or Edges Obsessively Physical Redirect Technique: Observe child walking on lines/cracks. After several minutes, approach and say "I see you're doing line-walking. Let's try crossing over the lines instead." Walk together deliberately stepping over lines/cracks for 20 steps. Then allow brief return to line-walking if desired. Practice alternating: 20 steps on lines, 20 steps crossing lines.
DIY Alternative Tool: Line-Walking Management: Designated line-walking area: Create taped lines specifically for line-walking (straight, curved, zigzag) - provides appropriate outlet Line-walking time limits: Timer for line-walking sessions (5 minutes), then different activity Balance beam alternative: Provide actual balance beam or 2x4 board on floor for legitimate balance practice Line variety: Create variety of line-walking challenges (different widths, heights, textures) - purposeful practice Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Tape patterns: Create elaborate tape patterns on floor - mazes, paths, games - purposeful line-following Hopscotch: Draw hopscotch patterns, combines line-walking with jumping Balance beam DIY: 2x4 board on floor, yoga mat rolled and taped, thick rope on floor - all provide line-walking alternatives Curb walking: Outside, practice walking on curbs (supervised) - functional line-walking skill
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Balance challenges: Activities requiring balance on narrow surfaces (balance beam, curb, low wall) Proprioceptive foot input: Activities providing foot input (barefoot walking on textures, foot massages, calf raises) Visual-motor integration: Line-following provides visual-motor practice - can channel into other activities (mazes, tracing, crafts) Gymnastics/dance: Classes teaching balance beam, barre work - appropriate line-walking outlets For Avoiders: Wide paths: Walk on wide, clear paths with no lines to navigate Avoid patterns: Keep environment simple without distracting lines/patterns Supported walking: Hold hand or rail, focus on destination not path Minimal visual complexity: Reduce visual environmental complexity Massage Techniques: Foot proprioception massage: Deep pressure massage of entire foot sole, 5 minutes each - increases foot awareness Ankle stability massage: Massage around ankle joints, 3 minutes each - these work hard for balance
Calf massage: Line-walking requires calf control, massage thoroughly, 5 minutes each Lower leg comprehensive: Full lower leg massage from knee to toes, 10 minutes each leg Vestibular Integration: Balance challenge: Line-walking challenges balance system - may be seeking vestibular input Visual-vestibular integration: Following lines integrates visual tracking with vestibular balance control Obsessive features: If compulsive (can't not walk on lines), may need OCD-specific interventions Manifestation 7: Zigzag or Serpentine Walking Patterns Physical Redirect Technique: Observe child's zigzag walking pattern. Join them walking zigzag briefly, then say "Let's try a different pattern - straight walking." Walk straight line together for 20 steps, counting. Then try wide gentle curves. Then tight zigzags. Practice various patterns: straight, gentle curve, tight zigzag, circle - builds pattern variety and motor control.
DIY Alternative Tool: Pattern Walking System: Pattern rotation chart: Chart showing different patterns to practice (straight, zigzag, circle, figure-8), rotate daily Cone course: Set up cones creating various patterns child navigates through Floor tape patterns: Multiple taped patterns on floor, child follows different ones at different times Pattern cards: Draw card showing which pattern to walk (adds cognitive element and variety) Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Slalom walking: Set up objects to zigzag around (chairs, pillows, toys) - purposeful zigzag Dancing: Many dances involve zigzag patterns - structured pattern movement Sports drills: Soccer dribbling through cones, basketball weaving drills Nature walks: Walking trails naturally have curves and zigzags - functional pattern walking Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Complex motor planning: Create elaborate obstacle courses requiring varied movement patterns
Sports participation: Soccer, basketball, skating - activities with directional changes Dance/movement classes: Choreographed movement with various patterns Agility training: Ladder drills, cone drills, agility course - structured pattern practice For Avoiders: Straight paths only: Simple, straight walking without turns Gradual curves: If any turns, very gradual and predictable Supported navigation: Adult guides through any pattern changes Minimal complexity: Keep movement patterns simple and predictable Massage Techniques: Lateral leg muscles: Zigzag walking uses lateral leg muscles intensely, massage outer and inner thigh, 5 minutes each leg Hip abductor/adductor massage: Directional changes work these muscles, thorough massage, 5 minutes each side Core rotation massage: Zigzag walking requires core rotation, massage obliques and back, 7 minutes Balance integration: Massage while child practices standing balance on one foot - integrates proprioception
