Vestibular Integration: Multi-directional vestibular input: Zigzag patterns provide vestibular input from multiple directions - rich stimulation Motor planning development: Complex patterns require and build motor planning skills Cognitive engagement: Pattern walking engages cognitive planning areas of brain Manifestation 8: Walking Backwards for Extended Periods Physical Redirect Technique: When notice backward walking, approach from side (safe - they can see you) and say "I see you're going backwards. Let's do 10 backward steps together, then 10 forward steps." Count backward steps together, then turn and count forward steps together. Practice alternating: 10 backward, 10 forward, repeat 3 times. Builds awareness and control. DIY Alternative Tool: Backward Walking Management: Backward walking zones: Designate safe areas for backward walking (clear, no obstacles), rest of areas forward only
Mirror practice: Practice backward walking watching self in mirror - builds spatial awareness Backward step counter: Set daily limit for backward walking (100 steps), child tracks own backward steps Game format: Backward walking as part of games (musical chairs walking backward, red light/green light backward) Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Backward walking path: Create safe taped path for backward walking practice Moonwalk practice: Teach moonwalk dance move - cool way to go backward with purpose Backward races: Structured backward walking races with clear safe path Video feedback: Record backward walking, watch together - increases body awareness Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Bilateral backward walking: Practice backward walking focusing on equal use of both legs Backward obstacle course: Navigate backward through cones, around objects (supervised)
Sports with backward: Basketball defense drills, dancing, skating - activities including backward movement Vestibular challenge: Backward walking is more vestibularly challenging than forward - good therapeutic activity For Avoiders: Forward only: Only forward walking, avoid backward movement Supported backward: If must go backward, hold hand or wall Minimal backward: Limit backward movement to absolute minimum Visual monitoring: If any backward movement, constantly look behind Massage Techniques: Posterior leg focus: Backward walking uses back of legs differently, massage hamstrings and calves, 5 minutes each leg Lower back massage: Backward walking can strain lower back, massage thoroughly, 7 minutes Hip extensor massage: Backward walking uses hip extensors (glutes), massage deeply, 5 minutes each side Vestibular calming: After challenging backward walking, calming massage focusing on sub-occipital area, 5 minutes
Vestibular Integration: Increased vestibular challenge: Backward movement more challenging than forward - requires more vestibular processing Motor planning: Backward walking requires motor planning and spatial awareness Therapeutic value: Backward walking actually a therapeutic activity in many therapy programs
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 5. VESTIBULAR STIMMING > C. Movement Pattern Stimming > Level 2: Complex Motor Patterns
Causation: Over-stimulated: Complex patterns require focus; blocks overwhelming input Under-stimulated: Intense, varied movement provides rich sensory input Sensitivity: Vestibular + proprioceptive + motor planning integration Mastery: Perfecting movement patterns provides accomplishment Cognitive: Motor planning practice; body-brain connection development Sensory Profile: Extreme Seeker: Creates increasingly complex challenges Athlete: Thrives on physical challenge and movement variety Motor Planning: Using movement to develop coordination and body awareness Description: Elaborate movement sequences Manifestation 1: Animal Walks for Extended Periods (Bear Crawl, Crab Walk, Bunny Hops) Physical Redirect Technique: When child has been doing animal walks extensively, join them briefly in the animal walk. Then say "Let's try walking like humans now." Stand up together, walk normally for 20 steps. Then say "Let's play animal walk relay - one trip as bear, one trip as human, one trip as crab." Structure alternates animal walks with regular walking.
DIY Alternative Tool: Animal Walk Management: Animal walk circuit: Create circuit with different animal walks at each station (bear crawl, crab walk, bunny hops, frog jumps, regular walking) Animal walk timer: Set timer for 5 minutes animal walking, then 10 minutes other activities Animal walk cards: Draw cards showing different movements (animals AND regular movements), follow card drawn Fitness routine: Integrate animal walks into exercise routine (2 minutes bear crawl, 2 minutes rest, 2 minutes crab walk) Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Obstacle course: Create course requiring various movements including animal walks - purposeful use Animal walk races: Structured races with family comparing different animal walks Follow the leader: Take turns leading with different movements (mix animal walks and regular movements) YouTube animal walk videos: Follow along with structured animal walk workout videos
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Heavy work circuit: Animal walks provide intense proprioceptive input - include in daily heavy work routine Timed challenges: "How fast can you bear crawl across the room?" - adds challenge and purpose Gymnastics class: Classes teaching proper animal walk form plus other skills Daily routine: 15 minutes morning and afternoon of structured animal walk exercises For Avoiders: Regular walking only: Avoid animal walks and other complex movements Upright movements: Keep all movement in natural upright position Minimal joint loading: Avoid weight-bearing on hands/arms Comfortable movement: Only movements that feel natural and comfortable Massage Techniques: Shoulder and arm focus: Animal walks load shoulders/arms heavily, deep massage 7-10 minutes each arm Wrist and hand massage: Weight-bearing on hands strains these areas, massage thoroughly 5 minutes each
Core strengthening massage: Animal walks require strong core, massage abdominal and back muscles, 7 minutes Full body proprioceptive: After animal walks, full body deep pressure massage integrating input, 15 minutes Vestibular Integration: Inverted head position: Some animal walks (bear crawl) put head lower than body - vestibular challenge Proprioceptive loading: Animal walks provide intense whole-body proprioceptive input - very organizing Motor planning: Different animal walks require various motor patterns - builds motor planning skills Manifestation 2: Dancing or Movement Routines Repeated 10-100+ Times Physical Redirect Technique: Count child's routine repetitions. At 10 repetitions, say "Pause! That was great dancing. Let's rest and watch someone else dance now." Show them video of professional dancing for 3 minutes (gives visual dance input without movement). Then allow 10 more routine repetitions if desired. Alternates doing with watching/resting.
DIY Alternative Tool: Dance Routine Management: Repetition counter: Use counter app, set maximum repetitions per session (20 reps) Routine rotation: Create 3-4 different routines, must rotate between them (prevents excessive repetition of one) Performance schedule: Schedule times when routines are "performed" (morning show, afternoon show, evening show) containing dance to specific times Learning mode: Time spent creating NEW moves/routines vs. repeating existing ones Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Mirror practice: Practice routine in front of mirror -increases body awareness, may reduce repetitions needed Video recording: Record routine, watch playback together - provides visual feedback Teach others: Child teaches routine to family member - makes repetition purposeful Music variety: Dance to different music styles, adapt routine to different tempos Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers:
Dance class enrollment: Structured class teaching choreography - appropriate outlet for dance repetition Just Dance video game: Follows on-screen choreography, provides structure and variety Create performances: Work toward actual performances (family show, recital) - gives purpose to practice Varied dance styles: Explore ballet, hip hop, jazz, tap - variety maintains interest For Avoiders: Minimal dancing: Avoid dance and repetitive movements Seated movement: If any movement, seated swaying or arm movements only Slow movements: Only slow, controlled movements, no fast dancing Observation: May prefer watching others dance rather than dancing Massage Techniques: Full body athletic massage: After extensive dancing, comprehensive massage like athletic recovery, 20-30 minutes Leg focus: Dancing uses legs intensely, thorough leg massage from hip to ankle, 10 minutes each leg
Foot and ankle care: Dance stresses feet/ankles, deep massage and gentle mobilization, 5 minutes each Back and core: Dance requires strong back/core, massage these areas thoroughly, 10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Multi-sensory integration: Dancing integrates vestibular, proprioceptive, auditory, and visual - rich sensory experience Bilateral coordination: Dance develops bilateral coordination and motor planning Cognitive-motor link: Learning choreography builds memory and motor planning together Manifestation 3: Parkour-Style Movements Over Furniture and Objects Physical Redirect Technique: When child is doing parkour movements on furniture, approach calmly and say "Stop and sit." Once stopped, say "Parkour belongs outside on safe equipment, not on furniture. Let's go outside/to designated area." Immediately redirect to appropriate location. If can't go outside, redirect to approved indoor activity (obstacle course on floor, jumping on designated cushions). Establish clear rule: furniture for sitting, parkour for outside/gym.
DIY Alternative Tool: Safe Parkour Alternatives: Outdoor parkour course: Create safe outdoor course using sturdy boxes, logs, low walls, platforms (supervision required) Indoor obstacle course: Floor-level course using cushions, taped lines, tunnels (no furniture climbing) Parkour class enrollment: Many gyms offer parkour classes with proper equipment and instruction Parkour zone designation: Specific outdoor area designated for parkour practice with clear boundaries Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Cushion course: Large floor cushions arranged as stepping stones, jump between them safely Tape course: Create elaborate taped floor course requiring jumping, balancing, crawling - no furniture needed Basement/garage setup: If available, set up safe jumping/climbing area with crash mats Playground structures: Daily playground visits utilizing climbing structures appropriately Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured parkour time: Daily scheduled time for supervised parkour practice in appropriate location
Ninja warrior courses: Create safe ninja warrior-style challenges appropriate for child's skill level Climbing wall access: Rock climbing gym membership provides safe climbing outlet Gymnastics class: Gymnastics teaches vaulting, jumping, tumbling safely with instruction For Avoiders: Ground-level activities: All activities on stable ground, no climbing or jumping Avoid heights: Stay away from elevated surfaces Slow movement: Controlled, careful movement always Supported activities: Activities with adult support nearby Massage Techniques: Impact absorption massage: After parkour, massage areas absorbing impact (feet, ankles, knees, wrists), 10 minutes Joint compressions: Compress all major joints after parkour, 10 seconds each - adds organizing proprioceptive input Full body recovery: Comprehensive massage like athletic recovery, 20-25 minutes Injury prevention focus: Check for any soreness, massage preventatively, ice if needed
Vestibular Integration: Complex vestibular challenge: Parkour combines multiple movement planes - very challenging vestibular activity Risk assessment: Teach risk assessment skills alongside parkour skills - important safety learning Motor planning: Parkour requires advanced motor planning - builds these skills intensely Manifestation 4: Gymnastic Movements in Sequences (Handstands, Rolls, Cartwheels) Physical Redirect Technique: When child is doing gymnastic sequences repetitively, count sequences with them. At 10 sequences, say "Time for a gymnastics break!" Have them do static stretching (10 different stretches, 20 seconds each) - maintains gymnastics theme while giving break. Then allow 10 more sequences if desired. Alternates dynamic movement with static stretching. DIY Alternative Tool: Gymnastics Sequence Management: Sequence counter: Track sequences per session, set maximum (20-30 sequences) Routine variation: Create 3-4 different sequences, must rotate between them
Skill progression chart: Chart tracking mastery of different skills, work on weakest skills not just favorites Performance format: Work toward creating polished routine for performance rather than endless repetition Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Gymnastics mat: Invest in basic gymnastics mat for safe home practice (8-10 ft long) Video tutorials: Follow gymnastics tutorial videos teaching new skills Yoga integration: Blend gymnastics with yoga - similar movements, adds mindfulness component Trampoline gymnastics: If have trampoline, practice gymnastics skills on it (supervised) Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Gymnastics class enrollment: Structured class with proper equipment and progressive skill teaching Daily practice routine: 20-30 minute structured practice including warm-up, skills, cool-down stretching Conditioning integration: Add strength/conditioning exercises between sequences (10 sequences, 20 push-ups, 10 sequences, 30 crunches)
Skill mastery focus: Work on perfecting form rather than quantity - quality over quantity For Avoiders: No gymnastics: Avoid inverted positions and gymnastics movements Gentle stretching only: Simple stretching without dynamic movements Supported positions: Any positions fully supported by floor/furniture Slow, controlled: If any movement, very slow and controlled Massage Techniques: Wrist and shoulder priority: Gymnastics stresses these areas, deep massage 7-10 minutes each Spinal alignment check: Gentle massage ensuring spinal alignment after inversions/flexibility work, 7 minutes Flexibility enhancement: Massage combined with gentle stretching, 15 minutes Recovery focus: Sports massage techniques focusing on muscle recovery, 20 minutes Vestibular Integration: Multiple planes: Gymnastics involves movement through all planes - comprehensive vestibular input Inverted positions: Handstands, rolls provide inverted vestibular input - very stimulating
Bilateral integration: Gymnastics requires bilateral coordination - integrates both brain hemispheres Manifestation 5: Specific Hand-Foot Coordination Patterns Physical Redirect Technique: Observe child's specific coordination pattern. Join them doing the pattern briefly, then say "Let's try a different pattern." Teach them new pattern (cross-crawl pattern, alternate hand-foot touches, bilateral movements). Practice new pattern together 10 repetitions. Then allow return to their preferred pattern if desired. Goal is building pattern variety. DIY Alternative Tool: Coordination Pattern System: Pattern library cards: Create cards showing 10-15 different coordination patterns, child draws cards and practices different patterns Mirror practice: Practice patterns in front of mirror - visual feedback improves coordination Bilateral integration focus: Ensure patterns include bilateral and cross-lateral movements Music pairing: Pair different patterns with different music styles
Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Dance coordination: Learn dance moves requiring specific hand-foot patterns (grapevine, box step, salsa steps) Martial arts basics: Learn basic martial arts stances and movements - structured coordination patterns Sports skills: Dribbling (hand-foot coordination), jumping rope, hopscotch - functional patterns Musical instruments: Drums or piano require hand-foot coordination patterns Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Cross-lateral exercises: Activities crossing body midline (march touching opposite knee, cross-crawls) Complex pattern training: Progressively more complex patterns building motor planning Bilateral activities: Activities using both sides simultaneously (swimming, climbing, bilateral catching) Rhythm-based: Patterns performed to specific rhythms adds auditory-motor integration For Avoiders: Simple patterns: Only simple, basic movement patterns Unilateral first: Master one-side movements before bilateral Slow practice: Very slow, controlled practice of any patterns
Supported positions: Practice patterns while sitting or well-supported Massage Techniques: Bilateral symmetrical massage: Massage both sides simultaneously supporting bilateral integration Cross-pattern massage: Massage right arm while child lifts left leg (and vice versa) - cross-lateral integration Limb awareness massage: Massage each limb individually building proprioceptive awareness Coordination integration: Massage while guiding through gentle movement patterns Vestibular Integration: Motor planning development: Specific patterns require and build motor planning skills Bilateral integration: Many patterns integrate both brain hemispheres Proprioceptive awareness: Patterns require awareness of where body parts are in space Manifestation 6: Jumping Patterns with Specific Sequences Physical Redirect Technique: Count child's jumping pattern repetitions. At 10 repetitions, say "Jump break!" Have them do 10 slow squats instead (maintains leg work, changes pattern). Then allow 10 more jump pattern repetitions. Alternates jumping with different leg exercise. If child insists on more jumping immediately, redirect to different activity entirely for 5 minutes.
DIY Alternative Tool: Jumping Pattern Management: Pattern variation cards: Cards showing different jumping patterns (hopscotch, jump rope patterns, alternating foot jumps), must use variety Jump counter: Count jump pattern repetitions, set maximum per session (50-100 jumps) Hopscotch variety: Create different hopscotch patterns requiring different jumping sequences Video jump games: Just Dance, Dance Dance Revolution - jumping patterns with visual guidance Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Jump rope routines: Learn different jump rope patterns and tricks Trampoline patterns: Practice different jumping patterns on trampoline (if available) Chalk patterns: Draw jumping patterns on driveway/sidewalk with chalk, follow patterns Fitness jumping: Jumping jacks, star jumps, tuck jumps, split jumps - variety of jump types Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured jumping routine: 10 minutes 2-3x daily including multiple jump types and rest periods
Jump training: Progressive jump training (single, double, triple jumps; height goals; patterns) Sports with jumping: Basketball, volleyball, jump rope team - sports featuring jumping Plyometric training: If age-appropriate, structured plyometric exercises For Avoiders: No jumping: Avoid all jumping activities Stepping only: Step up onto low step instead of jumping Supported landing: If must jump, very soft landing surface Minimal impact: Low-impact activities only Massage Techniques: Calf and foot intensive: Jumping stresses these areas heavily, 7-10 minutes each calf and 5 minutes each foot Knee joint attention: Massage around knee joint (not directly on it), 3-5 minutes each knee Hip and glute massage: Jumping uses these for power, massage deeply, 7 minutes Achilles tendon care: Gentle massage of Achilles tendon after jumping, 2-3 minutes each
Vestibular Integration: Vertical vestibular input: Jumping provides strong vertical acceleration/deceleration - intense vestibular input Motor planning: Specific patterns require sequencing and motor planning Proprioceptive impact: Landing provides strong joint compression - organizing proprioceptive input Manifestation 7: Climbing Up and Down Repeatedly (Stairs, Ladders, Furniture) Physical Redirect Technique: Count climbing repetitions. At 10 ascents/descents, say "Climbing break! Let's rest your muscles." Have them sit, drink water, do gentle stretching for 3 minutes. Then allow 10 more climb cycles if desired. If climbing continues excessively, set timer: "You can climb for 10 more minutes, then we do a different activity." DIY Alternative Tool: Climbing Management System: Climb counter: Track climbs per session, set daily maximum (30-40 climbs) Stair circuit: Create circuit - climb stairs, do activity at top, descend, do activity at bottom, repeat
Climbing schedule: Designate specific times for climbing (morning 15 min, after school 20 min) Alternative heights: Rotate between stairs, step stool, low ladder - varies climbing experience Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Step-ups: Use bottom stair or sturdy box for step-up exercises (up-down-up-down) Stair games: Climb stairs in different ways (one foot, sideways, tiptoe, heel-walking) Delivery service: Give child items to carry upstairs/downstairs - functional climbing Stair intervals: Fitness routine using stairs (climb slow 5x, fast 5x, march-step 5x) Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Rock climbing: Gym membership for indoor rock climbing - safe, supervised, challenging climbing Playground climbing: Daily playground visits focusing on climbing structures Climbing class: Many gyms offer children's climbing classes Hiking trails: Nature hikes with elevation changes provide extensive climbing opportunities
For Avoiders: Minimal climbing: Avoid stairs and climbing when possible Elevator/escalator use: Use alternatives to stairs when available Hand rail required: Always hold railing when must use stairs Very slow climbing: Take stairs one at a time, very carefully Massage Techniques: Full leg massage: Climbing works entire leg, comprehensive massage hip to ankle, 10 minutes each leg Glute focus: Climbing uses glutes intensely, deep massage, 7 minutes Calf and shin: Both areas work hard in climbing, massage thoroughly, 5 minutes each leg Lower back: Climbing can strain lower back, massage carefully, 7 minutes Vestibular Integration: Vertical movement: Climbing up/down provides vertical vestibular input Proprioceptive loading: Weight-bearing climbing provides intense proprioceptive input Motor planning: Navigating climbing requires planning and coordination Manifestation 8: Obstacle Course Creation and Repetition
Physical Redirect Technique: After child has completed their obstacle course multiple times, approach and say "You've mastered that course! Time to create a NEW course." Help them design different course using different obstacles and movements. Run new course together 3 times. Then alternate: old course 3 times, new course 3 times. Builds flexibility and creativity. DIY Alternative Tool: Obstacle Course Management: Course rotation system: Create 4-5 different courses, rotate which one used each day Course modification: Every 5 completions, must modify one element of course Timed challenges: Instead of endless repetition, time each completion, try to beat personal record Family course: Family members take turns adding obstacles to course - collaborative and varied Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Indoor course elements: Cushions to jump over, tape lines to walk, chairs to go under, hula hoops to jump through
Outdoor course: Use natural elements (logs, rocks, trees) plus portable items (cones, ropes, boxes) Sensory station course: Each obstacle station includes sensory element (touch texture, find hidden item, listen for sound) Skill variety: Ensure course includes jumping, crawling, balancing, climbing, throwing - comprehensive skills Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Elaborate courses: Create increasingly complex courses adding cognitive challenges (count while jumping, recite alphabet while crawling) Timed competitions: Race against timer or family members adding competitive element Themed courses: "Lava floor," "jungle adventure," "ninja training" - imaginative themes maintain interest Progressive difficulty: Start with easier course version, gradually make more challenging For Avoiders: Simple courses: Very simple, predictable courses with no surprises Slow completion: Navigate course very slowly and carefully Optional elements: Can skip obstacles that feel too challenging
Supported practice: Adult nearby for reassurance Massage Techniques: Full body comprehensive: Obstacle courses use all muscle groups, thorough full-body massage, 20-30 minutes Recovery focus: Address any muscle soreness from intense course repetition Joint attention: Check all major joints (ankles, knees, hips, wrists, shoulders), massage around each Cool-down integration: Massage serves as cool-down after intense obstacle course activity Vestibular Integration: Multi-sensory integration: Obstacle courses integrate vestibular, proprioceptive, visual, tactile, cognitive Varied vestibular input: Courses provide vestibular input from multiple directions and types Motor planning: Planning how to navigate course builds motor planning skills
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 5. VESTIBULAR STIMMING > C. Movement Pattern Stimming > Level 3: Extreme Movement Seeking
Causation: Over-stimulated: Extreme input can "reset" overwhelmed nervous system Under-stimulated: Severe vestibular under-responsiveness; needs intense input Sensitivity: High threshold for movement sensation; typical input doesn't register Thrill-Seeking: May seek adrenaline rush from risk or speed Danger Unawareness: May not perceive risk appropriately; poor interoception Sensory Profile: Extreme Seeker: Appears "fearless"; no apparent fear of heights or speed Risk-Taker: May require strict supervision for safety High Threshold: Doesn't get dizzy or nauseous from movement that affects others Description: High-intensity or risk-seeking vestibular activities Manifestation 1: Climbing to Dangerous Heights Repeatedly Physical Redirect Technique: If child is at dangerous height, calmly say "Stop and hold on tight. I'm coming to help you down." Once down safely, sit together and say "That height is too dangerous. Let's find safer climbing." Immediately take to appropriate climbing location (rock climbing gym, playground climbing structure, safe tree). Establish clear rule about maximum safe heights with visual markers if possible.
DIY Alternative Tool: Safe Height Management: Height markers: Mark "safe height" on trees, climbing structures with colored tape - climbing above marker not allowed Supervised climbing only: All climbing requires adult supervision, no solo climbing Climbing alternatives: Provide challenging but safe climbing options (rock climbing gym membership, playground regular visits) Skill-appropriate challenge: Match climbing difficulty to actual skill level, not fearlessness level Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Indoor climbing wall: If possible, install small climbing wall with crash mat (professional installation recommended) Basement pull-up bar setup: Monkey bars or pull-up bar configuration allowing safe climbing/hanging Structured outdoor climbing: Identify safe trees/structures, establish rules for their use Climbing class enrollment: Professional instruction teaches both skills and safety Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers (HIGH RISK - Requires Intensive Management):
Daily climbing outlet: MUST provide daily safe climbing opportunities to reduce dangerous seeking Rock climbing gym: Multiple weekly visits to indoor climbing gym - safe, supervised, progressive difficulty Adrenaline alternatives: Other activities providing "rush" (trampoline parks, zip lines, roller coasters) - safer adrenaline Body awareness training: Help child recognize when engaging in dangerous vs. safe climbing For Avoiders: Ground activities only: All activities on ground level Avoid heights entirely: Stay away from elevated areas Low climbing acceptable: If any climbing, only very low (1-2 feet maximum) Constant support: Adult hand-holding for reassurance Massage Techniques: Full body check: After high climbing, check entire body for any injuries or strains, massage gently, 15-20 minutes Anxiety release: If height-seeking is thrill-seeking, massage can help release tension/anxiety, 15 minutes
Grounding focus: Heavy, grounding massage emphasizing feet and legs, 10 minutes Calming protocol: Slow, rhythmic, calming massage after intense climbing, 15-20 minutes Vestibular Integration: EXTREME seeking: Dangerous height-seeking indicates very high vestibular threshold - needs intensive vestibular sensory diet Lack of fear: May have poor interoception (body awareness) not recognizing danger - needs interoceptive training Professional assessment: This level of seeking requires occupational therapy evaluation and intervention Manifestation 2: Jumping from High Surfaces (Seeking Impact and Free-Fall Sensation) Physical Redirect Technique: If about to jump from dangerous height, say firmly "STOP! Do not jump from there!" Help them down safely. Once down, say "Jumping from high places can break bones. We need to find safe jumping." Immediately redirect to safe jumping location (trampoline, crash pit, gymnasium with mats). Establish clear maximum safe jumping heights.
DIY Alternative Tool: Safe Jumping System: Height limits: Clearly mark maximum jump heights (tape on playground equipment, rules for furniture) Landing surface requirements: May jump only onto very soft surfaces (crash mats, ball pit, deep sand) Supervised jumping only: All jumping from any height requires adult supervision Progression training: Start with low heights, only progress when demonstrating safe landing skills Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Crash mat jumping: Stack couch cushions/gymnastics mats, allow jumping onto these from LOW approved heights Trampoline with dismount: Practice trampoline jumps with safe dismounts onto surrounding padding Ball pit jumping: If space allows, jump into ball pit - provides falling sensation safely Foam pit access: Some gyms have foam pits - schedule regular visits Sensory Integration Activities:
For Seekers (HIGH RISK - Requires Intensive Management): Trampoline park weekly: Multiple weekly visits providing safe jumping outlet Parkour class: Structured class teaching safe jumping and landing techniques Gymnastics with tumbling: Structured tumbling teaching proper landings High-impact sports: Wrestling, martial arts, rugby - controlled high-impact activities For Avoiders: No jumping: Avoid all jumping, especially from heights Stepping down only: Step down carefully from any height Fear valid: Respect fear of heights and falling Ground activities: All activities on stable ground Massage Techniques: Impact absorption focus: After jumping, massage feet, ankles, knees, hips thoroughly - areas absorbing impact, 15 minutes Spinal check: Gentle spinal massage ensuring alignment after impact, 7 minutes Heel and arch: Deep massage of heels and arches which absorb landing impact, 5 minutes each foot
Ice if needed: If any soreness, ice massage on impact areas, 5 minutes Vestibular Integration: Free-fall sensation seeking: Seeking the free-fall vestibular sensation - very intense input Proprioceptive impact: Landing impact provides strong proprioceptive input through joints EXTREME threshold: This behavior indicates very high vestibular threshold requiring intensive sensory diet Manifestation 3: Seeking Extreme Playground Equipment (Highest, Fastest) Physical Redirect Technique: At playground, before child goes to extreme equipment, establish rules: "You can go on the tall slide/high monkey bars, but I stay right here watching and you must use them safely." Position yourself to supervise. If unsafe behavior, immediately say "Stop. That's not safe. Come down and take a break." After 5-minute break, may return with reviewed safety rules. DIY Alternative Tool: Playground Safety Management:
Playground rules chart: Visual chart showing playground rules (hands on equipment, feet placement, etc.) Equipment rotation: Must rotate between extreme and moderate equipment - no exclusive focus on most extreme Buddy system: Can use extreme equipment only when specific adult watching Skill demonstration: Must demonstrate safe use of moderate equipment before advancing to extreme Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Home vestibular equipment: Swing set, trapeze bar, climbing structure in yard - controlled extreme play Trampoline with enclosure: Provides intense jumping safely enclosed Slip-n-slide: Outdoor water play provides speed safely Bike riding: Controlled speed and movement challenge Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Daily playground time: Regular playground visits essential for providing needed vestibular input Adventure parks: Occasional visits to adventure/trampoline parks - safe extreme experiences
Progressive challenges: Start moderate, gradually work toward more extreme appropriately Skill building: Focus on building actual skills making extreme equipment use safer For Avoiders: Gentle equipment only: Swings with low amplitude, small slides, climbing structures near ground Avoid extreme: Stay away from highest, fastest equipment Supported use: Adult very nearby for any equipment use Observation: May prefer watching others on equipment Massage Techniques: Post-playground recovery: After intense playground use, full body massage, 15-20 minutes Specific injury prevention: Check hands, arms, shoulders (from hanging), legs (from running/jumping) Cooling down: Massage serves as cool-down after vigorous play Grounding: Emphasis on grounding after intense vestibular input, 10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Seeking maximum input: Consistently choosing most extreme equipment indicates high vestibular needs Sensation threshold: May not feel moderate vestibular input - needs extreme to register
Safety concern: Need to balance providing needed input with safety - requires close supervision Manifestation 4: Riding Bikes/Scooters at Maximum Speed Physical Redirect Technique: When child is riding at unsafe speed, call their name loudly "STOP!" Once stopped, approach and say "That speed is too fast and dangerous. Let's practice safe speed." Walk bike/scooter with them at safe speed for 2 minutes. Then allow them to ride at moderate speed. If speed increases dangerously again, take bike/scooter away for 10-minute break. Gradual speed increases only as safety skills improve. DIY Alternative Tool: Speed Management System: Speed zones: Mark zones with cones/chalk - slow zone (walking speed), medium zone (jogging speed), only designated areas for faster riding Supervised riding only: All bike/scooter riding requires adult supervision until safety demonstrated consistently
Protective gear mandatory: Helmet, knee pads, elbow pads required for ALL riding - no exceptions Racing alternatives: Set up timed courses where going carefully/accurately matters more than pure speed Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Obstacle courses: Create bike/scooter courses emphasizing control over speed Slow races: Who can ride slowest without falling - teaches control Follow the leader: Adult leads at safe speeds, child follows Delivery missions: Ride to deliver items to destinations - adds purpose beyond speed Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Daily riding time: Structured riding sessions in safe areas (parks, quiet streets, driveways) Skill progression: Learn actual bike skills (turns, stops, obstacle navigation) not just speed BMX/skateboard parks: If age-appropriate, supervised time at parks with proper equipment Racing with rules: Structured races with safety rules, adult supervision, protective gear
For Avoiders: Very slow riding: Ride only at walking speed Flat surfaces only: Avoid hills, uneven surfaces Training wheels extended: Keep training wheels longer if needed Supportive environment: Ride only with adult close by Massage Techniques: Leg focus: Riding uses legs intensely, thorough leg massage, 10 minutes each leg Lower back care: Riding position can strain back, massage carefully, 7 minutes Hand and forearm: Gripping handlebars creates tension, massage hands and forearms, 5 minutes each Neck and shoulders: Riding position affects these areas, massage thoroughly, 7 minutes Vestibular Integration: Speed sensation seeking: High-speed riding provides intense linear vestibular acceleration Risk-taking: May not accurately perceive danger - needs safety education and limits Visual-vestibular integration: Fast riding integrates vision with vestibular - challenging processing
Manifestation 5: Diving, Flipping, or Aerial Movements Physical Redirect Technique: If attempting unsafe aerial movements, say firmly "Stop! Aerial movements need proper training and safe environment." If at pool, establish diving rules based on skill level. If attempting flips on ground/furniture, redirect immediately to safe location (gymnastics gym, trampoline with supervision). Never allow unsupervised aerial movements. DIY Alternative Tool: Aerial Movement Safety System: Professional instruction required: Gymnastics, diving, or parkour classes - no self-taught aerials Appropriate equipment only: Aerials only on trampoline, into pool, or on gymnastics equipment with mats Progression requirements: Must master foundational skills before attempting advanced aerials Supervision mandatory: All aerial movements require trained supervisor present Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Trampoline practice: If have trampoline with safety net, practice basic jumps working toward aerials gradually
Pool diving: Practice diving in pool with proper depth (9+ feet for diving) Forward rolls: Practice gymnastics rolls as stepping stone toward aerial skills Professional facilities: Use gymnastics gyms with foam pits, trained coaches Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Gymnastics enrollment: Essential for safe aerial skill development Diving lessons: If seeking diving, professional diving lessons Trampoline classes: Many facilities offer trampoline classes teaching safe aerial skills Parkour training: Structured parkour classes with professional instructors For Avoiders: No aerials: Avoid all flipping, diving, aerial movements Feet-on-ground: All activities with feet maintaining ground contact Head-above-heart: Avoid inverted positions Gradual exposure: If must participate (school requirement), very gradual gentle exposure with support Massage Techniques: Spinal alignment priority: After aerial movements, careful spinal massage ensuring alignment, 10 minutes
Neck care: Aerials can strain neck, gentle thorough neck massage, 7 minutes Shoulder girdle: Aerials stress shoulders, deep massage, 7 minutes Full body check: Check entire body for any strain or injury, 15-20 minutes Vestibular Integration: EXTREME vestibular input: Aerials provide maximum vestibular stimulation - rotational, inverted, accelerating High skill requirement: Requires advanced motor planning, body awareness, vestibular processing Safety critical: This level of seeking REQUIRES professional instruction - too dangerous for self-teaching Manifestation 6: Skateboarding/Rollerblading with Tricks Physical Redirect Technique: When attempting tricks beyond skill level, say "Stop. That trick requires more practice. Let's work on basics first." Have them demonstrate foundational skills (straight riding, turning, stopping). Only when basics mastered consistently may they attempt tricks, and only with proper safety equipment and supervision.
DIY Alternative Tool: Skateboarding Safety System: Skill progression chart: Visual chart showing skill progression (balance → riding → turning → stopping → basic tricks → advanced tricks) Protective gear non-negotiable: Helmet, wrist guards, knee pads, elbow pads required ALWAYS - no riding without Supervised learning: All new trick attempts require adult supervision Skate park rules: Learn and follow all skate park etiquette and safety rules Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Balance board practice: Practice balance on indo board or balance board - builds skateboarding skills safely Driveway/garage practice: Flat safe area for practicing basics Skate park visits: Regular visits to actual skate parks (with supervision) Video instruction: Follow reputable skateboarding tutorial videos teaching proper progression Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured skate sessions: Regular sessions with skill-building focus, not just free skating
Lessons if available: Professional skateboarding lessons teach safe progression Skate community: Join skateboarding community/groups with safety emphasis Cross-training: Strengthen balance, coordination, core through other activities For Avoiders: No skateboarding: Avoid skateboarding/rollerblading entirely Stable alternatives: Scooter, bike with training wheels - more stable options Slow, supported: If must try, very slow with adult support Protective gear: If trying, maximum protective gear for confidence Massage Techniques: Ankle priority: Skateboarding stresses ankles, thorough massage around ankle joints, 5 minutes each Foot care: Feet work hard for balance, deep massage, 5 minutes each Wrist protection: Falls often impact wrists, massage preventatively, 5 minutes each Core and back: Balance requires core/back engagement, massage these areas, 10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Balance challenge: Skateboarding challenges vestibular balance systems intensely
Visual-vestibular integration: Requires integrating vision with vestibular for balance Proprioceptive feedback: Skateboard movement provides continuous proprioceptive feedback Manifestation 7: Seeking Amusement Park Rides (Rollercoasters, Drop Towers) Physical Redirect Technique: At amusement park, establish ride plan before entering: "You can ride 2 extreme rides, then we do 2 gentle rides, then another extreme ride." Use visual schedule if helpful. After each extreme ride, mandatory 20-minute break doing calming activities (eating, sitting, watching shows) before next ride. DIY Alternative Tool: Amusement Park Management: Ride rotation system: Alternate extreme rides with moderate and gentle rides Token system: Give specific number of "extreme ride tokens" per park visit (3-5 tokens) Recovery time requirement: Minimum 20 minutes between extreme rides Post-ride check-in: After each ride, assess how feeling (dizzy, nauseous, excited) - builds body awareness
Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Home vestibular alternatives: When craving ride sensations, use home equipment (swinging, spinning, jumping on trampoline) VR rides: Virtual reality ride experiences (if age-appropriate and available) Ride videos: Watch POV videos of rides - provides visual vestibular input Playground "rides": Swings, merry-go-rounds, spinners provide ride-like input Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Planned park visits: Schedule regular amusement park visits (monthly/quarterly) - having scheduled visits may reduce constant craving Ride variety: Try all types of rides (spinning, dropping, speeding, inverting) - varied vestibular input Responsibility building: As child gets older, teach self-monitoring of vestibular tolerance Alternative thrill-seeking: Rock climbing, zip-lining, parasailing - other safe "thrill" activities For Avoiders: Gentle rides only: Carousels, train rides, gentle boat rides, shows No pressure: Never pressure to ride rides causing distress
Ground activities: Focus on games, food, shows, character meetings Exit strategy: Know child can always say "I want to stop" on any ride Massage Techniques: Post-park recovery: After amusement park day, thorough evening massage, 30 minutes Vestibular integration: Focus on sub-occipital, temples, jaw areas, 10 minutes Anti-nausea support: If nauseous, wrist pressure points, cool compress on neck, gentle massage Grounding emphasis: Heavy grounding massage focusing on feet and legs after floating/dropping sensations, 15 minutes Vestibular Integration: Maximum vestibular input: Extreme rides provide maximum possible vestibular stimulation - all types simultaneously Tolerance building: Regular exposure can build vestibular tolerance (within safe limits) Self-awareness: Learning to recognize "too much" vestibular input - important interoceptive skill Manifestation 8: Swimming/Diving with Underwater Somersaults and Movements
Physical Redirect Technique: When child is doing excessive underwater movements, call them to pool edge. Say "Water break - out of pool for 5 minutes." During break, have them drink water, sit quietly. Explain "Lots of underwater spinning can make you dizzy and unsafe. Let's limit underwater tricks to 5 at a time, then surface for rest." DIY Alternative Tool: Underwater Movement Management: Surface time requirements: Every 5 underwater movements, must surface and rest at edge for 1 minute Buddy system: Swimming with buddy who monitors each other's underwater time/movements Designated underwater play time: Specific portions of swim time for underwater movements, other time for regular swimming Movement variety: Ensure swimming includes regular swimming strokes, not just underwater acrobatics Alternative Stimulation (Household Items):
Bath time movement: Allow underwater movements during bath time (safer, controlled environment) Goggles use: Goggles allow seeing underwater, may satisfy some visual-vestibular seeking Pool games: Structure underwater activities (treasure hunting, swimming through hoop) - purposeful underwater time Diving practice: If deep enough pool, structured diving practice (lessons recommended) Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Swimming lessons: Formal lessons teaching various strokes and underwater skills properly Synchronized swimming: If available, synchro swimming involves underwater movements with structure Diving lessons: Structured diving lessons if appropriate depth pool available Water polo: Team sport with lots of underwater movement, swimming, competition For Avoiders: Shallow water only: Stay in water where can always touch bottom Minimal submersion: Keep head above water mostly Flotation devices: Use floaties, noodles for security
Gradual exposure: Very slow introduction to water activities with lots of support Massage Techniques: Post-swim massage: After swimming, thorough massage helps prevent muscle soreness, 15-20 minutes Shoulder and arm focus: Swimming uses these heavily, deep massage, 10 minutes Neck alignment: Underwater movements can stress neck, careful massage, 7 minutes Warming massage: If cold from water, brisk massage to warm up, 10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Multi-sensory input: Water provides vestibular, proprioceptive (resistance), and tactile input simultaneously Reduced gravity: Underwater feels different gravity - unique vestibular experience Rotational movements: Underwater somersaults provide intense rotational vestibular input in reduced-gravity environment
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 5. VESTIBULAR STIMMING > D. Vestibular Avoidance Stimming > Level 1: Movement Resistance
Causation: Over-stimulated: Vestibular input is overwhelming or nauseating Sensitive: Over-responsive vestibular system; movement feels extreme Anxiety: Fear of losing balance or control; gravitational insecurity Past Trauma: Previous negative experience with movement Low Muscle Tone: Movement is exhausting; poor postural control Sensory Profile: Avoider: Extreme vestibular defensiveness; movement causes distress Cautious: Gravitational insecurity; fear of falling or being off-balance Motion Sensitive: Easily nauseous from movement; may vomit Description: Avoiding typical movement activities Manifestation 1: Refusing Playground Equipment (Swings, Slides, Merry-Go-Rounds) Physical Redirect Technique: When child refuses playground equipment, don't force. Say "It's okay to not want to swing today. Let's find something you do want to do." Offer ground-based alternatives (sandbox, digging, drawing with chalk). If working on exposure, start very small: "Can you just sit on the swing while it's still? Just sitting, no moving." Build from there over many sessions.
DIY Alternative Tool: Gentle Exposure System: Gradual hierarchy: Create visual hierarchy of playground activities from least to most challenging (touching equipment → sitting still on equipment → tiny movement → more movement) Comfort zone expansion: Each playground visit, try ONE very slightly more challenging activity Choice emphasis: Child always has choice - forced activities increase anxiety/avoidance Reward system: Small rewards for trying slightly challenging activities (sticker, high-five, favorite activity after) Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Ground-based play: Focus on activities child finds comfortable (sand, water play, ball games, chalk drawing) Supportive adult: Adult sits on swing/slide with child - makes it less scary Stationary equipment exploration: Let child explore equipment while it's still (sit on still swing, sit on top of slide without going down)
Peer modeling: Watch other children using equipment happily - vicarious exposure Sensory Integration Activities: For Avoiders (Gradual Exposure Approach): Start with ground: Lots of ground-based playground activities building confidence Static equipment first: Climbing structures, balance beams - movement child controls Tiny increments: When ready, smallest possible movement on swing (adult pushes 1 inch, 2 inches, gradually increasing) Success focus: Celebrate every small brave step, never force or shame For Seekers: N/A - This manifestation is avoidance-specific Massage Techniques: Pre-playground calming: Before playground, 10-minute calming massage to reduce anxiety Grounding focus: Deep pressure on legs and feet, helps child feel grounded and secure, 7 minutes Post-playground success: After playground (regardless of what child tried), positive massage celebrating their effort, 10 minutes Anxiety release: If child shows anxiety, slow rhythmic massage particularly calming, 10-15 minutes
Vestibular Integration: Vestibular over-responsiveness: Avoiding movement indicates vestibular system too sensitive - movement feels overwhelming Gravitational insecurity: Fear of feet leaving ground, fear of falling - vestibular-based anxiety Gradual desensitization: Very slow, gentle, child-controlled exposure can gradually increase tolerance Manifestation 2: Fear of Feet Leaving Ground (Jumping, Climbing) Physical Redirect Technique: When child shows fear of feet leaving ground, validate feeling: "I understand jumping feels scary to you. That's okay." Offer tiny incremental challenge: "Could you stand on this book?" (½ inch elevation). Start incredibly small. Next session: "Could you step down from this book?" Each success builds confidence. Never force, always encourage. DIY Alternative Tool: Incremental Height Exposure: Height hierarchy: Create visual hierarchy from easiest to hardest (standing on flat floor → standing on 1" board → stepping down from 1" → standing on 2" → etc.)
Supportive equipment: Use very secure sturdy equipment (solid step stool vs. wobbly stool) Hand-holding allowed: Always allow child to hold adult hand for security Progress tracking: Chart showing tiny accomplishments builds confidence and motivation Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Carpet vs. hard floor: Practice tiny jumps on soft carpet first - feels safer Cushion landing: Stack soft cushions, practice stepping onto cushions - soft landing builds confidence Therapeutic ball: Sitting on therapy ball with feet touching floor - tiniest "leaving ground" exposure Parent participation: Adult does tiny jump, child tries - modelling helps Sensory Integration Activities: For Avoiders (Gradual Exposure): Ground-based strength: Build leg strength through ground-based activities (squats, lunges, walking) Tiny increments: Stepping on books increasing in thickness, stepping down from very low surfaces
Trampoline introduction: Stand on trampoline with feet not leaving surface - just feeling the give Proprioceptive building: Heavy work activities building body confidence (pushing, pulling, carrying) For Seekers: N/A - This manifestation is avoidance-specific Massage Techniques: Leg grounding massage: Very firm pressure massage from hip to ankle, 10 minutes each leg - helps child feel legs/feet connection to ground Foot awareness: Deep pressure massage of entire foot sole, 5 minutes each - increases proprioceptive foot awareness Anxiety release: If child shows anxiety about feet leaving ground, slow calming massage, 15 minutes Success celebration: After any brave attempt, positive affirming massage, 10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Gravitational insecurity: Core vestibular issue - child doesn't trust vestibular system to keep them safe Postural insecurity: May have poor postural responses - doesn't trust body to catch balance
Gradual tolerance building: Very gentle systematic desensitization can help, but must be child-paced Manifestation 3: Extreme Caution on Stairs or Uneven Surfaces Physical Redirect Technique: When child is navigating stairs/uneven surfaces with extreme caution, stay close for security. Say "I'm right here with you. Take your time." Offer hand if child wants it. Don't rush. After navigating surface, praise: "You did it! You were so careful and safe." Build confidence through successful experiences at child's pace. DIY Alternative Tool: Stair/Surface Navigation Support: Practice stairs: If possible, practice on same stairs repeatedly (home stairs) - familiarity builds confidence Visual supports: Tape or mark each step with colored tape - visual cue for foot placement Railing emphasis: Teach to always hold railing, make it automatic habit
Two-feet-per-step okay: It's fine to put both feet on each step - safety and confidence more important than speed Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Practice surfaces: Create practice uneven surfaces safely (pillows on floor, foam pieces, yoga mat) Gradual challenges: Start with tiny unevenness (thick rug), gradually increase (thicker foam, bigger bumps) Supervised practice: Practice stairs going up and down slowly with adult right there Step stool practice: Practice stepping up/down from low step stool - controlled height Sensory Integration Activities: For Avoiders (Gradual Exposure): Balance building: Practice balance on flat ground first (standing on one foot, walking line), builds confidence Proprioceptive input: Heavy work before navigating challenging surfaces helps nervous system feel more organized Visual compensation: Teach to use vision to compensate for vestibular uncertainty - look carefully at each step
Success experiences: Ensure lots of successful experiences on slightly challenging surfaces, building confidence For Seekers: N/A - This manifestation is avoidance-specific Massage Techniques: Leg and ankle stability: Massage around ankles and up legs, 10 minutes each leg - increases proprioceptive awareness Foot grounding: Deep pressure foot massage, 5 minutes each foot - helps feel stable Pre-challenge calming: Before navigating challenging surface, brief calming massage, 5 minutes Post-success celebration: After successfully navigating surface, positive massage, 10 minutes Vestibular Integration: Postural control issues: May have poor vestibular-postural integration - doesn't automatically adjust balance Visual dependence: May be over-relying on vision to compensate for vestibular issues Fear of falling: Vestibular insecurity creates legitimate fear - needs support and gradual building Manifestations: Discomfort in elevators or escalators- not available
Resistance to riding in vehicles (motion sickness)-not available Preferring sedentary activities exclusively-not available Distress when tilted or moved by others- not available Gripping onto stable surfaces during movement-not available
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 5. VESTIBULAR STIMMING > D. Vestibular Avoidance Stimming > Level 2: Postural Stability Seeking
Causation: Over-stimulated: Stable positions prevent overwhelming vestibular input Sensitive: Poor vestibular processing; can't accurately sense body position Anxiety: Need for control and security; fear of falling Compensatory: Using visual or tactile input to compensate for poor vestibular function Developmental: Delayed vestibular-proprioceptive integration Sensory Profile: Extreme Avoider: Cannot tolerate instability; severe gravitational insecurity Compensatory: Over-relying on other senses (vision, touch) for balance Fearful: Anxiety-based avoidance of movement Description: Maintaining stable, grounded positions Manifestations: Always keeping both feet on ground Sitting instead of standing whenever possible Lying down instead of sitting Holding onto walls, furniture, or people while moving Taking stairs very slowly with tight grip on railings Walking close to walls for security Refusing to walk on unstable surfaces (grass, sand, gravel)
Keeping center of gravity low (crouching, squatting)
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 5. VESTIBULAR STIMMING > D. Vestibular Avoidance Stimming > Level 3: Vestibular Overload Responses
Causation: Over-stimulated: Severe vestibular over-responsiveness; movement is intolerable Sensitive: Vestibular system extremely sensitive; minimal input causes distress Medical: Possible vestibular disorder (labyrinthitis, BPPV, etc.) Neurological: Central vestibular processing dysfunction Protective: Behavioral responses prevent sensory assault Sensory Profile: Crisis-Level Avoider: Movement triggers fight-or-flight response Medical Concern: Requires vestibular therapy and/or medical evaluation Functional Impact: Movement avoidance significantly limits activities Description: Extreme reactions to movement input Manifestations: Vomiting from movement (cars, swings, spinning) Panic attacks when feet leave ground Meltdowns after movement activities Dizziness from minimal movement (standing up, turning head) Disorientation lasting long after movement stops Refusing all movement activities completely Extreme carsickness or motion sickness Balance difficulties affecting daily function
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 6. ORAL/GUSTATORY STIMMING
(Mouth, Taste, and Eating-Related)
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 6. ORAL/GUSTATORY STIMMING > A. Oral Motor Stimming > Level 1: Mouthing and Chewing
Causation: Over-stimulated: Oral input is organizing and calming Under-stimulated: Mouth has high nerve density; provides strong sensory input Sensitivity: Oral-motor seeking; craves proprioceptive input to jaw and mouth Self-Soothing: Oral stimulation releases calming chemicals (similar to nursing/pacifiers) Developmental: Regression to infant self-soothing patterns Anxiety: Chewing reduces stress and anxiety Sensory Profile: Seeker: Constant chewing throughout day; destroys multiple items weekly Anxious: Chewing increases during stress or uncertainty Oral Motor Needs: Under-responsive oral system needs intense input IDENTIFYING SENSORY SEEKERS VS AVOIDERS: Sensory Seeker Signs: Child constantly puts items in mouth, destroys 5+ items weekly through chewing, seeks chewy foods, actively looks for things to bite, chewing increases when bored or under-stimulated Sensory Avoider Signs: Pushes away items near mouth, resists teeth brushing, limited food textures accepted, gags easily, covers mouth protectively
Description: Using mouth on non-food items MANIFESTATION 1: Chewing on clothing (sleeves, collars, drawstrings) Physical Redirection Technique: "Hand-to-Shoulder" Redirect: When you notice the child bringing clothing to mouth, gently place your hand on their shoulder and apply firm pressure (like a weighted touch). Say "Shoulders down, hands down." Guide their hands to their lap or to a replacement item. The shoulder pressure activates proprioceptive receptors and interrupts the automatic hand-to-mouth pattern. DIY Alternative Tool: Fabric Chew Necklace: Cut a clean cotton t-shirt into a long strip (2 inches wide, 30 inches long). Braid three strips tightly together. Tie ends to create a necklace. Dampen the fabric and freeze for 1 hour before use for added sensory input. Cost: Free using old clothing.
Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Frozen washcloth: Wet a clean washcloth, twist it, and freeze for 2 hours. Let child chew on this for 5-10 minutes. The cold provides numbing input, and the texture satisfies chewing need. Silicone pot holder: Clean kitchen silicone pot holders have great chewing texture. Attach to keychain for portability. Coffee stirrer straws: The thick, rigid straws from coffee shops are excellent for chewing. Cut to 3-inch lengths to prevent choking. Child can chew while doing homework or watching TV. Occupational Therapy Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Resistive Chewing Exercises: Provide crunchy foods every 2 hours (carrots, apples, celery). Have child chew on one side for 10 chews, then switch sides. This provides the proprioceptive input they crave while being functional.
Jaw Strengthening Games: Blow bubbles through a straw into water (add dish soap for extra bubbles). Resistance of water provides oral motor input. Do 3 sets of 10 blows. Chewy Food Breaks: Set timer for every 90 minutes. Offer beef jerky, dried mango, fruit leather, or gummy bears. Make it a "chew break" routine. For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Oral Desensitization: Use a soft baby toothbrush. Let child brush their own hand first, then you gently brush outside of their cheeks (not inside mouth) for 5 seconds. Gradually increase over weeks. Vibration Introduction: Use an electric toothbrush (turned off) around outside of mouth for 10 seconds daily. When tolerated, turn on for 3 seconds on the back of their hand, then cheek.
Sensory Integration Activities: Deep Pressure Mouth Massage: Using clean hands, provide firm pressure to child's cheeks (outside). Press and hold for 5 seconds, release. Repeat 5 times. This calms the oral sensory system. Oral Motor Obstacle Course: Set up stations: (1) Blow cotton balls across table with straw, (2) Suck water through crazy straw, (3) Chew dried fruit for 20 chews, (4) Blow whistle 5 times. Complete circuit twice daily. Massage Techniques: Jaw Massage: Place fingers on jaw joint (where jaw meets ear). Make small circles with firm pressure for 30 seconds on each side, 3 times daily. Cheek Compression: Using flat palms, press both cheeks simultaneously toward center of face. Hold 5 seconds, release. Repeat 10 times before meals. MANIFESTATION 2: Biting pencils, pens, or markers
Physical Redirection Technique: "Tap and Replace": Tap child's elbow firmly three times (creates proprioceptive input). Say "Pencil down, chew up" while placing an appropriate chew item in their other hand. The elbow tap breaks the automatic behavior pattern. DIY Alternative Tool: Pencil Topper Chew: Cut 3-inch sections from aquarium tubing (available at pet stores, $3 for 10 feet). Slide onto pencils/pens. The tubing is safe, chewable, and washable. Can add texture by wrapping thin rubber bands around the tubing. Alternative Stimulation: Eraser caps with texture: Buy pencil cap erasers (10 for $1). Let child chew these instead of the pencil itself—they're designed to be on the mouth end. Coffee stirrer pencil attachment: Tape a thick coffee stirrer to the side of the pencil. This gives something to chew that isn't the working end.
Rubber pencil grips: The bumpy rubber grips (sold for handwriting) can be chewed safely. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Pre-Work Chew Session: Before homework/desk work, provide 5 minutes of intensive chewing (bagel, thick pretzel, jerky). This "fills the tank" before concentration tasks. Chew-and-Write Timer: Set timer for 5 minutes. Child writes, then gets 1-minute chew break with appropriate item. Gradually increase writing time. Gum Chewing (age 5+): Allow sugar-free gum during desk work. The constant chewing satisfies oral need while working. For Sensory Avoiders: Pencil Awareness Training: Have child hold pencil and look at it before starting work. Say "This is for writing, not mouth." Practice putting it down after each sentence. Sensory Integration: Bilateral Mouth Work: Have child push tongue against inside of one cheek while you press that cheek from outside. Hold 5 seconds per side, 5 repetitions. This provides organizing input to oral system.
Massage: Lip Massage: Using clean finger, press along upper lip (under nose) with firm pressure, moving side to side. Then lower lip. Repeat 3 times. Do before focus tasks. MANIFESTATION 3: Chewing on toys, especially plastic or rubber Physical Redirection: "Squeeze and Swap": When child has toy in mouth, squeeze their shoulders firmly and say "Toy down." Immediately place designated chew toy in hand. The shoulder squeeze provides input that replaces what they sought from chewing. DIY Alternative: Frozen Silicone Teether: Pour water into ice cube tray. Insert popsicle sticks. Freeze. Once frozen, let child suck/chew on ice pops. For older kids, freeze fruit juice instead. Alternate: Buy baby teething toys (they're designed for mouthing), cost $5-10 for a set. Alternative Stimulation:
Silicone kitchen utensils: Silicone spatulas, basting brushes, or ice cube trays can be chewed (after thorough washing). The texture is similar to toys but designated for chewing. Clean dog chew toys: New, unused rubber dog toys (specifically marked non-toxic) can serve as heavy-duty chew items. Bonus: They're designed to withstand chewing! Rubber jar openers: The circular rubber gripper pads used to open jars have excellent chew texture. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Toy Texture Exploration: Provide variety of textures to mouth under supervision (bumpy ball, smooth stone, soft fabric, rough sponge). Let child explore 2 minutes each. This satisfies curiosity and provides varied input. Frozen Fruit Station: Keep frozen grapes, berries, mango chunks available. Every 2 hours, child gets 10 pieces to eat slowly. The cold and chewing provide significant sensory input.
For Sensory Avoiders: Toy Touch-Only Practice: Have child hold toy in hands only, exploring with fingers. Praise staying away from mouth. Gradually build tolerance to having objects near face without mouthing. Sensory Integration: Face Tapping: Using fingertips, gently tap around child's mouth in a circle. Start with 10 taps, build to 30. This alerts the oral system and can reduce seeking behavior. Massage: Whole Face Massage: Using flat palms, press gently on forehead, then cheeks, then chin. Hold each for 5 seconds. The full-face input helps organize sensory system. MANIFESTATION 4: Mouthing fingers, hands, or nails Physical Redirection: "Fist Squeeze and Pull": Gently take child's hand that's approaching mouth. Make it into a fist and squeeze firmly for 5 seconds. Then pull/stretch each finger outward. This proprioceptive input to hands can satisfy the need that was driving hand-to-mouth behavior.
DIY Alternative: Textured Gloves: Take old gloves. Hot-glue small buttons, felt pieces, or fabric scraps to fingertips. Child wears these and can chew on textured fingertips instead of skin. Wash weekly. Alternative Stimulation: Popsicle stick guards: Keep fingers busy holding popsicle sticks (can add flavoring by rubbing with lemon or applying small dot of jam to lick). Finger puppet chews: Make finger puppets from felt. Child wears these and chews the puppet, not the finger. Band-aids with texture: Apply band-aids to commonly mouthed fingers. The texture is different from skin and less satisfying to mouth. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Hand Fidget Box: Fill container with: stress ball, theraputty, small textured toys, fabric squares. When urge to mouth hands arises, child gets item from box instead.
Scented Hand Cream: Apply strongly scented lotion to hands. The smell can remind child not to mouth them. Choose unpleasant-tasting scent (lavender, tea tree). Keep Hands Busy Protocol: Every 30 minutes, provide 5-minute hand activity: play-doh, drawing, building blocks. Busy hands don't go to mouth. For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Hand Massage: Before situations where mouthing increases (stress, boredom), massage child's hands firmly for 2 minutes. This provides calming input. Sensory Integration: Hand Joint Compression: Hold child's hand. Press each finger joint together firmly, moving from fingertip to knuckle. Repeat 3 times per finger, both hands. Provides organizing proprioceptive input. Massage: Palm Pressure Points: Using thumb, press firmly into center of child's palm. Make small circles with pressure. 30 seconds per hand, 3-5 times daily.
MANIFESTATION 5: Chewing on hair (own or others') Physical Redirection: "Hair Up, Hands Down": Approach child from side. Gently sweep hair behind shoulder away from mouth. Place firm hand on top of child's head for 3 seconds (grounding pressure). Guide hands to replacement activity. DIY Alternative: Hair Elastics with Chew Attached: Tie hair up in ponytail. Attach a chew tube or thick ribbon to the hair elastic (make sure it won't tangle). If child reaches for ponytail, they encounter the chew item instead. Alternative Stimulation: Ribbon chews: Attach grosgrain ribbon (textured fabric ribbon) to child's collar or backpack strap. Keep it 4-6 inches so it's accessible but not in the way. Child can chew ribbon instead of hair. Yarn braids: Braid colorful yarn (3 strands, 8 inches long). Attach to zipper pull or backpack. Yarn texture satisfies chewing need.
Fabric hair ties: Use fabric hair scrunchies (the cloth-covered elastics). These are safer to chew than regular elastics. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Heavy Work Before High-Risk Times: Before school/homework (when hair chewing peaks), do 10 minutes of: push-ups against wall, carrying heavy books, chair push-ups. This loads the nervous system so seeking decreases. Chew Schedule: Set phone alarm for every hour. When alarm sounds, child gets 2-3 minutes with designated chew item. This provides regular oral input. For Sensory Avoiders: Hair Awareness Training: Practice braiding or styling hair without bringing it near mouth. Reward attempts. Sensory Integration: Scalp Massage: Firmly massage child's scalp using fingertips in circular motions. Cover entire head. 3-5 minutes daily. This provides input to the area they're seeking when pulling hair to mouth.
Massage: Neck and Shoulder Massage: Often hair chewing involves neck movement. Massage neck muscles firmly, then shoulders. This releases tension that might drive the behavior. MANIFESTATION 6: Biting on chewy jewelry or chewable items Physical Redirection: "Jewelry Down, Breathe": Touch child's sternum (center chest) firmly. Say "Breathe in, breathe out" while you model it. The chest touch activates the parasympathetic nervous system. Then redirect to appropriate chew item. DIY Alternative: Homemade Chew Necklace: String large wooden beads (untreated, craft store $3) on thick cotton cord. Tie securely. Wood is safe to chew and has satisfying texture. Alternatively, string silicone beads sold for teething (available online, $8 for 50). Alternative Stimulation: Chewable jewelry specifically designed: ARK Therapeutic, Chewigem, and SentioCHEWS sell chew jewelry ($8-15). While not DIY, they're durable and designed for this purpose.
Silicone bracelet stacks: Wear multiple silicone bracelets (like Livestrong-style). These can be pulled and chewed. Keychain chews: Attach chew items to belt loop or backpack. Always accessible. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Chew Rating System: Have child rate their "chew need" from 1-5. At level 3+, they get chew item for 5 minutes. This builds self-awareness. Texture Variety: Rotate 3-4 different chew items with different textures. Monday: smooth silicone. Tuesday: bumpy rubber. This prevents habituation. For Sensory Avoiders: Gradual Exposure: Start with smooth chew item. Hold it only. Next week, touch to closed lips. Build tolerance slowly. Sensory Integration: Mouth Pressure Exercises: Using clean finger (yours or child's), press firmly on roof of mouth, then inside cheeks, then under tongue. Hold each 5 seconds. This intensive oral input can reduce constant chewing need.
Massage: Jaw Hinge Massage: Place fingers just below ears where jaw hinges. Make firm circles for 45 seconds. This relaxes jaw muscles that may be driving chewing. MANIFESTATION 7: Gnawing on bottle caps, straws, or utensils Physical Redirection: "Drop and Clench": Say "Drop it" while gently pressing on child's jaw muscles (sides of face). This creates awareness. Then have them clench teeth together hard for 5 seconds, release. Repeat 3 times. The clenching provides jaw input without chewing objects. DIY Alternative: Straw Collection: Keep collection of various straws (regular, wide, crazy straws, silicone reusable straws). These are designed to be in mouth and are inexpensive. Replace when worn. Cost: $5 for 50. Alternative Stimulation: Reusable silicone straws: Buy food-grade silicone straws ($8 for 6-pack). These are durable, chewable, and washable.
Spoon chews: Baby spoons (soft plastic or silicone) can be chewed safely. Keep in pocket or pencil case. Bottle caps on a ring: Collect clean plastic bottle caps. Use zip-tie or keyring to connect them. Creates a chew chain. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Drinking Through Resistive Straw: Thickened drinks (smoothies, milkshakes) through regular straw provide intense oral motor input. Offer 2-3 times daily. Bite-and-Hold Exercises: Give child thick pretzel rod or carrot stick. Have them bite and hold (don't chew) for 10 seconds. Release. Repeat 5 times. This provides sustained jaw pressure. For Sensory Avoiders: Utensil Touch Desensitization: Let child touch various utensils to hands, cheeks, then lips (outside only). Build comfort gradually. Sensory Integration: Straw Blowing Games: Blow cotton balls across table, blow bubbles in water, blow pinwheel. These activities provide oral motor input without chewing.
Massage: Temporal Mandibular Joint (TMJ) Massage: Place fingers on jaw joint. Open and close mouth while applying gentle pressure to joint. 10 repetitions, 3 times daily. MANIFESTATION 8: Chewing on blankets, pillows, or furniture edges Physical Redirection: "Pull Away and Ground": Physically remove item from mouth (gently). Place both your hands on child's shoulders with firm pressure. Count to 5 slowly. This grounding pressure helps them transition from the behavior. DIY Alternative: Designated Chew Blanket Corner: Take small corner of old blanket (8x8 inches). Fold and stitch it multiple times to create a thick, chewable corner. Attach to current blanket with ribbon. Child can chew this designated section. Alternative Stimulation: Chew tags on blankets: Sew thick ribbon or fabric tags onto corners of blanket. These become the "chew zones."
Furniture corner protectors: While designed for safety, the foam/rubber corner guards have interesting textures and can redirect chewing from furniture itself. Teething blankets: Purchase baby "lovey" blankets with attached teether corners ($8-12). These work for older children too. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Pre-Sleep Chew Routine: Since blanket/pillow chewing often happens at bedtime, provide 10 minutes of intensive chewing right before bed (crunchy snack, chew toy). This satisfies the need. Bedtime Oral Motor Routine: Blow bubbles, drink thick smoothie through straw, chew gum. Creates bedtime ritual that addresses oral needs. For Sensory Avoiders: Soft Item Introduction: Let child choose a soft item they like. Keep it away from face initially, gradually building comfort. Sensory Integration: Full Body Deep Pressure Before Bed: Roll child in blanket like burrito. Apply firm pressure all over body. This full-body input can reduce localized oral seeking.
Massage: Face and Jaw Massage Before Sleep: Massage entire face, jaw, and neck for 5 minutes before bed. This can prevent nighttime chewing.
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 6. ORAL/GUSTATORY STIMMING > A. Oral Motor Stimming > Level 2: Tongue and Lip Movements
Causation: Over-stimulated: Internal oral movements provide controllable input Under-stimulated: Tongue and lips rich with sensory receptors; provides input Sensitivity: Exploring oral-motor capabilities and sensations Habitual: May develop into unconscious habit over time Tic-like: May have compulsive quality; feels "incomplete" without action Sensory Profile: Seeker: Constant oral movement throughout day Anxious: Increases during concentration or stress Oral Fixation: Strong need for oral stimulation IDENTIFYING SENSORY SEEKERS VS AVOIDERS: Seeker Signs: Constant tongue movement visible when concentrating, makes clicking sounds frequently, lips always moving, seeks oral stimulation actively Avoider Signs: Minimal mouth movement, doesn't like things near mouth, doesn't explore with tongue, restricted oral movements Description: Moving tongue, lips, or mouth structures MANIFESTATION 1: Tongue thrusting (pushing against teeth) rhythmically Physical Redirection: "Tongue on Roof": When you observe thrusting, gently tap under child's chin 3 times. Say "Tongue up" and model pressing your tongue to roof of your mouth. Have child copy you and hold for 10 seconds.
DIY Alternative: Peanut Butter Spot Game: Place tiny dab of peanut butter (or cream cheese, sunflower butter) on roof of child's mouth. They must use tongue to lick it off. This gives tongue a job and strengthens upward movement. Alternative Stimulation: Mouth position stickers: Place small sticker inside upper lip or on roof of mouth (edible paper). Child must manipulate with tongue to remove it. Tongue depressor exercises: Use clean popsicle stick. Child pushes against it with tongue in different directions. This channels the pushing urge productively. Whistling practice: Learning to whistle requires specific tongue positioning and gives tongue appropriate work. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Tongue Obstacle Course: Set up stations: (1) Lick lollipop 10 times, (2) Touch tongue to nose (try), (3) Stick tongue out/in 10 times quickly, (4) Hold tongue on roof of mouth for 30 seconds. Complete twice daily.
Tongue Strengthening: Hold tongue depressor between tongue and roof of mouth. Try to pull it out while child holds with tongue. 10 repetitions. Ice Chip Melting: Place small ice chip in mouth. Child must keep it on tongue (not chew). Let it melt completely. This gives tongue sustained sensory work. For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Tongue Touch: Use electric toothbrush (off) to touch tip of tongue for 1 second. Build tolerance gradually. This addresses under-responsiveness that may drive thrusting. Sensory Integration: Oral-Facial Stimulation: Using finger cot or gloved finger, provide firm pressure to various points inside mouth (gums, inner cheeks, roof, under tongue). This comprehensive input helps organize oral system. Massage: External Tongue Massage: From outside, massage the area under child's chin with firm pressure. Make small circles over entire under-chin area. 60 seconds, 3 times daily.
MANIFESTATION 2: Licking lips excessively (causing chapping or redness) Physical Redirection: "Lips Together, Breathe Nose": When you see licking, touch child's philtrum (the line between nose and upper lip) firmly with your finger. Say "Close lips, breathe through nose." Model closed-mouth breathing for 5 breaths together. DIY Alternative: Lip Balm with Unpleasant Taste: Apply very minty or medicated lip balm (Carmex, Burt's Bees). The strong taste reminds child not to lick.
