Plus, if they do lick, the flavor is a deterrent. Alternative Stimulation: Flavored lip balm station: Let child apply lip balm every 30 minutes. The application satisfies oral focus, and keeping lips coated prevents chapping that might trigger more licking. Drink bottle always available: Often licking is actually thirst. Keep water bottle accessible so they can sip instead of lick lips.
Humidifier: If licking is response to dry lips, increase humidity in environment (especially bedrooms). OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Lip Exercises: Exaggerate lip movements: pucker like fish (hold 5 seconds), smile wide (hold 5 seconds), press lips together hard (hold 5 seconds). Repeat 10 times. This satisfies need for lip movement/stimulation. Lollipop Licking Practice: Provide lollipop or popsicle 2 times daily. This gives a productive licking activity. Mirror Work: Have child watch themselves in mirror. Count how many seconds they can go without licking lips. Try to beat personal record. For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Lip Touch: Use soft brush (clean makeup brush) to touch around lips. Build tolerance to sensation so they don't lick to "fix" discomfort. Sensory Integration: Lip Massage: Using clean finger, massage lips in circular motions with firm pressure. Outer edge, then directly on lips. This deep input can reduce excessive licking.
Massage: Perioral Massage: Massage all around mouth area in a square pattern (above upper lip, cheeks on both sides, below lower lip). Firm pressure. 45 seconds, 4-5 times daily. MANIFESTATION 3: Clicking tongue repeatedly (100+ times per session) Physical Redirection: "Click Count and Stop": Don't try to stop clicking mid-stream. Instead, say "I hear clicking. Make 5 more clicks, then stop." Count them together. This gives control and closure to the pattern. Then redirect. DIY Alternative: Clicker Toy: Buy an actual clicker (dog training clicker, $2). When child wants to click, they can use the clicker instead of tongue. Provides similar auditory feedback with external object. Alternative Stimulation: Musical tongue sounds: Teach child to make other tongue sounds: rolling Rs, "tsk-tsk," popping. Create a repertoire so they have variety.
Beatboxing or rhythm games: Channel clicking into musical rhythm making. Makes it purposeful. Mouth harp/jaw harp: Inexpensive instrument ($5) that makes sounds with mouth movements. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Scheduled Clicking Time: Set timer for 5 minutes, 3 times daily. During this time, clicking is allowed and encouraged. Outside these times, redirect. Sound-Making Alternatives: Provide other ways to make satisfying sounds: harmonica, whistle, kazoo. 5-minute sessions. Tongue Position Games: Play "Simon Says" with tongue positions (touch left cheek, touch right cheek, stick out, pull in). Gives tongue purposeful movements. For Sensory Avoiders: Quiet Mouth Time: Practice keeping mouth completely still for increasing time periods. Use visual timer. Sensory Integration: Bilateral Tongue Work: Have child push tongue against inside of cheek while you push that cheek from outside (resistive). Switch sides. 10 repetitions each side. Organizes oral system.
Massage: Jaw and Cheek Massage: Massage jaw muscles and cheeks with firm circular pressure. 90 seconds per side, before times when clicking typically increases. MANIFESTATION 4: Sucking on tongue or cheeks Physical Redirection: "Release and Relax": Touch child's cheeks on both sides simultaneously with firm pressure. Say "Let go, relax mouth." Model opening your mouth and relaxing jaw. Have child copy and hold relaxed position for 10 seconds. DIY Alternative: Thicker Drinks: Provide drinks that require stronger sucking (smoothies, milkshakes, yogurt drinks through straw). This satisfies sucking need appropriately. Alternative Stimulation: Lollipops or hard candy: Allows sucking in a functional way. Choose sugar-free options. Frozen fruit to suck: Freeze grapes, berries, or mango chunks. Child sucks on these instead of cheeks.
Sports bottle with small opening: The restrictive opening requires stronger sucking action. Fill with water for continuous access to appropriate sucking. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Straw Drinking Routine: Every 90 minutes, provide thick liquid through straw. Must drink 8 oz. This schedules sucking input regularly. Bubble Blowing: Blow bubbles through various wand sizes. Requires sustained mouth/cheek control. 10 minutes, twice daily. Harmonica Playing: Requires controlled breathing and mouth positioning. 5-10 minutes daily. For Sensory Avoiders: Cheek Awareness: Have child puff out cheeks with air, hold 5 seconds. This creates internal awareness without sucking. Sensory Integration: Intra-Oral Massage: With gloved finger, massage inside of cheeks with firm circular pressure. Both sides, 30 seconds each. This provides intense input that may reduce seeking.
Massage: External Cheek Massage: Using flat palms, press cheeks together toward center of face. Hold 5 seconds, release. 10 repetitions, 3 times daily. MANIFESTATION 5: Pushing tongue against roof of mouth repeatedly Physical Redirection: "Tongue Down and Swallow": Place finger under child's chin with firm upward pressure. Say "Swallow" which naturally resets tongue position. Then guide them to let tongue rest flat on floor of mouth. DIY Alternative: Popsicle/Ice Chips: Sucking on popsicles or ice requires tongue to work against cold item held against roof of mouth. Provides similar sensation appropriately. Alternative Stimulation: Small foods on roof of mouth: Cheerios, raisins, or mini marshmallows. Child places on roof of mouth and maneuvers with tongue to swallow. Oral sensory toys: Textured spoons or oral massage tools designed to touch roof of mouth.
Crunchy foods requiring tongue manipulation: Goldfish crackers, pretzels—foods that child moves around in mouth with tongue. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Tongue Strengthening Exercises: Place tongue on roof of mouth and push hard while counting to 10. Rest. Repeat 5 times. Provides intense input purposefully. Food Retrieval Game: Place small piece of food (cereal, raisin) on roof of mouth. Child must use tongue to move it around mouth without using hands. This gives tongue a job. Resistance Activities: Use tongue depressor. Child pushes against it with tongue in different directions (up, down, sides). 10 pushes each direction. For Sensory Avoiders: Gradual Palate Touch: Use soft toothbrush to gently touch roof of mouth for 1 second. Build tolerance slowly over weeks. Sensory Integration:
Full Oral Stimulation: Use NUK brush or similar oral tool. Massage gums, roof of mouth, inside cheeks, and tongue with varied pressure. 3-5 minutes daily. Massage: Under-Jaw Massage: Massage entire area under jaw and chin with firm pressure. This externally stimulates the area corresponding to inside the mouth. 90 seconds, 3 times daily. MANIFESTATION 6: Lip smacking or popping sounds Physical Redirection: "Quiet Lips": When sounds occur, place one finger vertically over your own lips (shh gesture). Say "Quiet lips" and have child press their lips together firmly for 5 seconds. The pressure provides input to replace the sound-making. DIY Alternative: Quiet Signal Card: Make a card that says "Quiet Lips" with a picture. When child makes sounds, show card as visual reminder. Child then does 3 actions: press lips together, take deep breath, continue activity.
Alternative Stimulation: Whisper practice: Channel mouth sounds into purposeful whispering. Whispering requires specific lip control. Silent mouth exercises: Practice opening/closing mouth silently in front of mirror. Makes them aware of sound production. Humming instead: Redirect sound-making to humming, which is more socially acceptable. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Scheduled Sound Time: Designate 5 minutes, 3 times daily, when lip sounds are encouraged. "This is your sound time—make all the sounds you want!" Lip Massage Before Activities: Massage lips firmly for 30 seconds before entering environments where sounds are inappropriate (classroom, library). This preemptive input may reduce sounds. Making Purposeful Sounds: Teach different lip sounds child can make (motor sounds, animal sounds). Make it purposeful play rather than random stimming. For Sensory Avoiders:
Lip Vibration Exercises: Practice making "motor boat" sounds (brrr with lips). Builds lip awareness and control. Sensory Integration: Lip Compression: Using fingers, gently press lips together from outside. Hold 3 seconds, release. Repeat 10 times. Provides organizing input to lips. Massage: Perioral (Around Mouth) Massage: Massage in square around mouth with firm pressure. Include upper lip, lower lip, and corners. 60 seconds, multiple times daily. MANIFESTATION 7: Chewing on inside of cheeks or lips Physical Redirection: "Release and Breathe": Place both hands on child's cheeks from outside. Apply gentle inward pressure. Say "Let go inside, breathe out." As they exhale, the tension releases. Hold position for 5 seconds. DIY Alternative: Mint or Cinnamon Gum: Strong-flavored gum provides something appropriate to chew. The flavor also reminds them they're chewing gum, not cheeks.
Alternative Stimulation: Chewy foods scheduled regularly: Provide chewy foods every 2 hours (fruit leather, dried mango, gummy bears, jerky). This satisfies chewing need externally. Ice chips: Keep in mouth to suck/gently chew. The cold sensation is novel and different from cheek-chewing. Chew tools: ARK's Probe or similar can be placed in specific areas inside mouth to provide alternative chewing surface. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Cheek Puffing Exercises: Puff out one cheek, hold 5 seconds. Switch to other cheek. Then puff both. Repeat 10 times. This provides internal cheek stimulation without biting. Resistive Chewing Schedule: Set timer for every 90 minutes. When it rings, provide 3-5 minutes of intensive chewing (hard pretzel, carrot, apple, bagel). Facial Exercises: Make exaggerated faces in mirror (fish face, lion face, surprised face). This moves cheek and mouth muscles in varied ways.
For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Intra-Oral Touch: Using clean finger with finger cot, gently touch inside of cheeks. 3 seconds per side. Build tolerance gradually. Sensory Integration: Bilateral Cheek Work: Place fingers inside mouth on one cheek. Place other hand on outside of same cheek. Gently press together for 5 seconds. Switch sides. Repeat 5 times. This bilateral input is organizing. Massage: External Cheek Massage: Using fingertips, massage cheek muscles in circular motions with firm pressure. Cover entire cheek area. 45 seconds per side, 3-5 times daily, especially before high-chewing times. MANIFESTATION 8: Making exaggerated mouth movements (open-close, stretching) Physical Redirection: "Freeze Face": When movements occur, say "Freeze!" and touch child's jaw lightly. Have them hold still for 5 seconds. Then say "Normal face" and model a neutral, relaxed expression. Practice together.
DIY Alternative: Mirror Feedback: Keep small mirror accessible. When movements start, have child look in mirror and describe what they see. Self-awareness often reduces behavior. Alternative Stimulation: Purposeful face exercises: Turn movements into structured activity. "Make 5 big mouths, 5 small mouths, 5 circle mouths." This satisfies need in controlled way. Facial yoga: Look up "face yoga" videos. These exercises use exaggerated movements purposefully for muscle tone. Silly face time: Designate specific times to make silly faces together. Gets it out of system. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Facial Muscle Workout: Set up routine: (1) Open mouth wide 10 times, (2) Pucker lips 10 times, (3) Stretch mouth in smile 10 times, (4) Move jaw side to side 10 times. Do twice daily.
Chewing Gum: Provides sustained jaw movement in more typical way. Singing/Talking Activities: Channel mouth movements into purposeful activities like singing, reciting, or storytelling. For Sensory Avoiders: Awareness Training: Practice keeping face still. Use timer—how long can they maintain neutral face? Gradually increase time. Sensory Integration: Full Face Massage: Massage forehead, cheeks, jaw, around mouth, under chin with firm pressure. Complete circuit takes 2-3 minutes. Do before activities requiring facial control. Massage: Jaw Joint Massage: Place fingers on jaw joints (in front of ears). Make firm circles while child gently opens/closes mouth. 45 seconds, multiple times daily.
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 6. ORAL/GUSTATORY STIMMING > A. Oral Motor Stimming > Level 3: Extreme Oral Stimming
IDENTIFYING SENSORY SEEKERS VS AVOIDERS: Extreme Seeker Signs: Self-injurious oral behaviors, cannot stop even when causing damage, consuming dangerous items, aggressive seeking, distress when unable to access oral input Extreme Avoider Signs: Fear responses to oral input, physical illness from mild oral stimulation, complete refusal of oral care, panic responses Causation: Over-stimulated: Extreme oral input attempts to regulate overwhelming system Under-stimulated: Severe under-responsiveness; needs intense input to register Sensitivity: Craves strong proprioceptive feedback to jaw and teeth Pica: May indicate nutritional deficiency (iron, zinc) or sensory disorder Medical: Dental issues causing need to bite/grind Behavioural: May be communication or learned behavior Sensory Profile: Extreme Seeker: Dangerous level of oral seeking; requires intervention Pica Diagnosis: Consuming non-nutritive substances; medical concern Self-Injurious: Biting self or others requires immediate behavioural support
Description: Intense or potentially harmful oral behaviours MANIFESTATION 1: Biting self (hands, arms) leaving marks ⚠️ SAFETY NOTE: This behavior requires immediate occupational therapy evaluation and may need behavioral intervention plan. Physical Redirection: "Stop-Block-Compress": If bite is about to occur, block by placing cushion or stuffed animal in path. Say "Stop, bite this instead." If already biting, don't pull away quickly (may cause injury). Instead, gently press on either side of jaw where it hinges while saying "Let go, gentle mouth." DIY Alternative: Protective Arm Sleeves: Cut the legs off old leggings or socks to make arm sleeves. Child wears these on commonly bitten areas. Add extra padding (sew cotton batting inside) over most targeted spots. Alternative Stimulation: Bite blocks: Thick rubber blocks designed for biting (search "ARK Bite Block" or similar). Keep multiple available at all times.
Frozen bagels: Extremely hard and safe to bite with significant force. Keep several in freezer. Rubber dog toys: Heavy-duty rubber toys designed for aggressive chewing dogs. Ensure non-toxic. OT Activities: For Extreme Sensory Seekers: Intensive Oral Motor Program: Must work with OT, but includes: (1) Deep pressure massage inside mouth 3x daily, (2) Resistive biting activities every hour (bite on special tools), (3) Heavy work protocol (pushing, pulling, carrying) every 90 minutes to load nervous system. Biting Replacement Training: At first sign of agitation that leads to biting, immediate intervention: provide maximum oral input (frozen bagel + chew tool + crunchy food + deep pressure massage). Set timer for 5 minutes of intensive oral work. Calming Sensory Diet: Incorporate throughout day: weighted blanket, deep pressure hugs, joint compressions, rocking, heavy work tasks. Goal is to keep nervous system regulated so extreme seeking doesn't occur.
Crisis Response Protocol: Protective gear worn during high-risk times Always have replacement bite item immediately available Never punish biting—it's sensory need, not behavior choice Track triggers (times, situations, activities) and provide preventive input before these Sensory Integration: Wilbarger Protocol: This is a specific brushing and joint compression protocol done by trained individuals. Requires OT training but involves brushing arms, legs, back with specific brush followed by joint compressions. Done every 90-120 minutes. Massage: Deep Pressure Full Body Massage: Before high-risk times, provide deep pressure massage to whole body. 10-15 minutes. Use firm pressure, slow strokes. Include arms (where biting occurs) with extra attention. MANIFESTATION 2: Biting others during interactions ⚠️ SAFETY NOTE: Requires behavioral intervention plan and OT support immediately. Physical Redirection:
"Block and Redirect": If bite is imminent, block with soft object (pillow, stuffed animal). Say firmly "No biting people. Bite this." If bite occurs, remain calm (strong reaction reinforces). Remove child from situation. Provide appropriate bite item immediately. DIY Alternative: Social Biting Protocol Card: Create card with pictures: (1) Feel like biting, (2) Take chew toy, (3) Bite toy not person. Laminate and attach to child at all times during social situations. Alternative Stimulation: Always available chew tools: Child wears chew necklace or has chew tool in pocket at all times during social time. Pre-social oral input: Before any social situation, provide 10 minutes of intense oral motor activity: crunchy snack, frozen fruit, chew toy, thick smoothie through straw. Scheduled sensory breaks: During social time, break every 15-20 minutes for oral input.
OT Activities: For Extreme Seekers: Social Story About Biting: Create book with pictures: "When I feel like biting, my body needs input. I can bite my chew toy. I cannot bite people. Biting people hurts them." Read daily. Replacement Behavior Training: Role play situations where biting urge occurs. Practice reaching for chew tool instead. Reward heavily. Intensive Oral Motor Schedule: Every 30 minutes during waking hours, child gets 3-5 minutes of oral input (chewing, sucking, biting appropriate items). Sensory Integration: Preventive Heavy Work: Before social situations, complete 10-minute heavy work circuit: push against wall (10 reps), chair pushups (10 reps), carry heavy books across room (5 trips), animal walks (bear, crab, donkey kicks). Massage: Pre-Social Deep Pressure: Before social interactions, provide 5 minutes of deep pressure touch: firm massage to shoulders, arms, back. Wrap tightly in blanket with firm pressure. This calms system.
MANIFESTATION 3: Consuming non-food items (pica): paper, dirt, chalk ⚠️ MEDICAL EMERGENCY: Requires immediate medical and OT evaluation. May indicate nutritional deficiency. Physical Redirection: "Stop-Remove-Replace": If caught in act, calmly say "Stop, not for eating." Remove item from mouth (don't dig—may push further back). Immediately offer safe alternative: crunchy snack, ice chips, or chew tool. Then provide drink to clear mouth. DIY Alternative: Environmental Control: Remove all pica items from environment completely. Not as alternative but as safety measure. Then provide sensory-similar safe alternatives: rice cakes for paper-seekers, edible dirt cups (crushed cookies) for dirt-seekers. Alternative Stimulation: Edible alternatives that match sought texture: For paper: rice paper, fruit leather, seaweed snacks For dirt: cocoa powder, crushed cookies, chocolate pudding with graham cracker "dirt"
For chalk: Tums (chewable calcium), white chocolate, yogurt-covered raisins Sensory bins with edible materials: Dry cereal to run hands through, cooked pasta to squish, pudding for messy play. Satisfies exploration urge safely. Constant oral input schedule: Every 30 minutes, child must consume something: water, crunchy snack, chew toy, ice chips. Keeps mouth busy. OT Activities: For Extreme Sensory Seekers: Medical Evaluation First: Check iron, zinc, and other mineral levels. Pica often indicates deficiency. Intensive Oral Motor Program: Under OT supervision: (1) Intra-oral massage 3x daily, (2) Varied textures to mouth under supervision, (3) Resistive chewing exercises, (4) Strong flavor exposure (sour, salty, bitter). Comprehensive Sensory Diet: Whole body approach: (1) Heavy work every 90 min, (2) Deep pressure activities throughout day, (3) Movement breaks hourly, (4) Oral input every 30 minutes.
Environmental Management: Complete supervision in any area where pica items present. Gradually build to independence with constant redirection and replacement. Sensory Integration: Full Body Sensory Integration Sessions: Work with OT on: brushing protocol, joint compressions, vestibular input (swinging, spinning), proprioceptive activities (pushing, pulling, carrying). Done multiple times daily to regulate entire nervous system. Massage: Calming Full Body Massage: 15-20 minutes of slow, deep pressure massage to entire body. Do 2-3 times daily. Include extra focus on arms, hands, face, jaw. MANIFESTATION 4: Gagging self with fingers or objects SAFETY WARNING: Requires immediate professional evaluation. Risk of choking and aspiration. 1. Physical Redirection: "Hands Down, Breathe Out": Approach calmly. Place one hand on child's shoulder, other hand gently guiding their hand away from mouth. Say "Hands down, big breath out" while modeling deep exhale. The exhale naturally stops gag reflex. Guide hands to safe oral tool immediately.
DIY Alternative: Oral Fidget Kit in Sealed Container: Create box that only opens with adult help. Inside: various chew tools, textured spoons, oral massage tools, popsicles. When gagging urge occurs, child requests box and adult supervises selection of safe item. Alternative Stimulation: Back-of-tongue stimulation (SUPERVISED ONLY): Using NUK brush or Z-Vibe with appropriate tip, adult provides firm pressure to back of tongue for 3-5 seconds. This provides deep input to the area child seeks without triggering gag. Cold stimulation: Freeze smoothie or juice in popsicle mold. Licking/sucking provides back-of-throat sensation safely. Thick liquids through straw: Yogurt drinks, smoothies require strong sucking that stimulates throat area. OT Activities: For Extreme Sensory Seekers: Oral Desensitization Program (OT-supervised): Gradual progression: Week 1-2: Touch outside of lips with various textures
Week 3-4: Touch inside of lips, front of tongue Week 5-6: Touch middle of tongue Week 7-8: Touch back third of tongue (never to gagging point) All done with proper tools, never fingers or unsafe objects Gag Reflex Work: OT can teach graduated exposure to reduce hypersensitive gag reflex OR provide appropriate input if seeking deep sensation. This must be individualized based on assessment. Replacement Behavior Chain: Create sequence child follows when urge occurs: (1) Recognize urge, (2) Find adult, (3) Request "throat need," (4) Adult provides safe deep oral input with proper tool. Sensory Integration: External Throat/Neck Input: Since internal gagging provides vagal nerve stimulation, provide external alternatives: firm massage down sides of neck, firm pressure under chin, gentle pressure on throat area (externally, never restricting airway).
Massage: Neck and Shoulder Massage: Deep pressure massage to entire neck, shoulder, and upper back area. 10 minutes, 3 times daily. This area connects neurologically to throat and may reduce internal seeking. MANIFESTATION 5: Excessive drooling from constant mouthing Physical Redirection: "Swallow Check": Set timer for every 5 minutes. When it beeps, touch child's throat/chin and say "Swallow." Have them deliberately swallow, then close mouth for 10 seconds. This builds awareness. DIY Alternative: Absorbent Bandana/Scarf: Child wears bandana around neck to catch drool. Change every 2 hours. Less stigmatizing than bib. Sew absorbent fabric (flannel, fleece) into triangle shape with ties. Alternative Stimulation: Sour/tart foods regularly: Lemon slices, sour candy, pickles. Sour taste triggers automatic swallowing response. Chilled items: Cold reduces drooling. Keep water bottle, ice chips, frozen fruit available.
Straw drinking: Requires lip closure and triggers swallowing. Every 30 minutes, child drinks 4 oz through straw. 4. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers (oral motor low tone contributing): Oral Motor Strengthening Blow exercises: bubbles, whistles, harmonica (10 min, 3x daily) Sucking exercises: thick smoothies, applesauce through straw Lip closure practice: hold popsicle stick between lips (no teeth) for 30 seconds, 10 reps Cheek strengthening: push tongue against cheek while adult pushes from outside Swallow Training: Practice deliberate swallowing every 15 minutes while awake. Use timer as reminder. Jaw Stability Work: Bite-and-hold exercises with resistive items (thick pretzels, carrots). Hold bite without chewing for 10 seconds. 5. Sensory Integration: 1. Intra-Oral Stimulation: Using appropriate oral motor tools, provide stimulation to: gums (upper and lower), inside cheeks, tongue (all surfaces), roof of mouth. This alerting input can improve oral awareness and muscle tone.
6. Massage: 1. Facial Muscle Massage: Firm massage to: cheeks (circular motions), jaw muscles, under chin, lips. 3-5 minutes, multiple times daily. Increases circulation and muscle tone. MANIFESTATION 6: Teeth grinding (bruxism) causing dental damage ⚠️ DENTAL CONCERN: Requires dental evaluation and possible night guard. Physical Redirection: "Jaw Release": When grinding occurs, place hands on both sides of child's face over jaw muscles. Apply gentle pressure and say "Open, relax." Guide them to open mouth slightly and consciously relax jaw. Hold relaxed position for 10 seconds. DIY Alternative: Daytime Awareness Reminder: Place small stickers in child's environment (bathroom mirror, desk, car dashboard). Each sticker reminds them to check: "Is my jaw clenched? Relax it." Alternative Stimulation: Chew breaks scheduled: Every 60-90 minutes, provide 5 minutes of intensive chewing (gum, tough bagel, beef jerky, carrots). This satisfies jaw need appropriately.
Night guard: Must be fitted by dentist. Protects teeth during sleep grinding. Jaw exercises before sleep: 10 minutes of: wide mouth opening/closing, side-to-side jaw movements, gentle self-massage. Tires jaw muscles before bed. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers (seeking proprioceptive input to jaw): Heavy Jaw Work Protocol: Morning: tough breakfast (bagel, thick toast, hard fruit) Every 2 hours: resistive chewing activity (5 min) Before bed: jaw exercises + massage Stress Management: Often grinding increases with stress/anxiety. Implement calming strategies: deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, weighted blanket, rocking. Daytime Awareness Training: Teach child to notice when jaw is clenched. Practice deliberately relaxing jaw 20 times daily. For Nighttime Grinding: Bedtime Routine: (1) Jaw massage (5 min), (2) Warm compress on jaw (3 min), (3) Gentle stretching (open wide 10x, move side to side 10x), (4) Progressive muscle relaxation including face/jaw.
Sleep Positioning: Some positions reduce grinding. Try elevating head slightly or side-sleeping with small pillow between knees (reduces overall muscle tension). Sensory Integration: Joint Compression to Jaw: Place hands on both sides of jaw. Have child open/close mouth while you provide gentle resistance/compression to jaw joint. 10 reps, 3x daily. Massage: Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ) Massage: Place fingers on jaw joints (in front of ears) Make small circles with firm pressure for 60 seconds Then massage jaw muscles (sides of face) for 60 seconds Massage temples for 30 seconds Do this 3x daily and especially before bed MANIFESTATION 7: Chewing holes through clothing regularly Physical Redirection: "Shirt Down, Tool Up": When you see clothing approaching mouth, gently pull shirt away from mouth while simultaneously placing chew tool in hand. Say "Shirt is for wearing, this is for chewing."
DIY Alternative: Chew Tool Attachments on Clothing: Sew loops onto collar/neckline of shirts. Attach chew tools to these loops with ribbon or cord. When child reaches for clothing, they encounter the chew tool instead. Alternative Stimulation: Sacrificial clothing: Designate specific old shirts as "chew shirts" for home use. Child knows these are acceptable to chew. Replace when damaged. Chew jewelry always worn: Silicone chew necklaces worn at all times. Multiple backups in every environment (car, school, home). Clothing made of less appealing textures: Smooth athletic fabric is less satisfying to chew than cotton. May reduce behavior. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Oral Motor Diet: Schedule oral input throughout day: 7 AM: crunchy breakfast 9 AM: chewy snack 11 AM: chew tool + heavy work
1 PM: resistive lunch foods 3 PM: frozen fruit 5 PM: chewy snack 7 PM: chew tool session Before bed: oral massage Clothing Awareness Training: Practice putting on shirt while saying "This stays away from mouth." Reward minutes/hours without chewing clothing. Replacement Training: At first sign of clothing moving toward mouth, prompt child to reach for chew tool. Reward immediately. Over time, this becomes automatic. Sensory Integration: Heavy Work + Oral Input Combined: Before times when clothing chewing peaks (during concentration, anxiety, boredom), provide: 5 minutes heavy work (wall pushes, chair pushups, carrying items) immediately followed by 5 minutes oral input (chew tool, crunchy snack). This combination addresses both needs. Massage: Full Body Calming Massage: Often clothing chewing is self-soothing. Provide alternative soothing through 10-minute deep pressure massage to whole body, 2x daily.
MANIFESTATION 8: Inserting inappropriate objects in mouth CHOKING HAZARD: Requires constant supervision and safety planning. Physical Redirection: "Stop, Show Me": If you see object heading to mouth, say "Stop. Show me with your hands, not your mouth." Guide them to explore object with hands only. If already in mouth, calmly say "Give it to me" while extending your hand. Trade for appropriate oral item immediately. DIY Alternative: Appropriate Oral Exploration Kit: Fill container with variety of safe oral exploration items: different textured chews, oral massage tools, safe household items that can be mouthed (silicone spatula, new baby teethers, etc.). Supervised access only. Alternative Stimulation: Sensory bins with oral-safe materials: Create bins with items safe to mouth: silicone beads, rubber shapes, smooth stones (too large to swallow), baby toys. Child explores these under supervision.
Oral sensory toys rotation: Keep 8-10 different oral toys. Rotate 4 at a time so there's always novelty. Heavy oral input before free play: Before situations where inappropriate mouthing occurs, provide 10 minutes of intensive appropriate oral input. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Oral Exploration Program (Supervised): Under OT guidance, systematically explore safe textures/items orally: smooth, bumpy, soft, hard, cold, warm. This satisfies exploratory need safely while building discrimination. Hand Exploration First: Teach sequence: (1) See new object, (2) Touch with hands first, (3) Examine visually, (4) Ask adult if mouth-safe, (5) If yes, explore with mouth. Build this pattern through practice. Environmental Safety + Replacement: Child-proof environment completely. Have 3-4 appropriate oral items always available and visible. When child reaches for inappropriate item, immediate redirection to appropriate one.
Sensory Integration: Oral Discrimination Training: Present various textures/items. Child explores with hands first, then mouth (if safe). Adult asks: "How does it feel? Bumpy? Smooth? Hard? Soft?" Builds oral awareness and discrimination skills. Massage: Calming Protocol Before Free Play: Before times when mouthing occurs, provide: 5 minutes full body deep pressure massage, joint compressions to all major joints, 3 minutes oral massage. This preemptive input may reduce seeking.
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 6. ORAL/GUSTATORY STIMMING > B. Taste and Food Texture Stimming > Level 1: Flavor Seeking
Causation: Over-stimulated: Strong flavors provide focusing input Under-stimulated: Taste receptors under-responsive; needs intense flavors Sensitivity: Exploring taste sensation and preferences Preference: May genuinely prefer intense flavors neurologically Nutritional: May indicate deficiency (salt craving = mineral need) Sensory Profile: Seeker: Constantly seeking intense flavor experiences Selective: Only eats foods with specific strong flavors Under-Responsive: Typical flavors don't register; needs extreme tastes IDENTIFYING SENSORY SEEKERS VS AVOIDERS: Seeker Signs: Constantly requests strong flavors, adds excessive seasoning, seeks sour/spicy/salty foods, taste-tests everything, eats same strong-flavored foods repeatedly Avoider Signs: Refuses foods with strong flavors, only eats bland foods, gags at smell of flavourful foods, extremely limited food preferences Description: Seeking specific or intense taste experiences MANIFESTATION 1: Craving extremely sour foods constantly Physical Redirection:
"Wait and Rate": When child requests sour food, have them wait 30 seconds. During wait, rate their "sour need" 1-5. If 3+, provide sour item. Teaching delayed gratification and self-awareness. DIY Alternative: Sour Water Station: Fill water bottle with water + fresh lemon/lime juice. Child can access this anytime for sour flavor without excessive candy consumption. Add stevia if too sour. Alternative Stimulation: Homemade sour snacks: Frozen lemon/lime slices to suck Apple slices dipped in lemon juice Homemade "sour spray" (lemon juice in spray bottle) Frozen grapes rolled in citric acid powder (from baking aisle) Sour schedule: Rather than constant access, schedule sour breaks every 90 minutes. Set timer, provide sour item when it rings. Sour alternatives: Pickles, sauerkraut, kimchi, kombucha (small amounts), plain yogurt, green apples, grapefruit.
OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Taste Exploration Program: Present 5 different sour intensities (mild to extreme). Child rates each 1-5. Helps build awareness of how much sourness they actually need. Sour + Activity Pairing: Provide sour item right before activities requiring focus (homework, reading). The strong sensory input can be alerting and organizing. Graduated Sour Weaning: If consumption is excessive/problematic, gradually reduce intensity: Week 1: Extreme sour, Week 2: Very sour, Week 3: Moderately sour, etc. Replace with other sensory inputs. For Sensory Avoiders: Mild Flavor Introduction: Start with barely-detectable flavors. Add tiny drop of lemon to water. Over weeks, gradually increase. Sensory Integration: Full Sensory Diet: Often intense flavor seeking indicates under-responsive system. Incorporate: heavy work, deep pressure, movement activities, and varied sensory experiences throughout day to generally "wake up" sensory system.
Massage: Pre-Meal Oral Massage: Before meals, massage around mouth, jaw, and cheeks for 2-3 minutes. This alerting input may reduce need for extreme flavors during meal. MANIFESTATION 2: Seeking very salty foods excessively ⚠️ MEDICAL NOTE: Excessive salt craving may indicate adrenal issues or mineral deficiency. Consult doctor. Physical Redirection: "Substitute Check": When child requests salt, offer water first. Often thirst masquerades as salt craving. If still wanting salt after drinking, provide measured amount. DIY Alternative: Controlled Salt Access: Put salt in shaker with only 2-3 holes (vs many). Limits amount child can add at once. Alternatively, mix salt with herbs/spices so less salt is needed for flavor. Alternative Stimulation: Naturally salty foods: Celery, olives, pickles, cheese, seaweed snacks, deli meat, salted nuts (in moderation).
Salt alternatives: Mrs. Dash or other salt-free seasonings, nutritional yeast (savory/salty flavor), miso paste (in soup or on vegetables). Mineral-rich foods: If salt craving indicates mineral deficiency, provide: leafy greens, nuts, seeds, whole grains, mineral water. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Taste Training: Present 5 saltiness levels. Have child identify which is too much, just right, too little. Builds awareness. Other Intense Flavors: Provide other strong flavors (sour, spicy, bitter) to satisfy need for intensity without excessive salt. Medical Investigation: If craving is persistent and intense, have doctor check: electrolytes, adrenal function, mineral levels. Sensory Integration: General Alerting Activities: Salt seeking often indicates under-responsive system. Provide alerting input: cold water on face, jumping, fast movement, crunchy foods, upbeat music. Massage: Energizing Massage: Quick, light tapping massage to arms, legs, back. Stimulating rather than calming. May reduce need for intense sensory input from salt.
MANIFESTATION 3: Wanting spicy foods beyond age-typical Physical Redirection: "Cool Down First": Before providing spicy food, offer cold milk or yogurt. Explain "We need cooling food ready." This creates slight delay and ensures safety items available. DIY Alternative: Graduated Spice Options: Create 3-level spice station: Mild (paprika), Medium (chili powder), Hot (cayenne). Child chooses level. Gives control while you manage intensity. Alternative Stimulation: Spicy snack options: Mild: pepperoni, pepper jack cheese Medium: hot sauce on popcorn, spicy chips Hot: jalapeño slices, hot salsa Other intense sensory experiences: Cold foods (popsicles, ice), sour foods, crunchy/hard foods. Varies the type of intensity. Temperature play: Sometimes cold is as alerting as spice. Offer frozen grapes, ice water, popsicles. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Spice Exploration: Safely explore various spice levels. Teach body awareness: "How does your mouth feel? How does your belly feel?"
Cooling Strategies: Teach that milk/yogurt/bread cool spice. Empowers child to manage intensity. Alternative Alerting Input: Before meal, provide 5 minutes of alerting activities: jumping jacks, cold water on face, fast music, dancing. May reduce need for extreme spice. Sensory Integration: Proprioceptive Loading: Heavy work before meals: carry groceries, push/pull heavy objects, animal walks. This deep input may satisfy seeking behavior so intense flavors less needed. Massage: Firm Pressure Massage: Deep pressure massage to whole body before meals. Satisfies intense sensory need through different channel. MANIFESTATION 4: Eating same foods repetitively (10-50+ times per week) Physical Redirection: "First/Then with New Food": "First [preferred food], then [new food], then [more preferred food]." Small exposure to variety while honoring preference. DIY Alternative: Food Journal: Child keeps simple log: draw or write what they ate. Visual representation helps them see the repetition and may motivate variety.
Alternative Stimulation: Variations of preferred food: If loves chicken nuggets: try different brands, shapes, homemade versions If loves pasta: try different shapes, colors, temperatures Small changes while maintaining core food Preferred food in new contexts: Eat it in different place, on different plate, at different time. Builds flexibility. Food chaining: Identify what child likes about the food (texture? flavor? temperature?). Find similar foods sharing those properties. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers (seeking predictability): Food Exploration (Non-Eating): Week 1: Look at new food Week 2: Touch new food Week 3: Smell new food Week 4: Lick new food Week 5: Take tiny bite, can spit out Week 6+: Try eating small amount Same Food, New Way: If child eats chicken nuggets daily, try: different sauce, different shape, cut up vs whole, cold vs hot. Tiny variations build flexibility.
Social Eating: Eat together. Model trying new foods enthusiastically. Don't pressure, just expose. For Sensory Avoiders: Safe Food + New Food: Always include preferred food at meals. New food is "explore only, not required to eat." Pressure Off: Remove all pressure to try new foods. Often pressure increases avoidance. Let curiosity naturally develop. Sensory Integration: Non-Food Sensory Variety: If food variety is limited, ensure variety in other sensory areas: different textures to touch, various movement experiences, multiple types of play. Builds general flexibility. Massage: Calming Pre-Meal Routine: Before meals with new foods, 5-minute calming massage. Reduces anxiety that may drive food rigidity. MANIFESTATION 5: Licking or tasting non-food items to explore flavor Physical Redirection: "Smell Don't Taste": When child reaches to lick item, intercept and say "Smell it instead." Hold item under nose. Satisfies curiosity more safely.
DIY Alternative: Smell Exploration Kit: Create box of safe items with interesting smells (spices, extracts, essential oils on cotton balls in sealed bags). When child wants to explore, offer this instead. Alternative Stimulation: Taste-safe exploration materials: Food-grade flavoring extracts (vanilla, almond, lemon) on cotton swabs Edible flowers, herbs from garden Various spices (cinnamon stick to lick, etc.) Supervised taste exploration: Set up "tasting station" with tiny amounts of many flavors. Explores taste safely with variety. Redirect to appropriate tasting: Keep interesting food flavors available (sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami). When urge to lick arises, offer food alternative. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Taste Exploration Program: Systematically explore flavors under supervision: Week 1: Sweet varieties (honey, sugar, fruit) Week 2: Sour varieties
Week 3: Salty varieties Week 4: Bitter varieties Week 5: Umami varieties Builds taste database through safe exploration Hand-First Rule: Teach: "First touch with hands. Ask adult. Then maybe mouth." Build this habit. Taste Journaling: Child draws/describes tastes they explore. Channels exploration into learning activity. Sensory Integration: Multi-Sensory Exploration: Teach child to explore items through multiple senses: look, touch, smell, listen. Reduces reliance on taste as primary exploration method. Massage: Oral Massage Before Exploration Time: Provide deep input to oral area before free play. May reduce seeking behavior during play. MANIFESTATION 6: Requesting strong-flavored foods (pickles, vinegar, hot sauce) Physical Redirection: "Strong Flavor Time": Designate specific times for strong flavors (after school, before dinner). When requested outside these times, remind "Strong flavor time is at 3pm."
DIY Alternative: Strong Flavor Station: Set up accessible area with: pickle jar, hot sauce bottle, lemon juice, vinegar-based dressings. Child can access small amounts independently. Alternative Stimulation: Variety of strong flavors available: Pickled vegetables (cucumbers, carrots, beets) Fermented foods (sauerkraut, kimchi) Vinegar-based salad dressings Hot sauce varieties Strong cheeses (blue, feta, aged cheddar) Anchovies, capers, olives Make-your-own strong flavors: Pickle vegetables together, make hot sauce, create salad dressing. Involves child in process. Strong flavor scheduled throughout day: Rather than unlimited access, provide at regular intervals. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Flavor Intensity Scale: Child rates foods 1-10 on intensity. Helps them identify how much intensity they need vs want. Alternate Intense Sensory Input: Before requesting strong flavors, try: cold water on face, jumping 20 times, pushing against wall, squeezing stress ball. Sometimes need is general arousal, not specifically flavor.
Strong Flavor Meal Planning: Involve child in planning meals that include strong flavors appropriately: tacos with hot sauce, salad with vinaigrette, sandwich with pickles. Sensory Integration: Alerting Activities Before Meals: 10 minutes before meals: upbeat music, movement (dancing, jumping), cold wash cloth on face. Alerts system so less need for extreme flavor alerting. Massage: Stimulating Massage: Light, brisk tapping massage to arms, legs, back. Provides alerting input through different channel. MANIFESTATION 7: Adding excessive seasoning to foods Physical Redirection: "Three Shake Rule": Allow child to shake seasoning 3 times, then must stop and taste. If still needs more, 3 more shakes. Creates awareness and control. DIY Alternative: Personal Seasoning Container: Give child their own small seasoning shaker with controlled holes. Feels like autonomy but limits amount.
Alternative Stimulation: Seasoning variety: Instead of excessive amount of one seasoning, offer multiple types: garlic salt, onion powder, herbs, spices. Variety satisfies need for flavor without excessive amount. Strong-flavored foods naturally: Choose foods with inherent strong flavors so less seasoning needed. Texture addition: Sometimes need is sensory input, not flavor. Try: crunchy toppings (nuts, seeds, croutons), crispy onions, bacon bits. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Cooking Involvement: Child helps cook, adding seasonings under supervision. Learns appropriate amounts through practice. Taste Testing: Add little seasoning, taste, add more, taste. Builds awareness of how flavor builds. Alternative Sensation: Try: squeeze lemon on food, add hot sauce, include pickles on side. Different ways to add intensity. Sensory Integration: Pre-Meal Sensory Input: Before meals, 5-10 minutes of intense sensory activity: bear hugs, joint compressions, fast movement. Loads system so less seeking during meal.
Massage: Hand and Arm Massage Before Meals: Since seasoning involves hand movements, massage hands and arms before meals. May reduce driven quality of the behavior. MANIFESTATION 8: Seeking bitter flavors (coffee grounds, dark chocolate) Physical Redirection: "Bitter Time": Similar to other strong flavors, designate times when bitter items available. Creates structure around the seeking. DIY Alternative: Safe Bitter Options: Provide appropriate bitter items: dark chocolate (70%+), cocoa nibs, tonic water, black tea, coffee (diluted for children), raw cacao powder in smoothie. Alternative Stimulation: Bitter foods in diet: Dark leafy greens (kale, arugula) Brussels sprouts, broccoli rabe Grapefruit, cranberries Dark chocolate Black coffee/tea (age-appropriate amounts) Bitter scheduled: Rather than unlimited access to coffee grounds or other inappropriate items, schedule bitter snacks 2-3 times daily.
Mix bitter with other flavors: Dark chocolate with sea salt, coffee with milk, greens with lemon juice. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Bitter Exploration: Safe exploration of bitter flavors in appropriate contexts: cooking with cocoa, trying different dark chocolates, tasting various teas. Understanding Bitter: Explain that bitter taste tells us about food (some poison is bitter, coffee is bitter but safe). Makes seeking educational. Alternate Intense Input: Often bitter seeking indicates need for strong sensory input. Provide through other channels: proprioceptive, vestibular, tactile. Sensory Integration: General Sensory Diet: Incorporate varied intense sensory experiences throughout day to satisfy seeking in multiple ways, reducing fixation on one type (bitter). Massage: Oral and Facial Massage: Deep pressure massage to jaw, cheeks, around mouth. 3-5 minutes, 2-3 times daily. Satisfies oral sensory need through touch.
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 6. ORAL/GUSTATORY STIMMING > B. Taste and Food Texture Stimming > Level 2: Texture-Based Food Stimming
IDENTIFYING SENSORY SEEKERS VS AVOIDERS: Seeker Signs: Only seeks specific textures (crunchy or smooth), explores food texture extensively, prefers intense textures, texture is more important than flavor Avoider Signs: Refuses mixed textures, gags at certain textures, extremely limited accepted textures, texture varies causes distress Causation: Over-stimulated: Specific textures are comforting and predictable Under-stimulated: Seeking specific oral-motor input (crunch = proprioceptive) Sensitive: Oral tactile defensiveness; can only tolerate certain textures Control: Need to control oral sensory experience completely ARFID: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder may be present Sensory Profile: Crunchy Seeker: Needs proprioceptive input through jaw; seeks resistive foods Smooth Seeker: Oral tactile defensive; can't tolerate mixed or complex textures Avoider: Extreme selectivity limits nutrition; may require feeding therapy Description: Selecting or avoiding foods based on texture
MANIFESTATION 1: Only eating crunchy foods Physical Redirection: "Crunchy First, Then Try": Honor the need while introducing flexibility. "First eat your crunchy carrot, then let's try one bite of [softer food]." DIY Alternative: Add Crunch to Everything: While working on flexibility, make accepted foods crunchy: freeze them, dehydrate them, add crunchy toppings, toast them. Alternative Stimulation: Maximum crunch options: Raw vegetables: carrots, celery, bell peppers, cucumber, jicama Fruits: apples, pears, grapes (freeze for extra crunch) Crackers, rice cakes, popcorn, pretzels Nuts and seeds (age-appropriate) Toast, crispy bacon, chips Freeze-dried fruits/vegetables Frozen vegetables eaten while still frozen Make soft foods crunchy: Add granola to yogurt Put crushed crackers on mac and cheese Top casseroles with crispy onions Bread and fry foods Non-food crunching: Chew tools, ice chips, gum. Satisfies the sensory need outside meals.
OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers (seeking proprioceptive jaw input): Pre-Meal Jaw Work: Before meals, 5-10 minutes of: chewing gum, biting on chewy tube, chewing dried fruit/jerky, crunching ice. Loads the jaw so intense need reduced during meal. Food Chaining for Texture: Current food: Crunchy carrot Next step: Cooked carrot that's still slightly crunchy Next: Softer cooked carrot Eventually: Soft cooked carrot Gradual progression over weeks/months Heavy Work Before Meals: 10 minutes of: push-ups against wall, carrying heavy items, chair dips, animal walks. General proprioceptive input throughout body may reduce need for it specifically in jaw. For Sensory Avoiders (oral defensiveness—crunchy only tolerable texture): Texture Desensitization (Outside Mouth First): Week 1-2: Touch various textures with hands (wet, sticky, smooth, rough) Week 3-4: Touch textures to arms, legs
Week 5-6: Touch textures to face (outside mouth) Week 7+: Very gradually introduce to mouth area No Pressure Exposure: Present new textures at meals but ZERO pressure to eat. "This is just to look at today." Reduces anxiety. Choose One Texture to Expand: Pick texture slightly different from crunchy (maybe crispy, then eventually slightly softer). Work on expanding within that texture family first. Sensory Integration: Oral Motor Activities: Blow whistles, blow bubbles, suck through straws, blow cotton balls across table. Exercises oral muscles in ways that don't involve eating, building tolerance. Massage: Jaw Massage Before Meals: Deep pressure massage to jaw muscles, temporal area, under chin. 3-5 minutes. Calms oral area before potentially stressful eating. MANIFESTATION 2: Only eating smooth foods (purees, yogurt, applesauce)
Physical Redirection: "Smooth Now, Expand Later": Accept current state while working gradually toward variety. Don't make meals battleground. DIY Alternative: Blender is Your Friend: While working on expansion, puree EVERYTHING. Child still gets nutrition, just in accepted texture. Alternative Stimulation: Maximum smooth options: Yogurt (all flavors) Applesauce, pureed fruits Smoothies, protein shakes Pudding, mousse Pureed soups Mashed potatoes, pureed vegetables Ice cream, frozen yogurt Hummus, guacamole Baby food pouches (for all ages if needed) Nut butters Thicker to thinner progression (or reverse): Start with texture child tolerates Very gradually change consistency Mix in tiny amounts of less-preferred texture Over months, slowly increase proportion Temperature variation: If texture limited, vary temperature: cold, room temp, warm. Adds variety without texture change. OT Activities:
For Sensory Seekers (seeking smooth texture): Sensory Play with Smooth Textures: Play with pudding, shaving cream, yogurt, smooth play-doh. Touch exploration with hands builds tolerance that can transfer to mouth. Smooth to Slightly Textured: Add tiny amounts of texture to smooth foods: Week 1: Pure smooth yogurt Week 2: Yogurt with 5 tiny sprinkles mixed in Week 3: Yogurt with 10 sprinkles Very gradual over months Self-Feeding Empowerment: Let child choose, prepare, serve their smooth foods. Control reduces anxiety. For Sensory Avoiders (oral tactile defensiveness): Oral Desensitization Program: Use electric toothbrush (off) around outside of mouth for 10 seconds daily Progress to (on) for 3 seconds Use textured washcloths on face at bath time Gradually build tolerance to varied sensations on face/mouth
Food Exploration (Not Eating): Touch foods with hands while playing Messy sensory play with various textures Build tactile tolerance generally "One Tiny Taste" Rule: Once per day, child touches tongue to food with different texture. Can immediately spit out. Just exposure, no pressure. Sensory Integration: Brushing Protocol (Wilbarger): Under OT guidance, systematic brushing of arms, legs, back followed by joint compressions. Done every 90 minutes. Reduces overall tactile defensiveness which may transfer to oral area. Massage: Face and Mouth Massage: Firm massage around mouth, on cheeks, jaw. 5 minutes, 3 times daily. Desensitizes area and builds tolerance. MANIFESTATION 3: Avoiding mixed textures (soup with chunks, casseroles) Physical Redirection: "Separate Plate": Present meal components separately on divided plate. Child can combine if desired but not required. Removes pressure.
DIY Alternative: Deconstructed Meals: Instead of casserole, serve each ingredient separately. Eventually child may combine on their own terms. Alternative Stimulation: Everything separated: Instead of soup with chunks: smooth soup + separate plate of crackers/meat Instead of casserole: noodles in one section, meat in another, vegetables in another Instead of sandwich: bread, meat, cheese all separate Let child eventually combine when ready Predictable mixed textures first: Trail mix (can see all components) Cereal with milk (expected) Yogurt with visible fruit (can remove if needed) Very gradual mixing: Week 1: Foods touching but separate Week 2: Small overlap Week 3: Slightly mixed Months of progression OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders (oral defensiveness with unpredictability): Food Predictability: Use clear containers so child sees exactly what's in foods before eating.
Practice Picking Out: Give bowl of mixed foods. Child picks out preferred items. Tolerates presence without eating. Builds comfort. Messy Play Outside Meals: Play with mixed-texture materials (water beads + rice, shaving cream + toys). Builds tolerance to mixed input through hands. Sensory Integration: Increase Predictability Overall: Use visual schedules, routine, prepare child for changes. Reducing overall anxiety may increase food flexibility. Massage: Calming Full Body Massage Before Meals: 10 minutes deep pressure massage. Calms nervous system so less reactive to mixed textures. Due to character limits, I'll continue with the remaining manifestations. Should I proceed with the rest of Level 2 and 3 of food stimming, then move to olfactory stimming, and finally the sensory diet protocol and planning table?
MANIFESTATION 4: Eating same-texture foods exclusively for months Physical Redirection: "Texture Day": Designate one day per week as "new texture day." Just one meal, one food, minimal pressure. Other days honor current preferences. DIY Alternative: Texture Chart: Create visual chart showing different textures (crunchy, smooth, chewy, crispy, etc.). Child places stickers on textures they've tried. Makes expansion into a game. Alternative Stimulation: Variety within preferred texture: If only crunchy: try carrots, apples, chips, pretzels, crackers, celery, cucumber, nuts If only smooth: try yogurt, pudding, applesauce, smoothies, mashed potatoes, ice cream Expand choices while maintaining texture safety Texture bridge foods: Find foods that have elements of both current and target texture: Between crunchy and soft: granola bars, cookies, toast with spread Between smooth and chunky: yogurt with tiny seeds, smooth soup with tiny pasta
Sensory substitution: If texture is comfort/regulation tool, provide OTHER regulation tools: weighted blanket, rocking chair, quiet space, music. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Texture Exploration Schedule: Monday: Touch 3 new textures with hands Wednesday: Smell 2 new food textures Friday: Lick 1 new texture (can spit out) Very gradual, low-pressure exposure Non-Food Texture Play: Daily sensory bins with varied textures. Builds general flexibility: rice, beans, water beads, sand, shaving cream, play-doh, slime, fabrics. Food Play (Not Eating): Cook together, touch ingredients, play with food textures. No eating required. Builds familiarity and comfort. Sensory Integration: Varied Sensory Diet Throughout Day: Since food texture is limited, ensure LOTS of varied sensory input in other areas: varied movement, different sounds, various tactile experiences. Builds overall sensory flexibility.
Massage: Varied Touch Massage: Use different textures during massage: soft brush, rough washcloth, smooth lotion, textured ball. Builds tactile tolerance through body which may transfer to mouth. MANIFESTATION 5: Examining food texture extensively before eating Physical Redirection: "Three Touch Rule": Child can touch food 3 times to examine, then must decide: eat or not eat. Limits compulsive examination while honoring need to check. DIY Alternative: "Inspection Station": Have separate plate for examining. Child inspects there, then transfers to eating plate. Separates examination from eating. Alternative Stimulation: Clear containers for food storage: Child can see food before serving. Reduces surprise and need for extensive examination. Predictable food sources: Same brands, same preparations. More predictability = less need to examine. Food cards with photos: Take photos of accepted foods. Child refers to cards before meals. "This is what chicken nuggets look like today."
OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers (needing control/predictability): Structured Examination Routine: Look at food: 10 seconds Touch food: 3 times Smell food: 2 sniffs Then eat or decline Structure reduces anxiety-driven examination Food Preparation Involvement: When child helps prepare, they know exactly what went into it. Reduces need for examination. Social Stories: Create book about "Foods can look different but still be good." Photos of same food looking different ways. Builds flexibility. Sensory Integration: Control in Other Areas: Give child LOTS of choices throughout day (clothes, activities, schedule). May reduce need for control specifically around food. Massage: Calming Hand Massage Before Meals: Since examination involves hands, massage hands deeply before meals. 3 minutes. May reduce compulsive quality. MANIFESTATION 6: Spitting out foods with unexpected textures
Physical Redirection: "Napkin Ready": Always have napkin available. If texture unexpected, child knows they can spit into napkin. Permission reduces anxiety. DIY Alternative: "Spit Bowl": Small bowl at child's place. If something doesn't work, they can spit into bowl without drama. Normalized response. Alternative Stimulation: Maximum predictability: Same foods prepared same way Avoid restaurants/new foods during high-stress times When trying new foods, explain texture beforehand: "This is crunchy and then creamy" Texture descriptions: Before meals, describe what each food will feel like: "The carrots are crunchy. The potatoes are smooth and soft." "One chew" rule: If texture unexpected, child can chew once and spit out. Honors their response while encouraging brief try. OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders (oral defensiveness): Texture Tolerance Building:
Start with tiny amounts Can spit out immediately Gradually increase: 1 chew before spitting, 2 chews, eventually swallow May take months per texture "Brave Bites": Create chart. Each time child tries texture without spitting, gets sticker. Small rewards for trying (NOT for swallowing). Flavor Before Texture: Sometimes loving the flavor motivates tolerating texture. Start with preferred flavors in new textures. Sensory Integration: Oral Motor Games: Practice different tongue/mouth movements with appropriate items (not food): move chew tool around mouth, hold in different positions. Builds oral control. Massage: Desensitization Massage: Massage face, around mouth, jaw with varying pressure (light to firm) and textures (smooth hands, textured cloth). 5 minutes, 2x daily. MANIFESTATION 7: Only eating specific brand/preparation of foods Physical Redirection: "Blind Taste Test": Sometimes child THINKS it's different but wouldn't notice blind. Occasionally test this (gently, not deceptively).
DIY Alternative: Brand Chart: If specific brands are necessary, create shopping list with pictures. Ensures correct items purchased. Reduces mealtime stress. Alternative Stimulation: Stock up on accepted brands: If only one brand works, buy in bulk. Reduces stress of running out. Find similar alternatives: Identify what child likes about specific brand (texture, flavor, appearance). Find other brands with similar properties as backup. Prepare same way every time: If preparation matters (nuggets baked 15 minutes at 400°, no more, no less), write it down. Family consistency helps. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers (need for sameness): Gradual Brand Introduction: Week 1: New brand on separate plate, doesn't have to eat Week 2: Touch new brand Week 3: Smell new brand Week 4: Lick new brand
Week 5+: Try bite Extremely gradual Compare Game: Put accepted brand and new brand side by side. Discuss: "How are they same? How different?" Makes difference less threatening. Focus Expansion Elsewhere First: Work on flexibility in non-food areas (taking different routes, wearing different clothes). General flexibility may transfer to food. Sensory Integration: Increase Tolerance for Change: Practice small changes throughout day: sit in different chair, use different cup. Build "flexibility muscle." Massage: Grounding Massage Before Transitions: Before trying anything new (including new food brand), provide 5 minutes grounding deep pressure massage. Calms anxiety. MANIFESTATION 8: Mashing or modifying food texture before eating Physical Redirection: "Your Food, Your Choice": Allow modification without comment. It's adaptive strategy, not bad behavior. DIY Alternative: Tools for Modifying: Provide fork, spoon, child-safe knife. Let them modify as needed. May eventually decrease as comfort increases.
Alternative Stimulation: Pre-modified options: Offer foods already in preferred texture: Instead of needing to mash potatoes, serve them already mashed Instead of cutting meat into tiny pieces, serve ground meat Meet them where they are Modification permission: "You can make your food however you like it." Removes shame/pressure. Gradual tolerance: Very slowly, over months, serve foods slightly closer to original texture. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers (need for control): Food Preparation Participation: When child prepares food themselves (mixing, mashing, cutting), they have maximum control and may need less modification. Sensory Play with Modifiable Materials: Play-doh, slime, clay, moon sand. Practice modifying textures in play. Builds comfort with varied textures. "Modification Station": Special plate where child puts food to modify. Then transfers to eating plate. Makes it purposeful, not compulsive.
Sensory Integration: Proprioceptive Activities Before Meals: Heavy work (carrying, pushing, pulling) provides deep input that may reduce need for oral control behaviors. Massage: Hand and Arm Massage: Since modification involves hands, deeply massage hands and arms before meals. 3 minutes. May reduce driven quality.
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 6. ORAL/GUSTATORY STIMMING > B. Taste and Food Texture Stimming > Level 3: Extreme Food-Related Stimming
These behaviors require professional evaluation and ongoing treatment. IDENTIFYING SENSORY SEEKERS VS AVOIDERS: Extreme Seeker Signs: Pica, eating to point of discomfort for sensory satisfaction, consuming dangerous items, cannot stop eating certain textures Extreme Avoider Signs: Severe restriction affecting health, vomiting from texture exposure, fear-based food refusal, nutritional deficiency Causation: Over-stimulated: Extreme selectivity prevents sensory overwhelm Under-stimulated: Pica indicates severe oral sensory seeking Sensitive: Oral defensiveness so severe it limits safe nutrition ARFID: Clinical eating disorder requiring treatment Medical: Pica may indicate nutritional deficiency or GI issues Anxiety: Food-related anxiety preventing exploration Sensory Profile: Extreme Selector: Severe restriction affecting health; requires intervention Pica: Medical and sensory evaluation needed immediately Oral Defensive: Feeding therapy required for nutritional adequacy Description: Unusual or excessive food-related behaviors
MANIFESTATION 1: Eating non-food items regularly (pica): dirt, paper, soap ⚠️ MEDICAL EMERGENCY: Requires immediate medical evaluation for nutritional deficiencies and GI issues. Occupational therapy for sensory component. Behavioral therapy may be needed. Physical Redirection: "Stop, Trade, Supervise": If caught eating non-food: Stop immediately (calm, not panicked). Remove item gently. Offer edible alternative that provides similar sensory experience. Never leave unsupervised until behavior controlled. DIY Alternative: Edible Sensory Alternatives: For dirt eaters: "Edible dirt" (chocolate pudding + crushed Oreos) For paper eaters: Rice paper, fruit leather, very thin crackers For soap eaters: Mild-flavored foods (very plain crackers, rice cakes) For chalk eaters: Tums (calcium carbonate), white chocolate, yogurt-covered raisins Alternative Stimulation: Medical intervention first: Check iron, zinc, calcium, other minerals. Supplement as directed by doctor.
Supervised oral exploration: Provide varied edible textures to explore: crunchy, smooth, gritty, powder, etc. Under supervision, explore textures orally Satisfy curiosity safely Environmental safety: Remove ALL pica items from environment. 100% supervision when items present. Intensive oral sensory diet: Every 30 minutes: oral input (chew tool, crunchy snack, ice, gum) Before high-risk times: intensive oral motor work (10 minutes) OT Activities: For Extreme Sensory Seekers: Comprehensive Sensory Diet (OT-designed): Heavy work every 60-90 minutes Deep pressure activities throughout day Vestibular input (swinging, spinning) 3x daily Oral motor activities every 30-60 minutes Goal: Keep sensory system so well-regulated that extreme seeking decreases Oral Motor Intensity Program: Intra-oral massage 3x daily (5 minutes each) Varied food textures to explore (edible) Resistive chewing activities hourly
Temperature variations (cold and warm items) Strong flavors (sour, salty, spicy as appropriate) Behavioral Component: Immediate redirection every time Trade for appropriate item Never punish (it's sensory need, not misbehavior) Reinforce using appropriate items heavily Texture Exploration Program (Supervised): Provide varied edible textures that somewhat match sought non-edible items Satisfy curiosity in safe ways May reduce seeking if exploratory need met Sensory Integration: Wilbarger Brushing Protocol: Systematic brushing and joint compressions every 90-120 minutes throughout day. Reduces overall sensory seeking. Intensive Proprioceptive Program: Maximum heavy work: pushing, pulling, carrying, climbing, hanging. 15-20 minutes, 4-5 times daily. Massage: Full Body Deep Pressure Massage: 15-20 minutes, 2-3 times daily. Deep, slow pressure to entire body. Calms and organizes nervous system. Oral and Facial Massage: 5-10 minutes, 3-4 times daily. Deep pressure to jaw, cheeks, around mouth, inside mouth (with gloved finger).
Safety Protocol: Never leave child unsupervised Remove all pica items from environment Medical monitoring for intestinal blockages, poisoning Track what items sought (helps identify alternatives) Emergency plan if dangerous item consumed MANIFESTATION 2: Eating excessive quantities for sensory satisfaction (not hunger) ⚠️ MEDICAL CONCERN: Requires evaluation for underlying issues. May need dietitian, OT, and behavioral support. Physical Redirection: "Portion Control with Timer": Serve measured portion. Set timer for 20 minutes. When timer rings, meal is over. This creates boundary while allowing adequate eating time. DIY Alternative: Smaller Plates, Multiple Servings: Use small plates. Child can have seconds/thirds, but smaller portions slow intake and create natural pauses. Alternative Stimulation: High-volume, low-calorie foods: If eating for sensory satisfaction, provide foods that offer lots of oral work without excessive calories:
Raw vegetables (celery, carrots, bell peppers) Air-popped popcorn Watermelon, cantaloupe, berries Clear soups, broth Sugar-free gum Non-food oral input: Between meals, provide chew tools, ice chips, water. Satisfies oral sensory need without eating. Heavy work before meals: 10 minutes of proprioceptive input before eating. May reduce sensory-driven eating. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Oral Motor Schedule (Non-Food): 8 AM: Chew tool, 5 minutes 10 AM: Frozen fruit, slowly 12 PM: Lunch (timed, portioned) 2 PM: Gum or chew tool, 5 minutes 4 PM: Crunchy vegetable snack 6 PM: Dinner (timed, portioned) 8 PM: Sugar-free popsicle Schedules oral input throughout day, not just meals Mindful Eating Training: Eat without distractions (no TV, phones) Chew each bite 20 times Put utensil down between bites
Check in: "Am I still hungry or just wanting more sensation?" Sensory Substitution: When urge to eat arises (not hungry), do alternative sensory activity: jump on trampoline, push-ups, weighted blanket, deep pressure. Channel seeking to different input. Hunger vs. Sensory Awareness: Teach body awareness: "Is belly hungry? Or is mouth bored?" "What does hungry feel like? What does full feel like?" Rate hunger 1-5 before eating Sensory Integration: Comprehensive Sensory Diet: Provide heavy sensory input throughout day through non-food means: heavy work, deep pressure, movement. Reduces need to seek it through food. Massage: Pre-Meal Calming Massage: 10 minutes before meals, full body deep pressure massage. Calms system so eating is less driven. Regular Deep Pressure Throughout Day: Every 2-3 hours, 5-10 minute massage. Keeps sensory needs met.
MANIFESTATION 3: Refusing all but 3-10 foods (extreme food selectivity) ⚠️ NUTRITIONAL CONCERN: May indicate ARFID (Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder). Requires feeding therapy, OT, possible dietitian. Physical Redirection: "Safe Foods Always Available": Never force new foods. Always provide at least one accepted food at meals. Reduces anxiety. DIY Alternative: Accepted Foods List: Create visual list (photos) of all accepted foods. Keep list accessible. When stressed, child can point to what they'll eat. Alternative Stimulation: Maximize nutrition within accepted foods: Add protein powder to accepted drinks Mix pureed vegetables into accepted sauces Fortify accepted foods with vitamins/minerals Work with dietitian to ensure adequacy Vitamin supplementation: If diet too limited for adequate nutrition, supplement under medical guidance. Food chaining: Find foods similar to accepted ones:
Accepts chicken nuggets → try different brands → try breaded chicken strips → try grilled chicken fingers Very gradual expansion along similarity lines OT Activities (Must be under OT/feeding therapist guidance): For Severe Sensory Avoiders: Sequential Oral Sensory (SOS) Approach: Level 1: Tolerates new food on table (not touching) Level 2: Helps put food on plate Level 3: Touches food with finger/utensil Level 4: Food touches lips (can remove immediately) Level 5: Licks food (can spit) Level 6: Bites food (can spit) Level 7: Chews and spits Level 8: Chews and swallows tiny amount Each level may take weeks or months Play with Food (No Eating Pressure): Cook together Play with food textures (painting with pudding, building with vegetables) Reduce fear through non-eating exposure
Oral Motor Preparatory Activities: Blow bubbles, whistles, kazoos Suck through straws (varied thicknesses) Chew on chew tools Temperature exploration (ice, warm) Build oral strength and awareness Desensitization Program: Textured play (outside mouth): play-doh, slime, sand, water beads Face touching with varied textures: soft brush, washcloth, hands Gradually move toward mouth area over months Very slow, child-paced Sensory Integration: Full Sensory Diet: Often food selectivity improves when overall sensory processing improves. Comprehensive program addressing all senses, not just oral. Massage: Daily Calming Routines: Predictable, calming massage routines before meals. 10 minutes. Reduces anxiety that may drive selectivity. MANIFESTATION 4: Prolonged food holding in mouth (20-60+ minutes per bite) Physical Redirection: "Chew Timer": Set timer for reasonable chewing time (start at 5 minutes, gradually reduce to 2). When timer rings, must swallow or spit into napkin. Creates boundary.
DIY Alternative: Small Bites Rule: Child takes tiny bites (pea-sized). Easier to swallow, less overwhelming, less holding time needed. Alternative Stimulation: Foods that dissolve quickly: Popsicles, ice chips Thin crackers, wafers Foods that melt (cheese, chocolate) Reduces need for prolonged oral work Liquid nutrition: If holding is preventing adequate intake, supplement with smoothies, drinks, soups. Strong flavors: Sometimes flavor fades and holding continues. Strong-flavored foods may prompt swallowing when flavor disappears. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers (prolonging sensory experience): Oral Motor Strengthening: May indicate weak oral muscles making swallowing effortful Blow exercises, straw drinking, resistive chewing Build strength so swallowing easier Swallow Practice (With Non-Food): Practice with water, juice Feel throat when swallowing Build awareness of swallow mechanism Timer Training: Start at current duration (even if 20 minutes)
Gradually decrease by 30 seconds per week Very slow reduction of holding time For Sensory Avoiders (fear of swallowing): Rule Out Medical: Ensure no physical difficulty swallowing (dysphagia). May need ENT or GI evaluation. Trust Building: Never force swallowing. Let child control pace. Reduces fear. Alternative Textures: Try textures easier to swallow (smooth, moist, slippery). Sensory Integration: External Throat Stimulation: Massage throat area (externally) to build awareness of swallow mechanism. Massage: Neck and Throat Massage: Gentle massage down front and sides of neck. May facilitate swallowing. MANIFESTATION 5: Eating foods in specific order/ritual every time Physical Redirection: "Flexibility Practice": Once per week, ask child to eat one item out of order. "Today, let's try carrots before nuggets." Very gradual flexibility building.
DIY Alternative: Honor the Ritual: If not causing harm, allow it. Many people have food rituals. Work on flexibility in other areas if food rigidity is needed for comfort. Alternative Stimulation: Predictable rituals in other areas: If food ritual provides comfort/control, ensure child has other areas of predictability and control: morning routine, bedtime routine, weekend schedule. Written ritual: If ritual matters, write it down. Child can check off steps. Makes it concrete and manageable. Gradual changes: If flexibility needed, change ritual VERY slowly over months. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers (need for predictability): Choice Within Structure: "You can eat carrots or peas first today." Provides choice while building flexibility. Social Story About Change: Create book: "Sometimes foods come in different orders. That's okay. My belly doesn't mind. Food can be different and still good."
Practice Change in Play: Play with toy foods, practice different orders. Makes change less threatening. Sensory Integration: Build Flexibility Generally: Practice small changes throughout day. General flexibility often transfers to food. Massage: Grounding Massage Before "Different" Meals: If change is planned, provide calming massage first. MANIFESTATION 6: Smelling, licking, touching food without eating Physical Redirection: "Explore Then Decide": Allow 2-3 minutes of exploration. Set timer. When it rings, ask: "Eat or not eat today?" DIY Alternative: Exploration Plate: Separate plate for exploring. Food can be touched, smelled, licked there. Eating plate separate. Keeps exploration contained. Alternative Stimulation: Honor exploration as learning: This is how child learns about food. Not problematic unless preventing eating adequate nutrition. Non-food sensory exploration: Provide lots of sensory play opportunities with non-food items. May reduce food exploration need.
"Looking vs. Eating" foods: Some foods are just for exploring today. Others are for eating. Reduces pressure. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Structured Food Exploration Time: Designate 10 minutes before meals as "food exploration time." Can touch, smell, lick, not required to eat. After exploration time, regular meal begins. Cooking Together: Exploration during cooking is purposeful and educational. "Food Scientist" Play: Approach exploration as scientific experiment. Write down observations. Makes it learning activity. Sensory Integration: Multi-Sensory Exploration Throughout Day: If exploring food with all senses, ensure exploring environment with all senses too. This is learning style. Massage: Hand Massage Before Meals: Since exploration involves hands, massage hands before meals. May reduce compulsive quality. MANIFESTATION 7: Vomiting or gagging from non-preferred textures
⚠️ MEDICAL CONCERN: Ensure no physical cause (GI issues, esophageal problems). May need medical evaluation. Physical Redirection: "Stop Before Gag": Learn child's pre-gag signals. Stop immediately before gag occurs. Remove trigger food calmly. DIY Alternative: Gag Triggers List: Document what triggers gags. Avoid these completely while working on tolerance with feeding therapist. Alternative Stimulation: Only accepted textures: Until working with feeding therapist, only offer tolerated textures. Prevent repeated gagging (can sensitize further). Medical evaluation: Rule out: reflux, eosinophilic esophagitis, other GI issues. Feeding therapy: This level of reaction requires professional feeding therapy. OT Activities (Under professional guidance only): For Severe Oral Defensiveness: Desensitization (Extremely Gradual): May take 6-12+ months Start with textures far from mouth Progress to face, lips, inside mouth
Eventually food textures Must be done by trained therapist Gag Reflex Desensitization: Systematic exposure to gradually further back oral stimulation Done with proper tools, professional guidance Never force or trigger actual vomiting Safe Foods Only Approach: Sometimes best approach is accepting current textures while working on general sensory processing. Food battles can worsen situation. Sensory Integration: Whole Body Sensory Processing: Often oral hypersensitivity part of overall sensory processing disorder. Address globally. Massage: Calming Full Body Massage: Multiple times daily. May reduce overall sensory defensiveness over time. MANIFESTATION 8: Food neophobia (fear of new foods) affecting nutrition ⚠️ NUTRITIONAL CONCERN: May require dietitian to ensure adequate nutrition within accepted foods. Physical Redirection: "New Food on Table (Not Plate)": New food present at meals but not on child's plate. Just exposure, zero pressure.
DIY Alternative: Photo Menu: Before meals, show child photos of what will be served. Reduces surprise/anxiety.
