Alternative Stimulation: Fortify accepted foods: Work with dietitian to maximize nutrition from accepted foods while slowly expanding. Family meals without pressure: Eat together. Model trying foods. No pressure on child. "One touch" exposure: New food at table. Child can touch with finger. That's all. Over weeks, progress to: smell, lick, tiny bite. *OT Activities (Feeding therapy): For Anxiety-Based Avoidance: Anxiety Management First: Deep breathing before meals Calming music Weighted lap pad at table Remove pressure completely Food Play: Play with foods (no eating): make art, build structures, sensory play Reduces fear through non-eating exposure Social Stories: "New foods can be scary. I can look at them first. Then maybe touch. I don't have to eat new foods today. Maybe another day."
Food Chaining: Start with well-accepted food Find similar food (same color, or similar texture, or similar flavor) Very gradually bridge from accepted to new May take months per food Sensory Integration: Build General Confidence: Success in non-food areas may transfer confidence to food exploration. Massage: Calming Routine Before Meals with New Foods: 10 minutes deep pressure massage, predictable and calming.
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 6. ORAL/GUSTATORY STIMMING > C. Oral Avoidance/Defensive Stimming > Level 1: Food Texture Avoidance
Causation: Over-stimulated: Oral sensory system easily overwhelmed by texture Sensitive: Oral tactile defensiveness; textures neurologically unpleasant Anxiety: Fear-based avoidance of unpleasant oral experiences Gag Reflex: Heightened gag reflex triggered by textures Control: Need to control oral sensory input precisely Sensory Profile: Avoider: Moderate to severe oral defensiveness Selective: Nutrition at risk from limited variety Protective: Behaviors prevent gagging/vomiting response Description: Rejecting specific food textures Manifestations: Refusing any "mixed" textures (yogurt with fruit chunks) Gagging on certain textures immediately Refusing to try new foods based on appearance/texture Only eating 10-20 "safe" foods Extreme reactions to slimy, sticky, or wet foods Preferring processed foods over whole foods (consistent texture) Cutting food into tiny pieces or mashing completely Removing any visible texture variations (skin, seeds, chunks)
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 6. ORAL/GUSTATORY STIMMING > C. Oral Avoidance/Defensive Stimming > Level 2: Oral Defensiveness Behaviors
Causation: Over-stimulated: Oral area extremely sensitive to touch and sensation Sensitive: Oral tactile defensiveness affecting daily care routines Anxiety: Previous negative experiences create fear Control: Need complete control over what enters or touches mouth Sensory: Toothbrush vibration, minty flavors overwhelming Sensory Profile: Extreme Avoider: Oral defensiveness affecting health (dental hygiene) Protective: Fight-or-flight response to oral care Intervention Needed: Occupational therapy for oral desensitization Description: Protecting mouth from unwanted input Manifestations: Refusing teeth brushing or extreme resistance (daily battles) Refusal of dental care (cleanings, exams) Won't use certain toothpaste flavors or types Resistance to face washing near mouth Refusing kisses or facial affection Keeping lips tightly closed during activities Difficulty taking medicine (especially liquids) Resistance to face painting, lip balm, etc.
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 6. ORAL/GUSTATORY STIMMING > C. Oral Avoidance/Defensive Stimming > Level 3: Severe Oral Avoidance
Causation: Over-stimulated: Severe oral sensory processing disorder Sensitive: Oral hypersensitivity causing pain or extreme discomfort Medical: Possible underlying medical conditions (eosinophilic esophagitis, reflux) Trauma: Previous negative medical experiences (intubation, NG tubes) Neurological: Central processing disorder affecting oral sensation Sensory Profile: Crisis-Level Avoider: Oral input triggers extreme distress Medical Concern: Requires feeding therapy and medical evaluation Nutritional Risk: May require alternative feeding methods Description: Extreme rejection of oral stimulation Manifestations: Refusing to eat solid foods (liquid diet only) Vomiting from texture exposure Panic attacks during teeth brushing or dental care Only tolerating very specific temperature foods G-tube feeding due to oral refusal Inability to swallow pills (even tiny ones) Selective mutism related to oral awareness Complete refusal of oral medications
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 7. OLFACTORY STIMMING
(Smell and Scent-Related)
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 7. OLFACTORY STIMMING > A. Smell-Seeking Stimming > Level 1: Intentional Smelling
IDENTIFYING SENSORY SEEKERS VS AVOIDERS: Sensory Seeker Signs: Constantly smelling objects/people, seeks out scents actively, deep inhaling of smells, first response to new items is smelling, uses smell as primary sense for exploration Sensory Avoider Signs: Covers nose frequently, complains about smells others don't notice, refuses to enter areas due to smell, detects odors from far away, distressed by scents Causation: Over-stimulated: Familiar scents are organizing and calming Under-stimulated: Olfactory system under-responsive; needs intense input Sensitivity: Exploring and cataloging scent information Memory: Scent strongly tied to memory; using for comfort or recall Identification: Using smell as primary sense for object recognition Sensory Profile: Seeker: Constant smelling throughout day; primary sensory exploration Comfort-Seeking: Using familiar scents for emotional regulation Under-Responsive: Needs close, intense smelling to register scents
Description: Actively seeking and smelling objects or people MANIFESTATION 1: Smelling people (hair, clothing, skin) upon greeting Physical Redirection: "Wave and Step Back": When child approaches person and begins to lean in to smell, gently touch their shoulder and guide them to take a step back. Say "Wave hello" and model waving. The physical distance interrupt breaks the smell-seeking pattern while providing alternative greeting. DIY Alternative: Scented Greeting Card: Child carries a small card or piece of fabric with their favorite scent (lavender, vanilla extract, lemon). When greeting people, they can smell their own card instead of the person. Attach to keychain or keep in pocket. Alternative Stimulation: Personal scent collection: Create a small "smell kit" child carries: Cotton balls with different essential oils in small plastic bags
Scented lip balm or hand lotion Scented stickers Small sachet of dried herbs Child can smell these anytime instead of people Scented jewelry: Wear essential oil diffuser necklace or bracelet. Can smell own scent when needed. Before social interaction ritual: Smell preferred scent for 30 seconds before entering social situation. Pre-loads the sensory need. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Smell Schedule: Set timer for every 30-45 minutes. When it beeps, child gets 1-2 minutes to smell preferred scents from their collection. Regular input reduces driven seeking. Social Greeting Practice: Role play greetings with family Practice: wave, say hello, keep personal space Reward appropriate greetings heavily After appropriate greeting, child can smell their personal scent item Social Story: Create book: "People have smells. I like to smell things. But people don't like to be smelled. I can smell my special smell items instead. After I wave hello, I can smell my bracelet/card/lip balm."
Olfactory Exploration Time: Designate 15 minutes daily as "smell exploration time." Child can smell variety of appropriate items: spices, extracts, flowers, scented items. Satisfies curiosity in appropriate context. For Social Situations: Warning Alert System: Teach child to recognize when they're about to smell someone. Internal dialogue: "I want to smell. I should smell my bracelet instead." Replacement Object Always Present: Never in social situation without appropriate smell item available. Sensory Integration: Olfactory Discrimination Training: Present 5-10 different scents. Child identifies each, describes it. Builds conscious awareness of smell as sense. May reduce automatic seeking. Multi-Sensory Greetings: Teach child to greet with multiple senses appropriately: look (see their face), listen (hear their voice), touch (handshake/wave). Reduces reliance on smell alone. Massage: Pre-Social Deep Pressure: Before social situations, 5-10 minute deep pressure massage. Calms system and may reduce sensory seeking behaviors.
MANIFESTATION 2: Smelling objects before using them (books, toys, clothing) Physical Redirection: "Touch First, Then Quick Smell": When child reaches for object, guide their hand to touch it first. Say "Touch first, then one quick smell." Allow brief smell (3-5 seconds), then redirect to using the object. The touching provides alternate sensory input first. DIY Alternative: Smell Timer: Use small sand timer (3-5 seconds). Child can smell object while sand falls, then must move on. Visual boundary for smell duration. Alternative Stimulation: Scented items appropriate for prolonged smelling: Scented markers (Mr. Sketch brand) Scented stickers Scratch-and-sniff books Scented stuffed animals These are designed to be smelled, so behavior is appropriate Personal scent station: At home, create area with variety of scents child can access anytime:
Jars with cotton balls + essential oils Spice jars (cinnamon sticks, whole cloves) Dried flowers/herbs Scented candles (unlit, just for smelling) Scented soaps New item ritual: When getting new item, allow 1 minute of exploration including smelling. Then put item to use. Satisfies need while setting boundary. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Olfactory Exploration Journal: Child keeps journal of smells encountered Draw or write about each smell Makes seeking purposeful and educational Adds cognitive component that may slow automatic behavior Smell Identification Game: Present 10 items in covered containers (only smell opening) Child smells and identifies: cinnamon, lemon, vanilla, coffee, mint, etc. Builds conscious smell discrimination 10 minutes daily "Look, Touch, Smell, Use" Routine: Teach sequence for new items Look at it (5 seconds)
Touch it (5 seconds) Quick smell (3 seconds) Use it appropriately Practice until automatic Scheduled Smell Breaks: Every hour, 2-minute smell break Child accesses smell collection Regular input reduces constant seeking For School/Public Settings: Discrete Smell Tools: Scented chapstick (can apply and smell) Essential oil on cotton ball in small container Scented hand lotion Can be used discretely without drawing attention Sensory Integration: Olfactory Discrimination Training: Teach child to consciously notice smells rather than automatically seeking: "What do you smell right now?" "How many different smells can you identify?" "Which smell is strongest?" Builds awareness and control Other Sensory Input: Often intense smell seeking indicates under-responsive system. Provide intense input through other senses: proprioceptive (heavy work), vestibular (spinning, swinging), auditory (music), visual (colored lights).
Massage: Nasal Area Massage: Gently massage around nose, cheeks, forehead. May increase awareness of olfactory area and reduce automatic seeking. 2-3 minutes, several times daily. MANIFESTATION 3: Sniffing food extensively before eating (20-60+ seconds) Physical Redirection: "Three Smell Rule": Allow child to smell food 3 times (can be deep sniffs), then must take a bite or decline the food. Count aloud: "Smell one, smell two, smell three, now decide." DIY Alternative: Visual Menu with Scent Descriptions: Before meals, show child what will be served with description: "Tonight we're having spaghetti. It smells like tomatoes and basil." Reduces need to smell extensively if they know what to expect. Alternative Stimulation: Cooking involvement: When child helps cook, they smell throughout preparation. Extensive smelling during cooking may reduce need at eating time.
Smell card for meals: Before meal, provide cotton ball with food-related scent (basil, garlic, vanilla, cinnamon). Child smells this for 30 seconds, then meal begins. Strong-smelling foods: If smell is important to eating, provide foods with significant aroma: garlic bread, cinnamon toast, curry, herbs, etc. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Pre-Meal Smell Session: 5 minutes before meal, child explores various strong scents Essential oils, spices, extracts Fills the "smell tank" before eating May reduce meal-time smelling Smell and Describe: At meals, teach child to smell once and describe: "This smells sweet/spicy/savory" Makes smelling purposeful and brief Add cognitive component Smell Timer at Table: Place small timer at child's spot Can smell food for 10 seconds (timer runs) Then must proceed with eating
Gradually reduce time over weeks Sensory Integration: Olfactory Hierarchy for Eating: Some foods require more smell than others (appropriate) New foods: longer smell acceptable Familiar foods: brief smell only Help child categorize Massage: Pre-Meal Calming Routine: 5 minutes before meals, massage hands, arms, shoulders. Calms nervous system so eating is less sensory-driven. MANIFESTATION 4: Smelling own hands or body repeatedly Physical Redirection: "Hands Down, Smell This": When hands approach nose, gently press hands down to lap. Immediately offer appropriate scent item (scented lotion, chapstick, essential oil on cotton ball). The downward hand pressure provides proprioceptive input while replacing smell source. DIY Alternative: Scented Hand Lotion Routine: Apply strong-smelling lotion to hands every 2 hours. Gives hands a scent, makes smelling them more purposeful and acceptable. Choose scent child loves.
Alternative Stimulation: Scented personal care products: Scented hand soap Strong-smelling lotion Scented deodorant (age-appropriate) Scented shampoo/conditioner Makes body-smelling less noticeable/more typical Scented clothing/accessories: Lightly spray clothing with body spray Use scented laundry detergent Scented fabric in pocket Replace with appropriate item: Scented wristband or bracelet Scented necklace Cotton ball with essential oil in pocket Can smell these instead of body OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Body Smell Awareness: Discuss: everyone has a smell, it's normal Teach socially appropriate ways to smell self (brief, discrete) Practice in mirror: "Is this discrete or obvious?" Scent Application Ritual: Morning and afternoon: apply scented product Can smell hands for 30 seconds after application Then continue with day Replacement Training: When urge to smell hands/body arises, immediately use alternative
Practice sequence: feel urge → reach for scent item → smell that instead Reward heavily when alternative used Scheduled Self-Smell Times: Designate 3-4 times daily when body-smelling is allowed Bathroom, private room, etc. Other times, use alternatives Gradually reduce frequency Sensory Integration: Interoceptive Awareness: Often body-smelling is checking on self/self-awareness. Build other forms of body awareness: deep pressure, movement, position sense. Proprioceptive Activities: Heavy work before times when body-smelling peaks. May reduce seeking. Massage: Hand and Arm Massage: Since hands are frequently smelled, deeply massage hands and arms 3-4 times daily. Provides intense input to area. 3-5 minutes each session. MANIFESTATION 5: Seeking out specific scents (flowers, perfumes, cleaning products) Physical Redirection: "Safe Smell First": Before allowing access to sought scent (especially if potentially unsafe like cleaning products), redirect to safe alternative first. "First smell this [safe item], then we'll see about the other."
DIY Alternative: Personal Scent Collection: Create child's own collection of preferred scent categories: Floral: dried flowers, floral essential oils, perfume samples on cards Clean: diluted cleaning product scents (safe), fresh laundry, soap bars Food: vanilla extract, cinnamon, coffee beans, citrus peels Keep in accessible box child can open anytime Alternative Stimulation: Safe sources of preferred scents: Loves perfume: perfume sample cards from magazines/stores, body sprays Loves cleaning products: unscented cleaner + safe essential oils child can smell separately, bar soap collection Loves flowers: dried flower sachets, floral essential oils, fresh flowers in room Loves gasoline/markers: NOT safe to provide—redirect to other strong scents Scent layering: Use preferred scent categories in daily products: Floral shampoo, lotion, room spray Clean-scented laundry products Constantly available in environment
Rotational scent availability: Monday-Tuesday: floral scents accessible Wednesday-Thursday: food scents Friday-Saturday: clean scents Sunday: choice day Keeps novelty, maintains interest OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Scent Exploration Program: Systematically explore many scents within preferred category 10-15 minutes daily Satisfies curiosity and seeking Creates "scent library" in brain Scent Creation Activities: Make potpourri (dried flowers + oils) Create custom perfume blends (essential oils + carrier oil) Make scented play-doh (add extracts or oils) Make sachets for drawers/closets Purposeful, creative scent activities Scent Matching Game: Create matching pairs of scents Memory game format: find matching smell Makes seeking into structured activity Safe vs. Unsafe Scent Education: Teach which scents are safe to seek (flowers, food extracts, essential oils) Which are dangerous (cleaning products, gasoline, chemicals)
Why unsafe scents are harmful (can hurt lungs, make sick) Provide abundant safe alternatives Sensory Integration: Olfactory Discrimination: Often intense seeking indicates under-responsive system. Provide varied, strong scents regularly to "wake up" the system. Over time, may reduce intensity of seeking. Comprehensive Sensory Diet: Balance olfactory input with other intense sensory experiences. Reduces fixation on smell alone. Massage: Full Body Alerting Massage: If olfactory seeking indicates under-responsive system, provide alerting massage: quick, light touches all over body. Wakes up nervous system. 5 minutes, 2-3 times daily. MANIFESTATION 6: Carrying scented objects (sachets, essential oils, scented toys) Physical Redirection: "Smell Station": Designate specific places where scented items "live" (bedroom, backpack pocket, kitchen). When child wants to smell, they go to the station. Creates boundaries while allowing access.
DIY Alternative: Scent Bracelet: String dried flowers, wooden beads with essential oils, or scented felt pieces on elastic. Child wears this—scent available but hands-free. Alternative Stimulation: Wearable scent options: Essential oil diffuser necklace or bracelet (lava bead style) Scented chapstick on keychain Small sachet pinned inside clothing Scented hand lotion in pocket Always available without carrying bulky items Scented items integrated into daily objects: Scented bookmark Scented pencil toppers Scented eraser Scented stickers on water bottle Functional items that also provide scent Layered scent environment: Scented laundry products on clothing Scented shampoo/body products Scented room spray in bedroom Scented lotion on hands Ambient scent means less need to carry specific items OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Scent Dependence Evaluation: Is scent for comfort/regulation? (emotional need)
Is it for sensory input? (under-responsive system) Treatment differs based on function If Emotional Comfort: Gradually fade dependence while replacing with other comfort tools Week 1: Can carry scent item everywhere Week 2: Scent item stays in backpack, can access when needed Week 3: Scent item at home only, use before school Week 4+: Scent available but not constantly carried Replace with: deep pressure, fidgets, music, etc. If Sensory Input: Scheduled smell breaks (every 60-90 minutes) Access scent items at break times Between breaks, use other sensory input (chew tools, fidgets, movement) Gradually lengthen time between smell breaks Discrete Carrying Solutions: If carrying needed, make discrete: locket necklace with scent, pocket-size item, bracelet Reduces social stigma while meeting need Sensory Integration:
Alternative Regulation Tools: If scent is regulatory, teach multiple regulation strategies: Deep breathing Progressive muscle relaxation Heavy work activities Reduces reliance on one tool (scent) Massage: Portable Self-Massage: Teach child self-massage techniques they can do anywhere: Hand massage Shoulder squeezes Neck rolls Provides alternative self-regulation method MANIFESTATION 7: Requesting specific scented products obsessively Physical Redirection: "Request Limit": Set clear boundary: "You can ask about scents 2 times today. You've asked once. You have one more." Visual counter (tokens, stickers) helps child track. DIY Alternative: Scent Choice Board: Create board with pictures of 3-5 available scented options. Child points to choice once per designated time period (morning, afternoon). Gives control within structure. Alternative Stimulation: Scheduled access: Rather than requesting unpredictably, create schedule:
8 AM: morning scent time (5 minutes with preferred scent) 12 PM: lunch scent break 4 PM: after-school scent time 7 PM: bedtime scent routine Reduces requests because child knows when access occurs Variety within category: If obsessively requesting lavender, provide 5 different lavender products. Satisfies need with variety. Gradual exposure to other scents: While honoring preferred scent, slowly introduce others: Week 1: 100% preferred scent Week 2: 90% preferred, 10% new scent Gradual shifting over months OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Request vs. Access: Child can access certain scents independently (those in their room/box) Special scents require request but have schedule Reduces obsessive requesting Scent Rating System: Child rates their "scent need" 1-5 If 1-2: use available scents If 3-4: access preferred scent for 5 minutes
If 5: longer session with preferred scent Builds self-awareness Replacement Requests: When child requests scent, first try: "Can you use [available alternative] first?" If alternative satisfies, reinforces flexibility If not, provide requested scent Over time, alternatives work more often Social Story About Scent Availability: "I love [specific scent]. It helps me feel good. Sometimes I can use it and sometimes I have to wait. I can use my other scents while I wait. My favorite scent is special, so I save it for [specific times]." Sensory Integration: Function Analysis: Determine why this specific scent is critical. Is it: Calming? → Teach other calming strategies Alerting? → Provide other alerting input Emotionally comforting? → Build other comfort sources Sensory need? → Provide varied olfactory input
Massage: Substitute Comfort: If scent is comfort-seeking, provide deep pressure massage when child requests scent. Sometimes physical input satisfies underlying need. MANIFESTATION 8: Becoming distressed when preferred scent unavailable Physical Redirection: "Plan B Scent": Teach child: "If scent A isn't available, we use scent B." Create hierarchy of acceptable scents (most preferred to least preferred). Practice accessing backups before distress occurs. DIY Alternative: Backup Scent System: Keep preferred scent in multiple locations (home, car, school, grandparent's house) AND have 2-3 similar backup scents. Reduces chance of being caught without any acceptable option. Alternative Stimulation: Scent hierarchy creation: Most preferred: lavender from specific brand Also good: other lavender products Acceptable: other floral scents Will work in emergency: mint, vanilla, lemon Creates fallback options
DIY scent creation: Teach child to create their preferred scent: Essential oils + carrier oil Mix of several oils to match favorite Empowers child to recreate if unavailable Scent independence: Child has their own supply they control. Reduces anxiety about availability. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers with Anxiety: Scent Flexibility Training: Week 1: Use preferred scent 100% of time Week 2: Try backup scent once, followed immediately by preferred Week 3: Use backup scent twice this week Week 4: Alternate days (preferred/backup) Very gradual expansion of accepted scents Coping Strategy Training: When preferred scent unavailable, use coping sequence: Deep breath (count to 4) Use backup scent Deep pressure (hug self, squeeze hands) Positive self-talk: "I can handle this. The backup scent will help."
Practice when NOT in distress first Distress Tolerance Building: Practice brief periods without scent while calm Start with 30 seconds Gradually increase Use other regulation tools during wait Builds tolerance for unavailability Social Story: "Sometimes my favorite scent isn't available. This makes me feel worried/upset. I can use my backup scent. I can take deep breaths. I can ask for a hug. Soon I will have my favorite scent again." Sensory Integration: Multiple Regulation Strategies: If distress occurs when scent unavailable, child is over-reliant on one tool. Build regulation toolbox: Deep pressure Movement Music Breathing techniques Counting Visualization Multiple options reduce dependence on scent alone Massage: Calm-Down Massage Protocol: When distress occurs due to scent unavailability, immediately provide deep pressure massage:
Both hands on shoulders, firm pressure Massage down arms with firm strokes Hand squeezes 3-5 minutes until calm returns Over time, massage alone may calm without scent
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 7. OLFACTORY STIMMING > A. Smell-Seeking Stimming > Level 2: Scent Collection and Preference
Causation: Over-stimulated: Specific scents provide predictable organizing input Under-stimulated: Favorite scents provide maximum olfactory stimulation Sensitivity: Strong scent preference; neurological preference for certain smells Emotional: Scents tied to positive memories or feelings Regulation: Using scent as primary regulation tool Sensory Profile: Seeker: Actively collects and seeks preferred scents Selective: Very specific scent preferences; rejects others Dependent: Relies on scent for emotional regulation Description: Seeking specific scents repeatedly MANIFESTATION 1: Collecting scented items (candles, lotions, perfumes) excessively Physical Redirection: "Rotation System": Child can keep 10 scented items accessible. Others stored away. Weekly, can swap 2 items in/out. Creates limit while allowing collection. DIY Alternative: Scent Library: Create organized system: labeled boxes/containers for scent collection. Makes collection purposeful/organized rather than chaotic accumulation. Alternative Stimulation:
Structured collection: Limit by category: 5 floral, 5 food, 5 clean scents Clear boundaries on collection size When new scent acquired, old one donated/discarded Collection becomes learning: Create scent journal describing each item Research scent origins (where does lavender grow? What makes vanilla?) Makes collecting educational Sharing collection: Child teaches others about their scents, shares favorites. Makes collection social/purposeful. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Collection Evaluation: Which scents actually used regularly? (keep) Which never used? (release) Reduces accumulation of unused items Quality Over Quantity: Teach that 10 wonderful scents better than 50 mediocre ones Save money/space for truly special items Scent Curation: Make scent collection an art/hobby Display beautifully Share with others Creates pride rather than hoarding Sensory Integration: Channel Collecting Into Other Areas: Often intense collecting indicates seeking/control needs. Provide other acceptable collecting outlets: rocks, stickers, cards. Spreads drive across multiple interests.
Massage: Organizing Activity: Sort scent collection together while receiving deep pressure (weighted lap pad, compression vest). Makes organization calming rather than stressful. MANIFESTATION 2: Applying scented products (lotion, lipstick) excessively Physical Redirection: "Two Pumps Rule": For lotion/body spray: only 2 pumps/sprays at a time. Count together. Set timer for 2 hours before can reapply. DIY Alternative: Diluted Products: Put products in spray bottles diluted with water or mix lotion with unscented. Child can apply more frequently but less concentration each time. Alternative Stimulation: Application schedule: 7 AM: Morning application 10 AM: Mid-morning 1 PM: After lunch 4 PM: After school 7 PM: Bedtime Scheduled times reduce constant application Strong, long-lasting products: Choose highly scented products that last longer. Reduces need for frequent reapplication.
Scent layering properly: Use scented shampoo + lotion + body spray in same scent family. Creates lasting scent environment. OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Application Awareness: "Can you still smell it?" Check before reapplying Often scent still present but child habituated Teaches to check rather than automatically reapply Timer System: Set timer when product applied Cannot reapply until timer rings Gradually lengthen time between applications Consequence Education: Too much scent bothers others Can irritate skin Wastes product/money Teaches moderation Sensory Integration: Olfactory Adaptation: Child may habituate to smell quickly (can't smell it anymore). Teach: "You may not smell it but others do." Massage: Hand Massage After Application: After applying scented product, massage hands for 2 minutes. The hand attention/input may reduce urge to immediately reapply.
MANIFESTATION 3: Seeking same scent repeatedly (smelling marker 50+ times daily) Physical Redirection: "Smell Five Times, Then Away": When child reaches for repeatedly-smelled item, allow 5 deliberate smells while counting together, then physically move item to different location. Set timer for 30 minutes before item accessible again. DIY Alternative: Scent Rotation Schedule: Have 5 similar scents. Each day, one is "today's scent." Other days, different scents used. Reduces fixation on single item while maintaining scent category child loves. Alternative Stimulation: Multiple sources of same scent: If loves marker smell: scented markers, dry erase markers, permanent markers (supervised), marker-scented air freshener Variety within sameness Can rotate through sources, getting same scent from different items Scheduled access with duration limit: Every 90 minutes: 2-minute smell session with preferred item
Use timer to signal end Regular schedule reduces obsessive seeking Fading procedure: Week 1: Can smell preferred item every 30 min Week 2: Every 45 min Week 3: Every 60 min Week 4+: Every 90 min Gradually extends time between access OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Smell Satiation Sessions: Designate 15 minutes, 2x daily as "intensive smell time" Child can smell preferred scent as much as wanted during this time Outside these times, limited to scheduled brief smells Often intensive sessions reduce constant seeking Alternative Alerting/Calming Activities: Before times when repetitive smelling peaks, provide alternative input: If scent is calming: deep pressure, slow rocking, dim lights, quiet music If scent is alerting: jumping, cold water on face, crunchy snacks, fast music
Meets underlying need through different channel Scent Diary: Track when/why child seeks specific scent Pattern identification: bored? anxious? transitioning? under-stimulated? Address underlying triggers rather than just limiting behavior Replacement Training: When urge to smell marker arises, first do: 10 jumping jacks, drink water, chew gum Sometimes alternative input satisfies need If not, then access marker briefly Over time, alternatives work more frequently Sensory Integration: Olfactory Habituation: Constant exposure to same scent causes habituation (can't smell it anymore), which drives more seeking. Rotating scents prevents habituation while satisfying need. Comprehensive Sensory Diet: If fixated on one scent repeatedly, likely indicates under-responsive system seeking intense input. Provide intense input across ALL senses throughout day. Reduces fixation on olfactory alone. Massage: Nasal and Facial Massage: Before high-seeking times, massage around nose, sinuses (cheeks, forehead), under eyes. 3-5 minutes. May satisfy attention to nasal area without repeated smelling.
MANIFESTATION 4: Creating scent rituals (smelling specific items before activities) Physical Redirection: "Quick Smell": When ritual is about to begin, set visual timer for 10 seconds. Child can smell during those seconds, then timer rings and activity proceeds. Shortens ritual while honoring need. DIY Alternative: Ritual Card: Create visual card showing: (1) Smell item for 10 seconds, (2) Deep breath, (3) Begin activity. Makes ritual structured and briefer. Alternative Stimulation: Formalize appropriate rituals: Before bed: smell lavender sachet for 30 seconds Before school: smell energizing scent (citrus, peppermint) Before homework: smell focus blend Makes rituals purposeful rather than compulsive Gradual fading: Week 1: Full ritual as child needs it Week 2: Shorten by 10 seconds Week 3: Shorten another 10 seconds
Eventually: brief smell becomes sufficient Alternative rituals: Teach other transition rituals: Deep breathing Counting to 5 Physical movement (stretch, jump) Gives options beyond just scent OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Ritual Function Analysis: What does ritual provide? Comfort? Transition help? Sensory input? Control? Address function directly: Comfort: teach multiple comfort strategies Transition: create transition plan with multiple elements Sensory: provide sensory input before activity begins Control: give child other areas of control Ritual Flexibility Training: Practice doing activity WITHOUT ritual occasionally Start with low-stakes activities Prove to child they CAN do it without ritual Builds confidence and flexibility Social Story About Rituals: "I like to smell [item] before [activity]. It helps me feel ready. Sometimes I can smell it and sometimes I can't. I can also [alternative] to feel ready. I am strong and can do activities even if I can't do my ritual."
Sensory Integration: Sensory-Based Transition Support: If ritual provides transition support, replace with other sensory transitions: Heavy work before new activity Movement break Deep pressure Multiple sensory-based options beyond scent Massage: Pre-Activity Massage: Instead of scent ritual, provide brief (2-3 minute) massage before activities: Hand squeezes Shoulder pressure Arm massage Provides sensory input and transition support MANIFESTATION 5: Refusing to use unscented items Physical Redirection: "Try First, Then Scented": Establish rule: first use unscented version for 1 minute, then can switch to scented. Often once using item, scent becomes less critical. DIY Alternative: Add Scent to Unscented Items: Put drop of essential oil on unscented items (lotion, soap, etc.). Child participates in scenting items. Gives control and meets need. Alternative Stimulation: Scent everything appropriately:
Add essential oils to: lotion, shampoo, body wash, laundry detergent Choose scented versions of products Meet preference rather than fighting it Gradual scent reduction: If goal is accepting unscented items, fade gradually: Week 1: Full scent strength Week 2: 90% scented + 10% unscented mixed Week 3: 80% scented + 20% unscented Very slow dilution over months Natural scents: Some items have inherent scents even if "unscented": Coconut oil smells like coconut Shea butter has natural scent May be acceptable alternatives OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Scent Independence: Teach child to add their own scents: Mix essential oils into unscented base Add vanilla extract to lotion Empowers child, makes any item "scented" Scented vs. Unscented Challenge: Blind test: can child actually tell difference?
Sometimes resistance is habit, not true sensory need If can't tell difference, helps reduce insistence Cost-Benefit Discussion: Scented items cost more Not always available Sometimes unscented is only option Teaching flexibility as practical life skill Sensory Integration: Environmental Scent Saturation: If child's environment is richly scented (room spray, scented candles, essential oil diffuser), individual items matter less. They're already surrounded by scent. Massage: Scented Massage: When doing massage, use scented oils. Associates pleasant experience with scent, may reduce need for every single item to be scented. Manifestations: Collecting scented items (candles, lotions, perfumes) excessively Carrying scented objects (sachets, essential oils, scented toys)-not available Applying scented products excessively (lotion, chapstick) Seeking same scent repeatedly (smelling marker 50+ times daily) Creating scent rituals (smelling specific items before activities)
Requesting specific scented products obsessively- not available Refusing to use unscented items Becoming distressed when preferred scent unavailable-not available
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 7. OLFACTORY STIMMING > A. Smell-Seeking Stimming > Level 3: Unusual Smell-Seeking
⚠ These behaviors have safety concerns and require close supervision and intervention. Causation: Over-stimulated: Strong, unusual scents provide maximum organizing input Under-stimulated: Severe olfactory under-responsiveness needs extreme input Sensitivity: Neurological preference for specific chemical compounds Danger: May not recognize dangerous chemical smells as harmful Social: Using smell as primary connection method (inappropriate socially) Sensory Profile: Extreme Seeker: Seeks potentially harmful scents; requires supervision Under-Responsive: Typical scents don't register; needs intense input Safety Concern: May inhale dangerous chemicals; education needed Description: Seeking socially inappropriate or concerning scents MANIFESTATION 1: Smelling inappropriate items (garbage, dirt, feces) ️⚠ SAFETY CONCERN: Risk of disease transmission and social inappropriateness. Physical Redirection: "Stop and Block": If child approaches inappropriate item, physically block access while saying "Not safe for smelling." Immediately redirect to safe alternative with similar properties (see below). Never allow access to truly unsafe items.
DIY Alternative: "Earthy" Scent Alternatives: Create safe versions of sought smells: For dirt smell: potting soil in sealed container with small holes, coffee grounds, cocoa powder For garbage smell: aged compost in sealed container (supervised), strong cheese, fermented foods For fecal smell: (this is most concerning—seek OT immediately) aged cheese, certain fermented foods NOTE: Never provide actual unsafe items; only safe smell approximations Alternative Stimulation: Supervised exploration of "unusual" scents: Blue cheese, aged cheese (strong smell) Durian fruit (famously strong odor) Fermented foods: kimchi, sauerkraut, fish sauce Very ripe fruit Aged compost (in sealed container) Vinegar Provides strong, unusual smells in safe ways Olfactory exploration program: Work with OT to systematically explore SAFE smells across spectrum: Pleasant: vanilla, lavender, rose Neutral: paper, wood, fabric
Unpleasant-but-safe: vinegar, old shoes, strong cheese Satisfies curiosity about full range of smells Complete environmental control: Never unsupervised near sought items Lock trash cans, bathroom doors if needed 100% supervision until behavior controlled OT Activities: For Extreme Sensory Seekers: Medical Evaluation First: Rule out: pica, OCD, zinc deficiency, neurological issues This level of unusual seeking may indicate medical issue Intensive Sensory Diet: Seeking inappropriate items indicates EXTREME under-responsiveness Need very intense sensory input throughout day: Heavy work every 60 minutes Strong flavors (sour, spicy, bitter) Temperature extremes (ice, warm) Deep pressure constantly (weighted vest, compression clothing) Very strong but SAFE smells regularly Goal: Fill sensory needs so intensely that seeking reduces Behavioral Component: Immediate redirection EVERY time No access to inappropriate items ever
Heavy reinforcement for using appropriate smell alternatives May need behavioral intervention plan (BCBA involvement) Social Skills Training: Explicitly teach: these items are not for smelling Why: make you sick, others think it's weird, spreads germs What to do instead: ask adult for safe smell item Practice appropriate smell-seeking Sensory Integration: Comprehensive Assessment: This level of seeking requires full sensory processing evaluation. Often part of larger sensory processing disorder needing intensive OT. Wilbarger Protocol: Brushing and joint compressions 6x daily. May reduce extreme seeking. Massage: Multiple Daily Deep Pressure Sessions: 15-20 minutes, 3-4 times daily. Full body deep pressure. Intensive input may reduce drive to seek extreme olfactory input. MANIFESTATION 2: Smelling people excessively or inappropriately ⚠️ SOCIAL CONCERN: Can lead to social rejection and misunderstandings.
Physical Redirection: "Personal Space Boundary": Teach arm's length rule. When greeting people, extend arm—this is minimum distance. If child moves closer to smell, adult physically guides them back to arm's length. "We stay this far from people." DIY Alternative: Social Script Card: Child carries card with pictures: (1) Wave hello, (2) Say "Hi," (3) Keep arm's length away. Adult prompts card use before social interactions. Alternative Stimulation: Pre-social olfactory input: Before social situations, 10 minutes of intensive smell exploration with preferred scents Loads the system so less driven to smell people Smell substitute always available: Scented bracelet, necklace, or pocket item When urge to smell person arises, smell own item instead "Smell people in photos": Provide photos of family members with their associated scent (mom's perfume on photo corner, dad's cologne). Can smell photo instead of person.
OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Social Skills Training: Role play greetings 20+ times Practice: wave, verbal greeting, maintain distance Reward appropriate greetings heavily Practice with family, then friends, then acquaintances Social Story: "People have smells. I like to know how people smell. But smelling people makes them uncomfortable. It's too close. I can smell my special smell item instead. I can wave and say hi. This is what friends do." Read daily, especially before social events Video Modeling: Watch videos of appropriate greetings Make video of child doing appropriate greeting Watch own video before social situations Distance Training: Use hula hoop or rope circle as visual boundary Practice staying outside the circle when greeting person inside Makes "personal space" concrete and visible
Sensory Integration: Alternative Connection Methods: Often smelling people is attempting connection/recognition. Teach other ways to connect: Visual: look at faces Auditory: listen to voices Social: ask questions, share interests Multi-sensory connection beyond smell Massage: Pre-Social Grounding: Before social situations, 10 minutes deep pressure massage. Calms and organizes system. May reduce sensory-seeking behaviors in social settings. MANIFESTATION 3: Seeking strong chemical smells (gasoline, markers, nail polish) ⚠️ DANGER: Toxic chemicals can cause brain damage, respiratory issues, and death. This is a medical emergency. Physical Redirection: "Block Access Completely": These items must be locked away, 100% inaccessible. If child attempts to access, physical barrier (adult blocks) + immediate redirection to safe alternative. NEVER allow access even briefly. DIY Alternative: Safe "Strong Chemical" Alternatives:
Strong, safe scents: eucalyptus oil, peppermint oil, tea tree oil (very diluted), camphor (in sealed container) Industrial smells (safe versions): rubber toys, new tennis balls, leather items NOTE: These are approximations only; child must NEVER access actual toxic chemicals Alternative Stimulation: Extremely strong but safe scents: Undiluted essential oils (in sealed container, supervised sniffing only): eucalyptus, peppermint, tea tree, camphor Ammonia-free smelling salts (athletic use) Extremely strong coffee beans Horseradish, wasabi (food items with strong smell) Vick's VapoRub Tiger Balm All must be supervised Environmental lockdown: All chemicals locked in car trunk or high locked cabinet Gasoline vehicles locked, keys hidden Nail polish, cleaners, paints completely inaccessible 100% supervision in any environment with chemicals Medical intervention: This level of seeking requires immediate medical and OT evaluation
May indicate severe sensory processing disorder, pica, or other condition OT Activities: For Extreme Sensory Seekers: CRISIS-LEVEL INTERVENTION: This is not typical sensory seeking—this is dangerous Requires: medical evaluation, intensive OT, possible psychiatric evaluation, behavioral intervention plan Immediate Safety Protocol: Never alone All chemicals locked Adults trained in recognition and intervention Emergency plan if chemical exposure occurs (Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222) Intensive Sensory Diet (OT-Designed): Maximum sensory input ALL day through safe means: Heavy work every 45-60 minutes (pushing, pulling, carrying) Strong safe smells every 30-60 minutes Deep pressure constantly (weighted vest/compression garment) Strong flavors (sour candies, spicy foods, bitter foods) Temperature extremes (ice, warm compress) Vestibular input (swinging, spinning) 3x daily Proprioceptive input (joint compressions) 6x daily Goal: Sensory system SO satisfied through safe means that dangerous seeking reduces
Education: Teach explicitly: these chemicals are poison Can kill you, hurt your brain, make you very sick Show pictures/videos about chemical safety Age-appropriate but clear messaging about danger Replacement Training: When urge to smell chemicals arises: Step 1: Recognize urge ("I want to smell something strong") Step 2: Tell adult immediately Step 3: Adult provides safe alternative (strong essential oil, smelling salts, etc.) Step 4: Heavy reinforcement for using appropriate alternative Practice 20+ times when NOT in crisis Sensory Integration: Full Sensory Processing Evaluation: This behavior indicates severe sensory processing disorder. Requires comprehensive evaluation and intensive OT intervention. Possible Medical Issues: Check for: zinc deficiency, neurological issues, psychiatric conditions. This is beyond typical sensory seeking. Massage: Maximum Deep Pressure Multiple Times Daily: 20-minute sessions, 3-4 times per day. Entire body, very firm pressure. May help satisfy intense sensory needs through safe channel.
EMERGENCY PROTOCOL: If child inhales chemicals: Fresh air immediately, call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222), seek emergency medical care If chemicals in eyes: Flush with water 15 minutes, seek emergency care If chemicals ingested: Call Poison Control immediately, do NOT induce vomiting unless instructed MANIFESTATION 4: Huffing or deep inhaling of strong scents ⚠️ MEDICAL CONCERN: Can indicate dangerous huffing behavior or simply very intense sensory seeking. Requires evaluation. Physical Redirection: "Gentle Sniff Only": When child begins deep inhaling, place hand on their shoulder and say "Gentle sniff" while modeling a brief, shallow sniff. Physically guide if needed—lift their head away from item after brief sniff. DIY Alternative: Breathing Technique Training: Teach "smell the flower" breathing: brief sniff through nose (1-2 seconds), then normal breathing. Practice with safe scents until automatic.
Alternative Stimulation: Safe strong scents with limited access: Provide strong scents in closed containers with small holes Prevents deep huffing, allows only brief sniffing Examples: essential oils in roller bottles, solid perfume, spice jars with shaker tops Breathing exercises: Channel deep breathing urge into: Blowing bubbles Blowing pinwheels Blowing cotton balls across table Harmonica, recorder, whistle Provides deep breathing sensation safely Alternative respiratory input: Cold air inhalation (stand by open freezer briefly) Steam inhalation (safe temperature) Breathing exercises (4-7-8 breathing) OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Distinguish From Huffing: Is child seeking sensory input from SMELL? → Sensory seeking Is child seeking lightheaded/altered state? → Huffing behavior (requires immediate psychiatric/medical intervention) Different treatments based on function If Sensory Seeking: Teach appropriate depth of sniffing
Practice with safe scents daily 1-2 second sniff, then item away Reward appropriate sniffing Respiratory Exercises: Belly breathing exercises 3x daily Provides attention to breathing without scent May satisfy respiratory component Intensive Input Through Other Channels: If seeking intense sensation via deep inhalation, provide through other means: Heavy work (maximum proprioceptive input) Strong tastes (sour, spicy) Temperature (ice, warmth) Deep pressure Reduces need for intense olfactory input Sensory Integration: Vestibular Input: Sometimes head rush sought from deep inhaling is actually vestibular seeking. Provide: swinging, spinning, hanging upside down, rolling. May reduce respiratory seeking. Massage: Chest and Shoulder Massage: Since deep breathing involves chest/diaphragm, massage chest (appropriate touch), shoulders, upper back. 5-10 minutes, 2-3 times daily. Provides attention to respiratory area. MANIFESTATION 5: Smelling body odours (own or others) repeatedly
Physical Redirection: "Quick Check, Then Done": Allow one brief smell (3 seconds) to "check," then redirect hands away from body area. Use timer if needed. DIY Alternative: Scented Body Products: Use strongly scented deodorant, body wash, lotion. If body must be smelled, at least it smells pleasant and is more socially acceptable. Alternative Stimulation: Personal care product routine: Morning: scented soap, scented lotion, scented deodorant Midday: reapply lotion or body spray Evening: scented body wash Body always has pleasant scent if child smells it Scented accessories: Wearable items with scent (bracelet, necklace) near body. When urge to smell body arises, smell accessory instead. Body awareness through other senses: Mirror checks (visual body awareness) Body scanning exercises (interoceptive awareness) Reduces reliance on smell for body awareness
OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Function Analysis: Why smelling body? Comfort? Checking? Sensory input? Anxiety? Comfort: teach other self-soothing Checking: teach visual checking Sensory: provide alternative input Anxiety: teach anxiety management Social Skills Training: Teach: smelling own body is private behavior (bathroom, bedroom only) Smelling others' bodies is never appropriate Practice appropriate alternative behaviors Hygiene Education: Good hygiene means body doesn't have strong odor Teach: shower, deodorant, clean clothes Reduces body odor that might drive smelling Sensory Integration: Interoceptive Work: Often body smelling is attempt at interoceptive awareness (sensing internal body state). Teach other interoceptive awareness methods: Body scan meditation Naming emotions/sensations Noticing heart rate, breathing, temperature Hunger/fullness awareness Massage: Full Body Massage for Body Awareness: Regular massage builds body awareness through touch rather than smell. 10-15 minutes daily. May reduce need to smell body for awareness.
MANIFESTATION 6: Seeking decaying or rotting smells ⚠️ MEDICAL/SAFETY CONCERN: May indicate pica, nutritional deficiency, or sensory processing disorder. Exposure to decay can cause illness. Physical Redirection: "Not Safe, Try This": Block access to decaying items completely. Immediately redirect to safe "aged" smell alternatives (see below). Never allow access to actual rotting items. DIY Alternative: Safe "Aged" Smell Alternatives: Very aged cheese (blue cheese, Limburger) Fermented foods (sauerkraut, kimchi, miso) Overripe fruit (supervised, still safe to eat) Aged vinegar Mushrooms Fish sauce (very small amount) Provide strong, fermented smells without actual decay/danger Alternative Stimulation: Supervised exploration of unusual but safe smells: Visit farmers market: smell aged cheeses, fermented items Cooking with fermented foods together Composting (sealed system, supervised) Makes interest educational and safe
Science education: Teach about decomposition, bacteria, fermentation Channel curiosity into learning Books, videos about decomposition Complete environmental control: All trash sealed in closed containers, inaccessible Compost locked No access to any decaying items 100% supervision outdoors OT Activities: For Extreme Sensory Seekers: Medical Evaluation Immediately: Check: zinc deficiency, pica, GI issues, neurological problems This is not typical sensory seeking Intensive Sensory Diet: Need maximum sensory input across all systems: Heavy work every 60 minutes Strong (safe) smells regularly Strong flavors (aged cheese, fermented foods, strong spices) Deep pressure constantly Goal: Satisfy seeking through safe channels so unsafe seeking reduces Behavioral Intervention: Immediate redirection every time Heavy reinforcement for using safe alternatives May need BCBA involvement Olfactory Exploration Program: Systematically explore ALL smell categories safely:
Sweet, sour, bitter, floral, woody, musky, fermented, etc. Satisfies curiosity about smell spectrum Reduces fixation on one category (decay) Sensory Integration: Full Assessment Required: This level of unusual seeking indicates serious sensory processing disorder requiring comprehensive OT intervention. Massage: Intensive Daily Deep Pressure: 20 minutes, 3 times daily. Very firm pressure. May reduce extreme sensory seeking. Manifestations: Difficulty regulating when preferred scent unavailable-not available Using scent-seeking as primary social interaction-not available
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 7. OLFACTORY STIMMING > B. Smell Avoidance/Defensive Stimming > Level 1: Scent Sensitivity
IDENTIFYING SENSORY AVOIDERS: Avoider Signs: Covers nose frequently, complains about smells others don't notice, refuses to enter areas due to smell, detects odors from far away, shows distress from scents, asks others to not wear perfume/cologne Causation: Over-stimulated: Olfactory system over-responsive; smells are overwhelming Sensitive: Heightened smell detection; can't filter olfactory input Anxiety: Unexpected smells cause distress and unpredictability Past Experience: Previous negative smell experiences create sensitivity Neurological: Olfactory processing differences in autism Sensory Profile: Avoider: Moderate olfactory defensiveness Sensitive: "Supersmeller"; detects odors below typical threshold Selective: Tolerates some scents but not others Description: Noticing and reacting to smells others don't detect MANIFESTATION 1: Commenting on smells others don't notice Physical Redirection: "I Hear You, Coping Strategy": Acknowledge child detected smell ("You noticed a smell"), then immediately implement coping strategy (see below). Validation + action reduces need for repeated commenting.
DIY Alternative: Smell Awareness Chart: Child rates smells 1-10 (intensity) and notes reaction. Over time, identifies patterns (which smells are actually problematic vs just noticeable). Builds self-awareness. Alternative Stimulation: Preferred scent always available: Carry pleasant scent (lavender, vanilla, peppermint) When unpleasant smell detected, smell preferred scent instead Masks/replaces unpleasant odor Nose-breathing filters: Breathe through fabric (scarf, bandana with pleasant scent) Reduces odor intensity Nasal adaptation training: When safe smell detected, practice staying near it for increasing durations Builds tolerance gradually OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Smell Exposure Hierarchy: List smells from least to most bothersome Gradually expose to smells, starting with least bothersome Very slow desensitization over months Example: Level 1: Picture of flower (no smell) Level 2: Flower scent from 10 feet away
Level 3: Flower scent from 5 feet away Level 4: Flower scent from 1 foot away Level 5: Brief direct smell Coping Strategy Training: When smell detected: Step 1: Notice smell Step 2: Rate intensity (1-10) Step 3: If 6+, use coping strategy (preferred scent, breathing through mouth, leave area) Step 4: If under 6, practice tolerating briefly Desensitization Through Pleasant Scents: Start with scents child loves Gradually introduce less-preferred but not unpleasant scents Eventually tolerate neutral scents Builds general olfactory tolerance Sensory Integration: Olfactory Discrimination: Teach child to identify: Is smell actually unpleasant/dangerous, or just noticeable? Builds ability to distinguish worth-commenting-on smells from ignorable ones. Massage: Calming Nasal Area Massage: Gentle massage around nose, sinuses, forehead. May reduce olfactory hypersensitivity. 3-5 minutes, 2-3 times daily.
MANIFESTATION 2: Detecting food cooking from far distances Physical Redirection: "Close Windows, Pleasant Scent": When child detects cooking smell from far away, offer to close windows/doors if possible, provide pleasant scent to child, turn on fan for ventilation. DIY Alternative: Air Purifier in Child's Space: HEPA air purifier with activated carbon filter in child's room. Reduces odor infiltration significantly. Alternative Stimulation: Competing pleasant scent: Essential oil diffuser in child's space Strongly scented candle (unlit, just for smell) or wax melts Creates preferred scent that competes with/masks cooking smells Advance warning: "We're cooking dinner in 10 minutes. Please go to your room and turn on your air purifier." Prepares child, reduces surprise/distress Ventilation: Kitchen exhaust fan during cooking Open windows in cooking area
Reduces smell spread throughout home OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Gradual Exposure to Food Smells: Start with cold foods (no cooking smell) Progress to room-temperature foods Then foods cooked in different room Eventually can tolerate cooking in same room Very gradual over months/years Pleasant Food Smell Exploration: Find foods child LIKES the smell of (baking cookies, popcorn, cinnamon rolls) Increase exposure to those smells Builds positive associations with food cooking smells Cooking Participation: When child helps cook, they control the experience May reduce aversion through familiarity and control Start with pleasant-smelling foods Sensory Integration: Olfactory Desensitization: This is olfactory hypersensitivity. OT can work on graduated exposure to reduce over-responsiveness over time. Massage: Pre-Meal Calming: Before meals (when cooking smells present), provide calming input: weighted lap pad, deep pressure, quiet space. Reduces stress response to smells.
MANIFESTATION 3: Refusing to enter areas due to scent Physical Redirection: "Breathing Technique Entry": Teach child to take three deep breaths through mouth while entering challenging space. Count together: "Breathe one, breathe two, breathe three, now enter." The focused breathing distracts from smell while providing control. DIY Alternative: Scent Mask System: Child wears cloth face mask with drops of preferred essential oil on inside. When entering challenging space, puts on mask. Creates portable scent barrier. Alternative Stimulation: Pre-entry preparation: Before entering challenging space: smell preferred strong scent for 30 seconds This "loads" olfactory system with preferred smell May temporarily mask unpleasant smell Scented scarf/bandana: Wear around neck Pull up over nose when needed Has drops of pleasant essential oil Mouth breathing practice:
Teach: "When smell bothers you, breathe through mouth" Significantly reduces odor detection Practice until automatic OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Graduated Exposure to Challenging Spaces: Week 1: Stand outside challenging space for 10 seconds Week 2: Step just inside door for 5 seconds, leave Week 3: Enter for 15 seconds Week 4: Enter for 30 seconds Very gradual exposure over months Always have "escape plan"—child can leave anytime Safe Space Modification: If child must be in challenging space regularly (classroom, store): Work with management to improve ventilation Request unscented cleaning products Use air purifier if possible Seat child near window/door Reward System: Heavy reinforcement for entering challenging spaces Earn preferred activity/item for tolerating smell Builds motivation to try Control and Choice:
Let child choose: which entrance to use, where to stand, how long to stay Control reduces anxiety and increases tolerance Sensory Integration: General Anxiety Reduction: Often smell avoidance ties to anxiety. Address overall anxiety through: deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, therapy if needed. Reduces all avoidance behaviors. Massage: Pre-Challenge Calming Routine: Before entering challenging space, 5-10 minute deep pressure massage. Calms nervous system so less reactive. MANIFESTATION 4: Covering nose in public spaces Physical Redirection: "Discrete Covering": Teach socially acceptable alternatives to obvious nose covering: pinch bridge of nose briefly (looks like thinking), scratch nose while blocking nostrils, cough into elbow (blocks nose briefly), hold hand near face casually. DIY Alternative: Medical Mask: In current times, wearing mask in public is socially acceptable. Provides legitimate smell barrier without drawing attention. Can add preferred scent inside mask.
Alternative Stimulation: Discrete scent tools: Scented chapstick applied under nose Dab of essential oil on upper lip (very small amount) Scented tissue held near nose Less obvious than hand covering Breathing modification: Shallow nose breathing Mouth breathing primarily Reduces odor intake Scented jewelry near face: Essential oil necklace Scented scarf Can position near nose discretely OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Social Awareness Training: Discuss: covering nose might hurt others' feelings Practice discrete alternatives Role play various scenarios Build socially appropriate coping strategies Public Space Desensitization: Visit public spaces during low-traffic times (fewer smells) Gradually increase exposure Practice tolerance for increasing durations Start with least-challenging public spaces (library vs mall) "Nose Covering" Alternative Skills: Teach 5 discrete ways to cope without obvious covering
Practice each until natural Child chooses which to use when Pre-Outing Preparation: Before public outings: Deep pressure massage Smell preferred scent Review coping strategies Set realistic duration goal Plan breaks/escape route Sensory Integration: Systematic Desensitization: OT-guided graduated exposure to public space smells. Start with brief exposures, gradually increase. Over months/years, tolerance improves. Massage: Post-Outing Regulation: After challenging public outings, provide calming massage. 10-15 minutes. Helps child recover from sensory stress. MANIFESTATION 5: Complaining about perfumes or scented products Physical Redirection: "One Comment, Then Cope": Allow child to comment once: "I smell perfume." Then say: "You commented. Now use coping strategy." Prevents repetitive complaining while acknowledging detection. DIY Alternative: Scent-Free Environment Advocacy: Create scent-free zones: child's room, car, classroom (with teacher support). Reduces exposure so child isn't constantly overwhelmed.
Alternative Stimulation: Request accommodations: Ask family members to use unscented products Request teacher announce: "We have student sensitive to scents. Please minimize perfume/cologne." Reduces problematic exposures Competing scent: Child wears their own preferred scent Helps mask others' scents Air quality improvement: Air purifiers in main living spaces HEPA filters Reduces scent intensity OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Accommodation vs. Tolerance Balance: Some situations: reasonable to request scent-free (home, child's room) Other situations: must build tolerance (public spaces, school) Help child distinguish when to advocate vs when to cope Intensity Rating System: Teach child to rate perfume smell 1-10 If 1-3: practice tolerating without comment If 4-6: use coping strategy quietly If 7-10: advocate for moving away/leaving Builds discrimination and appropriate response
Exposure to Pleasant Perfumes: Find perfumes child finds tolerable or even pleasant Gradual exposure to these first Builds general perfume tolerance May generalize to less-preferred scents Social Communication Training: Teach appropriate ways to address scent issues: NOT: "You smell bad! That perfume is gross!" YES: "Excuse me, I'm sensitive to scents. Could I move to a different seat?" Practice polite advocacy Sensory Integration: Olfactory Desensitization Program: Systematic OT-guided exposure to various scented products. Very gradual. May reduce hypersensitivity over time. Massage: Regular Calming Routines: Daily massage regardless of scent exposure. Keeps baseline nervous system calmness high. May reduce overall reactivity. MANIFESTATION 6: Noticing changes in familiar smells immediately Physical Redirection: "Good Noticing, Now Transition": Acknowledge: "You noticed something changed. Good awareness!" Then redirect: "Now let's [continue activity]." Validates noticing without allowing fixation.
DIY Alternative: Change Warning System: When changes will occur (new soap, different detergent), warn child in advance: "Tomorrow we're using new soap. It smells like lavender." Reduces surprise-related distress. Alternative Stimulation: Gradual product changes: Mix 90% old product + 10% new for first week 80/20 next week Slow transition reduces shock of change Consistent products when possible: Keep frequently-used products consistent Only change when necessary Reduces change frequency Smell preview: Before using new product, let child smell it separately Builds familiarity before actual use OT Activities: For Sensory Seekers (using smell for predictability): Change Tolerance Building: Practice small changes in low-stakes situations Different soap in bathroom child rarely uses Gradually increase change exposure Builds flexibility around smell changes "Same But Different" Game:
Collect multiple versions of same scent (3 brands of lavender soap) Child smells all, discusses similarities/differences Teaches: things can smell slightly different but still be same category Change Warning Routine: Always announce changes 24 hours in advance when possible Reduces surprise Child prepares mentally Focus on Positive: "New soap smells fresh/clean/nice" Frame changes positively rather than as loss of familiar Sensory Integration: General Flexibility Training: Work on flexibility in all areas (schedule, activities, routines). General flexibility often transfers to smell flexibility. Massage: Transition Massage: When changes occurring, provide extra massage sessions. Helps child manage change-related stress. MANIFESTATION 7: Requesting unscented products only Physical Redirection: "Unscented First, Scented Later": In situations where unscented unavailable, allow child to use unscented version of different product first (unscented soap instead of scented shampoo). Partial accommodation while building flexibility.
DIY Alternative: Stock Unscented Options: Keep unscented versions of all products child uses. Makes preference easy to honor at home. Alternative Stimulation: Honor the preference: Unscented products widely available This is reasonable accommodation Use unscented: soaps, shampoos, detergents, lotions Lightly scented bridge: If child must use scented product (school soap, restaurant bathroom): Start with very lightly scented options "Free & clear" products have minimal scent DIY unscented: Make own products: castile soap + water (unscented) Baking soda + coconut oil (deodorant) Simple, unscented alternatives OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Scent Exposure Hierarchy: Level 1: Unscented only (current) Level 2: Very lightly scented product on hand only (not near face) Level 3: Lightly scented product on arms Level 4: Lightly scented product on body (not face)
Level 5: Lightly scented product on face (wash off quickly) Over months/years, may build tolerance Emergency Scented Product Plan: Practice using scented products (when unscented unavailable) In low-stress situations first Builds confidence that "I CAN handle it if needed" Preference vs. Need Assessment: Is unscented truly necessary or preferred? Practice occasionally using lightly scented to prove tolerance exists May reduce rigid insistence Sensory Integration: Olfactory Desensitization: Gradual exposure to mild scents. May reduce hypersensitivity over time, making scented products more tolerable. Massage: Massage With Unscented Oil: Provide massage using unscented carrier oil. Positive association with touch may eventually allow scented massage oils. MANIFESTATION 8: Distress in areas with multiple competing scents Physical Redirection: "Exit and Reset": When distress begins in multi-scent environment, immediately exit. Go to fresh air. Deep breathing. Then return for shorter duration. Prevents full meltdown while building tolerance incrementally.
DIY Alternative: Sensory Rescue Kit for Outings: Small bag containing: mask with preferred scent, essential oil roller, mints (provides competing smell from inside mouth), earplugs (reduces total sensory load), sunglasses (reduces visual input, making smells easier to tolerate). Alternative Stimulation: Single strong preferred scent: When in multi-scent environment, smell one strong preferred scent Dominates olfactory system, masks multiple competing smells Essential oil on cotton ball, strongly scented lip balm, etc. Mouth breathing + mint: Breathe through mouth (reduces smell detection) Suck on strong mint (provides internal competing smell) Combination significantly reduces external smell impact Limit time in challenging environments: Quick shopping trips (in and out) Off-peak times (fewer people = fewer perfumes/scents) Online shopping when possible OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders:
Graduated Exposure to Multi-Sensory Environments: Week 1: Enter store, stay 2 minutes, leave Week 2: Stay 5 minutes Week 3: Stay 10 minutes Very gradual exposure builds tolerance Always have exit plan Competing Scent Training: Practice using preferred scent to mask others Experiment with which scents work best as masks Build skill in managing multi-scent environments Sensory Load Management: Multi-scent environments are overwhelming because total sensory load is high (smells + sounds + lights + people) Reduce other sensory input: Wear sunglasses (reduces visual) Wear noise-canceling headphones (reduces auditory) Hold parent's hand (provides grounding) When other inputs reduced, smells more manageable Pre-Outing Preparation: Before challenging environments: Discuss what to expect Review coping strategies Set realistic time limit Plan reward for successful navigation
Heavy sensory input (proprioceptive, deep pressure) before leaving Sensory Integration: Multi-Sensory Integration: Often overwhelm in complex environments is multi-sensory, not just olfactory. Comprehensive sensory diet addressing all systems may reduce overall sensitivity. Massage: Pre and Post-Outing Massage: Before challenging outings: 10 min calming massage. After: 15 min regulating massage. Supports nervous system before and after stress.
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 7. OLFACTORY STIMMING > B. Smell Avoidance/Defensive Stimming > Level 2: Scent Avoidance Behaviors
Causation: Over-stimulated: Smells trigger nausea, headaches, or sensory overload Sensitive: Severe olfactory defensiveness; smells neurologically painful Anxiety: Fear of encountering overwhelming scents Medical: Possible migraines triggered by scents; heightened during hormonal changes Control: Need to control olfactory environment completely Sensory Profile: Extreme Avoider: Severe olfactory defensiveness affecting daily function Medical: May experience physical symptoms (nausea, headaches) from scents Protective: Behaviors prevent sensory overload meltdowns Description: Actively avoiding or escaping smell stimuli MANIFESTATION 1: Leaving rooms due to cooking smells Physical Redirection: "Three-Breath Challenge": Before leaving room, child must take three deep breaths through mouth while staying. Count together. If still intolerable after three breaths, may leave. Often tolerance improves during breathing. DIY Alternative: Scent-Filtered Air Supply: Set up fan in child's area that pulls air from outside or different room. Creates personal air stream that doesn't contain cooking smells.
Alternative Stimulation: Preferred scent in personal space: Essential oil diffuser in child's room running during cooking times Creates strong competing scent in child's space May allow staying in general home area even if avoiding kitchen Warning and ventilation: Announce cooking 15 minutes before starting Child goes to room, closes door, turns on air purifier Kitchen exhaust fan and windows open Minimizes smell spread Cooking schedule: Cook at predictable times daily Child plans activities elsewhere during those times Routine reduces surprise and anxiety OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Cooking Smell Hierarchy: Create list of cooking smells from least to most bothersome: Example: baking cookies (least) → frying fish (most) Gradually expose to smells in hierarchy order Start with briefest exposure to least bothersome
Over months, work up hierarchy Positive Cooking Experiences: Find foods child likes the smell of (cinnamon rolls, popcorn, baking cookies) Cook these regularly Builds positive associations with cooking smells May generalize to other cooking smells Gradual Duration Increase: Week 1: Stay in home (not kitchen) during cooking for 2 minutes Week 2: Stay 5 minutes Week 3: Stay 10 minutes Very slow tolerance building Participation Reduces Aversion: When child helps cook, they control experience Know what smells to expect Builds ownership and tolerance Start with pleasant-smelling foods Sensory Integration: Olfactory Desensitization: Systematic graduated exposure to cooking smells under OT guidance. May reduce hypersensitivity over time. Massage: Pre-Meal Routine: Before dinner cooking time, provide 10-minute calming massage. Helps child enter high-smell time in calm state.
MANIFESTATION 2: Refusing to go to specific locations (restaurants, stores) due to scent Physical Redirection: "Quick Visit First": Before full visit, do brief exposure (drive by, walk to entrance but don't enter, enter for 1 minute). Builds familiarity and proves tolerance possible. Then attempt longer visit. DIY Alternative: Scent Survival Kit for Outings: Pack small bag: mask with preferred scent drops, essential oil roller for temples/upper lip, strong mints, stress ball, comfort item. Having tools readily available increases willingness to attempt. Alternative Stimulation: Location alternatives: Some restaurants/stores are less scented than others Choose locations with better ventilation, outdoor seating, minimal artificial scent Build tolerance in easier environments first Timing strategy: Visit during off-peak times (fewer people = fewer perfumes/colognes) Cooler weather (windows open = better ventilation)
Right after opening (smells not built up yet) Advance preparation: Call ahead: ask about ventilation, scented products used Request outdoor seating, table by door/window Some accommodations possible if requested OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Graduated Exposure Program: Week 1: Drive past location daily (exposure with no pressure) Week 2: Park in lot, look at building Week 3: Walk to entrance Week 4: Enter for 30 seconds (already knowing you'll leave) Week 5: Enter for 1 minute Week 6+: Gradually increase duration May take months but builds real tolerance Competing Motivation: Choose locations child really WANTS to go to Favorite restaurant, store with desired item Motivation helps overcome discomfort Start with highly-desired locations Success-Based Approach: Set very achievable goals "We're going in for 2 minutes. If you make it 2 minutes, you succeeded!"
Heavy reinforcement for attempting Build confidence through small successes Location Familiarization: Look at photos of location online Discuss what to expect Plan route through store Familiarity reduces anxiety, increases tolerance Sensory Integration: Total Sensory Load Reduction: Often location avoidance is about total sensory overwhelm, not just smell. Reduce other inputs: Sunglasses for visual overwhelm Headphones for auditory overwhelm Hold hand for grounding Makes smells more manageable when other inputs controlled Massage: Pre-Outing Calming Protocol: Before challenging outings, 15-minute deep pressure massage routine. Creates calm baseline that makes tolerating sensory challenges easier. MANIFESTATION 3: Holding breath when passing scented areas Physical Redirection: "Mouth Breathing Walk": When approaching scented area, start mouth breathing before reaching it. Practice: "Breathe through mouth, walk through, keep mouth breathing." Models and cues appropriate response.
DIY Alternative: "Breath Break" Training: Teach that holding breath is temporary solution only. Practice: take deep breath through mouth, hold 5 seconds while walking through scented area, resume normal (mouth) breathing. Prevents prolonged breath-holding which can cause dizziness. Alternative Stimulation: Scented handkerchief: Small cloth with preferred scent Hold to nose while passing scented area Breathe preferred scent instead of ambient scent Strong mint: Suck on peppermint while walking through scented area Provides internal competing scent Allows normal breathing Quick passage: Move quickly through scented areas Minimizes exposure time Less need for breath-holding OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Breathing Technique Training: Practice mouth breathing in non-challenging situations first Build automatic mouth-breathing response Apply in challenging situations once skilled Scent Tolerance Intervals: Practice tolerating scented area for increasing durations:
Week 1: Walk through quickly (3 seconds exposure) Week 2: Walk through slowly (5 seconds) Week 3: Pause in area for 2 seconds Gradual exposure builds tolerance Alternative Coping Strategies: Since breath-holding is unsustainable, teach alternatives: Mouth breathing Shallow breathing Holding scented item to nose Multiple options beyond breath-holding Sensory Integration: Respiratory Calming: Teach diaphragmatic breathing for general calming. Well-regulated nervous system tolerates smells better. Massage: Chest and Diaphragm Massage: Gentle massage to chest, ribs, upper abdomen (diaphragm area). May reduce breath-holding tendency by creating respiratory awareness. MANIFESTATION 4: Breathing through mouth exclusively to avoid smells Physical Redirection: "Gradual Nose Breathing": In low-smell environments, practice brief nose breathing: "Breathe through nose for 3 breaths, then mouth breathing is okay." Very gradual tolerance building.
DIY Alternative: "Nose Breathing Times": Designate specific safe times/places for nose breathing: outdoors in fresh air, child's own room, morning before anyone else awake. Builds nose-breathing habit in safe contexts. Alternative Stimulation: Acceptance approach: If mouth breathing allows function without distress, it's adaptive strategy May not need to change Focus on building tolerance in specific situations only Preferred scent exposure: When smelling scents child loves, practice nose breathing "This smells good! Let's smell it through our nose."
