Builds positive nose-breathing associations Respiratory health education: Teach about nose filtering/warming air Benefits of nose breathing for health May motivate working toward nose breathing OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Scent-Free Environment Nose Breathing: Practice nose breathing in environments with minimal scent Outdoors in nature, child's room with air purifier
Build nose-breathing skill/comfort May eventually transfer to more scented environments Olfactory Desensitization: Systematic exposure to mild scents while nose breathing Very gradual Start with barely-detectable pleasant scents Over months, increase intensity "Smell Check" Routine: Several times daily, child does brief nose breathing to "check" for smells If tolerable, continues; if not, returns to mouth breathing Builds awareness and flexibility Sensory Integration: General Sensory Desensitization: Often olfactory hypersensitivity part of larger sensory processing differences. Comprehensive OT addressing all systems may reduce olfactory defensiveness. Massage: Facial and Nasal Massage: Gentle massage around nose, sinuses. May reduce olfactory sensitivity over time, making nose breathing more tolerable. MANIFESTATION 5: Wearing masks or covering nose constantly Physical Redirection: "Mask Schedule": Create schedule for mask wearing: "Mask on in public, mask off at home in your room, mask optional in car." Provides structure rather than constant wearing.
DIY Alternative: Discrete Scent Barrier: Use discrete alternatives to obvious mask: scarf that can cover nose, high collar shirt, bandana. Provides protection while being less obvious socially. Alternative Stimulation: Scented mask: Add preferred scent to inside of mask Turns barrier into pleasant smell experience May be willing to remove occasionally if mask provides good smell Gradual mask fading: Start with mask always Week 5: Remove mask in car Week 10: Remove in home common areas Week 15: Remove in low-scent public spaces Very gradual reduction Alternative barriers: High turtleneck (can pull up over nose when needed) Scarf (pull up as needed) Gives control without constant obvious mask OT Activities: For Sensory Avoiders: Function Analysis: Why mask needed? Protection from overwhelming smells? Anxiety? Both?
Protection need: work on olfactory desensitization Anxiety: work on anxiety management Different interventions based on function Safe Spaces Without Mask: Identify spaces child feels safe without mask Practice mask-free time in these spaces Gradually expand mask-free zones Social Skills Around Mask: In current world, masks less stigmatized But teach child to explain if asked: "I'm sensitive to smells. The mask helps." Builds self-advocacy Mask Dependence Assessment: Is mask actually needed or has it become habitual? Experiment with mask removal in low-scent situations May discover more tolerance than expected Sensory Integration: Comprehensive Sensory Diet: If relying heavily on mask, indicates significant olfactory sensitivity. Need OT program addressing sensory processing globally. Massage: Face Massage for Desensitization: Regular facial massage may reduce sensitivity around nose/mouth area. Over time, may reduce need for constant barrier.
Manifestations: Opening windows regardless of weather-not available Refusing foods based solely on smell (won't try)-not available Distress from perfumes, lotions, or scented products on others-not available
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 7. OLFACTORY STIMMING > B. Smell Avoidance/Defensive Stimming > Level 3: Severe Olfactory Avoidance
Causation: Over-stimulated: Severe olfactory over-responsiveness; smell causes pain Sensitive: Extreme olfactory processing disorder Medical: Olfactory hypersensitivity; possible migraines or neurological condition Trauma: Previous severe reaction to smell creating phobia Anxiety: Scent-triggered panic disorder Sensory Profile: Crisis-Level Avoider: Smell triggers fight-or-flight response Medical Concern: Requires occupational therapy and/or medical evaluation Functional Impact: Scent avoidance severely limits activities and social participation Description: Extreme reactions to smell stimuli Manifestations: Vomiting from certain smells Panic attacks triggered by scents Refusal to enter buildings with "smell history" Complete avoidance of certain places (restaurants, stores, schools) Extreme reactions to body odors or natural smells Inability to tolerate family members using scented products Meltdowns triggered by unexpected smells Functional limitations from scent avoidance
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 8. INTEROCEPTIVE STIMMING
(Internal Body Sensations)
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 8. INTEROCEPTIVE STIMMING > A. Body Function Awareness Stimming > Level 1: Breathing Manipulation
Causation: Over-stimulated: Controlled breathing provides regulation and calming Under-stimulated: Noticing and controlling breath provides interoceptive input Sensitivity: Exploring respiratory system sensations Anxiety: Breath control reduces anxiety and panic Awareness: Poor interoceptive awareness; focusing on breath builds connection Sensory Profile: Seeker: Experimenting with varied breathing patterns for sensation Regulator: Using breath control for emotional/physiological regulation Anxious: Breath manipulation to manage anxiety or panic Description: Consciously altering breathing patterns Manifestations: Holding breath for extended periods (10-60+ seconds repeatedly) Hyperventilating intentionally (rapid breathing) Deep breathing exercises obsessively Panting or rapid shallow breathing patterns Sighing excessively (10-50+ times per hour) Breathing through mouth only or nose only exclusively Creating breathing rhythms (count-based patterns) Making breathing sounds audible deliberately
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 8. INTEROCEPTIVE STIMMING > A. Body Function Awareness Stimming > Level 2: Heart Rate and Circulation Awareness
Description: Focusing on cardiovascular sensations Causation: Over-stimulated: Heart rate awareness provides tangible focus during anxiety Under-stimulated: Poor interoceptive awareness; monitoring to build connection Sensitivity: Exploring cardiovascular system consciously Anxiety: Health anxiety about heart function Regulation: Using heart rate as biofeedback for emotional state Sensory Profile: Seeker: Actively seeks experiences that alter heart rate to feel difference Anxious: Checking heart function compulsively due to health anxiety Interoceptive Builder: Developing awareness of internal body sensations Manifestations: Checking pulse repeatedly (20-100+ times daily) Listening to own heartbeat excessively Seeking activities that elevate heart rate then monitoring Pressing on chest to feel heartbeat Becoming anxious about heart rate or rhythm Lying still to notice heartbeat sensations Changing position to affect blood flow sensation (head rush)
Noticing and commenting on pulse in different body parts
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 8. INTEROCEPTIVE STIMMING > A. Body Function Awareness Stimming > Level 3: Digestive and Elimination Focus
Description: Heightened awareness of digestive/elimination processes Causation: Over-stimulated: Focusing on internal sensations as distraction from external overwhelm Under-stimulated: Poor interoceptive awareness; difficulty reading body signals Sensitivity: Heightened awareness of internal sensations Anxiety: Health anxiety focused on digestive system Medical: Possible GI issues causing heightened awareness Sensory Profile: Over-Aware: Hypersensitive to internal sensations; may over-report issues Under-Aware: Difficulty reading signals; may have accidents or miss hunger cues Anxious: Digestive anxiety interfering with function Manifestations: Excessive focus on hunger and fullness sensations Monitoring bowel/bladder sensations constantly Delayed bathroom use despite awareness (holding) Compulsive bathroom visits (checking) Noticing digestive sounds and sensations excessively Anxiety about digestive processes Over-reporting stomach aches or nausea Restrictive eating due to digestive awareness
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 8. INTEROCEPTIVE STIMMING > B. Pain and Temperature Stimming > Level 1: Temperature Seeking
Description: Seeking hot or cold sensations Causation: Over-stimulated: Extreme temperatures provide organizing "reset" Under-stimulated: Temperature receptors under-responsive; needs extreme input Sensitivity: Exploring thermal sensations Regulation: Temperature changes affect physiological arousal Pain Threshold: May not accurately sense dangerous temperatures Sensory Profile: Seeker: Actively seeks extreme temperatures for stimulation Under-Responsive: Doesn't feel typical temperature ranges; needs extreme Danger: May not respond to pain from temperature; risk of burns or frostbite Manifestations: Seeking very hot showers or baths (potentially unsafe temperatures) Playing with ice excessively (holding, sucking, rubbing on skin) Preference for very cold or very hot foods/drinks Seeking cold floors or surfaces to lie on Wrapping in heavy blankets even when hot Putting hands in cold water repeatedly Seeking heating pads or warmth sources constantly
Alternating between hot and cold sensations
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 8. INTEROCEPTIVE STIMMING > B. Pain and Temperature Stimming > Level 2: Pain Seeking
Description: Engaging in potentially painful activities Causation: Over-stimulated: Intense sensation can paradoxically calm overwhelmed system Under-stimulated: High pain threshold; typical pain sensations don't register Sensitivity: Under-responsive pain system; needs intense input to feel Endorphin: Pain may trigger endorphin release providing reward Danger: May not recognize harmful situations; poor safety awareness Sensory Profile: Extreme Seeker: High pain threshold; appears "doesn't feel pain" Under-Responsive: Delayed or absent pain response; safety concern Self-Injurious: Requires intervention if causing significant harm Manifestations: Seeking deep pressure that others find painful Engaging in "rough play" seeking impact Biting self or others hard Picking at skin until bleeding Seeking spicy/painful foods excessively Enjoying physical sensations others avoid (intense massage) Not reacting to injuries (cuts, bruises, burns) Seeking activities that result in falls or impacts
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 8. INTEROCEPTIVE STIMMING > B. Pain and Temperature Stimming > Level 3: Pain Avoidance/Hypersensitivity
Description: Extreme sensitivity to pain sensations Causation: Over-stimulated: Pain sensations amplified; neurologically painful Sensitive: Hyperalgesia (heightened pain sensitivity) Anxiety: Fear of pain limits activities Past Trauma: Previous painful experiences create fear Medical: Possible underlying pain disorders (fibromyalgia, etc.) Sensory Profile: Avoider: Extreme pain sensitivity; minor stimuli cause significant pain Medical Concern: May require pain management evaluation Functional Impact: Pain sensitivity limits daily activities Manifestations: Crying from minor bumps or touches Refusing activities due to fear of pain Excessive reaction to medical procedures (shots, blood draws) Over-reporting pain from minimal causes Refusing to wear certain clothes (seams hurt, tags hurt) Extreme distress from hair brushing or grooming Avoiding playground due to fear of injury Panic from dental work or medical exams
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 9. COMPLEX/MULTI-SENSORY STIMMING > A. Combined Sensory Stimming > Level 1: Two-System Combinations
Description: Stimming engaging two sensory systems simultaneously Causation: Over-stimulated: Multiple inputs create powerful organizing effect Under-stimulated: Combination provides richer sensory experience Sensitivity: Integrating sensory systems through simultaneous input Regulation: Multiple systems engaged = stronger regulatory effect Preference: Neurologically prefers combined sensory experiences Sensory Profile: Multi-Sensory Seeker: Naturally combines inputs for maximum effect Integrated: Good sensory integration allows smooth multi-sensory processing Efficient: Uses multiple systems simultaneously for faster regulation Manifestations: Visual + Auditory: Watching spinning fan while humming Tactile + Proprioceptive: Squeezing playdough while pressing hard Vestibular + Visual: Spinning while watching hands flutter Oral + Tactile: Chewing while rubbing soft fabric Auditory + Proprioceptive: Making vocal sounds while jumping Visual + Tactile: Watching fingers touch different textures Olfactory + Tactile: Smelling and touching same object repeatedly
Vestibular + Proprioceptive: Rocking while hugging self tightly
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 9. COMPLEX/MULTI-SENSORY STIMMING > A. Combined Sensory Stimming > Level 2: Three+ System Combinations
Description: Complex stimming engaging multiple sensory systems Causation: Over-stimulated: Complex multi-sensory input provides maximum organization Under-stimulated: Severe under-responsiveness requires multiple intense inputs Sensitivity: Building sensory integration through rich experiences Regulation: Maximum regulatory effect from engaging many systems Whole-body: Preference for whole-body sensory experiences Sensory Profile: Extreme Seeker: Needs maximum sensory input from multiple sources Integration Builder: Developing sensory integration through complex experiences Intense Regulator: Requires intense multi-sensory input to achieve regulation Manifestations: Visual + Auditory + Vestibular: Spinning while humming and watching lights blur Tactile + Proprioceptive + Oral: Chewing while squeezing and pressing hard Visual + Tactile + Olfactory: Watching, touching, and smelling same object Vestibular + Proprioceptive + Auditory: Jumping while making loud sounds and seeking heavy landing Multiple systems during activities: Dancing involves visual (watching movement), vestibular (spinning), proprioceptive (muscle use), auditory (music)
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 9. COMPLEX/MULTI-SENSORY STIMMING > B. Ritualistic and Patterned Stimming > Level 1: Simple Routines
Description: Repetitive patterns with sensory components Causation: Over-stimulated: Routines provide predictability reducing anxiety Under-stimulated: Pattern provides cognitive + sensory stimulation Sensitivity: Need for predictability and control OCD Features: Compulsive need to complete pattern Regulation: Routine provides organization and security Sensory Profile: Control-Seeker: Needs predictability; routines provide security Pattern-Focused: Cognitive satisfaction from patterns + sensory input Anxious: Routines reduce anxiety about unpredictable environment Manifestations: Touching objects in specific sequence (door, wall, chair - repeat) Walking same path repeatedly (around furniture, specific routes) Organizing/reorganizing objects in patterns Repeating phrases while performing actions Specific bedtime routines with sensory elements Morning routines that must be identical daily Eating foods in specific order every time Touching body parts in sequence repeatedly
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 9. COMPLEX/MULTI-SENSORY STIMMING > B. Ritualistic and Patterned Stimming > Level 2: Complex Rituals
Description: Elaborate sequences with multiple sensory elements Causation: Over-stimulated: Complex rituals provide maximum control and organization Under-stimulated: Elaborate routines provide sustained sensory/cognitive input Sensitivity: Severe need for predictability and order OCD: Clinical OCD may be present; compulsive rituals Anxiety: Rituals prevent overwhelming uncertainty Sensory Profile: Extreme Control-Seeker: Cannot function without rituals OCD Features: Compulsive completion; distress if interrupted Functional Impact: Rituals significantly impact daily schedule Manifestations: Multi-step routines involving various sensory inputs (touch 5 things, spin twice, hum specific tune, jump three times) Elaborate bedtime rituals taking 30-90+ minutes Food preparation rituals (specific arrangement, order, tools) Transition rituals between activities Social interaction rituals (specific greetings, handshakes) Cleaning/organizing rituals with specific steps Morning routines requiring 1-2 hours "Checking" rituals for reassurance (doors locked, items in place)
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 9. COMPLEX/MULTI-SENSORY STIMMING > B. Ritualistic and Patterned Stimming > Level 3: Rigid Routines with Meltdown Risk
Description: Inflexible patterns causing distress if disrupted Causation: Over-stimulated: Routines are only source of control; disruption unbearable Under-stimulated: Rituals provide essential sensory organization Sensitivity: Extreme rigidity; can't adapt to change OCD: Severe OCD requiring treatment Anxiety: Severe anxiety disorder; rituals are compulsive safety behaviors Autism: Rigidity common in autism; resistance to change Sensory Profile: Crisis-Level: Routine disruption triggers severe dysregulation Clinical Concern: Requires behavioral therapy and/or medication Functional Impact: Rigidity severely limits flexibility and participation Manifestations: Meltdowns if routine varies even slightly Hours-long rituals interfering with daily life Inability to transition without specific ritual Distress lasting hours after routine disruption Aggressive responses to routine interruption Refusing activities if routine can't be completed Family members required to participate in rituals Complete shutdown if unexpected change occurs
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 9. COMPLEX/MULTI-SENSORY STIMMING > C. Social and Interactive Stimming > Level 1: Social Sensory-Seeking
Causation: Over-stimulated: Social touch provides organizing input Under-stimulated: Seeking proprioceptive/tactile input through social contact Sensitivity: Social interaction provides multi-sensory experience Connection: Sensory-seeking AND social connection simultaneously Misunderstanding: May not understand social boundaries around touch Sensory Profile: Social Seeker: Uses relationships for sensory satisfaction Tactile Seeker: Primarily seeking touch; social element secondary Boundary Challenges: Difficulty understanding personal space rules Understanding Social Sensory Profiles Social Sensory Seekers - Simple Indicators: Constantly seeking hugs, touch, physical contact Gets very close to people (no personal space awareness) Touches others frequently (hair, clothes, skin) Loves rough play, wrestling, tickling Seeks out social situations for physical aspect Always wants to be near or touching someone Climbs on people, pushes against them High-fives everyone repeatedly Social Sensory Avoiders - Simple Indicators:
Avoids hugs, physical contact Needs significant personal space Uncomfortable when people get close Doesn't like being touched unexpectedly Prefers parallel play over interactive play Backs away when people approach Stiffens during hugs or touch Prefers playing alone Description: Using social interaction for sensory input Manifestation 1: Seeking Hugs or Physical Contact Frequently (10-50+ Per Day) Physical Redirect Technique: When child approaches for yet another hug, receive the hug warmly but briefly (3 seconds). As hug ends, place hands on child's shoulders, make eye contact and say "That was a good hug. Now your body needs different input. Let's do wall push-ups together." Guide them to wall, do 10 push-ups together. This satisfies touch need appropriately while transitioning to proprioceptive input. DIY Alternative Tool: Hug Schedule and Alternatives:
Hug tokens: Create 10 cardstock circles with hearts on them. Child gets 10 "hug tokens" per day. When wants hug, gives token. When tokens gone, use hug alternatives instead. Hug timer: Set specific "hug times" (every hour on the hour, child gets 1 hug). Between times, use alternatives. Hug pillow: Large body pillow or weighted stuffed animal (3-5 lbs) child can hug anytime. Sew tight pillowcase that provides resistance when hugged. Self-hug vest: Cut bottom off compression shirt, child wears as vest providing ongoing hug sensation. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Compression wraps: Wrap child firmly in blanket (burrito roll), leave for 5 minutes - provides hug-like pressure Weighted lap pad: 3-5 lb lap pad provides pressure sensation similar to hugging, use during seated activities
Therapy ball squeezes: Hug large therapy ball or beach ball tightly, squeeze hard 10 times Pillow sandwich: Child lies between two couch cushions, adult presses top cushion down firmly for 1 minute Self-hugging: Teach child to hug themselves tightly (wrap arms around own body, squeeze 10 seconds, release, repeat 5 times) Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Scheduled hug times: Set specific hug times throughout day (8am, 12pm, 3pm, 6pm, bedtime) - child knows when hugs are coming, reduces random seeking Deep pressure alternatives: Between hugs, provide deep pressure through weighted vest (wear 20 minutes 3x daily), weighted blanket, compression clothing Partner activities: Activities involving appropriate physical contact (partner yoga, dance class, martial arts) - socially appropriate touch Appropriate touch games: "Red Light Green Light" with high-fives, handshake games, back-pat games - structures touch socially
For Avoiders: Hug warnings: Always warn before hugs "May I give you a hug?" Wait for consent Side hugs only: Offer side hugs or shoulder squeezes instead of full frontal hugs - less overwhelming Handshakes/high-fives: Use these instead of hugs - briefer, less intense touch Child controls duration: Child decides when hug ends, respects their tolerance Massage Techniques: 15-minute deep pressure massage routine: Morning and evening, comprehensive deep pressure massage - may reduce hug-seeking throughout day Self-massage teaching: Teach child to give themselves arm squeezes, shoulder presses, leg compression - empowers self-regulation Hug substitute massage: When child seeks hug, offer "Would you like a quick back massage instead?" (2-3 minutes firm pressure massage) Pressure point focus: Massage shoulders, upper back where hugs provide pressure, 5-7 minutes
Social Skills Integration: Counting hugs: Help child become aware of frequency "You've asked for 8 hugs this hour. Let's try hug alternatives now." Appropriate vs. inappropriate: Teach which people appropriate to hug (family, close friends with permission) vs. inappropriate (strangers, acquaintances, teachers without permission) Alternative greetings: Teach variety of greetings - wave, high-five, fist bump, thumbs up - not always hugs Reading social cues: Teach child to notice if person leans away, stiffens, or looks uncomfortable - signs hug not welcome Manifestation 2: Standing Very Close to People (Violating Personal Space) Physical Redirect Technique: When child is standing too close to someone, approach from behind, place hand gently on their shoulder and say "[Name], let's check your space." Guide them to take 2 steps backward. Use visual: "You should be able to extend your arms and not touch the person." Have them extend arms to check distance. Practice this distance awareness repeatedly.
DIY Alternative Tool: Personal Space Teaching Tools: Hula hoop personal space: Child wears hula hoop around waist (or holds in front) - visual representation of personal space bubble. Practice walking near others without hoop touching them. Arm's length rule: Paint or mark child's arms with washable marker at wrist. Teach "If you extend your arm and your mark touches someone, you're too close." Floor tape markers: In common spaces (kitchen, living room), use colored tape to mark "standing spots" with appropriate distance between them. Personal space mat: Small carpet square or mat (2x2 feet) child stands on - teaches "this is my space, that person has their space too." Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Proprioceptive input before social situations: Before social settings, 10 minutes heavy work (carrying, pushing, pulling) - helps child feel where their body is in space
Weighted backpack: Child wears backpack with 2-3 lbs of books during social situations - provides body awareness reducing space invasion Large stuffed animal carry: During social times, child carries large stuffed animal - creates physical barrier maintaining appropriate distance Visual boundaries: Use furniture, rugs, or objects to create visual boundaries showing where to stand Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Body awareness activities: Activities building sense of where body is in space (obstacle courses, crawling through tunnels, moving in tight spaces) Spatial games: "How close can you get without touching?" games - builds spatial awareness Mirror practice: Practice standing at appropriate distances in front of mirror - visual feedback Proprioceptive loading: Heavy work before social situations (wall push-ups, carrying heavy items) helps child feel body boundaries
For Avoiders: Large personal space: Allow child to maintain larger personal space than typical - respects their needs Warning when approaching: Always announce yourself before getting close "I'm going to stand next to you now" Side-by-side not face-to-face: Stand beside child rather than directly facing - less threatening Escape routes: Ensure child always has clear path to move away if feeling crowded Massage Techniques: Body boundary massage: Massage outlining child's body boundaries (massage along arms, legs, sides) building awareness of where body ends and space begins, 10 minutes Proprioceptive emphasis: Deep pressure massage on all body parts helping child "feel" their whole body, 15 minutes Pre-social massage: Before social situations, 5-minute focused massage on shoulders, arms, back - increases body awareness
Spatial massage game: Massage child while they lie with arms/legs extended - helps them feel their full spatial extent Social Skills Integration: Social stories: Create story with pictures showing appropriate distances for different situations (talking to friend = arm's length, waiting in line = 2 feet, sitting on bus = personal seat) Distance categories: Teach different distances for different relationships: Strangers: 4+ feet Acquaintances: 2-4 feet Friends: 1-2 feet Family: Closer okay with permission Practice scenarios: Role-play various social situations practicing appropriate distances Video feedback: Record child in social situations, watch together noticing distances Manifestation 3: Touching Others' Hair, Clothing, or Skin Physical Redirect Technique: When child reaches to touch someone's hair/clothing, gently intercept hand mid-air. Say "[Name], we use words not touch. If you like [their hair/shirt], say 'I like your hair' instead." Guide their hand back to their side or into their own lap. Redirect to appropriate touch: "You can touch your own hair" or "Let's feel this soft blanket instead."
DIY Alternative Tool: Touch Alternatives System: Texture basket: Create basket filled with various textures (fur fabric, silk, rough burlap, soft fleece, ribbons, feathers). When child wants to touch someone's hair/clothes, redirect to texture basket. Personal texture book: Make small book with different textured fabric swatches glued on each page. Child can carry and touch anytime. Fidget jewelry: Make bracelet or necklace with interesting textures (beads, soft fabric, smooth stones) child can touch their own jewelry instead of others. Touch cards: Cards showing ✓ (okay to touch: own items, offered items, pets with permission) and ✗ (not okay: other people's bodies, hair, clothing without permission). Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Hair alternatives: Doll with long hair child can brush, braid, style anytime Yarn "hair" attached to dowel rod (make simple yarn doll)
Their own hair - teach self-soothing through playing with own hair Hairbrush with soft bristles to use on own head Fabric alternatives: "Sensory square" - 6-inch square of favorite fabric texture child carries Soft scarf or piece of fleece to rub Velvet pillowcase or fabric child can stroke Fidget with fabric tags sewn on Skin alternatives: Lotion application - rub lotion on own arms provides skin touch sensation Silly putty, therapy dough to squeeze and manipulate Massage ball child rolls on own skin Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Scheduled touch time: Specific times daily (morning, after school, bedtime) child gets to play with different textures for 10-15 minutes Tactile exploration bins: Create bins with different materials (rice, beans, water beads, sand) child digs hands into and explores
Art with texture: Painting, finger painting, playdough, clay work - provides intense tactile input Self-care activities: Hair washing/brushing (own hair), lotion application, face washing - appropriate tactile self-stimulation For Avoiders: Minimize unexpected touch: Warn before any touch "I'm going to touch your arm now" Tolerate observation: Child can look at but not touch interesting textures Gradual exposure: If working on texture tolerance, very slow gentle introduction with child in control Respect boundaries: If child doesn't want to touch, don't force Massage Techniques: Hand and arm focus: Deep massage of hands and arms (areas wanting to reach and touch), 5-7 minutes each arm - may reduce seeking Textured massage tools: Use different massage tools (bumpy ball, textured roller, soft brush) during massage - provides tactile variety
Palm and finger massage: Thorough massage of palms and each finger, 5 minutes each hand - gives hands the tactile input they seek Self-massage teaching: Teach child to massage own hands, arms - empowers appropriate touch Social Skills Integration: Touch hierarchy teaching: GREEN (okay anytime): Own body, own belongings, offered items YELLOW (ask first): Pets, family members, friends RED (never without permission): Strangers, other people's bodies/belongings "Look with eyes" rule: Teach "When you see something interesting, look with your eyes and tell them with words 'I like your hair!'" Permission teaching: Role-play asking permission "May I touch your sweater? It looks soft" and accepting "No" gracefully Substitute phrases: Teach verbal alternatives: Instead of touching someone's soft hair, say "Your hair looks so soft!"
Social stories: Create story showing child that touching others without permission makes them uncomfortable (include faces showing emotions) Manifestation 4: Seeking Rough Play with Peers or Adults (wrestling, tickling) Physical Redirect Technique: When child is getting too rough during play, immediately say "Stop! Gentle freeze!" Everyone freezes in position. Say "[Name], your body is being too rough. Let's do strong pushing the right way." Guide them to push against wall (wall push-ups 10 times) or push against your hands (resistance game). Then may return to play with reminder "Gentle bodies with friends." DIY Alternative Tool: Rough Play Alternatives: Push wall station: Mark spot on wall with tape and hand outlines. When child needs rough play, send to "push wall spot" - push as hard as possible 10 times.
Resistance band play: Adult holds one end of resistance band, child pulls other end - provides rough play sensation safely. Pilllow fight boundaries: Designate specific time/place for supervised pillow fights with clear rules (no hitting faces, stop means stop, soft pillows only). Rough play token system: Child gets 3 "rough play" tokens per day. Each token = 10 minutes supervised rough play. When tokens gone, gentle play only. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Crash pad wrestling: Stack 6-8 couch cushions, child crashes into them, wrestles with them, pushes them around Pillow obstacles: Create course using pillows child pushes, climbs over, tunnels through Furniture pushing: Assign child to push heavy furniture (ottoman, chairs on carpet) - satisfies rough play need through work Tug-of-war: Play tug-of-war with towel or rope - provides rough play with clear rules and structure
Body sock wrestling: Child gets in body sock (tight lycra), wrestles to get out - intense proprioceptive input Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Structured rough play times: Schedule 15-20 minutes 2x daily for supervised rough play with clear rules Martial arts/wrestling class: Enroll in class teaching rough play appropriately with rules, respect, and supervision Heavy work circuit: Instead of rough play with people, intense physical work (push-ups, carrying, animal walks) 15 minutes 3x daily Crash and bang activities: Jumping into crash pad, breaking down cardboard boxes, pounding playdough - rough activities on objects not people For Avoiders: No rough play: Avoid all rough play and physically intense games Gentle activities: Board games, art, reading, building - calm activities Communicate boundaries: Teach child to say "No rough play, please" when others approach
Safe spaces: Provide areas where child can play knowing no rough play will occur Massage Techniques: Deep tissue sports massage: Provide intensity child seeks through deep, firm massage, 20 minutes Joint compressions: Firmly compress each major joint 10 seconds - intense proprioceptive input satisfying rough play need Resistive massage: Child pushes against massage (isometric) while receiving deep pressure Impact massage: Using massage tools or fists, pound lightly on large muscle groups (thighs, back) - controlled impact sensation Social Skills Integration: Rough play rules teaching: Always ask "Want to rough play?" before starting Stop immediately when anyone says "Stop" No hitting faces, necks, private areas Only rough play with people who said yes Rough play only in designated safe areas Intensity monitoring: Teach child to check in "Is this too rough?" during play
Gentle touch teaching: Practice and reinforce gentle touch: gentle high-fives, gentle hugs, gentle tags Reading reactions: Teach child to notice if play partner looks uncomfortable, hurt, or scared - signs to stop or gentle down Alternative outlets: If friend doesn't want rough play, what are alternatives? (Crash into pillows, do push-ups, play tug-of-war with adult) Manifestation 5: Tickling or Being Tickled Repeatedly Physical Redirect Technique: When child is seeking/giving excessive tickling, stop the tickling, make eye contact and say "Tickling is done now. Your body still needs strong touch. Let's do squeezes instead." Do "arm squeezes" - firmly squeeze child's arms from shoulder to wrist 3 times each arm. Or have them do wall push-ups. Provide the tactile/pressure input they're seeking without tickling.
DIY Alternative Tool: Tickle Alternatives System: Tickle timer: Use visual timer, tickling allowed only while timer runs (set 2 minutes maximum). When timer beeps, tickling stops, use alternatives. Tickle tickets: Child gets 3 "tickle tickets" per day, each ticket = 1 minute of tickling. Rations tickling throughout day. Pressure alternatives chart: Visual chart showing alternatives to tickling (squeezes, massage, bear hugs, rolling in blanket, crash pad jumping). Vibrating massager: Small handheld vibrating massager provides similar sensation to tickling without social component - child can use on self. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Light touch alternatives: Feather or soft makeup brush child uses on own arms/legs Cotton balls rubbed on skin Silk scarf dragge Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Light touch alternatives: Feather or soft makeup brush child uses on own arms/legs
Cotton balls rubbed on skin Silk scarf dragged slowly across arms Soft paintbrush strokes on arms/legs Pressure alternatives: Firm rubbing with hands instead of tickling Rolling with rolling pin on arms/legs (through clothes) Compression through tight clothing or wraps Massage with textured tools (bumpy ball, brush) Vibration alternatives: Electric toothbrush (turned on) held against arms/legs Vibrating phone or massager Sit on washing machine during spin cycle (supervised) Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Scheduled light touch time: 10 minutes 2x daily of appropriate light touch activities (soft brush on arms, feather touch, gentle stroking) Deep pressure prioritized: Provide LOTS of deep pressure throughout day - may reduce light touch seeking Tactile exploration bins: Bins with various textures child explores with hands - appropriate tactile input
Appropriate tickle games: Structure tickle games with clear rules (tickle for 10 seconds, stop, child's turn to request more or stop) For Avoiders: No tickling ever: Respect that tickling is overwhelming and unpleasant Deep pressure only: If any touch, only firm deep pressure, never light touch Control over touch: Child always controls when/if touch happens Warn before touch: Always announce before any touch "I'm going to touch your shoulder now" Massage Techniques: Alternative to tickling: When child seeks tickling, offer massage instead - "Instead of tickling, how about a back massage?" Light touch desensitization: If child excessively seeks light touch, may need gradual desensitization - work with OT Deep pressure massage: Provide deep, firm massage 15-20 minutes daily - may reduce light touch seeking
Textured tools massage: Use various textured tools during massage (bumpy ball, soft brush, textured roller) - provides sensory variety Social Skills Integration: Tickling consent rules: Always ask "May I tickle you?" before tickling anyone When someone says "Stop," MUST stop immediately - no exceptions If person is laughing but says stop, still MUST stop (laughter doesn't always mean "continue") Only tickle people who clearly said "Yes" to tickling Tickle awareness: Teach child that many people DON'T like tickling - it's not universally fun Alternative fun: If someone doesn't want tickling, what are other fun games? (Chase, hide-seek, ball games) Recognizing discomfort: Teach child to notice when tickling partner is actually uncomfortable (trying to get away, face showing distress, body stiffening) Reciprocity: If child wants to be tickled, teach appropriate ways to request "Would you tickle my back for 10 seconds please?"
Manifestation 6: High-Fiving or Handshaking Excessively Physical Redirect Technique: When child is excessively high-fiving/handshaking, receive the high-five/handshake, then hold their hand gently and say "That was a good high-five. One high-five is enough. Let's save the next one for later." Place their hand back at their side or in their lap. Redirect to alternative: "If you need hand action, try squeezing this ball" (hand them stress ball). DIY Alternative Tool: High-Five/Handshake Management: Greeting token system: Child gets 5 "greeting tokens" per social situation. Each token = 1 high-five or handshake. When tokens used, other greetings only (wave, nod, verbal greeting). Greeting variety chart: Visual chart showing 10 different greetings (wave, nod, smile, thumbs up, peace sign, fist bump, verbal hello, salute, bow, handshake). Must rotate through different greetings.
Hand fidget always available: Child keeps small fidget toy in pocket - squeeze this instead of excessive handshaking. Social script card: Card in child's pocket with script: "Hi!" (wave). If already greeted, script says "I already said hi to this person." Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Hand activities: Stress ball squeezing (keep in pocket for constant access) Therapy putty pulling and squeezing Hand clapping games (pat-a-cake, Miss Mary Mack) - structured hand contact High-five with wall (mark spot on wall with tape, high-five the wall) Greeting alternatives: Secret handshake family creates together - special, limited use increases value Fist bumps instead of high-fives (briefer, less repeatable) Elbow bumps, foot taps - silly alternatives that are less socially demanding Wave board - child waves at pictures of people on board when greeting urge arises
Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Hand proprioceptive input: Throughout day, provide intense hand input (squeeze therapy putty, hand grip strengthener, push hands together hard, finger resistance exercises) Structured greeting practice: Role-play appropriate greeting frequency - greet once, then conversation, not repeated greetings Hand massage routine: 5-minute hand massage 3x daily - satisfies hand sensory needs Handshake alternatives: Teach that not every greeting requires handshake - many alternatives exist For Avoiders: No handshakes required: Child not required to shake hands if uncomfortable Wave only: Waving from distance completely acceptable greeting Verbal greetings: "Hello!" is sufficient, no physical contact needed Prepare child: Warn if handshaking situation coming "At Grandma's, she might want to shake your hand. You can wave instead if you want."
Massage Techniques: Hand focus massage: Thorough massage of hands, fingers, palms, wrists - 5-7 minutes each hand, 3x daily Firm hand pressure: Very firm compression of each finger from base to tip Palm pressure points: Deep pressure in center of palm, between thumb and index finger Wrist rotations with pressure: Rotate wrist in circles while applying firm pressure Social Skills Integration: Greeting rules teaching: Greet each person ONCE when you see them If you already said hi, don't say hi again right away Look for cues person wants handshake (extending their hand) vs. doesn't (hands at sides, stepping back) In professional settings (doctor's office), handshake okay; casual settings (playground), less common Greeting frequency awareness: Help child become aware "You've high-fived that person 5 times in 10 minutes. That's too many. One high-five when you arrive, one when you leave."
Alternative interactions: If want to interact with someone, what are alternatives to repeated greetings? (Ask to play, start conversation, offer to share toy) Social stories: Create story showing child greeting someone once happily, then playing together - not greeting over and over Manifestation 7: Seeking Social Situations for Sensory Aspects (Not Social Connection) Physical Redirect Technique: When observe child entering social situation clearly for sensory aspects (going to group to crash into people, get hugs, touch things) rather than actual social engagement, gently redirect. Say "[Name], let's get your body what it needs first, then you can play with friends." Take them aside for 5 minutes of intense sensory input (jumping, crashing into cushions, deep pressure), THEN return to social situation.
DIY Alternative Tool: Sensory-First, Social-Second System: Pre-social sensory routine: Before any social situation (playdate, party, school), child does 10-minute sensory routine (jumping 100 times, spinning 20 times, wall push-ups 20 times, massage 5 minutes). Satisfies sensory needs BEFORE social demands. Sensory break schedule: During social situations, schedule sensory breaks every 20 minutes (2-minute break for sensory input, then return to social). Sensory area at parties: If hosting playdate/party, designate "sensory area" (trampoline, crash pad, quiet room with weighted blankets) where child can go for sensory input, then return to social. Social-sensory cards: Child carries cards: GREEN card = "I can handle social right now" YELLOW card = "I need sensory break soon" RED card = "I need sensory break NOW" Alternative Stimulation (Household Items):
Portable sensory kit for social situations: Small stress ball in pocket Fidget toy on keychain attached to pants Chew necklace Small weighted lap pad in backpack Sensory bottle to watch Pre-social sensory activities: Trampoline 10 minutes before social event Heavy backpack wearing during social situation Chewy snacks during social time (provide oral sensory input) Compression clothing worn under regular clothes During-social sensory opportunities: Volunteer for physical tasks (carrying things, setting up, cleaning up) Active games (tag, hide-seek) rather than seated games Sensory-rich activities (playdough, water play, messy art) during playdate Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Robust sensory diet BEFORE social: Ensure child's sensory needs thoroughly met before social demands - well-regulated child can better handle social interaction Sensory-rich social activities: Choose social activities that INCLUDE sensory input (swimming party, trampoline park outing, outdoor active play) rather than sedentary social (movie watching, tea party)
Movement breaks during social: Structure social time with movement breaks (play game 15 min, run around 3 min, play game 15 min) Small groups: Child may handle sensory needs better in smaller social groups (1-2 friends) vs. large parties For Avoiders: Low-sensory social situations: Quiet, calm social activities (board games, crafts, reading together) Escape routes: Ensure child always has option to leave social situation if overwhelmed Short social times: Start with 30-minute playdates, gradually increase as tolerated Familiar settings: Social situations in familiar, comfortable settings less overwhelming Massage Techniques: Pre-social calming massage: Before social situations, 10-15 minute calming massage helps organize nervous system for social demands Post-social recovery massage: After social situations, 15-20 minute massage helps child integrate sensory experiences and decompress
On-demand brief massage: During social situations (if at home), offer brief 3-5 minute massage breaks when child seems overwhelmed Teaching self-regulation: Teach child self-massage techniques to use during social situations (hand squeezes, shoulder presses) Social Skills Integration: Separating sensory from social: Help child understand "Your body needs sensory input (jumping, crashing, squeezing). Friends are for playing games together, talking, sharing. Let's meet body needs first, then play with friends." Appropriate sensory in social: Teach which sensory behaviors okay in social context (fidgeting with small toy, chewing gum quietly) vs. not okay (crashing into people, excessive touching) Recognizing social purpose: Teach child why we have social time - to connect with others, have fun together, build friendships - not just for sensory input
Balance teaching: "We need both sensory time AND social time. Sometimes together (active games), sometimes separate (sensory break, then social play)." Manifestation 8: Using People as "Tools" for Sensory Input (Climbing On, Pushing Against) Physical Redirect Technique: When child is climbing on or pushing against a person, immediately remove them physically (gently but firmly). Say "Stop. People are not for climbing. The wall/furniture is for pushing." Immediately redirect to appropriate alternative - take them to wall for wall push-ups, or to couch for climbing on furniture, or to crash pad for jumping. Provide the sensory input they need but through appropriate objects, not people. DIY Alternative Tool: People vs. Objects Teaching System: Visual sorting activity: Create two columns - "Okay to Push/Climb" (pictures of walls, furniture, climbing equipment, pillows) and "NOT Okay to Push/Climb" (pictures of people, pets, babies). Practice categorizing.
Designated push/climb objects: Mark specific furniture/areas with colored tape as "climbing zones" and wall spots as "pushing zones" - clear visual cues where to direct behavior. Life-size person cutout: Create cardboard life-size cutout of person with RED X over it = NOT for climbing/pushing. Keep near climbing areas as visual reminder. Alternative surfaces always available: Ensure child ALWAYS has access to appropriate climbing/pushing alternatives (climbing structure, therapy ball, wall) so they never "need" to use people. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Pushing alternatives: Wall push-ups station (mark wall with tape and hand outlines) Heavy furniture to push (ottoman on carpet) Adult holds their hands, child pushes against them in structured game (both standing, pushing hand-to-hand) Door pushing open (assign child to open all doors)
Climbing alternatives: Couch cushions stacked for climbing Sturdy low bookshelf or furniture (safe to climb) Indoor climbing structure or ladder Outdoor climbing: trees, playground equipment, rock walls Heavy work alternatives: Carry heavy laundry basket Push loaded wagon or cart Pull/drag heavy object on rope Dig in sand or dirt Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Continuous access to climbing/pushing: Child must have near-constant access to appropriate climbing and pushing outlets - if these needs aren't met, they'll use people Heavy work routine: 15-20 minutes 3x daily of intense heavy work (pushing, pulling, carrying, climbing) - satisfies proprioceptive needs reducing seeking from people Gymnastics/rock climbing classes: Structured settings teaching appropriate climbing with equipment Roughhousing rules: If child wants physical play with people, teach appropriate rough play rules (both people agree, clear boundaries, stop means stop)
For Avoiders: No climbing/pushing on people: Completely avoid this behavior - child uncomfortable with it Personal space respected: Ensure child's personal space always respected - they won't use others as tools Independent activities: Provide activities child can do independently without physical contact with others Massage Techniques: Whole body proprioceptive massage: Provide intense full-body deep pressure massage 20-30 minutes daily - gives body the input it's seeking from climbing/pushing on people Joint compressions full body: Compress every major joint firmly 10 seconds each - intense proprioceptive input Resistive massage: Child pushes against you while you massage (provides resistance they seek) Teaching body boundaries: During massage, emphasize "This is YOUR body. This is MY body. We each have our own bodies." Social Skills Integration:
People vs. Objects teaching: People: Have feelings, can get hurt, don't like being climbed on/pushed, ask for what they want, deserve respect Objects: Don't have feelings, meant for pushing/climbing (appropriate ones), can't get hurt Consent teaching: "Before you touch anyone, you must ask 'May I...?' and wait for YES. If they say NO or don't answer, the answer is NO." Empathy building: "How would YOU feel if someone climbed on you without asking? Would that hurt? Feel scary?" Build understanding of others' perspectives. Alternative requests: Teach child to request what they need appropriately: "I need to push something heavy. Can you help me push the couch?" (Requests help with appropriate activity vs. pushing against person) Social stories: Create story showing child that climbing/pushing on people:
Makes people feel hurt/uncomfortable Can cause injury Makes people not want to play with you vs. Using appropriate objects makes people happy and want to be your friend
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 9. COMPLEX/MULTI-SENSORY STIMMING > C. Social and Interactive Stimming > Level 2: Repetitive Social Patterns
Causation: Over-stimulated: Predictable social patterns reduce anxiety Under-stimulated: Social repetition provides sensory + social input Sensitivity: Need for predictability in unpredictable social world Communication: Using repetition to maintain interaction when language limited Regulation: Social patterns are organizing and comforting Sensory Profile: Pattern-Dependent: Needs social predictability for comfort Communicative: Using repetition functionally despite appearing rigid Anxious: Social unpredictability managed through repetitive patterns Description: Engaging in repetitive social interactions for stimulation Manifestation 1: Asking Same Questions Repeatedly Despite Knowing Answers Physical Redirect Technique: When child asks same question they've asked multiple times, instead of answering again, gently touch their shoulder and say "[Name], you've asked that question 3 times. You know the answer is [answer]. Let's move our bodies instead of asking again." Immediately engage in 2-minute movement activity (jumping jacks, running in place, animal walk across room). Physical activity interrupts the repetitive pattern.
DIY Alternative Tool: Question Management System: Question board: Create whiteboard or paper where frequently asked questions and their answers are written. When child asks, redirect them to read the board. "Remember, the answer is on your question board." Question tokens: Child gets 5 "new question tokens" per hour. Can ask new questions using tokens. Repeated questions don't get tokens - redirect to question board or remind "You already know this answer." Answer cards: Make small cards with common questions and answers. Child keeps these cards with them. When they want to ask repeated question, look at card instead. Question timer: "You may ask about [topic] once every hour. Let's set this timer. When it beeps in one hour, you can ask again if you still want to."
Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Oral motor alternatives: Chew necklace or chewy tube (provides oral sensory input that asking questions provides) Blow bubbles, blow into harmonica, blow up balloons Sing songs, hum, make sounds with mouth (appropriate vocalization alternatives) Sip very thick smoothie through straw (intense oral motor work) Communication alternatives: Talk about OTHER topics - create list of approved conversation topics, practice these Tell jokes, read books aloud, recite poems - other verbal activities Ask question game with NEW questions (provide list of interesting questions to ask) Anxiety management (often underlying repetitive questioning): Deep breathing exercises Heavy work activities (calms anxiety) Weighted lap pad while sitting Calming music or white noise Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Oral sensory diet: Throughout day, provide LOTS of oral sensory input (chewing, crunching, sucking, blowing) - may reduce need for repetitive verbal seeking
Communication-rich activities: Provide LOTS of opportunities for meaningful communication (conversations about interesting topics, storytelling, reading together, asking/answering NEW questions) Pattern satisfaction in other ways: If child loves patterns/repetition, provide this in non-social ways (sorting activities, watching same videos, reading same books) Anxiety reduction: If anxiety-driven, address anxiety through sensory diet (heavy work, deep pressure, predictable routines) For Avoiders: Respect need for predictability: Some children ask repeatedly because they NEED the predictability/reassurance of the same answer Provide written schedules: Visual schedules reduce need to ask about what's happening Reduce social demands: Less overall social communication demanded may reduce repetitive patterns Warnings for changes: Always warn before changes to routine (reduces anxiety and repetitive checking questions) Massage Techniques: Jaw and face massage: If repetitive questioning is oral-motor seeking, massage jaw muscles, 3-5 minutes
Calming full-body massage: If anxiety-driven, 15-20 minute calming massage before times when repetitive questioning typically occurs Scheduled massage breaks: When child asks repeated question, redirect: "Instead of asking again, let's do hand massage" (2-3 minutes) Self-regulation teaching: Teach child self-massage techniques to use when they feel urge to ask repeated questions Social Skills Integration: Question awareness: Help child become aware of pattern "You've asked me about dinner 5 times in the last hour. You already know the answer. Asking many times doesn't change the answer." One answer rule: "I will answer your question ONE time. Please listen carefully because I won't answer it again. After one answer, if you ask again, I'll remind you 'I already answered that.'" Alternative communication teaching: "Instead of asking the same question, you could:
Check your schedule board Check your question answer card Ask a NEW question Tell me something interesting instead" Understanding impact: "When you ask the same question many times, it makes people feel frustrated. They want to talk about new things, not answer the same question over and over." Patience teaching: "I know waiting is hard. While you wait for [dinner/event/etc], let's [activity] to help time pass." Manifestation 2: Requesting Same Stories, Songs, or Routines from Caregivers (100+ Times) Physical Redirect Technique: When child requests the same story/song for the 20th time that day, acknowledge their request: "I know you love that story." Then redirect: "We've read/sung it 20 times today. Now it's time for something different. Let's do [alternative] instead." Offer choice between 2-3 different options. If child persists, physically redirect to different activity - "Let's go jump on the trampoline instead."
DIY Alternative Tool: Story/Song Management System: Story tokens: Child gets 3 "favorite story tokens" per day. Can use tokens to request favorite story. When tokens gone, must choose different stories. Rotation schedule: Create visual schedule showing which story/song for which time of day (favorite at bedtime, different story at lunch, another after school). Child sees favorites are included but spread out. Recording system: Record child's favorite story/song. When they request it excessively, play the recording instead of live performance. Story variation: "We can read/sing the favorite, BUT you must choose one thing to change (different voice, add actions, change ending)." Introduces variation while honoring preference. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Auditory alternatives: Create playlist with favorite song plus 10 similar songs - gradually introduce variety
Audio books of favorite and similar stories White noise machine or calming music for background Child can listen to recordings on device independently Routine alternatives: Written schedule showing routine step-by-step (child can "read" routine instead of having it performed) Photo schedule of routine child looks at Child performs routine with dolls/toys (acting it out instead of requesting performance) Predictability in other areas: Provide lots of predictability in daily schedule Keep visual schedules consistent Maintain predictable mealtimes, bedtimes, activities Satisfy need for sameness in non-social ways Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Auditory sensory diet: Throughout day, provide rich auditory input (music, singing, audiobooks, nature sounds) - satisfies auditory seeking Vestibular input: Often repetitive requesting is self-soothing; provide alternative calming input (rocking, swinging, slow spinning)
Predictable sensory schedule: Keep sensory diet VERY predictable - satisfies need for sameness Pattern activities: Provide other patterned activities (sorting, lining up toys, watching same videos) - satisfies pattern-seeking For Avoiders: Honor need for sameness: Some children genuinely need the predictability and sameness Gradual introduction of new: Introduce new stories/songs very slowly, one at a time, mixed with favorites Control over changes: Child chooses when ready to try something new - never force Keep other things very predictable: If asking child to tolerate new story, keep everything else very same Massage Techniques: Calming massage with favorite song: During massage, play favorite song - pairs calming touch with auditory preference Rhythmic massage matching song: Massage in rhythm to favorite song's beat Predictable massage routine: Same massage routine every time (satisfies need for sameness)
Bedtime massage routine: If stories/songs requested most at bedtime, create predictable massage routine that partially replaces story time Social Skills Integration: Variety teaching: "Different stories/songs are also fun! Let's try this new one. If you don't like it, we can stop and read your favorite." Social reciprocity: "I've read your favorite story 3 times. Now you need to listen to the story I choose. We take turns choosing." Understanding limits: "Reading the same story 50 times would take all day. We don't have time for that. You can have it 3 times, then we do something else." Caregiver feelings: "When I read the same story 100 times, I get very bored and tired. I want to read stories that are new and interesting to me too."
Respecting others' needs: "Brother wants a different story. We need to take turns. This time we read his choice, next time your choice." Manifestation 3: Scripting Social Interactions (Same Greetings, Phrases) Physical Redirect Technique: When child uses scripted phrase, acknowledge it briefly, then physically redirect to flexible communication. For example, if child says same scripted greeting for 5th time, say "I heard you. Now let's talk about something NEW." Take their hand and guide them to something interesting in the environment: "Look at this [toy/picture/object]. Tell me about it." Redirects from script to spontaneous communication. DIY Alternative Tool: Script Flexibility System: Phrase variety cards: Create cards with 10 different ways to say the same thing: Instead of always "Hi, how are you?" also: "Hello!" "Hey!" "Good morning!" "What's up?" "How's it going?"
Child draws card, uses that greeting Conversation starter cards: Cards with various conversation topics child can choose from instead of repeating same scripts Flexibility practice: Role-play social situations multiple times using different phrases each time Video modeling: Record child using varied phrases in social situations, watch together, practice flexibility Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Oral motor alternatives: If scripting provides oral motor satisfaction, provide alternative oral activities (chewing, singing different songs, whistling, blowing) Pattern satisfaction elsewhere: If scripting satisfies need for patterns/sameness, provide patterns in non-social ways (sorting games, repetitive videos, lining up toys, same bedtime routine) Communication supports: Communication cards or device showing various conversation options Visual prompts for flexible phrases Social scripts with multiple options shown Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers:
Rich sensory diet: Well-regulated child has better flexible thinking - ensure robust sensory diet throughout day Oral sensory input: Provide lots of appropriate oral input (chewing, crunching, blowing) reducing need for verbal scripting Predictability in other areas: Provide lots of predictability in routines and environment - allows flexibility in communication Pattern activities: Satisfy pattern-seeking through appropriate activities (puzzles, building, sorting) For Avoiders: Respect need for scripts: Scripts provide security and predictability in scary social world Gradual script expansion: Add one new phrase per week to repertoire Safe practice: Practice new phrases in safe, comfortable settings before using in real situations Written supports: Provide written scripts with multiple options child can reference Massage Techniques: Jaw and mouth massage: If scripting is oral-motor, massage jaw area, 3-5 minutes
Calming massage: Anxiety often underlies scripting - regular calming massages may reduce need for rigid scripts Pre-social massage: Before social situations, 10-minute calming massage may help child be more flexible Grounding massage: Firm, grounding massage helps child feel safe enough to try new communication Social Skills Integration: Multiple ways to say things: Teach explicitly that there are MANY ways to express same idea - practice these Flexibility as strength: Reframe flexibility as positive skill: "Being able to say things different ways makes you a great communicator!" Social observation: Watch others (videos, real life) and notice they use varied phrases - "See, she said 'Hey there!' instead of 'Hi!' Both work!" Script library: Instead of one script, build library of options: "When I greet someone I can say: Hi, Hello, Hey, What's up, How's it going, Good morning..." Child chooses from library vs. same script always
Understanding impact: "When you say the exact same thing every time, people might think you're not really listening to them. Changing your words shows you're paying attention." Manifestation 4: Seeking Same Type of Play Repeatedly (Chase Games, Tickling) Physical Redirect Technique: When child requests same play activity for 10th time, acknowledge their preference: "I know you love chase!" Then set boundary: "We played chase 4 times already. Now we're playing something different. Your choice: [Option A] or [Option B]." Offer two different activities. Physically redirect to chosen activity - take their hand and move toward it, start engaging in new activity. DIY Alternative Tool: Play Variety System: Play menu: Create visual menu with 10-12 different play activities (pictures and words). Child chooses from menu. Rule: Can't choose same activity twice in a row.
Play rotation schedule: Visual schedule showing different activities at different times: 3:00 = Chase 3:15 = Blocks 3:30 = Drawing 3:45 = Child's choice (may choose chase again) Activity tokens: Child gets one token for favorite activity, plus tokens for 3 other activities. Must use all tokens before day ends (ensures variety). Same-but-different modifications: If child always wants chase, modify it: chase game with ball, chase on toes, slow-motion chase, freeze chase - introduces variation while honoring preference. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Vestibular alternatives (chase provides vestibular input): Swinging, spinning, jumping on trampoline, rolling down hills Any activity with movement satisfies same sensory need Social alternatives: Games with similar social structure (hide-and-seek has seeking element like chase) Turn-taking games (provides social interaction)
Cooperative games (playing together toward goal) Proprioceptive alternatives (rough play provides proprioceptive input): Heavy work activities (pushing, pulling, carrying) Crash pad jumping Pillow fights with rules Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Identify underlying sensory need: What sensory input does preferred play provide? (Chase = vestibular, tickling = light touch, rough play = proprioceptive) Provide that sensory input other ways: If loves chase for movement, provide lots of vestibular activities throughout day Satisfy need before play: Before playdate, 15 minutes of desired sensory input (jumping, spinning, crashing) - child may then be more flexible in play choices Broaden play repertoire: Gradually introduce new activities that provide SIMILAR sensory input (if loves chase/movement, try dancing, relay races, obstacle courses) For Avoiders: Respect play preferences: Child may avoid active/unpredictable play - honor this
Offer calm alternatives: Suggest calm, predictable play options (building, drawing, reading together) Small groups: May handle variety better with just one friend vs. group Control over play: Let child direct play - may be more flexible when in control Massage Techniques: Post-play calming: After active play, calming massage helps transition to different activity, 10 minutes Pre-play organizing: Before play, 5-minute massage may help child be more flexible in play choices Sensory-specific massage: If child seeks chase for movement, provide vestibular input through massage (rocking while massaging, rhythmic massage) Transition massage: When transitioning from favorite play to different play, brief 3-minute massage eases transition Social Skills Integration: Flexibility in friendship: "Friends like to play different games. If you only want to play chase, friends might not want to play with you. Playing different games makes you a better friend."
Turn-taking with activities: "This time we play chase because you want to. Next time we play hide-and-seek because I want to. Friends take turns choosing." Trying new things: "I know chase is your favorite. But let's try this new game. You might like it too! If you don't like it after 5 minutes, we can stop." Noticing others' preferences: "See, your friend looks bored with chase. Their face shows they want to try something new. Let's ask what they want to play." Reciprocity teaching: "You like when I play chase with you. Your friend likes when you play what THEY want. We give and take." Manifestation 5: Repeating Others' Physical Actions (Echopraxia) Physical Redirect Technique: When child is echoing another person's physical actions, gently touch their shoulder and say "[Name], you're copying [person]. Let's do YOUR own movements instead." Guide them to do a completely different action: If they were copying someone waving, have them do jumping jacks. If copying someone walking, have them skip instead. Redirects to independent movement.
DIY Alternative Tool: Independent Action System: Action cards: Create cards with different actions (jump, spin, clap, stomp, reach up, bend down). Child draws card and does THAT action instead of copying others. "My movement" vs. "Their movement" teaching: Two columns chart with "What I See Others Do" and "What I Choose to Do Instead" - visually separates observation from copying. Movement leader game: Structure turn-taking: "Now it's follow-the-leader time (copying okay), now it's independent time (everyone does own thing)." Child learns when copying appropriate vs. inappropriate. Mirror time: Provide large mirror where child watches SELF moving - builds awareness of own body separate from others. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Proprioceptive input (helps child feel own body): Heavy work before social situations (carrying, pushing, pulling)
Weighted vest or backpack during social time Deep pressure activities helping child feel body boundaries Movement activities alone: Solo dance time, obstacle course, animal walks Practice moving body independently before social situations Build repertoire of "my own movements" Visual blocking: Sunglasses or hat reducing visual input of others' movements Positioning child where they can't easily see others moving Activities where child focuses on task, not watching others Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Proprioceptive body awareness: Intensive proprioceptive activities throughout day help child feel their own body as separate entity Movement planning practice: Activities requiring motor planning (obstacle courses, new sports, dance choreography) - builds independent movement control Imitation in appropriate contexts: If child loves imitating, provide appropriate outlets (Simon Says, follow-the-leader games with clear structure, dance videos to imitate)
Visual-motor integration: Activities strengthening ability to translate what see into movement under their control (catch, sports, building from diagrams) For Avoiders: Reduce movement demands: Less pressure to move may reduce unconscious copying Parallel activities: Sit near others doing similar activity but not requiring interaction Individual space: Ensure child has own clear physical space separate from others Predictable movements: If any movement required, practice same movements repeatedly until automatic Massage Techniques: Body boundary massage: Massage outlining child's body, building awareness of self as separate from others, 10 minutes Proprioceptive intensive: Deep pressure on all body parts helping child FEEL their own body distinctly, 15 minutes Bilateral massage: Massage both sides of body simultaneously, reinforcing body symmetry and wholeness Grounding massage: Very firm foot and leg massage helping child feel grounded in own body
Social Skills Integration: Self-awareness teaching: "This is YOUR body. It moves how YOU decide, not how others move. What do YOU want your body to do?" Observation vs. copying: "It's okay to LOOK at what others do. But you don't have to DO what they do. You can choose your own movements." Appropriate imitation: "Sometimes copying is fun and okay - like in Simon Says or follow-the-leader. Other times we each do our own thing - like during recess or playtime." Understanding impact: "When you copy everything someone does, it can make them uncomfortable. They might think you're making fun of them. Doing your own movements shows respect." Building independence: Praise when child does own movements: "I love how you decided to jump while she was spinning! You made your own choice!"
Manifestation 6: Following People Around Constantly Physical Redirect Technique: When child is following someone constantly, gently touch their arm and say "[Name], [person] needs space. You need to stay here/play here now." Physically position child in different area with engaging activity. Set visual timer: "You stay here and [activity] until the timer beeps. Then you may check in with [person] ONE time." DIY Alternative Tool: Following Management System: Check-in schedule: Visual schedule showing when child may check in with person (every 30 minutes, on the hour, after completing activity). Between check-ins, must stay in own area. Physical distance markers: Use tape on floor or rugs to mark "child's space" and "other person's space." Child must stay in own space unless specifically invited.
Independence chart: Chart tracking time child spends in independent activity. Earn rewards for increasing independent time. Photo proximity: Take photos showing appropriate distance from people (3-6 feet) vs. too close (right next to/following). Child references photos. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Attachment alternatives: Weighted blanket or stuffed animal provides "company" feeling Pet to follow around (if family has pet) instead of person Audio of person's voice child can listen to when apart Photo of person child can look at when missing them Engagement activities: Highly engaging activities child wants to do (prevents boredom-driven following) Screen time, favorite toys, special activities reserved for independent time Sensory bins, art projects, building activities absorbing attention Connection scheduling: Schedule specific "together times" throughout day Child knows exactly when they'll have person's attention next
Reduces anxiety-driven following Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Vestibular input: Following provides continuous movement - provide alternative vestibular activities (swinging, rocking, pacing in designated area) Proprioceptive grounding: Heavy work and deep pressure help child feel secure alone (reduces need to follow for security) Visual input: If following to watch person, provide alternative visual activities (videos, books, art) Social connection alternatives: If following for connection, schedule frequent brief social times (every 20 minutes, 3-minute connection) For Avoiders: Respect need for proximity: Some children need close proximity to feel safe - honor this while working on gradual independence Gradual distance increase: Very slowly increase distance tolerance (start with same room, then can't see but can hear, then different room) Security objects: Provide comfort items when apart from person
Frequent check-ins: More frequent but brief check-ins may reduce constant following Massage Techniques: Grounding massage: Before independent time, grounding massage helps child feel secure enough to separate, 10 minutes Calming routine: Regular calming massages throughout day reduce anxiety that may drive following Brief connection massage: When child checks in, brief 2-minute massage provides connection, then back to independent activity Bedtime massage: Thorough evening massage helps child feel connected and secure overnight Social Skills Integration: Personal space and independence: "Everyone needs time alone or time to do their own activities. Following someone everywhere doesn't give them that space." Reading cues: "When someone closes door, that means they want privacy. When someone doesn't talk much, they might want quiet. Notice these signs." Appropriate proximity: Different situations require different distances:
Working/cooking/busy: Stay in different area Watching TV together: Sit nearby but not touching Playing together: Close proximity okay Someone's in bathroom/bedroom: Knock and wait, don't follow in Independence as strength: "Being able to play by yourself is an important skill. It shows you're growing up!" Scheduled connection: "We have together time at [times]. Between those times, we each do our own activities. That makes together time more special!" Manifestation 7: Initiating Same Social Routine with Different People Physical Redirect Technique: When child initiates same routine with yet another person (asking same questions, requesting same game, same greeting sequence), pause them mid-routine. Touch their shoulder and say "[Name], you did that routine with [previous person]. With [current person], let's try something NEW." Prompt them with alternative: "Try asking them about their day instead" or "Try playing a different game with this person."
DIY Alternative Tool: Routine Flexibility System: Person-specific interaction cards: Create cards for different people in child's life showing 3-4 different ways to interact with each person: With Grandma: Ask about her day, play cards, look at photos together, help cook With Friend: Play chase, build blocks, draw together, play ball Child chooses from options but has variety Interaction menu: Visual menu showing 10+ different social interactions. Must choose different one for each person encountered. Routine variation cards: If child MUST do routine, draw card showing one element to change (different question, different game, different greeting, different topic). Social script library: Instead of one script, provide library of multiple scripts for various situations. Alternative Stimulation (Household Items): Pattern satisfaction elsewhere: Sorting games, organizing toys, lining things up
Same bedtime routine, same morning routine Watching same videos, reading same books Provides pattern/sameness need in non-social contexts Predictability in environment: Very consistent daily schedule Same mealtimes, same locations for activities Visual schedules showing what happens when Environmental predictability may allow social flexibility Communication alternatives: If routine provides communication structure, provide other structured communication (conversation cards, communication device, social scripts with variety) Sensory Integration Activities: For Seekers: Robust sensory diet: Well-regulated child has better flexible thinking - ensure consistent sensory input throughout day Vestibular calming: If routines are soothing, provide alternative calming activities (rocking, swinging, deep pressure) Proprioceptive input: Heavy work before social situations may help child be more flexible Oral sensory: If routines involve verbal repetition for oral-motor input, provide alternatives (chewing, singing)
For Avoiders: Respect need for routines: Routines provide safety and predictability in social situations Gradual variation: Introduce tiny variations to routine very gradually Written support: Provide written versions of routine variations child can reference Practice in safe settings: Practice routine variations at home before trying in real social situations Massage Techniques: Pre-social calming: Before social situations, calming massage may reduce need for rigid routines, 10 minutes Anxiety-reducing massage: Regular massage throughout day reduces underlying anxiety driving routines, 15-20 minutes daily Routine massage: If child needs routines, create very predictable massage routine (satisfies need for sameness) Grounding before flexibility: Grounding massage before social situations helps child feel secure enough to try flexibility Social Skills Integration: People are different: "Each person is different and likes different things. When we talk to different people, we can say different things."
Flexibility makes better friend: "Friends like when you're interested in what THEY want to talk about or play, not just doing the same thing with everyone."
