Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Heavy Tactile Activities Before Stress: Before anticipated stressful events, engage in 5-10 minutes of heavy tactile activities: digging in rice bins, playing with kinetic sand, tearing paper, or squeezing playdough. This provides intense tactile input that reduces picking urges. Lotion Application Protocol: Apply thick, scented lotion to hands and arms slowly and thoroughly. This provides intense tactile input and makes skin picking less appealing (slippery). The scent provides olfactory regulation.
Resistive Finger Activities: Pull apart construction toys, open jars, or manipulate theraputty to provide resistance and proprioceptive input to fingers and hands. For Sensory Avoiders: Gentle Touch Alternatives: Rather than intense picking alternatives, provide soft, smooth textures to stroke (silk fabric, soft brush). Visual Monitoring: Use bandages or gloves on picked areas as both protection and visual reminder. The different sensation interrupts the picking pattern. Stress Reduction Focus: Since picking in avoiders often stems from anxiety rather than sensory seeking, focus on environmental stress reduction: quiet spaces, predictable routines, advance warning of changes. Massage Techniques: Arm and Hand Lymphatic Massage - Using gentle pressure, stroke from the shoulder down to the fingertips in long, slow movements. Repeat 10 times on each arm. This calming massage reduces stress and redirects touch to a positive experience rather than picking.
Cuticle and Nail Bed Massage - Gently massage around each nail bed and cuticle with oil or lotion for 30 seconds per finger. This provides targeted tactile input to the areas often picked and makes them less appealing to pick (moisturized and slippery). Full Hand Pressure Massage - Place the child's hand between both of yours and apply firm, even pressure for 10-15 seconds. Release and repeat 3-5 times per hand. This deep pressure is calming and reduces the urge to engage in picking behaviors. Manifestation 7. HUMMING SOFTLY DURING UNCERTAINTY Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Throat Touch Awareness" - Gently place your hand on the child's throat/neck area (externally, not pressing) and say, "I can feel your humming. Let's try silent breathing instead. Take three big breaths with me." This brings awareness to the vocal stimming and redirects to silent breath control.
DIY Redirection Tool: Humming Harmonica Card - Cut a small rectangle of wax paper or tissue paper and comb (making it slightly corrugated by running a comb across it). Fold it in half over a craft stick. The child can hum into this, and it vibrates, providing oral motor and auditory feedback similar to humming but creating a different sound that's less disruptive. Cost: ₹2-5. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Straw Whistle - Cut a plastic straw to 3-4 inches. Flatten one end slightly and cut a small triangle notch. The child can blow into it quietly, providing oral motor and auditory feedback similar to humming. The focus on breath control redirects from vocal humming. Cost: ₹2-5. Water Bottle Bubble Blowing - Fill a water bottle halfway with water. Provide a straw. The child blows bubbles in the water during uncertainty. This provides oral motor input, auditory feedback (gentle bubbling sound), and visual focus. Cost: ₹20-30 for reusable bottle.
Vibrating Toothbrush Sensation - Allow the child to hold a clean, vibrating electric toothbrush (turned on) against their cheek or chin during uncertain moments. The vibration provides similar sensory feedback to the vocal vibration of humming. Cost: ₹100-200 (can use an old electric toothbrush). Kazoo or Paper Whistle - Provide a kazoo or make a simple whistle from folded paper. The child can use this quietly during uncertainty, providing controlled oral motor and auditory output. Cost: ₹10-30. How to Use: Introduce the alternative during calm moments first: "Instead of humming, you can blow bubbles in your water bottle" Keep the tool accessible but discrete (in pencil case, pocket, attached to desk) Teach appropriate times and volumes: "You can use your whistle softly during independent work time"
Provide a visual cue: create a "quiet alternative" card the child can see as a reminder Coordinate with teachers if using in school settings to ensure it's acceptable Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Oral Motor Heavy Work: Before uncertain activities, engage in 5 minutes of oral motor input: chewing gum (if age-appropriate), crunching carrots or apples, drinking thick smoothies through a straw, or blowing cotton balls through a straw maze. This intense oral motor work reduces humming urges. Vocal Exercises with Purpose: Transform humming into structured vocal activities: animal sounds, singing songs quietly, or humming specific melodies. This makes the behavior purposeful rather than stimming. Vibration Input: Use a vibrating toy, phone, or massager on the cheeks, lips, or jaw before uncertain situations to provide external vibration that reduces the need for vocal vibration (humming).
For Sensory Avoiders: Silent Self-Regulation: Teach alternative silent coping strategies like slow breathing, pressing tongue to roof of mouth, or counting silently. Environmental Sound Masking: Provide soft background music or white noise through headphones during uncertain times. This reduces the internal need to create sound (humming). Visual Focus Tools: Redirect from auditory self-soothing (humming) to visual self-soothing: looking at calm pictures, watching a glitter jar settle, or focusing on a visual breathing pattern. Massage Techniques: Jaw and Facial Massage - With clean hands, gently massage the jaw muscles (the sides of the face below the cheekbones) in circular motions for 1-2 minutes. This releases tension that often triggers vocal stimming. Work from the jaw joint near the ears down to the chin.
Neck and Throat Massage - Very gently stroke down the front of the neck (over the throat area, not pressing on the windpipe) with soft pressure 10 times. This brings awareness to the vocal area and provides calming touch that can reduce humming urges. Chest Vibration Massage - Place your palm flat on the child's upper chest and gently pat or drum your fingers rhythmically for 30-60 seconds. This provides external vibration that can satisfy the internal vibration need that humming fulfills. Manifestation 8. ROCKING GENTLY DURING PROCESSING Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Grounding Shoulder Press" - Stand behind the child and place both hands firmly on their shoulders. Apply gentle downward pressure while saying, "Feel your weight in the chair. Press your feet flat on the floor. Let's count to five together." This proprioceptive input grounds the body and interrupts the rocking pattern.
DIY Redirection Tool: Weighted Lap Snake - Sew an old sock or tube of fabric into a long, thin shape and fill it with rice or dried beans (about 1-1.5 kg total weight). Tie or sew the end closed. The child drapes this across their lap during processing activities. The weight provides deep pressure and proprioceptive input that reduces rocking needs. Cost: ₹20-30. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Rocking Cushion Substitute - Place a partially deflated ball (basketball or soccer ball with some air let out) or a rolled towel under the chair seat. This allows small, controlled rocking movements while maintaining overall stability. Cost: Free or ₹200-300 for ball. Foot Swing Bar - Tie a resistance band, rope, or fabric strip between the front two legs of the chair (like a hammock under the chair). The child can swing their feet in this during processing, providing vestibular input without full body rocking. Cost: Free to ₹20.
Body Compression Band - Take a long elastic band or old bicycle inner tube and stretch it around the back of the chair and the child's back (not tight, just gentle pressure). This provides proprioceptive feedback that reduces rocking while still allowing small movements. Cost: Free to ₹30. Shifting Weight Bottle - Make a sealed bottle with water and glitter or colored oil. The child can hold this and slowly tilt it back and forth, watching the contents shift. The small hand movements provide vestibular input without full body rocking. Cost: ₹20-30. How to Use: Set up the tool before the processing activity begins (during homework, reading, listening to instructions) Allow the child to adjust the weight or resistance to their comfort level
Explain: "This heavy snake on your lap will help your body feel calm while you think" Combine with other sensory breaks: after 15-20 minutes, allow a full rocking or movement break Monitor effectiveness: if rocking continues, the weight may need adjustment or alternative approach needed Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Pre-Activity Rocking Time: Before processing tasks, allow 5 minutes of intentional rocking in a rocking chair, on a yoga ball, or in a swing. This satisfies the vestibular need proactively so it's less urgent during the task. Movement Breaks During Processing: Set a timer for every 10-15 minutes. When it rings, the child can stand up, do 5 spins in each direction, rock back and forth, or sway side to side for 30 seconds, then return to work.
Sitting on Therapy Ball: Replace the chair with a yoga/therapy ball (appropriate size for child's height). This allows constant small rocking movements while maintaining focus on the task. Alternative: place a cushion on a regular chair for subtle movement. Rocking Board Standing Desk: If possible, create a standing work area where the child stands on a balance or rocking board while processing information. For Sensory Avoiders: Stable, Supported Seating: Ensure the chair provides full back support, armrests if possible, and feet can rest flat on floor or footrest. Stability reduces anxiety-driven rocking. Heavy Blanket or Weighted Vest: Provide a heavy blanket over the shoulders or a weighted vest during processing. The weight grounds the body and reduces movement urges. Quiet, Calm Environment: Reduce environmental stimulation (lower lights, reduce noise, minimize visual distractions) so the child doesn't need to self-soothe through rocking.
Clear Structure and Expectations: Provide very clear explanations of what will happen during processing time. Uncertainty drives rocking in avoiders, so predictability reduces it. Massage Techniques: Full Back Pressure Massage - With the child seated, use firm pressure to press down the spine from shoulders to lower back, then out to the sides. Repeat 5-10 times. This proprioceptive input calms the nervous system and reduces rocking urges. Can be done over clothing. Shoulder Compressions - Stand behind the child and rhythmically squeeze and release both shoulders simultaneously for 1-2 minutes. This grounding input provides the rhythmic sensation rocking offers but without the movement. Hip and Thigh Pressure - With the child seated, press firmly on the tops of the thighs/hips for 5 seconds, release, and repeat 5 times. This grounds the lower body and reduces the rocking impulse that originates from the hips.
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 10. EMOTIONAL REGULATION STIMMING > A. Anxiety-Based Stimming > Level 2: Moderate Anxiety/Stress Response
Causation: Emotional: Moderate to high anxiety requiring regulation Dysregulation: Nervous system overwhelmed; using stimming to cope Coping: Primary coping mechanism for stress Escalation: Stimming intensity increases with stress intensity Profile: Stress-Responsive: Clear correlation between stressors and stimming Multi-System: Engages multiple sensory systems when stressed Observable: Others notice significant behaviour change during stress Description: Noticeable stimming increase during stress Manifestation 1. INTENSE PACING DURING WORRY OR PROBLEM-SOLVING Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Wall Lean Grounding" - When pacing intensifies, gently guide the child to stand facing a wall at arm's length. Have them place both palms flat on the wall and lean their weight into it (like a wall push-up position but just holding). Count to 20 together. This isometric proprioceptive input interrupts the pacing urge and provides heavy work that calms the nervous system.
DIY Redirection Tool: Pacing Path Markers - Use colored tape or chalk to create a specific path on the floor (a circle, figure-8, or straight line path). The child paces only on this designated path, making the behavior contained and purposeful. Add task elements: "Every time you reach the end, say one worry out loud" or "Count your steps each time around." Cost: ₹30-50 for tape. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Weighted Backpack - Fill a sturdy backpack with books or rice bags (1-3 kg depending on child's size). The child wears this during problem-solving. The weight provides proprioceptive input throughout the body, reducing the urgent need to pace. Cost: Free using existing backpack. Resistance Band Walking - Tie a resistance band (or fabric strip from old clothing) around the child's ankles loosely. When they walk, there's gentle resistance. This adds proprioceptive work to the pacing, making it more organizing for the nervous system. Cost: Free to ₹50.
Foot Weights - Make ankle weights by filling two long socks with rice or sand (0.5-1 kg each) and tying them around the ankles. Pacing with added weight provides heavy work input. Cost: ₹20-30. Stepping Stone Path - Place textured items on the floor (carpet squares, cushions, textured mats, cardboard pieces). If the child must pace, they step only on these items, adding tactile and proprioceptive input to the movement. Cost: Free using household items. How to Use: Don't forbid pacing entirely, as this increases anxiety; instead, redirect it Introduce weighted option: "Let's try wearing your backpack while you think this through" Create the designated path before the worry-inducing situation occurs Set boundaries: "You can pace in this room, but not beyond this line"
Combine with talk-it-out: "Tell me your worries while you walk your path" Gradually reduce pacing time: "Pace for 3 minutes, then we'll sit and problem-solve for 2 minutes" Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Heavy Work Circuit Before Problem-Solving: Before tackling difficult tasks, complete a 5-10 minute circuit: wall push-ups (10), chair push-ups (5), carrying heavy books across the room, animal walks (bear crawl, crab walk), jumping jacks (20). This intense proprioceptive and vestibular input reduces pacing needs. Pacing WITH Purpose: Transform pacing into purposeful movement: pace while bouncing a ball, walking lunges, high-knee marching, or heel-to-toe walking. This adds regulatory proprioceptive input to the vestibular movement. Seated Heavy Work Alternative: If pacing must stop, provide intense seated heavy work: pushing hands together hard (10 seconds, 5 reps), pressing palms on desk, squeezing stress ball as hard as possible.
For Sensory Avoiders: Minimize Need for Regulation: Reduce environmental stress that triggers pacing: lower stimulation, provide clear information about the problem, break tasks into smaller steps. Seated Alternatives: Provide a rocking chair or therapy ball to sit on. These allow movement in a contained, less overwhelming way than pacing. Grounding Visualization: Teach the child to visualize roots growing from their feet into the ground while seated. Pair with deep breathing to reduce pacing urges. Predictable Structure: Provide a clear problem-solving framework: "First we'll write down the problem, then think of 3 solutions, then pick one." Structure reduces anxiety-driven pacing. Massage Techniques: Leg Compressions - Have the child lie down or sit. Starting at the hip, use firm pressure to squeeze down each leg to the ankle, like squeezing toothpaste from a tube. Do each leg 5 times. This proprioceptive input calms the urge to pace and grounds the legs.
Foot Grounding Massage - Press very firmly into the soles of both feet for 30-60 seconds each. This activates pressure points that calm anxiety and reduces the flight response (pacing) by grounding the body. Full Body Bear Hug - Give the child a very firm, long hug (20-30 seconds) before problem-solving begins. This deep pressure activates the parasympathetic nervous system, reducing fight-or-flight response that triggers pacing. Manifestation 2. RAPID ROCKING DURING EMOTIONALLY CHARGED SITUATIONS Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Body Brake Hold" - Approach calmly and place both hands firmly on the child's shoulders or upper arms. Make eye contact and say, "I'm going to help your body slow down. Rock with me—slow... slow... slow..." Physically guide them into slower rocking, then into small forward-backward sways, then to stillness. This gradual reduction prevents abrupt stopping which can increase distress.
DIY Redirection Tool: Compression Vest Substitute - Take a snug-fitting t-shirt or tank top (one size smaller than the child's normal size) or a sports compression shirt if available. The child wears this during emotionally charged situations. The constant gentle pressure provides proprioceptive input that reduces rocking needs. Enhanced version: layer two snug shirts for more pressure. Cost: ₹100-200 or free using existing clothing. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Heavy Blanket Burrito - Wrap the child tightly in a heavy blanket or comforter (with head out, of course). The pressure and containment provide deep proprioceptive input. They can rock gently within the blanket, but the resistance makes it slower and more organized. Cost: Free. Rice or Bean Bag Hug - Make a large lap pad by filling a pillowcase with 3-5 kg of rice or beans and sewing it shut. During emotional situations, the child holds this against their chest/stomach like a hug while seated. The weight provides grounding proprioceptive input. Cost: ₹50-100.
Resistance Band Body Wrap - Wrap a resistance band or elastic fabric (like cut-up bicycle inner tube) around the child's torso and chair back. Not tight, just gentle pressure. This creates a "hug" from the chair that provides constant proprioceptive feedback, reducing rapid rocking. Cost: ₹30-50. Rocking Chair with Weight - If available, use a rocking chair but add weight to the child's lap (weighted blanket, rice bag, or stack of heavy books). The rocking is still possible but slowed and more organized due to the added weight. Cost: Free using household items. How to Use: Don't prevent all rocking immediately, as this may escalate distress Offer the compression or weighted option as soon as emotional charge begins: "Let's get your heavy blanket to help your body calm down"
If the child resists tools, stay nearby and use calming voice/presence Allow rocking to continue but within safe boundaries (on bed, on cushioned surface, not near hard objects or edges) Gradually introduce the weighted tool: "First let's rock together, then we'll try with your heavy blanket" Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Proprioceptive Heavy Work Before and During: At first signs of emotional escalation, engage in heavy work: pushing hands against wall, chair push-ups, squeezing large pillows between body and wall, or "sandwich" play (child is the filling, parents are bread applying firm pressure from both sides). Rocking With Deep Pressure: If rocking must occur, add deep pressure simultaneously: hold the child firmly while they rock, or have them rock while wrapped tightly in a blanket. The combination provides more sensory input and can de-escalate faster.
Alternative Vestibular Input: Redirect to other vestibular activities that are safer: spinning in an office chair, swinging (if available), rolling across the floor, or somersaults on a mat. For Sensory Avoiders: Prevent Escalation: Avoiders rock rapidly when overwhelmed by sensory input. Immediately reduce environmental stimulation: lower lights, reduce noise, remove people, eliminate visual clutter. Gentle Touch Only: Offer soft, gentle touch rather than firm pressure if the child is sensory-avoidant. A soft hand on the back, gentle stroke of the hair, or light hand-holding may be more calming. Create Safe Space: Designate a low-stimulation area (corner with soft lighting, quiet, minimal decoration). Guide child there during emotional escalation where rocking can occur safely without overstimulation. Co-Regulation Over Input: For avoiders, adult calm presence is more important than sensory tools. Sit nearby, breathe audibly and slowly, speak in soft, slow voice.
Massage Techniques: Rhythmic Back Pressure - With the child seated or lying down, place both palms on their upper back and apply rhythmic, firm pressure in a pattern that matches their rocking speed, then gradually slow the rhythm. Your hands "rock" on their back, then slow, helping their body match the decreasing rhythm. Arm and Leg Compression Sequence - Squeeze each arm and leg firmly from top to bottom (like the toothpaste technique) 3-5 times per limb. This full-body proprioceptive input calms the nervous system and can reduce rocking intensity. Head and Scalp Deep Pressure - Apply firm (but gentle) pressure with fingertips all over the scalp in circular motions for 2-3 minutes. This activates calming parasympathetic response and can help de-escalate rapid rocking.
Manifestation 3. AGGRESSIVE CHEWING ON OBJECTS DURING TESTS OR CHALLENGES Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Jaw Release Press" - Gently place your thumb on the child's jaw joint (just in front of the ear, where the jaw hinges). Apply gentle pressure while saying, "Let's relax your jaw. Open your mouth wide, now close it slowly." Guide them through three jaw releases. This brings awareness to the tension and interrupts the chewing pattern. DIY Redirection Tool: Braided Fabric Chew Necklace - Cut three long strips of cotton t-shirt fabric (about 1 inch wide, 18 inches long). Braid them tightly together and tie the ends to form a necklace that can go over the head. The child can chew on this braided section during challenges. The fabric provides resistance without being damaged quickly. Cost: Free using old t-shirts.
Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Coffee Stirrer/Straw Bundle - Bundle 5-7 plastic coffee stirrers or regular straws together with rubber bands on each end. The child can chew on the bundled end. The plastic provides firm resistance and the multiple pieces create different sensations. Replace when worn. Cost: ₹5-10. Silicone Spatula Handle - Clean silicone cooking spatulas have handles that provide excellent chewing resistance. The child can chew on the handle end (not the flat part) during tests. Easy to clean and very durable. Cost: ₹50-100 (dedicated for this purpose). Rubber Tubing Chew - Get a short piece (3-4 inches) of clean, food-grade silicone or rubber tubing (available at hardware stores). Seal one end with duct tape. The child chews on this; it provides excellent resistance and doesn't break down quickly. Cost: ₹20-40.
Wet Washcloth Ice Chew - Wet a washcloth, twist it tightly, place it in a plastic bag, and freeze it for 30 minutes before the test/challenge. The child chews on the cold, slightly stiff cloth. The cold provides extra sensory input. Can be prepped in advance for test days. Cost: Free. Dried Mango or Fruit Leather - Provide chewy dried fruit (dried mango strips, fruit leather, or dried apricots). These are edible, provide significant chewing resistance, and won't be forbidden in classroom settings. Cost: ₹30-50. How to Use: Have the chew tool on the child's body (worn as necklace, in pocket, attached to pencil case) before the test begins Practice using it during homework before actual test day For classroom use, coordinate with teacher: "My child has a chew tool to help focus. It's not food; it's a regulation tool"
Replace chew tools regularly as they wear down (fabric weekly, straws every few days) Combine with positive reinforcement: "Great job using your chew necklace instead of chewing on your pencil!" Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Pre-Test Oral Motor Heavy Work: 10-15 minutes before the test, engage in intense oral motor activities: chewing gum (if allowed), eating crunchy snacks (carrots, apples, pretzels), drinking thick smoothie through straw, or blowing up balloons. This intense input reduces chewing urges during the test. Jaw Strengthening Exercises: Regularly practice activities that strengthen jaw muscles: chewing on chewelry or chew tubes, biting on clean silicone bite plates, or therapeutic chewing exercises. Stronger muscles need less constant input. Bubble Blowing Before Tests: Spend 5 minutes blowing bubbles before the test. The oral motor work and breath control provide regulating input.
For Sensory Avoiders: Minimize Oral Input: If a child is generally sensory avoidant but chews during tests, it indicates anxiety rather than sensory-seeking. Focus on anxiety reduction rather than providing more oral input. Gentle Alternatives: Offer smooth, non-textured items to hold in the mouth (like a clean smooth spoon) rather than chewable items. Hand-Based Alternatives: Redirect to hand fidgets (smooth stone, fabric) to keep hands busy, which reduces the urge to bring objects to mouth. Test Anxiety Strategies: Address the root cause (test anxiety) through: practice tests, breaking work into smaller sections, extra time, quiet testing environment, or supportive check-ins during the test. Massage Techniques: Jaw Joint Massage - Place index fingers on the jaw joints (just in front of each ear). Apply gentle circular pressure for 1-2 minutes. This releases tension in the jaw that drives chewing behaviors.
Cheek and Mouth Area Massage - Using clean hands with gentle pressure, massage in circles around the outside of the mouth, over the cheeks, and along the jawline for 2 minutes. This provides oral-area sensory input that can reduce chewing urges. Gum and Inner Cheek Pressure - With clean hands (or use a clean spoon), apply gentle pressure to the gums and inner cheeks. Rub along the gum line inside the mouth. This internal oral massage provides deep pressure that satisfies the sensory need that drives chewing. Do this before the test/challenge begins. Manifestation 4. REPETITIVE VOCALIZATIONS DURING UNCERTAINTY Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Silent Voice Hold" - Gently place your hand on the child's throat/neck area (externally, not squeezing) and another hand on their chest. Say, "I can feel your voice. Let's hold our voices inside for 10 seconds and just breathe together." Count to 10 with deep breathing. This brings awareness to the vocalization and redirects to breath control.
DIY Redirection Tool: Vibration Humming Tube - Take an empty paper towel tube or rolled cardboard tube. The child hums into one end while holding the other end near their ear. The tube amplifies and changes the sound, providing similar auditory and oral-motor feedback but in a controlled way. They can also feel the vibration in their hands. Cost: Free. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Kazoo or Harmonica - Provide a cheap kazoo or harmonica. During uncertainty, the child can hum or blow into this (quietly if needed). This redirects vocal stims into purposeful sound-making with a tool. Cost: ₹20-50. Water Bottle Whistling - Fill a clean water bottle half-full and teach the child to blow across the top to make a whistling sound. During uncertainty, they can make controlled sounds this way instead of random vocalizations. Cost: Free using existing bottle.
Vibrating Toothbrush or Massager - Give the child a clean, vibrating electric toothbrush or small vibrating massager to hold against their cheek, jaw, or throat during uncertainty. The external vibration provides similar sensory input to the internal vibration of vocalizations. Cost: ₹100-300. Silent Vocalization Alternative - Teach the child to mouth words silently or whisper instead of full-voice vocalizations. Practice whispering or silent mouthing during calm times so it's available during uncertain moments. Cost: Free. Chewy Tube with Sound - Some commercial chewy tubes make slight whistling or squeaking sounds when bitten. If not available, partially deflate a small balloon and the child can squeeze it to make small squeaking sounds as an alternative to vocal stims. Cost: ₹10-30. How to Use:
Identify triggers for vocalizations (new situations, waiting, ambiguous instructions) and have tool ready Introduce the tool proactively: "When you're feeling unsure, you can use your kazoo quietly instead" Set volume boundaries: "You can hum into your tube, but keep it at a level that doesn't distract others" Practice using tools during calm times so they're familiar during uncertainty In group settings, arrange with the teacher for the child to use tools in a designated quiet area Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Oral Motor Input Before Uncertain Events: Before situations that cause uncertainty, provide 5-10 minutes of intense oral motor input: singing songs, making animal sounds, vocal warm-ups (scales, humming different notes), or blowing bubbles. This satisfies oral-motor and auditory sensory needs proactively.
Purposeful Vocal Activities: Transform vocalizations into structured activities: singing specific songs, counting out loud, reciting poetry, or telling stories. This makes the behavior purposeful rather than stimming. Vibration Tools: Regularly use vibrating tools on the face, jaw, and neck. This external vibration can reduce the need for internal vibration (vocalizations). Use for 3-5 minutes several times per day. For Sensory Avoiders: Address the Uncertainty: Avoiders vocalize from anxiety about uncertainty. Provide clear, specific information: "Here's what will happen next... then this... then this." Visual schedules and advance warnings reduce vocalization. Silent Self-Regulation: Teach silent coping strategies: slow breathing, counting silently in their head, or silent mantra ("I am okay, I am safe"). Reduce Auditory Overload: Uncertain situations may have too much auditory input (noise, instructions, conversations). Provide ear plugs, noise-canceling headphones, or quiet space to reduce overall auditory stress that triggers vocalizations.
Massage Techniques: Throat and Neck Massage - Very gently stroke down the front of the throat (externally, not on the windpipe) with light pressure 10 times. Then massage the neck muscles on the sides of the neck with gentle circular pressure. This brings awareness to the vocal area and provides calming touch. Do for 2-3 minutes. Jaw and Facial Vibration Massage - Using a vibrating massager or electric toothbrush (clean), apply gentle vibration to the jaw joints, cheeks, and around the mouth for 2-3 minutes before uncertain events. This provides external vibration that satisfies the sensory need that vocalizations meet. Chest and Shoulder Tension Release - Massage the upper chest and shoulders with firm circular pressure for 3-5 minutes. Tension in these areas often connects to vocal tension. Releasing it can reduce vocalization urges.
Manifestation 5. HAND-FLAPPING DURING EXCITEMENT OR ANXIETY Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Hand Press and Hold" - Gently take both of the child's hands in yours and press them together in a prayer position in front of their chest. Apply firm pressure (have them push their palms together hard) and count to 10 together. This proprioceptive input to the hands and arms interrupts the flapping and provides deep pressure that calms the nervous system. DIY Redirection Tool: Weighted Wrist Bands - Fill two long socks or wrist sweatbands with rice or sand (100-200 grams each) and tie or sew them closed. The child wears these on their wrists. The weight provides constant proprioceptive input to the arms, reducing the urge to flap, and adds resistance if flapping does occur. Cost: ₹20-30.
Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Stress Ball Power Squeezes - Provide a firm stress ball or make one by filling a balloon with flour or rice. During excitement or anxiety, the child squeezes the ball as hard as possible repeatedly instead of flapping. The intense proprioceptive input to the hands provides similar regulation. Cost: ₹10-50. Resistance Band Pulls - Take a resistance band or cut a strip from old tights/pantyhose. The child holds one end in each hand and pulls outward repeatedly during excitement/anxiety. This provides heavy work input to the arms and hands similar to flapping but more organizing. Cost: Free to ₹50. Hand Clapping Redirection - Instead of flapping, teach the child to clap their hands together forcefully. This provides similar bilateral movement and auditory feedback but is more socially acceptable and provides deeper proprioceptive input. Cost: Free.
Fabric or Ribbon Flapping - Attach ribbons, streamers, or strips of fabric to bracelets or handles. The child can wave these during excitement, still getting the visual and movement feedback of flapping but through an object. This can be more socially acceptable. Cost: ₹10-20. How to Use: Introduce weighted wrist bands during calm times first so the child adjusts to the sensation At first signs of flapping, redirect: "Let's use your power squeezes!" and hand them the stress ball Don't forbid flapping entirely, especially during high excitement (like birthday parties); instead, designate times/places where it's okay Practice the alternative (resistance band pulls, clapping) during calm times so it's automatic during excitement/anxiety Celebrate the redirection: "You used your squeezes instead of flapping! That's great body control!"
Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Heavy Work for Arms Before Trigger Events: Before anticipated excitement or anxiety, engage in 5-10 minutes of arm heavy work: wall push-ups (20), chair push-ups (10), wheelbarrow walking, carrying heavy objects, or hanging from monkey bars/door frame pull-up bar. This proprioceptive input to the arms reduces flapping urges. Bilateral Arm Activities: Engage both arms in purposeful bilateral movements: jumping jacks, swimming motions, rowing exercises, or dancing with arm movements. This provides similar bilateral motor input to flapping but in organized, purposeful ways. Weighted Vest During Trigger Times: If flapping occurs during specific activities (watching exciting videos, social events), have the child wear a weighted vest during these times. The full-body proprioceptive input reduces overall stimming needs.
For Sensory Avoiders: Reduce Triggers: If flapping is anxiety-driven (common in avoiders), focus on reducing environmental triggers: lower noise, reduce social pressure, provide clear expectations, offer breaks from overwhelming situations. Grounding Rather Than Movement: Instead of providing more movement input (which can overwhelm avoiders), focus on grounding: weighted lap pad, firm hugs, hand-holding, or pressing feet firmly into the ground. Safe Space Availability: Ensure the child can access a low-stimulation space when overwhelmed. Knowing escape is available reduces anxiety and subsequent flapping. Massage Techniques: Arm Compression Massage - Firmly squeeze from shoulder to hand on each arm, like squeezing toothpaste from a tube. Do 5 times per arm. This deep proprioceptive input to the arms calms the nervous system and reduces flapping urges.
Shoulder and Upper Back Pressure - Apply firm pressure with your palms to the shoulders and upper back for 10-15 seconds. Release and repeat 5 times. This grounds the upper body and reduces the urge for arm movements like flapping. Hand and Wrist Joint Compression - Hold each hand and apply firm pressure to each finger joint, the wrist, and the palm. Squeeze each area for 3-5 seconds. This targeted proprioceptive input to the hands reduces the need for flapping movements. Manifestation 6. SPINNING DURING OVERWHELM Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Anchor and Root" - Approach the child calmly and place both hands firmly on their shoulders or upper arms. Make eye contact if possible and say, "Stop spinning. Look at me. Feel my hands on your shoulders. Now let's plant your feet." Guide them to stand still with feet shoulder-width apart. Have them press their feet into the ground hard for 10 seconds. This grounding interrupts the vestibular-seeking behavior and provides proprioceptive input.
DIY Redirection Tool: Weighted Spinning Disc - Place a non-slip mat or textured surface (like a rubber car mat or yoga mat piece) on the floor. Add weight by placing a heavy book or bag of rice in the center. The child can stand on this and spin, but the texture and weight make the spinning more controlled and organizing. The textured surface provides tactile feedback to the feet during spinning. Cost: Free to ₹50. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Spinning Office Chair with Control - Use a desk/office chair that spins. The child sits and spins in the chair instead of standing and spinning. The seated position is safer and the chair's mechanics control the speed. Add a weighted lap pad while spinning to increase proprioceptive input. Cost: ₹1000-2000 (if purchasing) or free if available at home.
Spin and Spot Technique - Teach the child to spin while "spotting" (keeping eyes focused on one point, then quickly whipping head around to find that point again - ballet technique). Place a sticker or picture at eye level on the wall. The child practices spinning while spotting this visual target. This makes spinning more organized and less disorienting. Cost: Free. Hula Hoop Spinning - Instead of body spinning, the child spins a hula hoop around their body, arms, or on the ground. This provides visual vestibular input (watching the spinning) without the body spinning. Cost: ₹50-150. Spinning Tops or Fidget Spinners - Provide spinning toys. When the urge to spin arises, the child spins the toy instead and watches it. The visual vestibular input can partially satisfy the need. Cost: ₹20-100.
Swing Alternative - If available, redirect spinning to swinging. A swing provides vestibular input in a more controlled, safer way than spinning. Cost: Free if available at home/park. How to Use: Create a designated spinning space with clear boundaries: "You can spin in this area only" (carpeted area away from furniture/walls) Set spinning limits: "You can spin 5 times, then stop and stand still for 10 seconds" to prevent vestibular overload Introduce the office chair alternative: "Instead of spinning your body, let's try the spinning chair" Use a timer: "You can spin for 30 seconds, then we'll do deep breathing for 30 seconds" Redirect to alternative BEFORE spinning begins when you see overwhelm signs: "You're looking overwhelmed. Let's use the swing instead"
Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Vestibular Circuit Before Overwhelm: Proactively provide intense vestibular input through a movement circuit: 10 somersaults, 5 spins in each direction (controlled), 20 jumping jacks, rolling across the floor like a log (10 times), swinging for 5 minutes. This satisfies vestibular needs before overwhelm triggers spinning. Controlled Spinning Protocol: Allow spinning but make it therapeutic: spin 5 times clockwise, stop, touch 5 body parts (head, shoulders, knees, toes, hips), spin 5 times counter-clockwise, stop, do 5 jumping jacks. This provides vestibular input while adding organization and proprioceptive grounding. Alternative Vestibular Input: Redirect to other vestibular activities: trampolining, rolling down hills, hanging upside down from furniture (safely), or doing cartwheels. For Sensory Avoiders: Prevent Overwhelm: Spinning in avoiders indicates severe sensory overload. Immediately reduce ALL sensory input: move to quiet, dim space, minimize touch, reduce auditory input, eliminate strong smells.
No Additional Vestibular Input: Don't provide swinging or other movement as alternatives - avoiders are already vestibularly overwhelmed. Instead, provide grounding activities: heavy blanket, firm hugs, lying down flat, or deep pressure. Focus on Regulation, Not Redirection: The child isn't seeking vestibular input; they're dysregulated. Provide co-regulation: calm presence, slow breathing together, soft verbal reassurance rather than movement alternatives. Massage Techniques: Full Body Grounding Massage - With the child lying down (after spinning has stopped), apply firm pressure systematically from head to toe: press on head/scalp, shoulders, down arms to hands, chest, abdomen, hips, down legs to feet. Spend 15-20 seconds on each area. This full-body proprioceptive input grounds the vestibular system. Head and Neck Stabilization - Cup your hands around the child's head (sides of face/ears) and hold firmly but gently for 30 seconds. Then massage the base of the skull and neck with firm circular pressure for 2 minutes. This calms the vestibular system which is centered in the inner ear.
Joint Compression Sequence - Compress each major joint: press on shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles by applying firm downward pressure for 5 seconds each joint. This proprioceptive input to all joints helps reorganize the body after vestibular stimulation. Manifestation 7. COMPLEX RITUALS BEFORE STRESSFUL EVENTS Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Ritual Interrupt with Replacement" - When you notice the ritual beginning, gently interrupt with physical touch (hand on shoulder) and say, "I see you starting your routine. Let's do one calming breath together first." Guide one deep breath (4 counts in, 4 counts out). Then say, "Now you can do a SHORT version of your routine - pick the 3 most important steps only." This maintains some control for the child while reducing the ritual's intensity.
DIY Redirection Tool: Simplified Ritual Card - Create a laminated card (or use cardstock in a plastic sleeve) with 3 simple steps the child can do before stressful events. Use pictures and words: "1. Take 3 deep breaths (picture of lungs), 2. Squeeze hands 5 times (picture of hands), 3. Say 'I can do this' (picture of mouth)." The child follows this short ritual instead of the complex one. Cost: ₹10-20. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Ritual Object - Designate one small object (smooth stone, special coin, small toy) as the "calm object." Before stressful events, the child only needs to hold this object in their hand for 10 seconds instead of performing complex rituals. The object becomes the ritual. Cost: Free.
Abbreviated Physical Routine - Create a simple physical routine that takes 30 seconds: touch head, touch shoulders, touch knees, touch toes, clap hands 3 times, done. This replaces complex rituals with a consistent, brief physical sequence. Cost: Free. Timer-Limited Ritual - Use a visual timer (phone timer, kitchen timer, or draw a clock). The child can do ANY ritual they want, but only until the timer goes off (set for 2 minutes). This contains the ritual time without dictating specific actions. Cost: Free to ₹100. Ritual Box - Fill a small box with 5 sensory items (smooth stone, stress ball, fabric square, scented sachet, small toy). Before stressful events, the child picks one item, uses it for 30 seconds, and returns it. This replaces complex behavioral rituals with simple sensory rituals. Cost: Free to ₹50.
How to Use: Introduce simplified alternatives during low-stress times first: "Let's practice your new short routine" Gradually phase out complex rituals: "This week, let's do 5 steps instead of 10. Next week, we'll try 3 steps" Use positive reinforcement: "You used your short routine and still did great on the test!" Honor the child's need for control: "You can choose which 3 steps are most important to you" Be consistent: practice the new ritual daily during calm times so it feels automatic during stress Validate feelings: "I know your routine helps you feel ready. This shorter version will help you feel ready faster" Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Sensory-Rich Preparation Routine: Replace complex behavioral rituals with a consistent sensory routine: 5 minutes of heavy work (wall pushes, chair squats), 2 minutes of deep breathing, 1 minute of organizing activities (lining up pencils, organizing papers). This provides sensory regulation without complex rituals.
Physical Warm-Up Routine: Create a brief physical warm-up that becomes THE ritual: 10 jumping jacks, 5 arm circles each direction, 3 big stretches, 5 deep breaths. Do this exact sequence before every stressful event so it becomes the predictable ritual. Proprioceptive Anchoring: Before stressful events, provide intense proprioceptive input: firm hugs, joint compressions, wall push-ups. This calms the nervous system and can reduce the need for complex rituals. For Sensory Avoiders: Predictable Environment, Not Rituals: Avoiders develop rituals to create predictability in overwhelming environments. Instead of fighting the rituals, make the environment predictable: clear schedule, advance warnings, consistent routines throughout the day, visual schedules. Shorter, Gentler Rituals: Replace complex rituals with one gentle sensory activity: holding a soft object, looking at a calming picture, or deep breathing. Avoid intense sensory input which may increase overwhelm.
Address the Anxiety: Rituals often stem from anxiety about the stressful event. Provide information that reduces anxiety: "Here's exactly what will happen during the test... first this, then this, then this." Knowledge reduces ritual needs. Massage Techniques: Pre-Event Calming Massage Routine - Create a consistent 3-minute massage sequence that becomes THE ritual: 1 minute shoulder massage, 1 minute hand massage, 1 minute foot pressure. Do this exact sequence before every stressful event. The consistency is calming, and the deep pressure provides regulation. Pressure Point Calming - Teach the child (or parent) to press these calming points before stress: center of palm (10 seconds each hand), webbing between thumb and index finger (10 seconds each hand), center of forehead (10 seconds). This becomes a brief, portable ritual.
Self-Massage Ritual - Teach the child a quick self-massage: rub hands together fast (creating warmth), press palms together hard (10 seconds), shake hands out. This becomes their consistent pre-stress ritual that they can do independently anywhere. Manifestation 8. MULTIPLE STIMS SIMULTANEOUSLY DURING HIGH STRESS Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Full Body Reset" - This requires immediate, firm intervention. Approach calmly and use deep pressure: place both hands on the child's shoulders, apply firm downward pressure, and say in a calm, low voice, "We're going to reset your body. Stand up." Guide them to stand, then: "Push your hands against the wall as hard as you can for 10 seconds." Count together. Then: "Now press your feet into the floor. Feel yourself standing." This proprioceptive heavy work interrupts multiple stim pathways simultaneously.
DIY Redirection Tool: Crisis Sensory Kit - Create a small box or bag with high-intensity sensory items for crisis moments: ice pack wrapped in towel, strong-scented item (peppermint oil on cotton ball in sealed bag), very sour candy, weighted lap pad, chewy tube, and a stress ball. When multiple stims appear, offer the kit: "Pick TWO items from your kit right now." The intense sensory input from the kit can override the stimming urges. Cost: ₹200-500. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Ice Water Hand Plunge - Fill a bowl with ice water. When multiple stims occur, guide the child to plunge both hands into the ice water for 10-30 seconds. The intense sensory input interrupts all stim patterns simultaneously. Have a towel ready. Cost: Free.
Strong Scent Intervention - Keep a small bottle of strong scent (peppermint oil, eucalyptus oil, lemon juice, or even coffee grounds in a container). When multiple stims occur, have the child smell the strong scent for 10 seconds. The intense olfactory input can interrupt stim patterns. Cost: ₹50-200. Intense Proprioceptive Activity - Guide the child immediately into heavy work: push against a wall with full body weight for 20 seconds, do 10 squats, carry something heavy across the room, or do wall push-ups. The intense proprioceptive demand interrupts multiple stim pathways. Cost: Free. Compression Cocoon - Wrap the child tightly (but safely) in a heavy blanket or comforter immediately when multiple stims occur. The full-body deep pressure can interrupt all stim pathways simultaneously. The child can remain wrapped for 5-10 minutes while calming. Cost: Free.
Cold Pack or Vibration - Apply a cold pack (or bag of frozen vegetables wrapped in thin towel) to the back of the neck, or use a vibrating massager on the shoulders/back. The intense sensory input interrupts the multiple stim patterns. Cost: ₹50-300. How to Use: Multiple simultaneous stims indicate CRISIS-LEVEL stress - respond immediately and firmly but calmly Don't try to stop individual stims one by one; instead, provide ONE intense sensory input that overrides all of them Use calm, directive language: "Come with me now. We're going to use the ice water" After the intense sensory intervention, move to a quiet, low-stimulation space for recovery Stay with the child; don't leave them alone during crisis-level stimming After the crisis passes, debrief: "Your body was very stressed. Let's figure out what happened so we can prevent this next time"
Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Emergency Sensory Circuit: When multiple stims appear, immediately implement a high-intensity sensory circuit: 20 jumping jacks, 10 push-ups, 5 somersaults, run in place for 30 seconds, 10 deep breaths. The intense vestibular, proprioceptive, and interoceptive input can interrupt the crisis. Heavy Work Intervention: Implement immediate heavy work: push/pull heavy furniture, carry stack of heavy books, do chair push-ups repeatedly, or squeeze large pillows with full body. Continue for 5-10 minutes or until stims reduce. Deep Pressure Protocol: Apply deep pressure systematically: tight hug (20 seconds), compression down each arm and leg, weighted blanket, and lie flat under cushions or pillows (safely, face visible). Continue for 10-15 minutes. For Sensory Avoiders: Complete Sensory Reduction: Multiple stims in avoiders indicate severe sensory overload. Immediately remove ALL sensory input: move to dark, quiet room, remove all people except one calm caregiver, no talking, no touch unless the child requests it, no strong smells.
Safe Space Retreat: Have a pre-designated safe space (closet with cushions, tent, under desk with blanket). Guide child there immediately and allow them to decompress alone or with minimal caregiver presence. Gentle Co-Regulation: Sit nearby (not touching unless child requests), breathe slowly and audibly, speak minimally in soft voice, allow the child's nervous system to calm by mirroring your calm state. Massage Techniques: Crisis Deep Pressure Protocol - With the child lying down or seated, apply very firm pressure systematically: press down on shoulders (10 seconds), squeeze down each arm to hands (10 seconds per arm), press on hips (10 seconds), compress down each leg to feet (10 seconds per leg), press on feet (10 seconds each). Repeat the entire sequence 2-3 times. This intensive proprioceptive input can interrupt multiple stim patterns.
Emergency Scalp and Face Pressure - Apply firm (but not painful) pressure with your fingertips all over the scalp in circular motions for 2 minutes. Then gently but firmly press on the temples, cheekbones, jawline, and forehead. This intensive head and face pressure activates parasympathetic calming response. Bilateral Arm Squeezes - Squeeze both arms simultaneously from shoulders to hands repeatedly (like squeezing toothpaste tubes), 10 times. The bilateral proprioceptive input can help reorganize the nervous system when it's overwhelmed.
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > 10. EMOTIONAL REGULATION STIMMING > A. Anxiety-Based Stimming > Level 3: Severe Distress Stimming
Causation: Emotional: Severe anxiety, panic, or emotional dysregulation Meltdown: Sensory or emotional overload causing crisis response Trauma Response: Fight-or-flight activated Regulation Failure: Typical coping strategies insufficient Communication: Expressing unbearable internal state Profile: Crisis: Indicates severe distress requiring intervention Safety Concern: Risk of injury to self or others Support Needed: Requires crisis management and support strategies Description: Extreme stimming during crisis Manifestation 1. SELF-INJURIOUS STIMMING (HEAD-BANGING, BITING SELF) Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Immediate Safety Containment" - This is a CRISIS requiring immediate physical intervention to prevent injury. Approach quickly but calmly. For head-banging: place your hand between the child's head and the hard surface, or gently hold the head still with both hands on either side. For self-biting: gently but firmly redirect the mouth away from the body. Say in a calm, low voice: "I'm keeping you safe. Your body is safe." Then immediately move to deep pressure: firm hug, wrap in blanket, or have child lie down and apply gentle body weight/pressure.
DIY Redirection Tool: Crisis Safety Items - Keep immediately accessible: thick foam pieces or cushions to place between head and hard surfaces, soft fabric or silicone teething toys to redirect biting, and crash pads (stack of cushions/pillows on floor) where child can safely hit or crash. Cost: ₹200-500 using household items. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Crash Pillow Station - Create a permanent "safe crash zone": stack 4-6 firm pillows or cushions on the floor against a wall. When self-injury urges appear, redirect the child to crash into these pillows instead of hitting head on hard surfaces. The proprioceptive impact is similar but safe. Cost: Free using existing pillows. Bite Redirection Items - Keep multiple safe bite items accessible: clean towel rolled up, silicone pot holder, clean rubber spatula handle, or frozen washcloth. When self-biting begins, immediately place one of these in the child's mouth: "Bite this instead." Cost: Free to ₹50.
Cold Compress Application - Apply ice pack wrapped in towel to the area the child is targeting (forehead for head-banging, arm for biting). The intense cold sensation can interrupt the self-injury urge and provide alternative intense sensory input. Cost: ₹50 for reusable ice pack. Deep Pressure Alternatives - When self-injury begins, immediately provide alternative deep pressure: have child squeeze your hands as hard as possible, push against wall with head (safely, with your hands protecting), or bite down on a bite stick/teether as hard as they need. The pressure need is met safely. Cost: Free. How to Use: Self-injury requires IMMEDIATE intervention - do not delay Always prioritize safety: physically prevent injury while remaining calm After preventing immediate harm, provide intense sensory input: deep pressure, cold, proprioceptive work
Never leave a child alone who is engaging in self-injury After the crisis, seek professional help: occupational therapist, behavioral therapist, or medical evaluation Identify triggers: keep a log of when self-injury occurs to identify patterns Create a crisis plan with professionals: specific steps to follow when self-injury occurs Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Intensive Proprioceptive Protocol: Self-injury often indicates a need for extreme proprioceptive input. Provide intensive, daily proprioceptive activities: push/pull heavy objects for 15-20 minutes twice daily, carry weighted backpack, deep pressure brushing protocol (with OT guidance), joint compressions, therapeutic squeezing. Safe Impact Activities: Redirect the need for impact to safe activities: jump on trampoline, crash into crash pad repeatedly, hit pillows or punching bag, stomp feet hard, clap hands forcefully. These provide the intense input without injury.
Sensory Diet: Implement a structured, intensive sensory diet every 60-90 minutes throughout the day with OT guidance. Consistent sensory input can prevent the buildup that leads to self-injury. For Sensory Avoiders: Trauma-Informed Approach: Self-injury in avoiders often indicates severe pain, trauma, or unbearable internal state. Immediate medical and mental health evaluation is critical. This is beyond typical sensory strategies. Environmental Modification: Remove ALL possible triggering stimuli: eliminate fluorescent lights, reduce all noise, minimize touch, avoid strong smells, simplify visual environment. Professional Intervention Required: This level requires immediate professional support: occupational therapist, psychologist, behavioral therapist, and possibly medical evaluation. This is not a situation for home strategies alone. Massage Techniques: Crisis Deep Pressure Hold - After preventing immediate injury, provide sustained deep pressure: very firm hug lasting 2-5 minutes, lie the child down and place weighted blankets/cushions on them (face visible), or "sandwich" the child between two firm cushions with sustained pressure. Maintain until the child visibly calms.
Targeted Area Deep Massage - After the crisis, massage the area that was being injured (head, arm, etc.) with very firm pressure for 5-10 minutes. If head-banging: firm scalp massage. If biting arm: firm compression massage of the entire arm. This provides the deep pressure/pain input to that area without injury. Full Body Proprioceptive Massage - After crisis passes, provide intensive full-body massage with very firm pressure: compress all joints (shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles), squeeze all major muscle groups (arms, legs, back), and provide sustained pressure to hands and feet. Continue for 15-20 minutes. CRITICAL NOTE: Self-injurious behavior requires professional evaluation and intervention. These strategies are crisis management only, not treatment. Seek immediate help from occupational therapist, behavioral therapist, developmental pediatrician, or psychologist.
Manifestation 2. AGGRESSIVE STIMMING TOWARD OTHERS (HITTING, PULLING HAIR) Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Block and Redirect" - Physically block the aggressive action firmly but gently: catch the hitting hand, gently hold the hand away from the other person's hair. Say in a calm but firm voice: "Hitting/pulling hurts. Hands down." Immediately redirect to safe intense sensory input: "Push against my hands instead" (hold your hands up and have child push hard against them), or "Squeeze this" (provide stress ball or cushion to squeeze). Create physical distance between the child and the potential target if needed. DIY Redirection Tool: Hitting Alternative Station - Create a designated safe hitting area: hang a pillow from a doorway with string, set up a cushioned target (stack of pillows against wall), or fill a pillowcase with soft clothes/fabric to create a safe hitting bag. When the urge to hit appears, redirect: "Hit this instead." Cost: Free using household items.
Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Resistive Pull Toys - Provide items that can be safely pulled/tugged: stretch resistance bands between hands, pull apart large interlocking blocks, pull old t-shirts to rip them (if acceptable), or tug on a securely anchored rope. This redirects pulling to objects. Cost: Free to ₹50. Punching Alternatives - Set up safe punching activities: punch into a large container filled with foam pieces or crumpled paper, hit stack of pillows, knead/pound playdough or bread dough aggressively, or stomp on bubble wrap on the floor. Cost: Free to ₹100. Squeezing Alternatives - When the urge to hurt others appears, provide immediate squeezing alternatives: squeeze all the water out of a large sponge into a bowl repeatedly, squeeze large amount of thick playdough, crush aluminum cans (if safe), or squeeze your hands/forearms (adult providing hands for child to squeeze). Cost: Free.
Hair-Pulling Alternative - Provide safe pulling activities: pull dried grass from the ground, pull pages from an old phone book (if available), pull lint off velcro strips repeatedly, or pull apart cotton balls. Cost: Free. How to Use: Aggressive stimming toward others is NEVER acceptable - immediately stop and redirect Maintain firm boundaries: "You cannot hurt others. You can hit this pillow" Create physical distance if aggression continues: "You need space to calm down" After redirection, address the underlying need: "Your body needed to push/hit. Let's do wall pushes together" Never physically restrain unless absolutely necessary for safety - this can escalate aggression After incident, problem-solve with the child: "When you felt that urge, what could you do next time instead?"
Implement prevention: provide intensive proprioceptive activities BEFORE situations that typically trigger aggression Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Intensive Heavy Work Schedule: Aggressive stimming often indicates extreme proprioceptive need. Implement heavy work every 30-60 minutes: push-ups, carrying heavy items, tug-of-war with rope, pushing/pulling heavy furniture, wrestling with adults/siblings (with rules), or throwing heavy balls. Each session should be 5-10 minutes of intensive work. Safe Aggression Outlets: Provide daily aggressive play opportunities: punch pillows for 5 minutes, rip paper, throw balls at targets, stomp on cardboard boxes to flatten them, or pound playdough/clay. This meets the need for aggressive motor output safely. Full-Contact Activities: Consider activities that provide intensive body contact: wrestling, martial arts, gymnastics, or rock climbing. These provide extreme proprioceptive input in structured, safe ways.
For Sensory Avoiders: Immediate Crisis Management: Aggression in avoiders indicates unbearable overwhelm. Immediately reduce ALL environmental stimulation, create physical space from others, and allow recovery in a low-stimulation environment. Teach Escape Signals: Teach the child to communicate overwhelm BEFORE aggression: verbal cue ("I need space"), visual card (red card = need break), or gesture (raised hand). Honor these signals immediately every time. Prevent Situations: Identify what triggers aggressive stimming and modify the environment to prevent those situations until better coping is developed. Massage Techniques: Post-Aggression Bilateral Pressure - After the aggressive incident (when child is calmer), provide bilateral deep pressure massage: squeeze both arms simultaneously from shoulders to hands, squeeze both legs simultaneously from hips to feet. Do this firmly and rhythmically for 5 minutes. This bilateral input helps reorganize the nervous system.
Hand and Arm Intensive Massage - The hands and arms are often used in aggressive stimming. Provide intensive massage to these areas: firm squeezing of each finger, deep pressure to palms, compression of wrists, firm massage of forearms and upper arms. Spend 5-10 minutes on this targeted input. Containment Hold Massage - If the child accepts it, provide a firm containment hold (therapeutic holding): wrap arms around child from behind, apply firm steady pressure, rock gently, and speak softly. This is NOT restraint - the child can release if they want. This provides safety, containment, and deep pressure. Maintain for 3-5 minutes or until child calms. CRITICAL NOTE: Aggressive behavior toward others requires immediate professional intervention. Contact behavioral therapist, occupational therapist, or psychologist. These strategies are crisis management, not treatment. Safety of all individuals is paramount.
Manifestation 3. SCREAMING OR INTENSE VOCALIZATIONS Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Grounding Touch and Breathing" - Approach calmly despite the noise. Place one hand firmly on the child's chest and one on their back. Say in a calm, low voice (don't yell over the screaming): "I'm here. You're safe. Let's breathe together." Model slow, deep breathing. The firm bilateral pressure (chest/back) can help ground the child. If the child continues screaming, don't fight it - stay present and wait for a pause, then intervene with calming input. DIY Redirection Tool: Screaming Alternative Container - Designate a specific place and method for loud vocalizations: a pillow to scream into, a closet or bathroom where screaming is acceptable, or outside space where they can be loud. When intense vocalization urge appears, guide child to this space: "You can scream into your pillow" or "Let's go outside where you can be as loud as you need." Cost: Free.
Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Water Bottle Scream - Give the child a large, empty plastic bottle (2-liter bottle works well). They can scream into the bottle opening. The bottle muffles the sound and provides an echo effect that might satisfy the need for intense vocalization. Cost: Free. Singing/Humming Redirection - When intense vocalization urge appears, redirect to singing loudly, humming as loud as possible, or making animal sounds. These are purposeful vocalizations that provide similar motor and sensory output. Cost: Free. Physical Exertion to Fatigue Vocal System - Immediate intensive physical exercise can reduce vocal energy: running in place for 2 minutes, jumping jacks until fatigued, or running outside. Physical exhaustion reduces the energy available for screaming. Cost: Free. Breath-Control Activities - Redirect vocal energy into breath control: blowing up balloons (requires forceful exhalation), blowing bubbles, blowing cotton balls across table, or blowing through a straw into water. These use the same oral-motor systems as screaming but in controlled ways. Cost: ₹20-50.
Vibrating Alternatives - The vibration of screaming in the throat/chest may be part of the sensory need. Provide external vibration: electric toothbrush held to throat/chest, vibrating massager, or phone vibration held against throat (externally). Cost: ₹100-500. How to Use: Don't try to forcefully stop screaming - this often escalates it Stay calm yourself - your regulation helps the child regulate Offer alternatives calmly: "Here's your screaming bottle" without forcing acceptance After screaming subsides, address the underlying cause: pain, frustration, fear, overwhelm If screaming is frequent, implement a daily intensive sensory diet to prevent buildup Create a signal for when screaming is happening: "I see you need to scream. Let's go to your safe space" Validate the emotion: "You're feeling very big feelings. Your voice is showing me how big they are"
Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Oral-Motor Heavy Work: Provide intensive oral-motor activities throughout the day: chewing extremely crunchy or chewy foods (beef jerky, bagels, dried fruit), blowing activities (whistles, harmonicas, balloons), singing loudly, or using oral motor chew tools with resistance. Each session 5-10 minutes, multiple times daily. Breath Work Exercises: Teach and practice breath control exercises: blowing feathers across the table, blowing ping pong balls through straw obstacles, or practicing vocal exercises (scales, different volumes). This provides purposeful control over the vocal/breath systems. Whole-Body Calming Protocol: Implement full-body proprioceptive activities before situations that trigger screaming: 10 minutes of heavy work, joint compressions, deep pressure, and calming activities. For Sensory Avoiders: Emergency Sensory Reduction: Intense vocalization in avoiders indicates crisis-level overwhelm. Immediately: remove to quiet space, eliminate all sensory input, darken room, remove all people except one calm caregiver, no talking, no touch unless requested.
Prevent Overwhelm: Identify triggers (too much noise, too many people, confusing situations) and modify environment to prevent these situations. Escape Plan: Create and practice an escape plan: visual card that means "I need to leave NOW," designated safe space child can retreat to independently, and adult commitment to honor exit requests immediately. Massage Techniques: Throat and Chest Calming Massage - AFTER screaming subsides, provide gentle massage: very light strokes down the front of throat (externally, not on windpipe), gentle circular pressure on upper chest, and soft massage of shoulders and neck. Do this for 5-10 minutes. This soothes the areas that were just intensely activated. Jaw Release Massage - Screaming creates tension in the jaw. Massage the jaw joints (just in front of ears) with gentle circular pressure for 2-3 minutes. Massage the cheeks and around the mouth. This releases tension from intense vocalization.
Full Body Calming Sequence - After crisis, provide full-body calming massage: start at head (scalp massage), move to shoulders (firm pressure), down arms to hands (squeezing), chest (gentle pressure), abdomen (circular gentle pressure), legs (squeezing), and feet (firm pressure). Spend 15-20 minutes providing this full-body calming input. Manifestation 4. RUNNING OR FLEEING (VESTIBULAR ESCAPE) Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Intercept and Ground" - If safe to do so, physically intercept the running: step in front with arms out (like a gentle barrier), or if already running, run alongside and gently guide to a stop. Once stopped, immediately implement grounding: place hands on shoulders with firm pressure, guide to sit or lie down, and provide deep pressure. Say calmly: "You're safe. I've got you. Let's sit down together."
DIY Redirection Tool: Safe Running Zone - Designate a specific safe area where running IS allowed: a hallway, backyard, or section of a room. Mark the boundaries clearly with tape or visual markers. When the urge to run appears, redirect: "You can run back and forth in your running zone." This contains the behavior and provides the vestibular input safely. Cost: Free to ₹50 for marking tape. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Weighted Vest During Risk Times - Have the child wear a weighted vest (or backpack filled with books) during times when running/fleeing typically occurs. The weight provides proprioceptive input that can reduce the vestibular urge to run. Weight should be 5-10% of body weight. Cost: ₹500-1000 for vest, or free using backpack.
Resistance Running - Attach a resistance band or rope loosely around the child's waist (not tight enough to restrict, just provide resistance). The other end is held by an adult or anchored. When running urge appears, they can run against the resistance. The added proprioceptive work makes the running more organizing. Cost: ₹30-50. Running with Purpose - Redirect aimless fleeing into purposeful running: run to get an object and bring it back, run to touch each wall of a room in order, or run laps while counting. Making the running purposeful engages the cognitive system and can reduce the panic/escape component. Cost: Free. Alternative Vestibular Input - When running urge appears, immediately redirect to other intense vestibular activities: spinning in an office chair (10 times), somersaults (5 in a row), jumping on a mattress or trampoline (if available), or rolling across the floor repeatedly. Cost: Free to ₹300 for small trampoline.
How to Use: Running/fleeing indicates panic or escape response - prioritize safety first Don't chase aggressively - this can escalate panic Ensure environment is safe: lock doors to prevent running into dangerous areas (streets, stairs) After stopping, don't immediately discuss or problem-solve - first provide calming sensory input Identify triggers: What causes the flight response? Address those triggers. Create safety plans: visual schedule showing what comes next (reduces panic), safe person the child can go to, or safe space for retreat instead of running Practice calming strategies during non-crisis times so they're available during crisis Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Scheduled Intensive Running: Provide scheduled, purposeful running opportunities: morning run around the block, running games (tag, races), running laps with a timer, or treadmill time. Each session 15-30 minutes. Meeting the vestibular need proactively reduces urgent fleeing.
Vestibular Circuit: Create a movement circuit that provides intense vestibular input: running component, spinning component, jumping component, rolling component. Do this circuit 2-3 times daily. Cost: Free. Heavy Work Before Trigger Situations: Before situations that typically trigger running, provide 10-15 minutes of intensive proprioceptive work: push/pull heavy objects, carry weighted items, wall push-ups, or chair squats. This calms the system and reduces running urges. For Sensory Avoiders: Safety First: Running in avoiders is escape from unbearable stimulation. Ensure doors are locked, identify a safe person/space for the child to go to instead of panicked running. Eliminate Triggers: Identify what sensory input triggers fleeing (loud noise, crowds, bright lights, confusion) and eliminate or reduce these in the environment. Practice Safe Exits: During calm times, practice: "When you feel overwhelmed, you can say 'I need to leave' or go to your safe space" (specific designated area). Practice this routine repeatedly.
Environmental Modifications: Create predictable, low-stimulation environments. Reduce surprises and sudden changes that trigger panic responses. Massage Techniques: Post-Running Leg and Foot Massage - After running episode, massage the legs intensively: firm squeezing from hip to foot on each leg (5 times), deep pressure to feet, and gentle stretching of leg muscles. This provides proprioceptive input to the body parts that just experienced intense movement. Do for 10 minutes. Grounding Through Feet - Focus intensive massage on the feet: firm pressure to soles, squeeze each toe, press on heel, and massage all over each foot for 5 minutes per foot. This grounds the body through the feet and can reduce flight response. Full Body Containment - After running stops, provide full-body deep pressure: firm hug, wrap in blanket with firm pressure, or "sandwich" between cushions with sustained pressure. Maintain for 5-10 minutes. This contains the body that just felt compelled to flee and provides safety through deep pressure.
Manifestation 5. COMPLETE WITHDRAWAL AND SHUTDOWN Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Gentle Presence Without Demand" - Shutdown is not active stimming but is a severe stress response. Do NOT try to forcefully break through it. Instead, sit quietly nearby (not touching unless child initiates). Speak very softly and minimally: "I'm here. You're safe. Take your time." After 2-3 minutes of quiet presence, try gentle touch: soft hand on back or holding hand if accepted. Wait for the child to reengage on their timeline, which may take 10-30 minutes. DIY Redirection Tool: Safe Shutdown Space - Create a designated low-stimulation space for shutdowns: small tent, corner with blanket draped over to create a cave, under a table with cushions, or closet with soft items. When shutdown appears imminent, guide child there: "Let's go to your quiet space." This makes the shutdown location safe and contained. Cost: ₹200-500 or free using household items.
Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Weighted Blanket Cocoon - When shutdown occurs, gently place a heavy blanket over the child (ensuring face is visible and they can remove it). The deep pressure can be organizing and comforting during shutdown. Don't force if refused. Cost: ₹1000-3000 for weighted blanket, or make with heavy comforter. Sensory Comfort Items - Keep comfort items nearby during shutdown: soft stuffed animal, familiar blanket, smooth stone to hold, or special comfort object. Place these within reach (not forcing them on the child). They may gradually engage with these items as they emerge from shutdown. Cost: Free to ₹200. Minimal Sensory Input Space - During shutdown, reduce ALL sensory input: dim or turn off lights, eliminate noise (no talking, turn off TV/music), minimize visual stimulation (plain wall to look at), reduce smells, and limit touch to absolute minimum. Create sensory void to allow nervous system to recover. Cost: Free.
Gentle Rhythm Input - Some children respond to very gentle rhythmic input during shutdown: soft rocking, gentle patting, or slow rhythmic music played very softly. Try offering this gently - if the child resists, stop immediately. Cost: Free. How to Use: Shutdown is the nervous system's emergency brake - it indicates severe overload DO NOT demand, force, or rush the child during shutdown Accept that shutdown may last 20-60 minutes - this is the time needed for recovery Provide safety and quiet presence - your calm helps their system reset After shutdown ends, don't immediately return to demands - allow gradual reengagement Identify what led to shutdown and prevent those situations in the future Consider shutdown a sign that the child's sensory/emotional load exceeded their capacity - reduce overall daily demands
Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Prevention Through Sensory Diet: Shutdown in seekers indicates sensory starvation or extreme overwhelm. Implement consistent, intensive sensory diet: proprioceptive activities every 60-90 minutes throughout the day, vestibular input 2-3 times daily, and oral-motor activities regularly. Prevention is key. Recovery Protocol: After shutdown, provide gentle reengagement through preferred sensory activities: favorite movement activity, preferred tactile materials, or calming activities the child enjoys. Let the child guide the pace. Daily Regulation Routine: Create consistent daily routine with sensory input built in: morning movement, mid-day proprioceptive break, afternoon vestibular activity, evening calming activities. Consistency prevents buildup that leads to shutdown. For Sensory Avoiders: Prevention is Critical: Shutdown in avoiders means the sensory environment became unbearable. Dramatically reduce daily sensory demands: quiet environment, minimal transitions, predictable routines, low visual/auditory stimulation, gentle touch only.
Respect the Shutdown: Don't try to "fix" or rush shutdown. This is the nervous system protecting itself. Provide quiet, safe space and wait for the child to reemerge naturally. Environmental Overhaul: After shutdown, evaluate the entire environment and routine. What can be eliminated or reduced? What can be made more predictable? Create a sensory-friendly environment that prevents future shutdowns. Massage Techniques: Post-Shutdown Gentle Touch - AFTER the child emerges from shutdown (not during), offer very gentle massage: soft strokes down the back, gentle hand holding, or light pressure on shoulders. Keep it brief (2-3 minutes) and stop if the child resists. This reconnects the body to safe touch. Grounding Foot Massage - When the child is ready, provide foot massage with firm pressure: press into soles, squeeze feet, and apply steady pressure. This grounds the child back into their body after the dissociative experience of shutdown. Do for 5 minutes per foot.
