Optional Compression - If the child accepts it, provide joint compressions after shutdown: press on shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles (5 seconds each joint). This proprioceptive input helps reorganize the nervous system after shutdown. CRITICAL NOTE: Frequent shutdowns indicate the child's environment/demands exceed their capacity. This requires professional evaluation by occupational therapist and possibly psychologist. The environment must be modified to prevent shutdowns, as they indicate severe distress. Manifestation 6. DESTRUCTIVE STIMMING (BREAKING OBJECTS) Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Redirect Force Immediately" - Physically interrupt the destructive action: gently but firmly catch the arm/hand, remove the object, and say firmly: "We don't break things. You can break THESE instead." Immediately redirect to safe destructive activities (see below). If the child is mid-destruction and unsafe to interrupt, protect the child and others first, then clean up and redirect.
DIY Redirection Tool: Destruction Box - Create a box of items that CAN be destroyed: cardboard boxes to rip, old magazines/newspapers to tear, styrofoam to crush, bubble wrap to stomp, plastic bottles to crush, or cardboard tubes to flatten. When destructive urge appears, immediately provide the box: "You can destroy these things." Replace items regularly. Cost: Free using recyclables. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Safe Destruction Activities - Provide immediately: stack of paper to rip into tiny pieces, cardboard boxes to crush and flatten, old phone books to tear apart (if available), dried leaves/grass to crumble, or ice cubes to crush. These meet the need to destroy without harm. Cost: Free. Breaking-Feeling Activities - Redirect to activities that FEEL like breaking but aren't destructive: snap plastic building toys apart, pull apart Velcro strips repeatedly, pop large bubble wrap, or crush aluminum cans (if age-appropriate). Cost: Free to ₹50.
Physical Intensity Alternative - The urge to break often indicates need for intense proprioceptive output. Immediately redirect to: tearing an old t-shirt into strips (provide old clothing for this purpose), pulling apart clay or playdough, or punching/hitting a pillow pile. Cost: Free. Stomp Activities - If breaking involves foot-smashing: set up cardboard boxes flat on floor to stomp and flatten, bubble wrap sheets to stomp, or stack of paper cups to stomp. These provide similar downward force without destroying valued items. Cost: Free. How to Use: Destructive behavior is NEVER acceptable - immediately stop and redirect Keep the destruction box easily accessible during high-stress times Set firm boundaries: "You may not break [valued object]. You CAN break [destruction box items]" After incident, have child help clean up the damage (age-appropriate responsibility)
Problem-solve together: "When you felt like breaking something, you could have broken your cardboard instead" Implement heavy work activities before typical trigger times to prevent destruction urges Consider natural consequences: broken toy stays broken (don't immediately replace), child helps repair what was broken if possible Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Daily Intensive Heavy Work: Destructive stimming indicates need for EXTREME proprioceptive input. Implement multiple daily sessions (3-4 times) of intensive work: 15 minutes each of pushing/pulling very heavy objects, carrying maximum-weight items, tug-of-war with rope, or ripping apart very resistant materials. Safe Destruction Time: Schedule daily "destruction time": 10 minutes where child is allowed to safely destroy designated items (cardboard, paper, crushable items). Meeting this need proactively reduces inappropriate destruction.
Resistive Material Play: Provide daily access to materials that require intense force: very stiff clay to manipulate, resistive putty to tear apart, dough to pound and tear, or foam to rip. These materials require intense input to manipulate. For Sensory Avoiders: Crisis Management: Destruction in avoiders indicates rage/panic from overwhelming environment. Immediately remove child from overwhelming situation. Don't address destruction until child is fully regulated. Prevent Overwhelm: Identify environmental triggers (too much stimulation, unclear expectations, sensory overload) and eliminate these to prevent the rage that leads to destruction. Teach Appropriate Protest: Avoiders may destroy when they can't communicate "this is too much." Teach clear communication: "Say 'I need a break' instead of breaking things." Massage Techniques: Post-Incident Arm and Hand Massage - After destructive episode (when calm), provide intensive massage to the arms and hands that just engaged in destruction: firm squeezing down each arm, deep pressure to each finger, compression of wrists and elbows. This provides the proprioceptive input those body parts were seeking. Do for 10 minutes.
Full Body Heavy Pressure - Provide full-body deep pressure massage: very firm squeezing of all major muscle groups (arms, legs, back, shoulders), joint compressions, and sustained pressure. Spend 15-20 minutes providing intensive proprioceptive input through massage. Palm and Wrist Deep Pressure - The hands were active in destruction. Provide targeted deep pressure: press very firmly into palms, squeeze wrists firmly, and compress each finger joint. This satisfies the proprioceptive need in the specific body parts involved. Manifestation 7. STIMMING TO POINT OF EXHAUSTION OR INJURY Physical Technique to Break the Stimming Zone: "Physical Interruption and Redirection" - This requires immediate intervention as the child is in danger. Physically stop the behaviour: gently but firmly hold the body part that's stimming (arms for flapping, body for spinning, etc.), make eye contact, and say firmly: "Stop. Your body is hurt/tired. We're going to rest now." Guide the child to lie down or sit, and physically prevent resuming the behaviour if they try. Provide alternative intense sensory input immediately (deep pressure, ice, massage).
DIY Redirection Tool: Intensity Indicator and Timer - Create a visual intensity scale (1-5, with pictures showing calm to intense). Teach the child to check the scale during stimming. Set a timer for "safe" stimming duration (5 minutes). When timer goes off, mandatory 5-minute break with different activity. This creates built-in breaks before exhaustion/injury. Cost: Free to ₹50. Alternative Stimulation - Household Items: Rotating Sensory Activities - Create a rotation of 5-6 intense sensory activities on cards. The child picks a card, does that activity for 5 minutes (timed), then must pick a different card. This prevents perseveration on one stim to point of injury. Activities might include: ice water hand plunge, wall push-ups, squeezing stress ball, running in place, deep breathing, or jumping jacks. Cost: Free.
Forced Break System - Use a visible timer (visual timer app, kitchen timer, or sand timer). When timer goes off every 10 minutes during high-stim times, the child MUST stop the current activity and do a different activity for 2 minutes. This enforces breaks. Cost: Free to ₹100. Protective Equipment - If injury risk is high: use protective padding (knee pads, elbow pads, helmet if needed), soft surfaces (foam mats), or covering hard surfaces with cushions. This reduces injury risk while addressing the underlying issue. Cost: ₹200-1000. Intensity Alternatives - Provide alternatives that meet the need for intensity but have built-in exhaustion prevention: frozen items to hold (can only hold briefly before cold forces a break), cold shower/bath (temperature limits duration), or activities that require breaks (running sprints with rest periods). Cost: Free.
How to Use: Stimming to exhaustion/injury indicates severe dysregulation - this is beyond typical stimming Don't allow the behaviour to continue to injury - intervene earlier each time Create a safety plan: identify early warning signs, intervene at those signs, and redirect to safer alternatives Use timers and visual supports to create external structure the child's internal regulation can't provide After episodes, seek professional help - this level requires OT/behavioral intervention Consider whether pain is part of the cycle: some children stim intensely to create pain which then forces them to stop Medical evaluation may be needed to rule out underlying conditions (pain, seizure activity, etc.) Occupational Therapy & Sensory Integration Activities: For Sensory Seekers: Maximum Intensity Protocol: These children need MAXIMUM sensory input multiple times daily or they will seek it to point of injury. Implement 4-6 daily sessions of 20-30 minutes each: heavy work until fatigued, vestibular input until dizzy (safely), oral-motor work until jaw tired, or tactile input until satisfied. Meet the need fully to prevent dangerous self-stimulation.
Safe Exhaustion Activities: Channel the need for exhaustion into safe activities: running until tired (safe surface), swimming (exhausting and safe), climbing walls, or martial arts. Supervised activities where exhaustion occurs safely. Interrupted Stim Protocol: When unsafe stimming begins, immediately interrupt and redirect to maximum-intensity alternative: "Stop spinning. Do 20 jumping jacks NOW, then 10 push-ups, then we'll talk." Provide equal intensity in safer form. For Sensory Avoiders: Medical Evaluation: Stimming to exhaustion/injury in avoiders may indicate self-harm, pain, or severe distress. Immediate professional evaluation required. Environmental Emergency: The environment has become unbearable. Completely overhaul: remove all triggering stimuli, simplify all demands, provide constant safe space access, and minimize all expectations temporarily. Crisis Mental Health Support: This level of distress requires professional mental health intervention. Contact psychologist, psychiatrist, or crisis services.
Massage Techniques: Full Body Recovery Massage - After stimming to exhaustion, provide a complete recovery massage: gentle to firm pressure (depending on child's state) over entire body. Start with feet (grounding), move up legs, work on back, arms, and head. Spend 20-30 minutes. This helps the body recover and provides the deep touch it was seeking. Targeted Injury Prevention - If certain body parts are at risk (hands from hitting, head from banging, legs from running): provide extra massage focus on those areas daily. Very firm pressure, joint compressions, and sustained input to those vulnerable areas for 10-15 minutes daily. Pre-Exhaustion Intensive Input - BEFORE the child reaches the point of dangerous stimming, provide intensive massage: very firm pressure all over body, all joint compressions, sustained deep pressure, and long slow strokes. Do this 2-3 times daily for 15-20 minutes. This proactively meets the need for intense input.
CRITICAL NOTES: Stimming to exhaustion or injury is a medical and safety emergency This requires immediate professional evaluation: occupational therapist, developmental pediatrician, psychologist, and possibly neurologist These strategies are CRISIS management only, not treatment The child's safety is paramount - modify the environment and provide supervision to prevent injury while seeking professional help
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > SUMMARY TABLES > Intervention Approach Framework
For SEEKERS: Provide: Appropriate alternatives for sensory input Schedule: Regular sensory breaks with intense input Environment: Sensory-rich spaces with varied options Tools: Fidgets, chewelry, weighted items, movement opportunities Goal: Satisfy sensory hunger appropriately For AVOIDERS: Reduce: Overwhelming sensory input in environment Gradual: Slow desensitization with control Safe Spaces: Quiet, calm areas for retreat Warning: Advance notice before sensory experiences Goal: Increase tolerance while respecting limits For MIXED PROFILES: Assess: Each sensory system individually Customize: Provide seeking options for some, reduce input for others Flexible: Adjust based on current state and context Complex: Requires detailed sensory profile assessment
Comprehensive Stimming Guide > CONCLUSION
Stimming serves critical regulatory functions and should be: Understood as communication and self-regulation Respected as neurological need, not behavioral problem Supported with appropriate alternatives when harmful or limiting Never eliminated entirely; redirection, not suppression Key Principles: Function over form - WHY matters more than WHAT Safety first - Redirect if harmful, not if just different Appropriate alternatives - Meet need differently, not eliminate need Individual profiles - Each person's sensory needs are unique Environmental modification - Change environment, not just behavior Communication - Stimming often communicates unmet needs Respect - Stimming is valid, important, and deserves respect This guide is for educational purposes. Consult occupational therapists for personalized sensory assessment and intervention planning.
